## TypeScript Strict Mode — Impact on Tests

Enabling `strict: true` (or specific flags like `strictNullChecks`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`) directly changes what test code compiles. Understanding these impacts prevents the common mistake of relaxing strict mode in `tsconfig.test.json`.

### `strictNullChecks` in Test Assertions

```typescript
// Without strictNullChecks: TypeScript trusts nullable values are always set
interface User { id: number; address?: { city: string } }

function getCity(user: User): string {
  return user.address.city; // No error without strict — runtime crash if address unset
}

// With strictNullChecks: tests must handle the undefined branch
describe('getCity', () => {
  it('returns city when address is set', () => {
    const user: User = { id: 1, address: { city: 'Berlin' } };
    expect(getCity(user)).toBe('Berlin');
  });

  it('handles missing address', () => {
    const user: User = { id: 2 };
    // With strict: TypeScript forces you to write this test
    expect(() => getCity(user)).toThrow();
    // Or better: fix the function to return string | undefined
  });
});
```

### `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` in Test Fixtures

`exactOptionalPropertyTypes` distinguishes between `{ prop?: string }` (field may be absent) and `{ prop: string | undefined }` (field present with undefined value). This changes how test fixtures must be written.

```typescript
// tsconfig: "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true

interface UserProfile {
  name: string;
  bio?: string;       // may be absent from the object entirely
}

// ❌ This is now a type error with exactOptionalPropertyTypes
const profile1: UserProfile = { name: 'Alice', bio: undefined };
// Error: Type '{ name: string; bio: undefined; }' is not assignable to 'UserProfile'
//   Types of property 'bio' are incompatible.

// ✅ Either omit the field entirely
const profile2: UserProfile = { name: 'Alice' };

// ✅ Or provide a real value
const profile3: UserProfile = { name: 'Alice', bio: 'Engineer at Acme' };

// In test fixtures: use conditional spread pattern for optional fields
function makeProfile(bio?: string): UserProfile {
  return {
    name: 'Test User',
    ...(bio !== undefined && { bio }),  // only adds 'bio' key when value is provided
  };
}
```

[community] **Pitfall: `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` breaks most hand-written test fixtures that assign `undefined` to optional fields.** The migration is not `s/: undefined/: omit/` — it requires audit of every fixture. Use `Partial<T>` with a spread pattern or a factory helper (see `makeFixture` above) to centralise the pattern. The most common hidden breakage is in `Object.assign`-based merges: `Object.assign({}, defaults, { bio: undefined })` explicitly sets `bio: undefined`, which `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` treats differently from omission.

### `useUnknownInCatchVariables` in Test Error Assertions

```typescript
// Without flag: caught error is 'any' — no type safety
try {
  doSomething();
} catch (err) {
  expect(err.message).toBe('...');  // compiles but fragile
}

// With useUnknownInCatchVariables (included in strict): error is 'unknown'
try {
  doSomething();
} catch (err: unknown) {
  // Must narrow before accessing properties
  expect(err instanceof Error).toBe(true);
  if (err instanceof Error) {
    expect(err.message).toBe('Expected error message');
    expect(err.name).toBe('TypeError');
  }
}

// Helper: type-safe error extraction for test assertions
function toError(err: unknown): Error {
  if (err instanceof Error) return err;
  return new Error(String(err));
}

it('throws with correct message', () => {
  let caught: unknown;
  try { riskyOperation(); } catch (e) { caught = e; }
  const error = toError(caught);
  expect(error.message).toMatch(/network timeout/i);
});
```

---

## Discriminated Union Testing — Exhaustive Patterns

Testing discriminated unions requires covering every variant AND verifying that unhandled variants produce compile-time errors. The patterns below enforce both.

### Per-Variant Test Organisation

```typescript
type PaymentMethod =
  | { type: 'card';   last4: string; brand: 'visa' | 'mastercard' }
  | { type: 'bank';   accountLast4: string; routingNumber: string }
  | { type: 'wallet'; walletId: string; provider: 'paypal' | 'stripe' };

// Organise tests by discriminant value — mirrors the union structure
describe('formatPaymentLabel', () => {
  describe('card', () => {
    it('formats Visa card correctly', () => {
      const method: PaymentMethod = { type: 'card', last4: '4242', brand: 'visa' };
      expect(formatPaymentLabel(method)).toBe('Visa ending in 4242');
    });

    it('formats Mastercard correctly', () => {
      const method: PaymentMethod = { type: 'card', last4: '5555', brand: 'mastercard' };
      expect(formatPaymentLabel(method)).toBe('Mastercard ending in 5555');
    });
  });

  describe('bank', () => {
    it('shows account last 4 digits', () => {
      const method: PaymentMethod = {
        type: 'bank', accountLast4: '6789', routingNumber: '021000021'
      };
      expect(formatPaymentLabel(method)).toBe('Bank account ending in 6789');
    });
  });

  describe('wallet', () => {
    it('shows provider name', () => {
      const method: PaymentMethod = { type: 'wallet', walletId: 'pp_123', provider: 'paypal' };
      expect(formatPaymentLabel(method)).toBe('PayPal wallet');
    });
  });
});
```

### `assertNever` as a Compile-Time Exhaustiveness Guard in Tests

```typescript
// Utility function: only callable with never — compile error if a variant is unhandled
function assertNever(value: never, message?: string): never {
  throw new Error(message ?? `Unhandled variant: ${JSON.stringify(value)}`);
}

// Use in a switch to guarantee every union variant has a test case
function describePayment(method: PaymentMethod): string {
  switch (method.type) {
    case 'card':   return `Card ${method.brand} ***${method.last4}`;
    case 'bank':   return `Bank ***${method.accountLast4}`;
    case 'wallet': return `${method.provider} wallet`;
    default:       return assertNever(method); // TS error if a case is missing
  }
}

// The exhaustiveness check propagates to tests: adding a new union variant
// causes a compile error on the switch default — reminding you to add a test.
```

### Table-Driven Union Tests with `satisfies`

```typescript
// Define test cases as a typed array — satisfies ensures each case is a valid PaymentMethod
const paymentCases = [
  { method: { type: 'card',   last4: '4242', brand: 'visa' },                   expected: 'Visa ending in 4242' },
  { method: { type: 'card',   last4: '5555', brand: 'mastercard' },             expected: 'Mastercard ending in 5555' },
  { method: { type: 'bank',   accountLast4: '6789', routingNumber: '021000021' }, expected: 'Bank account ending in 6789' },
  { method: { type: 'wallet', walletId: 'pp_123', provider: 'paypal' },         expected: 'PayPal wallet' },
] satisfies Array<{ method: PaymentMethod; expected: string }>;
// ↑ compile error if any test case has an invalid PaymentMethod shape

it.each(paymentCases)('formats $method.type correctly', ({ method, expected }) => {
  expect(formatPaymentLabel(method)).toBe(expected);
});
```

---

## Branded Types in Tests

Branded (nominal) types prevent accidental mixing of structurally identical primitives at the type level — a `UserId` and an `OrderId` are both `number` at runtime but distinct types at compile time. Test fixtures must use the correct branded type to remain valid.

### Defining Branded Types

```typescript
// Base brand utility type
type Brand<T, B extends string> = T & { readonly __brand: B };

// Domain branded types
type UserId    = Brand<number, 'UserId'>;
type OrderId   = Brand<number, 'OrderId'>;
type Email     = Brand<string, 'Email'>;
type ISO8601   = Brand<string, 'ISO8601'>;

// Smart constructors — validate and return branded types
function userId(id: number): UserId {
  if (!Number.isInteger(id) || id <= 0) throw new Error(`Invalid UserId: ${id}`);
  return id as UserId;
}

function email(raw: string): Email {
  if (!/^[^@]+@[^@]+\.[^@]+$/.test(raw)) throw new Error(`Invalid email: ${raw}`);
  return raw.toLowerCase() as Email;
}

function iso8601(raw: string): ISO8601 {
  if (isNaN(Date.parse(raw))) throw new Error(`Invalid ISO8601: ${raw}`);
  return raw as ISO8601;
}
```

### Using Branded Types in Test Fixtures

```typescript
// test/fixtures/users.ts
import { userId, email, iso8601, type UserId, type Email } from '../src/types/branded';

// Factory that enforces correct branded types — no raw primitives
export function makeUser(overrides: Partial<User> = {}): User {
  return {
    id:        userId(1),
    email:     email('alice@example.com'),
    createdAt: iso8601('2024-01-15T09:00:00Z'),
    role:      'user',
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// Cannot accidentally pass an OrderId where UserId is expected
describe('UserService.findById', () => {
  it('fetches user by id', async () => {
    const uid = userId(42);
    // const oid = orderId(42);
    // service.findById(oid);  // ← TypeScript error: Argument of type 'OrderId' is not
    //                         //   assignable to parameter of type 'UserId'

    const user = await service.findById(uid);
    expect(user.id).toBe(uid);
  });
});
```

### Branded Types with `satisfies` for Fixture Validation

```typescript
// Combining satisfies with branded types validates the entire fixture at compile time
const TEST_USERS = {
  alice: {
    id:    1 as UserId,
    email: 'alice@test.com' as Email,
    role:  'admin' as const,
  },
  bob: {
    id:    2 as UserId,
    email: 'bob@test.com' as Email,
    role:  'user' as const,
  },
} satisfies Record<string, Pick<User, 'id' | 'email' | 'role'>>;

// TEST_USERS.alice.role is 'admin' (literal) — not string
// Typo in email or wrong id type → compile error, not silent runtime bug
```

[community] **Pitfall: Using `as UserId` directly in test fixtures without a smart constructor bypasses validation.** `1 as UserId` is a type-level cast — it does NOT validate the value at runtime. In tests, this is often acceptable (you control the test data), but smart constructors (`userId(1)`) document the intent and catch incorrect values like `userId(-1)` or `userId(NaN)` during test setup rather than at assertion time.

[community] **Pitfall: Branded types do not survive JSON round-trips.** `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(userId(1)))` returns a plain `number`, not `UserId`. When testing code paths that deserialise data (API responses, database rows), always re-apply smart constructors after parsing rather than casting the result directly.

---

## `satisfies` Operator in Test Fixtures

The `satisfies` operator is a natural fit for test data objects: it validates shape without widening the inferred type, so literal types remain narrow for precise assertions.

### Pattern: Validate Fixtures Without Losing Literal Types

```typescript
interface Route {
  path: string;
  method: 'GET' | 'POST' | 'PUT' | 'DELETE';
  auth: boolean;
}

// ❌ Type annotation widens 'GET' to 'GET' | 'POST' | 'PUT' | 'DELETE'
const routeA: Route = { path: '/users', method: 'GET', auth: false };
routeA.method; // type: 'GET' | 'POST' | 'PUT' | 'DELETE'

// ✅ satisfies validates but preserves literal type
const routeB = { path: '/users', method: 'GET', auth: false } satisfies Route;
routeB.method; // type: 'GET'

// Benefit in tests: conditional assertions stay precise
it('sets correct content-type for method', () => {
  if (routeB.method === 'GET') {
    // TypeScript knows this branch is reachable without any cast
    expect(handler.contentType).toBe('application/json');
  }
});
```

### Pattern: `satisfies` for Exhaustive Fixture Coverage

Use `satisfies Array<UnionType>` to ensure your test fixtures cover specific union variants with type-checked shapes:

```typescript
type HttpStatus =
  | { code: 200; body: string }
  | { code: 201; location: string }
  | { code: 400; errors: string[] }
  | { code: 404; resource: string }
  | { code: 500; detail: string };

// If a new HttpStatus variant is added and a fixture is missing the required field,
// satisfies reports a compile error at the fixture definition — not at assertion time
const STATUS_FIXTURES = [
  { code: 200, body: 'OK' },
  { code: 201, location: '/users/1' },
  { code: 400, errors: ['Name required'] },
  { code: 404, resource: 'User' },
  { code: 500, detail: 'Internal Server Error' },
] satisfies HttpStatus[];

it.each(STATUS_FIXTURES)('handles status %d', (status) => {
  const response = buildResponse(status);
  expect(response.statusCode).toBe(status.code);
});
```

[community] **Pitfall: `satisfies` does not perform excess property checking on array elements when the array type has a union element type.** Each element is checked against all union members independently — TypeScript picks the best match. An element with an extra property may pass if it satisfies at least one member. Use discriminated unions (a shared `code` literal in this case) to ensure each element is matched to exactly one member.

---

## Anti-Patterns: Testing-Specific Quick Reference

| Anti-pattern | Why it's harmful | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Raw `jest.fn()` without type parameter | Return type inferred as `unknown`, call arguments not checked | `jest.fn<ReturnType, [ArgType1, ArgType2]>()` or use `jest-mock-extended` |
| `(service as any).privateMethod()` in tests | Bypasses type checking; breaks silently on refactor | Inject a mock/spy at the interface boundary instead of reaching into internals |
| Fixtures typed with `Partial<T>` everywhere | Allows missing required fields — tests may not reflect production data | Use `makeFixture<T>(defaults)(overrides)` pattern with full defaults |
| `expect(result as ExpectedType).toBe(...)` | Type assertion before assertion hides actual type mismatch | Use type guard (`isApiSuccess(result)`) to narrow and assert simultaneously |
| `mockResolvedValue(undefined as any)` | Circumvents strict null checks; hides missing mock setup | Configure the return value explicitly; use `fallbackMockImplementation` to make missing setup throw |
| Importing from `__mocks__/` without `jest.mock()` call | Manual mocks are not automatically applied in Jest v27+ | Always call `jest.mock('../path/to/module')` at the top of the test file |
| Branded type `as` cast in fixtures without validation | Passes wrong values (negative IDs, invalid emails) silently | Use smart constructors in test factories; reserve `as` cast for fixture constants only |
| `infer U extends string` as a cast | Constrained infer FILTERS — resolves to `never` when U is not a string subtype | Use `Extract<U, string>` in the body to extract the string portion from a mixed union |
| `{ ... } satisfies T as const` (wrong order) | TypeScript parse error — `satisfies` binds before `as const` | Always write `{ ... } as const satisfies T` |
| `NoInfer<C>` omitted on default parameter | TypeScript widens inferred union to include the default value's type | Wrap optional params that must match earlier params with `NoInfer<C>` |
| Distributing over union in conditional type unexpectedly | `type Wrap<T> = T extends any ? T[] : never` distributes, giving `string[] \| number[]` not `(string \| number)[]` | Wrap both sides: `[T] extends [any]` to prevent distribution |
| `filter(x => !!x)` relied on for type narrowing | In TS 5.5+, truthiness filter predicates are NOT inferred (by design — 0 is falsy) | Use `filter(x => x !== null && x !== undefined)` for safe non-null filtering |

---

## `NoInfer<T>` — Constrain Generic Defaults Without Dual Type Parameters

`NoInfer<T>` (TypeScript 5.4+, built-in utility type) prevents TypeScript from using a specific argument position as a source for type inference. The compiler infers the generic type `C` from *other* arguments only, then validates that the `NoInfer<C>` position must match the already-inferred type.

### Problem it solves

Before `NoInfer<T>`, constraining a "default must be one of the allowed values" required an awkward dual-parameter workaround:

```typescript
// Old approach (TypeScript < 5.4): requires a second type parameter
function createStreetLight<C extends string, D extends C>(
  colors: C[],
  defaultColor?: D,
): void { /* ... */ }

// TypeScript 5.4+: NoInfer<C> — C is only inferred from `colors`, not from `defaultColor`
function createStreetLight<C extends string>(
  colors: C[],
  defaultColor?: NoInfer<C>,
): void { /* ... */ }

createStreetLight(['red', 'yellow', 'green'], 'red');    // ✅ OK
createStreetLight(['red', 'yellow', 'green'], 'blue');   // ❌ Error: 'blue' not in C
// Argument of type '"blue"' is not assignable to parameter of type
// '"red" | "yellow" | "green" | undefined'.
```

### Testing utilities pattern with `NoInfer`

`NoInfer<T>` is particularly useful in test fixture factories and assertion helpers where a default value must belong to the same union as the primary constraint:

```typescript
// Type-safe test fixture builder: ensures `defaultValue` is a valid member
// of the enum/union passed as `values` — not a widened version
function makeEnumFixture<T extends string>(
  values: readonly T[],
  defaultValue?: NoInfer<T>,
): { values: readonly T[]; defaultValue: T } {
  return {
    values,
    defaultValue: defaultValue ?? values[0]!,
  };
}

const statusFixture = makeEnumFixture(
  ['pending', 'active', 'archived'] as const,
  'active',        // ✅ valid — must be one of the three strings
);
// statusFixture.defaultValue: "pending" | "active" | "archived"

makeEnumFixture(['pending', 'active', 'archived'] as const, 'deleted'); // ❌ compile error

// Assertion helper: expected must be assignable to the inferred type, not a widener
function assertEqualTyped<T>(actual: T, expected: NoInfer<T>): void {
  expect(actual).toEqual(expected);
}

const user = { id: 1, name: 'Alice' };
assertEqualTyped(user, { id: 1, name: 'Alice' }); // ✅
assertEqualTyped(user, { id: 1, name: 'Alice', extra: true }); // ❌ excess property error
```

[community] **Pitfall:** `NoInfer<T>` is a hint to the *inference algorithm*, not a runtime check. If TypeScript cannot infer `T` from any non-`NoInfer` position, it falls back to `unknown`. Always ensure at least one parameter that is NOT wrapped in `NoInfer` provides the type inference anchor.

---

## TypeScript 5.4 — Closure Narrowing Preservation

TypeScript 5.4 improved narrowing inside closure callbacks. Before 5.4, TypeScript sometimes dropped narrowings established before a closure was defined, assuming the variable might have been reassigned by the time the closure ran. TypeScript 5.4 preserves narrowings when the variable's last assignment occurs *before* the closure is created.

```typescript
// TypeScript < 5.4: url was re-widened to string | URL inside the callback
// TypeScript 5.4+: url's narrowing is preserved in the closure
function buildUrls(url: string | URL, names: string[]): string[] {
  if (typeof url === 'string') {
    url = new URL(url); // last assignment — TypeScript 5.4 locks in URL here
  }
  // url is now URL — and this is preserved inside the .map callback:
  return names.map(name => {
    url.searchParams.set('name', name); // ✅ No error in 5.4+ (was error in 5.3)
    return url.toString();
  });
}
```

**Narrowing is disabled when a closure *also assigns* the variable:**

```typescript
function printValueLater(value: string | undefined) {
  if (value === undefined) {
    value = 'missing!';
  }

  setTimeout(() => {
    value = value; // assignment inside nested function — defeats narrowing
  }, 500);

  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log(value!.toUpperCase()); // still errors without !
    //          ~~~~~ possibly undefined — narrowing dropped because of the assignment above
  }, 1000);
}
```

**Testing impact:** Test code that uses `.map`, `.filter`, or `setTimeout` callbacks can now omit redundant null checks that TypeScript 5.3 required:

```typescript
// Before 5.4: needed explicit null assertion or guard inside the callback
function processUsers(users: (User | null)[], db: Database): void {
  const validUsers = users.filter((u): u is User => u !== null);
  validUsers.forEach(u => {
    // In 5.4: u is User here — no extra assertion needed
    db.save(u.id, u.name);
  });
}
```

[community] **Pitfall:** The 5.4 improvement only applies when the narrowed variable is **not mutated** inside any of the closures in scope. If even one callback in the same function assigns to the variable, TypeScript drops the narrowing for *all* closures in that function — not just the one that mutates it. Restructure the code to use a `const` alias (`const resolvedUrl = url`) to guarantee narrowing across all closures.

---

## Type-Safe `Result<T, E>` Pattern for Error Handling

TypeScript's `useUnknownInCatchVariables` (enabled by `strict: true` since 4.4) makes caught errors `unknown`, requiring a narrow before use. The `Result<T, E>` discriminated union pattern provides a functional alternative: callers never need to catch, and the type system enforces error handling.

```typescript
// Core Result type: success or typed failure — no throw required
type Result<T, E = Error> =
  | { ok: true;  value: T }
  | { ok: false; error: E };

// Smart constructors (free-function style, no class required)
const Ok  = <T>(value: T): Result<T, never>            => ({ ok: true, value });
const Err = <E>(error: E): Result<never, E>            => ({ ok: false, error });

// ---- Application code -----------------------------------------------

interface ApiError {
  status: number;
  message: string;
}

async function fetchUser(id: number): Promise<Result<User, ApiError>> {
  const res = await fetch(`/users/${id}`);
  if (!res.ok) {
    return Err({ status: res.status, message: await res.text() });
  }
  return Ok(await res.json() as User);
}

// Caller must handle both branches — no unchecked exception
async function displayUser(id: number): Promise<string> {
  const result = await fetchUser(id);
  if (!result.ok) {
    return `Error ${result.error.status}: ${result.error.message}`;
  }
  return `Hello, ${result.value.name}`;
}
```

### Testing `Result<T, E>` with type guards

```typescript
// test/helpers/result.ts

// Type guard for success variant — narrows to T
export function isOk<T, E>(result: Result<T, E>): result is { ok: true; value: T } {
  return result.ok === true;
}

// Type guard for failure variant — narrows to E
export function isErr<T, E>(result: Result<T, E>): result is { ok: false; error: E } {
  return result.ok === false;
}

// Assertion helper — throws with type context if not Ok
export function assertOk<T, E>(
  result: Result<T, E>,
  msg?: string,
): asserts result is { ok: true; value: T } {
  if (!result.ok) {
    const detail = JSON.stringify((result as { ok: false; error: E }).error);
    throw new Error(msg ?? `Expected Ok result, got Err: ${detail}`);
  }
}

// ---- Tests ----------------------------------------------------------

describe('fetchUser', () => {
  it('returns Ok with user on 200', async () => {
    vi.mocked(fetch).mockResolvedValue({
      ok: true, status: 200, json: async () => ({ id: 1, name: 'Alice' }),
    } as Response);

    const result = await fetchUser(1);
    assertOk(result);                         // narrows to { ok: true; value: User }
    expect(result.value.name).toBe('Alice');
  });

  it('returns Err with ApiError on 404', async () => {
    vi.mocked(fetch).mockResolvedValue({
      ok: false, status: 404, text: async () => 'Not Found',
    } as unknown as Response);

    const result = await fetchUser(999);
    expect(isErr(result)).toBe(true);
    if (isErr(result)) {
      expect(result.error.status).toBe(404);
      expect(result.error.message).toBe('Not Found');
    }
  });
});
```

[community] **Pitfall:** The `Result<T, never>` returned by `Ok()` and `Result<never, E>` returned by `Err()` can cause inference issues when collected into an array: `const results = [Ok(1), Err('bad')]` gives `Result<number, never>[] | Result<never, string>[]`. Fix: annotate the array type explicitly — `const results: Result<number, string>[] = [Ok(1), Err('bad')]`.

---

## TypeScript 5.5 — Inferred Type Predicates

TypeScript 5.5 automatically infers type predicate return types for simple filter functions. Before 5.5, `.filter()` returned `(T | null)[]` even with an explicit null check; with 5.5 it returns `T[]` automatically.

```typescript
// TypeScript < 5.5: birds is (Bird | undefined)[]
// TypeScript 5.5+: birds is Bird[]  — predicate is inferred automatically
function makeBirdCalls(countries: string[]): void {
  const birds = countries
    .map(country => nationalBirds.get(country))  // Map<string, Bird>.get → Bird | undefined
    .filter(bird => bird !== undefined);           // ← inferred as (b): b is Bird

  for (const bird of birds) {
    bird.sing(); // ✅ No error — TypeScript knows bird is Bird
  }
}
```

### Rules for predicate inference

TypeScript infers a predicate only when ALL four conditions hold:

1. No explicit return type or `is` annotation on the function
2. Single `return` statement with no implicit `return undefined`
3. The parameter is not mutated inside the function body
4. The return expression **type-checks** as a narrowing of the parameter

```typescript
// ❌ Truthiness checks are deliberately NOT inferred as predicates
//    because score === 0 is falsy but a valid number
const nums = [1, 0, 2, null].filter(x => !!x);
// nums: (number | null)[] — !! is not a type-safe predicate

// ✅ Explicit comparison → inferred as number[]
const nums2 = [1, 0, 2, null].filter(x => x !== null);
// nums2: number[]
```

### Breaking change for existing tests (5.4 → 5.5 migration)

```typescript
// Code that relied on widened inference will now produce errors:
const ids: (number | null)[] = [1, 2, null, 3].filter(x => x !== null);
ids.push(null); // ❌ Error in 5.5 — ids is now number[], not (number | null)[]

// Fix: annotate the variable type explicitly when you need the wider type
const ids2: (number | null)[] = [1, 2, null, 3].filter(x => x !== null) as (number | null)[];
// Or simply avoid the cast: keep the result as number[] and add null separately if needed
```

[community] **Pitfall:** Teams upgrading from 5.4 to 5.5 sometimes hit unexpected errors when `.filter()` results that previously accepted `null` pushes are now typed as the narrowed type. Search for `.filter(x => x !== null)` or `.filter(Boolean)` patterns and check whether any downstream push/assignment assumes the wider type.

---

## Conditional Types as Type-Level Test Helpers

Conditional types can encode compile-time type assertions — verifying that a generic function returns the expected type without any runtime overhead. These patterns complement runtime `expectTypeOf` assertions (Vitest) with zero-cost type-level checks.

### Pattern: `Expect<T extends true>` — Type-Level Assertion

```typescript
// Type-level assertion utilities
type Expect<T extends true> = T;
type Equal<A, B> = (<T>() => T extends A ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends B ? 1 : 2)
  ? true : false;
type Extends<A, B> = A extends B ? true : false;
type NotExtends<A, B> = A extends B ? false : true;

// ---- Type-level test cases (compile errors = test failures) ----------

// Verify that a utility type produces the expected output
type _test1 = Expect<Equal<Awaited<Promise<string>>,   string>>;
type _test2 = Expect<Equal<ReturnType<typeof parseInt>, number>>;
type _test3 = Expect<Equal<Parameters<typeof Math.max>, number[]>>;

// Verify discriminated union variants are exhaustive
type _test4 = Expect<Extends<{ ok: true; value: string }, Result<string, Error>>>;
type _test5 = Expect<Extends<{ ok: false; error: Error }, Result<string, Error>>>;
```

### Pattern: Type-Level Filtering Assertion

```typescript
// Type that resolves to true only when a function type accepts the given arg types
type AcceptsArgs<Fn, Args extends unknown[]> =
  Fn extends (...args: Args) => unknown ? true : false;

type _canAcceptNumber = Expect<AcceptsArgs<typeof parseInt, [string, number?]>>;

// Verify that a mapped type removes a specific key
type Without<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K>;
type _noPassword = Expect<Equal<
  keyof Without<{ id: number; name: string; password: string }, 'password'>,
  'id' | 'name'
>>;
```

### Pattern: Extract Generics from Complex Return Types

```typescript
// Extract the element type of a Promise-returning function's resolved value
type ResolvedElement<Fn extends (...args: never[]) => Promise<unknown[]>> =
  Awaited<ReturnType<Fn>> extends (infer Element)[] ? Element : never;

async function fetchUsers(): Promise<User[]> { return []; }

type FetchedUser = ResolvedElement<typeof fetchUsers>;
// type FetchedUser = User

// Use in tests to avoid repeating the type
function assertFetchedUser(value: unknown): asserts value is FetchedUser {
  expect(value).toMatchObject({ id: expect.any(Number), name: expect.any(String) });
}
```

[community] **Pitfall:** The `Equal<A, B>` helper using conditional types with a phantom `T` (the "identity trick") correctly distinguishes `string` from `string | undefined` but may give false positives when comparing `any` types. `Equal<string, any>` returns `true` because `any` absorbs all comparisons. For testing purposes, add a separate `NotExtends<A, any>` guard when the tested type must not be `any`.

---

## Distributive vs Non-Distributive Conditional Types — Testing Gotchas

Conditional types distribute over union members by default when the checked type is a bare type parameter. This subtlety causes surprising results in test type utilities.

```typescript
// Distributive (default): distributes over each member of the union
type ToArray<T> = T extends unknown ? T[] : never;
type Result1 = ToArray<string | number>;
// Result1: string[] | number[]  — NOT (string | number)[]

// Non-distributive: wraps both sides to prevent distribution
type ToArrayNonDist<T> = [T] extends [unknown] ? T[] : never;
type Result2 = ToArrayNonDist<string | number>;
// Result2: (string | number)[]

// Filtering with distributive types: keeps only matching members
type OnlyStrings<T> = T extends string ? T : never;
type StrOnly = OnlyStrings<string | number | boolean>;
// StrOnly: string  (number and boolean resolve to never and are removed)

// Practical: extract only function properties from a type
type FunctionProperties<T> = {
  [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends (...args: unknown[]) => unknown ? K : never;
}[keyof T];

interface MixedService {
  baseUrl: string;
  timeout: number;
  fetchUser(id: number): Promise<User>;
  saveUser(user: User): Promise<void>;
}

type ServiceMethods = FunctionProperties<MixedService>;
// "fetchUser" | "saveUser"

// Use in type-safe spy setup: only accept method names, not property names
function spyOnMethod<T>(
  obj: T,
  method: FunctionProperties<T> & keyof T,
): jest.SpyInstance {
  return jest.spyOn(obj as Record<string, unknown>, method as string);
}
```

[community] **Pitfall:** When writing union-filtering utility types for test helpers, always test both the distributive and union inputs explicitly. `OnlyStrings<string>` gives `string` whether or not distribution is enabled. The difference only appears with `OnlyStrings<string | number>`. Include a `type _testDistribution = Expect<Equal<OnlyStrings<string | number>, string>>` in your type tests.

---

## TypeScript 5.4 — Object.groupBy and Map.groupBy Type Safety

`Object.groupBy` and `Map.groupBy` (ES2024, added to TypeScript 5.4's `lib`) return `Partial<Record<K, T[]>>` — values are optional because TypeScript cannot prove every key will be produced. This requires a defensive access pattern.

```typescript
// lib: es2024 or esnext required
const items = [
  { status: 'active', name: 'Alice' },
  { status: 'inactive', name: 'Bob' },
  { status: 'active', name: 'Carol' },
];

// Return type: Partial<Record<"active" | "inactive", typeof items>>
const grouped = Object.groupBy(items, item => item.status);

// ❌ TypeScript 5.7+ with noUncheckedIndexedAccess: error — value may be undefined
const activeItems = grouped.active.map(u => u.name);
//                          ~~~~~~ Object is possibly 'undefined'

// ✅ Defensive access pattern
const activeItems = (grouped.active ?? []).map(u => u.name);

// ✅ With destructuring and defaults
const { active = [], inactive = [] } = grouped;

// Testing pattern: assert the grouped structure
it('groups users by status', () => {
  const result = Object.groupBy(items, item => item.status);

  // Use nullish coalescing for type-safe access in assertions
  expect(result.active ?? []).toHaveLength(2);
  expect(result.inactive ?? []).toHaveLength(1);
  expect(result.active?.[0]?.name).toBe('Alice');
});
```

[community] **Pitfall:** The `Partial<Record<K, T[]>>` return type means that even if you pass a union key type, TypeScript cannot guarantee all keys are present in the output. `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` makes this visible by adding `| undefined` to all index accesses. Teams that upgrade from TypeScript 5.3 to 5.7 and enable `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` together will see a flood of errors on `groupBy` result access — fix them with `?? []` defaults, not with `!` assertions.

---

## Anti-Patterns: Version-Upgrade Quick Reference

| Anti-pattern | Introduced in | Why it breaks | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `.filter(x => !!x)` expecting `T[]` | TS 5.5 | Truthiness does not infer a predicate; result stays `(T \| Falsy)[]` | Use `.filter(x => x !== null && x !== undefined)` |
| `grouped.key.map(...)` on `Object.groupBy` result | TS 5.4 / 5.7 (noUnchecked) | Value is `T[] \| undefined` — Partial record | Add `?? []` before `.map()` |
| `filter(x => x !== null)` assigned to `(T \| null)[]` variable | TS 5.5 | Inferred predicate narrows to `T[]`; push(null) now errors | Annotate as `(T \| null)[]` explicitly if you need the wider type |
| Closure over `let` variable expecting narrowing | TS < 5.4 | Narrowing was dropped in closures | Upgrade to 5.4+, or use a `const` alias after narrowing |
| `NoInfer<T>` omitted on config default param | TS 5.4 | Default value widens the inferred union (`'blue'` accepted) | Wrap the default param: `defaultColor?: NoInfer<C>` |
| `import assert { type: "json" }` syntax | TS 5.8 | `assert` keyword removed; only `with` is valid | Migrate to `import data from "./data.json" with { type: "json" }` |

## TypeScript 5.8 — Granular Branch Checking in Return Expressions

TypeScript 5.8 special-cases conditional (`? :`) expressions in `return` statements, checking each branch independently against the declared return type. Previously, `any | T` collapsed to `any`, masking real type errors.

```typescript
declare const untypedCache: Map<any, any>;

// TypeScript < 5.8: no error — any | string simplifies to any
// TypeScript 5.8+: each branch is checked independently
function getUrlObject(urlString: string): URL {
  return untypedCache.has(urlString)
    ? untypedCache.get(urlString)   // OK — cache returns any, widened to URL
    : urlString;                    // ❌ Error: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'URL'
}

// Fix: return URL from both branches
function getUrlObjectFixed(urlString: string): URL {
  const cached = untypedCache.get(urlString) as URL | undefined;
  return cached instanceof URL ? cached : new URL(urlString);
}
```

### Testing Impact

In test files, this catches fixture builders that return incorrect branch types under `any`-typed test doubles. If a mock helper has type `Map<any, any>`, the 5.8 check now enforces that the resolved branch still satisfies the declared return type.

[community] **Pitfall:** Teams with large `Map<any, any>` caches (often from third-party mocking libraries) will see new errors after upgrading to 5.8. The fix is to add an `as ReturnType` cast on the `get()` side, or — better — type the cache with its intended type rather than `any`. The 5.8 change is correct; the errors reveal latent bugs.

## TypeScript 5.8 — `--erasableSyntaxOnly` for Node.js Type Stripping

Node.js 22.6+ can strip TypeScript types at runtime via `--experimental-strip-types` without a separate compile step. The `--erasableSyntaxOnly` compiler flag validates that your code is compatible with this stripping — rejecting constructs that have runtime semantics and cannot simply be erased.

```typescript
// ❌ All of these produce errors under --erasableSyntaxOnly:

// 1. Parameter properties (generate runtime initialisation code)
class Config {
  constructor(public readonly apiKey: string) {}  // ❌ Not erasable
}

// 2. enum declarations (emit runtime objects)
enum Direction { Up = 'UP', Down = 'DOWN' }  // ❌ Not erasable

// 3. namespace with runtime content
namespace Utils {
  export const PI = 3.14;  // ❌ Not erasable
}

// 4. import = require() syntax
import express = require('express');  // ❌ Not erasable

// ✅ Replacements:

// 1. Explicit constructor body
class ConfigFixed {
  readonly apiKey: string;
  constructor(apiKey: string) { this.apiKey = apiKey; }
}

// 2. as const object (same inference, zero runtime cost)
const Direction = { Up: 'UP', Down: 'DOWN' } as const;
type Direction = typeof Direction[keyof typeof Direction];

// 3. ESM module or plain object
export const PI = 3.14;

// 4. ESM import
import express from 'express';
```

### tsconfig pattern for Node.js type stripping

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "erasableSyntaxOnly": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "module": "nodenext",
    "target": "esnext"
  }
}
```

[community] **Pitfall:** `--erasableSyntaxOnly` does NOT cover all runtime semantics — it only checks for TypeScript-specific erasable syntax. Decorators (which have runtime semantics) are separate and controlled by `experimentalDecorators`. Teams adopting Node.js native type stripping should audit for decorators separately.

---

## TypeScript 5.9 — `import defer` for Lazy Module Evaluation

`import defer` defers module *evaluation* (side-effect execution) until a property of the imported namespace is first accessed. This differs from dynamic `import()` — the module is loaded synchronously during the static analysis phase, but evaluation (code execution) is postponed.

```typescript
// ✅ Only namespace imports are allowed with import defer
import defer * as heavyLib from "./heavy-lib.js";
// Nothing in heavy-lib.js has run yet

// ... application setup ...

// Side effects execute at the first property access:
const result = heavyLib.process(data);  // heavy-lib.js evaluates here
```

### Key constraints

```typescript
// ❌ Named imports are not allowed
import defer { process } from "./heavy-lib.js";   // Syntax error

// ❌ Default imports are not allowed
import defer defaultExport from "./heavy-lib.js"; // Syntax error

// ✅ Re-export is allowed
export { heavyLib };
```

### Practical pattern: feature flags with lazy evaluation

```typescript
// analytics.ts — has expensive initialisation side effects
import defer * as analytics from "./vendor/analytics.js";

function initApp(config: AppConfig): void {
  setupCore(config);

  // analytics initialises only when feature is enabled
  if (config.analyticsEnabled) {
    analytics.init(config.analyticsKey);  // evaluation happens here
  }
}
```

### Runtime requirements

```json
// tsconfig.json — import defer only compiles with these module settings
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "preserve"   // or "esnext"
  }
}
```

[community] **Pitfall:** `import defer` defers *evaluation*, not *loading*. The module file must exist on disk and be parsed; only its top-level statements are held back. If a module has no top-level side effects, `import defer` has no observable benefit. Use it specifically for libraries with expensive initialisation code (analytics SDKs, heavy parsers, feature-flag clients).

---

## TypeScript 5.9 — ArrayBuffer / TypedArray Breaking Change

TypeScript 5.9 updated `lib.d.ts` so that `ArrayBuffer` is no longer a supertype of `TypedArray` types (including Node.js `Buffer`). Projects that pass `Buffer` values to APIs expecting `ArrayBuffer` will see new type errors.

```typescript
// ❌ Error in TypeScript 5.9+
function processBuffer(data: ArrayBuffer): void { /* ... */ }

const nodeBuffer = Buffer.from([1, 2, 3]);
processBuffer(nodeBuffer);
// Error: Type 'Buffer' is not assignable to type 'ArrayBuffer'
```

### Migration patterns

```typescript
// Option 1: Access .buffer property to get the underlying ArrayBuffer
processBuffer(nodeBuffer.buffer);

// Option 2: Be explicit with Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>
function processBuffer(data: Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>): void { /* ... */ }
processBuffer(nodeBuffer);  // OK — Buffer extends Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>

// Option 3: Accept the wider union
function processBuffer(data: ArrayBuffer | Uint8Array): void { /* ... */ }

// Option 4: Update @types/node (needed regardless)
// npm update @types/node --save-dev
```

[community] **Pitfall:** Tests that construct `Buffer.from(...)` and pass the result to functions typed as `ArrayBuffer` will fail type-checking after upgrading. The root fix is updating `@types/node` and then either using `.buffer` or broadening the function signature to `Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>`. Do not use `as ArrayBuffer` casts — they hide the actual type mismatch.

---

## TypeScript 6.0 — New Default Compiler Options

TypeScript 6.0 changes several compiler defaults to match the modern JavaScript ecosystem. Existing `tsconfig.json` files that rely on old implicit defaults will behave differently without changes.

### Changed defaults

| Option | Old default | New default | Impact |
|--------|-------------|-------------|--------|
| `strict` | `false` | `true` | All strict flags now on by default |
| `module` | `commonjs` | `esnext` | ESM output by default |
| `target` | `es5` | `es2025` | Modern runtime assumptions |
| `types` | all `@types/*` | `[]` (none) | **Must explicitly list types** |
| `rootDir` | inferred | `.` (tsconfig dir) | May affect output structure |

### Critical: `types: []` change

```typescript
// ❌ Error in TypeScript 6.0 — describe/it/expect not found
describe('MyService', () => {
  it('returns data', () => {
    expect(service.get()).toBeTruthy();
  });
});

// ✅ Fix: explicitly list needed types in tsconfig.json
```

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "types": ["node", "jest"]
  }
}
// Or for Vitest:
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "types": ["node", "vitest/globals"]
  }
}
```

### Removed features in 6.0

```typescript
// ❌ --outFile: Use a bundler (esbuild, rollup, webpack) instead

// ❌ --baseUrl alone for module resolution (confusing, use paths with full paths)
// Old (deprecated):
// { "baseUrl": "./src", "paths": { "@app/*": ["app/*"] } }
// New:
// { "paths": { "@app/*": ["./src/app/*"] } }

// ❌ --moduleResolution node (Node.js 10 algorithm): use nodenext or bundler
// { "moduleResolution": "nodenext" }

// ❌ module keyword for namespace (use namespace keyword)
module Foo { export const bar = 10; }  // ❌ Error in TS 6.0
namespace Foo { export const bar = 10; }  // ✅ Correct

// ❌ target: es5 removed — use es2015 or newer
```

### `dom.iterable` merged into `dom`

```json
// TS 6.0: dom.iterable and dom.asynciterable are included in dom
// Before:
{ "lib": ["dom", "dom.iterable"] }
// After (equivalent):
{ "lib": ["dom"] }
```

[community] **Pitfall:** The `"types": []` change is the most disruptive for test suites. Any project that relies on globally auto-included `@types/jest`, `@types/mocha`, or `@types/node` will see a flood of "Cannot find name 'describe'" errors. Always list `types` explicitly when upgrading to TypeScript 6.0. Set `"ignoreDeprecations": "6.0"` temporarily to defer removed-feature errors during migration, but remove it before adopting TypeScript 7.0.

---

## TypeScript 6.0 — New ES2025 Built-In APIs

TypeScript 6.0 targets `es2025` by default and ships with typings for new Stage 4 JavaScript APIs.

### `Map.getOrInsert` / `Map.getOrInsertComputed`

```typescript
// Before (verbose): check-then-set pattern
const cache = new Map<string, number>();
function getOrCompute(key: string, compute: () => number): number {
  if (!cache.has(key)) {
    cache.set(key, compute());
  }
  return cache.get(key)!;  // Non-null assertion needed
}

// After (ES2025): single call, no assertion needed
const cache = new Map<string, number>();

// Cheap default value — evaluated eagerly
const value = cache.getOrInsert('key', 0);

// Expensive computation — deferred with a callback
const computed = cache.getOrInsertComputed('key', () => expensiveCompute());
```

### `RegExp.escape`

```typescript
// ❌ Dangerous: user input contains regex metacharacters
function findExact(text: string, query: string): boolean {
  const regex = new RegExp(query);   // query = "a.b" matches "axb"!
  return regex.test(text);
}

// ✅ Safe: escape the string before embedding in a regex
function findExact(text: string, query: string): boolean {
  const escaped = RegExp.escape(query);  // "a.b" → "a\.b"
  const regex = new RegExp(`\\b${escaped}\\b`, 'g');
  return regex.test(text);
}

// Testing: validate regex escape behaviour
it('finds exact word matches only', () => {
  expect(findExact('a.b c d', 'a.b')).toBe(true);
  expect(findExact('axb c d', 'a.b')).toBe(false);  // dot is literal, not wildcard
});
```

[community] **Pitfall:** `RegExp.escape` is a runtime method — it exists only in environments that ship ES2025 support (Node.js 24+, modern browsers). Setting `"target": "es2025"` in TypeScript does NOT polyfill it. Add a runtime check or polyfill before using it in environments targeting Node.js < 24.

---

## Less-Known Utility Types: `ThisType`, `ThisParameterType`, `OmitThisParameter`

These three utility types address `this`-context patterns that often arise in object composition, method wrappers, and framework integrations.

### `ThisType<T>` — Contextual `this` in object literals

```typescript
// Pattern: object builder where methods need typed access to sibling data
type ObjectDescriptor<D, M> = {
  data?: D;
  methods?: M & ThisType<D & M>;  // this inside methods = D & M
};

function makeObject<D, M>(desc: ObjectDescriptor<D, M>): D & M {
  return { ...desc.data, ...desc.methods } as D & M;
}

const counter = makeObject({
  data: { count: 0 },
  methods: {
    increment()   { this.count++; },       // this.count is number ✅
    decrement()   { this.count--; },
    getValue(): number { return this.count; }
  }
});

counter.increment();
console.log(counter.getValue()); // 1
```

> Requires `"noImplicitThis": true` in `tsconfig.json` to enforce the typing.

### `ThisParameterType<T>` and `OmitThisParameter<T>`

```typescript
// Useful when working with functions that have an explicit this parameter
function toHex(this: Number): string {
  return this.toString(16);
}

// Extract the this requirement
type HexContext = ThisParameterType<typeof toHex>;
// HexContext = Number

// Create a version that can be called without a this context
const boundToHex: OmitThisParameter<typeof toHex> = toHex.bind(255);
console.log(boundToHex()); // "ff"

// Pattern: adapter that strips this from methods for callback use
function adaptMethod<T extends (this: any, ...args: any[]) => any>(
  instance: ThisParameterType<T>,
  fn: T,
): OmitThisParameter<T> {
  return fn.bind(instance) as OmitThisParameter<T>;
}
```

[community] **Pitfall:** `ThisType<T>` is a marker type — it does nothing by itself and has no runtime effect. It is only meaningful inside a mapped type or object literal type that is consumed by a generic function like `makeObject` above. Applying `ThisType<T>` to a standalone variable type annotation does nothing useful and is a common misuse.

---

## Advanced Mapped Types — Key Remapping with `as`

TypeScript 4.1+ supports key remapping in mapped types using an `as` clause. Combined with template literals, this creates powerful derivations without a new type and without losing information.

### Pattern: Generate getter/setter interfaces from data shape

```typescript
type Getters<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K];
};

type Setters<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as `set${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: (value: T[K]) => void;
};

interface User {
  name: string;
  age: number;
  email: string;
}

type UserGetters = Getters<User>;
// { getName: () => string; getAge: () => number; getEmail: () => string; }

type UserAccessors = Getters<User> & Setters<User>;
```

### Pattern: Event dispatcher — map union tags to handler types

```typescript
type SquareEvent = { kind: 'square'; x: number; y: number };
type CircleEvent = { kind: 'circle'; radius: number };
type AppEvent = SquareEvent | CircleEvent;

type EventHandlerMap<Events extends { kind: string }> = {
  [E in Events as E['kind']]: (event: E) => void;
};

type Handlers = EventHandlerMap<AppEvent>;
// { square: (event: SquareEvent) => void; circle: (event: CircleEvent) => void; }

// Type-safe dispatcher
function dispatch(handlers: Handlers, event: AppEvent): void {
  (handlers[event.kind] as (e: AppEvent) => void)(event);
}
```

### Pattern: Remove internal/metadata keys by filtering to `never`

```typescript
type PublicShape<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as K extends `_${string}` ? never : K]: T[K];
};

interface InternalConfig {
  _id: string;
  _version: number;
  name: string;
  timeout: number;
}

type PublicConfig = PublicShape<InternalConfig>;
// { name: string; timeout: number; }  — underscore-prefixed keys removed
```

[community] **Pitfall:** Key remapping with `as` only works with `keyof` iteration — you cannot remap arbitrary union keys in a single mapped type without first having an object type to iterate. If you need to remap a bare union of strings, create an intermediate `Record<UnionKey, unknown>` and then apply the remapping.

---

## TypeScript Performance — 2025+ Degradation Patterns

As codebases grow, TypeScript type-checking can become a bottleneck. These patterns are the leading causes of slow builds in 2025-era projects.

### 1. Large union types cause quadratic comparison time

```typescript
// ❌ Slow: 50+ union members compared pairwise — O(n²) comparisons
type AllEvents =
  | ClickEvent | HoverEvent | FocusEvent | BlurEvent | SubmitEvent
  | /* ... 45 more types */ ;

// ✅ Fast: shared interface that all events extend
interface BaseEvent { timestamp: number; source: string; }
interface ClickEvent extends BaseEvent { x: number; y: number; }
// TypeScript can compare via the shared interface, not pairwise union members
```

### 2. Inline conditional types re-evaluate on every use

```typescript
// ❌ Slow: this conditional re-executes everywhere Wrap<T> is used
function wrap<T>(x: T): T extends string ? StringWrapper<T> : NumberWrapper<T> {
  // ...
}

// ✅ Fast: named type alias is cached after first evaluation
type WrapResult<T> = T extends string ? StringWrapper<T> : NumberWrapper<T>;
function wrap<T>(x: T): WrapResult<T> { /* ... */ }
```

### 3. Intersection types vs. interface — merge cost

```typescript
// ❌ Slow: intersection must recursively merge properties on every access
type MyType = TypeA & TypeB & TypeC;

// ✅ Fast: interface creates a flat merged type once, detects conflicts early
interface MyType extends TypeA, TypeB, TypeC {}
```

### 4. Misconfigured `tsconfig.json` globs

```json
// ❌ Does NOT exclude nested node_modules — TypeScript still parses them
{ "exclude": ["node_modules"] }

// ✅ Correct — excludes all node_modules at any depth
{ "exclude": ["**/node_modules", "dist", "build"] }
```

### 5. Global type pollution from unused `@types` packages

```json
// ❌ Auto-includes @types/mocha globally, even in non-test source files
// (old tsconfig.json with no "types" field — TS 5.x default)

// ✅ Scope test types to test files using per-file tsconfig
// test/tsconfig.json:
{ "compilerOptions": { "types": ["node", "vitest/globals"] },
  "include": ["**/*.test.ts"] }
// src/tsconfig.json:
{ "compilerOptions": { "types": ["node"] },
  "include": ["**/*.ts"], "exclude": ["**/*.test.ts"] }
```

### 6. TypeScript 7.0 — upcoming Go native compiler

TypeScript's codebase is being ported to Go for TypeScript 7.0, targeting up to 10x faster builds. The JavaScript compiler will remain available for compatibility, but large projects should plan for the migration. Use `--stableTypeOrdering` (TypeScript 6.0 flag) to verify output equivalence between the current and upcoming native compiler during migration testing.

[community] **Pitfall:** Adding `skipLibCheck: true` to silence `.d.ts` errors is a common short-term fix that hides real type incompatibilities between library versions. Use it only during active migrations, not as a permanent setting. A better approach is to pin dependency versions and resolve the conflicts in library types explicitly.

## Anti-Patterns: TypeScript 5.8–6.0 Quick Reference

| Anti-pattern | Version | Why it breaks | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `enum Direction { ... }` in type-stripping codebases | TS 5.8 | `enum` has runtime semantics, not erasable | Replace with `as const` object + union type |
| `constructor(public x: T)` parameter properties in Node.js strip mode | TS 5.8 | Parameter properties emit initialisation code | Move to explicit `this.x = x` in constructor body |
| `untypedCache.get(k) : fallback` in a typed return | TS 5.8 | Each conditional branch now checked independently; `any` no longer masks wrong branch type | Cast `get()` result to the correct type or use `instanceof` guard |
| Passing `Buffer` to `ArrayBuffer` parameter | TS 5.9 | `Buffer` no longer subtypes `ArrayBuffer` | Use `.buffer` property or widen param to `Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>` |
| Relying on implicit `@types/*` resolution | TS 6.0 | `types: []` is the new default — no auto-include | Add `"types": ["node", "jest"]` (or equivalent) explicitly |
| `"module": "commonjs"` in new projects | TS 6.0 | Old default removed; new default is `esnext` | Explicitly set `"module": "commonjs"` if you still need CJS, else migrate to ESM |
| `"target": "es5"` | TS 6.0 | `es5` target removed | Use `"target": "es2015"` minimum; prefer `es2022` or newer |
| `baseUrl` without `paths` | TS 6.0 | `baseUrl` alone is deprecated | Move prefix to explicit `paths` entries with full relative paths |
| `namespace` vs `module` keyword confusion | TS 6.0 | `module Foo {}` syntax removed | Use `namespace Foo {}` exclusively |
| `import defer { named }` | TS 5.9 | Only namespace imports allowed with defer | Use `import defer * as ns from "..."` |

## Cycle 20 — 2026-05-13
<!-- sources: official (typescriptlang.org, TS 5.0–5.9 release notes) | community (microsoft/TypeScript Performance wiki) | iteration: 43 | score: 99/100 | date: 2026-05-13 -->

This cycle adds coverage for TypeScript 5.0–5.2 foundational features that had received only mention-level treatment in earlier cycles (const type parameters, ECMAScript decorators, decorator metadata, explicit resource management), consolidates TypeScript 5.8–5.9 production guidance with deeper code examples, expands compiler-performance community findings from the official Performance wiki, and adds a fresh node20 vs nodenext module stability quick reference.

### TypeScript 5.0 — `const` Type Parameters

`const T` on a generic function signals the compiler to infer tuple/array arguments as `readonly` literal tuples instead of mutable arrays, eliminating many call-site `as const` assertions.

```typescript
// Without const modifier — inference widens to string[]
function tagsToBadge<T extends readonly string[]>(tags: T): T {
  return tags;
}
const badge1 = tagsToBadge(["alpha", "beta"]);
// badge1: string[]  ← too wide for discriminated-union key lookups

// ✅ With const modifier — preserves tuple literals
function tagsToBadge<const T extends readonly string[]>(tags: T): T {
  return tags;
}
const badge2 = tagsToBadge(["alpha", "beta"]);
// badge2: readonly ["alpha", "beta"]  ← exact literals preserved

// Important: const modifier only applies to inline literals, not pre-bound variables
const existing = ["alpha", "beta"];
const badge3 = tagsToBadge(existing);
// badge3: string[]  ← variable was already widened before the call
```

**When to use:** Generic builders, routing tables, event-name registries — any API where callers pass literal arrays and downstream code needs to discriminate on exact values.

**Pattern — exhaustive route registry:**
```typescript
type RouteRecord<const T extends readonly string[]> = {
  [K in T[number]]: () => void;
};

function registerRoutes<const T extends readonly string[]>(
  paths: T,
  handlers: RouteRecord<T>
): void {
  for (const path of paths) {
    // handlers[path] is statically known to exist
  }
}

registerRoutes(
  ["/home", "/about"],
  { "/home": () => console.log("home"), "/about": () => console.log("about") }
);
// "/dashboard" in handlers would be a compile-time error
```

### TypeScript 5.0 — ECMAScript Standard Decorators

TypeScript 5.0 ships the stage-3 ECMAScript decorators proposal as the new default. This is **not** compatible with the legacy `--experimentalDecorators` flag; the two systems coexist but do not interoperate.

```typescript
// ---- Method decorator with ClassMethodDecoratorContext ----
function loggedMethod<This, Args extends unknown[], Return>(
  target: (this: This, ...args: Args) => Return,
  context: ClassMethodDecoratorContext<This, (this: This, ...args: Args) => Return>
): (this: This, ...args: Args) => Return {
  const methodName = String(context.name);
  return function (this: This, ...args: Args): Return {
    console.log(`→ ${methodName}(${args.map(String).join(", ")})`);
    const result = target.call(this, ...args);
    console.log(`← ${methodName} returned`);
    return result;
  };
}

class OrderService {
  @loggedMethod
  placeOrder(orderId: string, qty: number): boolean {
    return qty > 0;
  }
}

// ---- Auto-bind decorator using addInitializer ----
function bound(
  _target: unknown,
  context: ClassMethodDecoratorContext
): void {
  const name = context.name;
  context.addInitializer(function (this: Record<string | symbol, unknown>) {
    this[name] = (this[name] as Function).bind(this);
  });
}

class EventSource {
  @bound
  handleClick(event: MouseEvent): void {
    console.log(event.type, this);
  }
}
// handleClick can now be passed directly as an event listener without rebinding
```

**Key differences from `--experimentalDecorators`:**
- No `emitDecoratorMetadata` support — use decorator metadata (TS 5.2) instead.
- Parameter decorators are not part of the standard proposal.
- Decorators can be placed before or after `export` keyword — but not both.
- Well-typed decorators use generic `This`/`Args`/`Return` — avoids `any` in decorator bodies.

---

### TypeScript 5.2 — Decorator Metadata

TypeScript 5.2 adds `Symbol.metadata` support, giving decorators a shared metadata store on the class that survives tree-shaking and does not require `reflect-metadata`.

```typescript
// ---- Serialization via decorator metadata ----
const serializableFields = new WeakMap<object, string[]>();

function serialize(
  _target: unknown,
  context: ClassMemberDecoratorContext
): void {
  if (context.static || context.private) {
    throw new Error("@serialize only works on public instance members");
  }
  if (typeof context.name !== "string") {
    throw new Error("@serialize requires string property names");
  }
  let fields = serializableFields.get(context.metadata);
  if (!fields) {
    serializableFields.set(context.metadata, (fields = []));
  }
  fields.push(context.name);
}

function toJSON(instance: object): string {
  const meta = (instance.constructor as { [Symbol.metadata]?: object })[Symbol.metadata];
  const fields = meta ? serializableFields.get(meta) : undefined;
  if (!fields) throw new Error("No @serialize fields found");
  const payload: Record<string, unknown> = {};
  for (const field of fields) {
    payload[field] = (instance as Record<string, unknown>)[field];
  }
  return JSON.stringify(payload);
}

class User {
  @serialize id: number = 1;
  @serialize name: string = "Alice";
  passwordHash: string = "secret"; // Not serialized
}

console.log(toJSON(new User())); // {"id":1,"name":"Alice"}
```

**Required tsconfig for decorator metadata:**
```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2022",
    "lib": ["es2022", "esnext.decorators", "dom"]
  }
}
```

**Polyfill for environments without native support:**
```typescript
Symbol.metadata ??= Symbol("Symbol.metadata");
```

---

### TypeScript 5.2 — `using` and `await using` (Explicit Resource Management)

ECMAScript's explicit resource management proposal is now fully supported. Resources implementing `Symbol.dispose` (sync) or `Symbol.asyncDispose` (async) are automatically cleaned up when the enclosing scope exits — including on early `return` and `throw`.

```typescript
import { openSync, closeSync, unlinkSync } from "fs";

class TempFile implements Disposable {
  readonly path: string;
  private handle: number;

  constructor(path: string) {
    this.path = path;
    this.handle = openSync(path, "w+");
  }

  write(data: string): void {
    // ...
  }

  [Symbol.dispose](): void {
    closeSync(this.handle);
    unlinkSync(this.path);
  }
}

function processData(input: string): string {
  using tmp = new TempFile("/tmp/work.txt");
  tmp.write(input);
  return tmp.path; // file deleted as scope exits — even on throw
}

// ---- Async variant ----
class DbConnection implements AsyncDisposable {
  async [Symbol.asyncDispose](): Promise<void> {
    await this.close();
  }
  async close(): Promise<void> { /* ... */ }
}

async function runQuery(sql: string): Promise<unknown[]> {
  await using conn = new DbConnection();
  return conn.query(sql); // conn.close() called after return
}

// ---- Ad-hoc cleanup with DisposableStack ----
function withRawFd(path: string): number {
  const fd = openSync(path, "r");
  using stack = new DisposableStack();
  stack.defer(() => closeSync(fd));
  return fd; // fd closed when function returns
}
```

**Testing pattern — tear down mocks automatically:**
```typescript
function mockDate(isoString: string): Disposable {
  const original = Date.now;
  Date.now = () => new Date(isoString).getTime();
  return {
    [Symbol.dispose]() {
      Date.now = original;
    },
  };
}

it("formats the order timestamp", () => {
  using _mock = mockDate("2026-01-15T12:00:00Z");
  expect(formatOrderDate(Date.now())).toBe("Jan 15, 2026");
  // Date.now restored when the test block exits
});
```

---

### TypeScript 5.8 — `--erasableSyntaxOnly` for Node.js Type Stripping

Node.js 23.6+ can strip TypeScript type annotations natively without `tsc`, but only for "erasable" syntax — constructs that disappear completely after type removal. The `--erasableSyntaxOnly` flag enforces this at compile time.

**Erasable constructs (allowed):**
```typescript
// ✅ Type annotations — erased
const x: number = 42;
export interface Point { x: number; y: number; }
export type Alias = string | number;
import type { Foo } from "./foo.js";
```

**Non-erasable constructs (blocked by `--erasableSyntaxOnly`):**
```typescript
// ❌ enum — emits initialisation code
enum Direction { Up, Down, Left, Right }
// Fix: use as-const object + union type
const Direction = { Up: "Up", Down: "Down", Left: "Left", Right: "Right" } as const;
type Direction = (typeof Direction)[keyof typeof Direction];

// ❌ Parameter properties — emit assignments in constructor body
class Service {
  constructor(public readonly db: DbClient) {}
}
// Fix: explicit field + assignment
class Service {
  readonly db: DbClient;
  constructor(db: DbClient) { this.db = db; }
}

// ❌ Legacy import = require
import fs = require("fs");
// Fix: ESM import
import * as fs from "fs";

// ❌ Namespace with runtime body
namespace Utils { export function helper() { return 42; } }
// Fix: regular module-level exports
export function helper() { return 42; }
```

**Recommended tsconfig for Node.js native stripping:**
```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "nodenext",
    "target": "esnext",
    "erasableSyntaxOnly": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "strict": true
  }
}
```

---

### TypeScript 5.8 — Granular Branch Checking in Return Expressions

Before 5.8, the compiler checked the overall type of a conditional expression against the return type. From 5.8, each branch is checked individually. This surfaces bugs where one branch was previously masked by `any`.

```typescript
const cache = new Map<string, URL>();

// ❌ Pre-5.8: no error — `any | URL` simplified to `any` before checking
// ✅ 5.8+: error on the true-branch — Map.get() returns `URL | undefined`, not `URL`
function getUrl(key: string): URL {
  return cache.has(key)
    ? cache.get(key)  // ← error: URL | undefined not assignable to URL
    : new URL("https://example.com");
}

// Fix: narrow explicitly
function getUrlFixed(key: string): URL {
  const cached = cache.get(key);
  return cached ?? new URL("https://example.com");
}
```

[community] **Pitfall:** After upgrading to TS 5.8, CI may surface "X is not assignable to Y" errors in code that has been silently wrong since the `any`-spreading era. Treat each new error as a genuine bug to fix, not a false positive to suppress with `!` or `as`.

---

### TypeScript 5.9 — `import defer` for Lazy Module Evaluation

`import defer` loads the module's exports object immediately (so circular-dependency checks pass) but defers execution of module-level side effects until the first property access.

```typescript
// module: preserve or esnext required
import defer * as analytics from "./analytics.js";

function handleCheckout(cart: Cart): Order {
  const order = buildOrder(cart);
  // analytics module side-effects run only on first property access
  analytics.trackPurchase(order.id, order.total);
  return order;
}
```

**Key constraints:**
- Only namespace imports (`import defer * as ns`) are supported.
- Named imports (`import defer { fn }`) and default imports are syntax errors.
- TypeScript does not transform `import defer` — requires native runtime or bundler support.
- Works with `--module preserve` or `--module esnext`.

**Testing pattern — conditionally skip heavy analytics in unit tests:**
```typescript
// analytics.ts
export function trackPurchase(id: string, total: number): void {
  // calls external SDK — expensive in unit tests
}

// checkout.test.ts
import defer * as analytics from "../analytics.js";
vi.mock("../analytics.js", () => ({ trackPurchase: vi.fn() }));

it("builds the order", () => {
  const order = handleCheckout(makeCart());
  // analytics mock was never initialised until this line
  expect(vi.mocked(analytics.trackPurchase)).toHaveBeenCalledWith(order.id, order.total);
});
```

---

### TypeScript 5.9 — `--module node20` (Stable Node.js v20 Target)

`--module node20` is the stable, pinned equivalent of `nodenext` for Node.js v20 LTS. Unlike `nodenext` (which floats to the latest Node.js semantics), `node20` is fixed, making it suitable for libraries and CI environments that need reproducible builds.

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "node20",
    "target": "es2023",
    "strict": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true
  }
}
```

| Module option | Implies target | Stability | Recommended for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `nodenext` | `esnext` | Floating | Apps on latest Node.js |
| `node20` | `es2023` | Stable / pinned | Libraries, Node.js 20 LTS |
| `node18` | `es2022` | Stable | Node.js 18 LTS codebases |
| `commonjs` | (unchanged) | Legacy | CJS-only legacy packages |

**Pitfall:** Mixing `"module": "esnext"` with `"moduleResolution": "node20"` causes a TS 5.2+ error. The `module` and `moduleResolution` options must be from the same family (node16/node16, node20/node20, nodenext/nodenext).

### TypeScript Performance — Compiler Scaling Patterns [community]

Findings from the official Microsoft TypeScript Performance wiki, verified 2026-05-13.

**1. Interface extends over intersection types — quadratic vs. cached**
```typescript
// ❌ [community] Slow: intersection recalculates on every usage site
type ApiResponse = BaseResponse & PaginationMeta & ErrorEnvelope;

// ✅ Fast: interface merges once and caches the flat shape
interface ApiResponse extends BaseResponse, PaginationMeta, ErrorEnvelope {}
```
*Why:* Intersection types recursively merge on each access. Interfaces create a flat cached shape with conflict detection at definition time. At 10+ type parameters the difference compounds to seconds.

**2. Explicit return types on exported functions — reduced .d.ts inference cost**
```typescript
// ❌ [community] Slow for large codebases: compiler must infer and serialise
export function buildQuery(filters: FilterSpec) {
  return filters.items.map(/* complex transform */);
}

// ✅ Name the return type — inference computed once, referenced thereafter
export function buildQuery(filters: FilterSpec): QueryResult[] {
  return filters.items.map(/* complex transform */);
}
```
*Why:* Without an explicit return type, the compiler must infer the shape, serialise it to `.d.ts` import paths, and re-read it for every consumer file.

**3. Large union types — prefer interface hierarchies**
```typescript
// ❌ [community] Quadratic at 12+ members: all pairs compared on every intersect
type DomNode = DivEl | SpanEl | AnchorEl | ButtonEl | /* 20 more */;

// ✅ Shared base interface — pairwise comparisons reduced to subtype checks
interface DomNode { nodeType: number; textContent: string | null; }
interface DivEl extends DomNode { tagName: "DIV"; }
interface SpanEl extends DomNode { tagName: "SPAN"; }
```
*Why:* Union member elimination is O(n²) over union size. Discriminated unions via `tagName` allow the compiler to use narrowing rather than pairwise comparison.

**4. `types: []` in tsconfig — eliminate accidental global pollution**
```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "types": []
  }
}
```
[community] **Pitfall:** Without an explicit `types` list, TypeScript 5.x (before 6.0) auto-includes every `@types/*` package installed in `node_modules`. This pollutes global scope with test runner types (mocha `describe`/`it`) in non-test source files, causes false passes in type checking, and adds parsing overhead for types the app doesn't use. `types: []` provides 10–30% speedup with zero functional impact for most projects; add explicit entries (`"types": ["node"]`) only for packages that contribute actual globals.

**5. `skipLibCheck: true` — production caveats**

[community] **Pitfall:** `skipLibCheck: true` is ubiquitous in production tsconfigs because it eliminates errors in `.d.ts` files from library authors. However, it silently ignores real type incompatibilities between library versions (e.g., `@types/react` 18 vs `@types/react` 17 installed simultaneously). Use it only during active migrations; remove it and resolve genuine conflicts before shipping stable library code. A better long-term strategy is to pin `@types/*` versions and run `tsc --noEmit` with `skipLibCheck: false` in a separate lint step.

**6. Conditional types — cache with named aliases**
```typescript
// ❌ [community] Re-evaluated at every usage site
function wrap<T>(x: T): T extends string ? Wrapped<T> : Raw<T> { /* ... */ }

// ✅ Cached after first evaluation
type WrapResult<T> = T extends string ? Wrapped<T> : Raw<T>;
function wrap<T>(x: T): WrapResult<T> { /* ... */ }
```

---

### TypeScript 5.x — `satisfies` Operator: Advanced Patterns

The `satisfies` operator (introduced TS 4.9, matured in TS 5.x practice) validates against a type without widening the inferred type. This is distinct from a type annotation, which widens the type to the annotated shape.

```typescript
// ---- Pattern 1: Preserve literal types while validating shape ----
type StatusConfig = Record<"pending" | "active" | "closed", {
  label: string;
  color: string;
}>;

// Type annotation would widen all values to { label: string; color: string }
// satisfies preserves the exact object literal — label is still a string literal
const STATUS = {
  pending: { label: "Pending Review", color: "#FFA500" },
  active:  { label: "Active",         color: "#00C851" },
  closed:  { label: "Closed",         color: "#FF4444" },
} satisfies StatusConfig;

// ✅ STATUS.pending.color is string (not widened to string | unknown)
// ✅ Typo in key ("pendingg") is a compile error

// ---- Pattern 2: Exhaustive fixture coverage in tests ----
type UserFixture = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  role: "admin" | "viewer";
};

const USERS = [
  { id: "u1", name: "Alice", role: "admin"  },
  { id: "u2", name: "Bob",   role: "viewer" },
] satisfies UserFixture[];
// Adding a new required field to UserFixture turns all fixture objects into compile errors

// ---- Pattern 3: satisfies + as const chained (avoid pitfall) ----
// PITFALL [community]: satisfies does NOT narrow inside nested as-const records
const ROUTES = {
  home:    { path: "/",        exact: true  },
  profile: { path: "/profile", exact: false },
} satisfies Record<string, { path: string; exact: boolean }> as const;
// The `as const` must come AFTER satisfies, not before;
// if you reverse the order the type guard on satisfies sees a widened record

// ---- Pattern 4: Type-safe event bus registration ----
type EventMap = {
  userCreated: { id: string; name: string };
  orderPlaced: { orderId: string; total: number };
};

const handlers = {
  userCreated: (e) => console.log("New user:", e.name),
  orderPlaced: (e) => console.log("Order:", e.orderId, e.total),
} satisfies { [K in keyof EventMap]: (event: EventMap[K]) => void };
// handler parameter types are inferred from EventMap — no manual annotation needed
```

---

### TypeScript — Utility Types: Production Patterns

Condensed guide to the utility types most frequently misused or under-utilised in production codebases.

```typescript
// ---- Partial<T> — update payloads only ----
interface User { id: string; name: string; email: string; role: "admin" | "viewer"; }

// ❌ Anti-pattern: accepting User forces callers to provide every field
function updateUser(id: string, patch: User): Promise<User> { /* ... */ }

// ✅ Only changed fields required
function updateUser(id: string, patch: Partial<Omit<User, "id">>): Promise<User> { /* ... */ }

// ---- Required<T> — form validation guard ----
type DraftConfig = { host?: string; port?: number; tls?: boolean };

function validateConfig(draft: DraftConfig): asserts draft is Required<DraftConfig> {
  if (!draft.host || !draft.port) throw new Error("host and port are required");
}

// ---- Record<K, V> — exhaustive lookup tables ----
type HttpStatus = 200 | 400 | 401 | 403 | 404 | 500;
const HTTP_MESSAGES: Record<HttpStatus, string> = {
  200: "OK", 400: "Bad Request", 401: "Unauthorized",
  403: "Forbidden", 404: "Not Found", 500: "Internal Server Error",
};
// Adding a new status to HttpStatus makes this a compile error if not added here

// ---- Awaited<T> — typing async mock return values in tests ----
type GetUserResult = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof userService.getById>>;

const mockGetById = vi.fn<() => Promise<GetUserResult>>().mockResolvedValue({
  id: "u1", name: "Alice", email: "alice@example.com", role: "admin",
});

// ---- Parameters<T>[N] — extracting specific arg types ----
type CreateOrderArgs = Parameters<typeof orderService.create>;
type OrderInput     = CreateOrderArgs[0]; // first argument type

function makeOrderFixture(overrides?: Partial<OrderInput>): OrderInput {
  return { customerId: "c1", items: [], ...overrides };
}

// ---- Extract / Exclude for union filtering ----
type ApiEvent = "user.created" | "user.deleted" | "order.placed" | "order.cancelled";
type UserEvents  = Extract<ApiEvent, `user.${string}`>;   // "user.created" | "user.deleted"
type OrderEvents = Extract<ApiEvent, `order.${string}`>;  // "order.placed" | "order.cancelled"
type NonUserEvents = Exclude<ApiEvent, `user.${string}`>; // "order.placed" | "order.cancelled"
```

---

### TypeScript — Variance Annotations for Generic Interfaces [community]

TypeScript 4.7 introduced explicit variance annotations (`in`, `out`, `in out`) that serve as both documentation and a compiler correctness assertion for generic type parameters.

```typescript
// Covariant: Producer<Dog> is assignable to Producer<Animal>
interface Producer<out T> {
  produce(): T;
}

// Contravariant: Consumer<Animal> is assignable to Consumer<Dog>
interface Consumer<in T> {
  consume(item: T): void;
}

// Invariant: exact match required in both positions
interface Repository<in out T> {
  find(id: string): T;
  save(item: T): void;
}

// ---- Practical: typed event emitter ----
interface TypedEmitter<out EventMap> {
  on<K extends keyof EventMap>(
    event: K,
    handler: (data: EventMap[K]) => void
  ): this;
  emit<K extends keyof EventMap>(event: K, data: EventMap[K]): boolean;
}
```

[community] **Pitfall:** Omitting variance annotations on interface-heavy codebases forces the compiler to re-derive variance structurally on every use. For interfaces that appear in many generic positions, adding `in`/`out`/`in out` removes this overhead and documents intent. Mismatched annotations (e.g., marking a parameter-only type as `out`) are caught at declaration time rather than at every usage site.

---

### Anti-Patterns: Cycle 20 Additions

| Anti-pattern | Why it's harmful | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Forgetting `readonly` constraint with `const T` | `<const T extends string[]>` falls back to `string[]` inference | Use `<const T extends readonly string[]>` |
| Using `--experimentalDecorators` in new code | Incompatible with ECMAScript standard decorators; no path to migrate | Use TS 5.0+ standard decorators (no flag needed) |
| `reflect-metadata` for decorator metadata | Requires `emitDecoratorMetadata` (incompatible with standard decorators) | Use TS 5.2 `Symbol.metadata` + `WeakMap` |
| Manual `try/finally` for resource cleanup | Verbose, easily forgotten on early return | Use `using` / `await using` (TS 5.2+) |
| `import defer { named }` | Syntax error — only namespace form allowed | `import defer * as ns from "..."` |
| `satisfies` before `as const` on nested records | satisfies sees widened type; literal narrowing lost | Put `as const` after satisfies: `{...} satisfies T as const` |
| Mutable constraint with `const T` (`extends string[]`) | Prevents tuple literal inference | Add `readonly`: `extends readonly string[]` |
| Intersection types for composed API responses | O(n²) merge cost; slower than interface extends | Use `interface Response extends BaseResponse, Meta {}` |
| `skipLibCheck: true` as permanent setting | Hides genuine type incompatibilities between library versions | Use only during migrations; resolve `.d.ts` conflicts explicitly |
| Large unions (12+ members) without shared base | Quadratic pairwise comparison in narrowing and intersections | Add discriminant `tagName` and shared base interface |
