### TypeScript 5.9 — `import defer` for Lazy Module Evaluation

`import defer` is a new TC39 proposal-based feature (Stage 3) enabling deferred evaluation of namespace imports. The module is parsed and linked at startup but its body does not execute until the namespace is first accessed.

```typescript
// ✅ Only namespace imports are supported — no named or default imports
import defer * as analytics from "./analytics.js";
import defer * as heavyFeature from "./heavy-feature.js";

// Module body does NOT execute here — no side effects yet
console.log("App starting...");

// First property access triggers module evaluation
if (userWantsAnalytics) {
  analytics.track("page_view"); // ← only now does analytics.js execute
}

// ❌ NOT ALLOWED: named imports with defer
// import defer { track } from "./analytics.js"; // SyntaxError

// ❌ NOT ALLOWED: default imports with defer
// import defer defaultExport from "./analytics.js"; // SyntaxError
```

**Key constraints:**
- Only works with `--module preserve`, `esnext`, or higher. It is NOT transpiled/downleveled.
- `--module commonjs`, `es2015`, or `amd` will reject `import defer`.
- Use for modules with expensive side-effect initialization (database connections, heavy computation, feature flags) that are conditionally needed.

[community] **Pitfall — `import defer` in test suites:** Deferred modules behave differently under Jest/Vitest module mocking. If the mock is set up after the first access, the real module has already executed. Call `vi.mock()` / `jest.mock()` before any code path that triggers the namespace access, or switch to `import.meta.resolve()` + dynamic `import()` for test-controlled lazy loading.

### TypeScript 5.9 — Prescriptive `tsc --init` Defaults

TypeScript 5.9 overhauled `tsc --init` to emit an opinionated baseline. Teams starting new projects should use it directly rather than hand-crafting minimal configs.

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "nodenext",
    "target": "esnext",
    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "isolatedModules": true,
    "moduleDetection": "force",
    "noUncheckedSideEffectImports": true,
    "types": [],
    "sourceMap": true,
    "declaration": true,
    "declarationMap": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true
  }
}
```

**Notable new defaults explained:**
- `moduleDetection: "force"` — treats every `.ts` file as a module (not a script), preventing accidental global variable leakage in files that have no `import`/`export`.
- `noUncheckedSideEffectImports: true` — catches misspelled bare side-effect imports (`import "./typo-in-path.js"`) that were previously silently ignored.
- `types: []` — no `@types/*` auto-inclusion; add only what you use (e.g. `"types": ["node"]`).

[community] **Pitfall — upgrading existing projects to 5.9 `tsc --init` defaults:** `moduleDetection: force` changes ambient declaration merging behaviour. Files that previously relied on being treated as scripts (no top-level `import`/`export`) may need a bare `export {}` added to become modules. Run `tsc --noEmit` before adopting this flag on an existing codebase.

### TypeScript 6.0 — Breaking Default Changes: Migration Checklist

TypeScript 6.0 flips several long-standing defaults that affect every existing project. Treat each as a migration task before upgrading.

```typescript
// 1. strict: true is now the default
//    If your codebase compiled under "strict: false", add explicit
//    "strict": false to your tsconfig or address new errors.

// 2. module: esnext and target: es2025 are new defaults
//    Projects using require() must add "module": "commonjs" explicitly.

// 3. types: [] is now the default — explicit inclusion required
//    Before:  @types/node / @types/jest loaded automatically
//    After:   "types": ["node", "jest"] must be listed

// 4. rootDir: "." is now the default (tsconfig directory)
//    Output was: ./dist/index.js
//    Output is now: ./dist/src/index.js  ← BREAKS deploys!
//    Fix: "rootDir": "./src"

// 5. module "namespace Foo {}" keyword enforced
//    The old "module Foo {}" syntax is an error in TS 6.0
//    Use "namespace Foo {}" instead

// 6. import ... asserts {} is replaced by import ... with {}
//    Old: import data from "./data.json" assert { type: "json" }
//    New: import data from "./data.json" with { type: "json" }
```

**Graceful migration with `ignoreDeprecations`:**
```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "ignoreDeprecations": "6.0"
  }
}
```
This suppresses deprecation warnings during a phased migration but will be removed in TypeScript 7.0 — it is a temporary bridge, not a solution.

### TypeScript 6.0 — ES2025 APIs Now Natively Typed

TypeScript 6.0 ships built-in type definitions for ES2025 APIs that previously required polyfills or custom declarations.

```typescript
// 1. Temporal API — replace Date for all new time/date code
const now: Temporal.Instant = Temporal.Now.instant();
const yesterday = now.subtract({ hours: 24 });
const tomorrow  = now.add({ hours: 24 });

// PlainDate for calendar date without time
const today: Temporal.PlainDate = Temporal.Now.plainDateISO();
const nextWeek = today.add({ days: 7 });

// ZonedDateTime for timezone-aware operations (replaces moment-timezone)
const meeting = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from(
  "2026-06-15T14:30:00[America/New_York]"
);
const inTokyo = meeting.withTimeZone("Asia/Tokyo");

// 2. RegExp.escape — safe regex from user input (no more manual escaping)
function highlightWord(word: string, text: string): string {
  const pattern = new RegExp(`\\b${RegExp.escape(word)}\\b`, "gi");
  return text.replace(pattern, `<mark>$&</mark>`);
}

// ❌ Old (risky — user input could break the regex):
const dangerousPattern = new RegExp(`\\b${word}\\b`); // word = "c++" breaks this

// 3. Map/WeakMap upsert — replaces verbose has/set pattern
const cache = new Map<string, ComputedValue>();

// ❌ Old verbose pattern:
if (!cache.has(key)) {
  cache.set(key, computeExpensiveValue(key));
}
const value = cache.get(key)!;

// ✅ New getOrInsert:
const value = cache.getOrInsert(key, defaultValue);

// ✅ New getOrInsertComputed for lazy expensive computation:
const value2 = cache.getOrInsertComputed(key, (k) => computeExpensiveValue(k));
```

[community] **Pitfall — Temporal not polyfilled by Node.js:** Even with TypeScript 6.0 providing the type definitions, `Temporal` requires a runtime polyfill in Node.js versions below 22. Install `@js-temporal/polyfill` and check `globalThis.Temporal` before using. TypeScript's types will pass without error even if the runtime value is `undefined` at startup — this is a type-safety gap.

### TypeScript 6.0 — `--stableTypeOrdering` and the Road to TS 7.0

TypeScript 6.0 adds a new flag `--stableTypeOrdering` that previews behaviour coming in TypeScript 7.0's native Go port. The Go port introduces parallel type checking, which requires deterministic type ID assignment (previously types were ordered by processing sequence).

```typescript
// In TS 5.x: return type display depends on union member order
export function classify(n: number): "low" | "high" {
  return n < 50 ? "low" : "high"; // shows as "low" | "high"
}

// In TS 7.0 (or TS 6 with --stableTypeOrdering):
// Internal type IDs are sorted by content, not sequence.
// Union display may flip: "high" | "low" — ALPHABETICAL
// This is purely cosmetic for simple string unions but can cause
// test snapshot failures for expect(fn()).toMatchTypeOf().
```

**When to use `--stableTypeOrdering`:**
- Before upgrading to TS 7.0: run `tsc --stableTypeOrdering --noEmit` to detect type snapshot breakage early.
- Cost: approximately 25% type-check slowdown. Do not enable permanently on large codebases.

[community] **Pitfall — CI type-snapshot tests break silently after TS 7 upgrade:** Teams using `tsd` or `expect-type` with snapshot assertions on union display order will see failures after upgrading to TS 7.0. Run `--stableTypeOrdering` in CI before the upgrade to surface these failures early. The actual type safety is unchanged; only the display order differs.

### Template Literal Types — Advanced Production Patterns

Template literal types (introduced TS 4.1) enable string-level type safety for event systems, API routes, CSS-in-JS, and i18n keys. The patterns below address common production use cases that are under-documented.

```typescript
// ---- Pattern 1: Type-safe event emitter with property change events ----
type PropEventSource<T> = {
  on<K extends string & keyof T>(
    eventName: `${K}Changed`,    // string & keyof ensures literal inference
    callback: (newValue: T[K]) => void
  ): void;
};

interface User { name: string; age: number; email: string }

declare function makeWatched<T>(obj: T): T & PropEventSource<T>;

const user = makeWatched<User>({ name: "Alice", age: 30, email: "a@example.com" });
user.on("nameChanged", (newName) => newName.toUpperCase()); // newName: string ✅
user.on("ageChanged",  (newAge)  => newAge + 1);            // newAge: number ✅

// ---- Pattern 2: REST API route type builder ----
type HttpMethod = "GET" | "POST" | "PUT" | "DELETE" | "PATCH";
type ApiRoute<M extends HttpMethod, P extends string> = `${M} ${P}`;

type UserRoutes =
  | ApiRoute<"GET",    "/users">
  | ApiRoute<"POST",   "/users">
  | ApiRoute<"GET",    "/users/:id">
  | ApiRoute<"DELETE", "/users/:id">;

function handleRoute(route: UserRoutes): void { /* ... */ }

// ---- Pattern 3: CSS-in-JS theme keys with Lowercase<> intrinsic ----
type ColorToken  = "Primary" | "Secondary" | "Accent";
type ThemeObject = { [K in `color-${Lowercase<ColorToken>}`]: string };
//                  { "color-primary": string; "color-secondary": string; "color-accent": string }

const theme: ThemeObject = {
  "color-primary":   "#0066ff",
  "color-secondary": "#ff6600",
  "color-accent":    "#ffcc00",
};

// ---- Pattern 4: i18n namespace key typing ----
type Namespace  = "common" | "auth" | "dashboard";
type I18nKey<N extends Namespace, K extends string> = `${N}.${K}`;

function t<N extends Namespace>(ns: N): (key: `${N}.${string}`) => string {
  return (key) => key; // placeholder implementation
}
const authT = t("auth");
authT("auth.login");   // ✅
authT("auth.logout");  // ✅
// authT("common.ok"); // ❌ compile error — must start with "auth."
```

[community] **Pitfall — union explosion in template literal types:** When you interpolate multiple union positions (e.g. `` `${A | B}_${C | D | E}` ``), TypeScript generates every combination. With 4×5×3 members the type has 60 string literals, which the compiler must store and compare individually. The official recommendation is: "use ahead-of-time generation for large string unions" — compute the valid set programmatically and export a `const` array rather than relying on template literal cross-multiplication.

### TypeScript — `tsc --init` Best-Practice Config for Node.js 2026

The following tsconfig is the recommended starting point for a Node.js application in 2026, combining the TS 5.9 prescriptive defaults with explicit Node.js-specific settings.

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    // === Module system ===
    "module":           "node20",
    "moduleResolution": "node20",
    "target":           "es2023",

    // === Type safety ===
    "strict":                       true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess":     true,
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes":   true,
    "noImplicitReturns":            true,
    "noFallthroughCasesInSwitch":   true,
    "noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature": true,

    // === Module hygiene ===
    "verbatimModuleSyntax":         true,
    "moduleDetection":              "force",
    "noUncheckedSideEffectImports": true,
    "isolatedModules":              true,
    "types":                        ["node"],

    // === Output ===
    "rootDir":        "./src",
    "outDir":         "./dist",
    "sourceMap":      true,
    "declaration":    true,
    "declarationMap": true,

    // === DX ===
    "skipLibCheck":   true,
    "esModuleInterop": true
  },
  "include": ["src"],
  "exclude": ["**/node_modules", "**/.*/", "dist"]
}
```

**Why `node20` over `nodenext`:** `node20` pins to a stable, non-floating module target (implies `es2023`). `nodenext` floats to the latest Node.js version, which can introduce subtle breaking changes on Node.js version upgrades.

### TypeScript — Truthiness vs Equality Narrowing Pitfalls [community]

A commonly misunderstood narrowing distinction: truthiness checks silently swallow valid falsy values (`0`, `""`, `false`), while equality checks are explicit about which values are excluded.

```typescript
// ❌ Truthiness check hides the zero case
function processCount(count: number | null): string {
  if (count) {
    return `Found ${count} items`; // 0 items never reaches here!
  }
  return "No items";
}
processCount(0); // "No items" — WRONG: 0 is a valid count

// ✅ Equality check is explicit
function processCount(count: number | null): string {
  if (count !== null) {
    return `Found ${count} items`; // 0 correctly returns "Found 0 items"
  }
  return "No items";
}

// ❌ Truthiness on optional string swallows empty string
function greet(name?: string): string {
  if (name) return `Hello, ${name}`; // empty string "" falls to default
  return "Hello, stranger";
}
greet(""); // "Hello, stranger" — potentially wrong

// ✅ Explicit undefined check
function greet(name?: string): string {
  if (name !== undefined) return `Hello, ${name}`;
  return "Hello, stranger";
}
greet(""); // "Hello, " — correct: caller passed empty string intentionally
```

[community] **Pitfall — `!= null` vs `!== null`:** The loose inequality `!= null` eliminates both `null` and `undefined` in one check (a well-known JS quirk that TypeScript correctly models). This is intentional for optional-yet-nullable fields. Use it when you want to treat `null` and `undefined` identically; use `!== null` when they have different semantics (e.g., field explicitly set to null vs field omitted).

---

### TypeScript — `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature` Pattern [community]

Enabling `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature: true` enforces a disciplined split between known named properties and dynamic string-keyed index properties.

```typescript
interface AppConfig {
  debug:   boolean;     // known property
  version: string;      // known property
  [key: string]: unknown; // dynamic properties
}

const config: AppConfig = loadConfig();

// ❌ Rejected with noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature enabled:
config.debug;           // ✅ dot notation OK for known properties
config.someUnknown;     // ❌ Error: use bracket notation for index sig properties

// ✅ Must use bracket notation for dynamic access:
config["someUnknown"];  // OK — acknowledges this is a dynamic lookup
config["debug"];        // Also OK — dot vs bracket both work for known props

// Why this matters: dot notation implies certainty about the property.
// Requiring brackets for index-signature properties makes the uncertainty
// visible at the call site and forces the consumer to handle the unknown type.
```

[community] **Pitfall — forgetting this option when designing plugin-style configs:** A common pattern is `{ [plugin: string]: PluginOptions }` where some top-level keys are also known named properties. Without `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature`, teams access known props via dot notation and dynamic props via dot notation identically — hiding which accesses are safe. Enabling this flag surfaces every dynamic access.

### Anti-Patterns: Cycle 22 Additions

| Anti-pattern | Why it's harmful | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| `import defer { named }` syntax | Only namespace form supported; syntax error | Use `import defer * as ns from "..."` |
| `import defer` with `--module commonjs` | Not transpiled; requires native runtime support | Switch to `--module esnext` / `preserve`, or use dynamic `import()` |
| Missing `"types": []` in TS 6.0 | TS 6.0 default is `[]`; forgetting explicit list breaks `@types/node` | Add `"types": ["node"]` (or whichever packages you need) |
| Missing `"rootDir": "./src"` in TS 6.0 | Default is tsconfig dir — output goes to `./dist/src/` instead of `./dist/` | Always set `"rootDir": "./src"` explicitly |
| `module Foo {}` namespace syntax | Error in TS 6.0; conflicts with ECMAScript `module` proposal | Use `namespace Foo {}` instead |
| `import assert { type: "json" }` | Deprecated; removed in TS 6.0 | Use `import ... with { type: "json" }` |
| `--baseUrl` path resolution | Deprecated in TS 6.0; breaks module resolution in bundler mode | Use explicit `paths` entries with full relative prefixes |
| Truthiness check on `number \| null` | 0 is falsy; valid zero counts fall to the null branch | Use `!== null` for explicit narrowing |
| `config.dynamicProp` on index-sig interfaces | Hides uncertainty; should acknowledge dynamic access | Enable `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature`; use bracket notation |
| Large template literal cross-multiplications (4+ union positions) | Exponential type union expansion; compiler slowdown | Pre-generate valid strings programmatically; export as `const` array |
| Polyfill-free Temporal API usage | TS 6.0 types pass but Node.js &lt; 22 lacks runtime support | Install `@js-temporal/polyfill`; guard with `globalThis.Temporal` check |

### TypeScript 5.8 — `require()` of ECMAScript Modules in `--module nodenext`

Node.js 22 permits CommonJS modules to synchronously `require()` ESM files that do not contain top-level `await`. TypeScript 5.8 models this behavior under `--module nodenext`, allowing CJS consumers to import ESM libraries without a dual-publish setup.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json
// { "compilerOptions": { "module": "nodenext" } }

// ✅ CJS file requiring an ESM module (Node.js 22+)
// require-side.cjs
const esmModule = require("./esm-library.mjs");
esmModule.doSomething(); // TypeScript knows the full export shape

// ❌ Not allowed: ESM file with top-level await cannot be require()'d
// esm-with-tla.mjs
await setupDatabase();  // top-level await
export const db = createDb();

// require-side.cjs
const mod = require("./esm-with-tla.mjs"); // ❌ Runtime error in Node.js 22
```

**`--module node18` vs `--module nodenext`:**

| Feature | `node18` | `nodenext` |
|---------|----------|------------|
| `require()` of ESM | Not allowed | Allowed (Node 22+) |
| Import assertions (`assert {}`) | Allowed | Not allowed (deprecated) |
| `target` implied | `es2022` | `esnext` |

[community] **Pitfall — mixing `node18` and `nodenext` in monorepos:** When individual packages have different `--module` settings, a CJS wrapper package with `nodenext` can import ESM packages, but a package with `node18` cannot. Be explicit about which packages are CJS vs ESM and align `--module` per package. Using a shared `tsconfig.base.json` with `"module": "nodenext"` and overriding only where needed prevents configuration drift.

---

### TypeScript 5.8 — Granular Branch Checking in `return` Expressions

Before TypeScript 5.8, ternary and conditional expressions inside `return` statements were checked as a union. If any branch was typed `any`, the union collapsed to `any`, silently hiding type errors in the other branches. TypeScript 5.8 checks each branch independently against the declared return type.

```typescript
declare const untypedCache: Map<string, any>; // cache returns any

// ❌ BEFORE TypeScript 5.8: union of (any | string) = any — no error
function getUrlObject(urlString: string): URL {
  return untypedCache.has(urlString)
    ? untypedCache.get(urlString)  // any
    : urlString;                   // string — silently passed through
}

// ✅ AFTER TypeScript 5.8: each branch checked against URL
function getUrlObject(urlString: string): URL {
  return untypedCache.has(urlString)
    ? untypedCache.get(urlString)  // any — allowed (any is assignable to URL)
    : urlString;                   // ❌ Error: 'string' is not assignable to 'URL'
}

// ✅ Fix: construct the correct return type explicitly
function getUrlObjectSafe(urlString: string): URL {
  if (untypedCache.has(urlString)) {
    return untypedCache.get(urlString) as URL;  // cast at boundary
  }
  return new URL(urlString);  // ✅ correct type
}
```

[community] **Impact on existing codebases:** Teams relying on `any`-typed caches (Redis, LRU) as pass-through return values will see new errors after upgrading to 5.8. The fix is always correct: cast `any` results at the boundary with `as T` or use a typed wrapper. Do not suppress with `// @ts-ignore` — the error is a real bug.

---

### TypeScript 5.8 — Preserved Computed Property Names in Declaration Files

TypeScript 5.8 relaxes a long-standing restriction: exported classes with computed property names using exported `let` variables can now appear in declaration files. Previously TypeScript would widen the property to an index signature `[x: string]: T`, losing the specific property identity.

```typescript
// ✅ Now valid under TypeScript 5.8
export let propName = "theAnswer";

export class MyClass {
  [propName] = 42;  // Declaration emits [propName]: number (not [x: string]: number)
}

// Previously the .d.ts would emit:
//   class MyClass { [x: string]: number; }
// Now it emits:
//   declare let propName: string;
//   declare class MyClass { [propName]: number; }

// ❌ Still an error under --isolatedDeclarations
// (requires a deterministic single-file declaration emit)
export let dynamicKey = "result";
export class Computed {
  [dynamicKey] = 99;  // error: computed properties require type annotation
                       // under --isolatedDeclarations
}

// ✅ Use unique symbol for true static computed properties
const STATIC_KEY = Symbol("myKey");
export class WithSymbol {
  [STATIC_KEY] = "value";
}
```

[community] **Pitfall — `--isolatedDeclarations` users not affected by the relaxation:** The 5.8 improvement applies to standard `tsc`-emitted declarations. Projects using Babel, SWC, or esbuild with `--isolatedDeclarations` (required for single-file transform correctness) must still avoid computed property names with mutable variables. Prefer `const` string/symbol keys or explicit index signatures in those setups.

### TypeScript 5.9 — `ArrayBuffer` Type Hierarchy Breaking Change

TypeScript 5.9 updated `lib.d.ts` so that `TypedArray` types (including Node.js `Buffer`) are no longer sub-types of `ArrayBuffer`. This corrects a historical inaccuracy: `Buffer.buffer` returns an `ArrayBuffer`, but a `Buffer` instance is not itself an `ArrayBuffer`.

```typescript
// ❌ Previously allowed, now a compile error in TS 5.9
function processBuffer(buf: ArrayBuffer): void {
  const view = new Uint8Array(buf);
  // ...
}

declare const nodeBuffer: Buffer;
processBuffer(nodeBuffer);
// Error: Argument of type 'Buffer' is not assignable to parameter of type 'ArrayBuffer'

// ✅ Fix 1: pass the .buffer property explicitly
processBuffer(nodeBuffer.buffer);

// ✅ Fix 2: accept BufferSource (ArrayBuffer | ArrayBufferView)
function processData(src: BufferSource): void {
  const buf = src instanceof ArrayBuffer ? src : src.buffer;
  const view = new Uint8Array(buf);
}
processData(nodeBuffer);  // ✅ Buffer extends Uint8Array, which extends ArrayBufferView

// ✅ Fix 3: use explicit typed array parameter
function processTyped(data: Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>): void { /* ... */ }
processTyped(nodeBuffer);  // ✅ Node.js Buffer IS a Uint8Array
```

**Migration:** Run `npm update @types/node --save-dev` first — the updated type definitions already account for this correction and will eliminate most errors automatically.

[community] **Pitfall — streaming APIs accepting `ArrayBufferLike`:** Many Web Crypto, WebSocket, and stream APIs accept `ArrayBufferLike` (union of `ArrayBuffer | SharedArrayBuffer`). If your code passes `Buffer` to these APIs it now fails. The correct fix is `nodeBuffer.buffer` (extracts the underlying `ArrayBuffer`) — not casting with `as ArrayBuffer`, which can silently fail at runtime if the buffer is shared.

### TypeScript 6.0 — Less Context-Sensitive `this`-less Functions

Before TypeScript 6.0, the order of properties in an object literal affected how TypeScript inferred types for callback properties. Functions that did not reference `this` were considered "context-sensitive," meaning they could not be typed until all properties were processed. TypeScript 6.0 stops treating `this`-less functions as context-sensitive, enabling cross-property inference regardless of declaration order.

```typescript
declare function callIt<T>(obj: {
  produce: (x: number) => T;
  consume: (y: T) => void;
}): void;

// ✅ TypeScript 6.0: works regardless of property order
callIt({
  consume(y) { return y.toFixed(); },  // 'y' inferred as number from 'produce'
  produce(x: number) { return x * 2; },
});

// Previously only worked with 'produce' declared first:
callIt({
  produce(x: number) { return x * 2; },
  consume(y) { return y.toFixed(); }, // 'y' was unknown before 6.0 unless produce came first
});

// Pattern this enables: configuration objects with interdependent callbacks
function defineRoute<T>(config: {
  parse:  (raw: string) => T;
  handle: (parsed: T) => Response;
}): void { /* ... */ }

// ✅ Can declare 'handle' first without type annotations
defineRoute({
  handle(parsed) { return new Response(parsed.toString()); },
  parse(raw) { return JSON.parse(raw) as { id: number }; },
});
```

[community] **Practical impact:** Framework DSLs (like route/schema definitions, middleware pipelines) that rely on mutually-referencing callbacks benefit most. Previously, users had to manually annotate callback parameters or reorder properties — common sources of "why is `any` here?" confusion in library types.

---

### TypeScript 6.0 — Node.js `#/` Subpath Imports

Node.js's `package.json` `"imports"` field allows mapping internal aliases with the `#` prefix. TypeScript 6.0 now supports a `#/` prefix variant that directly maps a directory without requiring an extra path segment.

```json
// package.json — before: required extra segment after #
{
  "imports": {
    "#utils/*": "./dist/utils/*.js"
  }
}
```

```json
// package.json — TypeScript 6.0: #/ maps the root of dist directly
{
  "imports": {
    "#/*": "./dist/*.js"
  }
}
```

```typescript
// src/features/auth.ts
import * as tokenUtils from "#/utils/token.js"; // resolves to ./dist/utils/token.js

// Before TS 6.0, you'd need:
import * as tokenUtils from "#utils/token.js";
// (with the extra 'utils' segment baked into the alias key)

// ✅ Recommended tsconfig setting for subpath imports to resolve correctly:
// "moduleResolution": "nodenext" or "bundler"
```

[community] **Pitfall — `#/` only works in package contexts:** The `"imports"` field is per-package. Scripts run outside a package boundary (e.g., ts-node at the repo root, jest with `--rootDir` mismatch) do not resolve `#/` aliases. Use `moduleNameMapper` in Jest config or `tsconfig.json` `paths` as a parallel fallback during the transition.

---

### `using` Declarations — Disposal Order and Dependent Resource Patterns

TypeScript 5.2+ `using` declarations dispose in last-in, first-out (LIFO) order. When resources have dependencies — for example, a query object depends on a database connection — the declaration order must be inverted so the dependent resource is declared later and disposed first.

```typescript
// ❌ Anti-pattern: dependency declared after its dependency
async function runQuery() {
  await using db = await connect();      // declared first
  await using query = db.prepareQuery(); // depends on db

  // LIFO order: db disposed BEFORE query → query's close() may fail
}

// ✅ Correct: dependent resource declared last, disposed first
async function runQuery() {
  await using query = (await connect()).prepareQuery(); // chain inline
  // query disposed first, then the anonymous connection is torn down

  // — OR — declare in dependency order with explicit reversal:
  await using db    = await connect();    // independent
  await using query = db.prepareQuery();  // depends on db
  // LIFO: query disposed first, then db — correct ✅
}

// ✅ DisposableStack for dynamic resource collections
async function processFiles(paths: string[]) {
  await using stack = new AsyncDisposableStack();
  const handles = paths.map(p => stack.use(openFile(p)));
  // All handles disposed in reverse order on scope exit
  for (const handle of handles) {
    await processHandle(handle);
  }
}
```

[community] **Pitfall — `SuppressedError` swallows original exceptions:** If disposal throws after the main body threw, the original error becomes `e.suppressed` on the `SuppressedError`. Standard `catch (e)` blocks log the disposal error, not the original bug. Always inspect `e instanceof SuppressedError ? e.suppressed : e` in error handlers when using `using` with resources that can throw during cleanup (e.g., flushing buffers, committing transactions).

---

### Decorator Metadata — `WeakMap` Pattern for Encapsulated Field Registry

TypeScript 5.2's decorator metadata (`Symbol.metadata`) places metadata on the class object accessible to any consumer. Use a module-private `WeakMap` keyed on the metadata object to keep metadata encapsulated within the decorator's module.

```typescript
// serializer.ts — internal registry via WeakMap
const serializable = new WeakMap<object, string[]>();

type FieldContext =
  | ClassAccessorDecoratorContext
  | ClassGetterDecoratorContext
  | ClassFieldDecoratorContext;

export function serialize(
  _target: unknown,
  context: FieldContext
): void {
  if (context.static || context.private) {
    throw new Error("@serialize: only public instance members supported");
  }
  if (typeof context.name !== "string") {
    throw new Error("@serialize: symbol-named fields not supported");
  }
  let fields = serializable.get(context.metadata);
  if (!fields) {
    fields = [];
    serializable.set(context.metadata, fields);
  }
  fields.push(context.name);
}

export function toJSON(instance: object): string {
  const meta = (instance.constructor as any)[Symbol.metadata];
  const fields = meta ? serializable.get(meta) : undefined;
  if (!fields?.length) throw new Error("No @serialize fields found");

  const entries = fields.map(k => {
    return `${JSON.stringify(k)}: ${JSON.stringify((instance as any)[k])}`;
  });
  return `{ ${entries.join(", ")} }`;
}

// user.ts
import { serialize, toJSON } from "./serializer";

class User {
  firstName: string;
  lastName: string;

  @serialize
  age: number;

  @serialize
  get fullName(): string { return `${this.firstName} ${this.lastName}`; }

  toJSON() { return toJSON(this); }

  constructor(first: string, last: string, age: number) {
    this.firstName = first;
    this.lastName  = last;
    this.age       = age;
  }
}
```

**Why `WeakMap` over `Symbol.metadata` property directly:** The `WeakMap` key is the metadata object shared across the class hierarchy. External code cannot enumerate or access the `WeakMap` keys; the registry remains private to the decorator module. Direct `context.metadata[Symbol("myKey")]` assignment is visible (and enumerable) to any consumer that holds the class constructor.

[community] **Pitfall — inheritance and `Symbol.metadata`:** Subclasses inherit the parent's `Symbol.metadata` object. Decorators applied to both parent and child will register into the _same_ metadata object unless you explicitly create a new registry entry per class. With the `WeakMap` pattern, use `Object.create(parentMeta)` in a class decorator to fork the metadata chain.

---

### Function Overloads — Specificity Ordering Rule

TypeScript matches function overloads in top-down declaration order, resolving to the first matching signature. Placing general signatures before specific ones silently defeats narrowing: callers passing specific types get the general return type.

```typescript
// ❌ Anti-pattern: general before specific
declare function process(input: unknown): unknown;
declare function process(input: HTMLDivElement): string;
declare function process(input: HTMLElement): number;

const div = document.querySelector("div") as HTMLDivElement;
const result = process(div); // result: unknown — WRONG, should be string

// ✅ Correct: specific before general
declare function process(input: HTMLDivElement): string;
declare function process(input: HTMLElement): number;
declare function process(input: unknown): unknown;

const result2 = process(div); // result2: string — correct ✅

// ✅ Prefer union types over overloads for single-position differences
interface Parser {
  // ❌ Two overloads differing only in one parameter type
  parse(input: string): ParsedValue;
  parse(input: Buffer): ParsedValue;

  // ✅ Single signature with union
  parseUnified(input: string | Buffer): ParsedValue;
}

// ✅ Use optional parameters instead of arity-based overloads
// ❌ Over-specified overloads for optional params
declare function log(msg: string): void;
declare function log(msg: string, level: LogLevel): void;
declare function log(msg: string, level: LogLevel, ctx: object): void;

// ✅ Single signature
declare function log(msg: string, level?: LogLevel, ctx?: object): void;
```

[community] **Pitfall — callback overloads with different arities:** The TypeScript Do's &amp; Don'ts documentation specifically calls out callback parameter overloads. If a callback can accept `(data: T)` or `(data: T, elapsedTime: number)`, always declare the _maximum arity_ version only. Callers can always ignore trailing parameters; making the second parameter optional (rather than creating two overloads) produces the same flexibility with fewer signatures to maintain.

---

### `PickByValue<T, V>` — Custom Utility Type for Value-Filtered Picks

The built-in utility types operate on keys. `PickByValue` is a well-known community pattern that selects only properties whose value type extends a given type. It is useful for extracting all string fields, all function members, or all optional fields from a large interface.

```typescript
// Pattern: select keys whose values extend V, then Pick those keys
type PickByValue<T, V> = Pick<
  T,
  { [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends V ? K : never }[keyof T]
>;

// Inverse: omit keys whose values extend V
type OmitByValue<T, V> = Pick<
  T,
  { [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends V ? never : K }[keyof T]
>;

// Usage examples
interface ApiPayload {
  id:          number;
  name:        string;
  description: string;
  createdAt:   Date;
  updatedAt:   Date;
  isActive:    boolean;
  score:       number;
}

// Select only string fields
type StringFields = PickByValue<ApiPayload, string>;
// → { name: string; description: string }

// Select only Date fields
type DateFields = PickByValue<ApiPayload, Date>;
// → { createdAt: Date; updatedAt: Date }

// Omit all number fields (keep non-numbers)
type NoNumbers = OmitByValue<ApiPayload, number>;
// → { name: string; description: string; createdAt: Date; updatedAt: Date; isActive: boolean }

// Practical: type-safe form serialization — only string fields go to FormData
function toFormData(payload: PickByValue<ApiPayload, string>): FormData {
  const fd = new FormData();
  for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(payload)) {
    fd.append(k, v);
  }
  return fd;
}

toFormData({ name: "Alice", description: "Engineer" }); // ✅
// toFormData({ id: 1 });  // ❌ number field rejected
```

[community] **Pitfall — `PickByValue` with optional properties:** Optional fields `field?: string` have type `string | undefined` in `keyof`. If you use `extends string`, optional fields are excluded (because `string | undefined` does not extend `string`). Use `extends string | undefined` or `NonNullable<T[K]> extends V` to include optional string fields.

---

### `DeepReadonly<T>` — Recursive Immutability for Nested Configuration Objects

The built-in `Readonly<T>` is shallow: it makes the top-level properties read-only but leaves nested object properties mutable. `DeepReadonly<T>` is a community-standard recursive mapped type for truly immutable configuration and state objects.

```typescript
type DeepReadonly<T> =
  T extends (infer U)[]
    ? ReadonlyArray<DeepReadonly<U>>
    : T extends object
      ? { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }
      : T;

interface AppConfig {
  server: {
    host: string;
    port: number;
    tls: {
      cert: string;
      key:  string;
    };
  };
  features: string[];
}

const config: DeepReadonly<AppConfig> = {
  server: { host: "localhost", port: 8443, tls: { cert: "...", key: "..." } },
  features: ["auth", "logging"],
};

config.server.port = 80;          // ❌ Error: cannot assign to read-only property
config.server.tls.cert = "new";   // ❌ Error: deep readonly catches nested mutation
config.features.push("debug");    // ❌ Error: ReadonlyArray has no push method
config.features[0] = "analytics"; // ❌ Error: index signature is readonly

// ✅ Use DeepReadonly for injected configs in services
class AuthService {
  constructor(private readonly config: DeepReadonly<AppConfig>) {}
  getPort() { return this.config.server.port; } // read-only access is fine
}
```

[community] **Pitfall — `DeepReadonly` breaks Map/Set/Date method calls:** `DeepReadonly<Map<K, V>>` removes `set()`, `delete()`, `clear()` — but also breaks `get()` and `has()` on some TypeScript versions because the mapped type wraps the built-in methods. Use `ReadonlyMap<K, V>` and `ReadonlySet<T>` (both built-in since TS 3.4) for collections, and apply `DeepReadonly` only to plain object/array shapes.

---

### `NoInfer<T>` — Preventing Unwanted Inference at Call Sites

`NoInfer<T>` (TypeScript 5.4+) blocks the compiler from using a specific argument as an inference source for a generic type parameter. Without it, passing a "fallback" or "default" argument can cause TypeScript to widen `T` to include the fallback value type, defeating the purpose of the constraint.

```typescript
// Without NoInfer: defaultColor widens T to include "blue"
function createLight<C extends string>(
  colors: C[],
  defaultColor?: C,  // C can be inferred from this too
): void {}

createLight(["red", "yellow", "green"], "blue");
// T inferred as "red" | "yellow" | "green" | "blue" — "blue" leaked in!

// ✅ With NoInfer: defaultColor cannot contribute to T inference
function createLight<C extends string>(
  colors: C[],
  defaultColor?: NoInfer<C>,  // excluded from inference sources
): void {}

createLight(["red", "yellow", "green"], "blue");
// ❌ Error: "blue" is not assignable to "red" | "yellow" | "green"

createLight(["red", "yellow", "green"], "red"); // ✅

// Pattern: type-safe event system default handler
function createEventBus<K extends string>(
  events: K[],
  fallbackHandler?: NoInfer<(event: K) => void>,
): EventBus<K> { /* ... */ }

// 'fallbackHandler' cannot cause K to be widened to string
```

[community] **Pitfall — `NoInfer` is a hint, not a hard barrier on explicit type arguments:** `NoInfer<T>` only blocks _inference_ from that position. Callers can still pass a wide type if they explicitly annotate: `createLight<string>(["red"], "blue")` compiles fine because `T` was manually set to `string`. `NoInfer` is a UX guard for callers using type inference, not a runtime constraint.

---

### TypeScript 6.0 — `Map.getOrInsert` / `Map.getOrInsertComputed` Type-Safe Patterns

TypeScript 6.0 adds types for the Stage 4 ECMAScript Map upsert methods. These replace the common `has(k) ? get(k)! : (set(k, v), v)` pattern with a single expression, eliminating the non-null assertion.

```typescript
// ❌ Old pattern: has/get/set with non-null assertion
const cache = new Map<string, number[]>();

function addToGroup(key: string, value: number): void {
  if (!cache.has(key)) {
    cache.set(key, []);
  }
  cache.get(key)!.push(value); // non-null assertion required
}

// ✅ TypeScript 6.0: getOrInsert()
function addToGroup(key: string, value: number): void {
  cache.getOrInsert(key, []).push(value);
  // getOrInsert returns T (not T | undefined) — no assertion needed
}

// ✅ getOrInsertComputed() for expensive default values
const expensiveCache = new Map<string, LargeObject>();

function getOrCreate(key: string): LargeObject {
  return expensiveCache.getOrInsertComputed(key, () => {
    return buildExpensiveObject(key); // only called on cache miss
  });
}

// ✅ Common pattern: frequency counter
const freq = new Map<string, number>();
for (const word of words) {
  freq.set(word, (freq.getOrInsert(word, 0)) + 1);
}
```

**`WeakMap` equivalent:** `WeakMap` also receives `getOrInsert` and `getOrInsertComputed` in the same TC39 proposal. The same patterns apply for object-keyed caches.

[community] **Pitfall — `getOrInsert` mutates the map on every miss:** The method inserts the default value if the key is absent, even if the caller only needs to read. Callers must be aware that calling `getOrInsert` on a read-only `ReadonlyMap` interface causes a compile error — `ReadonlyMap` does not expose mutation methods. Type your maps as `ReadonlyMap<K,V>` for read-only consumers and `Map<K,V>` only where mutation is intended.

---

### TypeScript 6.0 — `RegExp.escape` for Type-Safe String Escaping

`RegExp.escape` is a Stage 4 TC39 proposal typed in TypeScript 6.0 as `(input: string) => string`. It eliminates the hand-rolled regex escape utilities that every TypeScript codebase previously wrote or imported.

```typescript
// ❌ Old: hand-rolled escape (brittle — easy to miss edge cases)
function escapeRegex(s: string): string {
  return s.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, "\\$&");
}

// ✅ TypeScript 6.0: built-in type for the native method
function matchWholeWord(word: string, text: string): RegExpMatchArray | null {
  const escaped = RegExp.escape(word); // return type: string
  const pattern = new RegExp(`\\b${escaped}\\b`, "g");
  return text.match(pattern);
}

matchWholeWord("hello.world", "Say hello.world today"); // ✅ dots escaped

// ✅ Type-safe utility: build dynamic patterns from user input
function highlightTerms(text: string, terms: string[]): string {
  const pattern = new RegExp(
    terms.map(RegExp.escape).join("|"),
    "gi"
  );
  return text.replace(pattern, m => `<mark>${m}</mark>`);
}
```

**Configuration:** Requires `"lib": ["es2025"]` or `"target": "es2025"` in `tsconfig.json`. TypeScript 6.0 sets `target` default to `es2025`.

[community] **Pitfall — `RegExp.escape` is not polyfilled by Node.js &lt; 24:** The method is available natively in Node.js 24+. For earlier Node.js versions, import a polyfill or the `regexp.escape` npm package. TypeScript's type definitions will not warn you if the runtime lacks the method — use a feature detection guard `if (typeof RegExp.escape === "function")` in environments that mix Node.js versions.

---

### Anti-Patterns: Cycle 23 Additions

| Anti-pattern | Why it's harmful | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| `require()` of ESM with top-level `await` in `nodenext` | Node.js 22 blocks this at runtime even though TypeScript may not catch it at compile time | Avoid top-level `await` in modules consumed via `require()`; use dynamic `import()` instead |
| Passing `Buffer` directly where `ArrayBuffer` expected | TS 5.9 removed the Buffer→ArrayBuffer subtype; now a compile error | Pass `.buffer` property or accept `BufferSource` in the function signature |
| Overloads ordered general-before-specific | First matching overload wins; general signature swallows specific callers | Declare specific signatures first, general fallback last |
| Two overloads differing only in a single parameter type | Union types express the same contract with fewer signatures | Replace with single signature using union parameter type |
| Arity-based overloads for optional params | Overloads create maintenance surface with no benefit | Use optional parameters in a single signature |
| `PickByValue` with `extends string` when optional fields needed | `string \| undefined` does not extend `string`; optional fields excluded | Use `extends string \| undefined` or `NonNullable<T[K]> extends V` |
| Shallow `Readonly<T>` on deeply nested config | Nested mutation still compiles silently | Use `DeepReadonly<T>` for config and state objects; `ReadonlyMap`/`ReadonlySet` for collections |
| `NoInfer<T>` expected to block explicit type argument widening | `NoInfer` only suppresses inference, not explicit type args | Combine `NoInfer` with runtime validation if hard runtime constraint needed |
| `map.get(key)!` after `map.has(key)` check | Non-null assertion is unsafe if the map is mutated between `has` and `get` | Use `map.getOrInsert(key, default)` (TS 6.0) or store `get` result in a variable and check it |
| `RegExp.escape` without Node.js version guard | Not available in Node.js &lt; 24; silent runtime error | Feature-detect or polyfill; pin `engines.node` to `>=24` in `package.json` if using it natively |

### TypeScript 5.7 — `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` for In-Place Execution

TypeScript 5.7 added `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions`, which rewrites relative `.ts`/`.mts`/`.cts` import paths to their JavaScript equivalents at compile time. This enables a "write `.ts` imports, ship `.js` imports" workflow without bundlers.

```typescript
// Source — developers write .ts extension explicitly
import { parseConfig } from "./config.ts";
import { buildIndex } from "../search/index.mts";

// Compiled output — TypeScript rewrites to .js/.mjs
// import { parseConfig } from "./config.js";
// import { buildIndex } from "../search/index.mjs";
```

**What is NOT rewritten:**

```typescript
// ❌ None of these are rewritten:
import { foo } from "./file";               // no extension — unchanged
import { bar } from "some-package/file.ts"; // non-relative npm path
import { baz } from "@scope/pkg/file.ts";   // scoped package path
import { qux } from "#/file.ts";            // package import map alias
import { quux } from "./already.js";        // already a JS extension
```

**Recommended tsconfig for Node.js ESM library projects:**

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "nodenext",
    "target": "esnext",
    "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "declaration": true,
    "declarationMap": true,
    "outDir": "./dist"
  }
}
```

[community] **Pitfall — `baseUrl`/`paths` aliases are not rewritten:** The flag only rewrites "naive" relative paths (those resolved solely by replacing the extension). Any path that goes through `baseUrl`, `paths`, or `package.json` `exports`/`imports` resolution is not touched. Alias imports like `@utils/token` must remain as-is and be resolved by the consuming bundler or a path-mapping tool.

---

### TypeScript 5.7 — Checks for Never-Initialized Variables in Closures

Before TypeScript 5.7, using an uninitialized `let` variable inside a nested function was not always caught. The compiler assumed the variable _might_ be initialized by the time the inner function is called. TypeScript 5.7 tightens this: if there is no assignment path at all, the error is now reported.

```typescript
// ❌ TypeScript 5.7 catches this — result is never assigned
function computeTotal(): number {
  let result: number;
  // Forgot to assign result before the closure
  const format = () => `Total: ${result}`;
  // Error: Variable 'result' is used before being assigned.
  return 0;
}

// ✅ Fix 1: initialize with a default value
function computeTotal(): number {
  let result: number = 0;
  const format = () => `Total: ${result}`;
  return result;
}

// ✅ Fix 2: make the type explicitly include undefined
function computeResultStr(): string {
  let result: number | undefined;
  const format = () => (result !== undefined ? `Total: ${result}` : "pending");
  return format();
}

// ❌ Another pattern now caught: variable only assigned in some branches
function getLabel(active: boolean): string {
  let label: string;
  if (active) {
    label = "Active";
  }
  // Error: Variable 'label' is used before being assigned (no else branch)
  return label.toLowerCase();
}

// ✅ Fix: cover all paths
function getLabel(active: boolean): string {
  const label = active ? "Active" : "Inactive";
  return label.toLowerCase();
}
```

[community] **Pitfall — suppressing the error with `!` instead of fixing it:** `label!.toLowerCase()` compiles but defers the bug to runtime. The TypeScript 5.7 check is detecting a genuine logic gap; the correct fix is always to ensure all branches assign the variable or to use `const` with a ternary/early return.

---

### TypeScript 5.7 — Validated JSON Imports (`import ... with { type: "json" }`)

Under `--module nodenext`, TypeScript 5.7 enforces import attributes for JSON files and validates that only default exports are used. This matches Node.js's runtime behavior which has required `with { type: "json" }` since Node.js 22.

```typescript
// ❌ Error: Missing import attribute in nodenext mode
import appConfig from "./app-config.json";
// Error: Importing a JSON file requires 'with { type: "json" }' assertion

// ✅ Correct: explicit attribute
import appConfig from "./app-config.json" with { type: "json" };
const version: string = appConfig.version; // ✅ default export only

// ❌ Error: Named exports not available for JSON imports
import * as cfg from "./app-config.json" with { type: "json" };
const v = cfg.version; // Error: JSON modules only export a default

// ✅ Access via default when using namespace import
const v2 = cfg.default.version; // ✅ works

// ✅ Dynamic import with attribute
const dynamicConfig = await import("./feature-flags.json", {
  with: { type: "json" },
});
const flags = dynamicConfig.default.flags; // ✅
```

**Type-safe wrapper pattern for JSON configs:**

```typescript
import rawConfig from "./config.json" with { type: "json" };

interface AppConfig {
  version: string;
  apiUrl: string;
  features: string[];
}

// ✅ Validate at import boundary using a schema parser (zod, valibot, etc.)
import { z } from "zod";
const AppConfigSchema = z.object({
  version:  z.string(),
  apiUrl:   z.string().url(),
  features: z.array(z.string()),
});

const appConfig: AppConfig = AppConfigSchema.parse(rawConfig);
// Type is now fully validated — not just `unknown` from the JSON import
```

[community] **Pitfall — `assert {}` vs `with {}` syntax divergence:** TypeScript 5.7+ under `nodenext` rejects `assert { type: "json" }` (the old syntax) in favour of `with { type: "json" }`. Projects that copy-pasted from older tutorials or StackOverflow answers will see new errors. Search for ` assert {` in your import statements and replace with ` with {` when upgrading to Node.js 22+ targets.

---

### TypeScript 5.6 — `--noCheck` for Separate Type-Check and Build Pipelines

TypeScript 5.6 added `--noCheck`, which emits JavaScript output without running any type-checking. This enables CI pipelines to run type-checking and transpilation as independent parallel jobs, cutting wall-clock build time for large monorepos.

```bash
# Parallel pipeline: type-check and transpile simultaneously
tsc --noEmit &          # Type-check only — no output, full diagnostics
tsc --noCheck &         # Transpile only — emits .js/.d.ts, no diagnostics
wait
```

**Combined with `--isolatedDeclarations` for library authors:**

```bash
# Fast parallel declaration emit + separate type check
tsc --noCheck --isolatedDeclarations  # Emit .d.ts files without checking
tsc --noEmit                          # Full semantic check in parallel
```

**GitHub Actions parallel jobs pattern:**

```yaml
jobs:
  typecheck:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx tsc --noEmit

  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx tsc --noCheck

  deploy:
    needs: [typecheck, build]  # Both must pass
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: npm run deploy
```

[community] **Pitfall — `--noCheck` can emit broken JavaScript:** If type errors would normally block `tsc`, `--noCheck` still emits `.js` files. Deploying the build output without the `typecheck` job passing is unsafe. Some teams accidentally drop the type-check job in pipeline refactors, leaving `--noCheck` as the only TypeScript invocation — the project then ships despite type errors. Always use `needs: [typecheck, build]` in the deploy job.

---

### TypeScript 5.6 — Iterator Helper Methods (`IteratorObject<T>`)

TypeScript 5.6 added types for the ECMAScript Iterator Helpers proposal (Stage 4). Generator functions and built-in iterators now expose `map`, `filter`, `take`, `drop`, `flatMap`, `reduce`, and `forEach` directly on the iterator, without materializing an array first.

```typescript
// ✅ Map and filter a generator without creating intermediate arrays
function* fibonacci(): Generator<number> {
  let [a, b] = [0, 1];
  while (true) {
    yield a;
    [a, b] = [b, a + b];
  }
}

// Take the first 10 even Fibonacci numbers — no Array.from() needed
const result = fibonacci()
  .filter(n => n % 2 === 0)
  .take(10)
  .toArray();
// result: [0, 2, 8, 34, 144, 610, 2584, 10946, 46368, 196418]

// ✅ Invert a Map using iterator helpers
function invertMap<K, V>(map: Map<K, V>): Map<V, K> {
  return new Map(map.entries().map(([k, v]) => [v, k] as [V, K]));
}

// ✅ Process a Set without converting to an array first
const seen = new Set<string>(["alpha", "beta", "gamma", "alpha"]);
const upper = seen.values()
  .filter(s => s.length > 4)
  .map(s => s.toUpperCase())
  .toArray();
// upper: ["ALPHA", "GAMMA"]
```

**New types in TypeScript 5.6:**

```typescript
// IteratorObject<T> — the type of iterator helper chains
const iter: IteratorObject<number> = [1, 2, 3].values();
const doubled: IteratorObject<number> = iter.map(x => x * 2);

// AsyncIteratorObject<T> — for async generators
async function* rangeAsync(n: number): AsyncGenerator<number> {
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) yield i;
}
const asyncIter: AsyncIteratorObject<number> = rangeAsync(5);
const asyncResult = await asyncIter.filter(x => x % 2 === 0).toArray();
```

[community] **Pitfall — iterator helpers require `"lib": ["es2025"]` or `"target": "es2025"`:** The methods are available in V8 (Node.js 22+, Chrome 122+) but TypeScript won't surface them without the matching lib. Adding `"lib": ["es2025", "dom"]` without the runtime to back it causes silent `TypeError: iter.filter is not a function` in Node.js < 22. Pin `"engines": { "node": ">=22" }` in `package.json` and verify your `target` matches.

### TypeScript Variance Annotations — `in` and `out` Modifiers

TypeScript 4.7 introduced explicit variance annotations for generic type parameters: `out T` marks a type parameter as covariant (only produced/returned), and `in T` marks it as contravariant (only consumed/accepted as input). These annotations both document API contracts and let the compiler skip expensive structural comparisons.

```typescript
// Covariant (out) — only produced/returned, never consumed as input
interface Producer<out T> {
  produce(): T;
}

// ✅ Covariant: Producer<Cat> is assignable to Producer<Animal>
declare class Animal {}
declare class Cat extends Animal {}
declare const catProducer: Producer<Cat>;
const animalProducer: Producer<Animal> = catProducer; // ✅ safe upcast

// Contravariant (in) — only consumed as input, never returned
interface Consumer<in T> {
  consume(item: T): void;
}

// ✅ Contravariant: Consumer<Animal> is assignable to Consumer<Cat>
declare const animalConsumer: Consumer<Animal>;
const catConsumer: Consumer<Cat> = animalConsumer; // ✅ safe (accepts any Animal)

// Invariant (no modifier) — both input and output
interface ReadWrite<T> {
  get(): T;
  set(value: T): void;
}
// ❌ Neither direction is safe for assignment without explicit cast
declare const catRW: ReadWrite<Cat>;
// const animalRW: ReadWrite<Animal> = catRW; // ❌ Error: invariant

// Bivariant (in out T) — both covariant and contravariant; rarely needed
// Useful as a compiler hint when you know the type is truly bivariant
interface Transform<in out T> {
  apply(fn: (x: T) => T): T;
}
```

**Practical example — read-only observable with `out`:**

```typescript
interface Observable<out T> {
  subscribe(observer: (value: T) => void): () => void;
  map<U>(fn: (value: T) => U): Observable<U>;
}

declare const successObs: Observable<{ ok: true; data: string }>;
// ✅ Observable<SuccessResponse> assignable to Observable<ApiResponse>
declare type ApiResponse = { ok: boolean };
const apiObs: Observable<ApiResponse> = successObs; // ✅ covariance allows this
```

[community] **Pitfall — adding `out` to a parameter that IS mutated causes a hard error:** TypeScript validates variance annotations structurally. If you mark `out T` on an interface that has a method accepting `T` as a parameter (contravariant use), the compiler errors immediately. This is intentional: the annotation mismatch reveals an unsafe assignment you might otherwise miss. Remove `out` from parameters that appear in both input and output positions.

### Template Literal Types — Type-Safe Event Systems and Route DSLs

Template literal types (TypeScript 4.1+) are most powerful when combined with mapped types to produce typed event emitter interfaces, route parsers, and HTTP client DSLs.

```typescript
// ---- Type-safe event emitter ----
type EventMap = {
  "user:created":  { id: string; name: string };
  "user:deleted":  { id: string };
  "order:placed":  { orderId: string; total: number };
  "order:shipped": { orderId: string; carrier: string };
};

interface TypedEmitter<M extends Record<string, unknown>> {
  on<K extends keyof M>(event: K, handler: (payload: M[K]) => void): void;
  off<K extends keyof M>(event: K, handler: (payload: M[K]) => void): void;
  emit<K extends keyof M>(event: K, payload: M[K]): void;
}

declare const emitter: TypedEmitter<EventMap>;

// ✅ Fully typed — payload inferred from event name
emitter.on("user:created", ({ id, name }) => console.log(id, name));
emitter.emit("order:placed", { orderId: "123", total: 99.99 });

// ❌ Wrong payload shape → compile error
// emitter.emit("user:deleted", { id: "1", name: "extra" });
// Error: Object literal may only specify known properties, 'name' does not exist
```

**Extracting path parameters from URL patterns:**

```typescript
// Extract /users/:userId/posts/:postId → { userId: string; postId: string }
type ExtractParams<S extends string> =
  S extends `${string}:${infer Param}/${infer Rest}`
    ? { [K in Param | keyof ExtractParams<Rest>]: string }
    : S extends `${string}:${infer Param}`
      ? { [K in Param]: string }
      : Record<string, never>;

type UserPostParams = ExtractParams<"/users/:userId/posts/:postId">;
// → { userId: string; postId: string }

function createRoute<const P extends string>(
  pattern: P,
  handler: (params: ExtractParams<P>, req: Request) => Response
): { pattern: P; handler: typeof handler } {
  return { pattern, handler };
}

const route = createRoute("/users/:userId/posts/:postId", (params) => {
  // params.userId and params.postId are both string — fully typed ✅
  return new Response(params.userId);
});
```

[community] **Pitfall — deep template literal type recursion hits depth limits:** TypeScript has a recursion limit (~50 levels) for conditional types. Complex path parameter extractors that recurse over long URL patterns hit "Type instantiation is excessively deep" errors. For production-grade route typing, use dedicated libraries (`hono`, `ts-rest`, `trpc`) which apply proven depth-bounding strategies and avoid hitting the limit in real-world route counts.

### `interface` vs `type` Alias — Performance and Structural Implications

The TypeScript Performance wiki recommends preferring `interface` over `type` alias for object shapes. The reason: interfaces create named types that the compiler can reference by identity (a single pointer), while intersection type aliases force structural expansion on every use site, increasing both check time and error message verbosity.

```typescript
// ✅ Prefer interface for object shapes — compiler caches the named type
interface UserRecord {
  id:    string;
  name:  string;
  email: string;
}

// ❌ Type alias with intersection forces re-expansion at every use site
type UserRecordIntersection = { id: string } & { name: string } & { email: string };

// ❌ Intersection — conflicts silently resolve to never
type A = { id: string };
type B = { id: number };
type AB = A & B; // AB.id = string & number = never (silent, hard-to-spot bug)

// ✅ interface extends — conflict caught at definition time
interface Base  { id: string }
// interface Extended extends Base { id: number } // ❌ Error at declaration!
// Forces reconciliation before the bug reaches callers

// ✅ Interfaces can extend multiple bases efficiently
interface AdminUser extends BaseUser, AuditTrail, RoleHolder {
  dashboardUrl: string;
}
// AdminUser is a single named type; compiler does not re-expand bases per call

// Union types and mapped types MUST use type aliases — no interface alternative
type Status        = "active" | "inactive" | "suspended";
type UserOrAdmin   = UserRecord | AdminUser;
type Nullable<T>   = T | null;
type Getters<T>    = { [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K] };
```

[community] **Pitfall — deeply nested intersection types from code generators:** OpenAPI, GraphQL codegen, and protobuf generators often emit deep intersection chains (`A & B & C & D & ...`). On projects with 500+ generated types, this pattern degrades incremental compile times significantly. A build that takes 30 seconds can drop to under 5 seconds by converting the generator output to `interface extends` chains. File a generator issue or post-process with a codemod.

### `satisfies` + `as const` — Preserving Literals Through Type Validation

`satisfies` validates a value against a type without widening it; `as const` preserves literal types on the value. Combining both is the canonical pattern when you need validation AND exact literal-type preservation.

```typescript
type ThemeColor = "primary" | "secondary" | "accent" | "muted";

interface DesignTokens {
  colors: Record<ThemeColor, string>;
  fontSizes: Record<string, string>;
}

// ✅ satisfies validates the shape; literals preserved (no widening to string)
const tokens = {
  colors: {
    primary:   "#0070f3",
    secondary: "#7928ca",
    accent:    "#ff4081",
    muted:     "#9e9e9e",
  },
  fontSizes: { xs: "0.75rem", sm: "0.875rem", md: "1rem", lg: "1.25rem" },
} satisfies DesignTokens;

// tokens.colors.primary is "#0070f3" (literal) — NOT widened to string ✅
// Adding an unknown key like "invalid" → compile error ✅

// Without satisfies — annotation widens all values to string
const tokensAnnotated: DesignTokens = { /* ... */ };
// tokensAnnotated.colors.primary is "string" — literal type lost ❌

// ✅ as const + satisfies for fully narrow read-only tokens
const tokensConst = {
  colors: { primary: "#0070f3", secondary: "#7928ca" },
} as const satisfies Pick<DesignTokens, "colors">;
// tokensConst.colors.primary is "#0070f3" (literal, readonly) ✅
// satisfies validates the shape after as const locks the literals
```

[community] **Pitfall — `as const` before `satisfies` vs `satisfies` without `as const`:** `{ ... } as const satisfies T` (const first) narrows ALL string values to readonly literals, then validates — so fields that legitimately need a `string` type (not a literal) will get an overly narrow type. Apply `as const` only where literal narrowing is actually needed, or use it on specific sub-objects rather than the entire expression.

---

### Opaque / Branded Types for Domain Modeling

Branded types prevent accidental mixing of structurally identical primitives at compile time. The pattern is critical in domain modeling where `UserId`, `OrderId`, and `ProductId` are all `string` under the hood but must never be interchangeable.

```typescript
// Core brand machinery — define once per project
declare const __brand: unique symbol;
type Brand<T, B> = T & { readonly [__brand]: B };

// Domain types
type UserId    = Brand<string, "UserId">;
type OrderId   = Brand<string, "OrderId">;
type ProductId = Brand<string, "ProductId">;
type Cents     = Brand<number, "Cents">;

// Smart constructors — single validation and branding point
function makeUserId(raw: string): UserId {
  if (!raw.startsWith("usr_")) throw new Error(`Invalid UserId: ${raw}`);
  return raw as UserId;
}

function makeCents(amount: number): Cents {
  if (!Number.isInteger(amount) || amount < 0)
    throw new Error("Cents must be a non-negative integer");
  return amount as Cents;
}

// Usage — compiler enforces brand boundaries
function getOrderForUser(userId: UserId, orderId: OrderId): void { /* ... */ }

const uid = makeUserId("usr_abc123");
const oid = "ord_xyz789" as OrderId; // internal trust boundary

getOrderForUser(uid, oid); // ✅
getOrderForUser(oid, uid); // ❌ Error: OrderId is not assignable to UserId

// Arithmetic on branded numbers
function addCents(a: Cents, b: Cents): Cents {
  return (a + b) as Cents;
}

const price: Cents = makeCents(1999);
// addCents(price, 200); // ❌ Error: number is not assignable to Cents
addCents(price, makeCents(200)); // ✅
```

**Testing helpers for branded types:**

```typescript
// Thin test helpers bypass smart constructors without losing brand safety
const testUserId    = (s: string): UserId    => s as UserId;
const testOrderId   = (s: string): OrderId   => s as OrderId;
const testCents     = (n: number): Cents     => n as Cents;

it("calculates order total correctly", () => {
  const order = buildOrder({
    userId: testUserId("usr_test"),
    total:  testCents(2999),
  });
  expect(order.total).toBe(2999);
});
```

[community] **Pitfall — JSON round-trips erase brands:** When a branded type is serialized to JSON and deserialized, the brand is lost — the result is a plain `string` or `number`. IDs from API responses must be re-branded at the deserialization boundary using a smart constructor or schema parser. Skipping this means unvalidated strings silently flow into branded fields, defeating the entire pattern.

---

### TypeScript 5.6 — `--noUncheckedSideEffectImports` Catches Misspelled Bare Imports

TypeScript 5.6 added `--noUncheckedSideEffectImports` (included in TypeScript 5.9's `tsc --init` defaults). It makes bare side-effect imports an error if the module cannot be resolved — catching `import "./missspelled-setup.js"` that previously compiled silently.

```typescript
// ❌ Without flag: silently succeeds even if file doesn't exist
import "./setup/register-interceptors.js"; // typo: file doesn't exist, no error

// ✅ With --noUncheckedSideEffectImports:
// Error: Cannot find module './setup/register-interceptors.js'
//        Did you mean './setup/register-interceptor.js'?

// ✅ Legitimate side-effect imports are unaffected when resolved:
import "reflect-metadata";     // found in node_modules ✅
import "./polyfills/index.js"; // found on disk ✅

// ✅ Ambient module declarations silence the error for intentional wildcards:
// ambient.d.ts
declare module "*.css" {}      // CSS imports allowed as side-effects
declare module "*.svg" {}      // SVG module side-effects
```

**Enable in tsconfig:**

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "noUncheckedSideEffectImports": true
  }
}
```

[community] **Pitfall — test setup files that import via moduleNameMapper aliases:** Some testing setups use bare imports to register custom matchers or polyfills at a path that only resolves via a Jest/Vitest `moduleNameMapper` entry — TypeScript doesn't know about runtime aliases. Enabling this flag breaks those setups until you add an `declare module "..."` ambient declaration or ensure the file is resolvable from TypeScript's perspective independently of the test runner.

---

### `Writable<T>` — Utility Type for Test-Time Mutation of Readonly Fixtures

TypeScript's `Readonly<T>` is useful for production immutability, but test code sometimes needs to mutate objects that are `readonly` in production. `Writable<T>` removes `readonly` modifiers, enabling controlled mutation in test helpers without `as any` casts.

```typescript
// Utility type — remove readonly from all top-level properties (shallow)
type Writable<T> = {
  -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K];
};

// Deep version for fully mutable nested objects
type DeepWritable<T> =
  T extends readonly (infer U)[]
    ? DeepWritable<U>[]
    : T extends object
      ? { -readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepWritable<T[K]> }
      : T;

// Production type — intentionally immutable
interface AppState {
  readonly userId:    string;
  readonly sessionId: string;
  readonly features:  readonly string[];
  readonly config:    readonly { readonly key: string; readonly value: string }[];
}

// ✅ Test helper: build mutable fixtures, return as readonly AppState
function makeTestState(overrides?: Partial<Writable<AppState>>): AppState {
  const defaults: Writable<AppState> = {
    userId:    "test-user",
    sessionId: "test-session",
    features:  ["auth"],
    config:    [{ key: "theme", value: "dark" }],
  };
  return { ...defaults, ...overrides } as AppState;
}

// ✅ DeepWritable for deeply nested mutations in complex fixture builders
function patchState(state: AppState, newUserId: string): AppState {
  const mutable: DeepWritable<AppState> = structuredClone(state) as DeepWritable<AppState>;
  mutable.userId = newUserId;
  mutable.config[0].value = "light"; // ✅ deep readonly removed
  return mutable as AppState; // re-cast after patching
}

// ❌ Bad pattern: casting to any to bypass readonly
// (state as any).userId = "mutated"; // bypasses all type checks
```

[community] **Pitfall — `Writable<T>` does NOT remove `readonly` from `ReadonlyArray<T>`:** The mapped type `-readonly [K in keyof T]` iterates declared named properties. `readonly T[]` is represented as `ReadonlyArray<T>`, a different interface from `Array<T>`. To make array fields mutable too, use `DeepWritable<T>` which handles the `readonly (infer U)[]` case explicitly, or replace the type annotation manually.

### Anti-Patterns: Cycle 24 Additions

| Anti-pattern | Why it's harmful | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Writing `.ts` extension in imports without `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` | TypeScript compiles but Node.js ESM rejects `.ts` at runtime — `ERR_UNKNOWN_FILE_EXTENSION` | Enable `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` so `.ts` is rewritten to `.js` in output, or always write `.js` in source imports |
| Using uninitialized `let` inside a nested closure (pre-TS 5.7) | Variable may never be assigned; inner function silently reads `undefined` — not caught before TS 5.7 | Initialize with a default or use `const` with a ternary; TS 5.7 now reports this as a compile error |
| Bare `import "./side-effect"` without `--noUncheckedSideEffectImports` | Typos in side-effect import paths silently compile — missing polyfill never executes | Enable `noUncheckedSideEffectImports: true` and add `declare module "..."` for any intentional ambient imports |
| Deploying from `tsc --noCheck` without a passing type-check job | `--noCheck` emits `.js` even when type errors exist — ships broken code | Always gate deployment on a passing `tsc --noEmit` job; make the deploy depend on both jobs |
| Using iterator helper methods (`.filter()`, `.map()`) without Node.js 22+ | Methods require Node.js 22+ and `"lib": ["es2025"]`; types exist but runtime throws | Check `engines.node` in `package.json`; polyfill or use `Array.from(gen()).filter(...)` on older targets |
| Applying `out T` variance annotation to a parameter also used as input | TypeScript validates annotations structurally and immediately errors | Remove `out` for parameters used in both input and output positions; use `in out T` (bivariant) or no annotation |
| Deep intersection types `A & B & C & D` for merged shapes | Forces structural re-expansion at every use site; degrades incremental build times | Prefer `interface D extends A, B, C {}` which creates a single named reference-comparable type |
| Using `as const` on a full `satisfies T` expression when some fields need `string` | Narrows ALL string values to literals — fields needing plain `string` become over-constrained | Apply `as const` selectively per sub-object or per field rather than at the top level |
| Passing branded type IDs as raw strings after JSON deserialization | JSON.parse returns `string`, not `UserId` — unvalidated strings bypass all brand invariants | Re-brand at the deserialization boundary using a smart constructor or schema parser |
| `as any` to mutate a `readonly` fixture in tests | Bypasses all type checks — interface refactoring won't catch stale test mutations | Use `Writable<T>` to spread-copy the fixture into a mutable shape with full type safety |
