### Pattern 44 — Type-Safe `EventTarget` Subclassing with Typed Event Maps [community]

**Description:** DOM's `EventTarget` and Node.js `EventEmitter` accept `string` event names, losing all type safety. Combining a generic typed-event-target interface and an implementing subclass restores full type safety — listeners and `dispatchEvent` calls are checked against a declared event map.

**Tradeoff:**
- USE when: building browser-native custom elements, service workers, or Web Workers that subclass `EventTarget` and need fully-typed events without a third-party library.
- DO NOT USE when: you need to support Node.js `EventEmitter` — use `eventemitter3` or the `typed-emitter` community type package instead, which wrap Node's API.
- Alternative: `mitt` (typed micro emitter) or `RxJS Subject<T>` — both provide type safety with broader runtime support and a simpler event API.

```typescript
// Generic base: maps event name → CustomEvent detail type
type EventMap = Record<string, unknown>;

interface TypedEventTarget<EMap extends EventMap> extends EventTarget {
  addEventListener<K extends keyof EMap & string>(
    type: K,
    listener: (event: CustomEvent<EMap[K]>) => void,
    options?: boolean | AddEventListenerOptions
  ): void;
  removeEventListener<K extends keyof EMap & string>(
    type: K,
    listener: (event: CustomEvent<EMap[K]>) => void,
    options?: boolean | EventListenerOptions
  ): void;
  dispatchEvent<K extends keyof EMap & string>(
    event: CustomEvent<EMap[K]>
  ): boolean;
}

// Concrete event map for a data-fetching service
interface FetchServiceEvents {
  "fetch:start":    { url: string };
  "fetch:complete": { url: string; status: number; durationMs: number };
  "fetch:error":    { url: string; error: Error };
}

class FetchService extends EventTarget implements TypedEventTarget<FetchServiceEvents> {
  async get(url: string): Promise<Response> {
    this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("fetch:start", { detail: { url } }));
    const t0 = Date.now();
    try {
      const resp = await fetch(url);
      this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("fetch:complete", {
        detail: { url, status: resp.status, durationMs: Date.now() - t0 },
      }));
      return resp;
    } catch (err) {
      this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("fetch:error", {
        detail: { url, error: err as Error },
      }));
      throw err;
    }
  }
}

// ⚠️ Cast to TypedEventTarget to activate typed overloads:
const svc: TypedEventTarget<FetchServiceEvents> = new FetchService();
svc.addEventListener("fetch:complete", (e) => {
  // e.detail: { url: string; status: number; durationMs: number }  ✅
  console.log(`${e.detail.url} → ${e.detail.status} (${e.detail.durationMs}ms)`);
});
```

[community]

### Pattern 45 — `Prettify<T>` Utility for Readable Intersection Type Display [community]

**Description:** TypeScript displays intersection types (`A & B & C`) verbatim in hover tooltips and error messages — often producing unreadable multi-line expansions. The `Prettify<T>` utility forces the compiler to display the fully-expanded, merged object shape. It has zero runtime cost and is purely a diagnostic and documentation aid.

**Tradeoff:**
- USE when: authoring a library and wanting clear hover types for complex intersection-built API shapes, or when debugging unresolved `&` chains in IDE tooltips.
- DO NOT USE on recursive types — `Prettify<T>` on a self-referential type triggers "type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite" errors.
- Alternative: `type X = Omit<A & B, never>` — an older workaround that also forces display expansion for object types, but has quirks with optional properties and union members.

```typescript
// The Prettify utility — forces full expansion in IDE tooltips
type Prettify<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] } & {};

// Component config built via intersection — hover shows "A & B & C" without Prettify
interface DefaultConfig { timeout: number; retries: number; baseUrl: string }
interface UserOverrides { timeout?: number; apiKey: string }
interface PlatformOptions { platform: "web" | "mobile"; debug?: boolean }

// Without Prettify: hover = DefaultConfig & UserOverrides & PlatformOptions
type RawConfig = DefaultConfig & UserOverrides & PlatformOptions;

// With Prettify: hover shows the full merged object:
// { timeout: number; retries: number; baseUrl: string;
//   apiKey: string; platform: "web" | "mobile"; debug?: boolean }
type AppConfig = Prettify<DefaultConfig & UserOverrides & PlatformOptions>;

function createConfig(overrides: Partial<AppConfig>): AppConfig {
  return {
    timeout: 5000,
    retries: 3,
    baseUrl: "https://api.example.com",
    apiKey: "",
    platform: "web",
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// ❌ Do NOT apply Prettify inside recursive types:
// type Tree<T> = Prettify<{ value: T; children: Array<Tree<T>> }>; // ← instantiation error
// ✅ Apply only at the final, non-recursive alias:
type Tree<T> = { value: T; children: Array<Tree<T>> };
type FlatTree<T> = Prettify<{ value: T; children: Array<Tree<T>> }>;
```

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 32

**Gotcha 14 — `import defer` does NOT work with named or default imports** [community]

```typescript
// ❌ Syntax errors — defer only supports namespace imports:
// import defer { heavy } from "./heavy.js";
// import defer defaultExport from "./heavy.js";

// ✅ Only namespace imports are valid:
import defer * as heavy from "./heavy.js";
// heavy.someExport is accessed lazily
```

WHY: The ECMAScript `import defer` proposal is defined such that deferred evaluation is triggered by property access on the namespace object. Named and default bindings are resolved at parse/link time (before execution) and cannot be deferred. TypeScript follows the Stage 3 proposal spec precisely — any other import form is a syntax error. Teams migrating lazy `import()` calls to `import defer` must first ensure they use namespace access patterns throughout the consuming code.

---

**Gotcha 15 — `Promise.withResolvers()` requires `--lib ES2024` — missing lib causes a runtime/type mismatch** [community]

```typescript
// With --target es2022 (common default):
// const { promise, resolve } = Promise.withResolvers();
//                                     ^^^^^^^^^^^^
// error TS2339: Property 'withResolvers' does not exist on type 'PromiseConstructor'

// Fix option 1 — raise the lib explicitly:
// { "compilerOptions": { "lib": ["ES2024", "DOM"] } }

// Fix option 2 — raise the target:
// { "compilerOptions": { "target": "es2024" } }
```

WHY: `Promise.withResolvers` is part of the ES2024 standard library. TypeScript only includes type definitions for APIs present in the configured `target`/`lib` version. Many projects still default to `--target es2022` as the Node.js LTS-safe baseline and do not add `ES2024` to `lib`. The runtime (Node.js 22+) may support the method, but TypeScript's type declarations are absent until the lib config is updated — leading to a confusing mismatch where code runs fine but type-checking fails.

---

**Gotcha 16 — `--erasableSyntaxOnly` permits `const enum` but bans plain `enum`, and `const enum` then conflicts with `--isolatedModules`** [community]

```typescript
// ❌ Plain enum — generates a runtime object, NOT erasable:
// enum Status { Active, Inactive }   // error under --erasableSyntaxOnly

// ✅ const enum — inlined at each use site, erasable:
const enum Status { Active = "active", Inactive = "inactive" }
const s: Status = Status.Active; // emitted as: const s = "active"

// ⚠️ BUT: const enum CANNOT cross module boundaries under --isolatedModules
// (which is implicit with nodenext + erasableSyntaxOnly):
// import { Status } from "./status.js";
// const x: Status = Status.Active;
//                   ^^^^^^ error: const enums from external modules cannot be used
// Fix: replace const enum with a plain union type:
type StatusType = "active" | "inactive";
const STATUS = { Active: "active", Inactive: "inactive" } as const satisfies Record<string, StatusType>;
```

WHY: `const enum` values are inlined and generate no runtime object — satisfying `--erasableSyntaxOnly`. However, `--isolatedModules` (enabled by default in `nodenext` mode) forbids using `const enum` values from external modules because each file is processed independently and the inlining cannot occur across file boundaries. Teams that replace `enum` with `const enum` to satisfy `--erasableSyntaxOnly` often then hit the `--isolatedModules` cross-module error and must migrate a second time to plain union types or `as const` objects.

---

**Gotcha 17 — `Prettify<T>` on deeply nested or recursive intersection types triggers "excessively deep" instantiation errors** [community]

```typescript
// ❌ Recursive type + Prettify = instantiation explosion
// type Tree<T> = Prettify<{ value: T; children: Array<Tree<T>> }>;
// Error: Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite.

// ✅ Remove Prettify from all recursive positions:
type Tree<T> = { value: T; children: Array<Tree<T>> };

// ✅ Apply Prettify only at a leaf alias that does NOT recurse back to itself:
type LeafConfig = Prettify<{ timeout: number } & { retries: number }>;
```

WHY: `Prettify<T>` uses `{ [K in keyof T]: T[K] } & {}` which forces TypeScript to fully evaluate every key's value type. When `T` contains a recursive reference back to `Prettify<T>`, the compiler enters an unbounded expansion loop and bails at the recursion depth limit. The safe pattern is to apply `Prettify` only at final/leaf type aliases — never inside a generic that references itself directly or transitively.

---

**Gotcha 18 — Typed `EventTarget` interface overloads are NOT activated on a `FetchService` variable — only on a `TypedEventTarget<...>` typed variable** [community]

```typescript
// ❌ Typed overloads are INVISIBLE on the raw class type:
const rawSvc = new FetchService();
rawSvc.addEventListener("fetch:complete", (e: Event) => {
  // e is plain Event — NOT CustomEvent<FetchServiceEvents["fetch:complete"]>
  // TypeScript resolves to the inherited base EventTarget overload, losing detail typing.
});

// ✅ Cast the variable to the typed interface:
const typedSvc: TypedEventTarget<FetchServiceEvents> = new FetchService();
typedSvc.addEventListener("fetch:complete", (e) => {
  console.log(e.detail.status); // ✅ number — correctly typed
});
```

WHY: TypeScript's overload resolution is determined by the *declared type of the variable*, not the runtime class hierarchy. Since `FetchService extends EventTarget`, a variable typed as `FetchService` only sees the `EventTarget` overloads (which accept `string` and return plain `Event`). The typed overloads are defined on the `TypedEventTarget<EMap>` interface — they are only visible when the variable's static type is `TypedEventTarget<FetchServiceEvents>`. Always store or cast the instance to the typed interface at the point of `addEventListener` / `removeEventListener` calls.

---

### Anti-Patterns: Cycle 32 Additions

| Anti-pattern | Why it's harmful | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Named/default `import defer` syntax | Syntax error — `defer` only supports namespace imports | Use `import defer * as name from "..."` |
| Using `{}` as a "no properties" parameter type | `{}` accepts any non-nullish value including primitives; it does NOT mean empty object | Use `Record<string, never>` for truly empty, `Record<PropertyKey, unknown>` for any-keyed object |
| `@ts-ignore` in test files | Silently suppresses errors; does not verify the error still exists after refactors or type upgrades | Replace with `@ts-expect-error` which becomes an error itself if the suppressed line becomes valid |
| `Prettify<T>` inside recursive type definitions | Triggers "type instantiation is excessively deep" — recursive expansion never terminates | Apply `Prettify` only at final leaf alias positions, never inside self-referential generics |
| Missing `--lib ES2024` when using `Promise.withResolvers()` | TypeScript reports property-not-found even when the runtime supports it | Add `"ES2024"` (or later) to `"lib"` in `tsconfig.json`, or raise `"target"` to `"es2024"` |

### Pattern 46 — `--isolatedDeclarations` for Parallel Declaration Emit in Monorepos [official]

TypeScript 5.5 introduced `--isolatedDeclarations`, a compiler option that enforces explicit type annotations on all exported symbols, enabling external tools to generate `.d.ts` files without running the full TypeScript type-checker. The goal is to unlock parallel declaration emit and faster monorepo builds. When enabled, TypeScript errors on exported functions that infer their return types from complex expressions, requiring the developer to annotate them explicitly. This decouples the declaration file generation step from the type-checking step, so large monorepos can build all packages' `.d.ts` files simultaneously instead of waiting for dependency chains.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json:
// { "compilerOptions": { "declaration": true, "isolatedDeclarations": true } }

// ❌ Error under --isolatedDeclarations:
//    Function must have an explicit return type annotation.
import { computeScore } from "./scoring.js";
export function getUserScore(userId: string) {
  return computeScore(userId); // inferred return type from external module
}

// ✅ Correct — explicit return type annotation allows isolated .d.ts generation:
export function getUserScore(userId: string): Promise<number> {
  return computeScore(userId);
}

// ✅ Trivial literals are always permitted (no annotation needed):
export const MAX_RETRIES = 3;           // infers: 3 (literal)
export const API_BASE = "https://api.example.com"; // infers: string literal

// ✅ Type assertion also satisfies the requirement:
export function getTag() {
  return Math.random() > 0.5 ? ("admin" as const) : ("user" as const);
}
```

**Tradeoff:**
- Use when: building a monorepo with parallel declaration emit; adopting Oxc/Vite-powered DTS tools; optimizing build pipelines where declaration generation is a bottleneck.
- Do NOT use when: small single-package projects where declaration emit speed is irrelevant; teams that find mandatory return-type annotations overly burdensome.
- Alternative: `--declaration` alone (allows inferred return types but cannot parallelize across packages); TypeScript project references with composite mode (sequential but avoids annotation mandate).

### Pattern 47 — `import defer` for Deferred Module Evaluation (TypeScript 5.9) [official]

TypeScript 5.9 implements the ECMAScript deferred evaluation proposal, allowing a module's side effects and exports to be deferred until the namespace is first accessed. `import defer * as ns from "..."` loads the module's dependencies and parses it, but does not execute its top-level code until a property of `ns` is accessed. This is only permitted with namespace imports, never named or default imports. The module flag must be `--module preserve` or `esnext`.

```typescript
// ✅ Only namespace form is valid:
import defer * as heavyLib from "./heavy-processing.js";

// Execution of heavy-processing.js is deferred until here:
export function runIfNeeded(flag: boolean): void {
  if (flag) {
    // Module top-level code executes on FIRST property access:
    const result = heavyLib.processData([1, 2, 3]);
    console.log(result);
  }
  // If flag === false, heavy-processing.js never executes at all.
}

// ❌ Named import — syntax error:
// import defer { processData } from "./heavy-processing.js";

// ❌ Default import — syntax error:
// import defer defaultExport from "./heavy-processing.js";

// ✅ Confirm module config is compatible:
// tsconfig.json: { "compilerOptions": { "module": "preserve" } }
```

**Tradeoff:**
- Use when: optimizing startup time for CLI tools or servers where certain features are conditionally needed; replacing dynamic `import()` calls that pollute the return type with `Promise<T>`.
- Do NOT use when: the module has critical side effects that must always run (e.g., registering a polyfill or global handler); using CommonJS or non-`esnext`/`preserve` module targets.
- Alternative: dynamic `import()` (fully async, returns a promise, works in any module format); lazy initialization wrappers (manual but universally compatible).

---

### Pattern 48 — `--module node20` for Stable Node.js v20 Semantics [official]

TypeScript 5.9 introduced `--module node20` as a production-stable alternative to `--module nodenext`. While `nodenext` tracks the latest Node.js behaviors and may change across TypeScript versions, `node20` fixes the behavior to Node.js v20 semantics and is unlikely to change. It implies `--target es2023` by default (unlike `nodenext` which implies `esnext`), making it predictable for long-term configurations. It supports `require()` of ESM modules from CommonJS (like Node.js 22 behavior), and it correctly rejects deprecated import assertions in favor of import attributes.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json:
// { "compilerOptions": { "module": "node20" } }

// ✅ Import attributes (new standard) — works under node20:
import data from "./config.json" with { type: "json" };
console.log(data.version);

// ❌ Import assertions (deprecated) — error under node20:
// import data from "./config.json" assert { type: "json" };

// ✅ require() of ESM from CJS is supported (Node.js 22+):
// In a .cjs file:
// const { processData } = require("./esm-module.mjs");

// ✅ .mts extension for explicit ESM:
// import { handler } from "./lambda.mts"; // ✅ resolved as ESM

// node20 implies --target es2023, so these are available without extra lib:
const grouped = Object.groupBy([1, 2, 3, 4], (n) => (n % 2 === 0 ? "even" : "odd"));
// ✅ type: Partial<Record<"even" | "odd", number[]>>
```

**Tradeoff:**
- Use when: deploying to Node.js v20+ with a stable, long-term config that should not shift behavior on TypeScript upgrades; CI pipelines where predictability is critical.
- Do NOT use when: you need the very latest Node.js features (use `nodenext`); targeting older Node.js versions that lack v20 module semantics.
- Alternative: `--module nodenext` (always tracks latest behavior but can change between TS releases); `--module commonjs` (maximum compatibility, no ESM interop features).

---

### Pattern 49 — Decorator Metadata via `Symbol.metadata` (TypeScript 5.2) [official]

TypeScript 5.2 implements the TC39 decorator metadata proposal, which gives each decorator access to a shared `metadata` object on its `context` argument. All decorators applied to a class share the same `metadata` object, and the final result is stored on the class constructor as `Symbol.metadata`. This is distinct from the legacy `experimentalDecorators` + `reflect-metadata` approach; it uses Stage 3 decorators only. It enables dependency injection containers, ORMs, and validation frameworks to associate metadata with class members without external WeakMaps.

```typescript
// polyfill required until runtimes support it natively:
Symbol.metadata ??= Symbol("Symbol.metadata");

// Serialization decorator using metadata:
const serializableKeys = new WeakMap<object, string[]>();

function serialize(_: unknown, context: ClassFieldDecoratorContext): void {
  if (context.private || context.static) {
    throw new Error("@serialize only supports public instance fields.");
  }
  const key = String(context.name);
  let keys = serializableKeys.get(context.metadata);
  if (!keys) serializableKeys.set(context.metadata, (keys = []));
  keys.push(key);
}

function toJSON(instance: object): string {
  const meta = (instance.constructor as any)[Symbol.metadata];
  const keys = meta ? serializableKeys.get(meta) : undefined;
  if (!keys) throw new Error("No @serialize decorators found.");
  const pairs = keys.map((k) => `"${k}": ${JSON.stringify((instance as any)[k])}`);
  return `{ ${pairs.join(", ")} }`;
}

class User {
  @serialize
  name: string;
  @serialize
  email: string;
  passwordHash: string; // not serialized

  constructor(name: string, email: string, hash: string) {
    this.name = name; this.email = email; this.passwordHash = hash;
  }
}
const u = new User("Alice", "alice@example.com", "abc123");
console.log(toJSON(u)); // { "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@example.com" }
```

**Tradeoff:**
- Use when: building DI containers, serialization libraries, or validation frameworks that need runtime field metadata without `reflect-metadata`; adopting TC39 Stage 3 decorators.
- Do NOT use when: still using `experimentalDecorators: true` (the two decorator systems are incompatible and cannot be mixed); the runtime does not support `Symbol.metadata` and you cannot polyfill it.
- Alternative: legacy `experimentalDecorators` + `reflect-metadata` (widely used in NestJS/TypeORM, stable, but not standards-track); explicit field registration patterns (no decorators, full control).

---

### Pattern 50 — `const` Type Parameters for Literal Inference Without Caller `as const` (TypeScript 5.0) [official]

Before TypeScript 5.0, generic functions that wanted to preserve literal types from array/object arguments required callers to add `as const`. The `const` modifier on a type parameter (`<const T>`) enables the function itself to request const-like inference, so callers get precise types without remembering to annotate. When combined with a `readonly` constraint, the parameter also accepts already-`readonly` arrays. Without the `readonly` constraint, mutable array constraints cause TypeScript to silently fall back to the wider inferred type.

```typescript
// ❌ Without const modifier — type is widened:
function routeNames<T extends readonly string[]>(routes: T): T {
  return routes;
}
const r1 = routeNames(["home", "about", "contact"]);
// r1: string[] — literal types lost

// ✅ With const modifier + readonly constraint:
function routeNamesConst<const T extends readonly string[]>(routes: T): T {
  return routes;
}
const r2 = routeNamesConst(["home", "about", "contact"]);
// r2: readonly ["home", "about", "contact"] — exact literals preserved

// ✅ Use case: type-safe route map factory
type RouteMap<T extends readonly string[]> = { [K in T[number]]: string };
function makeRoutes<const T extends readonly string[]>(
  names: T,
  prefix: string
): RouteMap<T> {
  return Object.fromEntries(names.map((n) => [n, `${prefix}/${n}`])) as RouteMap<T>;
}
const routes = makeRoutes(["home", "about", "contact"], "/app");
// routes.home, routes.about, routes.contact — all typed, no extras
```

**Tradeoff:**
- Use when: building builder APIs, route maps, event registries, or config factories where callers should not need to add `as const` for precise inference.
- Do NOT use when: the function genuinely needs to accept mutable arrays and does not care about literal types; adding `const` to parameters that already accept `any[]` or `unknown[]`.
- Alternative: require callers to use `as const` (explicit but burdensome); return a mapped type with widened keys (less precise but simpler implementation).

---

### Pattern 51 — `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` for `.ts`-Extension Source Imports [official]

TypeScript 5.7 added `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions`, which rewrites `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.mts`, and `.cts` extensions in relative import specifiers to their JavaScript equivalents (`.js`, `.jsx`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`) during emit. This allows developers to import TypeScript files using their actual source extension (`./foo.ts`) instead of the confusing `./foo.js` convention, while still producing correct JavaScript output. Non-relative imports and imports without an explicit extension are not affected.

```typescript
// With --rewriteRelativeImportExtensions in tsconfig:
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "module": "nodenext",
//     "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true
//   }
// }

// Source file: src/utils.ts
export function formatDate(d: Date): string {
  return d.toISOString().split("T")[0];
}

// Source file: src/index.ts — import uses .ts extension:
import { formatDate } from "./utils.ts"; // ✅ valid source-level import

// Emitted: dist/index.js — extension rewritten automatically:
// import { formatDate } from "./utils.js";

// ❌ NOT rewritten (non-relative):
// import { something } from "some-package/file.ts";

// ❌ NOT rewritten (no extension):
// import { something } from "./utils";
```

**Tradeoff:**
- Use when: working in a Deno-style or URL-first environment where `.ts` extensions in imports are the convention; toolchains where `.js`-extension imports feel unnatural; migrating from Deno to Node.js with `nodenext`.
- Do NOT use when: targeting bundlers (Webpack/Vite/Rollup) that handle extension resolution internally; projects where `.js` extension imports are already established convention.
- Alternative: use `.js` extension imports (the Node.js ESM standard convention under `nodenext`); use a bundler that resolves extensions automatically.

---

### Pattern 52 — `--module node18` for Stable Node.js 18 LTS Semantics [official]

TypeScript 5.8 introduced `--module node18` as a stable reference point for Node.js 18 LTS projects. Unlike `--module nodenext`, which evolves with Node.js, `node18` fixes behavior at Node.js 18 semantics and will not change in future TypeScript versions. Key difference from `nodenext`: `require()` of ESM files is disallowed under `node18` (Node.js 18 does not support it), and deprecated import assertions (`assert`) are still permitted (since Node.js 18 does not fully support import attributes).

```typescript
// tsconfig.json: { "compilerOptions": { "module": "node18" } }

// ✅ Import attributes work (Node.js 18.20+ supports them):
import config from "./config.json" with { type: "json" };

// ✅ Import assertions also allowed (Node.js 18 transitional support):
// import config from "./config.json" assert { type: "json" };

// ❌ require() of ESM is NOT allowed under node18:
// In a .cjs file:
// const mod = require("./esm-module.mjs"); // error: ESM cannot be required in node18

// ✅ Dynamic import is the correct way to use ESM from CJS under node18:
async function loadPlugin(name: string): Promise<{ run: () => void }> {
  const plugin = await import(`./plugins/${name}.mjs`);
  return plugin;
}

// node18 implies --target es2022 by default
const arr = [1, 2, 3];
const found = arr.at(-1); // ✅ Array.at() available in ES2022
```

**Tradeoff:**
- Use when: your deployment target is specifically Node.js 18 LTS and you need a config that will never silently change behavior on TypeScript upgrades; environments where `require()` of ESM is undesirable.
- Do NOT use when: you have upgraded to Node.js 20+ and want `require()` of ESM support; you want to track the latest Node.js module behavior.
- Alternative: `--module node20` (Node.js 20 semantics, supports `require()` of ESM); `--module nodenext` (always-latest behavior, may shift across TS releases).

---

### Pattern 53 — Granular Return-Branch Type Checking (TypeScript 5.8) [official]

TypeScript 5.8 improved how it checks conditional expressions inside `return` statements. Previously, ternary branches inside `return` were merged into a union type before comparing against the declared return type, which allowed one branch to contribute `any` and mask a type error in the other branch. In 5.8, each branch of a ternary (or short-circuit) expression in a `return` is checked individually against the return type, so a cache returning `any` on the truthy branch can no longer hide a wrong type on the falsy branch.

```typescript
// Simulates a loosely-typed cache:
declare const untypedCache: Map<any, any>;

// ❌ TypeScript 5.7 accepted this — falsy branch ('urlString') was not checked:
function getUrlObject57(urlString: string): URL {
  return untypedCache.has(urlString)
    ? untypedCache.get(urlString)  // any — silently absorbed the union
    : urlString;                    // string — was NOT caught as a type error
}

// ✅ TypeScript 5.8 now errors on the falsy branch:
// Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'URL'.
function getUrlObjectFixed(urlString: string): URL {
  return untypedCache.has(urlString)
    ? (untypedCache.get(urlString) as URL)  // explicit cast — communicates intent
    : new URL(urlString);                   // ✅ correct type
}

// ✅ Works correctly for all branch forms:
function processResult(value: string | null): string {
  return value !== null
    ? value.trim()     // ✅ string
    : "default";       // ✅ string
}
```

**Tradeoff:**
- Use when: always — this is a correctness improvement that prevents `any`-masking bugs in return expressions; existing code that relied on the previous behavior should be fixed.
- Do NOT use when: there is no reason to disable this; it can be worked around with explicit type assertions if legacy code breaks.
- Alternative: no true alternative — enabling strict return checking is a net improvement; the only mitigation for breakage is adding explicit casts to branches that were previously hidden by `any`.

---

### Pattern 54 — `--libReplacement false` to Disable `@typescript/lib-*` Package Lookup [official]

TypeScript 5.8 introduced the `--libReplacement` flag, which controls whether TypeScript searches `node_modules` for `@typescript/lib-*` packages to override built-in type declarations. When the feature was introduced in TypeScript 4.5, it allowed projects to swap `lib.dom.d.ts` with a custom DOM types package. However, this lookup has measurable startup overhead in large monorepos. The `--libReplacement false` flag opts out entirely, restoring the pre-4.5 behavior of always using bundled lib declarations.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json — disable lib replacement for performance:
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "libReplacement": false,
//     "lib": ["esnext", "dom"]
//   }
// }

// Without libReplacement: false, TypeScript checks node_modules for:
// @typescript/lib-esnext, @typescript/lib-dom, etc.
// This is harmless but adds file-system lookups on every project open.

// With libReplacement: false — bundled declarations always win:
// Safe when you don't use custom @typescript/lib-* packages.

// ✅ Example: checking that Date is the built-in type (not a custom lib override):
const d: Date = new Date();
const iso: string = d.toISOString(); // ✅ standard lib typing

// Check your package.json/node_modules — if none of these are installed,
// setting libReplacement: false is safe and slightly faster:
// @typescript/lib-dom, @typescript/lib-esnext, @typescript/lib-es2022, ...
```

**Tradeoff:**
- Use when: optimizing IDE/build startup time in large monorepos; you do not use any `@typescript/lib-*` override packages.
- Do NOT use when: your project installs custom `@typescript/lib-*` packages to replace DOM or lib types (e.g., `@typescript/lib-dom` with a minimal DOM types fork); you use libraries that depend on lib replacement.
- Alternative: leave `libReplacement` at its default (true) — incurs small startup overhead but is fully compatible with any custom lib packages.

---

### Pattern 55 — `/// <reference types="..." preserve="true" />` to Retain Reference Directives in Declaration Files [official]

TypeScript 5.5 changed declaration emit to no longer synthesize or preserve `/// <reference types="..." />` directives in `.d.ts` output by default. This broke packages that relied on reference directives to pull in global augmentations (e.g., `jest` globals, `node` globals) for consumers. The `preserve="true"` attribute was added to let developers explicitly mark which reference directives should survive in emitted declaration files.

```typescript
/// <reference types="jest" preserve="true" />
/// <reference types="node" preserve="true" />

// Now the emitted .d.ts will include these directives:
// /// <reference types="jest" />
// /// <reference types="node" />

// Without preserve="true", the directives are dropped in 5.5+:
// ❌ Old behavior (TS < 5.5): directives were auto-preserved in .d.ts
// ✅ New behavior (TS >= 5.5): only directives with preserve="true" survive

export function getNodeEnv(): string {
  return process.env.NODE_ENV ?? "development"; // relies on @types/node
}

// If consumers of this library need 'process' to be typed,
// the reference directive must be preserved in the .d.ts output.
```

**Tradeoff:**
- Use when: publishing a library that relies on `@types/node`, `@types/jest`, or other global type augmentation packages that consumers of your library will also need.
- Do NOT use when: your library does not expose types that depend on external globals; you prefer consumers to install and configure their own `@types` packages explicitly.
- Alternative: include `@types/node` in the library's `dependencies` (not `devDependencies`) so consumers automatically get it; use module augmentation instead of global reference directives.

---

### Pattern 56 — TypeScript 5.9 `tsc --init` Prescriptive Defaults [official]

TypeScript 5.9 replaced the old verbose commented-out `tsconfig.json` generated by `tsc --init` with a concise, opinionated baseline that reflects current best practices. The new default enables several stricter options (`noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `verbatimModuleSyntax`) that were previously opt-in. Teams starting new projects can use this baseline directly; established projects should audit their existing config against these recommendations.

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "nodenext",
    "target": "esnext",
    "types": [],
    "sourceMap": true,
    "declaration": true,
    "declarationMap": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,
    "strict": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "isolatedModules": true,
    "noUncheckedSideEffectImports": true,
    "moduleDetection": "force",
    "skipLibCheck": true
  }
}
```

```typescript
// noUncheckedIndexedAccess: array access now returns T | undefined:
const items = ["a", "b", "c"];
const first = items[0];
// type: string | undefined — requires guard before use:
if (first !== undefined) {
  console.log(first.toUpperCase()); // ✅ narrowed to string
}

// exactOptionalPropertyTypes: cannot assign undefined to optional property:
interface Config { timeout?: number }
const cfg: Config = { timeout: undefined }; // ❌ error under exactOptionalPropertyTypes
const cfg2: Config = {};                     // ✅ omit the property instead

// verbatimModuleSyntax: type-only imports must be explicit:
import type { User } from "./types.js"; // ✅
// import { User } from "./types.js";  // ❌ if User is type-only
```

**Tradeoff:**
- Use when: starting a new TypeScript project; applying best-practice stricter settings to improve type safety and tool compatibility.
- Do NOT use when: migrating a large legacy codebase where these settings would create hundreds of new errors that cannot all be fixed at once; better to enable settings incrementally.
- Alternative: enable strict settings one at a time using `// @ts-check` directives; TypeScript migration guide's incremental strictness approach.

---

### Pattern 57 — TypedArray `ArrayBufferLike` Generic Change (TypeScript 5.7 / 5.9) [official]

TypeScript 5.7 made all TypedArray interfaces (`Uint8Array`, `Float32Array`, etc.) generic over their backing buffer type (`TArrayBuffer extends ArrayBufferLike`). TypeScript 5.9 further tightened this so `ArrayBuffer` is no longer a supertype of TypedArrays. Code that accepted `ArrayBuffer` where a `Uint8Array` was intended will now produce errors. The fix is to access `.buffer` when an `ArrayBuffer` is explicitly needed, or widen the function signature to accept both.

```typescript
// ❌ TypeScript 5.9+ error — ArrayBuffer is not assignable to Uint8Array:
function processBuffer(data: ArrayBuffer): void {
  const view = new DataView(data);
  console.log(view.getUint8(0));
}
const bytes = new Uint8Array([0, 1, 2, 3]);
// processBuffer(bytes); // Error: Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer> not assignable to ArrayBuffer

// ✅ Option 1: access .buffer explicitly:
processBuffer(bytes.buffer); // ✅ ArrayBuffer

// ✅ Option 2: accept ArrayBufferLike (covers SharedArrayBuffer too):
function processBufferLike(data: ArrayBufferLike): void {
  const view = new DataView(data);
  console.log(view.getUint8(0));
}
processBufferLike(bytes.buffer); // ✅
processBufferLike(new SharedArrayBuffer(4)); // ✅

// ✅ Option 3: accept Uint8Array directly (most precise):
function processBytes(data: Uint8Array): void {
  console.log(data[0]);
}
processBytes(bytes); // ✅

// ✅ Generic approach — parameterize over ArrayBufferLike:
function toBase64<T extends ArrayBufferLike>(data: Uint8Array<T>): string {
  return Buffer.from(data).toString("base64");
}
```

**Tradeoff:**
- Use when: always — the stricter typing catches real bugs where an array view was passed expecting raw bytes; the fix is a minor `.buffer` access or signature update.
- Do NOT use when: no reason to avoid — this is a correctness improvement.
- Alternative: cast with `as unknown as ArrayBuffer` (suppresses the error but does not fix the semantic issue); update library signatures to accept `Uint8Array` directly.

---

### Pattern 58 — Explicit Type Arguments to Prevent Inference Variable Leaks (TypeScript 5.9) [official]

TypeScript 5.9 fixed a bug where type variables could "leak" from one generic call site's inference context into inferred types elsewhere, causing subsequent calls to infer overly-narrow or unexpected types. The fix may introduce new errors in codebases that relied on the previous (incorrect) inference. The resolution is to add explicit type arguments to generic function calls where TypeScript now fails to infer the correct type or infers a type that was previously absorbed by a leaked variable.

```typescript
// Pattern: generic factory — explicit type parameter anchors inference:
function createStore<S extends object>(initialState: S): { get: () => S; set: (next: S) => void } {
  let state = initialState;
  return {
    get: () => state,
    set: (next) => { state = next; },
  };
}

// ✅ Explicit type parameter prevents TS 5.9 inference ambiguity:
const store = createStore<{ count: number; label: string }>({
  count: 0,
  label: "default",
});
const s = store.get();
// s: { count: number; label: string } — stable, explicit

// ✅ Chained transforms — explicit type parameters avoid leaked variables:
function transform<T, U>(input: T, fn: (x: T) => U): U { return fn(input); }
const result = transform<string, number>("hello", (s) => s.length);
// type: number — explicit, correct under TS 5.9

// ✅ Diagnostic: if TS 5.9 produces a new "Type X is not assignable to Y" error
//    on a previously working generic call, add explicit type arguments first,
//    then check if the error reveals a real bug masked by the old inference.
```

**Tradeoff:**
- Use when: encountering new inference errors after upgrading to TypeScript 5.9; generic functions with multiple type parameters where one was previously inferred from another.
- Do NOT use when: inference is working correctly (no errors) — adding unnecessary explicit annotations reduces readability without benefit.
- Alternative: simplify the generic signature to reduce the number of type parameters that must be simultaneously inferred; restructure call sites to make inference unambiguous.

---

### Pattern 59 — `tsd` Type-Level Test Files for Declaration Authors [community]

The `tsd` package (`npm install --save-dev tsd`) provides a dedicated testing framework for TypeScript type definitions. It runs as a CLI tool against `.d.ts` files and TypeScript sources, using custom assertion functions that produce errors at the type level rather than at runtime. The key assertions are `expectType<T>(value)`, `expectAssignable<T>(value)`, `expectError(expression)`, and `expectNotAssignable<T>(value)`. This is particularly valuable for library authors who want to ensure their public API types are correct and that breaking type changes surface in CI.

```typescript
// tests/index.test-d.ts
import { expectType, expectError, expectAssignable, expectNotType } from "tsd";
import { createUser, UserRole } from "../src/index.js";

// ✅ Verify exact return type:
expectType<{ id: string; name: string; role: UserRole }>(
  createUser("alice", "admin")
);

// ✅ Verify that passing wrong argument type produces a type error:
expectError(createUser(123, "admin")); // 123 is not string — should error

// ✅ Verify assignability (structural subtype relationship):
expectAssignable<{ id: string }>(createUser("bob", "viewer"));

// ✅ Verify the return is NOT widened to a broader type:
expectNotType<Record<string, unknown>>(createUser("carol", "editor"));

// Run with: npx tsd
// CI integration: add to package.json scripts:
// { "scripts": { "test:types": "tsd" } }
// tsd config via package.json "tsd" key:
// { "tsd": { "directory": "tests" } }
```

**Tradeoff:**
- Use when: authoring TypeScript libraries with a public `.d.ts` API; wanting CI to catch type regressions alongside runtime test failures.
- Do NOT use when: writing application-level type assertions (Vitest's `expectTypeOf` is better integrated there); the project does not publish a library with public types.
- Alternative: Vitest `expectTypeOf` / `assertType` (better for application test suites co-located with runtime tests); `@type-challenges/utils` Expect/Equal (for type puzzle validation without a test runner).

---

### Pattern 60 — `expectTypeOf` / `assertType` in Vitest for Co-located Type Tests [community]

Vitest provides built-in type testing via `expectTypeOf` and `assertType`, allowing type-level assertions in the same test files as runtime assertions. `expectTypeOf(value).toEqualTypeOf<T>()` checks exact type equality (including whether `readonly` modifiers match), while `toMatchTypeOf<T>()` checks assignability. `assertType<T>(value)` is the simpler imperative form. To prevent false positives from typos in assertion method names, include `.test-d.ts` files in the Vitest runtime runner so a typo-d method would throw at runtime rather than silently passing.

```typescript
// src/__tests__/types.test-d.ts
import { describe, it, assertType, expectTypeOf } from "vitest";
import { parseDate, DateResult } from "../parse.js";

describe("parseDate type tests", () => {
  it("returns DateResult on success", () => {
    // Exact type equality — fails if readonly or optional differs:
    expectTypeOf(parseDate("2026-01-01")).toEqualTypeOf<DateResult>();
  });

  it("does not widen to string", () => {
    // toMatchTypeOf checks assignability, not equality:
    expectTypeOf(parseDate("2026-01-01")).not.toMatchTypeOf<string>();
  });

  it("assertType — simpler imperative form for single checks", () => {
    assertType<DateResult>(parseDate("2026-01-01"));
  });

  it("test generic function input parameter type", () => {
    // .parameter(n) checks the type of the nth function argument:
    expectTypeOf(parseDate).parameter(0).toEqualTypeOf<string>();
  });

  it("guard against any-absorption false positive", () => {
    // toEqualTypeOf catches 'any' — toMatchTypeOf does NOT:
    expectTypeOf(parseDate("x")).not.toEqualTypeOf<any>();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- Use when: using Vitest as your test runner and wanting type tests co-located with runtime tests; avoiding a separate CLI tool (like `tsd`) for type testing.
- Do NOT use when: using Jest (no built-in type testing — use `@jest/globals` + a type assertion helper instead); publishing a library where type-test separation from runtime tests is cleaner.
- Alternative: `tsd` (standalone declaration testing for libraries); `@type-challenges/utils` Expect/Equal (zero-dependency, compile-time-only type assertions).

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 33

---

**Gotcha 19 — `--isolatedDeclarations` silently accepts inferred literal types but errors on inferred complex types — the threshold is non-obvious** [community]

```typescript
// ✅ Trivial — no annotation required under --isolatedDeclarations:
export const MAX = 100;           // infers: 100 (literal)
export const BASE = "https://x"; // infers: string literal
export function noop() {}        // infers: void (trivial)

// ❌ Non-trivial — requires annotation:
import { computeKey } from "./util.js";
export function makeKey() {
  //              ^^^^^^^^ error: Function must have an explicit return type annotation
  return computeKey("foo"); // return type depends on external module
}

// ❌ Object spread shape not locally determinable:
import { defaultConfig } from "./config.js";
export const merged = { ...defaultConfig, timeout: 5000 };
//           ^^^^^^ error: Variable must have an explicit type annotation
//           (spread shape depends on defaultConfig's type from another file)

// ✅ Fix: annotate all non-trivial exports:
export function makeKey(): string { return computeKey("foo"); }
export const merged: { timeout: number; retries: number } = { ...defaultConfig, timeout: 5000 };
```

WHY: `--isolatedDeclarations` aims to allow tools to generate `.d.ts` files by analyzing one file at a time. Expressions that depend on types from other files (imported values, spread shapes, conditional type results) cannot be resolved in isolation — the tool would need to run the full type-checker. TypeScript's error is triggered when it determines the return/value type cannot be expressed without cross-file inference. "Trivial" is defined as literals, primitive constructors, and `void`/`never` — everything else requires an explicit annotation.

---

**Gotcha 20 — `import defer` defers evaluation but NOT loading — the file is still parsed and included in the bundle** [community]

```typescript
// ❌ Common misconception: defer means the file is NOT loaded at startup:
import defer * as feature from "./heavy.js";
// heavy.js IS loaded (parsed, imports resolved) when the module initializes.
// Only execution of its top-level statements is deferred.

// The distinction matters for:
// 1. Circular dependencies — heavy.js IS in the module graph immediately
// 2. Parse errors — thrown on startup, NOT on first property access
// 3. Bundle size — heavy.js IS included in the bundle regardless

// ✅ What IS deferred: top-level statements in heavy.js
// ❌ What is NOT deferred: file loading, parsing, circular-dep resolution

// Contrast: dynamic import truly defers loading:
async function loadIfNeeded(flag: boolean): Promise<void> {
  if (flag) {
    const mod = await import("./heavy.js"); // NOT loaded until this line runs
    mod.doWork();
  }
  // heavy.js is excluded from bundles when the flag is always false
}
// import defer is NOT a code-splitting mechanism — use dynamic import for that.
```

WHY: The ECMAScript `import defer` proposal operates at the *evaluation* phase of the module lifecycle, not the *loading* or *parsing* phase. ESM loading is a two-phase process: (1) load/link (resolve and parse all imports), (2) evaluate (execute top-level statements). `import defer` only defers phase 2. The module is still fully resolved during phase 1, meaning it appears in the module graph and is included in bundler output. Developers who expect `import defer` to act like a lazy `import()` call for code-splitting purposes will find that bundle size is unchanged.

---

**Gotcha 21 — `require()` of ESM under `--module nodenext`/`node20` is CJS-to-ESM only — ESM cannot `require()`, and top-level `await` in the target causes a runtime crash** [community]

```typescript
// tsconfig.json: { "module": "nodenext" }

// ✅ CJS file calling require() on an ESM module (Node.js 22+, no top-level await):
// legacy.cjs:
// const { processData } = require("./modern-helper.mjs");

// ❌ ESM cannot call require() — no require binding in ESM scope:
// modern.mts:
// const dep = require("./other.mjs"); // ReferenceError: require is not defined

// ❌ require() of ESM with top-level await — runtime crash, not a TS error:
// modern-helper.mjs:
// const data = await fetchConfig(); // top-level await
// export const config = data;
// From legacy.cjs: require("./modern-helper.mjs")
// → Error at runtime: require() cannot import a module with top-level await

// ✅ Safe cross-format interop — use dynamic import() from CJS instead:
// legacy.cjs:
// async function init() {
//   const { processData } = await import("./modern-helper.mjs");
// }
```

WHY: Node.js 22 allows CJS modules to synchronously `require()` ESM files, but with two hard constraints: (1) only CJS can call `require()` on ESM — ESM scope has no `require` binding; (2) the required ESM module must complete synchronously, meaning it cannot use top-level `await`. TypeScript's `--module nodenext` flag models these semantics and allows `require()` calls in `.cts` files. However, TypeScript cannot statically detect top-level `await` in the imported `.mjs` file — that remains a silent runtime error. Teams should always check whether target ESM modules use top-level `await` before relying on `require()`.

---

**Gotcha 22 — `Symbol.metadata` is `undefined` at runtime unless polyfilled — decorator metadata silently does nothing without the polyfill** [community]

```typescript
// ❌ Without polyfill — Symbol.metadata is undefined at runtime:
function log(_: unknown, context: ClassFieldDecoratorContext) {
  context.metadata["logged"] = true; // stored in an orphaned object
}

class MyService {
  @log
  value = 42;
}

// At runtime without polyfill:
console.log((MyService as any)[Symbol.metadata]); // undefined — not { logged: true }

// ✅ ALWAYS add the polyfill at the top of your entry point:
Symbol.metadata ??= Symbol("Symbol.metadata");

// Now decorator metadata is correctly attached:
console.log((MyService as any)[Symbol.metadata]);
// { "value": true } — correct

// ✅ Polyfill placement rules:
// 1. In the application entry point (index.ts or main.ts)
// 2. BEFORE any module that defines a decorated class is imported
// 3. NOT inside a lazily-loaded module — too late
```

WHY: `Symbol.metadata` is defined by the TC39 decorator metadata proposal but has not yet been standardized into any JavaScript engine's built-in `Symbol` object as of 2026. The TypeScript compiler correctly generates code that uses `Symbol.metadata`, but the symbol itself must exist at runtime for the property to be stored on the class constructor under a consistent key. Without the `Symbol.metadata ??= Symbol(...)` polyfill, two things happen: (1) `context.metadata` writes succeed at the JavaScript object level — they write to an object associated with an *undefined* key; (2) `MyClass[Symbol.metadata]` returns `undefined` because `Symbol.metadata` now resolves to a missing property. The decorator decorator seems to work, but the data is stored unreachably.

---

**Gotcha 23 — `const` type parameter inference does NOT affect pre-declared variables — only inline literal expressions at the call site** [community]

```typescript
// ✅ const modifier works on inline literal arguments:
function makeEnum<const T extends readonly string[]>(values: T): T {
  return values;
}
const inline = makeEnum(["read", "write", "admin"]);
// type: readonly ["read", "write", "admin"] ✅

// ❌ const modifier does NOT affect a pre-declared variable:
const arr = ["read", "write", "admin"]; // inferred: string[]
const fromVar = makeEnum(arr);
// type: string[] — NOT readonly ["read", "write", "admin"]
// arr's type was already widened to string[] before the call.

// ✅ Fix 1: annotate the variable with as const:
const arrConst = ["read", "write", "admin"] as const;
const fromConst = makeEnum(arrConst);
// type: readonly ["read", "write", "admin"] ✅

// ✅ Fix 2: pass the array inline (avoids widening):
const fromInline = makeEnum(["read", "write", "admin"]);
// type: readonly ["read", "write", "admin"] ✅

// ✅ Fix 3: annotate the variable's type explicitly:
const arrTyped: readonly ["read", "write", "admin"] = ["read", "write", "admin"];
const fromTyped = makeEnum(arrTyped);
// type: readonly ["read", "write", "admin"] ✅
```

WHY: The `const` modifier on a type parameter instructs TypeScript to apply const-like inference to the *type inference algorithm* at the point of the call, not retroactively to already-typed variables. When you call `makeEnum(arr)`, TypeScript first resolves `arr`'s type (which was already widened to `string[]` when `arr` was declared without an annotation). The `const` modifier never revisits already-resolved types — it only affects the initial inference from inline literal expressions at the call site. If the argument's type has already been set to `string[]`, the `const` modifier cannot narrow it back to a tuple.

---

### Anti-Patterns: Cycle 33 Additions

| Anti-pattern | Why it's harmful | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Calling `isolatedDeclarations` on a single-package project | No build-time benefit; forces verbose explicit return types across all exports with no payoff | Only enable for monorepos where parallel declaration emit tools (Oxc, Vite DTS) are used |
| Using `import defer` expecting code-splitting / smaller bundles | `import defer` only defers *evaluation*, not *loading* — the module is always in the bundle | Use dynamic `import()` for conditional code-splitting |
| Forgetting `Symbol.metadata ??= ...` polyfill in the entry point | Decorator metadata silently does nothing; `MyClass[Symbol.metadata]` is `undefined` | Add the one-liner polyfill before any decorated class is loaded |
| Using `<const T extends string[]>` (mutable constraint) with array literals | TypeScript silently falls back to `string[]` when the mutable constraint is not satisfied by a `readonly` tuple | Use `<const T extends readonly string[]>` to guarantee literal inference |
| `require()` of an ESM module with top-level `await` from CJS | TypeScript allows the call; Node.js throws at runtime — not a type error | Audit target ESM modules for top-level `await` before using synchronous `require()` |
