## Cycle 35 — 2026-05-14

<!-- sources: official | community | mixed | cycle: 35 | score: 91/100 | date: 2026-05-14 -->

### Overview

This cycle deepens coverage of TypeScript 5.7–5.9 features, Node.js ESM/CJS interop patterns under the new module modes, `--erasableSyntaxOnly` migration strategies, `import defer` correct usage, variance annotation pitfalls, expect-type / tsd type-level testing patterns, and community-sourced gotchas around inference, overload resolution, and branded type erosion.

---

### Pattern 1 — `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions`: Type-Safe `.ts`→`.js` Extension Rewriting for Node.js ESM Projects [official]

**Description.** TypeScript 5.7 introduced `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions`, which automatically rewrites `.ts`, `.mts`, and `.cts` import extensions to their JavaScript equivalents (`.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`) in the emitted output. This flag solves the long-standing friction where projects targeting Node.js ESM must write `import './foo.js'` in source files even though the actual file on disk is `foo.ts`. The rewrite happens only for relative imports — bare specifiers and package imports are untouched. Enabling the flag combined with `"module": "nodenext"` or `"module": "node20"` produces a project that is simultaneously readable (`.ts` extensions in source) and spec-compliant (`.js` extensions in output).

```typescript
// tsconfig.json
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "module": "nodenext",
//     "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true,
//     "outDir": "dist"
//   }
// }

// src/utils/math.ts
export function add(a: number, b: number): number {
  return a + b;
}

// src/index.ts — write the import with .ts extension in source:
import { add } from "./utils/math.ts";         // ✅ valid in source
// Emitted dist/index.js will contain:
// import { add } from "./utils/math.js";       // ✅ valid in Node.js ESM

// ❌ Old pattern without the flag — required .js extension in .ts source:
import { add } from "./utils/math.js";  // confusing: file is actually .ts
```

**Tradeoff.** The rewriting is purely at the TypeScript emission layer — bundlers that process TypeScript directly (Vite, esbuild, tsx) do not need or honour this flag. Enabling it in bundler-targeted projects creates a mismatch: the `.ts` source extensions are valid for `tsc`, but some bundlers may not resolve them. Reserve this flag for projects using `tsc` as the sole emitter (CLI tools, Lambda functions, pure Node.js apps). [official]

---

### Pattern 2 — `--module node18` vs `--module node20` vs `--module nodenext`: Choosing the Right Stability Guarantee [official]

**Description.** TypeScript 5.8 added `--module node18` and TypeScript 5.9 added `--module node20` as "frozen" module modes that lock in the exact Node.js 18/20 semantics at the time of TypeScript release. In contrast, `--module nodenext` is a moving target — it updates with each TypeScript release to track the latest stable Node.js behavior. For library authors publishing to npm, `node18` or `node20` provides a stable baseline that will not silently change under future TypeScript upgrades. Application teams tracking the LTS release cycle should match the mode to their actual runtime. The key behavioral difference between node18 and node20 is that node18 disallows `require()` of ESM files entirely, while node20 (and nodenext from TS 5.8 onward) permits `require()` of ESM files that do not contain top-level `await`.

```typescript
// Library tsconfig — use frozen mode for predictable semver behavior:
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "module": "node18",
//     "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
//     "declaration": true,
//     "target": "es2020"
//   }
// }

// app/src/loader.ts — Node 22 app using nodenext to get require-of-ESM:
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "module": "nodenext"
//   }
// }

// With --module node20 / nodenext on Node 22:
// lib/esm-helper.mts — ESM module with NO top-level await
export function escapeHtml(s: string): string {
  return s.replace(/&/g, "&amp;").replace(/</g, "&lt;");
}

// app/src/legacy-cjs-consumer.cts — CommonJS can require ESM if no TLA:
const { escapeHtml } = require("../lib/esm-helper.js"); // ✅ Node 22 allows
console.log(escapeHtml("<script>"));

// ❌ This fails at runtime if esm-helper contained: await somePromise at top-level
```

**Tradeoff.** Using `nodenext` in a library means downstream consumers on older Node.js versions may encounter declaration file errors if TypeScript updates the semantics of `nodenext` again. `node18` and `node20` never change their behavior; prefer them for published packages. Application code benefits from `nodenext` to automatically pick up new Node.js interop features as they stabilize. [official]

---

### Pattern 3 — `--erasableSyntaxOnly`: Preparing Codebases for Node.js Native TypeScript Stripping [official]

**Description.** TypeScript 5.8 added `--erasableSyntaxOnly`, which emits a compile-time error for any TypeScript-specific syntax that has *runtime semantics* — meaning it cannot be removed by simple character erasure. The affected constructs are: `enum` declarations, `namespace`s containing runtime values, parameter properties in class constructors, and `import =` / `export =` CommonJS-style assignments. This flag is essential for projects that want to run TypeScript directly in Node.js 22+ using `--experimental-strip-types` or the Bun/Deno native TypeScript runners — those runtimes strip types by erasure only and will crash at runtime on any of the blocked constructs. Enabling the flag is a zero-cost safety net even if you are not yet using native stripping; it makes a future migration to strip-types trivial.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json with the flag:
// { "compilerOptions": { "erasableSyntaxOnly": true } }

// ❌ These constructs cause compile errors under erasableSyntaxOnly:

enum Direction { Up, Down, Left, Right }
// Error: 'enum' is not allowed with --erasableSyntaxOnly

namespace Validators {
  export function isPositive(n: number): boolean { return n > 0; }
}
// Error: namespace with runtime code is not allowed with --erasableSyntaxOnly

class Greeter {
  constructor(public name: string) {}
  // Error: parameter properties not allowed with --erasableSyntaxOnly
}

// ✅ Erasable replacements:
const Direction = { Up: 0, Down: 1, Left: 2, Right: 3 } as const;
type Direction = (typeof Direction)[keyof typeof Direction];

// ✅ Regular module export replaces namespace runtime code:
export function isPositive(n: number): boolean { return n > 0; }

// ✅ Explicit property replaces parameter property:
class GreeterFixed {
  name: string;
  constructor(name: string) { this.name = name; }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `--erasableSyntaxOnly` is not included in `--strict` and must be opted into explicitly. Converting existing `enum` types to `as const` loses nominal type isolation (see Gotcha 27 in Cycle 34); add branded types if the codebase relied on enum identity preventing cross-assignment. Projects using `ts-node` with `transpileOnly` mode are not protected by this flag during development — only an actual `tsc` check or `ts-node` in full-typecheck mode will surface the error. [official]

---

### Pattern 4 — `import defer` for Side-Effect Deferral Without Code Splitting [official]

**Description.** TypeScript 5.9 (tracking TC39 Stage 2.7) supports `import defer * as ns from "./module.js"`, which loads the module into the bundle/process but delays the execution of its top-level code until the first property access on `ns`. This is semantically different from `import()`: `import defer` is a static import (present in the module graph, always loaded) but with deferred *evaluation*. The correct use case is startup performance: an expensive library whose initialization (WASM compilation, schema precompilation, singleton construction) should not block the main thread / process startup, but which is guaranteed to be needed at some point. It cannot be used as a code-splitting mechanism because the module bytes are always downloaded.

```typescript
// Only works with: "module": "preserve" or "module": "esnext" in tsconfig

import defer * as cryptoLib from "./crypto-lib.js";
// crypto-lib's top-level code does NOT run yet.
// Heavy key-schedule initialization, WASM loading, etc. is deferred.

function hashPassword(plain: string): string {
  // First property access triggers crypto-lib.js top-level code exactly once:
  return cryptoLib.sha256(plain);
}

// ✅ Compared to: always-eager static import
import * as cryptoLibEager from "./crypto-lib.js"; // Runs top-level immediately at app start

// ✅ Compared to: dynamic import (separate chunk / HTTP request, true lazy loading)
async function hashPasswordLazy(plain: string): Promise<string> {
  const { sha256 } = await import("./crypto-lib.js"); // separate network request
  return sha256(plain);
}

// ❌ import defer does NOT support named or default imports:
// import defer { sha256 } from "./crypto-lib.js";  // Syntax error
// import defer defaultExport from "./crypto-lib.js"; // Syntax error
```

**Tradeoff.** `import defer` only works under `--module preserve` (for bundlers) or `--module esnext` — it is not supported under `node18`, `node20`, or `nodenext` because Node.js does not implement deferred evaluation in its ESM loader. Bundlers (Vite, Rollup 4+, webpack 5.92+) that have adopted the TC39 proposal emit a thunk wrapper; bundlers that have not adopted it silently fall back to eager evaluation, giving you no performance benefit and no error. Always verify bundler support before relying on this for production startup optimizations. [official]

---

### Pattern 5 — Granular Return-Branch Checks (TypeScript 5.8): Catching `any` Leaks in Ternary Returns [official]

**Description.** TypeScript 5.8 introduced narrowing of each branch of a conditional expression when the expression appears directly inside a `return` statement. Before 5.8, if one branch of a ternary produced `any`, the entire return expression was silently `any`, hiding type errors in the other branch. Now TypeScript checks each branch independently against the declared return type. This catches a category of subtle runtime bugs where a cache hit path returned `any` (from an untyped cache map) while the cache miss path was typechecked correctly, but the `any` from the hit path suppressed the error on the miss path too.

```typescript
// TS < 5.8: the 'any' from untypedCache.get() infected the whole expression
declare const untypedCache: Map<string, any>;

function getUser(id: string): { name: string; age: number } {
  // TS 5.7: no error — cache branch is 'any', contaminates entire return
  // TS 5.8: Error on second branch: 'string' is not assignable to '{ name: string; age: number }'
  return untypedCache.has(id)
    ? untypedCache.get(id)            // branch 1: any — ok
    : id;                             // branch 2: string — now flagged! ✅
}

// ✅ Fix: type the cache properly or assert:
const typedCache = new Map<string, { name: string; age: number }>();

function getUserFixed(id: string): { name: string; age: number } {
  return typedCache.has(id)
    ? typedCache.get(id)!             // ✅ Map<K,V>.get() → V | undefined; ! asserts defined
    : fetchUserById(id);              // ✅ return type checked independently
}

declare function fetchUserById(id: string): { name: string; age: number };
```

**Tradeoff.** This is a technically breaking change in TypeScript 5.8: codebases that relied on `any`-contamination to suppress branch-level type errors will surface new errors. The fix is almost always to type the cache or external source correctly rather than silence the error. Adding `// @ts-ignore` on these returns is a signal that the source data type is underspecified and should be addressed with proper typing or a runtime validation step. [official]

---

### Pattern 6 — `--module node20` Implied `es2023` Target: Avoiding the `nodenext` esnext Trap for Libraries [official]

**Description.** `--module nodenext` implies `--target esnext`, which expands to whatever the latest ECMAScript version TypeScript recognises. For application code this is fine, but for libraries targeting Node.js 20 this is too aggressive: `esnext` may emit syntax only available in experimental proposals that Node 20 does not ship. TypeScript 5.9's `--module node20` solves this by implying `--target es2023`, which matches Node 20's V8 version (11.3) and is a stable baseline. Libraries built with `--module node20` can be distributed to any Node.js 20+ consumer without the risk of syntax downgrade issues from using an explicit `--target` that lags behind `nodenext`'s moving baseline.

```typescript
// ❌ Library tsconfig.json with nodenext risks emitting future-syntax:
// { "compilerOptions": { "module": "nodenext" } }
// Implied target: esnext — today this is ES2025+, may emit using/await using,
// Array.fromAsync, Set methods etc. that Node 20.0 does not support.

// ✅ Library tsconfig.json with node20:
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "module": "node20",
//     "strict": true,
//     "declaration": true,
//     "verbatimModuleSyntax": true
//   }
// }
// Implied target: es2023 — matches Node 20's stable feature set.

// ✅ Verify the implied target in CI:
// tsc --showConfig | grep target
// Expected: "target": "es2023"

export function groupRecords<K extends PropertyKey, V>(
  items: V[],
  keyFn: (item: V) => K
): Map<K, V[]> {
  const result = new Map<K, V[]>();
  for (const item of items) {
    const key = keyFn(item);
    const bucket = result.get(key) ?? [];
    bucket.push(item);
    result.set(key, bucket);
  }
  return result;
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `--module node20` is frozen at TypeScript 5.9's snapshot of Node.js 20 semantics. As Node.js 20 eventually receives additional V8 updates and TypeScript updates its `node20` mode accordingly, your compilation behavior may change — but only when you upgrade TypeScript. For long-term stability, pin a major TypeScript version in your library's `devDependencies`. [official]

---

### Pattern 7 — TypedArray Generic Change (`Uint8Array<TArrayBuffer>`): Updating `Buffer` and `ArrayBuffer` Usage for TS 5.7+ [official]

**Description.** TypeScript 5.7 made all TypedArray types generic over their backing buffer type: `Uint8Array<TArrayBuffer extends ArrayBufferLike = ArrayBufferLike>`. This change enables precise typing of `SharedArrayBuffer`-backed views vs. regular `ArrayBuffer`-backed views. The immediate impact is that `Buffer` from Node.js (which extends `Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>`) is no longer assignable to functions expecting `Uint8Array<ArrayBufferLike>` in some contexts, and `ArrayBuffer` is no longer a structural supertype of TypedArray instances. Projects that pass raw `Uint8Array` instances where the underlying buffer is needed must now use `.buffer` explicitly.

```typescript
// TS 5.7+: TypedArray types are now generic
// Uint8Array<TArrayBuffer extends ArrayBufferLike = ArrayBufferLike>

function processBuffer(buf: ArrayBuffer): void {
  const view = new Uint8Array(buf);
  console.log(view.byteLength);
}

const data = new Uint8Array([1, 2, 3]);

// ❌ TS 5.7+: Uint8Array<ArrayBufferLike> is not assignable to ArrayBuffer
// processBuffer(data); // Error: Type 'Uint8Array<ArrayBufferLike>' not assignable to 'ArrayBuffer'

// ✅ Use .buffer to extract the underlying ArrayBuffer:
processBuffer(data.buffer);  // data.buffer is ArrayBuffer

// Node.js Buffer gotcha:
import { Buffer } from "node:buffer";
const nodeBuf = Buffer.from([1, 2, 3]);

// ❌ May error with older @types/node before the generic update:
// const u8: Uint8Array = nodeBuf; // Buffer<ArrayBuffer> vs Uint8Array<ArrayBufferLike>

// ✅ Fix: update @types/node to >=22.x which applies the generic:
// npm install --save-dev @types/node@latest

// ✅ Fix 2: if you own the function signature, accept the generic form:
function processView<T extends ArrayBufferLike>(view: Uint8Array<T>): number {
  return view.byteLength;
}
processView(data);    // ✅ Uint8Array<ArrayBufferLike>
processView(nodeBuf); // ✅ Buffer<ArrayBuffer> extends Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>
```

**Tradeoff.** This change can surface dozens of errors in older codebases that treat TypedArrays and ArrayBuffers as interchangeable. The cleanest fix is usually to update `@types/node` and change functions that accept `ArrayBuffer` to accept `ArrayBufferLike` or the generic `Uint8Array<T>` form. Projects using `BufferSource` (Web API union of `ArrayBuffer | ArrayBufferView`) should be unaffected if they use that union type rather than the concrete `ArrayBuffer`. [official]

---

### Pattern 8 — `verbatimModuleSyntax` + `isolatedDeclarations`: The Modern Library Authoring Baseline [official]

**Description.** For library development in 2025, the recommended baseline combines `verbatimModuleSyntax: true` and `isolatedDeclarations: true`. `verbatimModuleSyntax` ensures that all `import type` / `export type` syntax is preserved verbatim in emitted declarations, preventing the ambiguous re-exports that caused `esModuleInterop` bugs in older setups. `isolatedDeclarations` ensures that every exported symbol has a type annotation sufficient to produce a `.d.ts` file without full type inference — enabling build tools like oxc-transform and swc to emit declaration files without running TypeScript's type checker. The combination makes the library consumable by all module systems and enables 10–100x faster declaration emit in monorepos.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json for library authoring
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "module": "node18",
//     "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
//     "isolatedDeclarations": true,
//     "declaration": true,
//     "declarationMap": true,
//     "strict": true
//   }
// }

// src/api.ts — must annotate all exported symbols explicitly:
// ❌ Without isolatedDeclarations: inferred return type is fine
export function createUser(name: string) {
  return { id: Math.random(), name };
  // Error under isolatedDeclarations: return type must be explicit
}

// ✅ With isolatedDeclarations: explicit return type annotation required
export function createUserFixed(name: string): { id: number; name: string } {
  return { id: Math.random(), name };
}

// ✅ Type-only import is preserved verbatim in .d.ts under verbatimModuleSyntax:
import type { UserRecord } from "./db-types.js";
export function findUser(id: number): UserRecord | null {
  return null; // stub
}
// Emitted .d.ts: import type { UserRecord } from "./db-types.js"; <- preserved
```

**Tradeoff.** `isolatedDeclarations` requires explicit return type annotations on all exported functions, which increases verbosity. The TypeScript Language Service provides a quick-fix "Infer return type" to automate this for existing code, but retrofitting a large library can require 100+ annotation additions. The long-term payoff is declaration emit that runs in parallel with type-checking (using esbuild-plugin-dts or oxc) rather than sequentially, which cuts monorepo CI times significantly. [official]

---

### Pattern 9 — `expect-type` Library: Fluent Compile-Time Type Assertions Without a Separate CLI [community]

**Description.** The `expect-type` library (used internally by Vitest's `expectTypeOf`) provides Jest-like assertion syntax that executes entirely at the TypeScript compiler level. Unlike `tsd`, it requires no separate test runner invocation — the assertions live in `.test-d.ts` or regular `.test.ts` files and fail at compile time (`tsc --noEmit`). The key methods are: `.toEqualTypeOf<T>()` for exact structural equality, `.toMatchObjectType<T>()` for partial structural matching (analogous to `toMatchObject`), `.toBeCallableWith()` for function signature testing, and sentinel methods `.toBeAny()`, `.toBeNever()`, `.toBeUnknown()` to catch overly-permissive or overly-restrictive inferred types. These sentinel checks are critical in test fixture builders — a builder returning `any` will silently pass all runtime assertions but signals type safety has been lost.

```typescript
import { expectTypeOf } from "expect-type";

// ✅ Exact structural equality (no extra properties, no widening):
expectTypeOf({ id: 1, name: "Alice" }).toEqualTypeOf<{ id: number; name: string }>();

// ✅ Partial matching (extra properties allowed):
expectTypeOf({ id: 1, name: "Alice", role: "admin" })
  .toMatchObjectType<{ id: number; name: string }>();

// ✅ Function signature check:
function greet(name: string): string { return `Hello ${name}`; }
expectTypeOf(greet).toBeCallableWith("world");
expectTypeOf(greet).returns.toEqualTypeOf<string>();
expectTypeOf(greet).parameter(0).toEqualTypeOf<string>();

// ✅ Detect any-escaped types in generic builders:
function makeFixture<T>(): T { return {} as T; }
// ❌ This would pass silently at runtime but is a type hole:
// expectTypeOf(makeFixture<User>()).toEqualTypeOf<User>(); // passes — but makeFixture returns `any` in practice

// ✅ Sentinel check catches it:
expectTypeOf(makeFixture<string>()).not.toBeAny();
// If makeFixture returns `any`, this compile-time assertion fails, surfacing the hole.

// ✅ Promise resolution types:
async function fetchUser(): Promise<{ id: number }> { return { id: 1 }; }
expectTypeOf(fetchUser).returns.resolves.toEqualTypeOf<{ id: number }>();
```

**Tradeoff.** `expect-type` assertions fail silently when TypeScript's `--noEmit` is not run as part of CI — the assertions are compile-time only and produce zero runtime output. Teams must explicitly add `tsc --noEmit` (or `vue-tsc --noEmit` for Vue projects) to the CI pipeline. Unlike `tsd`, which exits with a non-zero code when type assertions fail in its own test runner, `expect-type` errors appear only as TypeScript diagnostics. Intersection types can cause false assertion failures because TypeScript's structural equality for intersections does not always reduce to the expected form. [community]

---

### Pattern 10 — Variance Annotations (`in`, `out`, `in out`): When to Annotate and When to Trust Inference [official]

**Description.** TypeScript 4.7 added explicit variance annotations (`in` for contravariance, `out` for covariance, `in out` for invariance) on generic type parameters. These annotations serve two distinct purposes: performance and documentation. Explicitly annotating variance allows the checker to skip structural variance inference, which is expensive for deeply nested generics in high-volume types. However, variance annotations do NOT change the structural assignability behavior of the type — TypeScript always performs a final structural check, and an incorrect annotation (e.g., `out T` on an invariant type) will cause the checker to emit an error. The primary consumer of this feature is library authors defining large utility type APIs (like `ReadonlyArray` or framework signal types) where type-checking time is measurable.

```typescript
// ✅ Covariant (out): the type parameter only appears in output positions
interface Producer<out T> {
  make(): T;
  peek(): T | undefined;
}
// ✅ Producer<Dog> is assignable to Producer<Animal> (covariant):
declare const dogProducer: Producer<{ breed: string }>;
const animalProducer: Producer<object> = dogProducer; // ✅ allowed

// ✅ Contravariant (in): the type parameter only appears in input positions
interface Consumer<in T> {
  consume(value: T): void;
}
// ✅ Consumer<Animal> is assignable to Consumer<Dog> (contravariant):
declare const objectConsumer: Consumer<object>;
const dogConsumer: Consumer<{ breed: string }> = objectConsumer; // ✅ allowed

// ✅ Invariant (in out): parameter appears in both input and output positions
interface ReadWrite<in out T> {
  get(): T;
  set(value: T): void;
}

// ❌ Incorrect annotation causes a compile-time error — TypeScript enforces correctness:
interface BrokenProducer<out T> {
  make(): T;
  // Error: 'T' appears in contravariant position — annotation 'out' is wrong here:
  consume(value: T): void;
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Variance annotations only benefit types that are used in generic instantiation comparisons — if your type is only ever used structurally, there is no performance benefit. The official TypeScript docs explicitly warn: "Don't use variance annotations to force particular typing behavior — they will only cause errors if they're wrong, not grant new capabilities." The primary win is in monorepos where a shared `types` package is instantiated thousands of times during a build; annotating those types can cut typecheck time by 20–40% in large projects. [official]

---

### Pattern 11 — `noUncheckedSideEffectImports`: Detecting Unresolvable Side-Effect-Only Imports [official]

**Description.** TypeScript 5.9 added `--noUncheckedSideEffectImports`, which causes the compiler to error when a side-effect-only import (`import "./some-module"`) targets a file that cannot be resolved. Without the flag, TypeScript silently ignores unresolvable side-effect imports — a common footgun when refactoring file paths, removing polyfill packages, or migrating from one CSS-in-JS solution to another. The flag is most valuable in projects that import CSS, polyfills, or global setup modules as side effects, because a path typo would otherwise be invisible until a runtime failure revealed the missing side effect.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json: { "compilerOptions": { "noUncheckedSideEffectImports": true } }

// ❌ Side-effect import with a typo is now a compile error:
import "./setup/polyfils.js";  // Error: Cannot find module './setup/polyfils.js'

// ✅ Correct:
import "./setup/polyfills.js";

// ✅ CSS side-effect imports in projects with allowArbitraryExtensions:
// (The .css resolver must exist; with noUncheckedSideEffectImports, missing .css errors)
import "./styles/global.css";

// ✅ Using the flag to audit legacy setup files:
// If a Jest setup file import silently stopped resolving after a rename,
// noUncheckedSideEffectImports surfaces it at compile time rather than at test runtime:

// jest.config.ts:
// setupFilesAfterEach: ["<rootDir>/src/test-setup.ts"]
// If test-setup.ts imports a missing side effect — TypeScript now catches it.

// Pattern for testing: side-effect-only test helpers
import "./test-utils/matchers-setup.ts"; // Must exist or tsc errors
import "./test-utils/global-mocks.ts";   // Must exist or tsc errors
```

**Tradeoff.** This flag was not included in `--strict` in TypeScript 5.9. In TypeScript 6.0 it becomes `true` by default. Enabling it early will surface previously-ignored missing imports in legacy codebases — expect a burst of new errors on first adoption that require either fixing the paths or explicitly removing the dead imports. In test projects that use `import "./setup"` patterns extensively, this is a high-value flag to add before the TS 6.0 upgrade. [official]

---

### Pattern 12 — `tsd` vs `expect-type` vs Vitest `expectTypeOf`: Choosing a Type-Testing Strategy [community]

**Description.** Three dominant approaches exist for type-level testing in 2025. `tsd` is a standalone CLI that parses `$ExpectType` and `$ExpectError` comments and runs as a separate process — it is the oldest approach and requires no TypeScript configuration. `expect-type` (used as a library) integrates into existing test files and fails at `tsc` compile time; Vitest ships `expectTypeOf` built on the same implementation. Vitest's `expectTypeOf` is the lowest-friction choice for projects already using Vitest — type assertions co-locate with runtime assertions in `.test.ts` files and run in the same `vitest --typecheck` pass. The critical difference is failure mode: `tsd` fails the `tsd` process, `expect-type` in `.test.ts` fails `tsc --noEmit`, and Vitest `expectTypeOf` fails the Vitest run when `--typecheck` is enabled.

```typescript
// --- Approach 1: tsd (separate .test-d.ts file) ---
// Requires: npm install --save-dev tsd
// test-types.test-d.ts:
// import { expectType } from "tsd";
// import { greet } from "../src/greet.js";
// expectType<string>(greet("world"));  // pass
// expectType<number>(greet("world"));  // fail

// --- Approach 2: expect-type in any .test.ts file ---
import { expectTypeOf } from "expect-type";
import { greet } from "../src/greet.js";

test("greet return type is string", () => {
  expectTypeOf(greet).returns.toEqualTypeOf<string>(); // compile-time check
  // Runtime: this block is effectively empty — no assertions execute
});

// --- Approach 3: Vitest built-in expectTypeOf (preferred for Vitest projects) ---
import { describe, it, expectTypeOf } from "vitest";

describe("greet types", () => {
  it("returns a string", () => {
    expectTypeOf(greet("world")).toEqualTypeOf<string>();
  });
  it("parameter is string", () => {
    expectTypeOf(greet).parameter(0).toEqualTypeOf<string>();
  });
  // Run with: vitest --typecheck
});

// ✅ Gotcha check — always test for sentinel types to prevent silent any-widening:
it("result is not any", () => {
  expectTypeOf(greet("world")).not.toBeAny();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Vitest `--typecheck` requires running `tsc` under the hood; in large monorepos it adds significant time to the test pass. A common optimisation is to run `--typecheck` only on the affected packages in CI (using `turbo run typecheck --filter=[HEAD^1]` or similar) rather than on every commit. The `tsd` approach has the lowest setup cost but the most awkward syntax and no IDE integration for failures beyond "tsc says there is no $ExpectError here." For new projects, Vitest `expectTypeOf` is the recommended choice. [community]

---

### Pattern 13 — `Promise.withResolvers()` Type-Safe Pattern (ES2024 / TS 5.7+) [official]

**Description.** TypeScript 5.7's `--target es2024` and `--lib es2024` expose `Promise.withResolvers<T>()`, which returns `{ promise: Promise<T>, resolve: (value: T) => void, reject: (reason?: unknown) => void }`. This eliminates the classic "resolve/reject variables hoisted out of the Promise constructor" anti-pattern, which required `let resolve!: (v: T) => void` with a definite assignment assertion. The type-safe version makes the resolver types explicit and eliminates the need for the exclamation-mark assertion. It is particularly valuable in test utilities where a deferred promise is used to synchronize async events.

```typescript
// ❌ Classic anti-pattern: hoisted resolver with definite assignment assertion
let resolveUser!: (user: { id: number }) => void;
const userPromise = new Promise<{ id: number }>((res) => { resolveUser = res; });
// 'resolveUser' is typed correctly but the ! assertion is a smell.

// ✅ ES2024 Promise.withResolvers<T>():
const { promise: userPromise2, resolve: resolveUser2, reject: rejectUser } =
  Promise.withResolvers<{ id: number }>();

// Types are correctly inferred without assertions:
resolveUser2({ id: 42 });        // ✅ resolve: (value: { id: number }) => void
rejectUser(new Error("failed")); // ✅ reject: (reason?: unknown) => void

// ✅ Test utility pattern — deferred promise for synchronizing async test flows:
function createDeferred<T>() {
  const { promise, resolve, reject } = Promise.withResolvers<T>();
  return { promise, resolve, reject };
}

// In a test (Vitest):
it("emits value after subscription", async () => {
  const deferred = createDeferred<string>();
  const emitter = new EventEmitter();
  emitter.once("data", (v: string) => deferred.resolve(v));
  emitter.emit("data", "hello");
  await expect(deferred.promise).resolves.toBe("hello");
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `Promise.withResolvers` requires `--lib es2024` or `--lib esnext` — if your tsconfig uses an earlier lib (e.g., `es2022`) the method will not be in scope and you will get a "Property 'withResolvers' does not exist on type 'PromiseConstructor'" error. For projects that cannot move to es2024 target, a type-safe polyfill is trivial to implement. Node.js 22+ ships `Promise.withResolvers` natively; Node.js 18 does not — check your runtime compatibility. [official]

---

### Pattern 14 — `satisfies` + `as const` Interaction: When to Chain, When They Conflict [community]

**Description.** Chaining `satisfies SomeType` with `as const` on an object literal is a popular pattern for getting both structural validation AND literal type preservation. The order matters: `expr satisfies T as const` is parsed as `(expr satisfies T) as const` due to operator precedence — `satisfies` runs first (structural check against `T`), then `as const` is applied. The gotcha is that for arrays of objects, `as const` applied *after* `satisfies RouteConfig[]` cannot retroactively freeze the element types that `satisfies` already resolved to the interface form. Reversing the order — `as const satisfies readonly T[]` — locks the literals first, then validates the frozen array against the interface.

```typescript
type RouteConfig = {
  path: string;
  method: "GET" | "POST" | "PUT" | "DELETE";
};

// ✅ satisfies validates structure; literals preserved for simple object:
const getUsers = {
  path: "/users",
  method: "GET",
} satisfies RouteConfig;
// typeof getUsers.method → "GET"  (literal preserved — satisfies doesn't widen)

// ❌ Array of route configs — wrong order loses literal types on elements:
const routes = [
  { path: "/users", method: "GET" },
  { path: "/posts", method: "POST" },
] satisfies RouteConfig[];
// typeof routes[0].method → string (satisfies widened each element to RouteConfig)

// ✅ Correct order for arrays — as const first, then satisfies:
const routesFixed = [
  { path: "/users", method: "GET" },
  { path: "/posts", method: "POST" },
] as const satisfies readonly RouteConfig[];
// typeof routesFixed[0].method → "GET" ✅ — as const locks literals first

// ✅ Both satisfy RouteConfig (structural check passes) AND retain literals:
type FirstMethod = (typeof routesFixed)[0]["method"]; // "GET"
```

**Tradeoff.** The `as const satisfies T` order (const first, satisfies second) is the safer pattern for arrays and nested objects because it locks literal types before the structural check. For simple top-level object literals, `satisfies T` alone already preserves literals. Teams should codify which pattern to use in a project style guide — mixing both orders in the same codebase confuses readers about which direction inference flows. [community]

---

### Pattern 15 — `using` and `await using` in Test Setup/Teardown: Resource-Safe Fixtures Without Manual `afterEach` [official]

**Description.** TypeScript 5.2's `using` and `await using` declarations (Explicit Resource Management, Stage 4 in TC39 and shipping in Node.js 18+ via the harmony flag, Node.js 22 natively) enable automatic disposal of resources when a variable goes out of scope, using the `Symbol.dispose` / `Symbol.asyncDispose` protocol. In test code this replaces fragile `beforeEach`/`afterEach` pairs for resource cleanup. A test that opens a database connection, starts a server, or registers a spy can declare the resource with `using` and the disposal runs automatically at scope exit — whether the test passes, fails, or throws. The `SuppressedError` type is the key diagnostic for cleanup failures: it wraps both the original error and the disposal error.

```typescript
// Requires: "target": "ES2022" and "lib": ["esnext.disposable"] or "ES2026"

// ✅ Test helper implementing Disposable:
class MockServer implements Disposable {
  private httpServer: { close(): void };
  readonly url: string;

  constructor(port: number) {
    this.httpServer = startTestServer(port);
    this.url = `http://localhost:${port}`;
  }

  [Symbol.dispose](): void {
    this.httpServer.close();
  }
}

declare function startTestServer(port: number): { close(): void };

// ✅ In a Vitest/Jest test — no afterEach needed:
it("processes user creation via HTTP", async () => {
  using server = new MockServer(3001);
  // [Symbol.dispose] runs when this block exits — even if the assertion throws

  const response = await fetch(`${server.url}/users`, {
    method: "POST",
    body: JSON.stringify({ name: "Alice" }),
  });

  expect(response.status).toBe(201);
});

// ✅ Async disposal for database connections:
class TestDb implements AsyncDisposable {
  constructor(public readonly pool: { end(): Promise<void>; query(sql: string): Promise<unknown> }) {}

  async [Symbol.asyncDispose](): Promise<void> {
    await this.pool.end();
  }
}

declare function createTestPool(): { end(): Promise<void>; query(sql: string): Promise<unknown> };

it("reads from test DB", async () => {
  await using db = new TestDb(createTestPool());
  const rows = await db.pool.query("SELECT 1");
  expect(rows).toBeDefined();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The `using` declaration is only available inside a block scope — it cannot be used at module level or in `describe` callbacks that set up shared state across multiple `it` blocks. For shared fixture state across a `describe`, continue using `beforeEach`/`afterEach` with explicit teardown calls. Also, Vitest 1.x does not automatically understand `using` inside test bodies for async disposal sequences; ensure the Vitest version is 2.x+ which aligns with the TC39 spec's execution order for `await using`. [official]

---

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha 29 — `--erasableSyntaxOnly` does NOT error on same-file `const enum` — but `const enum` in published `.d.ts` files is still a runtime hazard under native type stripping** [community]

```typescript
// ✅ Regular enum: ERRORS under --erasableSyntaxOnly (has runtime code)
// enum Status { Active = "ACTIVE" }  // Error: enum not allowed

// ✅ const enum in the SAME file: does NOT error (values inlined and erased)
const enum Direction { Up = "UP", Down = "DOWN" }
const dir: Direction = Direction.Up; // inlined to "UP" — erasable ✅

// ❌ const enum declared in a .d.ts consumed from another package — RUNTIME HAZARD:
// types/shared.d.ts:
//   const enum SharedStatus { Pending = 0, Active = 1 }
//
// src/consumer.ts:
//   import type { SharedStatus } from "shared-types";
//   const s: SharedStatus = SharedStatus.Active;
//
// With Node.js --experimental-strip-types or Bun/Deno type erasure:
// The TypeScript inlining never happened. strip-types erases types but leaves:
//   const s = SharedStatus.Active  →  ReferenceError at runtime.
// --erasableSyntaxOnly does NOT catch this cross-.d.ts pattern.

// ✅ Fix: Enable isolatedModules: true — it DOES error on cross-.d.ts const enum imports.
// ✅ Replace const enum in published .d.ts with as const objects:
// export const SharedStatus = { Pending: 0, Active: 1 } as const;
// export type SharedStatus = (typeof SharedStatus)[keyof typeof SharedStatus];
```

WHY: `--erasableSyntaxOnly` checks whether the *source file being compiled* contains non-erasable constructs. A `const enum` defined in the same source file is inlined by `tsc` before erasure, so the flag passes it. However, a `const enum` imported from a `.d.ts` file (a third-party or monorepo package) bypasses `tsc`'s inlining when using native type-stripping runtimes — the runtime strips type annotations but does not perform constant inlining. The result is a reference to an identifier that does not exist. `--isolatedModules: true` (or `verbatimModuleSyntax`) correctly errors on this pattern as a necessary complement to `--erasableSyntaxOnly` for fully safe native-strip projects.

---

**Gotcha 30 — `import defer` evaluation guarantee depends on bundler support — unsupported bundlers silently fall back to eager evaluation** [community]

```typescript
// ✅ Spec-compliant runtimes (Chromium 124+, Bun 1.1+, Node.js 23 with --experimental-vm-modules):
import defer * as heavyLib from "./heavy-lib.js";
// heavyLib's top-level code does NOT run here in spec-compliant runtimes.

// ❌ In webpack < 5.94 or esbuild (no implementation as of 2025-Q2):
// import defer is silently treated as a regular eager import.
// heavy-lib.js top-level code runs immediately. No compile error. No runtime error.
// The startup optimization is silently lost.

// ✅ Bundler support checklist (2025):
// webpack:  >= 5.94.0  (requires experiments.deferredImports: true in config)
// Rollup:   >= 4.17.0
// Vite:     tracks Rollup — verify with vite@latest
// esbuild:  NOT implemented (tsup/unbuild based on esbuild also unaffected)

// ✅ Runtime verification — detect eager evaluation in tests:
// In heavy-lib.js:
// let _sideEffectRan = false;
// export const _markEvaluated = (() => { _sideEffectRan = true; return _sideEffectRan; })();
//
// In test:
// import defer * as heavyLib from "./heavy-lib.js";
// it("defers module evaluation", () => {
//   // If truly deferred, _sideEffectRan has not run yet:
//   expect(heavyLib._markEvaluated).toBe(true); // triggers evaluation NOW
// });
```

WHY: TypeScript only validates the *syntax* of `import defer` — it does not check whether the target bundler or runtime supports deferred evaluation semantics. A project using tsup or esbuild to bundle will compile without errors but receive eager evaluation silently. Because the optimization is invisible to normal functionality tests (the module is still loaded, just at a different time), the regression will only appear in startup-time benchmarks. Teams should add a runtime guard or an integration test that verifies the deferred evaluation timing if startup performance is the motivation for adopting `import defer`.

---

**Gotcha 31 — `satisfies` on a generic function call site does NOT constrain the generic parameter — it only validates the output type** [community]

```typescript
// Developers expect satisfies to "push" the type into the generic, like an annotation.
// It does NOT — satisfies only validates the OUTPUT of the expression.

function makeConfig<T extends Record<string, unknown>>(config: T): T {
  return config;
}

// ❌ Misconception: satisfies will constrain T to { port: number } and reject extra props
const cfg = makeConfig({ port: 8080, debug: "yes" }) satisfies { port: number };
// TypeScript infers T as { port: number; debug: string } from the argument.
// Then satisfies checks: does { port: number; debug: string } satisfy { port: number }? YES.
// No error. typeof cfg → { port: number; debug: string } — debug is NOT rejected.

// ✅ To constrain the INPUT (and thus T), use an explicit type annotation on the variable:
const cfgStrict: { port: number } = makeConfig({ port: 8080, debug: "yes" });
// Error: Object literal may only specify known properties,
//        and 'debug' does not exist in type '{ port: number }'

// ✅ Alternatively, constrain the generic explicitly at the call site:
const cfgGeneric = makeConfig<{ port: number }>({ port: 8080, debug: "yes" });
// Error: Object literal may only specify known properties — debug not in { port: number }

// ✅ satisfies IS correct for validating that a widened type meets a minimum shape:
const appConfig = {
  port: 8080,
  debug: "yes",
  host: "localhost",
} satisfies { port: number }; // ✅ validates minimum shape without restricting extra keys
```

WHY: `satisfies` operates *after* type inference has already determined the type of the expression. It is a post-inference assertion, not a pre-inference constraint. This makes `satisfies` useful for checking that a value is compatible with a shape without widening the inferred type — but it cannot push constraint information backward into a generic function call. For input-constraining use cases, an explicit type annotation or explicit generic type argument is required. This is one of the most commonly misunderstood aspects of `satisfies`.

---

**Gotcha 32 — `verbatimModuleSyntax` rejects value-style re-exports of types — all type re-exports require explicit `export type { }` syntax** [community]

```typescript
// tsconfig.json: { "compilerOptions": { "verbatimModuleSyntax": true } }

// src/types.ts:
export interface UserRecord { id: number; name: string; }
export type UserId = number;
export class UserService { /* ... */ }

// src/index.ts — re-exporting:

// ❌ Error under verbatimModuleSyntax:
export { UserRecord } from "./types.js";
// Error: Re-exporting a type when 'verbatimModuleSyntax' is enabled
//        requires using 'export type'. Did you mean 'export type { UserRecord }'?

export { UserId } from "./types.js";
// Same error — UserId is a type alias.

// ✅ Fix: use export type for all type/interface re-exports:
export type { UserRecord } from "./types.js";
export type { UserId } from "./types.js";

// ✅ Class exports (which have runtime value) remain as value exports:
export { UserService } from "./types.js"; // ✅ UserService is a runtime value — no error

// ✅ Inline type modifier — export multiple from one line:
export { type UserRecord, type UserId, UserService } from "./types.js";
```

WHY: `verbatimModuleSyntax` requires that JavaScript module semantics are unambiguous from TypeScript syntax alone. When a re-export does not use `type`, TypeScript must keep it in the JavaScript output in case it is a runtime value. If it is actually type-only, this creates phantom exports in the emitted `.js` file that reference non-existent runtime identifiers — causing errors in strict ESM environments where imports are validated eagerly. By requiring `export type`, the flag ensures the emitted JavaScript is correct for every module system without TypeScript needing to consult cross-file type information.

---

**Gotcha 33 — `Array.isArray()` narrows `readonly T[]` to mutable `T[]` — mutations type-check correctly but crash at runtime on frozen arrays** [community]

```typescript
// Array.isArray narrows to the mutable form, stripping readonly silently.

function processInput(value: string | readonly string[]): string[] {
  if (Array.isArray(value)) {
    // TypeScript narrows value to string[] here — NOT readonly string[].
    // Array.isArray signature: (arg: unknown) => arg is any[]
    // The 'any[]' is mutable — readonly is erased by the narrowing.
    value.push("extra"); // ✅ No compile error — but may crash at runtime!
    return value;        // ✅ Assignable to string[] — readonly stripped
  }
  return [value];
}

const frozenArr = ["a", "b", "c"] as const;
processInput(frozenArr); // Runtime: frozenArr.push throws TypeError on frozen array!

// ✅ Fix 1: Custom type guard that preserves readonly:
function isReadonlyArray<T>(value: unknown): value is readonly T[] {
  return Array.isArray(value);
}

function processInputSafe(value: string | readonly string[]): readonly string[] {
  if (isReadonlyArray<string>(value)) {
    // value is now readonly string[] — push is not available ✅
    return value;
  }
  return [value];
}

// ✅ Fix 2: Use ReadonlyArray at function boundaries consistently:
function processInputBoundary(value: string | ReadonlyArray<string>): ReadonlyArray<string> {
  return Array.isArray(value) ? value : [value];
  // Not mutating — no issue. Mutation would require an explicit Array.from() copy.
}
```

WHY: TypeScript's built-in `Array.isArray` is typed as `(arg: unknown) => arg is any[]`. The `any[]` form is mutable — there is no corresponding `readonly any[]` overload because readonly is not a runtime concept and `Array.isArray` cannot distinguish mutable from frozen arrays at runtime. This means the narrowing always strips the `readonly` modifier, silently allowing mutation code to compile on an array that may have been frozen or declared `as const`. The fix is a custom `isReadonlyArray<T>` guard that narrows to `readonly T[]`, keeping the mutation constraint visible in the type system. Note: TypeScript may address this with a `ReadonlyArray` overload in a future release.

### Anti-Patterns: Cycle 35 Additions

| Anti-pattern | Why it's harmful | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Using `--module nodenext` for a published npm library | `nodenext` tracks the latest Node.js semantics and will change behavior with TypeScript upgrades, breaking consumers on older Node.js | Use frozen `--module node18` or `--module node20` so library semantics are stable across TypeScript releases |
| Using `import defer` expecting code-splitting / reduced bundle size | `import defer` defers module *evaluation*, not loading — the module is always in the bundle | Use dynamic `import()` for actual lazy loading; use `import defer` only for deferred side-effect initialization |
| Using `satisfies` to constrain generic call-site inputs | `satisfies` is a post-inference output check, not an input constraint — extra properties pass silently | Use an explicit type annotation on the variable or an explicit generic type argument to constrain the input |
| Re-exporting type-only symbols without `export type { }` under `verbatimModuleSyntax` | Creates phantom runtime exports in emitted JS that cause runtime errors in strict ESM environments | Use `export type { Symbol }` or `export { type Symbol }` inline syntax for all type-only re-exports |
| Calling `Array.isArray()` and then mutating — assuming readonly is preserved | `Array.isArray` narrows to mutable `T[]`, silently stripping `readonly` — mutations on frozen arrays cause runtime `TypeError` | Use a custom `isReadonlyArray<T>` type guard that narrows to `readonly T[]` to preserve mutation safety |
| Not adding `noUncheckedSideEffectImports: true` before upgrading to TS 6.0 | TS 6.0 enables this by default; missing side-effect imports silently ignored in TS 5.x will become compile errors | Enable the flag in TS 5.9 to surface and fix missing side-effect imports proactively |
| Using `const enum` in published `.d.ts` files with `erasableSyntaxOnly` enabled | `erasableSyntaxOnly` only checks the current file — cross-.d.ts const enum inlining is a runtime hazard under native type stripping | Replace `const enum` with `as const` objects in all published declaration files; also enable `isolatedModules: true` |
