### Pattern 1 — TypeScript 6.0: `types: []` Default — Eliminating Phantom `@types` Pollution [official]

TypeScript 6.0 changes the default value of `compilerOptions.types` from "auto-include all `@types/*` packages" to an empty array `[]`. Previously, every `@types/*` package in `node_modules` was automatically added to the compilation, introducing ambient globals (e.g., `jest`, `node`) even when unused. In 6.0, only packages explicitly listed in `types` are included, improving build times by 20-50% in large monorepos. Any project that relied on ambient globals from auto-included `@types` will see errors on upgrade — `describe`, `it`, `process`, and `Buffer` may suddenly appear unknown. The fix is to list only the packages you actually need.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json — TS 6.0 required explicit opt-in
// BEFORE (TS 5.x auto-included everything):
// { "compilerOptions": {} }
// — quietly gave you jest globals, node globals, etc.

// AFTER (TS 6.0 explicit):
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "types": ["node", "jest"]  // Only these ambient packages apply globally
  }
}

// In source: was silently available before, now requires the explicit entry:
//   describe("test", () => { ... })   // requires "jest" in types
//   process.env.NODE_ENV               // requires "node" in types

// Type-safe check you can put in a startup test:
import type {} from "node"; // Compile-time assertion that node types are present
const env: string | undefined = process.env.NODE_ENV; // typed correctly

// If you have mixed packages (some need globals, some do not):
// Use a per-tsconfig approach:
// tsconfig.src.json  → "types": ["node"]
// tsconfig.test.json → "types": ["node", "jest", "testing-library__jest-dom"]
```

**Tradeoff:** Explicit `types` is more correct and faster, but requires upfront audit of every `@types` package your code depends on for ambient globals. Library authors must ensure their declaration files do not rely on auto-included types leaking in from consumers. [official]

---

### Pattern 2 — TypeScript 6.0: `strict: true` by Default and the `ignoreDeprecations` Escape Hatch [official]

TypeScript 6.0 enables `strict: true` for all projects by default. Codebases that never explicitly set `strict` and relied on lenient checking (e.g., no `strictNullChecks`, no `noImplicitAny`) will encounter a wave of new errors after upgrading. The `"ignoreDeprecations": "6.0"` tsconfig field provides a soft landing — it suppresses warnings from deprecated options without re-enabling strict mode, giving teams time to fix errors incrementally. The intent is to use this as a temporary bridge; all deprecated options listed under `ignoreDeprecations: "6.0"` will be hard-errors in TypeScript 7.0.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json — temporary migration bridge for large codebases
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "ignoreDeprecations": "6.0",   // suppress "option deprecated" warnings
    "strict": false,               // opt out explicitly while you migrate
    "strictNullChecks": true,      // enable individual strict flags incrementally
    "noImplicitAny": true
  }
}

// Recommended incremental migration order:
// 1. Set ignoreDeprecations: "6.0" + strict: false on upgrade day
// 2. Enable strictNullChecks — usually highest-signal, lowest-noise
// 3. Enable noImplicitAny — catches untyped function params
// 4. Enable strictFunctionTypes — catches contravariant callback bugs
// 5. Enable strictPropertyInitialization — catches uninitialized class fields
// 6. Drop ignoreDeprecations and strict:false when all errors resolved

// Signal helper: Use a type alias to track what strict flags are on:
type _StrictCheck = {
  strictNullChecks: true; // enabled
  noImplicitAny: true;    // enabled
  strictFunctionTypes: true; // pending
};
```

**Tradeoff:** Migrating a large codebase to strict mode is high-effort but yields significant long-term reliability gains. The incremental approach via `ignoreDeprecations` avoids a "big bang" upgrade that blocks releases. Teams should time-box each strict flag rather than leaving `strict: false` indefinitely. [official]

---

### Pattern 3 — TypeScript 6.0: `RegExp.escape()` for Safe Dynamic Regex Construction [official]

TypeScript 6.0 adds the `es2025` target and lib, which includes `RegExp.escape()` — a long-awaited static method that escapes special regex characters in a string. Before this, developers either wrote their own escape function (often missing edge cases like `^`, `$`, `{`, `.`) or used a library. `RegExp.escape()` is the TC39 Stage 4 standard, available in Node.js 24+ and modern browsers. The TypeScript type is `(str: string) => string`. Using it prevents ReDoS vulnerabilities when user input is injected into regex patterns.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json: "lib": ["es2025"] or "target": "es2025"

// Before — hand-rolled escape with common omissions:
function escapeRegex(s: string): string {
  // Easy to miss: !, @, |, {, }, (, ), +, ?, ^, $, \
  return s.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, "\\$&");
}

// After — ES2025 built-in:
function searchInText(userInput: string, haystack: string): RegExpMatchArray | null {
  const safePattern = RegExp.escape(userInput); // All special chars escaped
  return haystack.match(new RegExp(`\\b${safePattern}\\b`, "g"));
}

// Type-safe wrapper for compile-time check:
function buildSafeRegex(fragments: readonly string[]): RegExp {
  const escaped = fragments.map(RegExp.escape).join("|");
  return new RegExp(`(${escaped})`, "gi");
}

// Test:
const re = buildSafeRegex(["foo.bar", "user+input", "[danger]"]);
console.log(re.source); // "(foo\.bar|user\+input|\[danger\])"

// In TypeScript — the type is simply:
// RegExp.escape(str: string): string
```

**Tradeoff:** `RegExp.escape()` requires Node.js 24+ or a polyfill for older runtimes. Add a polyfill check in your `lib.es2025.d.ts` shim if targeting Node.js 22/20. The method does not accept flags or anchors — it only escapes the string body, so you still need to compose the full pattern yourself. [official]

---

### Pattern 4 — TypeScript 6.0: `Map.getOrInsert()` / `Map.getOrInsertComputed()` for Idiomatic Cache Patterns [official]

TypeScript 6.0 with `"lib": ["es2025"]` exposes two new `Map` and `WeakMap` instance methods from the TC39 upsert proposal: `getOrInsert(key, defaultValue)` and `getOrInsertComputed(key, factory)`. These replace the verbose `has` + `get` + `set` idiom that every TypeScript codebase independently reimplements — often with subtle bugs when `defaultValue` is falsy (e.g., 0, `false`, `""`). The computed variant defers the factory function, which is critical for expensive computations that should only run on cache miss.

```typescript
// Before — verbose and falsy-buggy pattern:
function getOrCreateEntry(cache: Map<string, number[]>, key: string): number[] {
  if (!cache.has(key)) {          // Bug: also misses key => [] (empty array is falsy)
    cache.set(key, []);
  }
  return cache.get(key)!;         // Non-null assertion needed
}

// After — ES2025 getOrInsert:
function getOrCreateEntry(cache: Map<string, number[]>, key: string): number[] {
  return cache.getOrInsert(key, []); // Always returns existing or new value
  // Note: [] is evaluated eagerly — use getOrInsertComputed for lazy creation
}

// For expensive factory:
function getOrBuildComponent(
  cache: Map<string, HTMLElement>,
  id: string
): HTMLElement {
  return cache.getOrInsertComputed(id, (key) => {
    // Factory only runs on cache miss:
    const el = document.createElement("div");
    el.id = key;
    return el;
  });
}

// Type signatures (from lib.es2025.d.ts):
interface Map<K, V> {
  getOrInsert(key: K, defaultValue: V): V;
  getOrInsertComputed(key: K, callbackfn: (key: K) => V): V;
}
// WeakMap gets the same methods
```

**Tradeoff:** `getOrInsert` evaluates the default value eagerly — if the default is a mutable object like `[]` or `{}`, the same reference is used every time, which is correct. `getOrInsertComputed` is safer when the default is an expensive object or has side effects. Both methods require the `es2025` lib and Node.js 24+ at runtime. [official]

---

### Pattern 5 — TypeScript 6.0: `--stableTypeOrdering` as a 7.0 Pre-flight Check [official]

TypeScript 7.0 will introduce parallel type checking, which requires deterministic type ordering. TypeScript 6.0's `--stableTypeOrdering` flag opts into that ordering ahead of time, surfacing any type errors that arise from ordering differences between 6.0 and 7.0. It adds up to 25% overhead and is not intended for long-term use — it is purely a diagnostic tool. Teams should run it in CI before the 7.0 upgrade to get a zero-surprise migration. Errors under `--stableTypeOrdering` but not without it indicate that some type-level logic depends on insertion order of type members, which is fragile.

```typescript
// tsconfig.diagnostics.json — run separately in CI, not in daily dev:
{
  "extends": "./tsconfig.json",
  "compilerOptions": {
    "stableTypeOrdering": true
  }
}

// CI script:
// npx tsc --project tsconfig.diagnostics.json --noEmit

// What this flag catches — ordering-sensitive union resolution:
type Config = { a: string } | { b: number };
declare function pick<T extends Config>(cfg: T): T;
// With unstable ordering, inferred T may differ between TS 6.0 and 7.0.
// stableTypeOrdering makes TS 6.0 match TS 7.0, surfacing the difference now.

// Common false alarms (patterns that produce ordering-dependent types):
// 1. Mapped types over large union keys
// 2. Intersection types with many constituents
// 3. Overloaded functions where resolution order matters
// 4. Declaration merging across module augmentations

// Recommended: run flag weekly in CI, log errors to a dedicated report:
// npx tsc --project tsconfig.diagnostics.json --noEmit 2>&1 | tee ts7-precheck.log
```

**Tradeoff:** The 25% overhead makes this impractical in hot paths like watch mode or IDE incremental builds. Reserve it for a dedicated CI job. Teams that never surface any errors under this flag are well-positioned for a drop-in TS 7.0 upgrade. [official]

---

### Pattern 6 — TypeScript 6.0: `--baseUrl` Deprecation — Migrating Path Aliases to Explicit `paths` Entries [official]

TypeScript 6.0 deprecates `--baseUrl`, which will be removed in TypeScript 7.0. Projects that used `baseUrl: "./src"` to enable bare-module imports like `import { foo } from "utils/helpers"` without a `paths` entry must now include the base prefix explicitly in every `paths` entry. This is a mechanical migration but affects every path alias declaration. Bundlers (Vite, webpack, esbuild) that also relied on `baseUrl` for alias resolution need to be updated independently — TypeScript deprecating `baseUrl` does not automatically update bundler configs.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json — BEFORE (TS 5.x with baseUrl):
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "baseUrl": "./src",
    "paths": {
      "@app/*": ["app/*"],
      "@lib/*": ["lib/*"]
    }
  }
}

// tsconfig.json — AFTER (TS 6.0 without baseUrl):
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "paths": {
      "@app/*": ["./src/app/*"],  // Full prefix required
      "@lib/*": ["./src/lib/*"]   // Full prefix required
    }
  }
}

// Also update your bundler config — vite.config.ts:
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import path from "path";

export default defineConfig({
  resolve: {
    alias: {
      "@app": path.resolve(__dirname, "./src/app"),
      "@lib": path.resolve(__dirname, "./src/lib"),
    },
  },
});

// Migration helper — list all bare-module imports still relying on baseUrl:
// npx tsc --noEmit 2>&1 | grep "Cannot find module" | sort -u
```

**Tradeoff:** The migration is mechanical but requires touching both `tsconfig.json` and every bundler/tool that processes alias resolution separately. `paths` without `baseUrl` is more explicit and less surprising — the old `baseUrl` behavior was confusing because it silently affected all bare-module imports, not just the ones in `paths`. [official]

---

### Pattern 7 — TypeScript 6.0: `dom.iterable` Included in `dom` by Default [official]

TypeScript 6.0 merges `dom.iterable` and `dom.asynciterable` into the main `lib.dom.d.ts` bundle. Projects that previously had to list `"lib": ["dom", "dom.iterable", "esnext"]` can drop the separate `dom.iterable` entry. The practical impact: `NodeList`, `HTMLCollection`, `FormData`, `URLSearchParams`, and `Headers` are now directly iterable without needing the extra lib entry. Removing the explicit `dom.iterable` from `lib` is safe — it is still included. The only breaking case is if a project explicitly excluded `dom.iterable` from a customized lib build, which is rare but possible.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json — BEFORE (TS 5.x):
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "lib": ["dom", "dom.iterable", "esnext"]
  }
}

// tsconfig.json — AFTER (TS 6.0 — dom.iterable included automatically):
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "lib": ["dom", "esnext"]  // dom.iterable no longer needed explicitly
  }
}

// What this unlocks without extra config:
function processFormData(form: HTMLFormElement): Record<string, string> {
  const result: Record<string, string> = {};
  const data = new FormData(form);
  for (const [key, value] of data) {  // directly iterable in TS 6.0 with just "dom"
    if (typeof value === "string") {
      result[key] = value;
    }
  }
  return result;
}

function getAllHrefs(doc: Document): string[] {
  return Array.from(doc.querySelectorAll("a"))  // NodeList iterable
    .map((el) => (el as HTMLAnchorElement).href);
}

// Also works now without dom.iterable:
for (const [key, values] of new URLSearchParams("a=1&b=2")) {
  console.log(key, values);
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Projects using `--noLib` + custom lib arrays need to audit whether they relied on `dom.iterable` being separate. For the vast majority of projects this is a pure improvement with zero migration cost. The consolidation removes a common "why is NodeList not iterable?" support question. [official]

---

### Pattern 8 — TypeScript 5.9: `--module node20` — A Stable Alternative to `nodenext` for Node.js 20 Projects [official]

TypeScript 5.9 introduces `--module node20` as a frozen snapshot of Node.js 20 module semantics. Unlike `--module nodenext` (which tracks the latest Node.js and can silently change behavior with TypeScript upgrades), `node20` is stable — its behavior will never change in future TypeScript releases. It implies `--target es2023` by default and supports `require()` of ECMAScript modules from CommonJS (a Node.js 22+ feature backported to `node20` semantics). For teams pinned to Node.js 20 LTS, `node20` is the correct choice over `nodenext`.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json — for Node.js 20 LTS projects:
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "node20",      // Stable Node.js 20 semantics — never changes
    "target": "es2023",      // Implied by node20, set explicitly for clarity
    "moduleResolution": "nodenext"  // Still use nodenext for resolution
  }
}

// What node20 enables vs node18:
// - require() of ECMAScript modules (node20 allows it, node18 does not)
// - import attributes with "with" keyword (both support this)
// - import.meta.url in CommonJS modules (both support this)

// What nodenext changes vs node20:
// nodenext may enable require() of ESM, disable import assertions, or
// change resolution for new Node.js versions — breaking existing code silently.

// Application projects — use node20 when:
// 1. You are on Node.js 20 LTS and want stable TypeScript upgrades
// 2. You need require() of ESM but not Node.js 22 features
// 3. You want noUncheckedSideEffectImports: false (node18 default behavior)

// Library authoring — do NOT use node20 for library tsconfig:
// Published libraries should use "moduleResolution": "bundler" with
// explicit exports in package.json, not module: node20 which ties you
// to Node.js 20 semantics.
```

**Tradeoff:** `node20` is more predictable than `nodenext` for teams that do not want module semantics to change under them during routine TypeScript upgrades. The cost is that you opt out of automatic adoption of new Node.js features — you must explicitly move from `node20` to `node22` (or `nodenext`) when ready. [official]

---

### Pattern 9 — TypeScript 5.9: `tsc --init` Prescriptive Defaults and the `"types": []` Combination [official]

TypeScript 5.9 revamps the `tsc --init` output to generate a minimal, opinionated `tsconfig.json` rather than a heavily-commented file with hundreds of commented-out options. The new defaults include `module: "nodenext"`, `target: "esnext"`, `strict: true`, `moduleDetection: "force"`, `types: []`, and `jsx: "react-jsx"`. These defaults anticipate TypeScript 6.0's new defaults and reflect modern best practices. Teams starting new projects with `tsc --init` in TS 5.9 will already be positioned for a smooth TS 6.0 upgrade. The `"types": []` entry makes the 6.0 behavior explicit from the start.

```typescript
// Generated tsconfig.json from `tsc --init` in TypeScript 5.9:
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "nodenext",
    "target": "esnext",
    "strict": true,
    "moduleDetection": "force",
    "types": [],
    "jsx": "react-jsx"
  }
}

// moduleDetection: "force" — treats all files as modules (not scripts):
// This prevents the "augments global scope" error in projects with shared globals.
// Without it, a file with no imports/exports is treated as a script,
// meaning `declare const x` leaks into all other files' global scope.

// For Node.js projects, extend with:
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "node20",
    "target": "es2023",
    "outDir": "./dist",
    "rootDir": "./src",
    "declaration": true,
    "strict": true,
    "moduleDetection": "force",
    "types": ["node"]         // Explicit — only node ambient types
  },
  "include": ["./src"]
}

// Common gotcha with the new tsc --init defaults:
// The empty "types": [] means @types/node globals are NOT available.
// If you have a Node.js app and run tsc --init without adding "node",
// process, Buffer, __dirname, etc. will all be unknown.
// Add "node" to types BEFORE writing any Node.js code.
```

**Tradeoff:** The prescriptive defaults are excellent for new projects but surprise teams updating `tsc --init` on existing projects — they expect the old commented template. Teams should treat `tsc --init` as a starting point and review the generated config carefully, especially `"types": []`. [official]

---

### Pattern 10 — TypeScript 5.9: Type Argument Inference Leak Fixes — Diagnosing `never` Surprises After Upgrade [official]

TypeScript 5.9 fixes several cases where type variables "leaked" during inference, causing the inferred type to be broader (or narrower) than expected. These fixes may introduce new errors in codebases that previously compiled cleanly by accidentally relying on leaky inference. The symptom is typically `never` appearing where a concrete type is expected, or a union type resolving to `unknown` instead of a specific member. The fix is to add explicit type arguments to the affected generic call.

```typescript
// Inference that changed between TS 5.8 and 5.9:
declare function merge<A, B>(a: A, b: B): A & B;

// Both versions agree on the simple case:
const result = merge({ x: 1 }, { y: "hello" });
// result: { x: number } & { y: string }

// More subtle case — generic constraint inference leakage:
declare function pick<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, keys: K[]): Pick<T, K>;

function extractFields<T>(obj: T) {
  // TS 5.8: K might leak to include non-key fields in edge cases
  // TS 5.9: K is strictly inferred from the keys array, no leakage
  return pick(obj, Object.keys(obj) as Array<keyof T>);
}

// Fix pattern — add explicit type argument when 5.9 surfaces new error:
declare function transform<T, U>(value: T, fn: (v: T) => U): U;

// If TS 5.9 infers U as never:
// transform(someComplexValue, mapper)   // U infers as never due to fix
// Fix:
// transform<MyType, OutputType>(someComplexValue, mapper)  // explicit

// Diagnostic script to find affected call sites:
// npx tsc --noEmit 2>&1 | grep "never" | grep -v ".d.ts"
// These are candidates for explicit type arguments after TS 5.9 upgrade.
```

**Tradeoff:** The fixes are correctness improvements — the old behavior was technically wrong. Adding explicit type arguments is the right fix, not a workaround. The upgrade surface is usually small (1-5 call sites in typical codebases). Avoid using `as any` to suppress these errors — they indicate genuinely ambiguous type inference that should be made explicit. [official]

---

### Pattern 11 — TypeScript 6.0: `--moduleResolution bundler` + `--module commonjs` Combination for Legacy Migration [official]

TypeScript 6.0 allows `--moduleResolution bundler` to be combined with `--module commonjs`, which was previously a hard error. This combination provides a migration path for codebases that are stuck on the deprecated `--moduleResolution node` (node10) without being ready to switch to full ESM. The `bundler` resolution allows TypeScript to accept extensionless imports and re-exports that bundlers handle at build time, while `commonjs` module output keeps existing runtime code working. It is explicitly a transitional configuration, not a long-term target.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json — migration bridge for CommonJS projects:
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "commonjs",          // Output CJS (for existing Node.js code)
    "moduleResolution": "bundler", // Accept bundler-style extensionless imports
    "esModuleInterop": true        // Required in TS 6.0 (cannot be false)
  }
}

// What this allows that "moduleResolution: node" did not:
// 1. Package exports field is respected (bundler resolution reads "exports")
// 2. Extensionless imports work without errors:
import { foo } from "./utils";       // bundler resolution; NOT node (node10) resolution
import { bar } from "./components/"; // index file resolution in bundler mode

// Migration path:
// 1. Move from moduleResolution:node → moduleResolution:bundler + module:commonjs (TS 6.0)
// 2. Fix all errors from lost node10 resolution quirks
// 3. Migrate to ESM: change module:commonjs → module:preserve or node20
// 4. Eventually: moduleResolution:nodenext + module:node20 (final state)

// Deprecated options removed in TS 6.0 that you can no longer use with this:
// --moduleResolution classic — hard removed
// --moduleResolution node (node10) — deprecated, use bundler or nodenext
```

**Tradeoff:** This is a transitional configuration only. Using `bundler` resolution with `commonjs` output means your TypeScript typechecks differently from how the code actually runs — the bundler handles resolution, but the emitted CJS has `require()` calls. You may get false-positive "safe" imports that fail at runtime if the bundler is misconfigured. Always run integration tests after adopting this combination. [official]

---

### Pattern 12 — TypeScript 6.0: Less Context-Sensitivity on `this`-less Functions — Ordering-Independent Method Inference [official]

TypeScript 6.0 improves method type inference in object literals where some methods do not use `this`. Previously, when an object literal had methods in an order where a consuming method appeared before its producing counterpart, TypeScript would fail to infer the type from the producer, leaving the consumer's parameter as `any` or producing an error. In 6.0, functions that never reference `this` are treated as higher-priority inference candidates regardless of their order in the object literal. This mostly affects callback-heavy APIs (like React hooks options, stream processors, and plugin systems).

```typescript
// The canonical example — declare a generic object-taking function:
declare function callIt<T>(obj: {
  produce: (x: number) => T;
  consume: (y: T) => void;
}): void;

// TS 5.x — this FAILED if consume came before produce:
// callIt({
//   consume(y) { return y.toFixed(); },  // y is any — inference not yet available
//   produce(x: number) { return x * 2; },
// });

// TS 6.0 — works regardless of method order:
callIt({
  consume(y) { return y.toFixed(); },  // y: number — inferred from produce
  produce(x: number) { return x * 2; },
});

// Real-world pattern — middleware pipeline:
declare function createPipeline<T, U>(config: {
  parse: (raw: string) => T;
  transform: (parsed: T) => U;
  serialize: (result: U) => string;
}): (input: string) => string;

// TS 6.0: T and U infer correctly in any property order:
const pipeline = createPipeline({
  serialize: (result) => JSON.stringify(result), // result: { id: number; name: string }
  transform: (parsed) => ({ id: parsed.id, name: parsed.name.trim() }),
  parse: (raw) => JSON.parse(raw) as { id: number; name: string },
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The improvement is transparent — existing code that worked before still works, and some code that produced errors now compiles. The only edge case is if your code deliberately relied on a method being inferred as `(y: any)` due to ordering, which would be an unusual anti-pattern. This change requires no migration steps. [official]

---

### Pattern 13 — TypeScript 5.8: `require()` of ESM in `--module nodenext` — Dual-Publish Elimination Pattern [official]

TypeScript 5.8 adds support for typing `require()` calls to ECMAScript modules from CommonJS context under `--module nodenext`. Node.js 22 introduced the ability to `require()` synchronous ESM modules from CJS, and TypeScript 5.8 now correctly types this scenario rather than emitting an error. Library authors can ship pure ESM packages without needing to dual-publish CJS and ESM variants, because CJS consumers can now `require()` the ESM entry. The TypeScript type for a `require()`d ESM namespace is the module's exported interface, the same as for `import()`.

```typescript
// package.json — pure ESM package (no "main" CJS entry needed in Node.js 22+):
{
  "type": "module",
  "exports": {
    ".": "./dist/index.js"
  }
}

// In a CJS consumer (under --module nodenext, Node.js 22+):
// TypeScript 5.8 now allows typing this:
const { createUser } = require("@myorg/user-service"); // types from ESM package
// createUser: (name: string) => User — correctly inferred from the ESM .d.ts

// The ESM module:
export interface User { id: string; name: string; }
export function createUser(name: string): User {
  return { id: crypto.randomUUID(), name };
}

// In TypeScript — CJS caller (nodenext), file: user-caller.cts
const esmModule = require("@myorg/user-service");
const user: import("@myorg/user-service").User = esmModule.createUser("Alice");

// Restriction: only synchronous ESM can be required().
// Modules with top-level await CANNOT be required() — this is a Node.js constraint.
// TypeScript will error if the ESM module's .d.ts includes top-level await usage.

// Pattern to check: add this to your library's test suite:
// import { createRequire } from "module";
// const require = createRequire(import.meta.url);
// const lib = require("./dist/index.js"); // Must not throw
```

**Tradeoff:** This pattern eliminates the dual-publish burden for library authors, but requires Node.js 22+ at the consumer's runtime. For libraries targeting Node.js 18/20, dual-publish is still necessary. TypeScript types the `require()` correctly, but the runtime behavior depends entirely on the Node.js version — a missing gotcha is that Node.js 18/20 consumers who see TypeScript accept their `require()` will still get a runtime error. [official]

---

### Pattern 14 — TypeScript 5.8: Granular Return-Branch Checks Surfacing `any` Pollution in Ternaries [official]

TypeScript 5.8 introduces per-branch checking of conditional expressions used directly in `return` statements. Before this, the entire ternary was widened to the union of all branch types, then checked against the return type. This allowed `any` from one branch to silently suppress errors in adjacent branches. Now each branch is checked independently against the declared return type, catching bugs where a lookup into an `any`-typed cache or map silently bypassed type safety.

```typescript
// The canonical motivating example:
declare const untypedCache: Map<any, any>;

function getUrlObject(urlString: string): URL {
  // TS 5.7 and earlier — no error (any from .get() widened the whole ternary):
  // return untypedCache.has(urlString) ? untypedCache.get(urlString) : urlString;

  // TS 5.8 — error on the false-branch: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'URL'
  return untypedCache.has(urlString)
    ? untypedCache.get(urlString)  // any — passes (any is assignable to URL)
    : urlString;                   // string is not assignable to URL — now caught
}

// Fix — assert or cast the typed branch:
function getUrlObjectFixed(urlString: string): URL {
  const cached = untypedCache.get(urlString) as URL | undefined;
  return cached ?? new URL(urlString);
}

// Another common pattern this catches — mixed return types from object lookups:
const routeHandlers: Record<string, any> = {};

function getHandler(route: string): (req: Request) => Response {
  return routeHandlers[route] !== undefined
    ? routeHandlers[route]  // any — passes TS 5.8 check
    : (req: Request) => new Response("Not Found", { status: 404 }); // typed correctly
  // If the false branch returned a non-function, TS 5.8 would catch it.
}

// Rule of thumb after TS 5.8 upgrade:
// Any ternary in a typed return expression that previously compiled without
// explicit return type annotation is a candidate for review.
```

**Tradeoff:** This is a correctness fix — the old behavior silently allowed type errors. The upgrade may surface real bugs (false branches returning wrong types). The fix pattern is usually either to type the true-branch assertion explicitly, or to refactor to a non-ternary return with proper narrowing. [official]

---

### Pattern 15 — TypeScript 6.0: `Promise.try()` in ES2025 — Normalizing Sync Throws in Non-Async Contexts [official]

TypeScript 6.0's `es2025` lib includes `Promise.try()` — a TC39 Stage 4 method that wraps a potentially-throwing synchronous function in a Promise, avoiding the anti-pattern of mixing sync and async error handling. Unlike `new Promise(resolve => resolve(fn()))`, `Promise.try()` correctly handles synchronous throws and returns a `Promise<T>` where `T` is inferred from the callback return type. It is most useful in constructors, synchronous event handlers, and factory functions where using `async` would change the function signature.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json: "lib": ["es2025"] or "target": "es2025"

// Before — mixing sync throws with async error handling was fragile:
async function loadConfig(path: string): Promise<Config> {
  try {
    const raw = fs.readFileSync(path, "utf8"); // throws if missing
    return JSON.parse(raw) as Config;           // throws if invalid JSON
  } catch (err) {
    throw new ConfigError("Failed to load config", { cause: err });
  }
}

// After — Promise.try() normalizes sync throws into Promise rejection:
function loadConfig(path: string): Promise<Config> {
  return Promise.try(() => {
    const raw = fs.readFileSync(path, "utf8"); // sync throw → rejects the Promise
    return JSON.parse(raw) as Config;
  }).catch((err) => {
    throw new ConfigError("Failed to load config", { cause: err });
  });
}

// Type signature (from lib.es2025.d.ts):
// Promise.try<T>(callbackFn: () => T | PromiseLike<T>): Promise<T>
// T is inferred from the callback's return type.

// Use Promise.try when you cannot use async (constructors, event handlers):
class ConfigLoader {
  constructor(private readonly path: string) {}
  load(): Promise<Config> {
    return Promise.try(
      () => JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(this.path, "utf8")) as Config
    );
  }
}

// Note: inside async functions, Promise.try is redundant:
async function asyncLoad(path: string): Promise<Config> {
  // async already converts sync throws to rejections — no Promise.try needed
  const raw = fs.readFileSync(path, "utf8");
  return JSON.parse(raw) as Config;
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `Promise.try()` requires the `es2025` lib and Node.js 24+ (or a polyfill). In existing async functions it is redundant — async functions already convert synchronous throws to rejections. Its value is specifically in non-async contexts: constructors, synchronous event handlers, and factory functions where using `async` would change the function signature. [official]

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 36

**Gotcha 34 — `"types": []` in TS 6.0 silently breaks `process.env` and `__dirname` in Node.js projects** [community]

```typescript
// After upgrading to TypeScript 6.0 (or using tsc --init in TS 5.9),
// the generated tsconfig has "types": [] — an empty array.
// This means @types/node is NOT included, even if installed in node_modules.

// Error after TS 6.0 upgrade with "types: []":
const port = process.env.PORT ?? "3000"; // error: Cannot find name 'process'
const dir = __dirname;                   // error: Cannot find name '__dirname'

// Fix — add "node" to the types array:
// tsconfig.json:
// "types": ["node"]
```

WHY: TypeScript's old `types` default was "include all `@types/*` packages installed in `node_modules/@types`". This was a convenience shortcut that had a serious downside: adding `@types/jest` to your devDependencies silently made `describe`, `it`, and `expect` globals available everywhere — even in production source files. The TS 6.0 change forces you to declare which ambient type packages you actually want. The WHY behind the change is to make the compilation's global type surface explicit and auditable, not an accident of which `@types` packages happen to be installed.

---

**Gotcha 35 — `require()` of ESM in TypeScript compiles but fails at runtime on Node.js 18/20** [community]

```typescript
// TS 5.8 + --module nodenext: TypeScript accepts require() of an ESM package
// because it assumes Node.js 22+. But if your runtime is Node.js 18 or 20,
// this silently type-checks and then throws at runtime.

// In your CJS file (TS accepts this under nodenext):
const { foo } = require("some-esm-only-package"); // TypeScript happy
// Node.js 18/20 runtime: Error: require() of ES Module ... not supported

// Fix — use dynamic import which works in all Node.js versions from CJS:
async function loadEsmPackage() {
  const { foo } = await import("some-esm-only-package");
  return foo;
}
```

WHY: TypeScript's `--module nodenext` types `require()` of ESM as valid because Node.js 22 added this support. But TypeScript does NOT check your runtime Node.js version. If you are on Node.js 18 or 20 LTS, `require()` of ESM will throw a runtime `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM` error even though TypeScript was happy. The type system cannot express "this call only works on Node.js 22+". The safe default is to use dynamic `import()` for ESM packages, which works across all modern Node.js versions from any module format.

---

**Gotcha 36 — `satisfies` with a union interface does not give you the narrow member type on indexed access** [community]

```typescript
// satisfies checks that each entry conforms to the union, but the
// declared type of each entry as accessed from the record is the full union.

type Config = { tag: "a"; value: string } | { tag: "b"; value: number };
const configs = {
  first: { tag: "a", value: "hello" },
  second: { tag: "b", value: 42 },
} satisfies Record<string, Config>;

// configs.first.tag is "a" (literal) — accessing directly by name is narrow
// BUT when you destructure via a variable key:
function getConfig(key: string) {
  const entry = configs[key as keyof typeof configs];
  // entry: Config — the full union, not { tag: "a"; value: string }
  const { value } = entry; // value: string | number — not string!
}
```

WHY: `satisfies` is a post-inference check — it verifies that the right-hand side conforms to the type but does not annotate the variable with the conformance type. The inferred type of each named property is still the narrow literal type. However, when accessed through a variable key (even one constrained to `keyof typeof configs`), TypeScript widens to the union of all value types — which is the full `Config` union. This is because TypeScript cannot know which specific property is accessed at a call site that uses a variable key. The workaround is to access by specific literal key directly when the narrow type matters.

---

**Gotcha 37 — `noUncheckedSideEffectImports: true` in TS 6.0 breaks `import "reflect-metadata"` patterns** [community]

```typescript
// TypeScript 6.0 defaults noUncheckedSideEffectImports to true.
// TypeScript will ERROR on side-effect-only imports that
// cannot be resolved to a module with type declarations.

// Error in TS 6.0 with default settings:
import "reflect-metadata"; // Error: Cannot find module 'reflect-metadata'
                           // (even if it's installed — no .d.ts for side-effect entry)

// Common patterns affected:
import "zone.js";          // Angular projects
import "reflect-metadata"; // NestJS / TypeORM decorators
import "./styles.css";     // CSS side-effect imports (handled by bundler)
import "dotenv/config";    // Dotenv auto-configure

// Fix 1 — add @types for the package:
// npm install --save-dev @types/reflect-metadata

// Fix 2 — add a triple-slash reference or ambient declaration:
// In a global.d.ts:
declare module "reflect-metadata"; // tells TS "this is a valid module"

// Fix 3 — disable the flag if you have many untyped side-effect imports:
// tsconfig.json:
// "noUncheckedSideEffectImports": false
```

WHY: TypeScript's `noUncheckedSideEffectImports` flag causes TypeScript to verify that every `import "..."` without any imported bindings actually resolves to a type-checkable module. Before TS 6.0, side-effect imports that could not be resolved were silently ignored — TypeScript assumed the bundler or runtime would handle them. The new default makes TypeScript explicit about what it can and cannot verify. The most common breakage is in Angular and NestJS projects that use `import "reflect-metadata"` for decorator support, where `@types/reflect-metadata` has historically been an optional devDependency that many teams forgot to install.

---

**Gotcha 38 — `--baseUrl` deprecation in TS 6.0 breaks the bundler config independently of tsconfig — "type-checks pass but build fails"** [community]

```typescript
// After removing baseUrl from tsconfig.json (required for TS 6.0 migration),
// TypeScript's language server correctly resolves path aliases via "paths".
// BUT the bundler (webpack, Vite, esbuild) has its OWN alias config that
// is INDEPENDENT of tsconfig.json.

// If you update tsconfig.json but forget the bundler config:
// - TypeScript language server: correctly resolves @app/* via paths
// - Bundler at build time: still looks up @app/* using the OLD baseUrl logic
// - Result: type-checks pass, but the build fails or produces wrong output

// vite.config.ts — MUST be updated alongside tsconfig.json:
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import path from "path";

export default defineConfig({
  resolve: {
    alias: {
      // After (explicit absolute paths matching new tsconfig paths):
      "@app": path.resolve(__dirname, "./src/app"),
      "@lib": path.resolve(__dirname, "./src/lib"),
    },
  },
});

// jest.config.ts — ALSO needs updating:
export default {
  moduleNameMapper: {
    // Must be explicit — jest doesn't read tsconfig paths
    "^@app/(.*)$": "<rootDir>/src/app/$1",
    "^@lib/(.*)$": "<rootDir>/src/lib/$1",
  },
};
```

WHY: TypeScript's `baseUrl` was the only place where bare-module alias resolution was configured for both the TypeScript compiler and (historically) for Node.js-based tooling like `ts-node`. When `baseUrl` was present, some older bundler integrations (like `webpack` with `tsconfig-paths-webpack-plugin`) would auto-read the TypeScript config. Removing `baseUrl` while updating to explicit `paths` entries in `tsconfig.json` does not automatically propagate to bundlers — each tool has its own alias configuration that must be updated independently. The breakage is silent: TypeScript types are correct, but the runtime bundle resolves the wrong paths.

---

### Anti-Patterns: Cycle 36 Additions

| Anti-pattern | Why it's harmful | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Not adding `"types": ["node"]` after TS 6.0 upgrade for Node.js projects | TS 6.0 defaults `types` to `[]`, making `process`, `Buffer`, and `__dirname` unknown | Explicitly list `"types": ["node"]` (and `"jest"` for test files) in tsconfig |
| Using `--module nodenext` and `require()`-ing ESM packages on Node.js 18/20 | TypeScript 5.8 allows `require()` of ESM under nodenext, but this is Node.js 22-only — Node.js 18/20 throws `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM` at runtime | Use dynamic `import()` for ESM packages; or gate with a Node.js version check |
| Leaving `"ignoreDeprecations": "6.0"` in tsconfig permanently | Deprecated options will be hard-removed in TS 7.0; `ignoreDeprecations` is a migration bridge, not a permanent config | Time-box the migration window; remove `ignoreDeprecations` and fix all deprecated option errors before TS 7.0 ships |
| Using `--stableTypeOrdering` in dev/watch mode | The flag adds up to 25% overhead — it is a one-shot diagnostic tool for TS 6.0 → 7.0 migration, not a daily compile flag | Reserve `stableTypeOrdering` for a dedicated CI job; remove it after completing the 7.0 pre-flight |
| Using `Promise.try()` inside `async` functions | Inside an `async` function, synchronous throws are already converted to rejections — `Promise.try()` adds overhead with no benefit | Use `Promise.try()` only in non-async contexts: constructors, synchronous event handlers, and factory functions |
| Not updating bundler alias config after removing `baseUrl` for TS 6.0 | TypeScript's `paths` updates fix IDE resolution but do not propagate to Vite/webpack/Jest alias configs — builds silently resolve wrong paths | Update Vite `resolve.alias`, webpack `resolve.alias`, and Jest `moduleNameMapper` alongside every `tsconfig.json` `paths` change |
| Relying on `dom.iterable` being a separate lib entry after TS 6.0 | TS 6.0 merges `dom.iterable` into `dom` — explicitly listing it still works, but tooling that checks for "required" libs may flag it as redundant | Remove `"dom.iterable"` from explicit `lib` entries; just use `"dom"` in TS 6.0+ projects |

| TC39 Promise.try Proposal | https://github.com/tc39/proposal-promise-try | Stage 4 — Promise.try() for normalizing sync throws to rejections, Node.js 24+ |
| TypeScript 6.0 Migration Guide | https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/migrating-from-javascript.html | baseUrl removal, types:[] migration, ignoreDeprecations usage, deprecated options table |

## Cycle 37 — 2026-05-14

This cycle adds 15 new patterns covering: TypeScript 7.0 / `tsgo` migration readiness checklist, `Prettify<T>` for layered API response modeling, template literal `infer` for URL path parameter extraction, labeled tuple types for typed middleware chains, `NonNullable<T>` + filter predicate factory, exhaustive switch + `never` + `satisfies` triple-lock, `satisfies` + `Record` for typed configuration registries, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` compatibility with the builder pattern, type-safe `Proxy<T>` for validation wrapping, `TemplateStringsArray` typed tagged templates with `const` inference, `abstract` class template method pattern, `@ts-expect-error` as precise negative test assertion, `infer` in conditional types for deep key extraction, `using` declarations in for-of loops for streaming resources, and `type` narrowing with `switch(true)` pattern (smart switch). Also adds 5 community gotchas and a key resources table.

### Pattern 1 — TypeScript 7.0 / `tsgo` Migration Readiness Checklist [official]

**Description.** TypeScript 7.0 is the first release built on the Go-native compiler (`typescript-go`, accessible today as `@typescript/native-preview`). The Go compiler targets 10× faster type-checking by eliminating the V8 JIT warm-up cost and enabling true parallel project checking. Teams can verify readiness today using three TypeScript 6.0 opt-in flags: `--stableTypeOrdering` (union ordering parity), `--isolatedDeclarations` (declaration emit without cross-file inference), and `npx @typescript/native-preview --noEmit` (direct native-compiler dry run). The native compiler targets exact semantic parity with the JS compiler — any divergence is a bug, not a feature.

```typescript
// package.json — add preview typecheck alongside the regular one
{
  "scripts": {
    "typecheck":         "tsc --noEmit",
    "typecheck:native":  "npx @typescript/native-preview --noEmit",
    "typecheck:7-prep":  "tsc --noEmit --stableTypeOrdering"
  }
}

// tsconfig.check-7.json — dedicated migration tsconfig (never use in prod)
{
  "extends": "./tsconfig.json",
  "compilerOptions": {
    "stableTypeOrdering": true   // matches TS 7.0 union ordering; ~25% slower
  }
}

// Step 1: Run both typecheck:native and typecheck, compare exit codes
// Step 2: Investigate any divergences — the JS compiler is the ground truth for now
// Step 3: Annotate all exported functions with explicit return types
//         (required by isolatedDeclarations for parallel .d.ts emit)
export function buildQuery(filters: Filter[]): Query {  // explicit ✅
  return filters.reduce<Query>(applyFilter, emptyQuery);
}
// Step 4: Remove `ignoreDeprecations: "6.0"` — all deprecated options must
//         be addressed before TS 7.0 removes them as hard errors
```

**Tradeoff.** The Go compiler's public API is not yet stable — custom TypeScript compiler plugins, language service extensions, and `ts.createProgram`-based codegen tools cannot yet migrate. Only type-checking and `.d.ts` emit are currently supported in the preview. Reserve the native compiler for CI type-checking; continue using the JS compiler for tooling that depends on the compiler API. [official]

---

### Pattern 2 — `Prettify<T>` for Layered API Response Modeling [community]

**Description.** REST API response types are often built by intersecting base shapes with status variants, adding `links` for HATEOAS, and extending with feature flags. Without intervention, TypeScript renders these in IDE hovers as a long unreadable intersection expression. A one-line `Prettify<T>` identity map forces the compiler to eagerly evaluate the type, producing a readable flat object in hover tooltips. The critical insight is that `Prettify<T>` is a no-op at runtime — the emitted JavaScript is identical — so it adds zero overhead while transforming the developer experience. Apply it at the final "export" boundary of each composed type, not at every intermediate step.

```typescript
// The Prettify utility — a pure compile-time readability tool
type Prettify<T> = {
  [K in keyof T]: T[K];
} & {};

// Layered API response composition
interface BaseEntity {
  id: string;
  createdAt: string;
  updatedAt: string;
}

interface UserFields {
  email: string;
  displayName: string;
  role: "viewer" | "editor" | "admin";
}

interface HateoasLinks<TRoutes extends string> {
  _links: Record<TRoutes, { href: string; method: string }>;
}

// Without Prettify: IDE hover shows the full intersection expression
type RawUserResponse = BaseEntity & UserFields & HateoasLinks<"self" | "delete">;

// With Prettify: IDE hover shows a clean flat object with all 8 keys listed
type UserResponse = Prettify<BaseEntity & UserFields & HateoasLinks<"self" | "delete">>;

// Use Prettify at test fixture generation boundaries too
type UserFixture = Prettify<
  Partial<UserFields> & Required<Pick<BaseEntity, "id">>
>;

// Deeply nested: apply recursively for nested intersection objects
type DeepPrettify<T> = {
  [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends object ? DeepPrettify<T[K]> : T[K];
} & {};
```

**Tradeoff.** `Prettify<T>` triggers eager type evaluation. On deeply recursive types (tree nodes, circular references), eager expansion causes "Type instantiation is excessively deep" errors. Apply it only at leaf/output types, never on self-referential types. Also, `DeepPrettify` compounds the expansion cost — profile with `tsc --extendedDiagnostics` if used on large schemas. [community]

---

### Pattern 3 — Template Literal `infer` for URL Path Parameter Extraction [official]

**Description.** TypeScript's template literal types support `infer` in conditional types, enabling compile-time extraction of dynamic segments from route pattern strings. The `infer` keyword inside a template literal match captures the variable portion of a string into a type variable. This enables fully typed route parameter dictionaries derived solely from the route definition string, with no separate type annotation or runtime parsing. The pattern composes with mapped types to produce `Params` objects where each key is a captured segment name — identical to what `react-router`, `hono`, or `express` does at runtime, but at the type level.

```typescript
// Extract all :param names from a route string like "/users/:id/posts/:postId"
type ExtractParams<Route extends string> =
  Route extends `${string}/:${infer Param}/${infer Rest}`
    ? Param | ExtractParams<`/${Rest}`>
    : Route extends `${string}/:${infer Param}`
      ? Param
      : never;

// Verify:
type P1 = ExtractParams<"/users/:id/posts/:postId">;
//   ^? "id" | "postId"
type P2 = ExtractParams<"/orgs/:orgId/teams/:teamId/members/:userId">;
//   ^? "orgId" | "teamId" | "userId"
type P3 = ExtractParams<"/health">;
//   ^? never

// Build a typed Params object from the route string
type RouteParams<Route extends string> = {
  [K in ExtractParams<Route>]: string;
};

// Type-safe route handler factory
function createHandler<Route extends string>(
  route: Route,
  handler: (params: RouteParams<Route>, req: Request) => Response
): { route: Route; handler: typeof handler } {
  return { route, handler };
}

const userPostHandler = createHandler(
  "/users/:userId/posts/:postId",
  (params) => {
    const { userId, postId } = params; // ✅ both typed as string
    return new Response(`User ${userId} post ${postId}`);
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** The recursive template literal conditional type hits TypeScript's ~100-level recursion depth limit on routes with more than ~20 segments. For deep routing trees, use a `Split<T, "/"> ` helper that converts the string to a tuple first, then iterate with `infer`. Also, this approach types all params as `string` — use `zod.string().transform(Number)` or a branded type smart constructor for numeric IDs at the parse boundary. [official]

---

### Pattern 4 — Labeled Tuple Types for Self-Documenting Middleware Chains (TypeScript 4.0) [official]

**Description.** TypeScript 4.0 introduced labeled elements in tuple types: `[label: Type, ...]`. Labeled tuples preserve parameter names in IDE tooltips when the tuple is spread into function parameters, making complex middleware chains and argument pipes self-documenting. Without labels, a tuple `[string, number, boolean]` shows `args_0`, `args_1`, `args_2` in tooltips — meaningless to a reader. With labels, `[userId: string, limit: number, dryRun: boolean]` communicates intent without a separate JSDoc comment or interface. The pattern is especially powerful when combined with `Parameters<F>` to preserve the original function's parameter names through wrapper layers.

```typescript
// Without labels — opaque in IDE hover
type QueryArgs = [string, number, boolean];

// With labels — self-documenting in hover and error messages
type LabeledQueryArgs = [userId: string, limit: number, dryRun: boolean];

// Middleware chain with labeled tuple pass-through
type Middleware<TArgs extends unknown[], TResult> = (
  next: (...args: TArgs) => TResult,
  ...args: TArgs
) => TResult;

// Labels are preserved through Parameters<F> extraction
function withLogging<TArgs extends unknown[], TResult>(
  fn: (...args: TArgs) => TResult
): (...args: TArgs) => TResult {
  return (...args) => {
    console.log("call", fn.name, args);
    return fn(...args);
  };
}

async function fetchUserPosts(
  userId: string,
  limit: number,
  dryRun: boolean
): Promise<Post[]> {
  return [];
}

const tracedFetch = withLogging(fetchUserPosts);
// tracedFetch hover: (userId: string, limit: number, dryRun: boolean) => Promise<Post[]>
// ✅ parameter names preserved — NOT (args_0: string, args_1: number, args_2: boolean)

// Named rest elements in tuple positions (TypeScript 4.2+)
type Pipeline<TMiddlewares extends unknown[]> = [
  name: string,
  ...middlewares: TMiddlewares,
  handler: () => void
];
```

**Tradeoff.** Labels are purely cosmetic for type-checking — two tuples `[a: string]` and `[b: string]` are structurally identical and assignable to each other. Labels do not enable nominal tuple matching. Additionally, labels are dropped when a labeled tuple is spread into a generic type variable (`T extends unknown[]`) unless the generic explicitly `extends` a labeled tuple pattern. [official]

---

### Pattern 5 — `NonNullable<T>` + Filter Predicate Factory for Type-Safe Array Transformations [official]

**Description.** TypeScript 5.5 introduced inferred type predicates, allowing `arr.filter(Boolean)` to narrow `(T | null | undefined)[]` to `NonNullable<T>[]` without a manual type guard. Before 5.5, this required an explicit type predicate function. Even post-5.5, complex filter predicates — those that also narrow the element's shape, not just its nullability — still require explicit annotation. The `NonNullable<T>` filter predicate factory is a composable pattern that handles both simple nullability filtering and shape-based narrowing in a single reusable utility.

```typescript
// TS 5.5+: simple nullability filter inferred automatically
const values: (string | null | undefined)[] = ["a", null, "b", undefined];
const strings: string[] = values.filter(Boolean); // ✅ inferred in TS 5.5+

// For complex compound predicates: explicit predicate factory
function isNonNullable<T>(value: T | null | undefined): value is NonNullable<T> {
  return value !== null && value !== undefined;
}

// Compose with shape-based predicates using intersection
function hasProperty<T, K extends PropertyKey>(
  key: K
): (value: T) => value is T & Record<K, unknown> {
  return (value): value is T & Record<K, unknown> =>
    typeof value === "object" && value !== null && key in value;
}

// Narrow: remove nulls AND narrow to only objects with 'id'
type MaybeRecord = { id: string; name: string } | { error: string } | null;
const records: MaybeRecord[] = [
  { id: "1", name: "Alice" },
  null,
  { error: "Not found" },
  { id: "2", name: "Bob" },
];

const withId = records
  .filter(isNonNullable)
  .filter(hasProperty("id")) as Array<{ id: string; name: string }>;
// ✅ withId: Array<{ id: string; name: string }>

// Generic pipeline helper combining both
function filterAndNarrow<T, U extends NonNullable<T>>(
  arr: (T | null | undefined)[],
  guard: (value: T) => value is U
): U[] {
  return arr.filter(isNonNullable).filter(guard) as U[];
}
```

**Tradeoff.** TypeScript's inferred type predicates in 5.5 only apply when the filter callback has a single `return` statement that is a truthiness check. Multi-expression predicates (with `&&`, `||`, or early returns) still require explicit annotation. When composing multiple `.filter()` calls in a pipeline, TypeScript re-evaluates the type at each step — consider combining predicates into a single guard function and filtering once to avoid redundant type-checking overhead on large arrays. [official]
