### Pattern 1 — TypeScript 5.5: Inferred Type Predicates from Filter Callbacks [official]

TypeScript 5.5 added the ability to automatically infer type predicates for functions whose return value is structurally tied to narrowing a parameter. The canonical use case is `.filter(x => x !== undefined)` — prior to 5.5 this still produced `(T | undefined)[]` even after filtering, requiring an explicit cast or a manually annotated type guard. With 5.5, TypeScript applies the same control-flow narrowing used inside function bodies to infer the return type as `x is T`, propagating the narrowing to the caller. The inference fires when the function has no explicit return type annotation, has a single return statement, does not mutate the parameter, and returns a boolean directly tied to a type refinement of the parameter.

```typescript
// TypeScript 5.5+ — inferred type predicates from filter callbacks

const nationalBirds = new Map<string, string>([
  ["US", "Bald Eagle"],
  ["AU", "Emu"],
]);

const countries = ["US", "CA", "AU", "DE"];

// Before TS 5.5: bird was (string | undefined)[] after filter
// After TS 5.5: bird is string[] — TypeScript infers the type predicate
const birds: string[] = countries
  .map(country => nationalBirds.get(country))
  .filter(bird => bird !== undefined);
//       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ inferred: (bird: string | undefined) => bird is string

// Explicit equivalent (no longer needed in TS 5.5+, but still valid):
function isDefined<T>(value: T | undefined): value is T {
  return value !== undefined;
}
const birdsExplicit: string[] = countries
  .map(country => nationalBirds.get(country))
  .filter(isDefined);

// Works for null as well
const values: Array<number | null | undefined> = [1, null, 2, undefined, 3];
const numbers: number[] = values.filter(v => v != null);
//                                           ^^^^^^^^^ inferred: v is number
```

**Tradeoff:** The inference only fires when the predicate function is simple enough for TypeScript's flow analysis to follow — no explicit return type annotation, no parameter mutation, a single return path. Complex multi-branch guard functions still require explicit `value is T` annotations. Over-reliance on inferred predicates means that adding a second return statement to a previously simple guard silently drops the predicate inference and widens the filtered type back to `(T | undefined)[]`, surfacing errors late.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 2 — TypeScript 5.5: `--isolatedDeclarations` for Parallel Declaration File Generation [official]

`--isolatedDeclarations` enforces that every exported symbol has an explicit type annotation, enabling declaration files to be generated from single files in isolation without needing the full type graph. This is the foundation of faster build pipelines where type-checking and declaration generation can be parallelized across workers. The flag is a strictness opt-in: it produces errors for any export whose type TypeScript would need to infer from the rest of the program to generate accurately. The companion `transpileDeclaration` API (also added in 5.5) performs single-file `.d.ts` generation for bundlers and build tools.

```typescript
// With --isolatedDeclarations enabled in tsconfig.json:
// { "compilerOptions": { "isolatedDeclarations": true } }

// ❌ Error: inferred return type requires cross-file information
export function getConfig() {
  //            ~~~~~~~~~~ error: Function must have explicit return type annotation
  return { host: "localhost", port: 3000 };
}

// ✅ Explicit annotation satisfies --isolatedDeclarations
export interface AppConfig {
  host: string;
  port: number;
}
export function getConfigSafe(): AppConfig {
  return { host: "localhost", port: 3000 };
}

// ✅ Also valid for exported variables
export const VERSION: string = "1.0.0";
export const MAX_RETRIES: number = 3;

// ✅ Classes are fine — constructor shapes are self-describing
export class UserService {
  constructor(private readonly db: Database) {}
  async findUser(id: string): Promise<User | null> {
    return this.db.users.findById(id);
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Enabling `--isolatedDeclarations` requires annotating every public export explicitly, which adds annotation burden in application code that was previously relying on inference. The benefit — faster parallel builds — is most significant in large monorepos with many packages. For single-package applications, the ergonomic cost may outweigh the build-speed benefit. The flag is best adopted incrementally per-package, starting with deeply imported utility packages rather than leaf application packages.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 3 — TypeScript 5.5: Regular Expression Syntax Validation at Compile Time [official]

TypeScript 5.5 added static syntax checking for regular expression literals. The compiler now parses regex syntax and reports errors for invalid patterns — unclosed groups, bad backreferences, duplicate capture group names, and invalid Unicode sequences — at compile time rather than at runtime. This catches a class of bugs that previously only surfaced when the regex was executed with a matching input string. The check is enabled by default for all regex literals and requires no configuration flag.

```typescript
// TypeScript 5.5 static regex validation

// ❌ Unmatched closing parenthesis
let re1 = /hello(world))/;
//                      ^ error: Unexpected ')'. Did you mean to escape it with backslash?

// ❌ Backreference to non-existent capture group
let re2 = /(\w+)\s\2/;
//                ^^ error: This backreference refers to a group that does not exist.

// ❌ Duplicate named capture group (invalid in non-disjunction context)
let re3 = /(?<name>\w+) (?<name>\d+)/;
//                        ^^^^ error: Named capturing groups with the same name are only allowed...

// ✅ Valid regex — TypeScript is silent
let re4 = /^(?<year>\d{4})-(?<month>\d{2})-(?<day>\d{2})$/;
const match = "2026-05-14".match(re4);
const year: string | undefined = match?.groups?.year; // properly typed

// ✅ Valid backreference to an existing group
let re5 = /(['"])(.*?)\1/; // matches strings in either single or double quotes

// TypeScript also validates flags:
// ❌ Unknown flag
// let re6 = /foo/q; // error: Unknown regex flag 'q'
```

**Tradeoff:** Static regex analysis validates syntax but cannot validate semantic correctness — TypeScript does not check whether a regex matches the intended patterns. Complex dynamic regexes constructed via `new RegExp(string)` are not checked, as the pattern is not a literal. The feature adds no runtime overhead and requires no configuration. The only edge case is rare false positives where TypeScript's regex parser lags behind the latest ECMAScript regex spec — verify with `--target` matching your runtime's regex support level.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 4 — TypeScript 5.5: Control-Flow Narrowing for Constant Indexed Accesses [official]

Prior to TypeScript 5.5, narrowing only applied to direct property accesses like `obj.key`, not to indexed accesses like `obj[key]`. TypeScript could not guarantee that `obj[key]` after a type check referred to the same slot if `key` was a variable. TypeScript 5.5 relaxes this restriction when both the object and the key are "effectively constant" — neither is reassigned between the check and the use. This makes dynamic-key patterns much more ergonomic in generic utility code without requiring manual casts.

```typescript
// TypeScript 5.5 — narrowing of obj[key] when both are effectively constant

function processField(
  record: Record<string, unknown>,
  key: string
): string {
  // Before TS 5.5: error — obj[key] is still unknown after typeof check
  // After TS 5.5: narrowed to string ✅
  if (typeof record[key] === "string") {
    return record[key].toUpperCase(); // ✅ recognized as string
  }
  return String(record[key]);
}

// Works with complex generic types
type EventMap = {
  click: MouseEvent;
  keydown: KeyboardEvent;
  resize: UIEvent;
};

function handleEvent<K extends keyof EventMap>(
  handlers: { [P in K]: (e: EventMap[P]) => void },
  type: K,
  event: EventMap[K]
): void {
  if (type in handlers) {
    // handlers[type] narrowed — TS 5.5 tracks both key and object as constant
    handlers[type](event); // ✅ no cast needed
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Narrowing only applies when TypeScript can prove the object reference and key variable are not mutated between the guard and the use. Any assignment to the object or key variable in a branch resets the narrowing. In async contexts, an `await` between the check and the use invalidates narrowing (see Gotcha 54), requiring a `const` capture. The improvement is purely ergonomic — it does not change runtime behavior — but it can surface latent errors in code previously accepted because the `unknown` type was not acted upon after the guard.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 5 — TypeScript 5.6: `IteratorObject` and Lazy Pipeline Patterns [official]

TypeScript 5.6 added full typings for the TC39 Iterator Helpers proposal, shipped in Node.js 22 and modern browsers. The new `IteratorObject<T>` type and its methods — `map`, `filter`, `take`, `drop`, `flatMap`, `reduce`, `toArray`, `forEach`, `some`, `every`, `find` — enable lazy, composable data pipelines without materializing intermediate arrays. TypeScript exposes these via a new `--strictBuiltinIteratorReturn` flag that differentiates between user-defined iterators (return type `any`) and built-in iterators (fixed `IteratorReturnResult` shape). Enabling `--strictBuiltinIteratorReturn` prevents unsafe access of `.value` before checking `.done`.

```typescript
// TypeScript 5.6 — IteratorObject lazy pipelines (Node.js 22+, modern browsers)
// tsconfig: "lib": ["es2025"] or "esnext"

function* naturals(): Generator<number> {
  let n = 1;
  while (true) yield n++;
}

// Lazy pipeline — no intermediate arrays allocated
const result = naturals()
  .filter(n => n % 2 === 0)        // even numbers only
  .map(n => n * n)                  // squared
  .take(5)                          // first 5
  .toArray();                       // materialize: [4, 16, 36, 64, 100]

// Working with DOM node lists lazily
function* domIter(list: NodeList): Generator<Element> {
  for (const node of list) {
    if (node instanceof Element) yield node;
  }
}
const inputValues: string[] = domIter(document.querySelectorAll("input"))
  .filter((el): el is HTMLInputElement => el instanceof HTMLInputElement)
  .map(input => input.value)
  .filter(v => v.trim().length > 0)
  .toArray();

// --strictBuiltinIteratorReturn distinguishes done types
function safeNext<T>(iter: BuiltinIterator<T, undefined>): T | undefined {
  const result = iter.next();
  return result.done ? undefined : result.value; // ✅ correctly typed
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Iterator helpers require Node.js 22+, Chrome 122+, or Firefox 131+. They are not polyfilled by TypeScript itself; a userland polyfill is needed for older environments. The `--strictBuiltinIteratorReturn` flag is a breaking change for code that passes user-defined iterators to slots expecting `BuiltinIterator`. The performance benefit — no intermediate array allocations for large data sets — is most valuable in streaming or processing pipelines, not small UI codebases.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 6 — TypeScript 5.6: Always-Truthy and Always-Nullish Condition Detection [official]

TypeScript 5.6 added errors for conditions that always evaluate the same way: regex literals used directly as booleans (always truthy), arrow functions on the left of `??` (functions are never nullish), and comparison results on the left of `??` (booleans are never nullish). These were previously silent bugs — the code compiled and ran, but the condition never did what the developer intended. The new errors fire under `--strict` mode and are invaluable for catching copy-paste mistakes in validation functions.

```typescript
// TypeScript 5.6 — always-truthy / always-nullish detection

// ❌ Regex literal is always truthy as a value (not calling .test())
if (/^\d+$/) {
//  ^^^^^^^^ error: This condition will always return true.
//           Did you mean to call `.test(...)`?
  console.log("matched");
}
// ✅ Fix: call .test() with the actual string
const input = "123";
if (/^\d+$/.test(input)) {
  console.log("matched");
}

// ❌ Arrow function left of ?? — functions are never nullish
const handler = (() => "default") ?? "fallback";
//              ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ error: Left side of '??' is never nullish

// ❌ Boolean comparison result left of ?? — booleans are never null/undefined
const value = (x > 0) ?? false;
//            ^^^^^^^^ error: Left side of '??' is never nullish

// ✅ Only use ?? when the left side can genuinely be null or undefined
const safeFallback = someOptionalValue ?? "default";

// ❌ Return of regex literal without .test() in boolean context
function isEmail(s: string): boolean {
  return /^\S+@\S+\.\S+/; // error: a RegExp is always truthy
}
// ✅ Fix:
function isEmailSafe(s: string): boolean {
  return /^\S+@\S+\.\S+/.test(s);
}
```

**Tradeoff:** These new errors catch real bugs but can surface in existing codebases that relied on the patterns silently (even if incorrectly). The most disruptive case is existing arrow-function-as-fallback patterns using `??` where the developer meant to use `||` for falsy checking. The fix is mechanical in all cases and the errors are accurate — there are no false positives in these categories.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 7 — TypeScript 5.7: Never-Initialized Variable Detection in Nested Closures [official]

TypeScript's control-flow analysis already caught variables used before assignment in linear code paths. TypeScript 5.7 extended this to nested functions and closures: if an inner function captures a variable from an outer scope, TypeScript now checks whether the outer variable is definitely assigned at all paths that can precede the inner function's call. This catches a common async initialization bug where a variable is declared in an outer scope and assigned inside a setup function, but the inner callback can run before the setup completes.

```typescript
// TypeScript 5.7 — never-initialized variable detection in closures

// ❌ Variable used in closure before any assignment path
function setupHandler(): () => void {
  let result: number;
  // TS 5.7 error: Variable 'result' is used before being assigned
  function printResult() {
    console.log(result); // error — result may never be assigned before this runs
  }
  return printResult;
}

// ❌ Async initialization race — common real-world case
class DataService {
  private cache: Map<string, string>;
  constructor() {
    this.loadCache(); // async — cache may not be set when first method call happens
  }
  private async loadCache(): Promise<void> {
    this.cache = await fetchRemoteCache(); // assigned async
  }
  getEntry(key: string): string | undefined {
    return this.cache?.get(key); // ✅ safe with optional chaining
  }
}

// ✅ Fix: use definite assignment assertion when the invariant holds at runtime
class SafeService {
  private cache!: Map<string, string>; // ! = definite assignment assertion
  async init(): Promise<void> {
    this.cache = await fetchRemoteCache();
  }
  getEntry(key: string): string | undefined {
    return this.cache.get(key); // safe — caller must call init() first
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The improved detection is more conservative: it may flag code patterns that are technically safe at runtime (e.g., a closure invoked only after a synchronous assignment always runs first). When TypeScript cannot prove the ordering, it errors. The fix is to use the definite assignment assertion (`!`) where you have a runtime guarantee TypeScript cannot see, or to restructure the code to make the assignment visible before the closure is created. Over-use of `!` defeats the purpose of the check — prefer restructuring when possible.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 8 — TypeScript 5.7: `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` for `.ts` Source Imports [official]

TypeScript 5.7 introduced `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions`, which rewrites `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.mts`, and `.cts` extensions in relative import specifiers to their corresponding `.js`, `.jsx`, `.mjs`, and `.cjs` counterparts during compilation. This enables writing source files with explicit `.ts` extensions (which Node.js 22.6+ supports via `--experimental-strip-types`) while producing correct `.js`-extension imports in compiled output. It bridges the "write `.ts` imports for clarity" convention with the "emit `.js` imports for Node.js ESM compatibility" requirement.

```typescript
// With --rewriteRelativeImportExtensions in tsconfig.json

// Source file: src/index.ts
import { formatDate } from "./utils/date.ts";   // explicit .ts extension
import { parseConfig } from "./config/index.ts";

// Compiled output: dist/index.js
// import { formatDate } from "./utils/date.js";   // auto-rewritten to .js
// import { parseConfig } from "./config/index.js";

// Works with all TypeScript extension variants:
import { helper } from "./lib/helper.mts";  // → "./lib/helper.mjs" in output
import { db } from "./db/client.cts";       // → "./db/client.cjs" in output

// Non-relative imports are NOT rewritten (node_modules, bare specifiers):
import { z } from "zod";        // unchanged
import path from "node:path";   // unchanged

// tsconfig.json excerpt:
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true,
//     "module": "nodenext",
//     "outDir": "./dist"
//   }
// }
```

**Tradeoff:** `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` only rewrites relative specifiers — absolute imports, bare module specifiers, and `node:` prefixed imports are unchanged. It does not validate that the rewritten path exists at the target location; a mistyped filename with a `.ts` extension produces a runtime import error, not a compile-time error (unless `--moduleResolution nodenext` catches it). The option is most valuable in monorepos with explicit `.ts` imports for in-repo cross-package references; in projects using path aliases, the alias resolver handles extension mapping independently.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 9 — TypeScript 5.8: `--erasableSyntaxOnly` for Node.js `--experimental-strip-types` Compatibility [official]

Node.js 23.6+ supports `--experimental-strip-types`, which strips TypeScript type annotations at runtime without transpilation — but only for TypeScript constructs that are purely additive (erasing them leaves valid JavaScript). TypeScript 5.8's `--erasableSyntaxOnly` flag enforces this constraint at compile time: it errors on `enum` declarations, `namespace`/`module` declarations, parameter properties in constructors, and legacy `import =` / `export =` syntax — all constructs that require transpilation rather than erasure. Enabling this flag ensures your TypeScript source is compatible with strip-types runtimes and build tools like esbuild or SWC that do type-stripping only.

```typescript
// With --erasableSyntaxOnly in tsconfig.json:

// ❌ enum — requires transpilation (emits runtime object)
enum Direction { Up, Down, Left, Right }
// error: 'enum' is not allowed with erasableSyntaxOnly

// ✅ Fix: const object + union type (purely type-level)
const Direction = { Up: "Up", Down: "Down", Left: "Left", Right: "Right" } as const;
type Direction = typeof Direction[keyof typeof Direction];

// ❌ namespace — emits a runtime IIFE
namespace Validators {
  export function isEmail(s: string): boolean { return s.includes("@"); }
}

// ✅ Fix: use a plain module export
export function isEmail(s: string): boolean { return s.includes("@"); }

// ❌ Parameter property — requires constructor body transformation
class UserModel {
  constructor(public readonly id: string, private name: string) {}
  // error: parameter properties are not allowed with erasableSyntaxOnly
}

// ✅ Fix: explicit property declarations
class UserModelSafe {
  readonly id: string;
  private name: string;
  constructor(id: string, name: string) {
    this.id = id;
    this.name = name;
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Adopting `--erasableSyntaxOnly` is a breaking change for any codebase using `enum`, `namespace`, or parameter properties — all historically popular TypeScript features. The migration is mechanical but can be high-volume in large codebases. Teams that compile TypeScript before deployment gain no runtime benefit but may value the consistency of using only erasable syntax as a stylistic discipline aligned with strip-only toolchains.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 10 — TypeScript 5.8: Computed Property Names Preserved in Declaration Files [official]

Prior to TypeScript 5.8, when a class or object had a computed property name using an entity name (e.g., `[propName]` where `propName` is an exported constant), TypeScript collapsed it to an index signature (`[x: string]: T`) in the generated `.d.ts` file. This lost the specific property name information and produced incorrect type inference for consumers of the declaration file. TypeScript 5.8 preserves the original computed property name in the emitted declaration, so the `.d.ts` accurately reflects the runtime shape.

```typescript
// TypeScript 5.8 — computed property names preserved in .d.ts

// shared-lib/index.ts
export const propName = "theAnswer" as const; // type: "theAnswer"

export class MyClass {
  [propName] = 42; // computed property using the exported constant
}

// Before TS 5.8 — generated .d.ts was (WRONG):
// export declare class MyClass {
//   [x: string]: number; // ← collapsed to index signature
// }

// After TS 5.8 — generated .d.ts is (CORRECT):
// export declare const propName: "theAnswer";
// export declare class MyClass {
//   [propName]: number; // ← preserves the specific property reference
// }

// Consumer now gets correct inference:
// import { MyClass, propName } from "shared-lib";
const instance = new MyClass();
const value: number = instance[propName]; // ✅ correctly typed as number
// const wrong = instance["someOtherKey"]; // ❌ error: index signature not present
```

**Tradeoff:** The improved `.d.ts` output is more accurate but also more fragile: if `propName` is not exported from the library, the computed property in the `.d.ts` becomes unresolvable to consumers. Developers relying on computed property names from non-exported constants will see new errors after upgrading to TypeScript 5.8 and must either export the constant or switch to a string literal property name. The change is a correctness fix; any code that worked only because of the inaccurate index-signature collapse was relying on incorrect types.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 11 — Variance Annotations (`in`/`out`) for Explicit Covariance and Contravariance [community]

TypeScript computes variance structurally, which for complex generic types can be expensive and can produce surprising results when the computed variance does not match developer intent. TypeScript 4.7 introduced explicit variance annotations: `out T` marks `T` as covariant (safe to widen on assignment), `in T` as contravariant (safe to narrow on assignment), and `in out T` as invariant. Adding these annotations both documents intent and allows TypeScript to skip the expensive structural variance computation. They are verified — TypeScript errors if the annotation contradicts the actual structural variance.

```typescript
// Explicit variance annotations — TypeScript 4.7+

// Covariant: producer/reader — assign Subtype to Supertype slot
interface ReadonlyContainer<out T> {
  getValue(): T;
  // ❌ Cannot have: setValue(value: T): void — requires invariance
}

// Contravariant: consumer/writer — assign Supertype to Subtype slot
interface WriteOnlyContainer<in T> {
  setValue(value: T): void;
  // ❌ Cannot have: getValue(): T — requires invariance
}

// Invariant: both read and write
interface MutableContainer<in out T> {
  getValue(): T;
  setValue(value: T): void;
}

// Practical example: typed event emitter
interface TypedEmitter<in out Events extends Record<string, unknown>> {
  on<K extends keyof Events>(event: K, handler: (data: Events[K]) => void): void;
  emit<K extends keyof Events>(event: K, data: Events[K]): void;
}

// Covariant Result type — safe to assign Result<Dog> to Result<Animal>
type Result<out T, out E extends Error = Error> =
  | { ok: true; value: T }
  | { ok: false; error: E };

declare const dogResult: Result<Dog>;
const animalResult: Result<Animal> = dogResult; // ✅ allowed with `out T`
```

**Tradeoff:** Explicit variance annotations are verified by TypeScript — annotating `out T` on an interface that structurally requires invariance (has both a `T` producer and consumer) produces an error. This is correct behavior but means you must fully understand variance implications before adding annotations. The performance benefit (skipping structural variance computation) is only measurable in extremely large type graphs. For most codebases the primary value is documentation clarity, not performance.

**Tag:** [community]

---

### Pattern 12 — `using` Declarations for Deterministic Resource Cleanup (TC39 Explicit Resource Management) [official]

TypeScript 5.2 introduced support for the TC39 Explicit Resource Management proposal: the `using` declaration (and `await using` for async cleanup). A `using` declaration binds a variable to a value implementing `Symbol.dispose` (or `Symbol.asyncDispose`); TypeScript guarantees the `dispose` method is called at block exit — even on exception. This replaces try/finally blocks for resource cleanup and enables RAII-style patterns for database connections, file handles, mutex locks, and test fixtures that need guaranteed teardown.

```typescript
// TypeScript 5.2+ — `using` declarations for resource management
// tsconfig: "lib": ["es2022", "esnext.disposable"] or "esnext"

// Define a disposable resource
class DatabaseConnection implements Disposable {
  private conn: Connection;
  constructor(url: string) {
    this.conn = openConnection(url);
  }
  query(sql: string): Row[] {
    return this.conn.execute(sql);
  }
  [Symbol.dispose](): void {
    this.conn.close(); // called automatically at block exit
  }
}

// `using` — dispose() called automatically even if an exception is thrown
function processData(): void {
  using db = new DatabaseConnection("postgres://localhost/mydb");
  const rows = db.query("SELECT * FROM users");
  // ... process rows ...
  // db[Symbol.dispose]() called here — no try/finally needed
}

// Async variant for async cleanup
class AsyncFileHandle implements AsyncDisposable {
  static async open(path: string): Promise<AsyncFileHandle> {
    return new AsyncFileHandle(await fs.open(path, "r"));
  }
  private constructor(private handle: fs.FileHandle) {}
  async read(): Promise<Buffer> {
    return (await this.handle.read()).buffer as Buffer;
  }
  async [Symbol.asyncDispose](): Promise<void> {
    await this.handle.close(); // async cleanup
  }
}

async function readFile(path: string): Promise<Buffer> {
  await using file = await AsyncFileHandle.open(path);
  return file.read();
  // file[Symbol.asyncDispose]() called automatically
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `using` declarations require runtime support for `Symbol.dispose` — available in Node.js 18.2+ and modern browsers. TypeScript compiles `using` to a try/finally block with a helper when targeting older environments, adding code size. The ergonomic improvement over explicit try/finally is significant, especially for nested resource management. The main footgun is throwing from `[Symbol.dispose]` — exceptions thrown by `dispose()` replace the original body exception (see Gotcha 61). Use `await using` and `AsyncDisposable` for any cleanup that requires async I/O.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 13 — Branded Types for Test Fixture Identity Safety [community]

TypeScript's structural type system means that two objects with the same shape are assignable to each other, even when they represent fundamentally different concepts. In test code, this leads to passing a `UserId` (a `string`) where a `ProductId` (also a `string`) is expected. Branded types use a phantom type tag to make structurally identical types incompatible at the type level while remaining identical at runtime. This eliminates an entire class of transposition bugs in test fixtures and function signatures.

```typescript
// Branded types for test fixture safety — zero runtime overhead

declare const __brand: unique symbol;
type Brand<T, B extends string> = T & { readonly [__brand]: B };

// Create distinct branded types
type UserId = Brand<string, "UserId">;
type ProductId = Brand<string, "ProductId">;
type OrderId = Brand<string, "OrderId">;
type TimestampUTC = Brand<number, "TimestampUTC">;

// Type-safe factory functions — the only way to create branded values
const UserId = (id: string): UserId => id as UserId;
const ProductId = (id: string): ProductId => id as ProductId;
const TimestampUTC = (ms: number): TimestampUTC => ms as TimestampUTC;

// Test fixture using branded types — prevents accidental mixups
const fixtures = {
  userId: UserId("user-abc-123"),
  productId: ProductId("prod-xyz-789"),
  createdAt: TimestampUTC(Date.UTC(2026, 4, 14)),
};

// Function requiring specific branded type
async function fetchOrder(
  userId: UserId,
  productId: ProductId
): Promise<Order> {
  return {} as Order;
}

// ✅ Correct: branded values passed in correct positions
await fetchOrder(fixtures.userId, fixtures.productId);

// ❌ Compile-time error: ProductId not assignable to UserId
// await fetchOrder(fixtures.productId, fixtures.userId);

// ❌ Compile-time error: plain string not assignable to UserId
// await fetchOrder("raw-string", fixtures.productId);
```

**Tradeoff:** Branded types have zero runtime overhead — the brand is a phantom type existing only at the type level. However, they require discipline at the seam between branded and unbranded code: every place where external data enters (API responses, database rows, form inputs) needs to cast to the branded type via the factory function. In large teams, remembering which factory to call adds cognitive overhead. A partial adoption (branding only IDs, not timestamps) is a reasonable incremental strategy.

**Tag:** [community]

---

### Pattern 14 — `satisfies` Operator for Config Object Validation Without Type Widening [community]

The `satisfies` operator (TypeScript 4.9) validates that an expression matches a given type without widening the inferred type to that type. For test fixtures and configuration objects this is the ideal tool: TypeScript verifies the shape is correct (compile-time safety) while preserving the literal types of all values (for inference downstream). Using `as SomeType` or `: SomeType` widens string literals to `string` and numeric literals to `number`, losing precision needed for discriminated union narrowing and autocomplete.

```typescript
// `satisfies` for config/fixture validation without widening

type HttpMethod = "GET" | "POST" | "PUT" | "DELETE" | "PATCH";

interface RouteConfig {
  method: HttpMethod;
  path: string;
  requiresAuth: boolean;
  rateLimit?: number;
}

// ✅ `satisfies` validates shape AND preserves literal types
const apiRoutes = {
  getUser:    { method: "GET",    path: "/users/:id", requiresAuth: true  },
  createUser: { method: "POST",   path: "/users",     requiresAuth: false },
  updateUser: { method: "PUT",    path: "/users/:id", requiresAuth: true  },
  deleteUser: { method: "DELETE", path: "/users/:id", requiresAuth: true  },
} satisfies Record<string, RouteConfig>;

// Literal types preserved — method is "GET", not HttpMethod
const method = apiRoutes.getUser.method; // type: "GET" (not HttpMethod)

// ❌ Using a type annotation widens the literal type:
const apiRoutesWidened: Record<string, RouteConfig> = {
  getUser: { method: "GET", path: "/users/:id", requiresAuth: true },
};
const methodWidened = apiRoutesWidened.getUser.method; // type: HttpMethod (widened)

// Exhaustive test coverage validation
type Scenario = "success" | "notFound" | "unauthorized" | "serverError";
const testCases = {
  success:      { status: 200, body: { id: "123" } },
  notFound:     { status: 404, body: { error: "Not Found" } },
  unauthorized: { status: 401, body: { error: "Unauthorized" } },
  serverError:  { status: 500, body: { error: "Internal Server Error" } },
} satisfies Record<Scenario, { status: number; body: object }>;
// ✅ TypeScript errors if a Scenario variant is missing from testCases
```

**Tradeoff:** `satisfies` is purely compile-time — it adds no runtime check. The validation only runs when the source file is type-checked; it will not catch invalid data arriving at runtime via JSON parsing or external APIs. `satisfies` requires TypeScript 4.9 or later, which may be a constraint for libraries supporting older versions. The operator cannot be used with expressions that require type narrowing across branches — only the declared shape is checked, not runtime-discriminated variants.

**Tag:** [community]

---

### Pattern 15 — `${configDir}` Template Variable for Portable Multi-Package TSConfig [official]

TypeScript 5.5 introduced the `${configDir}` template variable for `tsconfig.json` field values. Previously, relative paths in `tsconfig.json` were resolved relative to the config file's own location, which broke when using `extends` to share a base config across multiple packages in a monorepo — relative paths in the base config resolved from the base config's location, not the extending config's location. `${configDir}` always expands to the directory of the config file that contains it, making monorepo base configs portable without path gymnastics.

```typescript
// ${configDir} in tsconfig.json — always resolves to the extending file's directory

// packages/shared/tsconfig.base.json (BEFORE — broken):
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "typeRoots": ["./node_modules/@types"],  // resolved from packages/shared/ — WRONG
//     "paths": { "@app/*": ["./src/*"] }       // resolved from packages/shared/ — WRONG
//   }
// }

// packages/shared/tsconfig.base.json (AFTER — correct):
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "typeRoots": ["${configDir}/node_modules/@types", "${configDir}/types"],
//     "outDir": "${configDir}/dist",
//     "declarationDir": "${configDir}/dist/types",
//     "rootDir": "${configDir}/src",
//     "paths": {
//       "@app/*": ["${configDir}/src/*"]
//     }
//   }
// }

// packages/api/tsconfig.json extending the base:
// { "extends": "../shared/tsconfig.base.json" }
// → ${configDir} expands to packages/api/ when extended — paths now resolve correctly!

// packages/web/tsconfig.json extending the same base:
// { "extends": "../shared/tsconfig.base.json" }
// → ${configDir} expands to packages/web/ — each package gets its own resolution root

// Validate the base config is portable:
function validateConfigPath(resolvedPath: string): boolean {
  // Each package's resolved outDir should be within that package's directory
  return resolvedPath.startsWith(process.cwd());
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `${configDir}` only works in TypeScript 5.5 and later — using it in a project that needs to support older TypeScript versions (e.g., a published library's own type-checking toolchain) requires a version guard. The variable is only valid in `tsconfig.json` string values, not in TypeScript source files. In monorepos where packages have heterogeneous directory structures (some with `src/`, some without), a single base config using `${configDir}` may still need per-package overrides for `rootDir` and `outDir`.

**Tag:** [official]

---

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 41

**Gotcha 60 — `--isolatedDeclarations` errors on exported functions with inferred return types from `.filter()` chains — enabling it on a large existing codebase surfaces hundreds of errors simultaneously** [community]

```typescript
// ❌ With --isolatedDeclarations, this export fails because the return type
// cannot be determined from this file alone (depends on User type inference chain):
export function getActiveUsers(users: User[]) {
  //             ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ error: Function must have explicit return type annotation
  return users.filter(u => u.isActive).map(u => ({ id: u.id, name: u.name }));
}

// ✅ Fix 1: add explicit return type annotation
export function getActiveUsers(users: User[]): Array<{ id: string; name: string }> {
  return users.filter(u => u.isActive).map(u => ({ id: u.id, name: u.name }));
}

// ✅ Fix 2: extract a named interface for reuse
export interface ActiveUser { id: string; name: string; }
export function getActiveUsersSafe(users: User[]): ActiveUser[] {
  return users.filter(u => u.isActive).map(u => ({ id: u.id, name: u.name }));
}
```

WHY: `--isolatedDeclarations` requires that every exported symbol's type can be determined from the current file alone, without evaluating the full type graph of imported modules. A `.filter().map()` chain produces an inferred return type whose structure depends on the `User` type (imported from elsewhere) — generating the declaration requires following the inference chain, which requires the full type graph. Adding `--isolatedDeclarations` to a large existing codebase surfaces every export relying on cross-file inference, typically hundreds of errors. The fix is always mechanical (add a return type annotation) but must be applied to every affected export. Adopt `--isolatedDeclarations` incrementally, starting with new packages or a feature-flagged sub-project, rather than enabling it globally at once.

---

**Gotcha 61 — `using` declarations do not interact with `try/catch` the way developers expect — exceptions thrown by `[Symbol.dispose]` replace the original exception from the block body** [community]

```typescript
// ❌ Misconception: dispose() exception is swallowed when body also throws
class BadResource implements Disposable {
  [Symbol.dispose](): void {
    throw new Error("cleanup failed!"); // replaces the original error
  }
}

function riskyOperation(): void {
  using r = new BadResource();
  throw new Error("original error"); // thrown first
  // dispose() runs next, throws "cleanup failed!" — original error is lost!
}

try {
  riskyOperation();
} catch (e) {
  // e.message === "cleanup failed!" — NOT "original error"
  // Original error is silently replaced
  console.error((e as Error).message);
}

// ✅ Fix: never throw from dispose() — suppress and log instead
class SafeResource implements Disposable {
  [Symbol.dispose](): void {
    try {
      this.cleanup();
    } catch (disposeError) {
      // Log without re-throwing — preserves the original exception
      console.error("Cleanup failed (non-fatal):", disposeError);
    }
  }
  private cleanup(): void { /* close handles, release locks, etc. */ }
}
```

WHY: The TC39 Explicit Resource Management proposal specifies that when both the body of a `using` block and `[Symbol.dispose]` throw, the disposal error replaces the body error — only the disposal error propagates. This differs from Java's try-with-resources, which preserves the original exception and suppresses the disposal error. The JavaScript/TypeScript behavior means bugs in `dispose()` silently hide the actual error that triggered cleanup. The rule of thumb is: `[Symbol.dispose]` must never throw. Wrap all cleanup logic in try/catch inside `dispose()` and log failures without re-throwing; the original exception will then propagate unmodified.

---

**Gotcha 62 — Branded types break JSON serialization round-trips — `JSON.parse()` returns `unknown`/`any`, not the branded type, creating a silent type gap at runtime boundaries** [community]

```typescript
type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: "UserId" };
const UserId = (id: string): UserId => id as UserId;

// ❌ JSON round-trip loses the brand — JSON.parse() returns any/unknown
const serialized = JSON.stringify({ userId: UserId("user-123") });
const deserialized = JSON.parse(serialized);
// deserialized.userId is type: any — NOT UserId

// ❌ Accessing it as UserId requires explicit re-branding (or it silently becomes any):
// const userId: UserId = deserialized.userId; // no error under noImplicitAny=false

// ✅ Fix: use a schema validation library that re-brands on parse
import { z } from "zod";
const UserIdSchema = z.string().brand<"UserId">();
const UserResponseSchema = z.object({
  userId: UserIdSchema,
  name: z.string(),
});

// Parse + validate in one step — re-brands automatically at the boundary
const parsed = UserResponseSchema.parse(JSON.parse(serialized));
const typedId: z.infer<typeof UserIdSchema> = parsed.userId; // ✅ UserId type
```

WHY: Branded types are a purely compile-time construct — the brand phantom property does not exist at runtime. When you serialize a branded value to JSON and parse it back, you get a raw string (the underlying type), not a branded string. TypeScript cannot automatically re-brand parsed data because it does not know the origin of dynamically parsed content. Every API response, database read, or user input flowing into branded-type slots must pass through a validation/coercion layer (Zod, Valibot, io-ts) that applies the brand at the boundary. Omitting this layer creates a silent type gap between the branded types visible in your IDE and the unbranded values flowing at runtime.

---

**Gotcha 63 — `satisfies` does not narrow inside `if` branches and is not a runtime validator — it validates the declared shape at compile time only** [community]

```typescript
type Shape =
  | { kind: "circle"; radius: number }
  | { kind: "square"; side: number };

// ✅ satisfies validates the shape correctly at compile time
const myShape = { kind: "circle", radius: 5 } satisfies Shape;
// myShape.radius accessible because literal type "circle" is preserved

// ❌ Misconception: satisfies works on unknown/dynamic data as a type guard
function processShape(input: unknown): void {
  // This is a compile-time check, NOT a runtime guard:
  const shape = input satisfies Shape;
  // error: 'unknown' is not assignable to type 'Shape'
  // Even if it were, no runtime check is emitted
}

// ❌ satisfies is evaluated at compile time and emits NO JavaScript
// The following compiles to just: const validated = { kind: "circle", radius: 5 };
const validated = { kind: "circle" as const, radius: 5 } satisfies Shape;

// ✅ Fix: use a type guard function for runtime validation
function isShape(x: unknown): x is Shape {
  return (
    typeof x === "object" && x !== null &&
    "kind" in x &&
    ((x as any).kind === "circle" || (x as any).kind === "square")
  );
}

// ✅ Or a schema validator for full parse + type-narrowing:
import { z } from "zod";
const ShapeSchema = z.discriminatedUnion("kind", [
  z.object({ kind: z.literal("circle"), radius: z.number() }),
  z.object({ kind: z.literal("square"), side: z.number() }),
]);
```

WHY: `satisfies` is evaluated at compile time as a structural assignment check — it does not affect the code emitted to JavaScript. Using `x satisfies T` in an expression does not check `x` at runtime; it only asks the TypeScript compiler to verify that `x`'s compile-time type is assignable to `T`. If `x` is `unknown` or comes from a runtime boundary (JSON.parse, API response, user input), `satisfies` cannot help — you need a type guard function, a schema validator, or a manual narrowing. The confusion arises because `satisfies` looks syntactically similar to `instanceof` or `typeof`, which are runtime operators.

---

**Gotcha 64 — TypeScript 6.0's `strict: true` default enables `noImplicitOverride` — class methods that shadow parent methods without an explicit `override` keyword now error on upgrade** [community]

```typescript
// After upgrading to TypeScript 6.0 (strict: true by default):

class Base {
  greet(name: string): string {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
  }
  render(): void { /* base render logic */ }
}

// ❌ Error with noImplicitOverride (enabled via strict: true in TS 6.0):
class Derived extends Base {
  greet(name: string): string {
  //    ~~~~~ error: Method 'greet' will overwrite the base type method.
  //          Add the 'override' modifier
    return `Hi, ${name}!`;
  }
}

// ✅ Fix: add explicit override modifier
class DerivedSafe extends Base {
  override greet(name: string): string { // ✅ intent is explicit
    return `Hi, ${name}!`;
  }
}

// ✅ Bonus: noImplicitOverride catches typos that create accidental new methods
class TypoDerived extends Base {
  // ❌ 'renders' does NOT override 'render' — it creates a new method!
  // With noImplicitOverride, attempting to write `override renders()` would
  // produce: error: Method 'renders' ... does not exist in type Base
  renders(): void { /* BUG: this never overrides base render() */ }
  // Fix: override render(): void { /* ... */ }
}
```

WHY: `noImplicitOverride` was introduced in TypeScript 4.3 as an optional flag and became part of `strict: true` in TypeScript 6.0's updated defaults. It enforces that any class method shadowing a base class method must be explicitly marked with `override`. The dual benefit is documentation (intent is explicit) and error detection (typos creating new methods instead of overriding existing ones are caught immediately). The breaking change for TypeScript 6.0 upgraders is that all existing subclasses with implicitly overriding methods require the `override` modifier. The fix is mechanical: search for method names matching base class methods and add `override`. Running `tsc --strict --noEmit` before the upgrade surfaces all affected sites.

---

### Anti-Patterns: Cycle 41 Additions

| Anti-pattern | Why it's harmful | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Enabling `--isolatedDeclarations` globally on a large existing codebase in a single step | Surfaces hundreds of "missing return type" errors simultaneously, blocking CI and disrupting the team | Enable per-package incrementally, starting with leaf utility packages; run `tsc --isolatedDeclarations --noEmit` in a separate diagnostic script before adding to `tsconfig.json` |
| Throwing from `[Symbol.dispose]` in a `using` block | The disposal error replaces the original body error, silently losing the root cause exception | Wrap all cleanup logic in try/catch inside `dispose()`; log failures without re-throwing so the original exception propagates |
| Using branded types at API/database boundaries without a re-branding validation step | `JSON.parse()` returns unbranded values; accessing them as branded types creates a silent runtime/type gap | Pair branded types with a schema validator (Zod `.brand<"T">()`) at every external data boundary |
| Using `satisfies` as a runtime type guard on `unknown` data | `satisfies` is compile-time only; it emits no runtime check | Use an explicit type guard function or schema validator for runtime validation; reserve `satisfies` for literal objects constructed in source code |
| Defining class methods that shadow base class methods without `override` after upgrading to TypeScript 6.0 | `noImplicitOverride` (now part of `strict: true`) will error on all implicit overrides, and typos creating accidental new methods are not caught | Add `override` to all intentional overrides; run `tsc --strict --noEmit` before upgrading to identify all affected sites |
| Using `enum` in code that must run through `--experimental-strip-types` or esbuild type-stripping | `enum` requires transpilation (it emits a runtime IIFE); type-stripping tools cannot handle it and will fail at runtime | Replace `enum` with `as const` objects plus a derived union type: `const E = { A: "A" } as const; type E = typeof E[keyof typeof E]` |
| Using `${configDir}` in tsconfig base configs targeting TypeScript 5.4 or older | `${configDir}` is a TS 5.5 feature; older versions treat it as a literal string path, causing incorrect resolution silently | Verify `typescript` peer dependency minimum is `>=5.5` before using `${configDir}` in shared base configs |
