## Cycle 42 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 1 — TypeScript 5.8: Granular Return-Branch Checking Catches `any`-Masked Type Errors [official]

TypeScript 5.8 changed how the type checker validates `return` statements containing conditional expressions. Previously, when a conditional expression like `condition ? anyValue : concreteValue` was returned, TypeScript would collapse the two branches into a union (`any | ConcreteType`), which simplified to `any` — hiding genuine type errors in the concrete branch. TypeScript 5.8 now checks each branch of a ternary in a `return` statement individually against the declared return type, surfacing errors that were previously swallowed by `any` contamination. This matters most in codebases that use untyped caches, legacy `Map<any,any>` stores, or third-party libraries with loose typings.

```typescript
// TypeScript 5.7 and earlier: NO error — any contaminates the union
declare const untypedCache: Map<any, any>;

function getUrlObject_old(urlString: string): URL {
  return untypedCache.has(urlString)
    ? untypedCache.get(urlString) // returns any — union becomes any | URL → any
    : urlString;                  // ← hidden bug: string is not URL
}

// TypeScript 5.8+: error on the string branch
function getUrlObject(urlString: string): URL {
  return untypedCache.has(urlString)
    ? untypedCache.get(urlString)
    : urlString;
    // ~~~~~~~~~~
    // error: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'URL'.
}

// ✅ Fix: add explicit cast or construct the URL
function getUrlObjectSafe(urlString: string): URL {
  return untypedCache.has(urlString)
    ? (untypedCache.get(urlString) as URL)
    : new URL(urlString);
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Upgrading to TypeScript 5.8 will surface new errors in files that return conditional expressions where one branch involves `any`. These errors are real bugs that were previously hidden, but they require manual inspection — some are safe casts, others are genuine runtime type mismatches. Run `tsc --noEmit` before upgrading and budget time to audit each new error.

---

### Pattern 2 — TypeScript 5.8: `require()` of ESM in `--module nodenext` (Node.js 22+) [official]

Node.js 22 introduced support for synchronously `require()`-ing ECMAScript module files, removing the long-standing CJS/ESM interoperability barrier. TypeScript 5.8 reflects this change: with `--module nodenext`, TypeScript no longer errors when CJS code calls `require()` on a file whose package resolves to ESM. This enables library authors to publish a single ESM entry point consumable by both ESM `import` and CJS `require()` callers on Node.js 22+ without dual-publishing. ESM files that contain top-level `await` remain un-`require()`-able and TypeScript continues to error on those.

```typescript
// package.json (library)
// { "type": "module", "exports": { ".": "./dist/index.js" } }

// consumer.cjs — running on Node.js 22+
// tsconfig.json: { "compilerOptions": { "module": "nodenext" } }

// TypeScript 5.7: error — cannot require() ESM
// TypeScript 5.8+: ✅ no error when module: nodenext and Node 22 semantics apply
const myLib = require("my-esm-library");

// ❌ Still errors: top-level await in the ESM file makes require() impossible
// require("lib-with-top-level-await");

// ✅ Type-safe usage after require()
interface MyLib { greet(name: string): string; }
const lib = require("my-esm-library") as MyLib;
console.log(lib.greet("world"));

// Best practice: prefer dynamic import for code that should also run in ESM contexts
async function useLib(): Promise<void> {
  const { greet } = await import("my-esm-library");
  console.log(greet("world"));
}
```

**Tradeoff:** This feature is gated to Node.js 22+ semantics via `--module nodenext`. Projects that must support Node.js 18/20 should stick to `--module node18`/`node16` respectively, which disallows `require()` of ESM. Mixing `nodenext` with older Node.js runtimes will compile without errors but fail at runtime on the `require()` call.

---

### Pattern 3 — TypeScript 5.8: `--erasableSyntaxOnly` for Node.js Native TypeScript Execution [official]

Node.js 23.6 (and later) added `--experimental-strip-types`, which removes TypeScript syntax by stripping type annotations without transpilation — no `tsc` step required. However, this stripping cannot handle TypeScript constructs that emit JavaScript (enums, namespaces with runtime code, parameter properties, `import =` aliases, `export =`). TypeScript 5.8's `--erasableSyntaxOnly` flag makes the compiler error on any of these non-erasable constructs, guaranteeing that the compiled output is safe to strip-execute by Node.js. It is the companion flag to `--isolatedDeclarations` in a "type-strip-first" workflow.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json
// { "compilerOptions": { "erasableSyntaxOnly": true } }

// ❌ error: 'enum' is not allowed with --erasableSyntaxOnly (emits runtime IIFE)
enum Direction { Up = "UP", Down = "DOWN" }

// ✅ Fix: use const assertion object + derived union type
const Direction = { Up: "UP", Down: "DOWN" } as const;
type Direction = typeof Direction[keyof typeof Direction]; // "UP" | "DOWN"

// ❌ error: namespace with runtime code
namespace MathUtils { export const PI = 3.14159; }

// ✅ Fix: plain object
const MathUtils = { PI: 3.14159 } as const;

// ❌ error: parameter property (emits field assignment in ctor body)
class Point {
  constructor(public x: number, public y: number) {}
}

// ✅ Fix: explicit field declarations
class PointSafe {
  x: number;
  y: number;
  constructor(x: number, y: number) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
}

// ❌ error: import alias (CommonJS-style require)
import path = require("path");

// ✅ Fix: standard ESM import
import * as path from "path";
```

**Tradeoff:** Enabling `--erasableSyntaxOnly` is a one-way door for each file — once you migrate away from enums and parameter properties, the code is more portable but the ergonomics of parameter properties are lost. Parameter properties are idiomatic in TypeScript classes; teams must decide whether native Node.js execution is worth the added verbosity. For libraries targeting broad runtimes, the tradeoff strongly favors `--erasableSyntaxOnly`; for application code locked to a build pipeline, it is optional.

---

### Pattern 4 — TypeScript 5.8: `--module node18` as a Stable Config Point [official]

TypeScript 5.8 introduced `--module node18` alongside the existing `--module nodenext`. The `nodenext` mode always reflects the behavior of the latest stable Node.js release, which means its semantics can change across TypeScript versions (e.g., TypeScript 5.8 added `require()` of ESM under `nodenext` to match Node.js 22). `--module node18` provides a frozen configuration that targets Node.js 18 LTS semantics: no `require()` of ESM, import assertions (`assert`) are still valid (not yet deprecated for Node.js 18), and the CJS/ESM distinction is strictly enforced. Projects that must remain compatible with Node.js 18 LTS should pin to `--module node18` rather than `nodenext` to avoid inadvertently relying on Node.js 22+ behaviors.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json for a Node.js 18 LTS service
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "node18",       // frozen Node 18 semantics
    "moduleResolution": "node16",
    "target": "es2022",
    "strict": true
  }
}

// With --module node18:
// ✅ import assertions still valid (Node 18 supports them)
import data from "./data.json" assert { type: "json" };

// ❌ require() of ESM still errors (Node 18 does not support it)
// const lib = require("esm-only-package"); // error

// With --module nodenext (TypeScript 5.8):
// ❌ import assertions now error (Node 22 deprecated assert syntax)
// import data from "./data.json" assert { type: "json" };
// ✅ require() of ESM is allowed (Node 22 supports it)

// Migration path when moving from Node 18 → 22:
// 1. Change "module": "node18" → "nodenext"
// 2. Replace all assert { type: "json" } → with { type: "json" }
// 3. Remove any require()-of-ESM workarounds (now supported natively)
```

**Tradeoff:** Pinning to `--module node18` gives stability but requires a deliberate migration step when moving to newer Node.js releases. Using `--module nodenext` always stays current but means TypeScript version upgrades can introduce new compilation errors when Node.js semantics change. For long-lived LTS services, `node18`/`node20` etc. is safer. For actively evolving microservices, `nodenext` is more forward-compatible.

---

### Pattern 5 — TypeScript 5.7: `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` for Writing `.ts` Imports in Source Files [official]

Prior to `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions`, the TypeScript convention was to write imports without file extensions (`import x from "./foo"`) or to write `.js` extensions even in `.ts` source files (the "write the output extension" rule required by `--module nodenext`). TypeScript 5.7 introduced `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions`, which allows developers to write `.ts` extensions in source files — TypeScript rewrites them to `.js` (or `.mjs`/`.cjs` for `.mts`/`.cts`) in the emitted output. This makes source files more readable and eliminates the cognitive overhead of writing `.js` extensions in `.ts` files. Only relative imports (starting with `./` or `../`) are rewritten.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json
// { "compilerOptions": { "module": "nodenext", "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true } }

// ✅ New: write .ts extensions in source — they get rewritten to .js on emit
import { parseUser } from "./user-parser.ts";
import type { User } from "../models/user.ts";

// TypeScript emits: import { parseUser } from "./user-parser.js";
//                  import type { User } from "../models/user.js";  ← removed (type-only)

// ❌ Not rewritten: bare specifiers, package imports, absolute paths
import { z } from "zod";             // NOT rewritten (package)
import { readFile } from "node:fs";  // NOT rewritten (node: prefix)
// import x from "/abs/path.ts";    // NOT rewritten (absolute)

// ❌ Not rewritten: dynamic imports with non-literal strings
const mod = await import(getModulePath()); // NOT rewritten (non-literal)

// ✅ Rewritten: dynamic imports with string literals
const helpers = await import("./helpers.ts"); // → "./helpers.js"
```

**Tradeoff:** `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` only works for relative imports, so codebases relying on path aliases (via `paths` in tsconfig) or `baseUrl` resolution still need either no-extension imports or a separate bundler step. Additionally, the option can confuse tools that process TypeScript files without understanding this rewriting rule. Teams should verify that all scripts (linters, bundlers, test runners) are aware of the rewriting behavior before enabling it.

---

### Pattern 6 — TypeScript 5.7: Never-Initialized Variable Detection in Nested Closure Capture [official]

TypeScript has long detected "used before assigned" errors for local variables, but the analysis was limited to direct reads within the same function scope. TypeScript 5.7 extends this analysis to detect variables that are never initialized before being captured by a nested function. If a variable is declared but no code path assigns it before its first read in a closure, TypeScript 5.7 reports an error, catching a class of latent bugs where a developer forgets to assign the variable in all branches before defining the closure.

```typescript
// TypeScript 5.6 and earlier: no error (closure capture not analyzed)
function processItems(items: string[]): () => string {
  let result: string;
  // BUG: result never assigned if items is empty
  if (items.length > 0) {
    result = items.join(", ");
  }
  // Returns a closure that captures potentially-uninitialized result
  return () => result; // ← TypeScript 5.6: no error here
}

// TypeScript 5.7+: error caught
function processItemsSafe(items: string[]): () => string {
  let result: string;
  //  ~~~~~~ error: Variable 'result' is used before being assigned.
  if (items.length > 0) {
    result = items.join(", ");
  }
  return () => result;
}

// ✅ Fix 1: provide a default value
function processItemsFixed1(items: string[]): () => string {
  let result: string = ""; // definite initialization
  if (items.length > 0) {
    result = items.join(", ");
  }
  return () => result;
}

// ✅ Fix 2: use a ternary to guarantee initialization on all paths
function processItemsFixed2(items: string[]): () => string {
  const result = items.length > 0 ? items.join(", ") : "";
  return () => result;
}
```

**Tradeoff:** This new error is a genuine safety improvement, but it can trigger false positives in code that uses manual two-phase initialization patterns (declare then assign in a setup block). Teams upgrading to TypeScript 5.7 should run `tsc --noEmit` and review each new "used before assigned" error: most are real bugs, but some will require adding a definite assignment assertion (`result!`) or restructuring into a single-pass initialization.

---

### Pattern 7 — TypeScript 5.6: `--noUncheckedSideEffectImports` for Catching Bare Import Typos [official]

Side-effect imports (imports with no binding, like `import "some-polyfill"`) were previously never checked for module resolution errors — TypeScript silently ignored them when the module could not be found. TypeScript 5.6 added `--noUncheckedSideEffectImports`, which applies the same module resolution checks to side-effect imports as to named imports. Typos in polyfill paths, CSS imports, or initialization modules that were silently swallowed now produce compile-time errors. The flag is opt-in (not part of `strict`) because many projects import CSS, image files, or web worker scripts that require ambient module declarations.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json
// { "compilerOptions": { "noUncheckedSideEffectImports": true } }

// Without the flag: silent (no error even if the module doesn't exist)
import "reflect-metadata";          // ← silently passes even if uninstalled
import "./styles/main.css";         // ← silently passes even if file missing

// With --noUncheckedSideEffectImports:
import "reflact-metadata";          // ❌ error: Cannot find module 'reflact-metadata'
import "./styles/main.csss";        // ❌ error: Cannot find module './styles/main.csss'

// ✅ For CSS/image/asset imports: add ambient module declarations
// src/globals.d.ts
declare module "*.css" {}
declare module "*.svg" {}
declare module "*.png" {}

// Now these are valid with the flag enabled:
import "./button.css";     // ✅ matched by '*.css' ambient declaration
import heroImage from "./hero.png"; // ✅ matched by '*.png' ambient declaration

// ✅ For web workers or dynamic assets:
declare module "comlink-loader!*" {}
import MyWorker from "comlink-loader!./worker";
```

**Tradeoff:** Enabling `--noUncheckedSideEffectImports` on an existing project often reveals missing ambient module declarations for CSS modules, image imports, and worker loaders. The flag is strongly recommended for new projects but requires an ambient declaration audit for existing codebases. The benefit is significant: typos in polyfill paths (e.g., `reflect-metadata` vs `reflact-metadata`) are a real source of runtime bugs that are currently invisible at compile time.

---

### Pattern 8 — TypeScript 5.6: `IteratorObject` and Lazy Iterator Pipeline Pattern [official]

TypeScript 5.6 introduced the `IteratorObject` type to model JavaScript's built-in iterator helper methods (`map`, `filter`, `take`, `drop`, `flatMap`, `reduce`, `forEach`, `find`, `every`, `some`, `toArray`) that are now part of the ECMAScript iterator protocol. Unlike array methods, iterator helpers are lazy — intermediate operations do not allocate new arrays. This enables efficient pipeline processing of potentially infinite sequences or large datasets where early termination saves significant work.

```typescript
// TypeScript 5.6: IteratorObject with lazy pipeline helpers
function* generateIds(start = 1): Generator<number> {
  let id = start;
  while (true) yield id++;
}

// Lazy pipeline: no intermediate arrays allocated
const firstFiveEvenSquares: number[] = generateIds()
  .filter(n => n % 2 === 0)     // lazy — no array
  .map(n => n * n)               // lazy — no array
  .take(5)                       // lazy — no array
  .toArray();                    // materializes only at the end
// Result: [4, 16, 36, 64, 100]

// Typed custom iterator extending IteratorObject
class InfiniteCounter extends Iterator<number> {
  private value = 0;
  next(): IteratorResult<number, undefined> {
    return { value: this.value++, done: false };
  }
}

// Map iterator helpers work on built-in iterables too
function invertMap<K, V>(map: Map<K, V>): Map<V, K> {
  return new Map(map.entries().map(([k, v]) => [v, k]));
}

// --strictBuiltinIteratorReturn flag: BuiltinIteratorReturn becomes undefined
// Forces explicit done-check before using value
function* uppercase(iter: Iterator<string, undefined>) {
  while (true) {
    const { value, done } = iter.next();
    if (done) break;
    yield value.toUpperCase(); // value narrowed to string (not string|undefined)
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Iterator helpers require ES2025 (or a polyfill). Projects targeting older environments must either polyfill or convert to array-based pipelines. The lazy evaluation model also means errors inside `filter`/`map` callbacks are thrown at the call site of `toArray()` or iteration, not at the declaration of the pipeline — this can make stack traces harder to read. Use `toArray()` early when debugging to get immediate error messages.

---

### Pattern 9 — Key Remapping with `as` in Mapped Types for Property Name Transformation [official]

TypeScript 4.1 added the ability to remap property keys within mapped types using the `as` clause. Combined with template literal types and `Capitalize`/`Uncapitalize` intrinsics, this enables powerful structural transformations: generating getter/setter pairs, creating event name types, filtering out specific keys, and producing API clients from data models — all at the type level without runtime overhead. Key remapping with `never` is the idiomatic way to conditionally exclude properties from a mapped type.

```typescript
// Pattern 1: Generate typed getter methods from a data model
interface UserModel {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  createdAt: Date;
}

type Getters<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K];
};

type UserGetters = Getters<UserModel>;
// { getId: () => string; getName: () => string; getCreatedAt: () => Date; }

// Pattern 2: Filter properties by value type using `never`
type PickStrings<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as T[K] extends string ? K : never]: T[K];
};

type StringFields = PickStrings<UserModel>;
// { id: string; name: string; } — Date fields excluded

// Pattern 3: Generate type-safe event emitter event names
type EventMap<T extends Record<string, unknown>> = {
  [K in keyof T as `${string & K}Changed`]: (prev: T[K], next: T[K]) => void;
};

type UserEvents = EventMap<UserModel>;
// { idChanged: (prev: string, next: string) => void;
//   nameChanged: (prev: string, next: string) => void;
//   createdAtChanged: (prev: Date, next: Date) => void; }

// Pattern 4: Cross-union dispatch map
type SquareEvent = { kind: "square"; side: number };
type CircleEvent = { kind: "circle"; radius: number };
type EventHandlers = {
  [E in SquareEvent | CircleEvent as E["kind"]]: (event: E) => void;
};
// { square: (event: SquareEvent) => void; circle: (event: CircleEvent) => void; }
```

**Tradeoff:** Key remapping with template literals can produce opaque types that are hard to read in IDE tooltips — a `Getters<UserModel>` hover shows the expanded form, not the alias name. For shared utility types, add explicit interface aliases with `extends` to give them readable names. Also, the `string & K` cast in `Capitalize<string & K>` is required because `keyof T` can include `number` and `symbol`; omitting it causes a type error.

---

### Pattern 10 — Template Literal Types for Type-Safe Event and Route Definitions [official]

Template literal types combine with union types to generate precise string literal unions at the type level, enabling compile-time validation of event names, URL route parameters, and CSS property combinations. The cross-multiplication behavior (two unions in a template produce all combinations) can generate hundreds of valid string types from a handful of atomic unions. Combined with `infer` in conditional types, they support extracting dynamic segments from string patterns.

```typescript
// Route parameter extraction with infer + template literals
type ExtractRouteParams<Route extends string> =
  Route extends `${string}:${infer Param}/${infer Rest}`
    ? Param | ExtractRouteParams<`/${Rest}`>
    : Route extends `${string}:${infer Param}`
      ? Param
      : never;

type UserRouteParams = ExtractRouteParams<"/users/:userId/posts/:postId">;
// "userId" | "postId"

// Type-safe route builder
function buildRoute<R extends string>(
  route: R,
  params: Record<ExtractRouteParams<R>, string>
): string {
  return Object.entries(params).reduce(
    (acc, [key, value]) => acc.replace(`:${key}`, value),
    route
  );
}

const url = buildRoute("/users/:userId/posts/:postId", {
  userId: "u123",
  postId: "p456",
});
// url: "/users/u123/posts/p456"

// Missing param causes a compile error:
// buildRoute("/users/:userId", {}); // error: Property 'userId' is missing

// CSS property generation from atomic parts
type Axis = "x" | "y";
type Side = "top" | "bottom" | "left" | "right";
type PaddingKey = `padding-${Side}` | `margin-${Side}`;
// "padding-top" | "padding-bottom" | "padding-left" | "padding-right"
// | "margin-top" | ...
```

**Tradeoff:** Deeply recursive template literal types (like `ExtractRouteParams`) can cause significant type checker slowdowns on complex route strings. TypeScript sets a recursion depth limit (around 100 levels); routes with many segments can hit this limit. For production router types, prefer flatter patterns or use established libraries like `react-router`'s type definitions. The compile-time route parameter extraction pattern is most useful for small, bounded route sets.

---

### Pattern 11 — TypeScript 5.0 Standard Decorators: Well-Typed Method Decorators [official]

TypeScript 5.0 introduced standardized ECMAScript decorators, which differ fundamentally from the legacy `--experimentalDecorators` implementation. Standard decorators use a context object (`ClassMethodDecoratorContext`, `ClassFieldDecoratorContext`, etc.) and support a well-typed generic signature. The `addInitializer` hook on the context allows decorators to run code after the class is constructed, enabling patterns like method auto-binding that were previously only possible with `--experimentalDecorators`. Stacking decorators applies them bottom-up (inner first).

```typescript
// Well-typed method decorator — generic over `this`, args, and return
function memoize<This, Args extends unknown[], Return>(
  target: (this: This, ...args: Args) => Return,
  context: ClassMethodDecoratorContext<This, (this: This, ...args: Args) => Return>
): (this: This, ...args: Args) => Return {
  const cache = new Map<string, Return>();
  return function (this: This, ...args: Args): Return {
    const key = JSON.stringify(args);
    if (cache.has(key)) return cache.get(key)!;
    const result = target.call(this, ...args);
    cache.set(key, result);
    return result;
  };
}

// Auto-bind decorator using addInitializer
function bound<This, Args extends unknown[], Return>(
  _target: (this: This, ...args: Args) => Return,
  context: ClassMethodDecoratorContext<This, (this: This, ...args: Args) => Return>
): void {
  const methodName = context.name;
  context.addInitializer(function (this: This) {
    // `this` is the class instance at construction time
    (this as Record<string | symbol, unknown>)[methodName] =
      (this as Record<string | symbol, unknown>)[methodName].bind(this);
  });
}

class Calculator {
  @memoize
  expensiveCompute(n: number): number {
    return n * n; // expensive in practice
  }

  @bound
  handleClick(event: MouseEvent): void {
    console.log("clicked at", event.x, event.y);
  }
}

const calc = new Calculator();
// handleClick is pre-bound — safe to pass as callback
document.addEventListener("click", calc.handleClick);
```

**Tradeoff:** Standard decorators (TypeScript 5.0+) and legacy `--experimentalDecorators` are mutually exclusive — you cannot mix them in the same project. Many popular frameworks (Angular, NestJS, TypeORM) still use `--experimentalDecorators` and `--emitDecoratorMetadata`. Migrating to standard decorators requires waiting for framework support. Standard decorators also do not support parameter decorators, which are used by NestJS for dependency injection. Check your framework's roadmap before switching.

---

### Pattern 12 — Variance Annotations (`in`/`out`) for Generic Type Performance and Explicitness [official]

TypeScript 4.7 introduced explicit variance annotations `in` (contravariant) and `out` (covariant) for generic type parameters. Normally, TypeScript infers variance by structurally analyzing type parameter usages — a process that can be expensive for deeply nested generic types. Annotating variance explicitly short-circuits this structural analysis, improving type checking performance for library-level utility types. Beyond performance, explicit variance makes the type contract self-documenting: `out T` communicates "this type only produces T values", `in T` communicates "this type only consumes T values".

```typescript
// Without annotations: TypeScript infers variance (slower for complex types)
interface Functor<T> {
  map<U>(fn: (value: T) => U): Functor<U>;
}

// With explicit variance: TypeScript skips structural inference
interface CovariantBox<out T> {    // out = covariant: Box<Dog> extends Box<Animal>
  readonly value: T;
  map<U>(fn: (value: T) => U): CovariantBox<U>;
}

interface ContravariantSink<in T> { // in = contravariant: Sink<Animal> extends Sink<Dog>
  accept(value: T): void;
}

// ❌ Violation: out T cannot appear in an input (contravariant) position
interface BadBox<out T> {
  setValue(value: T): void; // error: Type parameter 'T' is not valid
                             // here since it can lead to unsoundness
}

// Practical usage: typed event emitter
interface TypedEmitter<in TEvent> {
  emit(event: TEvent): void;
}

// A handler for Animal events also handles Dog events (contravariance)
declare const animalHandler: TypedEmitter<{ name: string }>;
// Can be passed anywhere a TypedEmitter<{ name: string; breed: string }> is expected
// because it handles all possible animals, including dogs

// Performance-critical generic utility type
interface ReadonlyList<out T> {
  readonly length: number;
  get(index: number): T;
  [Symbol.iterator](): Iterator<T>;
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Explicit variance annotations cause the compiler to error when a type parameter is used in a position that violates the declared variance. This is a correctness benefit but it can be noisy when adding `out T` to an existing mutable type — it immediately flags all mutating methods. Add variance annotations incrementally starting with purely read-only or write-only types; avoid annotating types that genuinely serve both covariant and contravariant roles.

---

### Pattern 13 — `infer` with `extends` Bounds for Constrained Type Extraction [official]

TypeScript 5.4 introduced the ability to add type constraints to `infer` type variables using `infer X extends Constraint`. Before this addition, conditional types using `infer` would capture the full unconstrained type, requiring a subsequent conditional to check the constraint. With bounded `infer`, the constraint check and extraction happen in a single conditional, producing cleaner utility types and avoiding the redundant "wrap in conditional, check, unwrap" pattern.

```typescript
// Before TypeScript 5.4: two-step extraction (verbose)
type FirstStringElement_Old<T extends readonly unknown[]> =
  T extends readonly [unknown, ...unknown[]]
    ? T[0] extends string
      ? T[0]
      : never
    : never;

// TypeScript 5.4+: single-step with bounded infer
type FirstStringElement<T extends readonly unknown[]> =
  T extends readonly [infer First extends string, ...unknown[]]
    ? First
    : never;

type Result1 = FirstStringElement<["hello", 1, true]>; // "hello"
type Result2 = FirstStringElement<[42, "world"]>;       // never (first is number)

// Extract numeric literal from a tuple's second position
type SecondNumber<T extends readonly unknown[]> =
  T extends readonly [unknown, infer Second extends number, ...unknown[]]
    ? Second
    : never;

type S1 = SecondNumber<[string, 42, boolean]>; // 42

// Extract string keys from a Record type
type StringKeys<T> = {
  [K in keyof T]: K extends string ? K : never;
}[keyof T];

// Using bounded infer in template literal extraction
type UnwrapPromiseName<T extends string> =
  T extends `Promise<${infer Inner extends string}>` ? Inner : T;
type Unwrapped = UnwrapPromiseName<"Promise<string>">;    // "string"
type Unchanged = UnwrapPromiseName<"Observable<number>">; // "Observable<number>"
```

**Tradeoff:** Bounded `infer` requires TypeScript 5.4+; check your project's minimum TypeScript version before adopting. The syntax is not backward-compatible — projects supporting older TypeScript versions must use the two-step pattern. Also, `infer X extends SomeInterface` checks structural compatibility, not nominal identity, so `infer X extends string` captures any type assignable to `string`, which is just `string` and its literal subtypes.

---

### Pattern 14 — `satisfies` Operator for Config Validation While Preserving Literal Types [official]

The `satisfies` operator (TypeScript 4.9) validates that an expression matches a type without widening the expression's inferred type to that annotation. This is particularly valuable for configuration objects, route definitions, and constant maps where you want both compile-time shape validation and preservation of narrow literal types for downstream inference. A type annotation (`const x: T = value`) widens to `T`; `satisfies T` validates against `T` but retains the narrow inferred type.

```typescript
// Problem: annotation widens literal types, losing autocomplete fidelity
const routes_annotated: Record<string, { path: string; method: string }> = {
  getUser: { path: "/users/:id", method: "GET" },
  createUser: { path: "/users", method: "POST" },
};
// routes_annotated.getUser.method is typed as `string` — no autocompletion

// Solution: satisfies validates shape, retains narrow types
const routes = {
  getUser: { path: "/users/:id", method: "GET" as const },
  createUser: { path: "/users", method: "POST" as const },
} satisfies Record<string, { path: string; method: "GET" | "POST" | "PUT" | "DELETE" }>;

// routes.getUser.method is typed as `"GET"` — autocomplete works perfectly
type GetUserMethod = typeof routes.getUser.method; // "GET"

// Practical: type-safe color palette with hex validation
type HexColor = `#${string}`;
const palette = {
  primary: "#3B82F6",
  secondary: "#6366F1",
  error: "#EF4444",
} satisfies Record<string, HexColor>;

// Each value is still narrowed to its literal: palette.primary is "#3B82F6"
// But non-hex strings would error:
// const badPalette = { primary: "blue" } satisfies Record<string, HexColor>; // error

// Exhaustive enum-like mapping with satisfies
type Weekday = "Mon" | "Tue" | "Wed" | "Thu" | "Fri";
const workHours = {
  Mon: 8, Tue: 8, Wed: 8, Thu: 8, Fri: 7,
} satisfies Record<Weekday, number>;
// Adding a new Weekday to the type will cause a compile error here — enforced completeness
```

**Tradeoff:** `satisfies` is a compile-time-only operator (like a type assertion, it emits no JavaScript). It does not perform runtime validation. When the object is constructed from dynamic data (user input, API responses), you still need a runtime validator (Zod, Valibot). Also, `satisfies` does not allow excess properties in some contexts — if the type has no index signature, extra properties cause an error, which can be surprising when constructing partial fixtures.

---

### Pattern 15 — Declaration Merging: Augmenting Third-Party Modules and Global Scope [official]

TypeScript's declaration merging allows you to extend types defined in external modules or the global scope without modifying the original source. Module augmentation adds properties to existing interfaces from `node_modules` (e.g., extending Express's `Request`, augmenting `Window`, or adding custom fields to `process.env`). Ambient module declarations provide types for untyped modules (CSS, SVG, WASM) or fix incomplete `@types` packages. These patterns are essential for framework integration and gradual typing of legacy JavaScript dependencies.

```typescript
// 1. Augment an Express Request with a typed user property
import "express";
declare module "express" {
  interface Request {
    user?: { id: string; roles: string[] };
  }
}

// Now in request handlers:
import { Request, Response } from "express";
function protectedRoute(req: Request, res: Response): void {
  if (!req.user) { res.status(401).end(); return; }
  // req.user is now { id: string; roles: string[] } — no cast needed
  const { id, roles } = req.user;
}

// 2. Extend the Window interface for a third-party analytics script
declare global {
  interface Window {
    analytics: {
      track(event: string, properties?: Record<string, unknown>): void;
    };
  }
}
window.analytics.track("page_view", { path: location.pathname });

// 3. Type-safe process.env with string literal keys
declare global {
  namespace NodeJS {
    interface ProcessEnv {
      readonly NODE_ENV: "development" | "production" | "test";
      readonly DATABASE_URL: string;
      readonly JWT_SECRET: string;
    }
  }
}
// process.env.NODE_ENV is now "development" | "production" | "test" — not string
const env: "development" | "production" | "test" = process.env.NODE_ENV;

// 4. Ambient module for CSS modules
declare module "*.module.css" {
  const classes: Record<string, string>;
  export default classes;
}
import styles from "./Button.module.css";
const className: string = styles.button; // ✅ typed
```

**Tradeoff:** Module augmentation is powerful but fragile — the augmentation only applies when the augmenting file is included in the compilation (via `include`, `files`, or `references`). If the augmentation file is excluded from `tsconfig.json`, augmented types silently disappear with no error. Always place global augmentations in a `*.d.ts` file that is explicitly included in `tsconfig.json`, and add a comment explaining why the file must be kept. Augmenting third-party types also creates tight coupling to those types' internal structure; interface changes in library updates can silently break your augmentation.

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 42

**Gotcha 65 — TypeScript 5.8's granular return-branch checking surfaces new errors in codebases that return `any`-typed cache values in ternary expressions — these were previously silently accepted** [community]

```typescript
// ❌ Pattern that worked silently in TypeScript ≤5.7 but now errors in 5.8
const responseCache = new Map<string, any>();

function getCachedUser(id: string): { name: string; email: string } {
  return responseCache.has(id)
    ? responseCache.get(id)       // returns any — ok in ≤5.7
    : { name: "unknown", email: "" }; // ← 5.7: any union hides this branch check
                                      // ← 5.8: BOTH branches checked separately
}
// In TypeScript 5.8, the second branch is checked against the return type independently.
// If the `any` branch returns are fine, but a third refactor branch returns wrong type,
// the error is now caught.

// ✅ Fix: type your caches properly
const typedCache = new Map<string, { name: string; email: string }>();
function getCachedUserSafe(id: string): { name: string; email: string } {
  return typedCache.get(id) ?? { name: "unknown", email: "" };
}
```

WHY: In TypeScript 5.7 and earlier, when checking the return type of `condition ? anyExpr : typedExpr`, the two branches were unified into a single type first (`any | { name: string; email: string }` = `any`), then that union was checked against the return type. Since `any` is assignable to everything, the check always passed — even if the concrete branch returned an incompatible type. TypeScript 5.8 changed this to check each branch independently against the declared return type. This is strictly safer (the previous behavior was a soundness gap), but it surfaces errors in any function that returns a ternary where one branch yields `any`. The fix is always mechanical: either type the `any` source properly or add an explicit cast (`as ReturnType`) with a comment explaining why the cast is safe.

---

**Gotcha 66 — `--erasableSyntaxOnly` does not automatically convert enums — existing code using `enum` silently passes compilation until the flag is enabled, after which hundreds of errors appear** [community]

```typescript
// File: constants.ts — typical existing codebase pattern
enum HttpMethod {
  GET = "GET",
  POST = "POST",
  PUT = "PUT",
  DELETE = "DELETE",
}

enum StatusCode {
  OK = 200,
  Created = 201,
  BadRequest = 400,
  Unauthorized = 401,
  NotFound = 404,
}

// ❌ Both enums error with --erasableSyntaxOnly:
// error TS1294: This syntax is not allowed when 'erasableSyntaxOnly' is enabled.

// ✅ Migration: const assertion objects + derived union types
const HttpMethod = {
  GET: "GET",
  POST: "POST",
  PUT: "PUT",
  DELETE: "DELETE",
} as const;
type HttpMethod = typeof HttpMethod[keyof typeof HttpMethod];

const StatusCode = {
  OK: 200,
  Created: 201,
  BadRequest: 400,
  Unauthorized: 401,
  NotFound: 404,
} as const;
type StatusCode = typeof StatusCode[keyof typeof StatusCode];

// Note: string enum behavior is preserved. Numeric enum reverse mapping is LOST:
// Original: HttpMethod[HttpMethod.GET] === "GET" ← true for numeric enums
// After migration: no reverse lookup — access by key only
```

WHY: TypeScript's `enum` keyword emits a JavaScript IIFE (immediately invoked function expression) that creates a bidirectional mapping object at runtime. This means `enum` is not type syntax — it is value syntax that generates real JavaScript code. Node.js's `--experimental-strip-types` and similar tools (esbuild's `--loader=ts` in strip mode) can only remove type-only constructs by deleting them; they cannot transform `enum` into the IIFE equivalent. When `--erasableSyntaxOnly` is enabled, every `enum` declaration becomes a compile error. In a large codebase with dozens of enum files, this is a significant mechanical migration. Use a codemod (e.g., `ts-enum-to-const`) to automate the transformation, but verify that no code relied on the numeric reverse mapping (`Enum[Enum.Value]`) that const assertions do not provide.

---

**Gotcha 67 — Key remapping with `as` in mapped types silently produces an empty type when the remapping expression narrows all keys to `never`** [community]

```typescript
// ❌ Subtle: all keys filtered to never → empty object type (not an error)
interface Config {
  apiUrl: string;
  timeout: number;
  retries: number;
}

// Intended: pick only boolean properties
type BooleanKeys<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as T[K] extends boolean ? K : never]: T[K];
};

type ConfigBooleans = BooleanKeys<Config>;
// {}  ← empty object type! No error. No warning. Config has no boolean fields.

// ❌ Silent failure in a generic utility used downstream
function getBooleanDefaults<T>(config: T): BooleanKeys<T> {
  return {} as BooleanKeys<T>; // always returns {} if T has no boolean fields
}

// ✅ Fix: add a type-level assertion to detect unexpected empty results
type AssertNonEmpty<T extends Record<string, unknown>> =
  keyof T extends never ? "ERROR: No keys matched the filter" : T;

type ConfigBooleansChecked = AssertNonEmpty<BooleanKeys<Config>>;
// type ConfigBooleansChecked = "ERROR: No keys matched the filter"

// ✅ Better fix: document the filtering intent and test with a type assertion
type HasBooleanField<T> = BooleanKeys<T> extends Record<string, never> ? false : true;
type Check = HasBooleanField<{ active: boolean; name: string }>; // true
type CheckFail = HasBooleanField<Config>; // false
```

WHY: When a mapped type's `as` clause produces `never` for every key, TypeScript resolves the entire mapped type to `{}` (the empty object type). This is by design — `never` keys are excluded from the output, and if all keys are excluded, the result is a valid empty object type. TypeScript does not warn about this because `{}` is a legitimate type. The problem arises when a developer writes a filtering mapped type expecting it to extract something, and the filter silently matches nothing. This is especially subtle when the mapped type is a generic utility used across multiple types — the caller sees `{}` inferred for the return type and may not immediately realize the filter matched nothing. Add explicit `AssertNonEmpty` or `keyof T extends never` guards in tests when a mapped type filter is a core invariant of a utility type.

---

**Gotcha 68 — `--noUncheckedSideEffectImports` requires ambient module declarations for CSS, image, and worker imports — omitting them turns existing import patterns into errors after enabling the flag** [community]

```typescript
// Existing project without --noUncheckedSideEffectImports: all of these compile silently
import "./styles/reset.css";
import "./styles/App.css";
import logoUrl from "./assets/logo.png";
import workerPath from "./workers/heavy.worker.ts";

// After enabling --noUncheckedSideEffectImports without ambient declarations:
// ❌ error: Cannot find module './styles/reset.css'
// ❌ error: Cannot find module './styles/App.css'
// ❌ error: Cannot find module './assets/logo.png'
// ❌ error: Cannot find module './workers/heavy.worker.ts'

// ✅ Fix: add a global ambient declarations file
// src/global.d.ts (must be included in tsconfig.json's include array)
declare module "*.css" {}
declare module "*.scss" {}
declare module "*.sass" {}
declare module "*.png" { const url: string; export default url; }
declare module "*.jpg" { const url: string; export default url; }
declare module "*.svg" { const url: string; export default url; }
declare module "*.webp" { const url: string; export default url; }

// For web workers (varies by bundler):
declare module "*.worker.ts" {
  class WorkerFactory {
    constructor();
  }
  export default WorkerFactory;
}

// ✅ tsconfig.json: ensure the declarations file is included
// { "include": ["src/**/*.ts", "src/**/*.tsx", "src/global.d.ts"] }
```

WHY: `--noUncheckedSideEffectImports` applies module resolution checks to bare side-effect imports (`import "..."`) for the first time. Previously, TypeScript skipped resolution on these imports entirely — a deliberate choice because many projects import CSS, images, and workers that have no TypeScript types. Enabling the flag without first adding ambient declarations converts these historically silent imports into errors. The upgrade path is: (1) run `tsc --noEmit --noUncheckedSideEffectImports` to discover all failing imports, (2) add a `global.d.ts` with wildcard module declarations for each affected extension, (3) verify the file is included in `tsconfig.json`, then (4) enable the flag permanently. The benefit — catching typos in polyfill import paths — is significant enough to make this migration worthwhile.

---

**Gotcha 69 — Standard decorators (TypeScript 5.0+) and `--experimentalDecorators` are mutually exclusive within a project — importing a file that uses one model into a file configured for the other causes subtle type errors or runtime failures** [community]

```typescript
// ❌ Project mismatch: library uses standard decorators, consumer uses --experimentalDecorators
// (or vice versa)

// library/decorators.ts — standard decorator (TypeScript 5.0+ default)
export function log(
  target: (this: unknown, ...args: unknown[]) => unknown,
  context: ClassMethodDecoratorContext
): void {
  const name = String(context.name);
  return function (this: unknown, ...args: unknown[]) {
    console.log(`Calling ${name}`);
    return (target as Function).call(this, ...args);
  } as typeof target;
}

// consumer.ts — with --experimentalDecorators in tsconfig
import { log } from "./library/decorators";
class Service {
  @log  // ← type mismatch: experimental decorators expect different signature
  doWork(): void { /* ... */ }
}
// TypeScript emits inconsistent decorator call conventions for the two models.
// The result is a runtime failure or silent no-op decorator.

// ✅ Correct: ensure all decorator code in a project uses the same model
// tsconfig.json options:
// Standard decorators (default in TS 5.0+): no flag needed
// Experimental: { "experimentalDecorators": true, "emitDecoratorMetadata": true }

// ✅ Check which model a library uses:
// - Uses ClassMethodDecoratorContext → standard decorators (TS 5.0+ model)
// - Uses (target: any, key: string, descriptor: PropertyDescriptor) → experimental model
// - NestJS, TypeORM, Angular (pre-2024) → all use experimental model
```

WHY: TypeScript 5.0 introduced an entirely new decorator semantics aligned with the TC39 proposal — the decorator function signature, call convention, and emit strategy are fundamentally different from `--experimentalDecorators`. When `--experimentalDecorators` is enabled in `tsconfig.json`, TypeScript switches to the old model for the entire project; the new standard decorator syntax is not available. When a library compiled with standard decorators is imported into a project using `--experimentalDecorators`, the decorator functions have mismatched signatures — they expect a `ClassMethodDecoratorContext` but receive the old `(target, key, descriptor)` triplet (or vice versa), causing either a type error or a silent runtime malfunction. The fix is project-wide consistency: either all code uses standard decorators, or all code uses `--experimentalDecorators`. Migration from experimental to standard requires framework support (NestJS, Angular, etc.) which may not be ready yet.

---

### Anti-Patterns: Cycle 42 Additions

| Anti-pattern | Why it's harmful | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Returning a ternary expression where one branch is `any` without auditing the concrete branch's type safety (TypeScript 5.8+) | TypeScript 5.8 checks each ternary branch independently against the return type, surfacing hidden type errors that `any`-union collapse previously swallowed | Type caches as `Map<K, V>` instead of `Map<any, any>`; add explicit return type annotations to functions with ternary returns involving `any` sources |
| Enabling `--erasableSyntaxOnly` on a codebase without first migrating all `enum` declarations | Every `enum` becomes a compile error; doing this in one step in a large codebase blocks CI and disrupts the team | Run `tsc --erasableSyntaxOnly --noEmit` as a diagnostic before enabling; use a codemod to migrate `enum` → `as const` + union type incrementally |
| Writing filtered mapped types without testing for the empty-type edge case | `as never` remapping produces `{}` silently; callers infer `{}` instead of the intended type and no error is raised | Add `keyof T extends never ? ErrorSentinel : T` guards in type tests for any filtered mapped type utility |
| Enabling `--noUncheckedSideEffectImports` without first adding a `global.d.ts` with wildcard ambient declarations | All existing CSS, image, and worker side-effect imports become errors immediately | Audit `import "..."` patterns first with `--noEmit`, add wildcard ambient declarations, then enable the flag |
| Mixing standard decorators (TS 5.0+) with `--experimentalDecorators` across library/application boundaries | Decorator signatures are incompatible between the two models; the mismatch causes silent no-ops or runtime failures | Use one decorator model per project; prefer standard decorators for new code; check framework readiness before migrating existing decorator-heavy code |
| Writing `[K in keyof T as \`get${K}\`]` without casting `string & K` | `keyof T` includes `symbol` and `number`; template literal types require `string`, causing a type error | Always use `\`get${Capitalize<string & K>}\`` to constrain to string keys before applying template literal intrinsics |
| Using `--module nodenext` on a Node.js 18 project after upgrading to TypeScript 5.8 | TypeScript 5.8 added `require()` of ESM under `nodenext` (reflecting Node.js 22), meaning Node.js 18 users silently lose `import assertions` support and may encounter behaviors only valid in Node 22 | Pin to `--module node18` for Node.js 18 LTS projects; migrate to `nodenext` only when upgrading the runtime to Node.js 22+ |
