### Pattern 10 — Template Literal Types as Strongly-Typed Event Emitters [community]

Template literal types combined with mapped types and conditional types enable fully type-safe event emitter APIs where the set of event names and their payload types are both statically checked. Each event name is a string literal, and the payload type is derived from the event name through a lookup in a user-defined event map. This pattern eliminates the `any`-typed event payloads that plague untyped emitter libraries and makes `on`/`emit` calls self-documenting and IDE-navigable.

```typescript
// Define the event map: event name → payload type
type AppEvents = {
  "user:login":    { userId: string; timestamp: number };
  "user:logout":   { userId: string; reason: "manual" | "timeout" };
  "item:added":    { itemId: string; quantity: number };
  "item:removed":  { itemId: string };
  "error:network": { code: number; message: string };
};

// Extract all event names as a union of string literals
type EventName = keyof AppEvents; // "user:login" | "user:logout" | ...

// Type-safe emitter interface
interface TypedEmitter<Events extends Record<string, unknown>> {
  on<K extends keyof Events>(
    event: K,
    listener: (payload: Events[K]) => void
  ): this;
  emit<K extends keyof Events>(event: K, payload: Events[K]): boolean;
  off<K extends keyof Events>(event: K, listener: (payload: Events[K]) => void): this;
}

// ✅ Usage — fully type-checked
declare const emitter: TypedEmitter<AppEvents>;

emitter.on("user:login", ({ userId, timestamp }) => {
  // userId: string, timestamp: number — inferred ✅
  console.log(`${userId} logged in at ${timestamp}`);
});

emitter.emit("user:logout", { userId: "u1", reason: "timeout" }); // ✅

// ❌ Caught at compile time:
// emitter.emit("user:login", { userId: "u1", reason: "manual" });
//   ↑ error: 'reason' does not exist in type '{ userId: string; timestamp: number }'

// ✅ Utility: extract payload type for a given event
type PayloadOf<K extends EventName> = AppEvents[K];
type LoginPayload = PayloadOf<"user:login">; // { userId: string; timestamp: number }
```

**Tradeoff:** The event map type must be defined centrally and kept in sync with all emitter usages. If events are dynamically generated (e.g., from a server-sent schema), the static map cannot represent them and the pattern degrades to `Record<string, unknown>`. For plugin systems where event names are added at runtime, consider a registry pattern with module augmentation instead. [community]

---

### Pattern 11 — `const` Type Parameter: Preserving Literal Types Through Generic Functions [official]

TypeScript 5.0 introduced `const` type parameter modifiers, allowing generic functions to infer literal types (string literals, numeric literals, tuple types) rather than widening to their base types. Before this feature, passing a string literal to a generic `T extends string` parameter always inferred `T = string` unless the caller explicitly added `as const`. The `const` modifier on the type parameter makes the function behave as if all arguments were implicitly annotated with `as const`, without requiring the call site to do anything.

```typescript
// Without const modifier: T widens to string[]
function makeList<T extends string>(items: T[]): T[] {
  return items;
}
const list1 = makeList(["a", "b", "c"]);
//    ^? string[] — widened, not "a" | "b" | "c"

// ✅ With const modifier: T preserved as literal tuple
function makeConstList<const T extends readonly string[]>(items: T): T {
  return items;
}
const list2 = makeConstList(["a", "b", "c"]);
//    ^? readonly ["a", "b", "c"] — literal tuple preserved ✅

// ✅ Practical: type-safe route table
function defineRoutes<const T extends Record<string, { path: string; method: string }>>(
  routes: T
): T {
  return routes;
}

const routes = defineRoutes({
  home:   { path: "/",       method: "GET" },
  login:  { path: "/login",  method: "POST" },
  logout: { path: "/logout", method: "POST" },
});

type RouteName = keyof typeof routes;       // "home" | "login" | "logout" ✅
type HomeMethod = typeof routes.home.method; // "GET" — not string ✅

// ✅ Useful for discriminated union builders
function createAction<const T extends string, P>(
  type: T,
  payload: P
): { type: T; payload: P } {
  return { type, payload };
}

const loginAction = createAction("AUTH/LOGIN", { userId: "u1" });
// loginAction.type: "AUTH/LOGIN" — not string ✅
```

**Tradeoff:** The `const` modifier on a type parameter forces deep literal inference, which can sometimes produce overly-specific types that make union narrowing harder later. If a function is called with both literals and computed values in the same array, the tuple type becomes heterogeneous and less useful. Use `const T` when literal preservation is the primary goal; omit it when working with computed or dynamic values. [official]

---

### Pattern 12 — `satisfies` for Exhaustive Test Fixture Coverage [community]

The `satisfies` operator (TypeScript 4.9) validates that an expression conforms to a type without widening the inferred type of the expression. In test fixtures, this lets you define a fixture object that matches a union type while keeping each property typed as its specific literal value. Combined with `Record<VariantName, SomeType>`, `satisfies` enforces that every variant of a union has a corresponding fixture entry — adding a new variant to the union causes an immediate compile error in the fixture file.

```typescript
// Domain type
type UserRole = "admin" | "editor" | "viewer" | "guest";

type UserFixture = {
  id: string;
  role: UserRole;
  permissions: string[];
};

// ✅ satisfies enforces exhaustive fixture coverage for every UserRole
const USER_FIXTURES = {
  admin:  { id: "u1", role: "admin",  permissions: ["read", "write", "delete"] },
  editor: { id: "u2", role: "editor", permissions: ["read", "write"] },
  viewer: { id: "u3", role: "viewer", permissions: ["read"] },
  guest:  { id: "u4", role: "guest",  permissions: [] },
} satisfies Record<UserRole, UserFixture>;

// ✅ Each value preserves its literal types (not widened to UserFixture)
type AdminRole = typeof USER_FIXTURES.admin.role; // "admin" — not UserRole ✅

// ❌ Adding "moderator" to UserRole without adding a fixture causes a compile error:
// Property 'moderator' is missing in type
// '{ admin: ...; editor: ...; viewer: ...; guest: ...; }'
// but required in type 'Record<"admin" | "editor" | "viewer" | "guest" | "moderator", UserFixture>'

// ✅ Using fixtures in parameterized tests
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";

describe.each(Object.entries(USER_FIXTURES))("user role: %s", (roleName, fixture) => {
  it("has the correct role set on the fixture", () => {
    expect(fixture.role).toBe(roleName);
  });
  it("has a non-empty id", () => {
    expect(fixture.id.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Using `satisfies Record<K, V>` for exhaustive fixtures couples the fixture file tightly to the union definition. If the union is defined in a third-party package and has a new variant added in a minor release, all fixture files using `satisfies Record<K, V>` break until the fixture is updated. This tight coupling is a feature for internal types but a risk for external-dependency types. [community]

---

### Pattern 13 — `PropertyKey`-Based Key Narrowing with Mapped Types and `as` Clauses [community]

TypeScript's mapped type `as` clause (TypeScript 4.1+) enables key remapping during type transformation, producing new object shapes where the keys are derived from the original keys via template literal types or conditional types. Combined with `Extract` or `Exclude`, this creates powerful utilities for reshaping API response types, converting `snake_case` keys to `camelCase`, or stripping prefixes from event names — all without any runtime code.

```typescript
// Remap snake_case keys to camelCase at the type level
type SnakeToCamel<S extends string> =
  S extends `${infer Head}_${infer Tail}`
    ? `${Head}${Capitalize<SnakeToCamel<Tail>>}`
    : S;

type CamelCaseKeys<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as SnakeToCamel<K & string>]: T[K];
};

// ✅ API response type (from backend with snake_case keys)
type ApiUser = {
  user_id: string;
  first_name: string;
  last_name: string;
  created_at: string;
  is_active: boolean;
};

type DomainUser = CamelCaseKeys<ApiUser>;
// {
//   userId: string;
//   firstName: string;
//   lastName: string;
//   createdAt: string;
//   isActive: boolean;
// }

// ✅ Strip a prefix from event names
type StripPrefix<S extends string, Prefix extends string> =
  S extends `${Prefix}${infer Rest}` ? Rest : S;

type StripEventPrefix<T, Prefix extends string> = {
  [K in keyof T as StripPrefix<K & string, Prefix>]: T[K];
};

type RawEvents = {
  "on:click": MouseEvent;
  "on:focus": FocusEvent;
  "on:blur":  FocusEvent;
};

type CleanEvents = StripEventPrefix<RawEvents, "on:">;
// { click: MouseEvent; focus: FocusEvent; blur: FocusEvent; }

// ✅ Type test to verify the mapping
type _test = CleanEvents["click"]; // MouseEvent ✅
```

**Tradeoff:** Recursive template literal types like `SnakeToCamel` can hit TypeScript's instantiation depth limit on very deeply nested type expressions or extremely long strings. For production use, limit the recursion depth or add a depth counter. Key remapping with `as` clauses also does not produce runtime transformation code — you must implement the actual object key renaming separately, and keeping the runtime transformer and the type-level transformer in sync is a manual responsibility. [community]

---

### Pattern 14 — `NoInfer<T>` as a Generic Default Anchor [official]

TypeScript 5.4's `NoInfer<T>` utility type suppresses inference at a specific parameter site, forcing the generic to be resolved entirely from other parameters. A powerful extension of this pattern uses `NoInfer<T>` alongside a default parameter value that shares the same generic as the primary inference site. This creates functions that infer `T` from a required argument and then constrain an optional argument to exactly `T` — preventing the optional argument from accidentally widening the inferred type when passed.

```typescript
// ✅ NoInfer<T> as inference anchor for optional default values
function createStore<T>(
  initialState: T,
  validator?: (state: NoInfer<T>) => boolean,
  fallback?: NoInfer<T>
): { state: T; validate: () => boolean; reset: () => void } {
  let state = initialState;
  return {
    state,
    validate: () => validator?.(state) ?? true,
    reset: () => { state = fallback ?? initialState; },
  };
}

// ✅ T inferred as { count: number; label: string } from initialState only
const counterStore = createStore(
  { count: 0, label: "items" },
  (s) => s.count >= 0,                   // ✅ s: { count: number; label: string }
  { count: 0, label: "reset" }           // ✅ must match T exactly
);

// ❌ Without NoInfer — a mismatched fallback would widen T:
// createStore({ count: 0 }, undefined, { count: 0, extra: true });
//   ↑ Without NoInfer, T might widen to { count: number; extra?: boolean }

// ✅ Pattern: selector functions constrained by inferred state type
function select<TState, TResult>(
  state: TState,
  selector: (s: TState) => TResult,
  defaultValue: NoInfer<TResult>
): TResult {
  try {
    return selector(state) ?? defaultValue;
  } catch {
    return defaultValue;
  }
}

const store = { user: { name: "Alice", age: 30 } };
const name = select(store, (s) => s.user.name, "Anonymous");
//    ^? string — inferred from selector return, defaultValue constrained to string ✅
```

**Tradeoff:** `NoInfer<T>` only suppresses inference; it does not prevent assignment. After `T` is resolved, `NoInfer<T>` is structurally identical to `T`, so callers can still pass any `T`-compatible value to `NoInfer<T>` parameters. This is the desired behavior for an optional fallback, but it means `NoInfer` cannot be used to create a parameter that rejects all values post-inference. Use explicit validation logic or branded types for that level of restriction. [official]

---

### Pattern 15 — Discriminated Unions with `never`-Narrowed Exhaustiveness Checks at Runtime [community]

A common TypeScript pattern is to use `assertNever(x: never)` in the `default` case of a `switch` over a discriminated union. TypeScript's control flow ensures that if all union variants are handled, the type of `x` is narrowed to `never` by the time it reaches `default`. This check is purely compile-time, but the function can also throw at runtime to catch exhaustiveness violations introduced after a union is extended without updating all switch statements.

```typescript
// The classic assertNever utility
function assertNever(x: never, context?: string): never {
  throw new Error(
    `Unhandled discriminant: ${JSON.stringify(x)}` +
    (context ? ` in ${context}` : "")
  );
}

// ✅ Discriminated union
type Shape =
  | { kind: "circle";    radius: number }
  | { kind: "rectangle"; width: number; height: number }
  | { kind: "triangle";  base: number;  height: number };

function area(shape: Shape): number {
  switch (shape.kind) {
    case "circle":    return Math.PI * shape.radius ** 2;
    case "rectangle": return shape.width * shape.height;
    case "triangle":  return 0.5 * shape.base * shape.height;
    default:          return assertNever(shape, "area");
    // ↑ TypeScript error if a new variant is added without a case here ✅
  }
}

// ✅ Exhaustiveness via object map (alternative to switch)
const AREA_FN: { [K in Shape["kind"]]: (shape: Extract<Shape, { kind: K }>) => number } = {
  circle:    (s) => Math.PI * s.radius ** 2,
  rectangle: (s) => s.width * s.height,
  triangle:  (s) => 0.5 * s.base * s.height,
};
// ← adding "hexagon" to Shape without adding a key here is a compile error ✅

function areaV2(shape: Shape): number {
  return (AREA_FN[shape.kind] as (s: typeof shape) => number)(shape);
}

// ✅ Test: verify assertNever throws for unknown shapes at runtime
import { expect, it } from "vitest";
it("assertNever throws for unhandled discriminants", () => {
  const unknown = { kind: "hexagon" } as unknown as Shape;
  expect(() => area(unknown)).toThrow("Unhandled discriminant");
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The `switch` + `assertNever` pattern provides static exhaustiveness checking but requires the switch to be written manually for each callsite. The object-map pattern (`AREA_FN`) is more concise and enforces exhaustiveness at the type definition, but accessing `AREA_FN[shape.kind]` requires a cast if the types are not set up carefully. Both patterns are complementary: use the object map for data-driven dispatch and `assertNever` in `switch` statements for complex per-variant control flow. [community]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 44

**Gotcha 76 — TypeScript 5.8's per-branch return checks can surface errors in code that has been "working" for years due to implicit `any` propagation through ternaries** [community]

```typescript
// ❌ Code that silently passed TypeScript < 5.8
declare const registry: Map<any, any>;

function getHandler(name: string): (event: Event) => void {
  return registry.has(name)
    ? registry.get(name)  // returned any — propagated to return type
    : name;               // string — hidden behind any, no error
}
// TypeScript 5.8 now errors:
// Type 'string' is not assignable to type '(event: Event) => void'

// ✅ Fix: explicit cast at the cache access site
function getHandlerFixed(name: string): (event: Event) => void {
  return registry.has(name)
    ? (registry.get(name) as (event: Event) => void)
    : () => {};  // ← now correctly typed fallback
}

// ✅ Pattern: add a type-safe wrapper for untyped Maps
class TypedRegistry<K, V> {
  private map = new Map<K, V>();
  set(key: K, value: V): void { this.map.set(key, value); }
  get(key: K): V | undefined { return this.map.get(key); }
}
const handlerRegistry = new TypedRegistry<string, (event: Event) => void>();
```

WHY: Prior to TypeScript 5.8, when a ternary contained a branch returning `any`, the entire ternary expression resolved to `any` (because `any | T` collapses to `any` in TypeScript's type algebra). This meant that the other branch, even if it returned a clearly wrong type (like `string` where `URL` is expected), was silently swept under the `any` umbrella. TypeScript 5.8 changed this by checking each branch of a ternary in a `return` statement independently against the declared return type. This is a targeted breaking change — only `return` expressions with ternaries are affected, not general assignments — and it was deliberately narrow in scope to minimize disruption while catching the most impactful class of hidden bugs.

---

**Gotcha 77 — `--erasableSyntaxOnly` breaks parameter properties silently in downstream consumers if the library is shipped as TypeScript source (not compiled)** [community]

```typescript
// Library distributed as TypeScript source: lib/user.ts
export class User {
  constructor(
    public readonly id: string,     // ← parameter property
    public name: string,
    private email: string
  ) {}
}

// ❌ Consumer with --erasableSyntaxOnly enabled:
// import { User } from "../lib/user"; ← compile error
// Error: Parameter properties are not allowed with --erasableSyntaxOnly

// ✅ Fix for library authors: expand parameter properties before distribution
export class UserSafe {
  public readonly id: string;
  public name: string;
  private email: string;
  constructor(id: string, name: string, email: string) {
    this.id = id;
    this.name = name;
    this.email = email;
  }
}

// ✅ If you must keep parameter properties in source, compile to .js + .d.ts before shipping
// tsconfig.lib.json: { "compilerOptions": { "declaration": true, "outDir": "dist" } }
// package.json: { "main": "dist/user.js", "types": "dist/user.d.ts" }
// Consumers see compiled output — no parameter properties in the .d.ts
```

WHY: `--erasableSyntaxOnly` was designed for projects that run TypeScript directly via Node.js 23.6+ type stripping, Bun, or Deno, where the runtime strips type annotations without compiling. Parameter properties cannot be erased by simple text removal because they are syntactic sugar that generates both a field declaration and an assignment statement — a non-trivial transform. When a library ships TypeScript source (common in monorepos or "works with tsx" packages) and a consumer enables `--erasableSyntaxOnly`, the library's parameter properties become a compile error on the consumer's side even though the library never enabled the flag itself. The only safe fix for library authors targeting this audience is to expand parameter properties in source or compile to JavaScript before shipping.

---

**Gotcha 78 — `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` only rewrites relative imports — path aliases, npm packages, and `#internal` imports are NOT rewritten** [community]

```typescript
// tsconfig.json:
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "paths": { "@utils/*": ["./src/utils/*"] },
//     "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true
//   }
// }

// src/index.ts
import { helper } from "./local/helper.ts";       // ✅ REWRITTEN → ./local/helper.js
import { util }   from "@utils/format.ts";         // ❌ NOT rewritten — path alias
import { tool }   from "#internal/tool.ts";        // ❌ NOT rewritten — package import
import { lib }    from "some-package/entry.ts";    // ❌ NOT rewritten — npm package

// ❌ Runtime error in Deno/Bun: cannot resolve "@utils/format.ts"
// The alias is not rewritten to a .js extension in the output

// ✅ For path aliases, use a custom path plugin in your bundler/runner config
// Deno: import_map.json → map "@utils/" to the actual path
// Bun: bunfig.toml → configure path aliases
// tsx: tsconfig-paths + ts-node register

// ✅ Or avoid path aliases entirely in native-run TypeScript projects
// and use only relative imports (the rewrite will handle them)

// ✅ Diagnostic: check compiled output for alias imports
// tsc --outDir dist && grep 'from "@utils' dist/index.js
// If the alias appears unchanged, it will fail at runtime in non-Node runtimes
```

WHY: The `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` flag was designed with a narrow scope: it only modifies import specifiers that start with `./` or `../` and end with a TypeScript extension (`.ts`, `.tsx`, `.mts`, `.cts`). This scope was intentional — rewriting npm package imports or path aliases would require understanding the entire module resolution configuration and could produce incorrect rewrites if the alias resolution does not map 1:1 to a filesystem path. The flag is a low-risk, mechanical text substitution for the simple relative case. All other import formats require the developer to configure their runtime's module resolver (import maps, alias plugins, etc.) independently of TypeScript's compilation step.

---

**Gotcha 79 — TypeScript 5.7's TypedArray generic change causes `Type 'Uint8Array' is not assignable to type 'Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>'` errors when upgrading `@types/node`** [community]

```typescript
// ❌ Code that breaks after upgrading to TypeScript 5.7 + @types/node@22+
// Old @types/node: Uint8Array = Uint8Array (no type parameter)
// New @types/node: Uint8Array = Uint8Array<ArrayBufferLike>

function writeChunk(chunk: Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>): void {
  // ... write chunk to underlying buffer
}

// The error appears when passing a Uint8Array from a Node.js stream:
// readable.on("data", (chunk: Uint8Array) => {
//   writeChunk(chunk);
//   // ↑ Error: Argument of type 'Uint8Array<ArrayBufferLike>' is not assignable
//   //          to parameter of type 'Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>'
// });

// ✅ Fix Option 1: widen the parameter to accept ArrayBufferLike
function writeChunkFixed<T extends ArrayBufferLike>(chunk: Uint8Array<T>): void {
  const buffer = Buffer.from(chunk.buffer, chunk.byteOffset, chunk.byteLength);
  // work with buffer
}

// ✅ Fix Option 2: use Buffer (Node.js) which is always Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>
function writeChunkBuffer(chunk: Buffer): void {
  // Buffer is always Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer> in Node.js ✅
}

// ✅ Fix Option 3: accept the abstract constraint for maximum compatibility
function writeChunkAbstract(chunk: Uint8Array): void {
  // Uint8Array without a type parameter = Uint8Array<ArrayBufferLike> ✅
  // This is the most backward-compatible signature
}
```

WHY: TypeScript 5.7 made all `TypedArray` types generic over their buffer type (`ArrayBuffer` vs `SharedArrayBuffer` vs `ArrayBufferLike`). The default type parameter is `ArrayBufferLike` (the union of all buffer types), which means that `Uint8Array` without an explicit type argument now means `Uint8Array<ArrayBufferLike>`. Code that previously typed parameters as `Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>` (the specific type) now rejects `Uint8Array<ArrayBufferLike>` (the default) because `ArrayBufferLike` is not assignable to `ArrayBuffer` — it is the wider type. The fix is to either widen the parameter to `Uint8Array<T extends ArrayBufferLike>` or use the abstract `Uint8Array` (no parameter) which defaults to the widest form.

---

**Gotcha 80 — Computed property names in `.d.ts` files (TypeScript 5.8) reference the exported variable by name — renaming or deleting the variable breaks all consumers** [community]

```typescript
// Library: lib/keys.ts
export const SERIALIZE = "serialize";       // ← name referenced in .d.ts
export const DESERIALIZE = "deserialize";   // ← name referenced in .d.ts

// Library: lib/serializer.ts
import { SERIALIZE, DESERIALIZE } from "./keys.js";
export class JsonSerializer {
  [SERIALIZE](value: unknown): string { return JSON.stringify(value); }
  [DESERIALIZE]<T>(raw: string): T { return JSON.parse(raw) as T; }
}

// Generated .d.ts (TypeScript 5.8):
// import { SERIALIZE, DESERIALIZE } from "./keys.js";
// export class JsonSerializer {
//   [SERIALIZE](value: unknown): string;
//   [DESERIALIZE]<T>(raw: string): T;
// }

// ❌ Breaking change: renaming SERIALIZE → ENCODE in a minor version
// Consumers that reference [SERIALIZE] on JsonSerializer instances now get:
// Property '[SERIALIZE]' does not exist on type 'JsonSerializer'

// ✅ Guard against accidental renames: use unique symbol for stable contracts
export declare const SERIALIZE: unique symbol;
// unique symbol identity is tied to the declaration, not the name —
// but renaming the export is STILL a breaking change for consumers

// ✅ Best practice: treat computed property key exports as part of the public API
// Document them explicitly in CHANGELOG and semver accordingly
// Consider re-exporting as well-known constants from a stable entry point
```

WHY: When TypeScript 5.8 preserves computed property names in `.d.ts` files, it does so by emitting the variable name reference (e.g., `[SERIALIZE]`) directly in the declaration. This means the generated declaration file has an import dependency on the variable — and the variable name is now part of the public API contract of the library. If a library author treats these computed key variables as internal implementation details and renames or removes them in a semver-minor or patch release, all consumers that reference the computed property (e.g., `instance[SERIALIZE]()`) will receive a type error on upgrade. This is a new API-surface consideration that did not exist in TypeScript 5.7 and earlier, where such properties were either rejected or collapsed to index signatures.

---

**Gotcha 81 — `const` type parameters widen when the call site mixes literals with computed values in the same array argument** [community]

```typescript
// ✅ Fully literal: const T infers a precise tuple
function tag<const T extends readonly string[]>(items: T): T { return items; }

const pure = tag(["alpha", "beta", "gamma"]);
//    ^? readonly ["alpha", "beta", "gamma"] ✅

// ❌ Mixed literal + computed: T widens to string[]
const prefix = "omega";
const mixed = tag(["alpha", prefix, "gamma"]);
//    ^? readonly [string, string, string] — no literals preserved

// ❌ Also widens when computed via function call
const mixed2 = tag(["alpha", String(42), "gamma"]);
//    ^? readonly [string, string, string]

// ✅ Fix: pre-declare the computed value as a const to help narrowing
// This does NOT fix the problem — String(42) is still string at type level
// The only solution is to use literals directly or cast:
const mixed3 = tag(["alpha", "42" as const, "gamma"]);
//    ^? readonly ["alpha", "42", "gamma"] ✅ — explicit as const cast

// ✅ When mixing is unavoidable, prefer a union return type
function tagFlexible<const T extends string>(items: T[]): T[] { return items; }
const flexed = tagFlexible(["alpha", prefix]);
//    ^? string[] — clear: widened, no literal illusion
```

WHY: TypeScript's `const` type parameter modifier instructs the compiler to infer the most precise (deepest literal) type for each element in the argument. However, this inference is per-element, and computed values (variables, function calls, expressions) do not have literal types at the source level — they have their evaluated types (`string`, `number`, etc.). When a `const T` parameter receives an array containing a mix of string literals and string-typed variables, TypeScript cannot narrow the variable-typed elements to literals because they genuinely are not literals. The result is that the entire array element type widens to the base type, producing a homogeneous `readonly [string, string, string]` tuple rather than a heterogeneous literal tuple. This surprises developers who expect `const T` to "lock in" all values regardless of their source.

---

### Anti-Patterns: Cycle 44 Additions

| Anti-pattern | Why it's harmful | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Relying on `any`-propagation in ternaries to suppress return-type errors | TypeScript 5.8 checks each branch of a `return` ternary independently — `any \| string` no longer collapses to `any` | Add explicit `as T` casts at untyped-cache access sites; use typed wrappers for `Map<any, any>` |
| Enabling `--erasableSyntaxOnly` globally in a monorepo that transitively depends on library source using parameter properties | Parameter properties are non-erasable; they cause compile errors in consuming packages even if the library never opted in | Compile libraries to `.js + .d.ts` before sharing; expand parameter properties in source for native-run packages |
| Using path aliases (`@utils/foo.ts`) and expecting `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` to rewrite them | The flag only rewrites relative imports (`./`, `../`); path aliases, scoped packages, and `#internal` imports are untouched | Configure the runtime's module resolver (import maps, Bun aliases, Deno import map) for non-relative imports |
| Typing a function parameter as `Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>` after upgrading to TypeScript 5.7 | Node.js streams emit `Uint8Array<ArrayBufferLike>` (the wider default); the narrower `ArrayBuffer` type rejects it | Widen to `Uint8Array<T extends ArrayBufferLike>` or use unparameterized `Uint8Array` for maximum compatibility |
| Treating exported computed property key variables as internal implementation details | TypeScript 5.8 preserves computed key names in `.d.ts` — renaming the variable is a breaking API change | Document computed key exports in the public API changelog; version them as semver-breaking renames |
| Passing an array mixing string literals and computed values to a `const T` generic expecting all-literal inference | TypeScript cannot infer literals for computed values — the entire tuple widens to `string[]` | Use only inline literals, or cast computed values with `as const`; document the restriction in the API |
| Using `--module node18` for projects that plan to migrate to Node.js 22+ | `node18` is intentionally frozen and will not pick up Node.js 22 ESM `require()` semantics | Start with `--module nodenext` and pin the runtime version in `engines` instead of the TypeScript module target |

## Cycle 45 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 1 — TypeScript 5.9 `import defer`: Lazy Module Evaluation [official]

TypeScript 5.9 adds support for the TC39 `import defer` proposal, which allows a module's side effects and exports to be lazily evaluated — the module graph is fully loaded and linked at startup, but execution is deferred until the namespace is first accessed. Only namespace imports (`import defer * as ns from "..."`) are allowed; named and default deferred imports are not supported. The feature requires `--module preserve` or `--module esnext`. Modules containing top-level `await` cannot be deferred — they execute eagerly along with any async transitive dependencies, while only synchronous modules in the subtree remain deferred.

```typescript
// ✅ Only namespace import form is supported
import defer * as analytics from "./analytics.js";
import defer * as heavyLib from "./heavy-feature.js";

// Neither analytics nor heavyLib have executed yet —
// the module graph is loaded and linked but execution is suspended

function initializeApp(): void {
  const config = loadConfig();

  if (config.analyticsEnabled) {
    // First property access triggers synchronous evaluation
    analytics.init(config.analyticsKey);
  }

  // heavyLib never executes if this branch is never reached
  if (config.featureFlags.experimentalSearch) {
    heavyLib.attachSearchWidget(document.body);
  }
}

// ❌ Named import defer — NOT supported
// import defer { doSomething } from "./module.js";

// ❌ Default import defer — NOT supported
// import defer defaultExport from "./module.js";

// ✅ Dynamic import() is the async alternative when runtime conditions drive loading
async function loadOnDemand(): Promise<void> {
  const { doSomething } = await import("./module.js");
  doSomething();
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `import defer` keeps module loading synchronous (no `await` required at call sites) and avoids the infectious async propagation of `import()`, but it is only available with `--module preserve` or `esnext`, and cannot defer modules with top-level `await` — those fire eagerly, which can erode the startup benefit if a deferred dependency pulls in async transitive dependencies.

---

### Pattern 2 — TypeScript 5.9 `--module node20`: Stable Node.js 20 Semantics [official]

TypeScript 5.9 introduces `--module node20` as a stable, version-locked counterpart to `--module nodenext`. Like `node18`, it captures the ESM and CJS interop semantics of a specific Node.js release and does not change as Node.js evolves. Critically, `node20` implies `--target es2023` (not `esnext` like `nodenext` does), giving stricter, more predictable output. It also supports `require()` of ESM modules from CommonJS (a capability Node.js 20 introduced), aligning with `nodenext` on that dimension.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json for a Node.js 20 project
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "module": "node20",
//     "moduleResolution": "bundler",   // or "nodenext"
//     "target": "es2023",              // implicitly set by node20
//     "outDir": "./dist"
//   }
// }

// node20 allows CJS files to require() ESM modules (Node 20+ feature)
// file: consumer.cjs
const { readConfig } = require("./config.mjs");   // ✅ valid under node20

// Contrast with node18 — which disallows require() of ESM:
// const { readConfig } = require("./config.mjs"); // ❌ error under node18

// node20 uses es2023 target — includes Array.findLastIndex, Atomics.waitAsync
const last = [1, 2, 3].findLastIndex((x) => x < 3); // ✅ typed in es2023 lib

// nodenext would target esnext — picking up features not yet stable in Node 20
// Using node20 pins the lib to what Node 20 actually supports
```

**Tradeoff.** `--module node20` trades flexibility for predictability: your target and module semantics are frozen at Node.js 20's capability set, which prevents accidental reliance on newer runtime features. But if you target Node.js 22 or later, `node20` will not unlock `require()` of ESM with top-level `await` that Node.js 22 added — use `nodenext` for projects intended to stay current.

---

### Pattern 3 — TypeScript 5.9 Opinionated `tsc --init` Defaults [official]

Starting with TypeScript 5.9, `tsc --init` generates a minimal, prescriptive `tsconfig.json` with modern defaults rather than a heavily commented template with dozens of opt-in options. The new defaults include `"module": "nodenext"`, `"target": "esnext"`, `"strict": true`, `"verbatimModuleSyntax": true`, `"isolatedModules": true`, `"moduleDetection": "force"`, `"noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true`, `"exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true`, `"types": []`, and `"skipLibCheck": true`. This reflects community consensus on what a production-grade TypeScript project should look like by default.

```typescript
// Generated tsconfig.json from `tsc --init` in TypeScript 5.9:
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "module": "nodenext",
//     "target": "esnext",
//     "types": [],
//     "sourceMap": true,
//     "declaration": true,
//     "declarationMap": true,
//     "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
//     "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,
//     "strict": true,
//     "jsx": "react-jsx",
//     "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
//     "isolatedModules": true,
//     "noUncheckedSideEffectImports": true,
//     "moduleDetection": "force",
//     "skipLibCheck": true
//   }
// }

// Impact of noUncheckedIndexedAccess:
const arr: string[] = getStrings();
const first = arr[0];
//    ^? string | undefined  ← now explicit — must check before use

if (first !== undefined) {
  console.log(first.toUpperCase()); // ✅ safe
}

// Impact of exactOptionalPropertyTypes:
interface Config { timeout?: number }
const cfg: Config = {};
cfg.timeout = undefined; // ❌ error — undefined cannot be assigned to optional number
// Corrected: delete cfg.timeout;
```

**Tradeoff.** The prescriptive defaults catch more bugs out of the box and reduce "configuration archaeology" for new projects, but they introduce immediate migration friction in existing codebases: `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` can generate hundreds of `string | undefined` errors on first adoption, and `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` breaks patterns that assign `undefined` to optional properties to clear them.

---

### Pattern 4 — TypeScript 5.9 Type Argument Inference Leak Fix [official]

TypeScript 5.9 fixes a class of inference bugs where type variables from one part of an expression "leaked" into generic parameter inference for a different call in the same expression. This made some unsound code compile silently and causes new type errors on upgrade when the previously-accepted inference path was subtly wrong. The fix is most visible in multi-call chains and higher-order functions where the inferred type of one generic parameter was inadvertently constrained by a type variable it should not have seen.

```typescript
// Before TypeScript 5.9: a type variable from outer scope
// could incorrectly influence inner call inference
function wrap<T>(fn: () => T): () => T { return fn; }
function pair<A, B>(a: A, b: B): [A, B] { return [a, b]; }

// Previously: inferred [string, number] might leak into pair's A resolution
// in certain complex expressions involving overloaded signatures
const result = pair(wrap(() => "hello"), wrap(() => 42));
//    ^? [() => string, () => number] — now correctly inferred in TS 5.9

// Cases that break on upgrade: explicit cast required where inference was too wide
declare function pickFirst<T extends object>(
  candidates: T[],
  selector: (item: T) => boolean
): T | undefined;

declare function wrapResult<T>(value: T): { wrapped: T };

// TS 5.9 may require explicit T where leaked inference previously filled it
const found = pickFirst<{ id: number }>([{ id: 1 }], (x) => x.id === 1);
//           ^ explicit type arg now required if inference was relying on a leak

// Fix pattern: always specify explicit type arguments for higher-order generics
// where the type variable appears in both the array and the selector
```

**Tradeoff.** The fix makes TypeScript's generic inference more correct and predictable, but any codebase that relied on the leaked inference path (even accidentally) will see new errors. The errors typically require adding an explicit type argument to the offending call — a one-line fix per site, but potentially many sites in large codebases using complex generic utilities.

---

### Pattern 5 — TypeScript 4.7 Variance Annotations: `in`/`out` Modifiers for Type Parameters [official]

TypeScript 4.7 introduced explicit variance annotations — `out` for covariant type parameters (appear only in output/return positions) and `in` for contravariant type parameters (appear only in input/parameter positions). The combined `in out` marks a type parameter as invariant. These annotations serve two purposes: documentation of intent (enforced by the compiler) and a performance hint that lets TypeScript skip deep structural comparison in favor of comparing type arguments directly, which significantly speeds up checking of deeply recursive or circular generic types.

```typescript
// ✅ Covariant: T only appears in return/output position
interface Producer<out T> {
  produce(): T;
  // T cannot appear as a parameter — compiler enforces this
}

// Safe: Producer<Dog> is assignable to Producer<Animal>
const dogProducer: Producer<Dog> = { produce: () => new Dog() };
const animalProducer: Producer<Animal> = dogProducer; // ✅

// ✅ Contravariant: T only appears in parameter/input position
interface Consumer<in T> {
  consume(value: T): void;
}

// Safe: Consumer<Animal> is assignable to Consumer<Dog>
const animalConsumer: Consumer<Animal> = { consume: (a: Animal) => {} };
const dogConsumer: Consumer<Dog> = animalConsumer; // ✅

// ✅ Invariant: T appears in both positions — no substitutability
interface ReadWrite<in out T> {
  get(): T;
  set(value: T): void;
}
// ReadWrite<Dog> is NOT assignable to ReadWrite<Animal> — correct

// ✅ Performance: helps with deeply recursive types
type Tree<in out T> = {
  value: T;
  children: Tree<T>[];
};
// Without the annotation, each structural comparison traverses the full tree
// With it, TypeScript compares T arguments directly — significant speedup
```

**Tradeoff.** Variance annotations improve performance and catch incorrect subtyping in generic APIs, but they add noise for simple cases where TypeScript's structural checks are fast enough. The main value is in library code with complex recursive types, circular generics, or performance-sensitive type hierarchies — adding them to every generic interface is overkill and clutters the codebase.

---

### Pattern 6 — `satisfies` Operator for Narrow-Type Validation Without Widening [official]

The `satisfies` operator (TypeScript 4.9) validates that an expression conforms to a type without widening the inferred type. This is the correct tool for typed configuration objects, route definitions, and lookup tables where you want exhaustiveness and key-type safety but need to retain the most precise inferred types for downstream use. Unlike an explicit type annotation (which widens to the annotation type), `satisfies` keeps the literal or tuple type that TypeScript naturally infers.

```typescript
type Route = { path: string; method: "GET" | "POST" | "PUT" | "DELETE" };
type RouteMap = Record<string, Route>;

// ❌ Type annotation widens — path becomes string, autocomplete loses route names
const routes: RouteMap = {
  getUser:    { path: "/users/:id", method: "GET" },
  createUser: { path: "/users",     method: "POST" },
};
// routes.getUser     ← typed as Route, not the literal object
// routes.nonexistent ← no error! Record<string, Route> allows any string key

// ✅ satisfies validates shape but preserves literal key types
const typedRoutes = {
  getUser:    { path: "/users/:id", method: "GET" },
  createUser: { path: "/users",     method: "POST" },
} satisfies RouteMap;

// typedRoutes.getUser.method  ^? "GET"  (literal preserved)
// typedRoutes.nonexistent     ← TS error: property does not exist

// ✅ Exhaustive fixture with satisfies
type Locale = "en" | "fr" | "de";
const labels = {
  en: { save: "Save",       cancel: "Cancel"    },
  fr: { save: "Enregistrer", cancel: "Annuler"  },
  de: { save: "Speichern",  cancel: "Abbrechen" },
} satisfies Record<Locale, { save: string; cancel: string }>;
// Missing locale → compile error; extra locale → compile error
// labels.en.save ^? "Save"  (literal string, not widened to string)
```

**Tradeoff.** `satisfies` solves the classic tension between "I want type safety" and "I want the precise inferred type" — but it only validates at the declaration site. If the object is later mutated or passed into a function expecting the wide type, the widening happens at that boundary. For deeply nested objects, `satisfies` can produce confusing error messages because the violation appears at the top level even when only one nested property mismatches.

---

### Pattern 7 — Non-Distributive Conditional Types: Wrapping in Tuples to Suppress Union Distribution [official]

Conditional types in TypeScript are distributive by default: when the checked type `T` is a union, TypeScript maps the condition over each member independently. This is frequently the desired behavior (e.g., `Exclude<T, U>`) but becomes a footgun when you want to check the union as a whole — for example, testing whether an entire union is assignable to a constraint. Wrapping both sides of the `extends` in single-element tuples `[T] extends [U]` disables distributivity and treats the union atomically.

```typescript
// ❌ Distributive — evaluates each member independently
type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;

type A = IsString<string | number>;
//   ^? boolean  (distributes: IsString<string>=true | IsString<number>=false)

// ✅ Non-distributive — treats the full union atomically
type IsExactlyString<T> = [T] extends [string] ? true : false;

type B = IsExactlyString<string | number>;
//   ^? false  (string | number is NOT assignable to string as a whole)

type C = IsExactlyString<string>;
//   ^? true

// ✅ Practical: StrictEquals checks for type identity, not just assignability
type StrictEquals<X, Y> =
  (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends
  (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;

type D = StrictEquals<string, string>;         // true
type E = StrictEquals<string, string | number>; // false
type F = StrictEquals<any, string>;             // false

// ✅ Use case: type-level assertion helper for test suites
type Assert<T extends true> = T;
type _test1 = Assert<StrictEquals<ReturnType<typeof JSON.parse>, any>>;
```

**Tradeoff.** Non-distributive conditional types are powerful for type-level assertions and exhaustiveness checks, but the tuple-wrapping idiom is non-obvious to readers unfamiliar with TypeScript internals. The `StrictEquals` pattern using higher-rank type functions is even more opaque. Document the intent explicitly with comments, and prefer named utility aliases over inline tuple wraps in production code.

---

### Pattern 8 — `infer` with Constraint: `infer X extends Y` for Filtered Type Extraction [official]

TypeScript 4.8 added the `infer X extends Y` syntax, which adds a constraint to an `infer` variable within a conditional type. Previously, developers had to add a second conditional type layer to apply a constraint after inference. With the inline constraint, TypeScript infers the type, then checks it against the constraint — if the constraint fails, the entire conditional branch resolves to `never` instead of an unconstrained type.

```typescript
// ❌ Old pattern: two-stage conditional
type GetStringKeys<T> =
  T extends Record<infer K, unknown>
    ? K extends string ? K : never
    : never;

// ✅ New pattern: inline constraint on infer
type GetStringKeys<T> =
  T extends Record<infer K extends string, unknown> ? K : never;

type Keys = GetStringKeys<{ a: 1; b: 2; [n: number]: 0 }>;
//   ^? "a" | "b"  — number key excluded by the string constraint

// ✅ Extract tuple element types that are subtypes of a value type
type ExtractValues<T extends readonly unknown[]> =
  T extends readonly (infer V extends string | number)[] ? V : never;

type Vals = ExtractValues<["x", 1, true, "y", 2]>;
//   ^? "x" | 1 | "y" | 2  — boolean excluded by the string | number constraint

// ✅ Narrowing discriminant fields from a union
type ExtractKind<T, K extends string> =
  T extends { kind: infer D extends K } ? D : never;

type MyUnion = { kind: "create"; data: string } | { kind: "delete"; id: number };
type Kinds = ExtractKind<MyUnion, string>;
//   ^? "create" | "delete"
```

**Tradeoff.** Inline `infer X extends Y` eliminates boilerplate two-stage conditionals and makes the type's intent easier to read, but it changes behavior compared to an unconstrained `infer`: when the constraint fails, the branch produces `never` rather than the unconstrained type. This can be surprising when the intent was "infer whatever T has, then narrow" — in that case the two-stage form gives the author explicit control over the fallback.

---

### Pattern 9 — Template Literal Types as Strongly-Typed Route Parsers [community]

Template literal types can be composed recursively to parse string patterns at the type level — extracting path parameters from URL route strings, splitting command-line flag syntax, or validating dotted-key paths. The key building block is a conditional type with two `infer` positions inside a template literal, recursively consuming the string.

```typescript
// Extract path parameter names from Express-style route strings
type ExtractParams<Route extends string> =
  Route extends `${string}:${infer Param}/${infer Rest}`
    ? Param | ExtractParams<`/${Rest}`>
    : Route extends `${string}:${infer Param}`
      ? Param
      : never;

type Params = ExtractParams<"/users/:userId/posts/:postId">;
//   ^? "userId" | "postId"

// Build a typed params object from the route string
type RouteParams<Route extends string> = {
  [K in ExtractParams<Route>]: string;
};

// Type-safe route handler factory
function createHandler<const Route extends string>(
  route: Route,
  handler: (params: RouteParams<Route>, req: Request) => Response
): { route: Route; handler: typeof handler } {
  return { route, handler };
}

const userPostHandler = createHandler(
  "/users/:userId/posts/:postId",
  (params) => {
    // params.userId   ^? string ✅
    // params.postId   ^? string ✅
    // params.unknown  ← TS error: not in route pattern
    return new Response(`User ${params.userId}, Post ${params.postId}`);
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** Recursive template literal type parsing is elegant but has depth limits — TypeScript enforces a maximum recursion depth for conditional types (approximately 100 levels), so route strings with many segments can hit `Type instantiation is excessively deep` errors. For production routers with complex patterns, prefer a small set of well-tested helper types over unbounded recursion, and test inferred types explicitly with `type Assert<T extends true>` checks in your type test suite.

---

### Pattern 10 — Module Augmentation for Library Type Extension Without Forking [community]

TypeScript's module augmentation mechanism allows adding new declarations to an existing module's exported types without modifying the original `node_modules` source. This is the correct pattern for extending third-party library types, adding missing method overloads, or attaching application-specific metadata to framework interfaces. Augmentations must be in a file that is a module (has at least one `import` or `export`), and they apply globally to the augmented module throughout the compilation unit.

```typescript
// Augmenting Express's Request interface to add application-specific fields
// file: types/express-augment.d.ts

import "express"; // Must be a module (has import/export)

declare module "express-serve-static-core" {
  interface Request {
    // Added by auth middleware — always present after auth check
    user?: { id: string; roles: string[] };
    // Added by request-id middleware
    requestId: string;
    // Added by locale middleware
    locale: "en" | "fr" | "de";
  }
}

// Augmenting a third-party event emitter library to add typed event maps
declare module "eventemitter3" {
  interface EventEmitter<EventTypes extends Record<string, unknown[]>> {
    // Adding a once() overload that returns a Promise
    onceAsync<K extends keyof EventTypes & string>(
      event: K
    ): Promise<EventTypes[K]>;
  }
}

// Augmenting global scope — must be in a module file
export {};
declare global {
  interface Window {
    // Analytics object injected by script tag
    analytics: {
      track(event: string, props?: Record<string, unknown>): void;
    };
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Module augmentation is the cleanest way to extend third-party types, but it is globally scoped — every file in the compilation unit sees the augmented types. This means an augmentation that adds a required field to `Request` immediately makes all existing code that constructs mock `Request` objects fail type checks. Prefer making augmented fields optional (`?`) when they represent lazily-added middleware data, and document that augmentation files must be included in `tsconfig.json`'s `include` or `files` array.

---

### Pattern 11 — `using` / `await using` Declarations for Deterministic Resource Cleanup [official]

TypeScript 5.2 implements the TC39 Explicit Resource Management proposal: `using` for synchronous disposables and `await using` for asynchronous ones. When a `using` variable goes out of scope — whether via normal exit, `return`, `throw`, or `break` — TypeScript calls `[Symbol.dispose]()` on the value. This replaces `try/finally` blocks for resource cleanup and makes lifecycle boundaries explicit at the variable declaration site.

```typescript
// Implementing Symbol.dispose on a custom resource
class DatabaseConnection {
  constructor(private readonly url: string) {
    console.log(`Opened connection to ${url}`);
  }

  query(sql: string): unknown[] { return []; }

  [Symbol.dispose](): void {
    console.log(`Closed connection to ${this.url}`);
    // Release underlying socket/handle
  }
}

// Implementing Symbol.asyncDispose for async cleanup
class FileHandle {
  constructor(private readonly path: string) {}

  async write(data: string): Promise<void> { /* ... */ }

  async [Symbol.asyncDispose](): Promise<void> {
    await flushAndClose(this.path);
  }
}

// Usage — cleanup is guaranteed even if an exception is thrown
async function processData(url: string, path: string): Promise<void> {
  using db = new DatabaseConnection(url);     // disposed on scope exit
  await using file = new FileHandle(path);    // awaited on scope exit

  const rows = db.query("SELECT * FROM users");
  await file.write(JSON.stringify(rows));
  // Both db and file are disposed/closed here — even if write() throws
}

// DisposableStack for dynamic groups of resources
function openMultiple(urls: string[]): Disposable {
  const stack = new DisposableStack();
  for (const url of urls) {
    stack.use(new DatabaseConnection(url));
  }
  return stack; // disposing stack disposes all connections in LIFO order
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `using` declarations make cleanup intent immediately readable and are harder to accidentally forget than `try/finally`, but they require target `ES2022` or lower with the `esnext.disposable` lib, and the `using` keyword is a reserved word in TypeScript 5.2+ — introducing it in a codebase that uses `using` as a variable name (uncommon but possible) requires renaming. For async resources, `await using` adds implicit `await` at scope exit, which can be surprising in performance-sensitive loops.

---

### Pattern 12 — Branded / Opaque Types for Nominal Typing in a Structural System [community]

TypeScript's structural type system accepts any value with the right shape regardless of its declared type name. Branded types add a phantom type property (never assigned at runtime) to create distinct, non-interchangeable types from the same underlying primitive. This prevents functions that accept `UserId` from accidentally receiving a `OrderId` even though both are `string` at runtime.

```typescript
// Brand helper — the intersection with { readonly __brand: Brand }
// adds a phantom property that only exists at type level
declare const __brand: unique symbol;
type Brand<T, Brand> = T & { readonly [__brand]: Brand };

// Domain-specific branded primitives
type UserId  = Brand<string, "UserId">;
type OrderId = Brand<string, "OrderId">;
type Cents   = Brand<number, "Cents">;
type Pixels  = Brand<number, "Pixels">;

// Constructor functions — the only place `as` casts appear
const UserId  = (id: string):  UserId  => id  as UserId;
const OrderId = (id: string):  OrderId => id  as OrderId;
const Cents   = (n: number):   Cents   => n   as Cents;

// Type-safe function signatures
function chargeOrder(userId: UserId, orderId: OrderId, amount: Cents): void {
  // Implementation omitted
}

const uid = UserId("u-123");
const oid = OrderId("o-456");
const amt = Cents(1999);

chargeOrder(uid, oid, amt);     // ✅
chargeOrder(oid, uid, amt);     // ❌ Error: OrderId not assignable to UserId
chargeOrder(uid, oid, 1999);   // ❌ Error: number not assignable to Cents

// Branded types survive equality and arithmetic — only the TYPE differs
const doubled: Cents = Cents(amt * 2); // ✅ arithmetic preserves brand
```

**Tradeoff.** Branded types eliminate an entire class of mixing bugs at zero runtime cost, but they require discipline: every entry point that creates a branded value must go through the constructor function, and third-party APIs return plain `string`/`number` that must be explicitly wrapped. Teams adopting branding mid-project will encounter many "not assignable" errors at API boundaries where raw primitives flow in — plan a gradual migration by adding brands at the outermost boundaries first.

---

### Pattern 13 — Recursive Mapped Types: Deeply `Readonly` and `DeepPartial` [community]

TypeScript's built-in `Readonly<T>` and `Partial<T>` are shallow — they do not recurse into nested objects. Community patterns implement deep variants using recursive conditional mapped types. The key technique is to check whether each property value is itself an object before applying the recursion, while carefully handling edge cases: `Date`, `RegExp`, `Map`, `Set`, and array types should generally not be recursed into (or must be handled with special cases to avoid destroying their interface).

```typescript
// DeepReadonly: recurse into plain objects, leave class instances / arrays as-is
type DeepReadonly<T> =
  T extends (infer U)[]                  ? ReadonlyArray<DeepReadonly<U>>
  : T extends ReadonlyArray<infer U>     ? ReadonlyArray<DeepReadonly<U>>
  : T extends Map<infer K, infer V>      ? ReadonlyMap<K, DeepReadonly<V>>
  : T extends Set<infer U>               ? ReadonlySet<DeepReadonly<U>>
  : T extends Date | RegExp | Function   ? T   // leave atomic types intact
  : T extends object                     ? { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }
  : T;

// DeepPartial: same structural recursion, making every property optional
type DeepPartial<T> =
  T extends (infer U)[]           ? DeepPartial<U>[]
  : T extends ReadonlyArray<infer U> ? ReadonlyArray<DeepPartial<U>>
  : T extends Date | RegExp | Function ? T
  : T extends object              ? { [K in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[K]> }
  : T;

// Usage
interface Config {
  server: { host: string; port: number; tls: { cert: string; key: string } };
  db:     { url: string; poolSize: number };
}

type FrozenConfig = DeepReadonly<Config>;
// FrozenConfig.server.tls.cert is readonly string — write rejected by TS

function mergeConfig(base: Config, overrides: DeepPartial<Config>): Config {
  // deep merge implementation
  return base;
}
mergeConfig(defaultConfig, { server: { port: 8443 } }); // ✅ partial override
```

**Tradeoff.** Deep utility types are useful at API and configuration boundaries, but they are computationally expensive for the TypeScript compiler — deeply nested objects with many properties can significantly increase type-checking time. Prefer `DeepReadonly` at module entry points for frozen configuration objects rather than applying it universally throughout the codebase. Also note that class instances (which carry method prototypes) can produce unexpected structural types when recursed into; the `Date | RegExp | Function` guard handles common cases but not all class hierarchies.

---

### Pattern 14 — `Extract` and `Exclude` as First-Class Discriminant Filters [official]

`Extract<T, U>` and `Exclude<T, U>` are standard utility types that filter union members based on assignability. They are most powerful when used with discriminant literals to pull apart or suppress specific variants of a discriminated union — replacing long `T extends { kind: "a" } ? T : never` conditionals with concise, readable filters that compose well with mapped types and conditional type chains.

```typescript
type Event =
  | { kind: "click";  x: number; y: number }
  | { kind: "keydown"; key: string }
  | { kind: "resize"; width: number; height: number }
  | { kind: "error";  message: string; code: number };

// Extract specific variants by discriminant
type PointerEvent = Extract<Event, { kind: "click" | "resize" }>;
//   ^? { kind: "click"; x: number; y: number } | { kind: "resize"; ... }

// Exclude error events from public handler signatures
type SafeEvent = Exclude<Event, { kind: "error" }>;
//   ^? { kind: "click"; ... } | { kind: "keydown"; ... } | { kind: "resize"; ... }

// Compose with mapped types: build a handler registry typed by event kind
type HandlerMap<E extends { kind: string }> = {
  [K in E["kind"]]: (event: Extract<E, { kind: K }>) => void;
};

const handlers: HandlerMap<SafeEvent> = {
  click:  (e) => console.log(e.x, e.y),    // e is { kind: "click"; x, y }
  keydown:(e) => console.log(e.key),
  resize: (e) => console.log(e.width, e.height),
};

// Error handling separated from business logic
function dispatch(event: Event): void {
  if (event.kind === "error") { reportError(event); return; }
  handlers[event.kind](event as never); // narrowed by Exclude
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `Extract` and `Exclude` compose cleanly with mapped types and produce highly readable union-manipulation code, but the assignability semantics of `Extract<T, U>` mean it matches any union member that is assignable to `U`, not just exact matches. A union member with extra properties is still extracted if it satisfies `U`. Use a discriminant literal (e.g., `{ kind: "click" }`) rather than a structural type to ensure precise filtering.

---

### Pattern 15 — `--noUncheckedSideEffectImports`: Catching Unresolvable Side-Effect-Only Imports [official]

TypeScript 5.6 added `--noUncheckedSideEffectImports`, which causes TypeScript to report an error when a side-effect-only import (`import "./styles.css"`) cannot be resolved. Previously, TypeScript silently ignored unresolvable side-effect imports because they have no named exports to check. The flag is included in the TypeScript 5.9 `tsc --init` defaults, making unresolvable imports a build error rather than a silent no-op.

```typescript
// Without --noUncheckedSideEffectImports:
import "./does-not-exist.css";    // ← silently ignored — no error
import "./polyfill-maybe.js";     // ← silently ignored even if file is missing

// With --noUncheckedSideEffectImports (TS 5.6+, default in TS 5.9 init):
import "./does-not-exist.css";
// ❌ Error: Cannot find module './does-not-exist.css' or its type declarations.

import "./polyfill-maybe.js";
// ❌ Error: Cannot find module './polyfill-maybe.js'

// ✅ Fix: declare module for known side-effect imports with no TS source
// types/css.d.ts
declare module "*.css" {}          // wildcard ambient module for CSS
declare module "*.scss" {}

// ✅ Fix: or add the JS file, or use a bundler plugin that provides types
// ✅ For polyfills shipped as npm packages, use a package with type declarations
import "core-js/stable";           // ✅ resolves via node_modules/@types/core-js

// tsconfig that enables the flag (now default in tsc --init):
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "noUncheckedSideEffectImports": true
//   }
// }
```

**Tradeoff.** `--noUncheckedSideEffectImports` catches typos in import paths and prevents phantom imports that never actually execute, but it requires a wildcard ambient module declaration for every non-TypeScript file type your bundler handles (CSS, SCSS, SVG, fonts, etc.). Projects adopting Vite or webpack alongside TypeScript often have a `types/` directory full of `declare module "*.ext" {}` declarations — this flag makes those declarations mandatory rather than optional.

---

**Gotcha 82 — `import defer` evaluation fires synchronously on the first property access — there is no way to defer evaluation further or check "has it evaluated yet"** [community]

```typescript
import defer * as config from "./expensive-config.js";

// ❌ Misunderstanding: this reads config lazily on every call
function getTimeout(): number {
  return config.REQUEST_TIMEOUT; // evaluation fires HERE on first call
}

// On subsequent calls, the module is already evaluated — no second defer
// There is no `isDeferredAndUnevaluated(config)` or similar check
// Once evaluated, config behaves identically to a regular namespace import

// ✅ To truly load conditionally, use dynamic import() instead
async function getTimeoutLazy(): Promise<number> {
  const { REQUEST_TIMEOUT } = await import("./expensive-config.js");
  return REQUEST_TIMEOUT;
}
```

WHY: `import defer` is a module-graph-level optimization, not a demand-load mechanism. The entire module graph (including the deferred module) is fetched, parsed, and linked at program startup — only the JavaScript execution is deferred until first property access. This means `import defer` does not reduce network latency or bundle size; it only reduces CPU time at startup by deferring the execution cost. If the goal is lazy network loading (code splitting), `import()` is the correct tool. Developers who expect `import defer` to work like dynamic `import()` are surprised to find the module is already in memory — just not yet executed.

---

**Gotcha 83 — TypeScript 5.9's `tsc --init` defaults include `"types": []`, which disables automatic `@types/*` loading — previously auto-loaded ambient types like `@types/node` stop working immediately** [community]

```typescript
// After running tsc --init in TypeScript 5.9, tsconfig.json contains:
// "types": []

// Effect: TypeScript no longer auto-discovers @types/* packages in node_modules
// This breaks ambient globals provided by @types packages:

import { readFileSync } from "fs"; // ✅ still works (explicit import)

const buf = Buffer.from("hello"); // ❌ Cannot find name 'Buffer'
// Buffer is a global from @types/node — disabled by "types": []

process.env.NODE_ENV; // ❌ Cannot find name 'process'
// process is a global from @types/node — disabled by "types": []

// ✅ Fix: explicitly declare the types you need
// tsconfig.json:
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "types": ["node"]   // only @types/node globals are loaded
//   }
// }

// Or import explicitly instead of relying on globals:
import process from "node:process"; // ✅ explicit module import
```

WHY: The new `tsc --init` default of `"types": []` reflects modern best practice: ambient globals are a footgun in large projects because they make it unclear which type declarations are in scope. However, this is a breaking change for Node.js projects that relied on `@types/node` globals (`Buffer`, `process`, `__dirname`, `setTimeout` with Node types) being auto-loaded. Running `tsc --init` on an existing project and not noticing the `"types": []` addition causes a cascade of "Cannot find name" errors for all previously ambient globals. Always audit the generated tsconfig before replacing an existing one.

---

**Gotcha 84 — TypeScript 5.9's `ArrayBuffer` hierarchy restructuring breaks `Buffer` assignability — `Buffer` (Node.js) is no longer directly assignable to `Uint8Array<ArrayBufferLike>` after the `lib.d.ts` change** [community]

```typescript
// TypeScript 5.9 lib.d.ts change: ArrayBuffer is no longer a supertype of TypedArray

// ❌ Previously valid, now errors in TS 5.9 with @types/node < 20.x:
function hashBytes(data: Uint8Array): string { return ""; }

const buf = Buffer.from("hello");
hashBytes(buf); // ❌ Argument of type 'Buffer' is not assignable to 'Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>'

// Root cause: Buffer extends Uint8Array<ArrayBufferLike>, but the function
// expects Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer> (more specific). The TypedArray generic
// parameter changed from ArrayBuffer to ArrayBufferLike in TS 5.7, and
// TS 5.9 tightened the hierarchy further.

// ✅ Fix 1: widen the parameter type
function hashBytes(data: Uint8Array<ArrayBufferLike>): string { return ""; }

// ✅ Fix 2: update @types/node (newer versions align Buffer's type)
// npm update @types/node --save-dev

// ✅ Fix 3: extract the raw buffer for APIs that genuinely need ArrayBuffer
function hashBytes(data: ArrayBuffer): string { return ""; }
hashBytes(buf.buffer); // pass the underlying ArrayBuffer
```

WHY: TypeScript 5.7 parameterized `TypedArray` types with their buffer type (`Uint8Array<TBuffer extends ArrayBufferLike>`), and TypeScript 5.9 completed the hierarchy restructuring so that `ArrayBuffer` is no longer a structural supertype of all typed arrays. Node.js's `Buffer` class has always been a `Uint8Array` subclass backed by `ArrayBufferLike` (not the narrower `ArrayBuffer`), but the old unparameterized type system accepted it anywhere `Uint8Array` was expected. After the 5.9 lib change, functions annotated with the specific `Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>` type reject `Buffer` values unless `@types/node` is updated to declare `Buffer` with the correct parameterized type.

---

**Gotcha 85 — Variance annotations (`in`/`out`) cause an error if the actual usage contradicts the declared variance — but only at the declaration site, not at call sites** [community]

```typescript
// ❌ Declaring out (covariant) but using T in an input position
interface BadProducer<out T> {
  get(): T;
  set(value: T): void; // ❌ Error: T appears in contravariant position
  // TypeScript 4.7+: Type parameter 'T' is declared as covariant
  // but is used in a contravariant position here.
}

// The error fires at the INTERFACE DEFINITION, not at sites that use BadProducer
// This means adding variance annotations to existing interfaces can break
// code that was previously accepted

// ✅ Correct: remove the set method or mark T as invariant
interface GoodProducer<out T> { get(): T; }          // covariant — no set
interface GoodState<in out T> { get(): T; set(v: T): void; } // invariant

// ❌ Silent hazard: an 'out' annotation that TypeScript cannot verify
// because the interface body is too complex triggers inference fallback,
// not an error — the annotation is accepted but may be structurally wrong
// Always test variance annotations with assignment checks:
declare let p1: GoodProducer<Dog>;
declare let p2: GoodProducer<Animal>;
p2 = p1; // ✅ should compile — covariance allows Dog → Animal in output
```

WHY: TypeScript's variance annotation checker validates that the declared variance (`in`/`out`) is consistent with how the type parameter is actually used throughout the interface or type alias body. When a `out`-annotated type parameter appears as a function parameter (a contravariant position), TypeScript immediately errors at the declaration site. This is good — it catches incorrect annotations — but it means adding `out` to an existing interface that happens to have a setter method will break the compile. The fix is to either remove the setter or promote to `in out` (invariant). The confusion arises because many developers add `out` hoping for a performance benefit without understanding which positions qualify as covariant.

---

**Gotcha 86 — `using` declarations do NOT call `[Symbol.dispose]` when the variable is never assigned (e.g., `using x = maybeNull()` where the function returns `null`)** [community]

```typescript
// Symbol.dispose is called on scope exit — but only if the value is non-null/undefined
// TypeScript allows using declarations with nullable types (Disposable | null)

function maybeOpenConnection(url: string | null): DatabaseConnection | null {
  if (!url) return null;
  return new DatabaseConnection(url);
}

async function run(url: string | null): Promise<void> {
  using conn = maybeOpenConnection(url);
  // If url is null, conn is null — Symbol.dispose is NOT called (nothing to dispose)
  // If url is provided, conn is a DatabaseConnection — Symbol.dispose IS called

  if (conn === null) return; // explicit null check required before use

  conn.query("SELECT 1"); // ✅ safe after null check
}

// ❌ Misunderstanding: assuming using always guarantees cleanup
// If the factory function throws BEFORE returning, using never assigns
// and Symbol.dispose is never called for that resource —
// but any previously-assigned using resources in the same scope ARE cleaned up

// ✅ For conditional resources, use DisposableStack to manage null safely
async function runSafe(url: string | null): Promise<void> {
  using stack = new DisposableStack();
  const conn = url ? stack.use(new DatabaseConnection(url)) : null;
  if (conn) conn.query("SELECT 1");
} // stack.dispose() called — handles the conditional resource safely
```

WHY: The `using` declaration's cleanup guarantee is conditional on the value being a non-null Disposable. TypeScript's type system allows `Disposable | null` as a `using` target, and the JavaScript runtime skips the `Symbol.dispose` call when the value is `null` or `undefined`. Developers who assume `using conn = getConn()` always disposes on scope exit are surprised to find that a null return silently bypasses cleanup. The `DisposableStack.use()` method is the safe API for conditionally-included resources: it only registers the resource if non-null and disposes all registered resources in LIFO order.

---

### Anti-Patterns: Cycle 45 Additions

| Anti-pattern | Why it's harmful | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Using `import defer` expecting lazy network loading or code splitting | `import defer` only defers CPU execution — the module graph is fully loaded and linked at startup; bundle size and network usage are unchanged | Use dynamic `import()` for code splitting; reserve `import defer` for startup CPU optimization with `--module preserve` or `esnext` |
| Running `tsc --init` on an existing project and replacing the existing tsconfig | The new TS 5.9 defaults include `"types": []` which disables auto-loading of `@types/*` globals, breaking `Buffer`, `process`, `__dirname` in Node.js projects | Diff the generated tsconfig against the existing one; adopt new settings incrementally; explicitly set `"types": ["node"]` if Node.js globals are needed |
| Annotating type parameters with `out` (covariant) when the interface has both getters and setters | TypeScript errors at the declaration site when a covariant `out` parameter appears in a contravariant (parameter) position — the error is at the definition, not at call sites | Use `in out` (invariant) for state-like interfaces; use `out` only for pure producer interfaces with no input positions |
| Passing `Buffer` directly to functions typed as `Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>` after upgrading to TypeScript 5.9 | `Buffer` extends `Uint8Array<ArrayBufferLike>` (wide); `ArrayBuffer` is narrower than `ArrayBufferLike` — TypeScript 5.9 lib restructuring rejects this assignment | Widen the parameter to `Uint8Array<ArrayBufferLike>`, update `@types/node`, or pass `buf.buffer` (the raw `ArrayBuffer`) |
| Assuming `using x = factory()` guarantees cleanup when `factory()` may return `null` | The JavaScript runtime skips `Symbol.dispose` for `null`/`undefined` values — cleanup is NOT guaranteed for nullable factory returns | Use `DisposableStack.use()` for conditionally-present resources; add explicit null checks before using the variable |
| Using `infer X extends Y` as a non-distributive conditional type guard | `infer X extends Y` still distributes over unions like any other conditional type — the constraint only filters the inferred type, not the distribution | Wrap in `[T] extends [U]` to disable distributivity when checking the full union; use `infer X extends Y` for filtering inferred types, not for union-level guards |
