## Cycle 46 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 16 — `NoInfer<T>`: Blocking Inference Site Pollution in Generic Functions [official]

TypeScript 5.4 introduced the `NoInfer<T>` utility type, which wraps a type parameter at a call-site position where you explicitly want TypeScript to *not* use that argument as an inference source. Without `NoInfer`, every parameter of type `T` contributes equally to the inferred `T`, allowing invalid values to silently widen the inferred union and pass type-checking. Wrapping a parameter in `NoInfer<T>` removes it from the inference contest entirely — TypeScript resolves `T` solely from the remaining unguarded parameters, then checks the `NoInfer<T>` parameter against the already-resolved `T`. This is the idiomatic way to enforce one parameter as the "canonical" source of inference while others serve as validation-only consumers.

```typescript
// Without NoInfer: TypeScript infers C as "red"|"yellow"|"green"|"blue"
// and silently accepts "blue" as a valid default
function createLight_BAD<C extends string>(colors: C[], defaultColor?: C): void {}
createLight_BAD(["red", "yellow", "green"], "blue"); // ✅ wrong: no error!

// With NoInfer: C is inferred from `colors` only; `defaultColor` is checked after
function createLight<C extends string>(
  colors: C[],
  defaultColor?: NoInfer<C>
): void {}

createLight(["red", "yellow", "green"], "blue");
// ❌ Error: Argument of type '"blue"' is not assignable to parameter
//    of type '"red" | "yellow" | "green" | undefined'

createLight(["red", "yellow", "green"], "red");   // ✅ OK

// Real-world pattern: event system with typed payload
function on<K extends string>(
  eventMap: Record<K, unknown>,
  event: NoInfer<K>,
  handler: (payload: unknown) => void
): void {}

on({ click: null, focus: null }, "blur", () => {});
// ❌ Error: "blur" is not assignable to "click" | "focus"
```

**Tradeoff.** `NoInfer<T>` only affects *inference* — it has no runtime footprint and is erased completely. It cannot enforce call-order semantics or multi-pass inference; if *all* arguments of type `T` are wrapped in `NoInfer`, TypeScript falls back to the constraint bound and accepts any valid `T`, which may be unexpectedly permissive.

---

### Pattern 17 — Inferred Type Predicates: Filter-Array Narrowing Without Manual `is` Annotations [official]

TypeScript 5.5 can automatically infer a type predicate return type for functions that satisfy four strict conditions: no explicit return type annotation, a single `return` statement, the function does not mutate the filtered parameter, and the return expression is a boolean tied to a type refinement of that parameter. When these conditions hold, `.filter(fn)` automatically narrows the result array element type — eliminating the most common need for manual `(x): x is NonNullable<T>` boilerplate. The inference is precise enough to distinguish `x !== null` (which narrows out `null`) from `!!x` (which narrows out both `null` and `undefined` but also `0`, `""`, `NaN` — TypeScript declines to infer a predicate from truthiness checks because they remove valid falsy values).

```typescript
// TypeScript 5.4 and earlier: birds is (Bird | undefined)[]
// TypeScript 5.5+: birds is Bird[]  — predicate inferred automatically
const birds = ["eagle", "sparrow", undefined, "hawk"]
  .map(name => name ? { species: name } : undefined)
  .filter(bird => bird !== undefined);

// birds.forEach(b => b.species); // ✅ no error — element type is Bird, not Bird|undefined

// ❌ Gotcha: truthiness check does NOT infer a predicate
const scores = [0, 1, 2, null, 3];
const truthy = scores.filter(s => !!s);
// truthy is still (number | null)[] — TypeScript refuses to infer
// because !!s also strips valid 0 values

// ✅ Explicit null check infers the predicate correctly
const nonNull = scores.filter(s => s !== null); // number[]

// Multi-condition guard — still inferred if single return
function isValidUser(u: { name?: string; age?: number } | null):
  u is { name: string; age: number } {
  return u !== null && typeof u.name === "string" && typeof u.age === "number";
}
const users = [{ name: "Alice", age: 30 }, null, { name: "Bob" }];
const valid = users.filter(isValidUser); // { name: string; age: number }[]
```

**Tradeoff.** The four-condition rule is strict by design — any implicit return path (including `if/else` with no explicit `return false`) or mutation of the parameter disables predicate inference and falls back to `boolean`. Wrapping a filter callback in an abstraction layer (e.g., `compose(isNotNull, isValidShape)`) also breaks inference; explicit `is` annotations remain necessary for composed predicates.

---

### Pattern 18 — `--isolatedDeclarations`: Enforcing Explicitly-Typed Exports for Parallel Build Pipelines [official]

The `--isolatedDeclarations` flag (TypeScript 5.5) requires every exported binding to have an explicit, annotatable type — sufficient for a single-file declaration emitter to produce `.d.ts` without a full program context. This enables parallel `.d.ts` generation by tools like `oxc-transform`, `swc`, and `ts-blank-space`, drastically cutting declaration build times in monorepos. The flag does not change runtime behavior and does not require `--isolatedModules`, but it does mandate annotations on exported functions, classes, variables with complex initializers, and re-exported `const enum` members. The companion `transpileDeclaration` API provides a programmatic single-file `.d.ts` emitter that assumes `--isolatedDeclarations` preconditions hold.

```typescript
// ❌ Error with --isolatedDeclarations: inferred return type cannot
// be determined from a single file without type-checking the body
export function computeConfig() {
  return { debug: process.env.DEBUG === "1", version: 42 };
}

// ✅ Explicit return type satisfies isolated declarations
export function computeConfig(): { debug: boolean; version: number } {
  return { debug: process.env.DEBUG === "1", version: 42 };
}

// ✅ Trivially inferable exports are fine (literal assignments)
export const MAX_RETRIES = 3;        // number literal — OK
export const API_URL = "https://..."; // string literal — OK

// ❌ Complex initializer requires annotation
export const defaultConfig = createConfig({ strict: true });
// ✅ Fix:
export const defaultConfig: AppConfig = createConfig({ strict: true });

// tsconfig.json
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "isolatedDeclarations": true,
//     "declaration": true
//   }
// }
```

**Tradeoff.** Enabling `--isolatedDeclarations` on an existing codebase typically surfaces dozens to hundreds of "missing explicit type annotation" errors on exported API surfaces, which must be fixed before the flag can be adopted. The annotation burden is intentional: it makes the public API surface explicit and auditable, which is a long-term maintenance benefit but a non-trivial migration cost.

---

### Pattern 19 — `const` Type Parameters: Preserving Literal Type Inference in Generic Calls [official]

TypeScript 5.0 introduced the `const` modifier on type parameters, which forces the compiler to infer the narrowest (most literal) type for an argument — equivalent to the inference that applies when a value is declared `as const`. Without `const`, a generic function receiving `["Alice", "Bob"]` infers `T = string[]`; with `const T`, it infers `T = readonly ["Alice", "Bob"]`. This eliminates the `as const` boilerplate at call sites while keeping call-site types flexible: the `const` modifier only affects *freshly-written literals* passed directly to the function — variables that were pre-declared and widened before the call are unaffected and still infer their widened type.

```typescript
// Without const modifier: T is inferred as string[]
function first<T extends readonly string[]>(arr: T): T[0] {
  return arr[0];
}
const r1 = first(["a", "b", "c"]); // type: string

// With const modifier: T is inferred as readonly ["a", "b", "c"]
function firstConst<const T extends readonly string[]>(arr: T): T[0] {
  return arr[0];
}
const r2 = firstConst(["a", "b", "c"]); // type: "a"

// Real-world: type-safe event bus with literal event names
function defineEvents<const T extends readonly string[]>(events: T): {
  [K in T[number]]: K
} {
  return Object.fromEntries(events.map(e => [e, e])) as any;
}

const Events = defineEvents(["userCreated", "userDeleted", "orderPlaced"]);
// Events.userCreated  → type: "userCreated"  (not string)
// Events.unknown      → ❌ compile error

// ❌ Pre-declared variable loses the const inference benefit
const myEvents = ["userCreated", "userDeleted"]; // already widened to string[]
const Events2 = defineEvents(myEvents); // T is string[], NOT a tuple
```

**Tradeoff.** The `const` modifier only affects inference — it does not make the inferred type immutable at runtime and does not prevent the caller from passing a mutable array; the `readonly` in the constraint handles that. For complex nested objects, `const` inference can produce very deep literal types that slow down the type checker and produce unwieldy hover output; consider constraining depth with `Readonly<T>` rather than full deep literal inference.

---

### Pattern 20 — Auto-Accessors (`accessor` Keyword): Paired Get/Set with Decorator Interception [official]

TypeScript 4.9 (and TC39 Stage 3 decorators in TypeScript 5.0) introduced the `accessor` keyword for class fields, which desugars a single declaration into a private backing field plus a public getter/setter pair. Auto-accessors are the recommended decorator target for the Stage 3 decorator proposal — unlike method decorators that replace a function, auto-accessor decorators receive an `{ get, set }` descriptor object and can intercept reads and writes while retaining the original backing storage. This enables reactive patterns (logging, validation, change notification) without the verbosity of manually writing a private field, a getter, and a setter on every decorated property.

```typescript
// Auto-accessor desugars to a private backing field + get/set pair
class User {
  accessor name: string = "";
  accessor age: number = 0;
}
// Equivalent to:
// #name_backing = "";
// get name() { return this.#name_backing; }
// set name(v) { this.#name_backing = v; }

// Stage 3 decorator intercepting auto-accessor reads and writes
function logged<This, Value>(
  target: ClassAccessorDecoratorTarget<This, Value>,
  context: ClassAccessorDecoratorContext<This, Value>
): ClassAccessorDecoratorResult<This, Value> {
  const { get, set } = target;
  return {
    get(this: This) {
      const val = get.call(this);
      console.log(`GET ${String(context.name)} → ${val}`);
      return val;
    },
    set(this: This, value: Value) {
      console.log(`SET ${String(context.name)} = ${value}`);
      set.call(this, value);
    },
    init(this: This, value: Value) {
      console.log(`INIT ${String(context.name)} = ${value}`);
      return value;
    },
  };
}

class Config {
  @logged accessor debug: boolean = false;
  @logged accessor port: number = 3000;
}

const cfg = new Config(); // INIT debug = false  INIT port = 3000
cfg.debug = true;         // SET debug = true
console.log(cfg.debug);   // GET debug → true
```

**Tradeoff.** Auto-accessors generate a private field with a mangled name in the emitted JavaScript (`#__name` or a `WeakMap` slot depending on target), which increases property count and slightly increases memory usage per instance. They are not compatible with the legacy `experimentalDecorators` + `emitDecoratorMetadata` pipeline — mixing old and new decorator styles in the same class causes a compile error. Because the backing field is truly private, subclasses cannot directly access the raw value; they must go through the getter/setter.

---

### Pattern 21 — `satisfies` Operator: Validate Shape Without Losing Narrowed Type [official]

The `satisfies` operator (TypeScript 4.9) validates that an expression is compatible with a type without widening the expression's inferred type to that constraining type. This solves a long-standing tension: using a type annotation (`const x: T = ...`) narrows type-checking but loses literal type information; using `as const` preserves literals but removes shape validation. `satisfies T` does both simultaneously — the compiler checks the shape constraint and then discards it, leaving the inferred literal type intact. It is particularly useful for configuration objects, route maps, color palettes, and any key-value structure where you want validated keys but need to retain literal value types for downstream inference.

```typescript
type Palette = Record<string, [number, number, number] | string>;

// ❌ Without satisfies: accessing .toUpperCase() errors because
// the type is widened to [number,number,number] | string
const palette: Palette = {
  red: [255, 0, 0],
  green: "#00ff00",
};
palette.green.toUpperCase(); // ❌ Error: [number,number,number]|string has no toUpperCase

// ✅ With satisfies: shape is validated AND literal types are preserved
const palette2 = {
  red: [255, 0, 0],
  green: "#00ff00",
} satisfies Palette;
palette2.green.toUpperCase(); // ✅ TypeScript knows it's a string

// Config pattern: catch typos while retaining autocomplete on values
interface TsConfig {
  compilerOptions?: { strict?: boolean; target?: string };
}

const tsconfig = {
  compilerOptions: { strict: true, tarjet: "esnext" }, // ❌ typo caught!
} satisfies TsConfig;

// Satisfies works inline too:
function compile(cfg: TsConfig) {}
compile({ compilerOptions: { stricct: true } } satisfies TsConfig); // ❌ typo caught
```

**Tradeoff.** `satisfies` is purely a compile-time check — it produces no runtime code. Because it does not widen the type, subsequent assignments to the variable are checked against the *inferred* literal type, not against the constraint; this can be surprising when a variable annotated `satisfies T` is later assigned a different-but-valid-T value that doesn't match the original literal. For mutable variables, combining `let x: T = ... satisfies T` (annotation + satisfies) may be preferable.

---

### Pattern 22 — `--erasableSyntaxOnly`: Stripping-Compatible TypeScript for Native Node.js Type Stripping [official]

TypeScript 5.8 introduced `--erasableSyntaxOnly`, a compiler flag that errors on any syntax construct that cannot be removed by a simple text-erasing pass — i.e., constructs that actually emit JavaScript output beyond mere type removal. The forbidden constructs are: `enum` declarations (which generate object literals), `namespace`/`module` blocks with runtime code (which generate IIFEs), parameter properties in constructors (which generate field assignments), and `import =`/`export =` assignments (which generate `require`/`module.exports` calls). This flag makes TypeScript source files directly runnable by Node.js 23.6+ `--experimental-strip-types` and the official `--strip-types` flag (stable since Node.js 22.10), as well as `ts-blank-space`, `oxc-transform`, and Deno's type stripper, all of which implement erase-only transforms.

```typescript
// ❌ Errors with --erasableSyntaxOnly (generates runtime code)
enum Direction { Up, Down, Left, Right }       // generates object literal
namespace Utils { export function helper() {} } // generates IIFE
class Point {
  constructor(public x: number, public y: number) {} // parameter properties
}
import fs = require("fs"); // generates require() call

// ✅ Replacements that are erasable
const Direction = { Up: 0, Down: 1, Left: 2, Right: 3 } as const;
type Direction = typeof Direction[keyof typeof Direction];

// Regular class — explicit field declarations are erasable annotations
class Point {
  x: number;
  y: number;
  constructor(x: number, y: number) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
}

import * as fs from "fs"; // standard ESM import — erasable

// tsconfig for native stripping:
// { "compilerOptions": { "erasableSyntaxOnly": true, "verbatimModuleSyntax": true } }
```

**Tradeoff.** Adopting `--erasableSyntaxOnly` on a legacy codebase often requires migrating away from `enum` (to `const` object + union type) and `namespace` (to ES modules), which can be a substantial refactor. The `const enum` variant is also banned — even though const enums inline their values, the declaration itself is not erasable without full type information. The long-term payoff is a codebase that is directly executable by any type-stripping runtime without a build step.

---

### Pattern 23 — `--module node18` and `require()` of ESM in `--module nodenext` [official]

TypeScript 5.8 added `--module node18` as a stable, frozen snapshot of Node.js 18 module semantics — it does not allow `require()` of ESM files and uses `assert` (deprecated) rather than `with` for import attributes. Separately, TypeScript 5.8 added support (under `--module nodenext`) for the Node.js 22+ behavior of allowing `require()` to synchronously load ESM files that contain no top-level `await`. This eliminates the need for "dual CJS+ESM" library publishing: a library can publish pure ESM and CommonJS consumers on Node.js 22+ can `require()` it directly. TypeScript models this by treating `.js`/`.mjs` imports from `.cts`/`.cjs` files under `nodenext` as valid when the target file is flagged as ESM and contains no top-level await.

```typescript
// Node.js 22+ allows require() of ESM (no top-level await)
// TypeScript 5.8 --module nodenext supports this:

// lib/utils.mts  (ESM)
export function greet(name: string): string {
  return `Hello, ${name}`;
}

// consumer.cts  (CommonJS)
// ✅ Under --module nodenext on Node 22+, this is valid:
const { greet } = require("./utils.js") as typeof import("./utils.js");
console.log(greet("world"));

// ❌ Still forbidden: require() of ESM with top-level await
// lib/config.mts
export const DB_URL = await fetch("/config").then(r => r.text()); // top-level await
// Requiring this from CJS still throws ERR_REQUIRE_ESM

// --module node18: stable, frozen (no require-of-ESM, import assertions with assert:)
// --module nodenext: tracks Node.js latest (includes require-of-ESM, import attributes with with:)
// --module node20: stable snapshot of Node 20 semantics (TypeScript 5.9+)
```

**Tradeoff.** The ability to `require()` ESM is runtime-version-gated: it only works on Node.js 22+ (and Node.js 20.17+ with `--experimental-require-module`). TypeScript's type checking under `nodenext` will accept the pattern, but deploying to Node 18 or 20 (below 20.17) will throw `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM` at runtime. Use `--module node18` to ensure type-level enforcement of the older, stricter semantics when your deployment target is Node 18.

---

### Pattern 24 — Regular Expression Syntax Checking [official]

TypeScript 5.5 introduced static analysis of regex literals — the compiler now parses regex syntax and reports errors for: unclosed groups, back-references to non-existent named groups, invalid escape sequences in unicode mode, and use of named capture groups (`(?<name>...)`) or lookbehind assertions (`(?<=...)`) when the `target` is below ES2018. This is zero-cost at runtime (regexes are unchanged) and requires no configuration. The check is performed on the regex literal text at compile time using the same regex engine rules as the target JavaScript engine, so the diagnostics are semantically correct rather than pattern-matched heuristics.

```typescript
// ❌ Syntax error: unbalanced closing paren
let r1 = /@robot(\s+(please|immediately)))? do task/;
//                                        ^ Unexpected ')'

// ❌ Back-reference to non-existent group \3
let r2 = /@typedef \{import\((.+)\)\.([a-zA-Z_]+)\} \3/u;
//                                                    ^ refers to group 3, only 2 exist

// ❌ Named capture group requires ES2018+ (target: ES2016 → error)
let r3 = /(?<year>\d{4})-(?<month>\d{2})/;
// Error: Named capture groups are only available when targeting 'ES2018' or later.

// ✅ Correct: target ES2018+
// tsconfig: { "target": "ES2020" }
let r4 = /(?<year>\d{4})-(?<month>\d{2})/;
r4.exec("2026-05")?.groups?.year; // "2026"

// ❌ Invalid: \d in non-unicode string mode is fine, but
//    \p{Letter} (unicode property escape) requires the 'u' flag
let r5 = /\p{Letter}+/;
// ✅ Fix:
let r6 = /\p{Letter}+/u;
```

**Tradeoff.** TypeScript only checks regex *literals* — dynamically-constructed `new RegExp(str)` patterns are not analyzed. The target-aware checks (named groups, lookbehind) are tied to the `target` compiler option, so a regex valid for ES2020 will produce errors if the project target is downgraded without updating the regex. Projects targeting old environments but relying on a polyfill for named groups will need to suppress these errors with `// @ts-ignore`.

---

### Pattern 25 — Iterator Helper Methods (`IteratorObject`): Lazy Pipeline Composition on Any Iterator [official]

TypeScript 5.6 added type support for the TC39 Iterator Helpers proposal, which lands the standard `Array`-like methods (`map`, `filter`, `take`, `drop`, `flatMap`, `reduce`, `forEach`, `some`, `every`, `find`, `toArray`) directly on the built-in `Iterator` prototype. These methods are lazy — they produce a new `IteratorObject` that computes values on demand without materializing an intermediate array. TypeScript models this with the new `IteratorObject<T, TReturn, TNext>` and `AsyncIteratorObject<T, TReturn, TNext>` types, which replace the older structural `Iterator<T>` interface for built-in iterators. The `--strictBuiltinIteratorReturn` flag (also 5.6) tightens the `BuiltinIteratorReturn` alias from `any` to `undefined`, surfacing previously-hidden mismatches in iterator protocol implementations.

```typescript
// Native generator — yields an infinite sequence lazily
function* naturals(): Generator<number> {
  let n = 0;
  while (true) yield n++;
}

// Iterator helpers compose without materializing arrays
const result = naturals()
  .filter(n => n % 2 === 0)   // even numbers
  .map(n => n * n)             // squares
  .take(5)                     // first 5
  .toArray();                  // materialize: [0, 4, 16, 36, 64]

// Set, Map, and string iterators also support helpers
const words = new Set(["hello", "world", "foo", "bar"]);
const longWords = words.values()
  .filter(w => w.length > 3)
  .toArray(); // ["hello", "world"]

// --strictBuiltinIteratorReturn: TReturn is undefined, not any
function* typed(): Generator<number, undefined> {
  yield 1;
  return undefined; // explicit undefined return required
}

// AsyncIteratorObject for async generators
async function* asyncStream(): AsyncGenerator<string> {
  for await (const chunk of fetchChunks()) yield chunk;
}
const firstThree = await asyncStream().take(3).toArray();
```

**Tradeoff.** Iterator helpers are a runtime feature requiring Node.js 22+, Chrome 117+, or Firefox 131+; they are not polyfillable without replacing the `Iterator.prototype` globally, which is invasive. TypeScript's type support correctly models the `IteratorObject` chain, but older targets that only have the structural `Iterator<T>` type will not expose these methods — type errors appear at the call site. For maximum compatibility, materialize with spread (`[...gen()]`) and use array methods; switch to iterator helpers only when the runtime target is known to support them.

---

### Pattern 26 — `verbatimModuleSyntax`: Eliminating Import Elision Ambiguity [official]

`verbatimModuleSyntax` (TypeScript 5.0) is a strict-mode replacement for the `importsNotUsedAsValues` + `preserveValueImports` pair that was deprecated in 5.0 and will be removed in TypeScript 6.0. Under this flag, every import is emitted as-is unless it is explicitly marked `import type` — there is no import elision logic. An `import { Foo } from "mod"` where `Foo` is only used as a type must be written `import type { Foo } from "mod"`, otherwise it is left in the output as a runtime import (which may trigger side effects or fail in environments where the module is type-only). This makes the semantic intent of every import explicit and predictable, which is essential for bundlers, type strippers, and `--isolatedDeclarations` tooling.

```typescript
// ❌ Ambiguous without verbatimModuleSyntax: elided or not?
import { SomeType, SomeClass } from "./module";
const x: SomeType = new SomeClass(); // SomeType used as type only

// With verbatimModuleSyntax, must split:
import type { SomeType } from "./module";     // ✅ erased completely
import { SomeClass } from "./module";          // ✅ kept as runtime import

// Mixed inline form also works:
import { type SomeType, SomeClass } from "./module";

// Re-exports must also be explicit:
export type { SomeType } from "./module"; // ✅ type-only re-export
export { SomeClass } from "./module";     // ✅ runtime re-export

// ❌ CommonJS-style exports are banned in ESM files under verbatimModuleSyntax:
module.exports = { SomeClass }; // ❌ Error: use ESM export syntax

// tsconfig pairing — standard modern setup:
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
//     "moduleResolution": "bundler",   // or "nodenext"
//     "module": "esnext"               // or "nodenext"
//   }
// }
```

**Tradeoff.** Enabling `verbatimModuleSyntax` on a large codebase typically produces hundreds of "This import is never used as a value and must use `import type`" errors. Automated codemods (`typescript-eslint/consistent-type-imports` auto-fix, or `ts-migrate`) can migrate most cases, but barrel files that re-export types and values from the same module often require manual attention. The flag is incompatible with `--module commonjs` in the sense that it still transpiles ESM syntax to CJS — it only prevents TypeScript from deciding for you which imports to elide.

---

### Pattern 27 — Declaration Merging: Extending Interfaces Across Files for Module Augmentation [community]

Declaration merging is TypeScript's mechanism for combining multiple declarations of the same name into a single type. While most commonly used for interface extension, its most powerful application is *module augmentation*: adding properties to types exported by third-party libraries without forking the library or using type casting. The `declare module "lib"` syntax reopens a module's ambient namespace from within any file, and the declarations inside are merged with the library's own declarations. This pattern is used pervasively in the ecosystem: Express adds `request.user`, Vue adds `ComponentCustomProperties` for plugin globals, and tRPC adds router types to the React Query context.

```typescript
// Augmenting Express Request with user property:
// src/types/express/index.d.ts
import { User } from "../models/user";

declare global {
  namespace Express {
    interface Request {
      user?: User;
    }
  }
}

// Now in any route handler:
app.get("/profile", (req, res) => {
  req.user?.id; // ✅ TypeScript knows about req.user
});

// Augmenting a third-party library (e.g., adding typed metadata to fastify):
declare module "fastify" {
  interface FastifyRequest {
    tenantId: string;
  }
}

// Augmenting global window for browser environment variables:
declare global {
  interface Window {
    __APP_CONFIG__: { apiUrl: string; featureFlags: Record<string, boolean> };
  }
}
window.__APP_CONFIG__.apiUrl; // ✅ typed

// Interface merging across files in the same project:
// a.ts
interface Plugin { name: string; }
// b.ts
interface Plugin { version: string; }
// Both files merge: Plugin = { name: string; version: string; }
```

**Tradeoff.** Module augmentation declarations must be in a *module file* (containing at least one import or export) — in a script file (no imports/exports), `declare module` opens a new ambient module rather than augmenting an existing one, silently creating a parallel type instead of extending the real one. The merged type is not validated against the original module's internal implementation; it is purely additive at the type level, so it is possible to declare a property that the library never actually sets at runtime.

---

### Pattern 28 — Template Literal Types as Type-Safe String Validators [community]

Template literal types (TypeScript 4.1) allow string types to be parameterized with union-driven pattern matching, enabling a form of structural typing for string values. Combined with conditional types and `infer`, they become a parsing mechanism that can extract route parameters, validate CSS values, enforce naming conventions, and generate event handler names from domain models — all at the type level with zero runtime cost. TypeScript ships four built-in intrinsic string manipulation types (`Uppercase<S>`, `Lowercase<S>`, `Capitalize<S>`, `Uncapitalize<S>`) that operate on string literal types, enabling case-normalization during type derivation.

```typescript
// Route parameter extraction
type ExtractParams<Route extends string> =
  Route extends `${string}:${infer Param}/${infer Rest}`
    ? Param | ExtractParams<`/${Rest}`>
    : Route extends `${string}:${infer Param}`
      ? Param
      : never;

type Params = ExtractParams<"/users/:id/posts/:postId">;
// type Params = "id" | "postId"

// Typed event handler names from model fields
type EventMap<T> = {
  [K in string & keyof T as `on${Capitalize<K>}Change`]: (
    value: T[K],
    prev: T[K]
  ) => void;
};

interface User { name: string; age: number; email: string; }
type UserEvents = EventMap<User>;
// { onNameChange: (value: string, prev: string) => void;
//   onAgeChange: (value: number, prev: number) => void;
//   onEmailChange: (value: string, prev: string) => void; }

// CSS property validation
type CSSUnit = "px" | "em" | "rem" | "vh" | "vw" | "%";
type CSSLength = `${number}${CSSUnit}`;

function setWidth(width: CSSLength): void { /* ... */ }
setWidth("100px");  // ✅
setWidth("2.5rem"); // ✅
setWidth("100");    // ❌ Error: missing unit
setWidth("big");    // ❌ Error: not a valid length
```

**Tradeoff.** Template literal types with multiple union branches generate a cross-product of all combinations: `type T = `${A | B}-${C | D}`` produces 4 variants for 2x2 unions, but a 10x10 union produces 100. TypeScript imposes a compile-time limit on template literal union size (approximately 100,000 members); exceeding it causes a "Type produces a union type that is too complex to represent" error. Keep union branches small, or use `string` as a fallback combined with runtime validation.

---

### Pattern 29 — `--noCheck` and Region-Prioritized Diagnostics: Separating Emit from Type-Checking [official]

TypeScript 5.6 introduced `--noCheck`, a flag that instructs the compiler to emit output files without performing type checking. This is primarily useful in CI pipelines where type checking and compilation are separate jobs, or when using `--isolatedDeclarations` tooling that handles `.d.ts` emit independently. Separately, TypeScript 5.6 added a language server protocol extension for *region-prioritized diagnostics*: editors can request diagnostics for the visible viewport region first, reducing perceived latency from >3000ms to ~140ms on large files. The `--noCheck` flag pairs naturally with `tsc --watch` in hot-reload development workflows where a separate `tsc --noEmit` job handles type checking asynchronously.

```typescript
// tsconfig for a split emit/check pipeline:
// emit.tsconfig.json — fast emit, no type checking
// { "extends": "./tsconfig.json", "compilerOptions": { "noCheck": true } }

// check.tsconfig.json — type checking only, no emit
// { "extends": "./tsconfig.json", "compilerOptions": { "noEmit": true } }

// Makefile targets:
// build: tsc -p emit.tsconfig.json          # fast, no type-check
// typecheck: tsc -p check.tsconfig.json     # full check, no output
// ci: make typecheck && make build          # parallel in CI

// --noCheck is also useful with transpilers that handle emit:
// esbuild src/index.ts --bundle --outfile=dist/bundle.js
// tsc --noEmit  # type-check only (separate from esbuild emit)

// ❌ Common mistake: using --noCheck with --declaration
// Declaration emit requires type information — --noCheck with --declaration
// produces .d.ts files that may be incorrect or incomplete.
// ✅ Use --isolatedDeclarations + a single-file d.ts emitter instead.
```

**Tradeoff.** `--noCheck` sacrifices the compile-time guarantee that the emitted JavaScript is type-safe — it is possible to ship broken runtime code that would have been caught by type checking. This is acceptable in workflows where type checking runs as a separate blocking job before deployment, but dangerous if the emit step can be merged without running the check step. Teams adopting `--noCheck` should gate their merge queue or deployment pipeline on a passing `tsc --noEmit` job.

---

### Pattern 30 — `--strictBuiltinIteratorReturn` and the `IteratorObject` Hierarchy [official]

TypeScript 5.6 introduced the `--strictBuiltinIteratorReturn` flag and a new `IteratorObject` class hierarchy to distinguish between the structural `Iterator<T>` interface (the minimal `{ next(): IteratorResult<T> }` duck type) and the concrete `IteratorObject<T, TReturn, TNext>` that built-in iterators (generators, `Map.values()`, `Set.keys()`, etc.) actually implement. Under the old types, `BuiltinIteratorReturn` was `any`, which silently accepted mismatched `TReturn` types. With `--strictBuiltinIteratorReturn`, `BuiltinIteratorReturn` becomes `undefined`, and any `Iterator` implementation used where `BuiltinIteratorReturn` is expected must explicitly type its return value as `undefined`. This catches real bugs where code assumed the `done: true` result's `value` was meaningful when it is always `undefined` for generators and built-in iterators.

```typescript
// Without --strictBuiltinIteratorReturn: BuiltinIteratorReturn = any
// With --strictBuiltinIteratorReturn: BuiltinIteratorReturn = undefined

// ❌ Bug caught by the flag: consuming the return value of a built-in iterator
function* gen(): Generator<number, undefined> {
  yield 1;
  yield 2;
  // implicit return undefined
}

const iter = gen();
let result = iter.next();
while (!result.done) {
  console.log(result.value); // number — ✅
  result = iter.next();
}
// After the loop: result.done is true, result.value is undefined
// ❌ Previously: result.value typed as any, masking the undefined
// ✅ Now: result.value typed as undefined — reads like .value?.toString() error correctly

// IteratorObject exposes helper methods; Iterator<T> (structural) does not
function consumeStructural(iter: Iterator<number>): number[] {
  // iter.map is not available — Iterator<T> is the minimal interface
  return [...{ [Symbol.iterator]: () => iter }];
}

function consumeBuiltin(iter: IteratorObject<number>): number[] {
  return iter.map(x => x * 2).toArray(); // ✅ helper methods available
}

// Type guard to check if an iterator supports helpers
function hasHelpers(iter: Iterator<unknown>): iter is IteratorObject<unknown> {
  return typeof (iter as any).map === "function";
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `--strictBuiltinIteratorReturn` is not part of `--strict` and must be opted into separately; it is enabled by default in the TypeScript 5.9 `tsc --init` output but not in existing tsconfigs. Enabling it on a codebase that manually implements `Iterator<T>` by returning objects with `{ value: SomeType, done: true }` (where `SomeType` is not `undefined`) will produce errors — the fix is either to change the return type to `undefined` or to use a different interface (`Iterator<T, SomeType>`) with explicit `TReturn`.

---

**Gotcha 87 — TypeScript 5.5 inferred type predicates silently change the element type of `.filter()` results — code that previously pushed `null` into the filtered array now errors** [community]

```typescript
// TypeScript 5.4 and earlier: nums is (number | null)[]
// TypeScript 5.5+: nums is number[]  — predicate inferred from x !== null
const nums = [1, 2, 3, null, 5].filter(x => x !== null);

// ❌ Was previously fine; now a compile error in 5.5+:
nums.push(null);
// Error: Argument of type 'null' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'

// This is a SILENT BREAKING CHANGE if you upgrade TypeScript without
// re-checking array mutation sites after filter calls

// ✅ Fix: explicitly annotate the array type if you need nullability
const numsNullable: (number | null)[] = [1, 2, 3, null, 5].filter(x => x !== null);
numsNullable.push(null); // ✅ now ok

// ❌ Another trap: truthiness filters also affect downstream types
const words = ["hello", "", "world", ""].filter(Boolean);
// words is now string[] in 5.5+ (empty string filtered as "falsy")
// WAIT — actually truthiness does NOT infer a predicate (per spec)
// .filter(Boolean) infers boolean return, not a type predicate
// words remains (string)[] — no change here
// The inferred predicate only applies to explicit !== null/undefined checks
```

WHY: TypeScript 5.5's inferred type predicate feature treats a function returning `x !== null` as a type predicate `(x): x is NonNullable<typeof x>`. When `.filter()` receives a type predicate, it narrows the element type of the result array from `T | null` to `T`. This is correct and desirable behavior, but it is a *breaking* semantic change for any code that subsequently mutates the filtered array to re-insert null values. The change is particularly subtle because it does not produce an error on the filter call itself — only on downstream mutation or assignment sites that assume the array still accepts null.

---

**Gotcha 88 — `--isolatedDeclarations` bans `export default` of anonymous arrow functions and object literals — two extremely common patterns that now require either a name or an explicit return type annotation** [community]

```typescript
// ❌ Both patterns are common and both fail under --isolatedDeclarations:

// Anonymous arrow function default export — cannot emit .d.ts without full inference
export default (x: number) => x * 2;
// Error: Default exports must have an explicit type annotation with
// --isolatedDeclarations.

// Object literal default export — shape cannot be inferred in isolation
export default { greet: (name: string) => `Hello ${name}` };
// Error: Default exports must have an explicit type annotation.

// ✅ Fix 1: add explicit return type annotation
export default (x: number): number => x * 2;

// ✅ Fix 2: name the expression and annotate
const double = (x: number): number => x * 2;
export default double;

// ✅ Fix 3: annotate the object literal with satisfies or a type
interface Greeter { greet(name: string): string; }
export default {
  greet: (name: string): string => `Hello ${name}`,
} satisfies Greeter;

// ❌ Also banned: export default with a class expression containing
// inferred property types from parameter properties
export default class {
  constructor(public value: number) {} // ❌ parameter property — erasable check too
}
```

WHY: `--isolatedDeclarations` requires every exported type to be computable from the syntax of a *single file* without resolving imports or running the full type inference engine. Anonymous arrow functions and object literals have no declared type at the export site — a declaration emitter must run the full type checker to determine their shape. The TypeScript team explicitly chose to error rather than fall back to `any` in the emitted `.d.ts`, because a `.d.ts` with `any` would silently destroy type safety for consumers. The fix is mechanical but widespread in codebases that follow the "export default arrow" pattern common in React component files.

---

**Gotcha 89 — `const` type parameter inference does not apply when the argument is a pre-existing variable — the narrowing only works for freshly-written object/array literals at the call site** [community]

```typescript
function route<const T extends readonly string[]>(paths: T): T {
  return paths;
}

// ✅ Fresh literal: T inferred as readonly ["home", "about", "contact"]
const r1 = route(["home", "about", "contact"]);
// r1[0] is type "home", not string

// ❌ Pre-existing variable: T inferred as string[] — const has no effect
const paths = ["home", "about", "contact"]; // already widened to string[]
const r2 = route(paths);
// r2[0] is type string, not "home"

// ❌ Returning a value and reassigning also defeats const inference
function getPaths() { return ["home", "about"]; } // returns string[]
const r3 = route(getPaths()); // T is string[]

// ✅ Workaround: use `as const` on the pre-existing variable
const paths2 = ["home", "about", "contact"] as const;
const r4 = route(paths2); // T is readonly ["home","about","contact"] ✅

// ❌ Subtle: const inference does NOT make the parameter readonly at runtime
// It only affects the inferred type; the JS array is still mutable
function mutateRoute<const T extends string[]>(paths: T): T {
  paths.push("404"); // No TS error — T is inferred as tuple but not readonly
  return paths;
}
// ✅ Fix: add readonly to the constraint
function safeRoute<const T extends readonly string[]>(paths: T): T {
  // paths.push("404"); // ❌ now a compile error
  return paths;
}
```

WHY: The `const` type parameter modifier instructs TypeScript to infer the argument type as if it were declared with `as const` — but only when the argument is a *fresh* object or array literal written directly at the call site. When the argument is a variable that was declared elsewhere, its type has already been widened to `string[]` (or `object`) by the earlier declaration, and that widened type is what the generic receives. The compiler cannot retroactively "un-widen" a pre-existing type. This is the same reason `as const` on a pre-declared variable at declaration time must be written at the declaration site, not at the usage site.

---

**Gotcha 90 — TypeScript 5.6's "always-truthy" check for nullish coalescing fires on legitimate defensive patterns, requiring a `// @ts-ignore` or a restructuring of the code** [community]

```typescript
// TypeScript 5.6: right operand of ?? is unreachable if left is never nullish
const port = Number(process.env.PORT) ?? 3000;
// ❌ Error: Right operand of '??' is unreachable because the left operand
//    is never nullish. 'Number()' always returns number, never null/undefined

// The intent was defensive default — Number() DOES return NaN for bad input,
// but NaN is not null/undefined so ?? doesn't help anyway
// ✅ Fix: use || for falsy fallback (NaN is falsy, 0 is falsy — be explicit)
const port2 = Number(process.env.PORT) || 3000;

// Another common false alarm pattern:
function getValue(): string { return computedValue; }
const label = getValue() ?? "default";
// ❌ Error: getValue() returns string (never nullish)

// ✅ Fix: only use ?? when the left operand can actually be null/undefined
function getValue2(): string | null { return computedValue || null; }
const label2 = getValue2() ?? "default";

// ❌ Arrow functions are always truthy — this fires in test code:
if (x => x > 0) {
  // "This kind of expression is always truthy" — the arrow function object
  // is always truthy even if the intent was to check if x is positive
}
// ✅ Fix: call the function
if ((x => x > 0)(someValue)) { /* ... */ }
```

WHY: TypeScript 5.6 added a lint-style check that fires when it can statically determine that a truthy or nullish check will always evaluate in one direction. The `??` check fires when the left side is typed as non-nullable (e.g., `string`, `number`, `boolean`) — exactly the cases where `??` has no effect. The check is correct: `Number()` always returns `number` (possibly `NaN`), so `?? 3000` will never activate. The surprising part is that `NaN ?? 3000` evaluates to `NaN` (because `NaN` is not `null`/`undefined`), which means the defensive pattern was already broken before TypeScript 5.6 pointed it out.

---

**Gotcha 91 — Computed property `override` checks (TypeScript 5.6) now catch symbol-keyed overrides that were silently ignored in earlier versions — adding `override` to a symbol method that doesn't exist in the base class is now an error, and *omitting* `override` on a symbol method that *does* exist is also flagged under `--noImplicitOverride`** [community]

```typescript
const tag = Symbol("tag");
const render = Symbol("render");

class Base {
  [tag](): string { return "base"; }
}

// ❌ TypeScript 5.5 and earlier: silently ignored; 5.6+ errors:
class Derived extends Base {
  override [render](): string { return "derived"; }
  // Error: This member cannot have an 'override' modifier because it is
  // not declared in the base class 'Base' (symbol 'render' not in Base)
}

// ❌ Under --noImplicitOverride: omitting override on [tag] is now an error
class Derived2 extends Base {
  [tag](): string { return "derived2"; } // Error: override keyword missing
}

// ✅ Correct:
class Derived3 extends Base {
  override [tag](): string { return "derived3"; } // ✅ overriding [tag] from Base
}

// ❌ Edge case: if `tag` is declared `const` but its value is computed at
// module load time from a Symbol.for() call, TypeScript may not be able
// to statically verify the symbol identity and will report a false positive —
// use the same const reference throughout rather than separate Symbol.for() calls
const sharedTag = Symbol.for("app.tag");
class A { [sharedTag]() {} }
class B extends A {
  override [sharedTag]() {} // ✅ same const ref — TypeScript can verify identity
}
```

WHY: Prior to TypeScript 5.6, the `override` modifier was only validated for string-named and number-indexed class members. Computed property names (including `Symbol` values) were silently accepted regardless of whether the base class had a matching member. TypeScript 5.6 extends the override checker to computed properties by comparing the const-reference identity of the symbol variable — if the same `const` variable is used in both the base and derived class, TypeScript can prove they refer to the same runtime symbol and validate the override correctly. This is a correctness improvement, but it breaks code that carelessly added `override` to symbol methods without a matching base method.
