## Cycle 49 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 61 — `using` Declarations for Deterministic Resource Cleanup (TypeScript 5.2 / ES2025) [official]

Implement `Disposable` (or `AsyncDisposable`) on any object that holds an OS- or process-level resource and use the `using` binding to guarantee cleanup at scope exit, even when exceptions are thrown.

```typescript
import * as fs from "node:fs";

// ── 1. Implement Disposable on a resource-owning class ──────────────────────
class TempFile implements Disposable {
  readonly path: string;
  private readonly _handle: number;

  constructor(path: string) {
    this.path = path;
    this._handle = fs.openSync(path, "w+");
  }

  write(data: string): void {
    fs.writeSync(this._handle, data);
  }

  [Symbol.dispose](): void {
    fs.closeSync(this._handle);
    fs.unlinkSync(this.path);
  }
}

// ── 2. using guarantees disposal at scope exit ──────────────────────────────
function processBatch(items: string[]): void {
  using tmp = new TempFile(".batch_work.tmp");
  for (const item of items) {
    tmp.write(item + "\n");
  }
  // [Symbol.dispose]() is called here automatically, even if an error is thrown
}

// ── 3. DisposableStack for ad-hoc registrations ─────────────────────────────
function doWork(): void {
  using stack = new DisposableStack();
  const conn = openConnection();          // hypothetical sync resource
  stack.defer(() => conn.close());
  // additional registrations in LIFO order
  const lock = acquireLock();
  stack.defer(() => releaseLock(lock));
  // lock released first, then conn closed
}

// ── 4. Async variant ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class DbConnection implements AsyncDisposable {
  async [Symbol.asyncDispose](): Promise<void> {
    await this.close();
  }
  async close(): Promise<void> { /* … */ }
}

async function query(): Promise<void> {
  await using db = new DbConnection();
  // db.close() is awaited on scope exit
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Requires `"target": "es2022"` or newer plus the `"lib": ["esnext.disposable"]` lib entry (or equivalent). Polyfills (`Symbol.dispose ??= Symbol("Symbol.dispose")`) are needed for runtimes below Node.js 22. The feature replaces ad-hoc `try/finally` blocks but does not replace RAII for languages where stack lifetimes are guaranteed at the machine level — GC still controls object lifetime between dispose calls. [official]

---

### Pattern 62 — Decorator Metadata via `Symbol.metadata` for Framework-Level Introspection (TypeScript 5.2) [official]

Use Stage-3 Decorator Metadata to attach reflection data from decorators in a standard, collision-free way, then read it at runtime to implement serialization, validation, or dependency injection without a separate `Reflect.metadata` polyfill.

```typescript
// ── 1. Declare the metadata shape ───────────────────────────────────────────
interface PropertyMeta { type: string; required: boolean }
const META_KEY = Symbol("serializable");

// ── 2. Write a decorator that pushes into metadata ───────────────────────────
function field(opts: Partial<PropertyMeta> = {}) {
  return function (_target: undefined, ctx: ClassFieldDecoratorContext) {
    const meta = (ctx.metadata[META_KEY] as PropertyMeta[] | undefined) ?? [];
    meta.push({ type: "unknown", required: true, ...opts, ...{ name: String(ctx.name) } } as any);
    ctx.metadata[META_KEY] = meta;
  };
}

// ── 3. Annotate a class ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class User {
  @field({ type: "string" })
  name!: string;

  @field({ type: "string", required: false })
  email?: string;
}

// ── 4. Read metadata at runtime ──────────────────────────────────────────────
function toJson(instance: object): string {
  const meta = instance.constructor[Symbol.metadata];
  const fields = (meta?.[META_KEY] ?? []) as Array<PropertyMeta & { name: string }>;
  const out: Record<string, unknown> = {};
  for (const f of fields) {
    const val = (instance as any)[f.name];
    if (f.required && val == null) throw new Error(`${f.name} is required`);
    out[f.name] = val;
  }
  return JSON.stringify(out);
}

const u = new User();
u.name = "Alice";
console.log(toJson(u)); // {"name":"Alice"}
```

**Tradeoff:** `Symbol.metadata` replaces the non-standard `Reflect.metadata` pattern from `reflect-metadata`. The polyfill `Symbol.metadata ??= Symbol("Symbol.metadata")` must run before any decorator-annotated class is loaded. Libraries that previously used `emitDecoratorMetadata` must migrate separately — the two systems do not interoperate. [official]

---

### Pattern 63 — Template Literal Type–Driven Event Map with Inferred Callback Signatures [official]

Use template literal types combined with `keyof` and indexed access types to build a strictly typed event emitter where invalid event names and wrong callback parameter types are caught at compile time.

```typescript
// ── 1. Domain model ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
interface UserEvents {
  login:   { userId: string; timestamp: number };
  logout:  { userId: string };
  update:  { userId: string; fields: Partial<{ name: string; email: string }> };
}

// ── 2. Template literal types derive the "on*" handler map ──────────────────
type HandlerMap<Events extends Record<string, unknown>> = {
  [K in keyof Events as `on${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: (payload: Events[K]) => void;
};

// ── 3. Type-safe emitter interface ───────────────────────────────────────────
type Emitter<Events extends Record<string, unknown>> = {
  emit<K extends keyof Events>(event: K, payload: Events[K]): void;
  on<K extends keyof Events>(event: K, handler: (payload: Events[K]) => void): void;
  off<K extends keyof Events>(event: K, handler: (payload: Events[K]) => void): void;
};

declare function createEmitter<Events extends Record<string, unknown>>(): Emitter<Events>;

// ── 4. Usage ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
const bus = createEmitter<UserEvents>();

bus.on("login", ({ userId, timestamp }) => {
  // userId: string, timestamp: number — fully inferred
  console.log(userId, new Date(timestamp));
});

// ❌ Compile error: payload type mismatch
// bus.emit("login", { userId: 1 }); // userId must be string

// ── 5. Derive handler map for class mixins ───────────────────────────────────
type UserHandlers = HandlerMap<UserEvents>;
// { onLogin: (p: {userId:string;timestamp:number}) => void;
//   onLogout: (p: {userId:string}) => void;
//   onUpdate: (p: {userId:string;fields:…}) => void }
```

**Tradeoff:** The `Capitalize<string & K>` cast is required because `K` may be `string | number | symbol`; without `string &` the `Capitalize` intrinsic errors. Template literal cross-products grow exponentially — avoid combining more than two large union types in a single template literal position. [official]

---

### Pattern 64 — Granular Return-Branch Checks with Typed `any` Maps (TypeScript 5.8) [official]

TypeScript 5.8 checks each branch of a ternary or `&&`/`||` return expression against the declared return type independently, catching bugs that previously hid behind `any` pollution from untyped caches or external data.

```typescript
// ── Pattern: properly typed cache avoids per-branch shadowing ───────────────
type RouteHandler = (req: Request, res: Response) => Promise<void>;
const handlerCache = new Map<string, RouteHandler>(); // typed, not Map<any,any>

function getHandler(route: string, fallback: RouteHandler): RouteHandler {
  // ✅ Both branches assignable to RouteHandler — no 5.8 error
  return handlerCache.has(route)
    ? handlerCache.get(route)! // non-null assertion: has() confirmed presence
    : fallback;
}

// ── What 5.8 now catches ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
declare const untypedCache: Map<any, any>;

function getUrl(key: string): URL {
  return untypedCache.has(key)
    ? untypedCache.get(key)   // ✅ any — still compiles
    : key;                     // ❌ 5.8 ERROR: 'string' not assignable to 'URL'
    //   Previously: any | string → any → silent. Now: branch checked individually.
}

// ── Safe rewrite ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
function getUrlSafe(key: string): URL {
  return untypedCache.has(key)
    ? (untypedCache.get(key) as URL)  // explicit assertion
    : new URL(`https://example.com/${key}`);
}
```

**Tradeoff:** This is a correctness improvement but is a **breaking change for code relying on `any`-widened ternary returns**. Migrations of large codebases that used `Map<any, any>` as an internal cache type typically require either introducing proper generics or adding explicit `as T` casts at the `get()` call site. Prefer fixing the underlying `Map` type rather than suppressing with `as`. [official]

---

### Pattern 65 — `await using` with `AsyncDisposableStack` for Composable Async Teardown [official]

Compose multiple async resources inside a single `AsyncDisposableStack` so that all teardowns happen in LIFO order and failures in one teardown do not suppress cleanup of the remaining resources.

```typescript
import type { AsyncDisposable } from "typescript";

// ── 1. Async-disposable database pool ────────────────────────────────────────
class Pool implements AsyncDisposable {
  constructor(readonly url: string) {}
  async query(sql: string): Promise<unknown[]> { return []; }
  async [Symbol.asyncDispose](): Promise<void> {
    console.log("pool closed");
  }
}

// ── 2. Async-disposable message bus ─────────────────────────────────────────
class Bus implements AsyncDisposable {
  async publish(topic: string, msg: unknown): Promise<void> { /* … */ }
  async [Symbol.asyncDispose](): Promise<void> {
    console.log("bus disconnected");
  }
}

// ── 3. Compose via AsyncDisposableStack ──────────────────────────────────────
async function runMigration(): Promise<void> {
  await using stack = new AsyncDisposableStack();

  const pool = stack.use(new Pool("postgres://localhost/app"));
  const bus  = stack.use(new Bus());

  // stack.defer for ad-hoc lambdas
  stack.defer(async () => console.log("audit log written"));

  const rows = await pool.query("SELECT id FROM users");
  await bus.publish("migration.complete", { count: rows.length });
  // On scope exit: audit log → bus.disconnect → pool.close (LIFO)
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `AsyncDisposableStack` is available in TypeScript 5.2+ with `"lib": ["esnext.disposable"]`. Errors thrown by dispose methods are wrapped in `SuppressedError` — if you catch exceptions from `await using` scopes you must check `e instanceof SuppressedError` to inspect both the original error and the suppressed disposal error. [official]

---

### Pattern 66 — `--erasableSyntaxOnly` for Node.js Native Type-Stripping Compatibility [official]

Enable `--erasableSyntaxOnly` in projects targeting Node.js 22.6+ or 23.6+ native `--experimental-strip-types` to get a compile-time guard against non-erasable TypeScript syntax that requires a build step.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json for native-strip-compatible code:
// { "compilerOptions": { "erasableSyntaxOnly": true, "verbatimModuleSyntax": true } }

// ── Constructs blocked by --erasableSyntaxOnly ─────────────────────────────

// ❌ Parameter properties
class Vec2 {
  constructor(public x: number, public y: number) {}  // ERROR
}
// ✅ Rewrite:
class Vec2Ok {
  x: number; y: number;
  constructor(x: number, y: number) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
}

// ❌ enum (has runtime JS output)
enum Dir { Up, Down }  // ERROR
// ✅ Rewrite with const object + satisfies:
const Dir = { Up: 0, Down: 1 } as const satisfies Record<string, number>;
type Dir = (typeof Dir)[keyof typeof Dir];

// ❌ import = require()
import fs = require("node:fs");  // ERROR
// ✅ Rewrite:
import * as fs from "node:fs";

// ❌ namespace with runtime value
namespace Config { export const version = "1"; }  // ERROR
// ✅ Rewrite: plain ES module exports
export const configVersion = "1";

// ✅ Allowed: type aliases, interfaces, type assertions, generics
type Opts = { timeout: number };
function fetch<T>(url: string): Promise<T> { return null!; }
```

**Tradeoff:** Adopting `--erasableSyntaxOnly` in a greenfield project is low-cost; retrofitting it in a codebase with widespread enums and parameter properties requires a migration pass. The flag improves interoperability with tools that strip types without a full TypeScript compile (esbuild, swc, Node.js `--experimental-strip-types`) but prevents using compile-time enum inlining for perf-sensitive integer tables. [official]

---

### Pattern 67 — Computed Property Names Preserved in `.d.ts` Files (TypeScript 5.8) [official]

Since TypeScript 5.8, computed property names whose keys are exported entity names survive declaration emit, enabling consumers to access the property using the same symbolic key without a type assertion.

```typescript
// ── lib.ts (published library) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
export const HOOK_KEY = "onBeforeRender" as const;

export class Renderer {
  [HOOK_KEY]?: () => void;  // ✅ preserved in .d.ts since TS 5.8
  render(): void { /* … */ }
}

// ── Emitted .d.ts (TypeScript 5.8+) ─────────────────────────────────────────
// export declare const HOOK_KEY: "onBeforeRender";
// export declare class Renderer {
//   [HOOK_KEY]?: () => void;  // key identity preserved
//   render(): void;
// }

// ── consumer.ts ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import { Renderer, HOOK_KEY } from "./lib";
const r = new Renderer();

// ✅ Property access via the imported key — type-safe
r[HOOK_KEY] = () => console.log("pre-render");

// ✅ TypeScript knows [HOOK_KEY] exists; no `as any` needed
function registerHook(target: Renderer, hook: () => void): void {
  target[HOOK_KEY] = hook;
}
```

**Tradeoff:** This only works when the computed key is an **exported const or let** with a string/number/symbol literal type. Object literal shorthand keys, `Symbol()` expressions, or non-exported variables still collapse to index signatures. When upgrading to TypeScript 5.8, verify that library consumers that previously used an index signature workaround still compile — the preserved declaration is structurally compatible but may surface new type narrowing at access sites. [official]

---

### Pattern 68 — `--module node18` as a Stable Forward-Compatible Reference for Node 18 LTS Projects [official]

Use `--module node18` instead of `--module node16` or `--module nodenext` in Node.js 18 LTS projects to get a fixed module mode that does not receive behavior changes as Node.js evolves, while still enabling ESM interop and proper `.mjs`/`.cjs` extension routing.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "module": "node18",
//     "moduleResolution": "node18",
//     "target": "es2022"
//   }
// }

// ── node18 vs nodenext differences ──────────────────────────────────────────
//
// Feature                      node18    nodenext
// require() of ESM files       ❌ error  ✅ allowed (Node 22+)
// import assertions             ✅ valid  ❌ deprecated (use import attributes)
// .mts / .cts / .mjs / .cjs    ✅ routed ✅ routed
// Stability over time           fixed     tracks Node.js latest

// ── Example: import attributes (nodenext) vs assertions (node18) ─────────────
// node18:
import data from "./data.json" assert { type: "json" };  // ✅ node18

// nodenext:
import data2 from "./data.json" with { type: "json" };   // ✅ nodenext

// ── Correct ESM-first import style for node18 ────────────────────────────────
// File: src/utils.mts
export function add(a: number, b: number): number {
  return a + b;
}

// File: src/index.mts — use explicit .mjs extension for ESM resolution
import { add } from "./utils.mjs";
console.log(add(1, 2));
```

**Tradeoff:** `node18` gives predictable behavior for the Node 18 LTS support window (until April 2025). Projects that need to support only Node 18 gain stability but give up `require(esm)` interoperability available in Node 22+. When Node 18 reaches EOL, migrate to `node20` or `nodenext` and audit import assertions that must become import attributes. [official]

---

### Pattern 69 — Named Tuple Elements with Mixed Labels for Self-Documenting APIs (TypeScript 4.0+) [official]

Label all elements of a function's tuple return type or parameter rest so that destructured bindings, IDE hover information, and error messages show meaningful names instead of generic `0`, `1`, `2` indices.

```typescript
// ── 1. Named tuple as return type ────────────────────────────────────────────
function usePagination(total: number, pageSize: number): [
  page:    number,
  setPage: (n: number) => void,
  pages:   number,
] {
  let page = 1;
  return [
    page,
    (n) => { page = n; },
    Math.ceil(total / pageSize),
  ];
}

const [page, setPage, totalPages] = usePagination(100, 10);
//     ^^^^  ^^^^^^^  ^^^^^^^^^^   — IDE shows label names on hover

// ── 2. Spreading preserves labels ────────────────────────────────────────────
type HasCoords = [x: number, y: number];
type HasDepth  = [z: number];
type Vec3 = [...HasCoords, ...HasDepth];
// Hover: [x: number, y: number, z: number]  ← labels preserved

// ── 3. Mixing optional and required labeled elements ─────────────────────────
type RequestSpec = [
  method: "GET" | "POST" | "PUT" | "DELETE",
  path:   string,
  body?:  unknown,
];

function request(...args: RequestSpec): Promise<Response> {
  const [method, path, body] = args;
  return fetch(path, { method, body: JSON.stringify(body) });
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Tuple element labels are documentation only — they do not affect structural assignability (a labeled `[x: number]` is assignable to `[number]`). Overly long tuples (> 4 elements) are better expressed as named objects; use labeled tuples primarily for React hook–style `[value, setter]` pairs and function overload helpers. TypeScript 4.2+ also allows leading/middle rest elements in labeled tuples, enabling precise variadic signatures. [official]

---

### Pattern 70 — `satisfies` + `as const` Combination for Exhaustive Config Objects with Literal Type Preservation [community]

Combine `satisfies` (TypeScript 4.9) with `as const` to get both the literal type preservation of `as const` and the structural validation of an annotation, without the type widening that a plain annotation introduces.

```typescript
// ── Without satisfies: annotation widens literals ───────────────────────────
type Palette = Record<string, [number, number, number]>;
const colors1: Palette = {
  red:   [255, 0, 0],
  green: [0, 255, 0],
};
// colors1.red has type [number, number, number] — lost the literal [255,0,0]

// ── With satisfies: validation without widening ──────────────────────────────
const colors2 = {
  red:   [255, 0, 0],
  green: [0, 255, 0],
  blue:  [0, 0, 255],
} satisfies Palette;
// colors2.red has type [255, 0, 0] (literal preserved!)
// colors2.purple — ❌ error (not in Palette constraint) ← still validated

// ── Combined with as const for deep immutability ─────────────────────────────
const routes = {
  home:    { path: "/",        method: "GET"  },
  profile: { path: "/profile", method: "GET"  },
  login:   { path: "/login",   method: "POST" },
} as const satisfies Record<string, { path: string; method: "GET" | "POST" }>;

type RouteKey = keyof typeof routes;          // "home" | "profile" | "login"
type RoutePath = typeof routes[RouteKey]["path"]; // "/" | "/profile" | "/login"

// ✅ Exhaustive switch is possible because literal types are preserved:
function getMethod(key: RouteKey) {
  return routes[key].method; // "GET" | "POST" — not widened to string
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `as const satisfies T` is evaluated right-to-left: `as const` freezes the literal types first, then `satisfies T` validates the shape. This means you cannot use `satisfies` to widen literals that `as const` froze — if you need the widened type for downstream use, annotate with `: T` instead and accept the literal loss. [community]

---

### Pattern 71 — Recursive Template Literal Types for Type-Safe URL Path Parsing [community]

Use recursive conditional types with template literal `infer` to parse URL path segments into a typed parameter record, enabling route handlers to receive fully typed `params` objects without runtime parsing code.

```typescript
// ── 1. Extract path params via recursive infer ───────────────────────────────
type ExtractParams<Path extends string> =
  Path extends `${string}:${infer Param}/${infer Rest}`
    ? { [K in Param | keyof ExtractParams<Rest>]: string }
    : Path extends `${string}:${infer Param}`
      ? { [K in Param]: string }
      : Record<never, string>;

// ── 2. Type-check at definition time ────────────────────────────────────────
type UserParams    = ExtractParams<"/users/:userId/posts/:postId">;
// { userId: string; postId: string }

type ArticleParams = ExtractParams<"/articles/:slug">;
// { slug: string }

type StaticParams  = ExtractParams<"/health">;
// Record<never, string>  (i.e. {})

// ── 3. Typed router factory ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
declare function route<P extends string>(
  path: P,
  handler: (params: ExtractParams<P>) => Response,
): void;

route("/users/:userId/posts/:postId", ({ userId, postId }) => {
  // userId: string, postId: string — fully typed, no manual annotation
  return new Response(`User ${userId} post ${postId}`);
});

// ❌ Compile error: 'badParam' does not exist in params
// route("/items/:id", ({ badParam }) => new Response(badParam));
```

**Tradeoff:** Recursive conditional types add to the instantiation depth counter. Paths with more than ~8 segments may hit TypeScript's recursion limit (`Type instantiation is excessively deep`). For production routing libraries, generate the param map via a code-generation step instead of relying on deep runtime recursion. [community]

### Pattern 72 — `using` + `DisposableStack` for Test Fixture Lifecycle Management [community]

In test files, use `using` and `DisposableStack` to manage test database connections, mock server instances, and temporary files so that teardown happens automatically regardless of test outcome.

```typescript
import { describe, it } from "vitest";

// ── 1. Disposable test server ────────────────────────────────────────────────
class TestServer implements Disposable {
  readonly port: number;
  constructor() {
    this.port = Math.floor(Math.random() * 10000 + 3000);
    // start listening synchronously
  }
  fetch(path: string): Promise<Response> {
    return globalThis.fetch(`http://localhost:${this.port}${path}`);
  }
  [Symbol.dispose](): void {
    // stop server
    console.log(`server on :${this.port} stopped`);
  }
}

// ── 2. Disposable DB transaction ─────────────────────────────────────────────
class TxFixture implements AsyncDisposable {
  constructor(private readonly db: { rollback(): Promise<void> }) {}
  async [Symbol.asyncDispose](): Promise<void> {
    await this.db.rollback(); // always rollback — keep DB clean
  }
}

// ── 3. Composed fixture with DisposableStack ─────────────────────────────────
describe("API tests", () => {
  it("returns user data", () => {
    using server = new TestServer();
    using stack  = new DisposableStack();
    stack.defer(() => console.log("extra cleanup"));

    // test code — cleanup guaranteed even if assertion throws
    expect(server.port).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `using` in test bodies requires Jest 29.7+ or Vitest 1.0+ with `"target": "es2022"` in the test tsconfig. Async test teardown needs `await using` but most test frameworks' `it()` callbacks accept async functions, making this pattern seamless. The pattern eliminates `afterEach` / `afterAll` state-threading boilerplate but requires all maintainers to understand `Symbol.dispose`. [community]

### Pattern 73 — `infer` with `extends` Bounds to Extract Specific Subtypes Without `Exclude` [official]

Since TypeScript 5.4, the `infer X extends Constraint` syntax lets conditional types extract only the subset of an inferred type that satisfies a bound, replacing chains of `Exclude<infer X, Y>` with a single, readable bound expression.

```typescript
// ── 1. Extract string keys only from a union ─────────────────────────────────
type StringKeys<T> = keyof T extends infer K extends string ? K : never;

type Keys = StringKeys<{ a: 1; b: 2; 0: 3 }>;
// "a" | "b"  (symbol and number keys excluded by the `extends string` bound)

// ── 2. Extract the return type only when it's a Promise ──────────────────────
type IfPromiseReturn<T extends (...args: any[]) => any> =
  ReturnType<T> extends infer R extends Promise<unknown>
    ? Awaited<R>
    : never;

async function loadUser(): Promise<{ id: string }> { return { id: "1" }; }
type UserData = IfPromiseReturn<typeof loadUser>; // { id: string }

// ── 3. Extract numeric literal values from a const union ─────────────────────
type NumericValues<T extends Record<string, unknown>> =
  T[keyof T] extends infer V extends number ? V : never;

const Status = { OK: 200, NOT_FOUND: 404, ERROR: 500 } as const;
type StatusCode = NumericValues<typeof Status>; // 200 | 404 | 500

// ── 4. Old approach (prior to TS 5.4) — verbose ──────────────────────────────
type StringKeysOld<T> = keyof T extends infer K
  ? K extends string ? K : never
  : never;
```

**Tradeoff:** The bound constraint `extends Constraint` applies after inference, meaning the inferred type is first captured unrestricted, then the bound filters it. If no members satisfy the bound, the whole conditional resolves to `never` — make sure to test the never case. This syntax is only available from TypeScript 5.4; tooling that re-processes TypeScript < 5.4 will fail to parse the bound. [official]

### Pattern 74 — Assertion Functions with `asserts` Return Type for Flow-Narrowing Helpers [official]

Declare a function's return type as `asserts condition` so that TypeScript treats the function as a type guard that throws on failure, narrowing the type at all points after the call without requiring an `if` branch.

```typescript
// ── 1. Basic assertion function ──────────────────────────────────────────────
function assert(condition: unknown, msg?: string): asserts condition {
  if (!condition) throw new Error(msg ?? "Assertion failed");
}

// ── 2. Typed assertion for nullable values ───────────────────────────────────
function assertDefined<T>(val: T | null | undefined, name = "value"): asserts val is T {
  if (val == null) throw new TypeError(`${name} must not be null/undefined`);
}

// ── 3. Usage — narrows without if-branch ────────────────────────────────────
function processUser(raw: unknown) {
  assert(typeof raw === "object" && raw !== null, "expected object");
  // raw: object (narrowed)

  const user = raw as { id?: string; name?: string };
  assertDefined(user.id, "user.id");
  // user.id: string (non-nullable narrowed)

  return user.id.toUpperCase(); // ✅ no optional-chain needed
}

// ── 4. Combine with discriminated union narrowing ────────────────────────────
type ApiResponse<T> = { ok: true; data: T } | { ok: false; error: string };
function assertOk<T>(res: ApiResponse<T>): asserts res is { ok: true; data: T } {
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`API error: ${res.error}`);
}

declare function fetchUser(): ApiResponse<{ name: string }>;
const result = fetchUser();
assertOk(result);
result.data.name; // ✅ narrowed — .data is always present after assertOk
```

**Tradeoff:** Assertion functions must be declared with a proper `asserts` return type — a function that throws but lacks the annotation does not narrow. Assertion functions that call into `Promise`-returning async code should be `async` and return `Promise<void>` with the asserts annotation only in the synchronous overload, since async assertions do not narrow in the current scope before the `await`. [official]

### Pattern 75 — `import type` Enforcement via `verbatimModuleSyntax` for ESM-Compatible Codebases [official]

Enable `"verbatimModuleSyntax": true` to force all imports that are only used as types to be written with `import type`, preventing TypeScript from silently eliding the import and breaking bundlers that rely on ESM static analysis for tree-shaking.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json: { "verbatimModuleSyntax": true }

// ── Without verbatimModuleSyntax: TypeScript silently elides type-only imports ─
import { User } from "./user";  // ← if User is only used as a type,
                                //   TS elides this at emit → bundlers see nothing

// ── With verbatimModuleSyntax: must be explicit ──────────────────────────────
import type { User } from "./user";          // ✅ type-only, always elided
import { createUser, type UserInput } from "./user"; // ✅ mixed: one value, one type

// ── Inline type imports within a value import ────────────────────────────────
import { connect, type ConnectionOptions } from "./db";
//                ^^^^
// ConnectionOptions is type-only; connect is a value — TS emits only: import { connect }

// ── Re-exports also require type keyword ─────────────────────────────────────
export type { User };                        // ✅
// export { User };                          // ❌ error under verbatimModuleSyntax if User is type-only

// ── Side-effect imports are unaffected ──────────────────────────────────────
import "./polyfill.js";                      // ✅ always preserved

// ── Practical benefit: no surprise "import not found" in bundlers ─────────────
// esbuild/rollup/Node native ESM all handle `import type` correctly;
// the explicit annotation removes ambiguity about whether the import has side effects.
```

**Tradeoff:** `verbatimModuleSyntax` is incompatible with `"module": "commonjs"` when CJS files use `import type` (you must use `require()` for value imports in CJS). For monorepos with mixed ESM/CJS packages, use per-package tsconfigs that set `verbatimModuleSyntax` only for ESM packages. The flag also forces you to add `type` to every re-export of a type, which is noisy but semantically correct. [official]

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 49

**Gotcha 102 — `using` declarations do NOT scope disposal to the nearest block — they scope to the nearest function body or module scope, so `using` inside an `if` block disposes at the end of the enclosing function** [community]

```typescript
function example(): void {
  if (condition) {
    using file = new TempFile("work.tmp");
    // Expected: file disposed when if-block exits
    // Actual:   file disposed when example() returns ← may hold resource longer than expected
  }
  doMoreWork(); // TempFile is still open here
}

// ✅ Wrap in a nested IIFE or a helper function to scope disposal:
function example2(): void {
  if (condition) {
    ((): void => {
      using file = new TempFile("work.tmp");
      // disposed here, at inner function exit
    })();
  }
  doMoreWork(); // file is now closed
}
```

WHY: The TC39 Explicit Resource Management proposal (Stage 4) defines `using` as scoped to the nearest **enclosing function or block scope entry** — specifically the "lexical environment" which corresponds to the function body, not arbitrary `{…}` blocks. This matches how `let`/`const` scoping works at the variable-lifetime level, not at the GC level. The disposal happens in the `finally` slot of the implicit `try/using/finally` that TypeScript emits around the entire function body. Developers coming from C++ RAII or C# `using` statements expect block-scoped disposal, but JavaScript/TypeScript `using` is function-scoped. Always wrap resource-bounded logic in its own function when you need sub-function scoping.

---

**Gotcha 103 — `satisfies` does NOT prevent excess property checking at assignment — it only validates the shape declared in the constraint, so properties that are absent from the constraint type are silently allowed on the value side** [community]

```typescript
type Config = { host: string; port: number };

// ❌ Misleading: no error for extra 'debug' property
const cfg = {
  host: "localhost",
  port: 3000,
  debug: true,  // ← NOT flagged by satisfies — Config doesn't mention 'debug'
} satisfies Config;

// Why: satisfies checks that the value is ASSIGNABLE to Config, not IDENTICAL to it.
// Structural typing means {host, port, debug} is assignable to {host, port}.

// ✅ To catch extra properties, use a mapped type helper:
type Exact<T, U extends T = T> = T & Record<Exclude<keyof U, keyof T>, never>;
const cfg2 = {
  host: "localhost",
  port: 3000,
  debug: true,  // ❌ now errors: 'debug' does not exist in Exact<Config>
} satisfies Exact<Config, typeof cfg2>;
```

WHY: TypeScript's structural type system considers any superset of the required properties to be assignable. The `satisfies` operator uses the same assignability rules — it does not perform exact-shape checking. This surprises developers who expect `satisfies` to act like a strict schema validator. The excess property check that TypeScript normally performs only applies when an object literal is **directly assigned** to a typed variable or passed to a typed parameter; `satisfies` deliberately avoids this restriction to preserve literal types on the extra properties.

---

**Gotcha 104 — `--erasableSyntaxOnly` rejects `const enum` even when the enum is only used as a numeric constant — `const enum` emits inlined numbers in the consumer but still requires a TypeScript compilation pass, which the flag explicitly forbids** [community]

```typescript
// ❌ With --erasableSyntaxOnly:
const enum Direction { Up = 0, Down = 1 }
// Error: 'const enum' declarations are not allowed with '--erasableSyntaxOnly'.

// Even this seemingly harmless usage fails:
const x: Direction = Direction.Up;  // ERROR — declaration itself is illegal

// ✅ Rewrite using as const + satisfies:
const Direction = { Up: 0, Down: 1 } as const satisfies Record<string, number>;
type Direction = (typeof Direction)[keyof typeof Direction]; // 0 | 1

const x2: Direction = Direction.Up; // ✅

// ✅ Or use a plain type alias with a numeric union:
type Dir = 0 | 1;
const Dir = { Up: 0 as Dir, Down: 1 as Dir } as const;
```

WHY: `const enum` is a TypeScript-specific feature that inlines numeric values at compile time by reading the emitting project's `const enum` declarations. This requires a full TypeScript type-resolution pass — it cannot be accomplished by a simple syntax-strip tool like `@swc-node`, `tsx`, or Node.js `--experimental-strip-types`. The `--erasableSyntaxOnly` flag enforces this constraint at the declaration site. The commonly cited workaround of adding `"isolatedModules": true` is not sufficient because `isolatedModules` only warns on cross-file `const enum` usage; `--erasableSyntaxOnly` bans the declaration entirely.

---

**Gotcha 105 — TypeScript 5.8 granular return-branch checking fires on legitimate `||`-based fallback returns whose right-hand side is a wider type, causing errors in code that previously relied on `any`-widening to pass** [community]

```typescript
// ── Before TypeScript 5.8: silent ────────────────────────────────────────────
declare function maybeString(): string | undefined;
function getLabel(): string {
  return maybeString() || "default";  // ✅ TS < 5.8: fine
}

// ── TypeScript 5.8 — granular branch checking: each branch checked separately ─
// For ||, left branch = maybeString() = string | undefined, right = "default"
// TS 5.8 checks both branches individually against the declared return type string:
// • left:  string | undefined — ❌ undefined not assignable to string → ERROR
// • right: "default"          — ✅

// ✅ Fix option 1: explicit non-null assertion
function getLabel2(): string {
  return maybeString()! || "default";
}

// ✅ Fix option 2: nullish coalescing (preferred)
function getLabel3(): string {
  return maybeString() ?? "default";
}

// ✅ Fix option 3: explicit conditional
function getLabel4(): string {
  const s = maybeString();
  return s !== undefined ? s : "default";
}
```

WHY: TypeScript 5.8's granular branch check was added to catch bugs where one arm of a conditional expression returns an incompatible type that previously hid behind union widening (especially `any`). The check applies to `||`, `&&`, and `?:` expressions in return positions. Legitimate `||`-based fallbacks whose left-hand side may return `undefined` now fail because `undefined` is checked as a standalone branch. The `??` operator (nullish coalescing) is semantically correct for this pattern and should be preferred over `||` in new code regardless of TypeScript version.

---

**Gotcha 106 — `verbatimModuleSyntax` combined with `"module": "commonjs"` causes a compile error for every `import type` statement in `.ts` files because CJS module resolution requires `require()` for all imports — you cannot mix ESM import syntax with CJS output** [community]

```typescript
// tsconfig.json: { "module": "commonjs", "verbatimModuleSyntax": true }

// ❌ Error: ESM-style imports are not allowed with verbatimModuleSyntax + CJS
import type { Foo } from "./foo";  // ERROR: Cannot use import/export syntax...

// ── Root cause ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
// verbatimModuleSyntax requires that the module format of every source file
// matches the tsconfig's "module" setting. CJS files must use require().
// TypeScript 5.0 introduced this restriction intentionally.

// ✅ Fix option 1: switch to ESM output
// tsconfig.json: { "module": "nodenext" or "esnext", "verbatimModuleSyntax": true }

// ✅ Fix option 2: use .mts extension for ESM files, .cts for CJS files
// .cts files: use require() — verbatimModuleSyntax enforces this
// .mts files: use import   — verbatimModuleSyntax enforces this

// ✅ Fix option 3: drop verbatimModuleSyntax for legacy CJS packages
// tsconfig.json: { "module": "commonjs" }
// and manually audit type-only imports to add `type` keyword for clarity

// ── Monorepo pattern: per-package tsconfig ────────────────────────────────────
// packages/cjs-lib/tsconfig.json: { "module": "commonjs" }            // no verbatimModuleSyntax
// packages/esm-lib/tsconfig.json: { "module": "nodenext", "verbatimModuleSyntax": true }
```

WHY: `verbatimModuleSyntax` was designed for the ESM world where `import` and `export` syntax maps one-to-one to the emitted output. When `"module": "commonjs"` is set, TypeScript emits `require()` calls for value imports and elides type imports entirely — this is fundamentally incompatible with the "emit exactly what you wrote" contract of `verbatimModuleSyntax`. The TypeScript team explicitly documents this restriction: the flag requires that the file's syntactic module format (ESM `import`/CJS `require`) match the declared `"module"` target. The safest migration path for mixed monorepos is to set `verbatimModuleSyntax` only on the ESM-output sub-packages and leave CJS packages on standard `"module": "commonjs"` settings.

---

### Anti-Patterns: Cycle 49 Additions

| Anti-pattern | Why it's harmful | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Using `using x = resource` and expecting disposal at the nearest `{}` block boundary | `using` scopes disposal to the enclosing function body, not the nearest block — resources may be held open far longer than intended | Wrap resource-bounded logic in a dedicated function or IIFE to limit the disposal scope |
| Relying on `satisfies` to enforce exact-shape checking (no extra properties) | `satisfies` uses structural assignability — supersets of the constraint type pass silently | Use an `Exact<T, U>` helper mapped type or a Zod/Arktype schema for runtime exact validation |
| Using `const enum` in codebases targeting native TypeScript stripping or `--erasableSyntaxOnly` | `const enum` requires a full TypeScript compilation pass to inline values — it cannot be stripped without type resolution | Replace `const enum` with `as const satisfies Record<string, number>` objects and a companion type alias |
| Returning `maybeValue || "default"` from a function declared to return a non-nullable type after upgrading to TypeScript 5.8 | TypeScript 5.8 checks each branch of `||` individually — the `undefined` branch now errors | Replace `||` fallbacks with `??` (nullish coalescing), which is semantically correct and always passes the branch check |
| Enabling `verbatimModuleSyntax` in a CJS tsconfig | The flag requires syntactic module format to match output — CJS output cannot use ESM import syntax | Set `verbatimModuleSyntax: true` only on ESM-output packages; use per-package tsconfigs in monorepos |
| Writing decorator metadata to `WeakMap` keyed on the class constructor instead of using `context.metadata` | WeakMap-based metadata does not survive tree-shaking and is not accessible via the standard `Symbol.metadata` key, breaking interoperability with other decorator libraries | Store metadata in `context.metadata[MY_KEY]` so that all Stage-3-compatible frameworks can read it |

### Pattern 76 — `import defer` for Lazy Module Evaluation (TypeScript 5.9) [official]

Defers module evaluation until at least one exported binding is first accessed, enabling startup-time performance gains in large applications with optional or rarely-used subsystems.

```typescript
// ── TypeScript 5.9 with --module preserve or esnext ──────────────────────────
import defer * as heavyAnalytics from "./analytics-module.js";
import defer * as pdfRenderer from "./pdf-renderer.js";

// Neither module executes yet — no side effects run at import time
// Module code executes lazily the first time an export is accessed

export function trackEvent(name: string): void {
  // analytics-module only executes on first call to trackEvent()
  heavyAnalytics.record(name);
}

export async function exportToPdf(data: unknown): Promise<Uint8Array> {
  // pdf-renderer only executes on first call to exportToPdf()
  return pdfRenderer.render(data);
}

// ── Constraint: only namespace imports ───────────────────────────────────────
// import defer { record } from "./analytics-module.js";  // ❌ named import — ERROR
// import defer defaultExport from "./analytics-module.js"; // ❌ default import — ERROR
import defer * as mod from "./analytics-module.js";        // ✅ namespace only
```

**Tradeoff:** `import defer` is not downleveled by TypeScript — it requires runtime or bundler support (e.g., native ESM in Node.js 20+, or a bundler that implements the TC39 proposal). Useful for CLI tools and web apps with feature-flagged subsystems; a poor fit for libraries because consumers may not support the syntax. Only works with `--module preserve` or `--module esnext`.

---

### Pattern 77 — `--module node20` for Stable Node.js 20 LTS Module Semantics [official]

Pins module resolution and emit to a specific Node.js major version rather than the floating `nodenext` target, giving monorepos a reproducible module contract that does not silently change as TypeScript's model of "the latest Node" advances.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "module": "node20",
//     "target": "es2023",
//     "moduleResolution": "bundler"  // ← also available; or omit to use node20's default
//   }
// }

// ── Effect on import resolution ──────────────────────────────────────────────
// node20 = CJS + ESM dual-mode with explicit .js extensions required in ESM files

// ✅ Relative ESM import must include extension
import { helper } from "./utils.js";

// ✅ JSON import requires type assertion (as in Node 20)
import config from "./config.json" with { type: "json" };

// ── Contrast with nodenext (floating) ────────────────────────────────────────
// nodenext tracks "latest Node LTS" — may change rules when TS ships a new version
// node20 is frozen to Node 20 semantics — no silent rule changes on TS upgrade
```

**Tradeoff:** `node20` gives determinism at the cost of manual upgrades — you must bump to `node22` (when available) to adopt new Node semantics. `nodenext` is more convenient but can introduce breaking resolution changes on TypeScript version bumps. Recommended for long-lived production codebases on a fixed Node LTS; `nodenext` is fine for greenfield projects where you intend to stay on the latest toolchain.

---

### Pattern 78 — TypeScript 5.9 Opinionated `tsc --init` with Modern Defaults [official]

TypeScript 5.9 redesigned the generated `tsconfig.json` from a commented-out everything file into a minimal opinionated starter that enables strictness features by default. Treating `tsc --init` output as a living reference prevents teams from shipping with dangerously permissive settings.

```typescript
// Generated tsconfig.json from `npx tsc --init` in TypeScript 5.9
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "module": "nodenext",
//     "target": "esnext",
//     "types": [],
//     "sourceMap": true,
//     "declaration": true,
//     "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
//     "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,
//     "strict": true,
//     "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
//     "isolatedModules": true,
//     "noUncheckedSideEffectImports": true,
//     "moduleDetection": "force",
//     "skipLibCheck": true
//   }
// }

// ── What each new default prevents ───────────────────────────────────────────
// noUncheckedIndexedAccess: array[n] is T | undefined, not T
// exactOptionalPropertyTypes: { x?: string } ≠ { x: string | undefined }
// noUncheckedSideEffectImports: "import './side-effect'" is flagged if module not found
// moduleDetection: "force": every file treated as a module (never ambient script)

// ── Migration guard: add these one by one to existing projects ───────────────
function unsafeOld(arr: string[]): string {
  return arr[0]; // ❌ With noUncheckedIndexedAccess: Type 'string | undefined' not assignable to 'string'
}
function safeNew(arr: string[]): string | undefined {
  return arr[0]; // ✅
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Enabling all defaults at once on an existing codebase can generate hundreds of errors. The recommended migration strategy is to add the new strict options one at a time per sprint, using `// @ts-expect-error` as a temporary escape hatch tracked by a TODO. New projects should accept all defaults unconditionally.

---

### Pattern 79 — `TypedArray` Generic Specialization to Avoid `ArrayBuffer` Assignability Errors (TypeScript 5.7 / 5.9 `lib.d.ts`) [official]

TypeScript 5.7 made TypedArrays generic over their buffer type (`Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>` vs `Uint8Array<SharedArrayBuffer>`). TypeScript 5.9 continued this tightening: `ArrayBuffer` is no longer a supertype of all TypedArray types, requiring explicit buffer types in function signatures.

```typescript
// ── TypeScript 5.9 lib.d.ts change ───────────────────────────────────────────
// ArrayBuffer is NOT a supertype of TypedArray anymore

function processBuffer(buf: ArrayBuffer): void {
  // ...
}

const data = new Uint8Array([1, 2, 3]);

// ❌ TypeScript 5.9: Argument of type 'Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>' not assignable to 'ArrayBuffer'
// processBuffer(data);

// ✅ Option 1: access .buffer explicitly
processBuffer(data.buffer);

// ✅ Option 2: accept both in the function signature
function processBufferOrView(buf: ArrayBuffer | ArrayBufferView): void {
  const buffer = ArrayBuffer.isView(buf) ? buf.buffer : buf;
  // ...
}
processBufferOrView(data); // ✅

// ✅ Option 3: specialize the generic
function processTyped<T extends ArrayBuffer | SharedArrayBuffer>(
  data: Uint8Array<T>
): T {
  return data.buffer;
}
const result = processTyped(data); // inferred as Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>
```

**Tradeoff:** Tighter assignability catches real bugs (passing a `SharedArrayBuffer` to a function expecting a transferable `ArrayBuffer`), but breaks existing code that relied on duck-typing. The most defensive fix is to use `ArrayBufferView` union rather than `ArrayBuffer` directly in public API signatures, which future-proofs against both typed and plain buffer inputs.

---

### Pattern 80 — Mapped Type Property Filtering with `never` Key Remapping [official]

TypeScript 4.1+ supports `as` clauses in mapped types for key remapping. Remapping a key to `never` removes that property from the output type entirely — enabling compile-time structural filtering without runtime overhead.

```typescript
// ── Filter out all method properties ─────────────────────────────────────────
type DataOnly<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as T[K] extends Function ? never : K]: T[K];
};

interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  greet(): string;
  serialize(): string;
}

type UserData = DataOnly<User>;
// Result: { id: number; name: string }

// ── Filter to only required (non-optional) properties ────────────────────────
type RequiredKeys<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as {} extends Pick<T, K> ? never : K]: T[K];
};

interface Config {
  host: string;
  port: number;
  timeout?: number;
  retries?: number;
}

type RequiredConfig = RequiredKeys<Config>;
// Result: { host: string; port: number }

// ── Filter to only string-valued properties ───────────────────────────────────
type StringProps<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as T[K] extends string ? K : never]: T[K];
};

type OnlyStrings = StringProps<User>;
// Result: { name: string }
```

**Tradeoff:** `never`-key remapping is purely type-level and compiles to nothing at runtime. The main risk is over-filtering: combining multiple `never` conditions using `|` or `&` in the `as` clause can produce surprising interactions because of conditional type distributivity. Always write unit-test-style type assertions (`type Check = Expect<Equal<Result, Expected>>`) when building utility mapped types for shared libraries.

---

### Pattern 81 — `Concrete<T>` Utility: Removing Optionality with `-?` Mapped Modifier [official]

The `-?` mapped type modifier removes optionality from all properties of a type, producing a variant where every field is required. This is useful for test fixture builders, form state models, and Redux action creators where all fields must be populated.

```typescript
// ── Built-in Required<T> uses -? ──────────────────────────────────────────────
// type Required<T> = { [P in keyof T]-?: T[P] };  // stdlib definition

// ── Custom deep variant ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
type DeepRequired<T> = {
  [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] extends object ? DeepRequired<T[K]> : T[K];
};

interface NestedConfig {
  db?: {
    host?: string;
    port?: number;
  };
  cache?: {
    ttl?: number;
  };
}

type StrictConfig = DeepRequired<NestedConfig>;
// Result: { db: { host: string; port: number }; cache: { ttl: number } }

// ── Test fixture builder using -? ─────────────────────────────────────────────
type FixtureOf<T> = {
  [K in keyof T]-?: NonNullable<T[K]>;
};

function makeFixture<T>(defaults: FixtureOf<T>): FixtureOf<T> {
  return defaults;
}

interface Order {
  id?: string;
  amount?: number;
  status?: "pending" | "complete";
}

const fixture = makeFixture<Order>({
  id: "ord-001",
  amount: 99,
  status: "pending",
  // ❌ Omitting any property is a compile error — exhaustive fixtures guaranteed
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `-?` removes optionality but does NOT remove `undefined` from the value type if the property was `T | undefined` (not just `T?`). Combine with `NonNullable<T[K]>` to strip `undefined` from values as well. Be aware that `Required<T>` from the stdlib only removes the `?` modifier — you need the `NonNullable` wrapper for complete non-nullability.

---

### Pattern 82 — `Awaited<T>` for Deeply Unwrapping Nested Promise Types [official]

`Awaited<T>` (TypeScript 4.5+) recursively unwraps `Promise<Promise<string>>` to `string` — unlike the earlier `UnwrapPromise<T>` community patterns that only peeled one layer. This enables precise typing for async utility functions, especially in test infrastructure.

```typescript
// ── Awaited<T> recursive unwrapping ──────────────────────────────────────────
type T1 = Awaited<Promise<string>>;            // string
type T2 = Awaited<Promise<Promise<number>>>;   // number
type T3 = Awaited<string | Promise<boolean>>;  // string | boolean

// ── Typing the return value of async factories ────────────────────────────────
async function createUser() {
  return { id: 1, name: "Alice", roles: ["admin"] as const };
}

type User = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof createUser>>;
// { id: number; name: string; roles: readonly ["admin"] }

// ── Use in test fixtures ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
async function setupDatabase(): Promise<{ db: { query: (sql: string) => unknown[] } }> {
  return { db: { query: () => [] } };
}

type DbContext = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof setupDatabase>>;
// { db: { query: (sql: string) => unknown[] } }

// ── Generic async pipeline ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
async function pipeline<T>(
  input: T,
  ...transforms: Array<(v: Awaited<T>) => unknown>
): Promise<unknown> {
  let current: unknown = await input;
  for (const t of transforms) current = await t(current as Awaited<T>);
  return current;
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `Awaited<T>` is correct for deeply nested promises but will also unwrap `.then()`-able objects (thenables) because it follows the `PromiseLike<T>` protocol — not just native `Promise`. This is semantically correct (it matches JavaScript's `await` semantics) but can surprise teams that expect only `Promise` instances to be unwrapped. Use `T extends Promise<infer U> ? U : T` if you specifically want to handle only native `Promise` types.

---

### Pattern 83 — `infer` with `extends` Constraint for Type-Safe Extraction [official]

TypeScript 4.7 introduced `infer X extends Constraint` inside conditional types. This eliminates the need for a separate `Extract` or `Exclude` step after the `infer`, and prevents the inferred variable from widening to a base type.

```typescript
// ── Without extends constraint (old pattern) ──────────────────────────────────
type GetStringUnion_Old<T> =
  T extends Array<infer U> ? (U extends string ? U : never) : never;

// ── With extends constraint (TS 4.7+) ────────────────────────────────────────
type GetStringUnion<T> =
  T extends Array<infer U extends string> ? U : never;

type Result = GetStringUnion<["a" | "b" | "c" | 1 | 2]>;
// Old: "a" | "b" | "c"   (two steps)
// New: "a" | "b" | "c"   (one step, cleaner)

// ── Extract a specific union member from a discriminated union ─────────────────
type FindByKind<T, K extends string> =
  T extends { kind: infer U extends K } ? T : never;

type Shape =
  | { kind: "circle"; radius: number }
  | { kind: "rect"; w: number; h: number }
  | { kind: "triangle"; base: number; height: number };

type Circles = FindByKind<Shape, "circle">;
// { kind: "circle"; radius: number }

// ── Infer number subtype ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
type PositivePort<T> = T extends `${infer N extends number}` ? N : never;
type Port = PositivePort<"8080">;  // 8080 (literal number, not string)
```

**Tradeoff:** `infer X extends Constraint` is strictly more expressive than the two-step pattern but can produce counter-intuitive results when the constraint is a wide type like `string` or `number` — the constraint acts as both a filter and a bound. When the inferred type does not satisfy the constraint, the entire conditional evaluates to `never` (not the fallback branch), which differs from an `Extract` wrapping the full type parameter. Test with at least one "should produce never" case to verify constraint behavior.

---

### Pattern 84 — Variance Annotations (`in` / `out`) for Faster Checking and Self-Documenting Generics [official]

TypeScript 4.7 added explicit variance annotations. Marking a type parameter as `out` (covariant) or `in` (contravariant) both documents the intended use and allows the compiler to skip expensive structural compatibility checks for large parameterized types.

```typescript
// ── Covariant: T only appears in output/producer position ─────────────────────
type Producer<out T> = {
  readonly value: T;
  create(): T;
};

// ── Contravariant: T only appears in input/consumer position ──────────────────
type Consumer<in T> = {
  consume(value: T): void;
};

// ── Invariant (default): T appears in both positions ─────────────────────────
type ReadWrite<in out T> = {
  get(): T;
  set(value: T): void;
};

// ── Assignability implications ────────────────────────────────────────────────
declare const stringProducer: Producer<string>;
declare let anyProducer: Producer<unknown>;

// ✅ Covariant: Producer<string> assignable to Producer<unknown>
anyProducer = stringProducer;

declare const anyConsumer: Consumer<unknown>;
declare let stringConsumer: Consumer<string>;

// ✅ Contravariant: Consumer<unknown> assignable to Consumer<string>
stringConsumer = anyConsumer;

// ── Performance benefit: large union/intersection types ───────────────────────
// Without annotations, TS walks the entire structure to check assignability.
// With out/in annotations, TS uses declared variance and skips structural walk.
```

**Tradeoff:** Variance annotations are optional, not enforced. If you annotate a type `out T` but accidentally add a consumer method, TypeScript will emit a variance annotation mismatch error — which is the intended behavior. The main risk is incorrectly annotating a mutable generic as `out`, leading to unsound assignments that previously would have been caught by structural checking. Only add variance annotations to types you own; never annotate imported types.

---

### Pattern 85 — `const` Type Parameters for Inferred Literal Tuples (TypeScript 5.0) [official]

The `const` modifier on a generic type parameter tells TypeScript to infer the narrowest possible type — the same inference that `as const` produces on a value — without requiring the caller to write `as const` at the call site.

```typescript
// ── Without const type parameter ─────────────────────────────────────────────
function makeRoute<T extends string[]>(paths: T): T {
  return paths;
}
const r1 = makeRoute(["/home", "/about"]); // string[]  ← widened

// ── With const type parameter (TS 5.0) ───────────────────────────────────────
function makeRouteConst<const T extends string[]>(paths: T): T {
  return paths;
}
const r2 = makeRouteConst(["/home", "/about"]); // ["/home", "/about"]  ← literal tuple

// ── Practical use: type-safe event emitter ────────────────────────────────────
function createEmitter<const Events extends string[]>(events: Events) {
  type EventName = Events[number];
  const listeners = new Map<EventName, Set<() => void>>();
  return {
    on(event: EventName, fn: () => void) {
      (listeners.get(event) ?? listeners.set(event, new Set()).get(event)!).add(fn);
    },
    emit(event: EventName) {
      listeners.get(event)?.forEach(fn => fn());
    },
  };
}

const emitter = createEmitter(["click", "hover", "focus"]);
emitter.on("click", () => console.log("clicked")); // ✅
// emitter.on("keydown", () => {}); // ❌ "keydown" not in "click" | "hover" | "focus"
```

**Tradeoff:** `const` type parameters only narrow at the call site — they do not propagate constness through assignment. If the caller stores the argument in a `let` variable before passing it, the inferred type widens back to the non-`const` form. The pattern works best with inline literal arguments (arrays, objects, strings). Unlike `as const`, `const T` does not make the inferred type `readonly`; you must add `readonly` to the constraint if immutability is required.

---

### Pattern 86 — `NoInfer<T>` to Block Type Argument Inference from a Specific Site [official]

`NoInfer<T>` (TypeScript 5.4) prevents a specific argument from participating in generic type inference while still participating in checking. This solves the classic "default value inference anchor" problem where a fallback argument widens the inferred type unexpectedly.

```typescript
// ── Problem without NoInfer ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
function createStore<T>(initial: T, fallback: T): T {
  return initial ?? fallback;
}
// ❌ TypeScript infers T = string | number from both arguments
const bad = createStore("hello", 42); // T = string | number — too wide

// ── Solution with NoInfer (TS 5.4) ────────────────────────────────────────────
function createStoreSafe<T>(initial: T, fallback: NoInfer<T>): T {
  return initial ?? fallback;
}
// ✅ T is inferred from `initial` only; `fallback` is checked against the inferred T
// const good = createStoreSafe("hello", 42); // ❌ Error: 42 not assignable to string
const good = createStoreSafe("hello", "world"); // ✅ T = string

// ── Real-world: typed config getter with typed default ────────────────────────
function getConfig<T>(key: string, fallback: NoInfer<T>): T {
  const value = process.env[key];
  if (value === undefined) return fallback;
  return JSON.parse(value) as T;
}

const port = getConfig<number>("PORT", 3000);        // ✅ fallback checked as number
const host = getConfig<string>("HOST", "localhost"); // ✅ fallback checked as string
```

**Tradeoff:** `NoInfer<T>` does not prevent the site from providing a type that widens `T` — it only prevents the site from contributing to the inference of `T`. If `T` is already inferred (or explicitly supplied) as a wide type, `NoInfer<T>` does not narrow it further. The idiom is most useful for "one inference anchor, one checking site" patterns (default values, fallbacks, comparable comparators).

---

### Pattern 87 — Template Literal Type Key Remapping for Getter/Setter Interfaces [official]

Combining `as` clause key remapping with template literal types in a mapped type generates an entire accessor interface from a plain data type — without code generation.

```typescript
// ── Generate getter interface ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
type Getters<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K];
};

// ── Generate setter interface ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
type Setters<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as `set${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: (value: T[K]) => void;
};

// ── Combine into a fluent builder ────────────────────────────────────────────
type Builder<T> = T & Getters<T> & Setters<T> & { build(): T };

interface UserData {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
}

declare function createBuilder<T>(defaults: Partial<T>): Builder<T>;

const user = createBuilder<UserData>({ id: 1 })
  .setName("Alice")
  .setEmail("alice@example.com")
  .build();

// ── Derived event listener map ────────────────────────────────────────────────
type OnEvents<T extends string> = {
  [K in T as `on${Capitalize<K>}`]: (event: K) => void;
};

type Handlers = OnEvents<"click" | "hover" | "focus">;
// { onClick: (event: "click") => void; onHover: ...; onFocus: ... }
```

**Tradeoff:** Template literal key remapping is entirely type-level, so no runtime code is generated. The tradeoff is IDE performance: types with large unions or deep mapped layers (>50 members) can noticeably slow down language server hover responses. Use `type` aliases with caching (a named intermediate type rather than an inline expression) to mitigate hover latency. Also note that `Capitalize<string & K>` is required rather than just `Capitalize<K>` because `keyof T` may contain `symbol` or `number` keys, and template literals only accept `string`.

---

### Pattern 88 — `satisfies` Operator for Config Objects with Per-Key Type Narrowing [official]

The `satisfies` operator (TypeScript 4.9) checks that a value matches a type without widening the inferred type to the constraint. This gives you the narrower literal/tuple/discriminated-union inference of an unannotated value plus the compile-time safety of a type annotation.

```typescript
// ── Without satisfies — annotation widens ─────────────────────────────────────
const config1: Record<string, string | string[]> = {
  host: "localhost",
  ports: ["3000", "3001"],
};
// config1.host is string | string[] — toUpperCase() not directly available

// ── With satisfies — constraint checked, narrow type preserved ─────────────────
const config2 = {
  host: "localhost",
  ports: ["3000", "3001"],
} satisfies Record<string, string | string[]>;
// config2.host is string — toUpperCase() works ✅
// config2.ports is string[] — map/filter work ✅

// ── Exhaustive colour palette ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
const palette = {
  red:   [255, 0,   0  ],
  green: [0,   255, 0  ],
  blue:  [0,   0,   255],
} satisfies Record<string, [number, number, number]>;

// Narrowed: palette.red is [255, 0, 0], not number[]
palette.red[0].toFixed(2); // ✅

// ── Combine with as const for full literal inference ─────────────────────────
const routes = ["/", "/about", "/contact"] satisfies string[];
// routes[0] is string (not "/" — satisfies alone doesn't make it readonly const)

const routesConst = ["/", "/about", "/contact"] as const satisfies string[];
// routesConst[0] is "/" ✅ — as const + satisfies gives narrowest type + constraint check
```

**Tradeoff:** `satisfies` does not prevent excess properties from being present on the value — it only validates that the value is assignable to the constraint type. Also, `satisfies` without `as const` does not produce literal/tuple types for array elements; you need `as const satisfies T` for full narrowing. In union constraints, `satisfies` uses structural assignability — a value that is a superset of one union member passes even if it is not a superset of all members.

---

### Pattern 89 — Opaque (Branded) Types via Intersection for Domain Primitive Safety [community]

Branded types prevent accidental interchange of structurally identical primitive types (e.g., `UserId` and `OrderId` are both `string` but should not be assignable to each other) without any runtime overhead.

```typescript
// ── Brand infrastructure ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
declare const __brand: unique symbol;
type Brand<T, B> = T & { readonly [__brand]: B };

// ── Domain primitives ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
type UserId  = Brand<string, "UserId">;
type OrderId = Brand<string, "OrderId">;
type Dollars = Brand<number, "Dollars">;

// ── Smart constructors (runtime validation + type narrowing) ──────────────────
function toUserId(raw: string): UserId {
  if (!raw.startsWith("usr_")) throw new Error(`Invalid UserId: ${raw}`);
  return raw as UserId;
}

function toDollars(amount: number): Dollars {
  if (amount < 0) throw new Error("Amount cannot be negative");
  return amount as Dollars;
}

// ── Type-safe API ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
function getOrder(userId: UserId, orderId: OrderId): void {
  console.log(`User ${userId} order ${orderId}`);
}

const uid = toUserId("usr_123");
const oid = "ord_456" as OrderId; // ← skip validation in tests only

getOrder(uid, oid); // ✅
// getOrder(oid, uid); // ❌ Argument of type 'OrderId' not assignable to 'UserId'

// ── Serialization/deserialization ─────────────────────────────────────────────
type Serialized<T extends Brand<string, string>> = string; // lose brand at boundary
function serialize(id: UserId): string { return id; }
function deserialize(raw: string): UserId { return toUserId(raw); }
```

**Tradeoff:** The `unique symbol` brand trick is entirely erased at runtime — brands add zero bytes to the compiled output. The cost is that smart constructors require a cast (`as UserId`) internally, which bypasses the brand check inside the constructor itself. Teams should avoid branching on branded values at runtime (the brand property does not exist); use them only as compile-time markers. JSON serialization/deserialization always loses brands — always re-validate through smart constructors at API boundaries.

---

### Pattern 90 — `Extract<T, U>` and `Exclude<T, U>` for Discriminated Union Slicing [official]

`Extract` and `Exclude` are the primary tools for carving discriminated unions into sub-unions at the type level — essential for reducing handler types and narrowing action unions in state machine patterns.

```typescript
// ── Union slicing ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
type Action =
  | { type: "fetch/pending" }
  | { type: "fetch/fulfilled"; data: unknown[] }
  | { type: "fetch/rejected"; error: Error }
  | { type: "reset" };

type AsyncActions = Extract<Action, { type: `fetch/${string}` }>;
// | { type: "fetch/pending" }
// | { type: "fetch/fulfilled"; data: unknown[] }
// | { type: "fetch/rejected"; error: Error }

type SyncActions = Exclude<Action, { type: `fetch/${string}` }>;
// | { type: "reset" }

// ── Type-safe reducer handler ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
type Handler<A extends { type: string }> = {
  [K in A["type"]]: (action: Extract<A, { type: K }>) => void;
};

const asyncHandler: Handler<AsyncActions> = {
  "fetch/pending":   (_a) => console.log("loading"),
  "fetch/fulfilled": (a) => console.log(a.data),   // ✅ data is available
  "fetch/rejected":  (a) => console.log(a.error),  // ✅ error is available
};

// ── Extracting from primitive unions ─────────────────────────────────────────
type Status = "active" | "inactive" | "pending" | "archived";
type LiveStatus = Extract<Status, "active" | "pending">;   // "active" | "pending"
type DeadStatus = Exclude<Status, "active" | "pending">;   // "inactive" | "archived"
```

**Tradeoff:** `Extract<T, U>` uses assignability (not equality) for matching — `Extract<string | number, string>` gives `string`, not the string literals. When filtering discriminated unions, use a shared property type (like `{ type: "specific" }`) rather than a primitive to ensure exact member extraction. Combining `Extract` with template literal types (`Extract<Action, { type: \`fetch/\${string}\` }>`) is powerful but slow with large unions — benchmark the language server if the union exceeds ~50 members.

---

### Community Gotchas

---

**Gotcha 107 — `import defer` only works with namespace imports — attempting to use named or default imports with `defer` is a syntax error in TypeScript 5.9, even though the TC39 proposal discusses named import support as a future extension** [community]

```typescript
// ── What the TC39 defer proposal currently allows ─────────────────────────────
import defer * as mod from "./module.js";   // ✅ namespace import only

// ❌ Named import — TypeScript 5.9 syntax error:
// import defer { foo, bar } from "./module.js";

// ❌ Default import — TypeScript 5.9 syntax error:
// import defer defaultExport from "./module.js";

// ── Workaround: destructure after access ──────────────────────────────────────
import defer * as mod2 from "./module.js";

// Access is deferred until this line:
const { foo, bar } = mod2; // ← destructuring triggers evaluation
```

WHY: The TC39 proposal for deferred module evaluation (Stage 3 as of 2025) intentionally restricts `defer` to namespace imports in its initial version. Named and default imports create a binding at parse time and are harder to defer lazily because the module must be evaluated to know whether the named export exists. TypeScript 5.9 implements the current proposal surface, not a future extension. Teams expecting named `defer` imports from a prototype or blog post will encounter a hard TypeScript syntax error with no auto-fix.

---

**Gotcha 108 — `const` type parameter inference widens back to non-literal types when the call-site argument is stored in a `let` variable before being passed — the `const` modifier only narrows at the point of the literal expression** [community]

```typescript
function narrow<const T extends string[]>(values: T): T {
  return values;
}

// ✅ Inline literal: narrows to tuple
const r1 = narrow(["a", "b", "c"]);  // type: ["a", "b", "c"]

// ❌ Variable: widens to string[]
let items = ["a", "b", "c"];
const r2 = narrow(items);            // type: string[] — not ["a", "b", "c"]

// ✅ Workaround: use as const at the variable declaration
const itemsConst = ["a", "b", "c"] as const;
const r3 = narrow([...itemsConst]);  // type: ["a", "b", "c"]
```

WHY: TypeScript's inference algorithm decides whether to narrow to literal types at the point where the type is first assigned to a binding. A `let` variable always receives a widened type (because `let` variables can be reassigned). The `const` generic parameter modifier only affects the inference from the argument expression at the call site — it cannot retroactively narrow a value that was already widened when it was stored in a `let` variable. The fix is to use `const` declarations and `as const` for the source array before passing it to the generic function.

---

**Gotcha 109 — `NoInfer<T>` does not prevent an explicitly supplied type argument from being wider than what would be inferred from the inference-participating sites — it only blocks a specific site from contributing to inference** [community]

```typescript
function pick<T>(obj: T, key: NoInfer<keyof T>): T[keyof T] {
  return obj[key];
}

const user = { id: 1, name: "Alice" };

// ✅ T inferred from obj only; key checked against inferred T
const name = pick(user, "name"); // ✅ "name" is keyof { id: number; name: string }
// pick(user, "missing");         // ❌ "missing" not in keyof user — good error

// ⚠️ Explicit T argument bypasses the NoInfer benefit:
const wide = pick<Record<string, unknown>>(user, "anything"); // ✅ No error — T was widened explicitly
```

WHY: `NoInfer<T>` only modifies the inference phase — it does not add a constraint that survives into the checking phase when `T` is explicitly provided. When the caller explicitly supplies a wide type argument, the `NoInfer<T>` site is checked against the wide `T`, so any value passes. The pattern is most reliable when callers always let `T` be inferred (i.e., when no explicit type argument is passed). If your API can accept explicit type arguments, document that `NoInfer` defaults are advisory, not enforced.

---

**Gotcha 110 — Variance annotations (`in`/`out`) on a generic type cause a hard compile error when the actual usage in the type body is inconsistent with the annotation — TypeScript checks structural variance against the declared annotation and errors rather than silently widening** [community]

```typescript
// ✅ Correct covariant annotation
type Producer<out T> = { get(): T };

// ❌ Incorrect: T used in contravariant (input) position but annotated `out`
// type BrokenProducer<out T> = { get(): T; set(v: T): void };
// Error: Type parameter 'T' is declared as covariant but is used in a contravariant position.

// ── Implication for refactoring ───────────────────────────────────────────────
// Adding a new method to a type that uses variance annotations may flip the variance
// and immediately break other code that relied on assignability under the old variance.

// ── Safe approach: annotate last ─────────────────────────────────────────────
// Build the type first, verify usage, then add in/out annotations as documentation.
type SafeProducer<T> = { get(): T };            // step 1: build
// type SafeProducer<out T> = { get(): T };     // step 2: annotate once stable
```

WHY: TypeScript enforces variance annotations by comparing the declared annotation against the structural variance computed from the type body. This is intentional — incorrect annotations would make the type unsound. The error fires immediately when the annotation does not match the body, not lazily at assignment sites. Teams adding `in`/`out` annotations to existing types as a performance optimization must audit all methods and properties first. Even a single new method added later by a colleague can break the annotation and generate a cascade of errors at every site where assignability relied on the declared variance.

---

**Gotcha 111 — The `-?` mapped modifier (as in `Required<T>`) removes the `?` optional flag but does NOT remove `undefined` from the value type when the property was explicitly typed as `T | undefined` — you need `NonNullable` to strip `undefined` from the value** [community]

```typescript
interface Form {
  name?: string;               // type = string | undefined, flag = optional
  email: string | undefined;   // type = string | undefined, flag = required
}

type StrictForm = Required<Form>;
// { name: string; email: string | undefined }
//                       ^^^^^^^^ — undefined NOT removed from email!

// Required<T> only removes the ? flag, not undefined from value types
// name becomes string ✅ because ? was the source of undefined
// email stays string | undefined ❌ because undefined was explicit in the value type

type TrulyStrict = {
  [K in keyof Form]-?: NonNullable<Form[K]>;
};
// { name: string; email: string }  ✅ — both ? flag and undefined stripped
```

WHY: TypeScript represents optionality in two independent ways: the `?` modifier on the property key (which adds `| undefined` to the value type in most strictness configurations) and an explicit `| undefined` in the value type. The `-?` mapped modifier only removes the first form — it does not transform the value type. This is a common source of bugs when using `Required<T>` on types received from an API schema generator (like `openapi-typescript`) where properties are typed as `T | undefined` rather than as optional. Always use `NonNullable` in combination with `-?` when building fixtures or strict validators.

---

**Gotcha 112 — `satisfies` with a union constraint validates assignability to the union as a whole — not to any specific member — so a value that is a superset of one union member passes even if it has extra properties that would fail excess-property checking under a direct annotation** [community]

```typescript
type Shape =
  | { kind: "circle"; radius: number }
  | { kind: "rect"; width: number; height: number };

// ❌ Direct annotation: excess property check fires
// const s: Shape = { kind: "circle", radius: 5, width: 100 }; // Error: 'width' is excess

// ⚠️ satisfies: no error — excess property check does NOT apply with satisfies
const s = { kind: "circle", radius: 5, width: 100 } satisfies Shape; // ✅ no error!

// WHY: satisfies uses assignability (structural), not excess property checking.
// { kind: "circle"; radius: 5; width: 100 } is assignable to Shape because
// it is assignable to the "circle" branch (which only requires kind + radius).
// The extra `width` property is not flagged.

// ✅ Workaround: use an identity function with an annotation for exact-shape checking
function asShape<T extends Shape>(shape: T extends Shape ? T : never): T {
  return shape;
}
// const exact = asShape({ kind: "circle", radius: 5, width: 100 }); // ❌ Error
```

WHY: `satisfies` and type annotations behave differently for excess properties. A direct type annotation on an object literal triggers the "excess property check" — a special rule that errors on properties not present in the declared type. `satisfies` does not trigger this special rule; it only performs standard structural assignability. This distinction matters for discriminated unions where you want to ensure a value is exactly one member — `satisfies` cannot enforce this. Use a typed helper function or Zod/ArkType schema parsing for runtime-enforced exact-shape checking on union members.
