### Anti-Patterns: Cycle 50 Additions

| Anti-pattern | Why it's harmful | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Using `import defer { foo }` or `import defer defaultExport` expecting named/default lazy loading | Only namespace imports (`import defer * as mod`) are supported in TypeScript 5.9 — named/default forms are syntax errors | Use `import defer * as mod` and destructure after first access |
| Storing an array in a `let` variable before passing to a `const`-typed generic parameter | The `let` binding widens the array to `string[]` before the `const` modifier can narrow it | Declare the array with `const` and use `as const` to preserve literal tuple types |
| Using `Required<T>` to strip `undefined` from API-generated types that use `T \| undefined` value types | `Required<T>` removes only the `?` modifier — explicit `undefined` in value types is unaffected | Use `{ [K in keyof T]-?: NonNullable<T[K]> }` to strip both optional flag and `undefined` from values |
| Applying variance annotations (`out T`) to mutable generics or types that will grow new methods | A single new method with `T` in input position will break the annotation and cause errors at every assignability site | Build the type fully before annotating; reserve `in`/`out` for stable, well-understood interfaces |
| Using `satisfies` as a substitute for excess-property checking on discriminated union members | `satisfies` uses structural assignability, not excess-property checking — supersets of a union member pass silently | Use a typed identity helper or a Zod/ArkType schema when exact-shape validation is required |
| Explicitly providing a wide type argument to a function that uses `NoInfer<T>` for a default parameter | Explicit type arguments bypass inference — `NoInfer` sites are checked against the wide explicit `T`, making any value valid | Document that explicit type arguments defeat `NoInfer` defaults; prefer letting `T` be inferred |

### Pattern 91 — Iterator Helper Methods for Lazy Pipelines (TypeScript 5.6) [official]

TypeScript 5.6 adds type support for the TC39 Iterator Helpers proposal, giving built-in iterators `map`, `filter`, `take`, `drop`, `flatMap`, `reduce`, `toArray`, `forEach`, and `some`/`every`/`find`. Unlike array methods, iterator helpers are **lazy** — they produce values on demand without materialising an intermediate array, making them ideal for large or infinite sequences.

```typescript
// Infinite generator — never call .toArray() without .take() first
function* positiveIntegers(): Generator<number> {
  let i = 1;
  while (true) yield i++;
}

// Lazy pipeline: no intermediate array allocated
const firstFiveSquaresOfEvens = positiveIntegers()
  .filter(n => n % 2 === 0)   // IteratorObject<number>
  .map(n => n * n)             // IteratorObject<number>
  .take(5)                     // IteratorObject<number>
  .toArray();                  // [4, 16, 36, 64, 100]

// Inverting a Map with iterator helpers — no intermediate spread
function invertMap<K, V>(map: Map<K, V>): Map<V, K> {
  return new Map(map.entries().map(([k, v]) => [v, k] as const));
}

// Iterator.from() adapts any iterable into an IteratorObject
const words = Iterator.from(["hello", "world", "foo"])
  .filter(w => w.length > 3)
  .map(w => w.toUpperCase());
console.log([...words]); // ["HELLO", "WORLD"]
```

**Tradeoff:** Iterator helpers require `"lib": ["ES2025"]` (or later) in `tsconfig.json`. Polyfilling via `core-js` or the `iterator-helpers-polyfill` package is necessary for runtimes below Node.js 22. Calling `.toArray()` on an unbounded iterator without `.take()` will hang — add a lint rule or helper that wraps infinite generators.

### Pattern 92 — `--noUncheckedSideEffectImports` to Catch Typos in Side-Effect-Only Imports [official]

TypeScript 5.6 introduced `--noUncheckedSideEffectImports`, which causes `import "missing-module"` to produce a type error when the module cannot be resolved. Without this flag, bare side-effect imports silently succeed even when the module path is wrong — a common source of missing polyfills or style sheets.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json
// { "compilerOptions": { "noUncheckedSideEffectImports": true } }

// ❌ Error: Cannot find module 'reflect-metadta' — typo!
import "reflect-metadta";

// ✅ Correct spelling
import "reflect-metadata";

// ✅ Ambient module declaration silences the error for intentional patterns
// global.d.ts:
declare module "*.css" {}
declare module "*.svg" {}

// Now this is valid:
import "./Button.css";
import logo from "./logo.svg";

// ✅ Dynamic side-effect import — same resolution rules apply
await import("./setup-global-mocks.js"); // errors if file does not exist
```

**Tradeoff:** Enabling this option in a brownfield project that uses CSS/asset imports requires adding ambient `declare module "*.css"` declarations first. The flag is off by default to avoid breaking existing codebases. Recommended to enable alongside `moduleResolution: bundler` or `node16/nodenext` for the most complete import safety picture.

---

### Pattern 93 — Disallowed Always-Truthy / Always-Nullish Checks (TypeScript 5.6) [official]

TypeScript 5.6 reports errors on conditions that can never change — specifically regex literals used as conditions (always truthy), arrow functions used as conditions (always truthy), and `??` applied to a left-hand side that can never be `null | undefined` (nullish check is unreachable). These represent almost-always accidental bugs.

```typescript
// ❌ Regex literal is always truthy — should call .test(value)
if (/^\d+$/) {
  console.log("This always runs");
}
// ✅ Correct:
if (/^\d+$/.test(input)) { ... }

// ❌ Arrow function is always truthy — missing invocation ()
const isValid = (x: number) => x > 0;
if (isValid) {          // Error: This condition will always be true
  applyTransform();
}
// ✅ Correct:
if (isValid(value)) { ... }

// ❌ Left side of ?? is a number literal — never nullish
const timeout = options.timeout ?? 5000;  // fine
const bad = 500 ?? options.timeout;       // Error: left side is never nullish

// ✅ Exception: while(true) and while(false) are idiomatic and still allowed
while (true) { processQueue(); }
```

**Tradeoff:** The check fires on expressions, not variables — `const alwaysTrue = true; if (alwaysTrue)` still compiles. Teams with deliberate "always-truthy" sentinel patterns (e.g., feature flags typed as `true`) should replace them with explicit `boolean` types or conditional compilation constants to avoid surprising future maintainers.

### Pattern 94 — `--noCheck` Flag for Emit-Only Builds (TypeScript 5.6) [official]

`--noCheck` skips all type-checking while still emitting JavaScript and declaration files. Combined with `--isolatedDeclarations`, this enables a CI pipeline where type-checking and code emission run in parallel, significantly reducing build latency for large monorepos.

```typescript
// Package.json scripts for parallel CI:
// "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit",
// "build": "tsc --noCheck",
// Run both in parallel: "ci": "npm run typecheck & npm run build"

// tsconfig.json for build-only emit
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "isolatedDeclarations": true,   // required for parallel .d.ts gen
    "declaration": true,
    "emitDeclarationOnly": false,
    "noCheck": true                 // skip type-checking in this invocation
  }
}

// With a bundler integration (esbuild/swc emit, tsc type-checks):
// esbuild src/index.ts --bundle --outdir=dist  &
// tsc --noEmit --watch                          &
// Both run concurrently — tsc errors do not block bundler output

// transpileDeclaration API (programmatic usage):
import { transpileDeclaration } from "typescript";
const result = transpileDeclaration(
  "export const version: string = '1.0.0';",
  { compilerOptions: { declaration: true } }
);
console.log(result.outputText); // "export declare const version: string;"
```

**Tradeoff:** `--noCheck` output may be unsound — you can emit broken JS if there are type errors. Always pair it with a separate `--noEmit` type-check step. Do not use `--noCheck` as the only compilation step in a release pipeline.

---

### Pattern 95 — `${configDir}` Template Variable for Portable `tsconfig.json` Paths (TypeScript 5.5) [official]

TypeScript 5.5 introduced `${configDir}` as a special template variable usable inside `tsconfig.json` path fields. It always resolves to the directory containing the current config file, even when that config is extended by another file in a parent directory. This eliminates path fragility in shared base configurations used across a monorepo.

```typescript
// packages/shared/tsconfig.base.json — base config lives here
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "typeRoots": [
      "${configDir}/node_modules/@types",   // resolves to packages/shared/node_modules/@types
      "${configDir}/types"                  // resolves to packages/shared/types
    ],
    "outDir": "${configDir}/dist",
    "rootDir": "${configDir}/src"
  }
}

// packages/api/tsconfig.json — extends base from a different directory
{
  "extends": "../shared/tsconfig.base.json",
  // ${configDir} in the base now resolves to packages/api/, NOT packages/shared/
  // So outDir becomes packages/api/dist  ✅
  // Without ${configDir}: outDir would have been relative to packages/shared/ ❌
  "include": ["src/**/*"]
}

// Root tsconfig.json — extends the same base at yet another level
{
  "extends": "./packages/shared/tsconfig.base.json",
  // ${configDir} resolves to the repo root ✅
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `${configDir}` is only supported in TypeScript 5.5+. Mixed monorepos where some packages use older TypeScript versions will see an "Unknown option '${configDir}'" error. Audit all packages' `typescript` dependency versions before adopting this pattern in a shared base config.

---

### Pattern 96 — Regular Expression Syntax Checking at Compile Time (TypeScript 5.5) [official]

TypeScript 5.5 validates regex literals for syntactic correctness and basic semantic issues — mismatched groups, illegal backreferences, and features that require a higher ECMAScript target than the project configures. Invalid regexes are caught at compile time rather than at runtime.

```typescript
// ❌ Unmatched closing paren — syntax error caught at compile time
const bad1 = /@robot(\s+(please|immediately)))? do task/;
//                                           ^^ extra )

// ❌ Backreference \3 but only 2 groups defined
const bad2 = /^(\w+)\s(\w+)\s\3$/;
//                               ^^ group 3 does not exist

// ❌ Named group reference requires ES2018 target; project targets ES2016
const bad3 = /^(?<year>\d{4})-(?<month>\d{2})$/u;
// Error: Named capturing groups require ES2018 target or later

// ✅ Correct: named groups with matching target
// tsconfig: { "target": "ES2018" }
const dateRegex = /^(?<year>\d{4})-(?<month>\d{2})-(?<day>\d{2})$/u;
const match = dateRegex.exec("2026-05-14");
if (match?.groups) {
  const { year, month, day } = match.groups;
  // year, month, day are all string | undefined — TypeScript knows the group names
}

// ✅ Backreference to existing group
const quotedString = /^(['"])(.*)\1$/; // \1 refers to group 1 ✅
```

**Tradeoff:** TypeScript checks syntax and backreferences but does not validate regex semantics at runtime (catastrophic backtracking, exponential patterns). Use a separate tool like `safe-regex` or `vuln-regex-detector` for ReDoS analysis. The compile-time check adds a small overhead to type-checking but zero overhead at runtime.

### Pattern 97 — `isolatedDeclarations` for Parallel Declaration Emit (TypeScript 5.5) [official]

`--isolatedDeclarations` requires all exported symbols to have explicit type annotations, enabling third-party tools (like `oxc-transform` or `swc`) to generate `.d.ts` files for each file in isolation — without needing full program context. This unlocks truly parallel declaration emit for large monorepos.

```typescript
// ❌ Error under --isolatedDeclarations: return type inferred, not explicit
export function computeTotal(items: CartItem[]) {
  return items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, 0);
}

// ✅ Explicit return type — isolatedDeclarations can emit .d.ts without full check
export function computeTotal(items: CartItem[]): number {
  return items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, 0);
}

// ❌ Re-export without explicit type — inference crosses file boundaries
export { someHelper } from "./utils"; // Error: must be type-annotated

// ✅ Type-only re-export is always fine
export type { SomeType } from "./utils";

// ✅ Value re-export with explicit annotation at source
// utils.ts: export function someHelper(): void { ... }  // explicit return type
export { someHelper } from "./utils"; // Now OK

// tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "isolatedDeclarations": true,
    "declaration": true
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Retrofitting an existing codebase with `--isolatedDeclarations` requires adding explicit return types to every exported function. TypeScript provides a quick-fix "Infer return type" but it must be applied file-by-file. Start with leaf packages in a monorepo (no internal dependencies) and work inward. The maintenance cost is justified only for large packages with heavy `.d.ts` generation times.

---

### Pattern 98 — New ECMAScript `Set` Methods for Set Algebra (TypeScript 5.5) [official]

TypeScript 5.5 added type definitions for the TC39 Set methods proposal: `union`, `intersection`, `difference`, `symmetricDifference`, `isSubsetOf`, `isSupersetOf`, and `isDisjointFrom`. These methods return new `Set` instances and never mutate the receiver, making them safe for immutable data flow patterns.

```typescript
// Requires "lib": ["ES2025"] or "lib": ["ESNext"]
const admins = new Set(["alice", "bob"]);
const editors = new Set(["bob", "carol", "dave"]);
const viewers = new Set(["eve", "frank"]);

// Set algebra — all methods return new Sets, no mutation
const allUsers    = admins.union(editors).union(viewers);
const adminEditors = admins.intersection(editors);   // Set { "bob" }
const onlyAdmins  = admins.difference(editors);      // Set { "alice" }
const exclusiveUsers = admins.symmetricDifference(editors); // Set { "alice", "carol", "dave" }

// Subset / superset / disjoint predicates — return boolean
const teamHasAdmin = admins.isSubsetOf(allUsers);          // true
const allEditorsAreUsers = editors.isSupersetOf(admins);   // false
const noOverlap = admins.isDisjointFrom(viewers);          // true

// Type-safe: all methods preserve the element type
function permittedRoles(
  userRoles: Set<string>,
  allowedRoles: Set<string>
): Set<string> {
  return userRoles.intersection(allowedRoles); // Set<string>
}
```

**Tradeoff:** These methods require a polyfill for Node.js < 22 and browsers without ES2025 support. Unlike lodash set utilities, the built-in methods only work with `Set<T>` — plain arrays and objects need to be wrapped first. The return type is always `Set<T>` with the same element type as the receiver, which means heterogeneous set operations require explicit casting.

---

### Pattern 99 — `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` for Source-Extension Imports (TypeScript 5.7) [official]

TypeScript 5.7 introduced `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions`, which rewrites `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.mts`, and `.cts` extensions in relative import paths to their JavaScript equivalents (`.js`, `.jsx`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`) in the emitted output. Combined with `--allowImportingTsExtensions`, this allows writing imports that exactly mirror the source file paths while producing spec-compliant ESM output.

```typescript
// Source: src/index.ts — write exact source paths
import { parseConfig } from "./config.ts";      // resolves to ./config.ts on disk
import { renderApp }   from "./ui/App.tsx";      // resolves to ./ui/App.tsx on disk
import { startServer } from "./server.mts";      // resolves to ./server.mts on disk

// Emitted: dist/index.js — extensions rewritten automatically
// import { parseConfig } from "./config.js";
// import { renderApp }   from "./ui/App.jsx";
// import { startServer } from "./server.mjs";

// tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "NodeNext",
    "allowImportingTsExtensions": true,
    "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true,
    "outDir": "./dist"
  }
}

// ⚠️  Non-relative paths (aliases, bare specifiers) are NOT rewritten
import { helper } from "@/utils";            // unchanged in output
import lodash from "lodash";                 // unchanged in output
// Only paths starting with ./ or ../ are rewritten
```

**Tradeoff:** `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` only applies to relative imports — path aliases (e.g., `@/`) still need to be handled by a bundler or path-mapping tool. The flag is mutually exclusive with `--allowImportingTsExtensions: false` and should not be combined with bundlers that already handle extension resolution, as the rewritten extensions may conflict with bundler expectations.

---

### Pattern 100 — Never-Initialized Variable Checks in Closures (TypeScript 5.7) [official]

TypeScript 5.7 extended "variable used before assigned" analysis to cover closure-captured variables. Previously, a variable that was only assigned inside a nested function or callback could escape uninitialized if the outer function returned before the assignment ran. The new check catches this entire class of bug.

```typescript
// ❌ Error (TS 5.7+): result is used before being assigned
function computeAndLog(): void {
  let result: number;

  function assign() {
    result = heavyComputation(); // assignment is in a closure
  }
  // If assign() is never called, result is uninitialised
  // TypeScript 5.7 now detects this:
  console.log(result); // Error: Variable 'result' is used before being assigned
}

// ✅ Fix 1: assign a default value
let result: number = 0;

// ✅ Fix 2: declare with definite assignment assertion (if you own the lifecycle)
let result!: number;

// ✅ Fix 3: return the value from the closure instead of capturing it
function computeAndLog(): void {
  const getResult = () => heavyComputation();
  console.log(getResult());
}

// ✅ Real-world pattern: async setup captured in outer scope
async function setup() {
  let db: Database;
  const connect = async () => { db = await Database.connect(); };
  await connect();
  return db!; // definite assignment assertion after verified lifecycle
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The new check may surface false positives in codebases that rely on "call before use" conventions where the call is guaranteed by external contracts (e.g., framework lifecycle hooks). Use `!` (definite assignment assertion) sparingly and only when the lifecycle is externally enforced. Prefer returning values rather than capturing via closure to make data flow explicit.

---

### Pattern 101 — Validated JSON Imports in `--module nodenext` (TypeScript 5.7) [official]

TypeScript 5.7 under `--module nodenext` requires import attributes (`with { type: "json" }`) when importing JSON files, matching Node.js's runtime requirement for JSON module loading. Missing attributes now cause a compile error instead of a silent runtime failure.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json
// { "compilerOptions": { "module": "NodeNext", "resolveJsonModule": true } }

// ❌ Error in TS 5.7 + nodenext: missing import attribute
import config from "./config.json";

// ✅ Correct: import attribute required
import config from "./config.json" with { type: "json" };
console.log(config.version); // string

// ✅ Dynamic import — also requires the assertion
const pkg = await import("./package.json", { with: { type: "json" } });

// ❌ Named imports from JSON are not allowed (JSON has only a default export)
import { version } from "./config.json" with { type: "json" }; // Error

// ✅ Destructure after default import
import pkgJson from "./package.json" with { type: "json" };
const { name, version } = pkgJson;

// ✅ Type-only JSON shape — use interface when you don't need the value
interface PackageJson {
  name: string;
  version: string;
  dependencies?: Record<string, string>;
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The `with { type: "json" }` syntax requires Node.js 22+ at runtime. For Node.js 18/20, use `assert { type: "json" }` (old syntax) but be aware it is deprecated. Teams targeting multiple Node.js versions should abstract JSON loading through a helper function that uses `fs.readFileSync` + `JSON.parse` to avoid the import-attribute complexity entirely.

---

### Pattern 102 — Template Literal Type Event Bus with Inferred Payload Types [official]

Template literal types combined with mapped types and index signatures create a fully type-safe event bus where both the event name and its payload type are constrained by a single source-of-truth schema type. This eliminates the need for manual overloads and keeps the event registry DRY.

```typescript
// Define the event schema once
type AppEvents = {
  userCreated:  { userId: string; email: string };
  orderPlaced:  { orderId: string; total: number };
  pageViewed:   { path: string; referrer?: string };
};

// Derive listener map from schema via template literal keys
type ListenerMap = {
  [K in keyof AppEvents as `on${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: (
    payload: AppEvents[K]
  ) => void;
};
// { onUserCreated: (p: {userId: string; email: string}) => void; ... }

// Type-safe event emitter
class TypedEmitter<Schema extends Record<string, unknown>> {
  private handlers = new Map<string, Set<(p: unknown) => void>>();

  on<K extends keyof Schema & string>(
    event: K,
    handler: (payload: Schema[K]) => void
  ): void {
    if (!this.handlers.has(event)) this.handlers.set(event, new Set());
    this.handlers.get(event)!.add(handler as (p: unknown) => void);
  }

  emit<K extends keyof Schema & string>(
    event: K,
    payload: Schema[K]
  ): void {
    this.handlers.get(event)?.forEach(h => h(payload));
  }
}

const bus = new TypedEmitter<AppEvents>();
bus.on("userCreated", ({ userId, email }) => console.log(userId, email)); // ✅ typed
bus.emit("userCreated", { userId: "u1", email: "a@b.com" });              // ✅
bus.emit("userCreated", { userId: "u1" });                                // ❌ missing email
```

**Tradeoff:** The `Capitalize` intrinsic type works only on string literals known at compile time — computed or runtime-concatenated keys will produce `string` not the specific capitalized type. For very large event schemas (100+ events), the mapped type derivation may increase check times; extract the map type into a named alias to allow TypeScript to cache the instantiation.

---

### Pattern 103 — `PropEventSource<T>` Pattern for Watched Object Callbacks [official]

The TypeScript handbook's `PropEventSource<T>` pattern uses template literal types with generic inference to create an `on(eventName, callback)` API where the callback's argument type is automatically inferred from the property name. This is the canonical illustration of type-level string manipulation unlocking strongly-typed callbacks.

```typescript
type PropEventSource<Type> = {
  on<Key extends string & keyof Type>(
    eventName: `${Key}Changed`,
    callback: (newValue: Type[Key]) => void
  ): void;
};

declare function makeWatchedObject<Type>(
  obj: Type
): Type & PropEventSource<Type>;

const person = makeWatchedObject({
  firstName: "Ada",
  lastName: "Lovelace",
  age: 1815,
});

// ✅ TypeScript infers callback argument type from property name
person.on("firstNameChanged", newName => {
  // newName: string — inferred from Type["firstName"]
  console.log(newName.toUpperCase());
});

person.on("ageChanged", newAge => {
  // newAge: number — inferred from Type["age"]
  if (newAge < 0) throw new RangeError("Age cannot be negative");
});

// ❌ Event name must end in "Changed"
person.on("firstName", () => {}); // Error: 'firstName' not assignable to '${Key}Changed'

// ❌ Typos caught at compile time
person.on("frstNameChanged", () => {}); // Error: not a valid key pattern

// Extension: use Uncapitalize to accept either casing
type FlexibleSource<T> = {
  on<K extends string & keyof T>(
    event: `${Uncapitalize<K>}Changed` | `${Capitalize<K>}Changed`,
    cb: (v: T[K]) => void
  ): void;
};
```

**Tradeoff:** The inference works only when the event name is a string literal at the call site — a variable of type `string` will not resolve `Key`. For large objects with many properties the cross-product of `${Key}Changed` union members can become very wide; use `Pick<T, SomeKeys>` to limit the watched surface if editor latency becomes noticeable.

### Pattern 104 — `--module preserve` for Bundler-Agnostic Mixed ESM/CJS Projects (TypeScript 5.4) [official]

`--module preserve` tells TypeScript to emit import/export syntax exactly as written — neither transforming ESM to CJS nor adding interop helpers. It is designed for bundler pipelines (Webpack, Vite, Rollup, esbuild) that consume TypeScript source directly and handle their own module format transformation.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json — for bundler-first projects
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "preserve",
    // Implicitly sets:
    // "moduleResolution": "bundler"
    // "esModuleInterop": true
    // "resolveJsonModule": true
  }
}

// With "module": "preserve", TypeScript leaves imports untouched
import * as fs from "node:fs";            // emitted as-is (ESM syntax)
import bar = require("./legacy-cjs");     // emitted as: const bar = require("./legacy-cjs")

// ✅ Allows mixing ESM and CJS import styles in one file (bundler resolves at build)
import { defineConfig } from "vite";      // ESM import
import { createRequire } from "module";
const require = createRequire(import.meta.url);
const pkg = require("./package.json");   // CJS require — both valid under "preserve"

// ❌ Do NOT use "module": "preserve" for direct Node.js execution without a bundler
// Node.js requires explicit .mjs/.cjs file extensions or package.json "type" field
// "preserve" does not emit file extensions
```

**Tradeoff:** `"module": "preserve"` does not apply any interop — the output is only usable by a bundler that understands both ESM and CJS syntax in the same file. If you need direct Node.js execution without a build step, use `"module": "nodenext"` instead, which enforces explicit file extensions and `package.json` `"type"` field.

### Pattern 105 — Checked Import Attributes via `ImportAttributes` Interface (TypeScript 5.4) [official]

TypeScript 5.4 introduced a global `ImportAttributes` interface that allows projects to constrain what attribute values are valid in `import ... with { ... }` statements. This enables compile-time validation of import attributes beyond just `type: "json"`.

```typescript
// global.d.ts — constrain valid import attributes for this project
interface ImportAttributes {
  type: "json" | "css" | "wasm";
}

// ✅ Valid — "json" is in the allowed union
import config from "./config.json" with { type: "json" };

// ✅ Valid — "css" allowed by the custom interface
import styles from "./Button.css" with { type: "css" };

// ❌ Error — "text" is not in the union
import readme from "./README.md" with { type: "text" };
// Error: Type '{ type: "text"; }' is not assignable to type 'ImportAttributes'

// ❌ Error — typo caught at compile time
import data from "./data.json" with { type: "jsoon" };

// Advanced: extend with optional attributes for bundler metadata
interface ImportAttributes {
  type: "json" | "css" | "wasm";
  lazy?: "true";    // optional bundler hint
}

import heavyLib from "./heavy.wasm" with { type: "wasm", lazy: "true" }; // ✅
import other from "./other.wasm" with { type: "wasm", lazy: "yes" };     // ❌
```

**Tradeoff:** The `ImportAttributes` interface is a module-augmentable global — if multiple `declare global` blocks or `.d.ts` files define conflicting `ImportAttributes` interfaces, TypeScript merges them by intersection, which may produce an `never`-typed `type` property. Keep the canonical definition in a single `global.d.ts` file and avoid re-declaring it in library code.

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 51

**Gotcha 113 — Iterator helper methods (`.map()`, `.filter()` etc.) on a generator return an `IteratorObject`, not an `Array` — passing the result to a function that expects `T[]` causes a type error even though the values are the same** [community]

```typescript
function* getIds(): Generator<number> { yield 1; yield 2; yield 3; }

const doubled = getIds().map(n => n * 2); // IteratorObject<number>, NOT number[]

// ❌ Error: IteratorObject<number> is not assignable to number[]
processIds(doubled);

// ✅ Materialise with .toArray()
processIds(doubled.toArray());

// ✅ Or spread (requires the iterator protocol, which IteratorObject satisfies)
processIds([...doubled]);

// ⚠️ Gotcha: iterator objects are single-use — iterating twice gives empty second pass
const iter = getIds().map(n => n * 2);
console.log([...iter]); // [2, 4, 6]
console.log([...iter]); // [] — exhausted!
```

WHY: `IteratorObject` implements the iterator protocol but is not an `Array`. Functions typed as `(items: T[])` require an actual array. Additionally, unlike arrays, iterator objects are stateful and can only be consumed once — spreading or calling `.toArray()` exhausts the iterator, and any subsequent iteration yields nothing. Teams migrating from lodash `_.map` (which returns arrays) to native iterator helpers must audit every downstream consumer.

---

**Gotcha 114 — `--noCheck` suppresses type errors but does NOT suppress emit errors — a file with a syntax error or an ambiguous export will still fail the build even with `--noCheck` enabled** [community]

```typescript
// broken.ts — syntax error
export function foo( {  // missing closing paren
  return "bar";
}

// Running: tsc --noCheck --outDir dist
// ❌ STILL FAILS: SyntaxError in broken.ts — noCheck does not bypass parse errors

// broken2.ts — ambiguous export (not a type error but an emit error)
export { helper };      // helper is not declared in this file
// ❌ STILL FAILS under --noCheck — module resolution error blocks emit

// ✅ --noCheck only skips:
//   • Type compatibility checks
//   • Inference errors
//   • Assignability errors
//   • Missing property errors
// --noCheck does NOT skip:
//   • Parse/syntax errors
//   • Unresolved module specifiers
//   • Circular reference detection
```

WHY: Developers adopting `--noCheck` for faster emit pipelines are sometimes surprised when the build still fails. The flag skips semantic type analysis — not the syntactic or module-resolution phases that TypeScript must complete before it can emit any output. A broken `import` statement or malformed syntax will always prevent emit regardless of `--noCheck`.

---

**Gotcha 115 — `${configDir}` in `tsconfig.json` is replaced at config parse time, not at module resolution time — it expands to the directory of the config file that contains it, NOT the directory of the root config that does the `extends`** [community]

```typescript
// packages/ui/tsconfig.json — BASE config
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "paths": {
      "@ui/*": ["${configDir}/src/*"]   // expands to packages/ui/src/*
    }
  }
}

// apps/web/tsconfig.json — EXTENDS the base
{
  "extends": "../../packages/ui/tsconfig.json"
  // ${configDir} in base resolves to packages/ui/, NOT apps/web/
  // So "@ui/*" → packages/ui/src/* — which is CORRECT for this use case
}

// ⚠️ Subtle trap: if you meant to point to the EXTENDING project's src,
// do NOT put ${configDir} in the base. Override the paths in the child config:
{
  "extends": "../../packages/ui/tsconfig.json",
  "compilerOptions": {
    "paths": {
      "@app/*": ["${configDir}/src/*"]  // correctly resolves to apps/web/src/*
    }
  }
}
```

WHY: `${configDir}` is evaluated relative to the file where the string physically appears. It was specifically designed to make base configs refer to their own files — not to produce paths relative to the extending config. This is useful for `typeRoots` and `outDir` in base configs but is the wrong tool when you want each extending project to point to its own local directories. Document the intended use in your base config to prevent teammates from adding `${configDir}` paths that should instead be in the child config.

---

**Gotcha 116 — TypeScript 5.6's "always-truthy" check fires on custom `isValid` function references used in a condition — it does NOT distinguish between accidentally checking a function reference vs. deliberately calling a predicate as a value** [community]

```typescript
// ✅ The check correctly catches accidental function-reference bugs:
const isPositive = (n: number) => n > 0;
if (isPositive) { ... }    // ❌ Error: This condition will always be true (forgot ())

// ⚠️  But it also fires on intentional functional patterns:
const validators: Array<(x: unknown) => boolean> = [isString, isNumber];
const firstValidator = validators[0];
// if (firstValidator) { ... }  // ❌ Error — even though checking "was an element found?" is valid

// ✅ Workaround for "does this slot have a function?" check:
if (firstValidator !== undefined) { ... }  // use explicit undefined check

// ⚠️  The check ALSO fires on class method references stored in variables:
class Guard {
  check = (x: unknown) => x != null;
}
const guard = new Guard();
const fn = guard.check;
if (fn) { ... }  // ❌ Error: always truthy

// ✅ Idiomatic fix — check the source, not the reference:
if (guard) { ... }           // check the object, not the method
```

WHY: The always-truthy check is a purely syntactic/structural analysis — it fires whenever a function-typed expression appears in a boolean context. TypeScript cannot determine intent: whether you are checking "is this callable?" or accidentally forgetting to call it. When an element from a `validators` array is retrieved by index, the type is `(x: unknown) => boolean`, which is always truthy. Use explicit `!== undefined` checks when you genuinely want to test for the presence of a function in a container.

---

**Gotcha 117 — `isolatedDeclarations` errors on exported generic functions that use conditional return types — even with an explicit annotation, some conditional type forms require full type-checking context to emit a valid `.d.ts`** [community]

```typescript
// ❌ Error under --isolatedDeclarations: conditional return type requires inference
export function narrowToString<T>(value: T): T extends string ? string : never {
  if (typeof value === "string") return value as any;
  throw new Error("not a string");
}
// Error: Return type annotation refers to 'T extends string ? string : never'
// but isolatedDeclarations cannot verify this without full program context

// ✅ Workaround 1: use function overloads with concrete return types
export function narrowToString(value: string): string;
export function narrowToString(value: unknown): string {
  if (typeof value === "string") return value;
  throw new Error("not a string");
}

// ✅ Workaround 2: wrap in a generic utility type that is declared separately
type NarrowResult<T> = T extends string ? string : never;
export function narrowToString<T>(value: T): NarrowResult<T> {
  if (typeof value === "string") return value as NarrowResult<T>;
  throw new Error("not a string");
}
// NarrowResult<T> is a named alias — isolatedDeclarations can reference it
// without computing the conditional type inline

// ✅ Workaround 3: cast return type to avoid the conditional entirely
export function narrowToString(value: unknown): string {
  if (typeof value !== "string") throw new Error("not a string");
  return value;
}
```

WHY: `isolatedDeclarations` requires that each file can produce its own `.d.ts` without seeing other files. Conditional return types that depend on a type parameter `T` are fine as named aliases, but inline conditional expressions in return position can reference type relationships that require program-wide type resolution. TypeScript 5.5 accepts some inline conditional forms and rejects others — the safest pattern is to extract any conditional type expression into a named alias declared before the function, which gives the `.d.ts` emitter a stable reference to write.

---

### Anti-Patterns: Cycle 51 Additions

| Anti-pattern | Why it's harmful | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Calling `.toArray()` on an `IteratorObject` and then iterating it again | Iterator objects are single-use — the second iteration yields nothing with no error | Store the result of `.toArray()` in a `const` variable; treat `IteratorObject` values as ephemeral |
| Using `--noCheck` as the only tsc step in a release pipeline | `--noCheck` skips type errors but not syntax and module-resolution errors; broken imports still fail | Always pair `--noCheck` emit with a separate `--noEmit` type-check job |
| Placing `${configDir}` paths in a base `tsconfig.json` when the intent is to resolve relative to each extending project's directory | `${configDir}` expands to the file it physically appears in — the base config's dir, not the extending config's dir | Override path-dependent options in the child `tsconfig.json` instead of the base |
| Checking a function variable in a boolean condition instead of calling it (`if (validate)`) | TypeScript 5.6 reports this as always-truthy; the intent (is a function present?) is better expressed as `!== undefined` | Use `if (validate !== undefined)` for presence checks; use `if (validate(value))` for result checks |
| Writing inline conditional return types on exported generic functions when `--isolatedDeclarations` is enabled | Some inline conditional forms cannot be emitted to `.d.ts` without full program context | Extract the conditional type into a named alias before the function declaration |
| Using bare side-effect imports without enabling `--noUncheckedSideEffectImports` | Typos in side-effect imports silently succeed — polyfills and CSS files may be silently missing | Enable `noUncheckedSideEffectImports: true` and add `declare module "*.css" {}` ambient declarations as needed |

## Cycle 52 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 106 — Granular Return-Branch Type Checking (TS 5.8)

TypeScript 5.8 special-cases conditional (ternary) expressions that appear directly inside `return` statements, checking each branch independently against the declared return type. Previously, an `any`-typed branch could "infect" the union and suppress a type error on the other branch. Now both branches must satisfy the return annotation.

```typescript
// ❌ Bug silently passed in TS 5.7 — the any from .get() hid the string return
declare const cache: Map<any, any>;

function getUrlObject(urlString: string): URL {
  return cache.has(urlString)
    ? cache.get(urlString)   // any — was accepted because any is assignable to URL
    : urlString;             // string — TS 5.8 now errors: string is not URL
}

// ✅ Correct: both branches satisfy the declared return type
function getUrlObjectFixed(urlString: string): URL {
  return cache.has(urlString)
    ? (cache.get(urlString) as URL)
    : new URL(urlString);
}

// ✅ Also correct: narrow the result before returning
function getUrlObjectNarrow(urlString: string): URL {
  const cached: unknown = cache.get(urlString);
  if (cached instanceof URL) return cached;
  return new URL(urlString);
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Existing codebases with `Map<any, any>` caches or similar loosely-typed APIs will see new errors on upgrade to TS 5.8. Use this as a forcing function to tighten cache typings to `Map<string, URL>` or use `unknown` with a runtime guard.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 107 — `--erasableSyntaxOnly` for Node.js Strip-Types Compatibility

TypeScript 5.8 introduces `--erasableSyntaxOnly`, which validates that your code uses only syntax that can be removed (erased) by a type stripper such as Node.js 23.6's `--experimental-strip-types`. Non-erasable constructs — `enum`, runtime `namespace`, parameter properties, and legacy `import =` / `export =` — cause compile errors.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json
// { "compilerOptions": { "erasableSyntaxOnly": true, "verbatimModuleSyntax": true } }

// ❌ enum — has runtime representation, cannot be erased
enum Direction { Up, Down, Left, Right }

// ✅ Alternative: const enum + satisfies or plain object
const Direction = { Up: "Up", Down: "Down", Left: "Left", Right: "Right" } as const;
type Direction = (typeof Direction)[keyof typeof Direction];

// ❌ Parameter properties — desugared by TypeScript compiler
class Point {
  constructor(public x: number, public y: number) {}
}

// ✅ Alternative: explicit field declarations
class PointSafe {
  x: number;
  y: number;
  constructor(x: number, y: number) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
}

// ❌ Namespace with runtime code
namespace Container {
  export function run() {}
}

// ✅ Alternative: plain module with named exports
export function run() {}
```

**Tradeoff:** Migrating a codebase with heavy enum or namespace usage to erasable syntax requires significant refactoring. Consider doing it incrementally: enable the flag in new code first and add a lint rule to block new non-erasable constructs.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 108 — `require()` of ESM Modules in `--module nodenext` (TS 5.8 / Node 22+)

Node.js 22 allows CommonJS files to `require()` ESM files that contain no top-level `await`. TypeScript 5.8 with `--module nodenext` now models this correctly, letting you import ESM packages from CJS entry points without dual-publishing. This eliminates the need for dynamic `import()` wrappers just to consume a pure-ESM library.

```typescript
// myLib/index.mts  (ESM, no top-level await)
export function greet(name: string): string {
  return `Hello, ${name}`;
}

// consumer/index.cts  (CommonJS)
// tsconfig: { "module": "nodenext" }
const { greet } = require("./myLib/index.mjs");
//      ^^^^^^^^ TypeScript 5.8 resolves this correctly as ESM

console.log(greet("world")); // Hello, world

// ❌ Still not allowed — ESM with top-level await
// const { greet } = require("./async-lib/index.mjs");
// → Runtime error: require() cannot be used on an ES module that uses top-level await
```

**Tradeoff:** This only works on Node.js 22+. If you support Node 18/20, guard with a runtime version check or keep the dynamic `import()` wrapper. Use `--module node18` flag to enforce the stricter (no-require-ESM) rules for Node 18 LTS targets.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 109 — `infer X extends Bound` Constrained Extraction

TypeScript 4.7 introduced the ability to add an `extends` constraint directly on an `infer` variable, eliminating nested conditional types for constrained type extraction. The inferred variable is narrowed to the bound at the point of use — no extra conditional is needed.

```typescript
// ❌ Old pattern: nested conditionals for constrained infer
type FirstStringLegacy<T> =
  T extends [infer S, ...unknown[]]
    ? S extends string ? S : never
    : never;

// ✅ New pattern: bound on the infer variable itself
type FirstString<T> =
  T extends [infer S extends string, ...unknown[]] ? S : never;

type A = FirstString<[string, number]>;    // string
type B = FirstString<["hello", number]>;   // "hello"
type C = FirstString<[boolean, number]>;   // never

// Practical: extract the numeric key from a tuple pair
type NumericKey<T> =
  T extends readonly [infer K extends number, infer _V] ? K : never;

type K1 = NumericKey<[1, "a"]>;  // 1
type K2 = NumericKey<[2, true]>; // 2

// Extract union of string keys from a record
type StringKeys<T> = keyof T extends infer K
  ? K extends string ? K : never
  : never;

interface User { id: number; name: string; email: string }
type UserStringKeys = StringKeys<User>; // "name" | "email"
```

**Tradeoff:** The bound is checked at infer time: if the inferred type does not extend the bound, the whole conditional resolves to `never`. This is usually what you want, but it can be surprising when a bound is almost-satisfied — use union bounds (`infer K extends string | number`) to capture wider cases.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 110 — Instantiation Expressions for Specializing Generics

TypeScript 4.7 added instantiation expressions: you can apply type arguments to a generic function or constructor without wrapping it in a new function. This is cleaner than arrow-wrapper patterns and preserves the original function's overload signatures.

```typescript
// ❌ Old pattern: wrapper function to specialize a generic
function makeStringSet() {
  return new Set<string>();
}

// ✅ Instantiation expression: no wrapper needed
const StringSet = Set<string>;
const s = new StringSet();  // type: Set<string>
s.add(42);                  // ❌ Error: 42 is not a string

// Works with generic functions too
function identity<T>(value: T): T { return value; }

const identityString = identity<string>;
identityString(123);  // ❌ Error: number not assignable to string
identityString("hi"); // ✅ "hi"

// Useful for factory maps
type Constructor<T> = new (...args: any[]) => T;

const factories: Record<string, Constructor<unknown>> = {
  map:  Map<string, number>,
  set:  Set<string>,
  // array: Array<string>,  // Array requires special handling
};

// Specialize API clients in a DI-style setup
declare function createClient<T>(endpoint: string): Promise<T>;
const createUserClient = createClient<User>;   // (endpoint: string) => Promise<User>
const createOrderClient = createClient<Order>; // (endpoint: string) => Promise<Order>
```

**Tradeoff:** Instantiation expressions do not work on non-generic values; TypeScript will error if the resolved type has no type parameters. They also cannot partially apply only some type arguments on a multi-parameter generic — all or none.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 111 — Variance Annotations (`in` / `out`) on Type Parameters

TypeScript 4.7 added explicit variance modifiers: `out T` marks a covariant position (T only appears as output), `in T` marks a contravariant position (T only appears as input), and `in out T` marks invariance. Explicit annotations speed up structural compatibility checks on recursive types and act as self-documenting contracts.

```typescript
// Covariant — T only in output positions (can assign Producer<Dog> to Producer<Animal>)
interface Producer<out T> {
  produce(): T;
}

// Contravariant — T only in input positions (can assign Consumer<Animal> to Consumer<Dog>)
interface Consumer<in T> {
  consume(value: T): void;
}

// Invariant — T in both positions (must be exact)
interface Channel<in out T> {
  send(value: T): void;
  receive(): T;
}

// TypeScript enforces the annotation:
interface BadProducer<out T> {
  consume(value: T): void; // ❌ Error: T used in contravariant position but declared 'out'
}

// Practical: typed event emitter with variance
interface Emitter<out TEvent> {
  on(event: string, handler: (e: TEvent) => void): void;
  // T only flows out through the handler parameter
}

declare const dogEmitter: Emitter<{ bark: string }>;
const animalEmitter: Emitter<object> = dogEmitter; // ✅ covariance allows this upcast
```

**Tradeoff:** Adding variance annotations to a public interface is a breaking change if the current structural type happens to allow variance that the annotation prohibits. Audit existing subtypes before adding `out`/`in` to an established interface.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 112 — `accessor` Auto-Accessor Keyword

TypeScript 4.9 introduced the `accessor` keyword for class members. It desugars to a private backing field plus a public `get`/`set` pair, making it the idiomatic way to declare an interceptable property — particularly useful as the target for class decorator interception patterns.

```typescript
class Temperature {
  accessor celsius: number;

  constructor(c: number) {
    this.celsius = c;
  }

  get fahrenheit() {
    return this.celsius * 9 / 5 + 32;
  }
}

// accessor desugars to:
// #__celsius: number
// get celsius() { return this.#__celsius; }
// set celsius(v) { this.#__celsius = v; }

// Decorator interception — a common use-case that drove the feature
function logged<T>(
  _target: ClassAccessorDecoratorTarget<unknown, T>,
  ctx: ClassAccessorDecoratorContext
): ClassAccessorDecoratorResult<unknown, T> {
  return {
    get(this: unknown) { return _target.get.call(this); },
    set(this: unknown, value: T) {
      console.log(`Setting ${String(ctx.name)} to`, value);
      _target.set.call(this, value);
    },
  };
}

class Config {
  @logged
  accessor threshold: number = 10;
}

const cfg = new Config();
cfg.threshold = 20; // logs: Setting threshold to 20
```

**Tradeoff:** `accessor` is a class-only feature and cannot be used on interface members or object literals. Mixing `accessor` with an explicit `get`/`set` pair of the same name is a compile error. The private backing field uses a mangled name, so direct reflection or serialization will not see it.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 113 — `satisfies` for Literal-Preserving Validation

The `satisfies` operator (TypeScript 4.9) validates that an expression conforms to a type without widening the inferred type to the annotation. This is the right tool when you want constraint-checking at the declaration site but need downstream code to see the specific literal/tuple types.

```typescript
type Color = "red" | "green" | "blue";
type RGB = [red: number, green: number, blue: number];

// ❌ Annotation approach: loses specificity
const paletteAnnotated: Record<Color, string | RGB> = {
  red: [255, 0, 0],
  green: "#00ff00",
  blue: [0, 0, 255],
};
paletteAnnotated.green.toUpperCase(); // ❌ Error: string | RGB has no toUpperCase

// ✅ satisfies: validates without widening
const palette = {
  red: [255, 0, 0],
  green: "#00ff00",
  blue: [0, 0, 255],
} satisfies Record<Color, string | RGB>;

palette.green.toUpperCase(); // ✅ green inferred as string
palette.red[0].toFixed(0);   // ✅ red inferred as [number, number, number]

// Catch typos at declaration time
const badPalette = {
  red: [255, 0, 0],
  mauve: "#800080",  // ❌ Error: 'mauve' is not in Color
} satisfies Record<Color, string | RGB>;
```

**Tradeoff:** `satisfies` does not assign a type — it only validates. If you need the wider type later (e.g., to pass to a function expecting `Record<Color, string | RGB>`), TypeScript will check compatibility at the call site anyway. When combined with `as const`, `satisfies` prevents widening while still ensuring structural validity.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 114 — `in` Operator Narrowing on `unknown` Objects (TS 4.9+)

Since TypeScript 4.9, using the `in` operator on an `object`-narrowed `unknown` value intersects the type with `Record<"propertyName", unknown>`, enabling safe property access without a cast. This supersedes the verbose `(obj as any).prop` pattern for runtime property sniffing.

```typescript
// ❌ Pre-4.9: required a cast to access an unknown property
function getName(value: unknown): string | undefined {
  if (typeof value === "object" && value !== null) {
    return (value as any).name; // unsafe cast
  }
}

// ✅ TS 4.9+: in-operator narrows to Record<"name", unknown>
function getNameSafe(value: unknown): string | undefined {
  if (typeof value === "object" && value !== null) {
    if ("name" in value) {
      // value: object & Record<"name", unknown>
      if (typeof value.name === "string") {
        return value.name; // ✅ fully narrowed to string
      }
    }
  }
}

// Practical: parsing untrusted JSON payloads
function parseApiError(payload: unknown): string {
  if (
    typeof payload === "object" &&
    payload !== null &&
    "error" in payload &&
    typeof payload.error === "string"
  ) {
    return payload.error;
  }
  return "Unknown error";
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The `in` narrowing only applies when the left-hand side is a string, number, or symbol literal, and the right-hand side has been narrowed to an object type. It does not help with array index access or dynamically computed property names — use `Object.hasOwn()` combined with a cast for those cases.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 115 — Template Literal Types for Type-Safe Event Bus

Template literal types allow you to construct string union types through interpolation and to constrain callback signatures based on the interpolated key. The canonical use-case is a watched-object or event-emitter API where each event name encodes its payload type.

```typescript
type PropEventSource<T> = {
  on<K extends string & keyof T>(
    eventName: `${K}Changed`,
    callback: (newValue: T[K]) => void
  ): void;
};

declare function makeWatchedObject<T>(obj: T): T & PropEventSource<T>;

const user = makeWatchedObject({ name: "Alice", age: 30, active: true });

// ✅ Callback type is inferred from the interpolated key
user.on("nameChanged",   (v) => v.toUpperCase()); // v: string
user.on("ageChanged",    (v) => v.toFixed(0));     // v: number
user.on("activeChanged", (v) => !v);               // v: boolean

// ❌ Typo: "name" is not a valid event name (must be "nameChanged")
user.on("name", () => {});

// ❌ Wrong payload type caught at compile time
user.on("ageChanged", (v: string) => v.toUpperCase()); // Error: string not assignable to number
```

**Tradeoff:** Template literal type unions grow combinatorially. Avoid interpolating two large unions together — the resulting type can slow the compiler and produce overwhelming error messages. For large schemas, generate the event map from a separate type alias rather than computing it inline.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 116 — Intrinsic String Manipulation Types for API Key Generation

TypeScript's built-in `Uppercase`, `Lowercase`, `Capitalize`, and `Uncapitalize` intrinsic types can be combined with template literal types to derive consistently-cased API keys, environment variable names, or CSS custom properties from a single source-of-truth type.

```typescript
type EnvKey<S extends string> = `REACT_APP_${Uppercase<S>}`;

type AppEnvKeys = EnvKey<"apiUrl" | "timeout" | "debugMode">;
// "REACT_APP_APIURL" | "REACT_APP_TIMEOUT" | "REACT_APP_DEBUGMODE"

// Build a type-safe env accessor
declare const env: Record<AppEnvKeys, string | undefined>;
const apiUrl = env["REACT_APP_APIURL"]; // string | undefined ✅

// Derive camelCase getter names from snake_case field names
type CamelGetter<S extends string> =
  S extends `${infer Head}_${infer Rest}`
    ? `get${Capitalize<Head>}${Capitalize<CamelGetter<Rest>>}`
    : `get${Capitalize<S>}`;

type G1 = CamelGetter<"user_name">;        // "getUserName"
type G2 = CamelGetter<"first_login_date">; // "getFirstLoginDate"

// CSS custom property prefix enforcer
type CSSVar<S extends string> = `--${Lowercase<S>}`;
type DesignToken = CSSVar<"PrimaryColor" | "SurfaceElevation">;
// "--primarycolor" | "--surfaceelevation"
```

**Tradeoff:** The intrinsic string utilities are not locale-aware — they use JavaScript's `toUpperCase()` / `toLowerCase()` defaults, which behave unexpectedly for certain locales (e.g., Turkish dotless-i). Do not rely on them for user-visible string transformations; use them only for compile-time key derivation.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 117 — `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` for Run-In-Place TypeScript (TS 5.7)

TypeScript 5.7's `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` option rewrites `.ts`/`.mts`/`.cts` extensions in relative import paths to their compiled JavaScript equivalents (`.js`/`.mjs`/`.cjs`) in the emitted output. This lets you write imports as `.ts` source-file references while still producing valid JS that Node.js can execute.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json: { "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true }

// ✅ Source file uses .ts extension directly
import { parseConfig } from "./config.ts";    // emitted as ./config.js
import { logger } from "../utils/logger.mts"; // emitted as ../utils/logger.mjs

// These are NOT rewritten (non-relative or already-correct):
import { z } from "zod";                      // untouched — bare specifier
import { foo } from "./foo";                  // untouched — no extension
import { bar } from "./bar.js";               // untouched — already .js

// Node.js 23+ can also run .ts files directly with --experimental-strip-types,
// making the round-trip consistent without a build step:
// node --experimental-strip-types src/index.ts
```

**Tradeoff:** This option is primarily useful for toolchain-free development (scripts, CLIs, monorepo tooling). For production builds with bundlers like esbuild or Webpack, the bundler already handles extension resolution and this flag may conflict with its expectations. Enable it in a dedicated tsconfig for scripts/tools, not in the main app tsconfig.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 118 — `NaN` Equality Guard and `Number.isNaN` Idiom

TypeScript 4.9 added a lint-style compile error when you compare a value directly against `NaN` using `===` or `!==`, since those comparisons are always `false` by IEEE 754 rules. The idiomatic replacement is `Number.isNaN()`, which TypeScript now suggests in the diagnostic message. This prevents a category of subtle numeric bugs where developers expect `x === NaN` to behave like a null check.

```typescript
declare let score: number;

// ❌ TS 4.9+ error: This condition will always return 'false'
//    since NaN !== NaN (IEEE 754)
if (score === NaN) {
  console.log("invalid score");
}

// ❌ Also always false
if (score !== NaN) {
  processScore(score); // ran even when score is NaN
}

// ✅ Correct: use Number.isNaN
if (Number.isNaN(score)) {
  console.log("invalid score");
}

// ✅ Or filter NaN out from an array with type predicate
function isValidScore(n: number): n is number {
  return !Number.isNaN(n) && Number.isFinite(n);
}

const scores = [10, NaN, 20, Infinity, 30];
const validScores = scores.filter(isValidScore); // [10, 20, 30]
```

**Tradeoff:** `Number.isNaN()` only returns `true` for the `NaN` value and does not coerce its argument, unlike the global `isNaN()` which coerces strings. Prefer `Number.isNaN()` for numeric validation in all cases. For the broader "is this a valid finite number?" check, combine it with `Number.isFinite()`.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 119 — `const` Type Parameters for Literal Inference Without `as const`

TypeScript 5.0 introduced the `const` modifier on type parameters, which instructs the type system to infer the argument as if `as const` were applied. This avoids requiring callers to append `as const` at every call site when a library wants to preserve literal types.

```typescript
// ❌ Without const modifier: infers widened types
function config<T extends object>(opts: T): T {
  return opts;
}
const c1 = config({ env: "production", port: 3000 });
// c1: { env: string; port: number } — literals widened

// ✅ With const modifier: preserves literals
function configConst<const T extends object>(opts: T): T {
  return opts;
}
const c2 = configConst({ env: "production", port: 3000 });
// c2: { env: "production"; port: 3000 } — literals preserved

// Practical: a type-safe route builder
function defineRoutes<const T extends Record<string, string>>(routes: T): T {
  return routes;
}
const routes = defineRoutes({
  home:    "/",
  about:   "/about",
  profile: "/profile/:id",
});

type RouteName = keyof typeof routes; // "home" | "about" | "profile"
type RoutePath = (typeof routes)[RouteName]; // "/" | "/about" | "/profile/:id"

// Without <const T>, RoutePath would be just string.
```

**Tradeoff:** `const` type parameters only preserve literal types when the argument is an object or array literal passed inline. If the argument is a variable with a widened type, inference still widens. Callers can still override with explicit type arguments. This feature does not work on non-generic parameters — it only controls inference on the constrained variable.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 120 — Checked Always-Truthy Function References (TS 5.6)

TypeScript 5.6 reports an error when a function-typed expression is used directly in a boolean condition without being called — this catches the common mistake of checking whether a method reference is defined instead of calling it and checking the result. The check fires on any function-typed value, including method references retrieved from arrays or maps.

```typescript
// ❌ TS 5.6 error: this condition will always be true
//    because a function reference is always truthy
const validators = [isNonEmpty, isEmail, isMaxLength(50)];
const validate = validators[0];
if (validate) {           // Error: 'validate' is a function — always truthy
  runValidation(validate);
}

// ✅ Fix 1: call the function and check the return value
if (validate(input)) {
  console.log("valid");
}

// ✅ Fix 2: check for presence explicitly when the value might be undefined
const maybeValidator: ((x: string) => boolean) | undefined = validators[0];
if (maybeValidator !== undefined) {
  runValidation(maybeValidator);
}

// ❌ Subtler: accidentally using method reference as guard
class Form {
  onSubmit?: () => void;

  submit() {
    if (this.onSubmit) {  // ✅ Fine — onSubmit is `() => void` | undefined
      this.onSubmit();
    }
  }
}

// ❌ But this fires if the type is non-nullable:
class RequiredForm {
  onSubmit: () => void = () => {};
  submit() {
    if (this.onSubmit) { // Error: always truthy — onSubmit is not optional
      this.onSubmit();
    }
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The check can produce false positives in JavaScript migration scenarios where a function slot might genuinely be overwritten with a falsy value through an untyped path. Suppress with `// @ts-expect-error` plus a comment, or widen the type to include `undefined` if the optional presence check is intentional.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 52

**Gotcha 118 — `--erasableSyntaxOnly` does not ban `const enum` usage in consuming files — only declarations; downstream `.d.ts` files using `const enum` still compile, but stripping fails at runtime** [community]

```typescript
// dependency/index.d.ts  (from an older package)
export const enum Status { Active = 0, Inactive = 1 }

// your-code.ts — with erasableSyntaxOnly: true
import { Status } from "dependency";
const s = Status.Active; // ✅ compiles — the declaration is in a .d.ts, not your source
// But at runtime under Node --experimental-strip-types, the enum value is absent
// because the .d.ts was never compiled into runtime JS by you
```

WHY: `--erasableSyntaxOnly` validates only the files in your compilation unit; it cannot see whether a dependency's `const enum` was correctly compiled into inline constants in its JS output. If a package ships only `.d.ts` with `const enum` and no matching runtime values, your strip-types build will produce `undefined` at the access site instead of the numeric constant. Always compile `const enum` dependencies or use `"isolatedModules": true` (which forbids cross-file `const enum` references) as an additional guard.

---

**Gotcha 119 — Template literal union cartesian explosion causes `Type instantiation is excessively deep` errors for even moderate-sized string unions** [community]

```typescript
// ❌ Explodes: 10 × 10 = 100 members, then used inside another literal → 1000 members
type A = "a1" | "a2" | "a3" | "a4" | "a5" | "a6" | "a7" | "a8" | "a9" | "a10";
type B = "b1" | "b2" | "b3" | "b4" | "b5" | "b6" | "b7" | "b8" | "b9" | "b10";
type AB = `${A}_${B}`; // 100 members — still ok
type ABPrefixed = `prefix_${AB}`; // 100 members — still ok
type Full = `${ABPrefixed}_suffix`; // starts slowing down with further nesting

// ✅ Use named intermediate aliases to control expansion depth
type ABAlias = `${A}_${B}`;          // computed once
type Full2   = `${ABAlias}_suffix`;  // references alias, not re-expands A × B
```

WHY: TypeScript computes template literal unions eagerly by expanding every combination at the point of use. Without intermediate aliases, deeply-nested template literal expressions force the compiler to recompute the cartesian product multiple times in the same type-check pass, leading to `Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite` errors. Breaking the computation into named aliases lets the compiler cache the intermediate result.

---

**Gotcha 120 — `satisfies` does not narrow the type inside the expression's own initializer — circular references still require explicit annotations** [community]

```typescript
// ❌ satisfies does not help when the object references itself
type TreeNode = { label: string; children: TreeNode[] };

const root = {
  label: "root",
  children: [
    { label: "child", children: [] },
  ],
} satisfies TreeNode;

// root.children[0] has type { label: string; children: never[] }
// NOT TreeNode — the inner object literal is not re-checked against TreeNode
// because satisfies only validates the outer shape, not recursively tightens
// each element of the children array to TreeNode.
const grandchild: TreeNode = root.children[0]; // ✅ compiles — structurally compatible
// But: root.children[0].children is inferred as never[] not TreeNode[]
root.children[0].children.push({ label: "x", children: [] }); // ❌ never[]
```

WHY: `satisfies` validates structural compatibility at the top level without re-annotating the inner type of each nested literal. Nested object literals pick up their most specific inferred type, which may be narrower than the constraint. For recursive data structures, annotate the variable explicitly (`const root: TreeNode = ...`) or use a helper function that enforces the recursive type: `function node(n: TreeNode): TreeNode { return n; }`.

---

**Gotcha 121 — Variance annotations break when an interface is extended without matching the same annotation — the subtype silently loses the variance guarantee** [community]

```typescript
interface Producer<out T> { produce(): T; }

// ❌ Extending without out — the subtype is now invariant
interface TransformProducer<T> extends Producer<T> {
  transform(value: T): T; // contravariant position — violates 'out'
}

// TypeScript errors here (correctly), but developers sometimes suppress it with:
// @ts-ignore — and the annotation is silently ignored in the subtype
declare const strProducer: TransformProducer<string>;
// The following assignment should fail but doesn't under ts-ignore suppression:
const objProducer: TransformProducer<object> = strProducer as any; // unsafe
```

WHY: Variance annotations are checked per-interface, not transitively enforced across an inheritance chain. When you extend a `<out T>` interface and add a method that uses `T` in a contravariant (input) position, TypeScript reports an error — but if that error is suppressed, the subtype proceeds without the `out` constraint being enforced, and the caller's code that relied on covariance to upcast may introduce type-unsafe assignments. Always redeclare the appropriate variance modifier on extending interfaces, and never suppress variance errors with `@ts-ignore`.

---

**Gotcha 122 — `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` rewrites imports inside `.d.ts` files too, which can break declaration consumers on older TypeScript versions** [community]

```typescript
// With rewriteRelativeImportExtensions: true, emitted .d.ts contains:
import { Config } from "./config.js"; // rewritten from ./config.ts

// ❌ If a consumer uses TS 4.x with "moduleResolution": "node" (classic),
//    it cannot resolve ./config.js without the actual file being present,
//    because classic resolution doesn't follow the .js → .ts remapping
//    that moduleResolution: "bundler" and "nodenext" do.
```

WHY: `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` was designed for projects where the emitted JS runs directly and the `.d.ts` files are consumed by a bundler-aware TypeScript version. When your package's `.d.ts` files reference `.js` extensions in relative imports and a downstream consumer uses `moduleResolution: "node"` (TypeScript < 4.7 classic algorithm), those `.js` references are not remapped back to `.ts` source files, causing `Cannot find module './config.js'` errors. If you publish a library, prefer writing extensionless relative imports (resolved by the module resolver) or ship both CJS and ESM outputs with separate declaration files.

---

### Anti-Patterns: Cycle 52 Additions

| Anti-pattern | Why it's harmful | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Using `enum` with `--erasableSyntaxOnly` enabled | Enums have runtime representation and cannot be stripped by Node.js `--experimental-strip-types` | Replace with `const` object + `typeof` union: `const E = { A: "A" } as const; type E = (typeof E)[keyof typeof E]` |
| Checking `if (fn)` where `fn` has a non-nullable function type | TS 5.6 reports this as always-truthy; intent is unclear | Use `if (fn !== undefined)` for optional presence, `if (fn(arg))` for result |
| Relying on `satisfies` to recursively narrow nested object literals | `satisfies` only validates structural compatibility at the top level; inner literals retain their inferred (possibly narrower) types | Annotate recursive types explicitly or use a typed constructor helper |
| Applying variance annotation `<out T>` to a base interface and then extending it with a method using `T` in an input position without re-declaring variance | The annotation is not transitively enforced; a suppressed error leaves the subtype covariant unsafely | Declare the correct variance modifier on every interface in the hierarchy |
| Passing a `Map<any, any>` cache result directly in a ternary return without casting | TS 5.8's per-branch return checking now catches the `any`-infected branch | Tighten the map's type parameter or guard with `instanceof`/`as` cast in the branch |
| Writing inline template literal type cartesian products from large unions without intermediate aliases | Type instantiation depth explodes; compiler produces "excessively deep" errors | Extract intermediate `type Alias = \`${A}_${B}\`` and reference the alias in the outer template |
