## Cycle 59 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 211** — Mapped Type with `as` Key Remapping to Build Getter Interfaces
```typescript
type Getters<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K];
};

interface UserProfile {
  name: string;
  age: number;
  email: string;
}

type UserGetters = Getters<UserProfile>;
// { getName: () => string; getAge: () => number; getEmail: () => string }

// Compose with a base class pattern
class ProfileStore implements Getters<UserProfile> {
  private data: UserProfile;
  constructor(data: UserProfile) { this.data = data; }
  getName()  { return this.data.name; }
  getAge()   { return this.data.age; }
  getEmail() { return this.data.email; }
}
```
Tradeoff: Key remapping with `as` and `Capitalize` cleanly generates accessor-interface shapes at the type level with zero runtime cost, but the pattern forces every property name through `string & K` intersection — omitting the `string &` cast causes a TS error because `K` alone is typed as `string | number | symbol`. The generated interface is also purely structural so classes implementing it must manually keep accessor names in sync with property additions.

---

**Pattern 212** — `EventConfig` Dispatcher via Union-Based Mapped Key Remapping
```typescript
type EventConfig<E extends { kind: string }> = {
  [Ev in E as Ev["kind"]]: (event: Ev) => void;
};

type ClickEvent  = { kind: "click";  x: number; y: number };
type FocusEvent  = { kind: "focus";  target: string };
type SubmitEvent = { kind: "submit"; formId: string };

type AppHandlers = EventConfig<ClickEvent | FocusEvent | SubmitEvent>;
// { click: (e: ClickEvent) => void; focus: (e: FocusEvent) => void; submit: (e: SubmitEvent) => void }

function dispatch<K extends keyof AppHandlers>(
  kind: K,
  handlers: AppHandlers,
  event: Parameters<AppHandlers[K]>[0]
): void {
  (handlers[kind] as (e: typeof event) => void)(event);
}
```
Tradeoff: Distributing over a discriminated union to produce an event-handler map is expressive and self-documenting — adding a new event variant automatically extends the map type with a new required handler key. The downside is that the `dispatch` helper requires a cast because TypeScript cannot yet correlate the generic `K` key with its narrowed parameter type inside the function body; this is a known limitation (microsoft/TypeScript#30581).

---

**Pattern 213** — `ExtractPII` Conditional Mapped Type for GDPR Field Auditing
```typescript
type Sensitive = { pii: true };

type ExtractPII<T> = {
  [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends Sensitive ? true : false;
};

type DBSchema = {
  id:        { format: "uuid" };
  username:  { type: string };
  email:     { type: string; pii: true };
  birthDate: { type: string; pii: true };
};

type PIIMap = ExtractPII<DBSchema>;
// { id: false; username: false; email: true; birthDate: true }

type PIIKeys<T> = {
  [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends Sensitive ? K : never;
}[keyof T];

type SensitiveFields = PIIKeys<DBSchema>; // "email" | "birthDate"
```
Tradeoff: Encoding data-classification as a type-level property and extracting it via conditional mapped types creates a compile-time GDPR surface map with no runtime overhead. However, the pattern is purely advisory — nothing prevents a developer from accessing a PII field at runtime. Enforcement still requires lint rules or runtime guards. The `PIIKeys` extraction step using `[keyof T]` can be confusing and should be documented in the codebase.

---

**Pattern 214** — `DeepPartial<T>` Recursive Mapped Type for Patch Payloads
```typescript
type DeepPartial<T> = T extends object
  ? { [K in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[K]> }
  : T;

interface Config {
  server: { host: string; port: number; tls: { cert: string; key: string } };
  logging: { level: string; format: "json" | "text" };
}

type ConfigPatch = DeepPartial<Config>;
// All fields optional at every depth

function applyPatch(base: Config, patch: ConfigPatch): Config {
  return {
    server: {
      host:  patch.server?.host  ?? base.server.host,
      port:  patch.server?.port  ?? base.server.port,
      tls: {
        cert: patch.server?.tls?.cert ?? base.server.tls.cert,
        key:  patch.server?.tls?.key  ?? base.server.tls.key,
      },
    },
    logging: {
      level:  patch.logging?.level  ?? base.logging.level,
      format: patch.logging?.format ?? base.logging.format,
    },
  };
}
```
Tradeoff: `DeepPartial` cleanly models patch/merge scenarios and avoids wide `Partial<Config>` that only makes top-level keys optional. The recursion is bounded at compile time for finite types but can cause slow type-checking on very deeply nested structures. Arrays inside the type become `(DeepPartial<Item>)[]`, which may be too permissive — an element patch array could omit required discriminant fields that are needed at runtime for array-item identification.

---

**Pattern 215** — `Concrete<T>` Mapped Modifier Removal to Enforce Required Shapes
```typescript
type Concrete<T> = {
  [K in keyof T]-?: NonNullable<T[K]>;
};

interface FormDraft {
  title?:       string;
  description?: string;
  tags?:        string[];
  publishAt?:   Date;
}

type PublishedPost = Concrete<FormDraft>;
// { title: string; description: string; tags: string[]; publishAt: Date }

function validateAndPublish(draft: FormDraft): PublishedPost {
  if (!draft.title)       throw new Error("title required");
  if (!draft.description) throw new Error("description required");
  if (!draft.tags?.length) throw new Error("at least one tag required");
  if (!draft.publishAt)   throw new Error("publishAt required");
  return draft as PublishedPost;
}
```
Tradeoff: The `-?` modifier removal combined with `NonNullable` produces a fully required, non-nullable shape from an optional draft without duplicating field declarations. The cast inside `validateAndPublish` is sound only if all guard conditions are exhaustive — a future field added to `FormDraft` will be silently absent from the runtime validation unless a linter rule (`@typescript-eslint/no-unnecessary-type-assertion` or strict checks) flags the cast. Prefer exhaustive validation utilities that iterate `Object.keys(result)` for critical paths.

---

**Pattern 216** — `FilteredKeys<T, U>` Utility for Type-Driven Property Selection
```typescript
type FilteredKeys<T, U> = {
  [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends U ? K : never;
}[keyof T];

type StringKeys<T>   = FilteredKeys<T, string>;
type FunctionKeys<T> = FilteredKeys<T, (...args: any[]) => any>;

interface ApiClient {
  baseUrl:    string;
  timeout:    number;
  apiKey:     string;
  get:        (path: string) => Promise<unknown>;
  post:       (path: string, body: unknown) => Promise<unknown>;
  retryCount: number;
}

type StringFields   = StringKeys<ApiClient>;   // "baseUrl" | "apiKey"
type MethodNames    = FunctionKeys<ApiClient>;  // "get" | "post"

// Build partial mocks from only the method subset
type MockMethods<T> = Pick<T, FunctionKeys<T>>;
type ApiMock = MockMethods<ApiClient>;
```
Tradeoff: `FilteredKeys` composes cleanly with `Pick` to build domain-specific subtype utilities without enumerating keys manually. The `[keyof T]` indexing trick to collapse the mapped type to a union is idiomatic but cryptic to developers unfamiliar with the pattern — a comment explaining "indexed distribution" is advisable. The conditional `extends` check uses structural subtyping so a `string`-returning function satisfies `FilteredKeys<T, string>` unexpectedly.

---

**Pattern 217** — Infer Return Type of Overloaded Functions via Last-Signature Rule
```typescript
// TypeScript resolves `infer` against the LAST (catch-all) overload signature
declare function parseValue(x: string): number;
declare function parseValue(x: number): string;
declare function parseValue(x: string | number): string | number;

type ParseValueReturn = ReturnType<typeof parseValue>; // string | number

// Work around by wrapping in a conditional infer extraction
type LastOverloadReturn<T> =
  T extends { (...args: any[]): infer R }
    ? R
    : never;

// When you own the overloads, prefer a single generic implementation
function parseValueGeneric<T extends string | number>(
  x: T
): T extends string ? number : string {
  return (typeof x === "string" ? Number(x) : String(x)) as any;
}

type PR1 = ReturnType<typeof parseValueGeneric<string>>; // number
type PR2 = ReturnType<typeof parseValueGeneric<number>>; // string
```
Tradeoff: The last-overload-wins rule for `infer` is intentional — TypeScript uses the most permissive (catch-all) overload for inference to avoid false negatives. Developers expecting the narrowest return type are surprised. The generic-function alternative avoids overloads entirely and gives per-call-site return type precision via conditional return types, but requires an `as any` cast inside the implementation body (or a type predicate chain) because TypeScript does not narrow conditional return types inside function bodies.

---

**Pattern 218** — Template Literal Union Cross-Product for Typed CSS Class Helpers
```typescript
type Size    = "sm" | "md" | "lg" | "xl";
type Variant = "primary" | "secondary" | "ghost";
type State   = "" | "-active" | "-disabled";

type ButtonClass = `btn-${Variant}-${Size}${State}`;
// 3 × 4 × 3 = 36 literal members in the union

// Type-safe class builder
function btnClass(
  variant: Variant,
  size: Size,
  state?: "active" | "disabled"
): ButtonClass {
  const suffix = state ? `-${state}` : "" as State;
  return `btn-${variant}-${size}${suffix}` as ButtonClass;
}

const c1 = btnClass("primary", "md");           // "btn-primary-md"
const c2 = btnClass("ghost",   "lg", "active"); // "btn-ghost-lg-active"
// btnClass("danger", "md"); // TS error: "danger" not assignable to Variant
```
Tradeoff: Template literal cross-product unions provide exhaustive, compiler-enforced class-name vocabularies. The union size grows multiplicatively — beyond ~1000 members TypeScript may emit "union too complex to represent" errors and fall back to `string`. For large design-token systems with 4+ axes, use a runtime validator (e.g., Zod) with a coarser string type rather than a full cross-product union, and reserve template literals for 2–3 axis combinations.

---

**Pattern 219** — `infer X extends string` Constrained Extraction for Typed Route Params
```typescript
// TypeScript 4.8+: infer with extends bound constrains extraction type
type ExtractRouteParams<T extends string> =
  T extends `${string}:${infer Param extends string}/${infer Rest extends string}`
    ? Param | ExtractRouteParams<`/${Rest}`>
    : T extends `${string}:${infer Param extends string}`
    ? Param
    : never;

type Params1 = ExtractRouteParams<"/users/:userId/orders/:orderId">; // "userId" | "orderId"
type Params2 = ExtractRouteParams<"/posts/:slug">;                   // "slug"
type Params3 = ExtractRouteParams<"/health">;                        // never

// Build a typed params record
type RouteParamRecord<T extends string> = Record<ExtractRouteParams<T>, string>;

function buildUrl<T extends string>(
  template: T,
  params: RouteParamRecord<T>
): string {
  return template.replace(/:([a-z]+)/gi, (_, key) => params[key as keyof typeof params]);
}

const url = buildUrl("/users/:userId/orders/:orderId", { userId: "42", orderId: "7" });
```
Tradeoff: Constrained `infer X extends string` (TS 4.8+) eliminates the need for a subsequent `Extract<X, string>` wrapping, making complex recursive route-param extraction concise. Recursive template literal types increase compilation time linearly with route depth; paths deeper than 6–7 segments may noticeably slow `tsc`. For large route registries, pre-compute param types once in a central route-map type rather than re-inferring per call site.

---

**Pattern 220** — `Awaited<T>` Deep Promise Unwrapping for Async Utility Types
```typescript
// Awaited<T> (TS 4.5+) recursively unwraps Promise<Promise<T>> to T
type DoubleWrapped = Awaited<Promise<Promise<string>>>; // string

// Real-world: derive the resolved value type of an async factory
type ResolvedConfig = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof loadConfig>>;

async function loadConfig() {
  return { dsn: "postgres://…", poolSize: 10 };
}

// Combine with conditional to get element type of async iterable
type AsyncIterableItem<T> =
  T extends AsyncIterable<infer U> ? U : never;

async function* generateIds(): AsyncGenerator<number> {
  yield 1; yield 2; yield 3;
}

type IdItem = AsyncIterableItem<ReturnType<typeof generateIds>>; // number

// Type-safe async accumulator
async function collectAll<T>(
  gen: AsyncIterable<T>
): Promise<T[]> {
  const out: T[] = [];
  for await (const x of gen) out.push(x);
  return out;
}
```
Tradeoff: `Awaited<T>` makes the return type of async utilities explicit and correct even with doubly-wrapped promises, which previously required manual `Promise<T>` unwrapping utilities. The type is fully recursive — it follows `PromiseLike<T>` not just native `Promise<T>` — so it works with thenables. The downside is that `Awaited<T>` is sometimes overly aggressive: `Awaited<() => Promise<number>>` is `() => Promise<number>` (functions are not unwrapped), so developers must combine it with `ReturnType` explicitly.

---

**Pattern 221** — Variance Annotations (`in`/`out`) for Generic Parameter Correctness
```typescript
// TypeScript 4.7+ variance annotations
interface ReadonlyBox<out T> {   // covariant — T only appears in output positions
  getValue(): T;
}

interface WriteonlyBox<in T> {   // contravariant — T only appears in input positions
  setValue(value: T): void;
}

// Covariant: ReadonlyBox<Dog> is assignable to ReadonlyBox<Animal>
declare class Dog { bark(): void }
declare class Animal { breathe(): void }

const dogBox: ReadonlyBox<Dog>    = { getValue: () => new Dog() };
const animalBox: ReadonlyBox<Animal> = dogBox; // OK — covariant

// Invariant without annotation (TypeScript default for mutable generics):
interface MutableBox<T> {
  get(): T;
  set(v: T): void;
}
// MutableBox<Dog> is NOT assignable to MutableBox<Animal>
```
Tradeoff: Explicit `in`/`out` variance annotations let TypeScript skip expensive structural compatibility checks for large generic types, reducing `tsc` time by up to 30% in monorepos with many deeply generic interfaces. They also serve as documentation — a reader immediately sees which positions a type parameter occupies. The cost is that incorrect annotations (marking a bivariant parameter as `out`) can unsoundly allow unsafe assignments; TypeScript does not yet verify annotation correctness at definition time for all cases.

---

**Pattern 222** — `satisfies` Operator for Exhaustive Constant Maps Without Widening
```typescript
type StatusCode = 200 | 201 | 400 | 401 | 403 | 404 | 500;
type HttpMeta   = { message: string; retryable: boolean };

const HTTP_META = {
  200: { message: "OK",                retryable: false },
  201: { message: "Created",           retryable: false },
  400: { message: "Bad Request",       retryable: false },
  401: { message: "Unauthorized",      retryable: false },
  403: { message: "Forbidden",         retryable: false },
  404: { message: "Not Found",         retryable: false },
  500: { message: "Server Error",      retryable: true  },
} satisfies Record<StatusCode, HttpMeta>;

// Preserves literal types — HTTP_META[200].message is "OK", not string
type OkMessage = typeof HTTP_META[200]["message"]; // "OK"

// Adding an unrecognised key triggers a compile error
// HTTP_META[418] would cause: Object literal may only specify known properties
```
Tradeoff: `satisfies` validates a value against a type constraint without widening the inferred type, preserving literal precision that an explicit annotation would lose. The trade-off is that `satisfies` does not refine the variable's type — the declared type of `HTTP_META` is still the structural inferred type, not `Record<StatusCode, HttpMeta>`. Consumers that accept `Record<StatusCode, HttpMeta>` need an explicit parameter type; passing `HTTP_META` directly works due to structural subtyping but the extra key safety is not propagated to call sites automatically.

---

**Pattern 223** — `NoInfer<T>` Utility to Anchor Generic Inference
```typescript
// TypeScript 5.4+ built-in NoInfer<T>
function createStore<T>(
  initial: T,
  validate: (value: NoInfer<T>) => boolean
): { get(): T; set(v: T): void } {
  let current = initial;
  return {
    get: ()  => current,
    set: (v) => { if (validate(v)) current = v; },
  };
}

// Without NoInfer, both arguments participate in T inference:
// createStore(0, v => v.length > 0) would infer T = number | { length: number }
// With NoInfer<T> on validate, T is anchored to `initial` = number
// The validate callback receives number, so v.length is a TS error
const numStore = createStore(0, v => v > -1);       // T = number
// createStore(0, (v: string) => v.length > 0);    // Error: string not assignable to number
```
Tradeoff: `NoInfer<T>` (TS 5.4+) solves a long-standing inference problem where "helper" parameters unintentionally widen the primary inferred type. It is zero-overhead at runtime (erased) and communicates intent clearly to readers. The limitation is that `NoInfer` can only be applied at the call-site via the type definition — it cannot be applied retroactively to a third-party generic. For older TypeScript versions, the workaround `[T] extends [NoInfer<T>]` is not available; use `T extends T ? (val: T) => bool : never` conditional tricks instead.

---

**Pattern 224** — `Readonly<T>` Shallow vs `DeepReadonly<T>` Recursive Immutability
```typescript
type DeepReadonly<T> = T extends (infer U)[]
  ? ReadonlyArray<DeepReadonly<U>>
  : T extends object
  ? { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }
  : T;

interface AppState {
  user: { name: string; roles: string[] };
  settings: { theme: "light" | "dark"; notifications: boolean };
}

type FrozenState = DeepReadonly<AppState>;
// user.roles is ReadonlyArray<string> — push/pop are compile errors
// settings.theme is readonly "light" | "dark"

function renderHeader(state: FrozenState): string {
  // state.user.name = "hack"; // TS error: readonly
  return `Hello, ${state.user.name} (${state.settings.theme})`;
}
```
Tradeoff: `DeepReadonly<T>` closes the gap left by the built-in `Readonly<T>` which only freezes the top level. Arrays and nested objects remain mutable under shallow `Readonly`, which is the root cause of accidental state mutations in reducers. The recursive mapped type adds compilation cost for deeply nested state trees but has no runtime cost. The pattern does not prevent `Object.assign` or spread mutations at runtime — it only blocks direct property assignment. Pair with `Object.freeze` for runtime safety in critical paths.

---

**Pattern 225** — `Parameters<T>` and `ConstructorParameters<T>` for Higher-Order Type Safety
```typescript
// Parameters<T> extracts argument tuple from a function type
type LogArgs = Parameters<typeof console.log>;         // [message?: any, ...optionalParams: any[]]

// ConstructorParameters<T> extracts constructor argument tuple
class HttpClient {
  constructor(
    readonly baseUrl: string,
    readonly timeout: number,
    readonly headers: Record<string, string>
  ) {}
}

type ClientCtorArgs = ConstructorParameters<typeof HttpClient>;
// [baseUrl: string, timeout: number, headers: Record<string, string>]

// Use for factory / DI container patterns
function createClient(...args: ClientCtorArgs): HttpClient {
  return new HttpClient(...args);
}

// Use Parameters to build typed curry wrappers
function withLogging<F extends (...args: any[]) => any>(
  fn: F
): (...args: Parameters<F>) => ReturnType<F> {
  return (...args) => {
    console.log("calling", fn.name, args);
    return fn(...args);
  };
}
```
Tradeoff: `Parameters<T>` and `ConstructorParameters<T>` make higher-order wrappers, factories, and DI containers fully type-safe without duplicating parameter declarations. The extracted tuple types are positional — adding a new constructor argument automatically updates the factory signature. The limitation is that rest-parameter tuples can be complex to work with when partially applying arguments; spreading `Parameters<F>` works for full forwarding but partial application requires `Parameters<F>[0]`, `Parameters<F>[1]` etc. indexing which becomes verbose beyond 3–4 args.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G153** — `string & Property` intersection required in mapped `as` clauses with `Capitalize`
Why this matters: When remapping keys via `as Capitalize<Property>`, TypeScript reports an error unless the operand is narrowed to `string`. The type of `Property` in a mapped type is `string | number | symbol`, and `Capitalize` only accepts `string`. Developers write `Capitalize<Property>` expecting it to work and see a cryptic "Type 'symbol' is not assignable to 'string'" error.
Fix: Always intersect the key with `string` inside template-literal mapped-type operations: `[K in keyof T as Capitalize<string & K>]`. The `string & K` intersection narrows `K` to the string subset and satisfies `Capitalize`'s constraint without changing the runtime behaviour.

---

**G154** — Distributive conditional types evaluate to `never` when passed `never`
Why this matters: A distributive conditional type `type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false` distributes over union members. When `T = never`, there are no union members to distribute over, so the result is `never` — not `false`. This breaks type-level boolean logic when `never` is a possible type argument, e.g., in utility types that use conditionals for filtering.
Fix: Guard against `never` before the distributive check: `type IsString<T> = [T] extends [never] ? false : T extends string ? true : false`. Wrapping in tuples `[T] extends [never]` prevents distribution and evaluates the check on `never` itself, returning the intended `false` branch.

---

**G155** — `as const` arrays spread into mutable copies, silently dropping `readonly`
Why this matters: `const arr = ["a", "b"] as const` produces `readonly ["a", "b"]`. But `const copy = [...arr]` produces `string[]` — a mutable, widened copy. Functions that accept `readonly string[]` and then spread the parameter internally give callers a false sense of immutability. The original `readonly` contract is not enforced on the spread result.
Fix: Explicitly re-annotate spread results: `const copy: readonly string[] = [...arr]`. For function parameters, declare them as `readonly T[]` (or `ReadonlyArray<T>`) rather than `T[]` to prevent callers from passing mutable arrays where readonly was expected, and use `[...arr] as const` when the output must remain a readonly tuple.

---

**G156** — Excess property checking only fires on freshly-written object literals, not references
Why this matters: TypeScript checks for extra properties only when an object literal is assigned directly to a typed location. If the literal is first stored in an intermediate `const` without a type annotation and later passed to a typed parameter, the excess-property check is skipped. A misspelled config key (e.g. `tiemout` instead of `timeout`) compiles silently, the value is ignored at runtime, and the real timeout never changes.
Fix: Use `satisfies` at the assembly site so the check fires before the variable is passed anywhere: `const cfg = { tiemout: 500 } satisfies RequestConfig` — this surfaces the typo immediately. Alternatively, annotate the intermediate `const` explicitly: `const cfg: RequestConfig = { tiemout: 500 }` (the annotation makes it a directly typed assignment, triggering the check).

---

**G157** — Generic parameter defaults silently widen inferred types after library upgrades
Why this matters: When a library adds a default to a previously required generic parameter (`type Box<T = unknown>` replacing `type Box<T>`), existing call sites that relied on inference continue to compile — but now receive `unknown` as the type argument instead of the previously-inferred concrete type. Code that was type-safe under inference can silently lose type precision, turning checked property accesses into `unknown`-typed accesses that require casts.
Fix: Audit call sites of upgraded APIs after adding or changing generic defaults. Explicitly supply type arguments at important API boundaries: `Box<MyType>` instead of relying on inference. When authoring library types, prefer narrow or `never` defaults for safety, and document the change in the changelog. The TypeScript `--noImplicitAny` flag does not catch this issue because `unknown` is explicit, not implicit.

---

## Cycle 60 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 226** — `Flatten<T>` with `infer Item` to Unwrap Nested Array Types
```typescript
// Recursively unwrap until we reach a non-array type
type Flatten<T> = T extends ReadonlyArray<infer Item>
  ? Flatten<Item>
  : T;

type DeepArray = string[][][];
type Element = Flatten<DeepArray>; // string

// Practical use: normalise heterogeneous collection return types
function flatten<T>(arr: T[][]): Flatten<T[][]>[] {
  return arr.flat() as any;
}

// Pair with Awaited for async arrays
type AsyncFlat<T> = Flatten<Awaited<T>>;
type Resolved = AsyncFlat<Promise<number[][]>>; // number
```
Tradeoff: Recursive conditional types elegantly unwrap arbitrarily deep arrays but TypeScript imposes a recursion depth limit (~100 levels). For genuinely unbounded nesting use a depth counter generic parameter; for most real-world data (2–4 levels) the plain recursive form is safe and far more readable.

---

**Pattern 227** — Branded / Nominal Types via `unique symbol` for Type-Safe IDs
```typescript
declare const __brand: unique symbol;
type Brand<T, B extends string> = T & { readonly [__brand]: B };

type UserId    = Brand<string, "UserId">;
type ProductId = Brand<string, "ProductId">;

function createUserId(raw: string): UserId {
  return raw as UserId;
}

// Error: Argument of type 'ProductId' is not assignable to parameter of type 'UserId'
function getUser(id: UserId): void { /* ... */ }

const pid = "p-42" as ProductId;
// getUser(pid); // TS2345 — caught at compile time, not runtime
```
Tradeoff: Branded types enforce domain identity at zero runtime cost by attaching a phantom property via `unique symbol`. The limitation is that construction sites must use explicit casts (`as UserId`) — this is intentional, acting as a "smart constructor" boundary — but if you cast carelessly at too many sites the brand provides no real safety. Centralise creation in factory functions to keep brand integrity.

---

**Pattern 228** — `const` Type Parameter (TypeScript 5.0) for Literal Inference Without `as const`
```typescript
// Before TS 5.0: callers had to write `as const` to preserve literals
function makeConfig<T extends readonly string[]>(keys: T): T {
  return keys;
}
const cfg = makeConfig(["a", "b"] as const); // needed as const

// TS 5.0+: declare the type parameter as `const` to infer literals automatically
function makeConfigV2<const T extends readonly string[]>(keys: T): T {
  return keys;
}
const cfg2 = makeConfigV2(["a", "b"]); // inferred as readonly ["a", "b"]

// Useful in route builders, state machine definitions, schema factories
function defineRoutes<const T extends Record<string, string>>(routes: T): T {
  return routes;
}
const routes = defineRoutes({ home: "/", about: "/about" });
type HomeRoute = typeof routes.home; // "/", not string
```
Tradeoff: `const` type parameters eliminate the ergonomic friction of requiring callers to annotate `as const`, making library APIs feel natural. The caveat is that the constraint `T extends readonly string[]` (or the appropriate readonly shape) is still required — omitting `readonly` causes the inferred tuple to be mutable, which may widen unexpectedly when the value is later assigned to a non-readonly variable.

---

**Pattern 229** — Variadic Tuple Types for Type-Safe Argument Composition
```typescript
type Prepend<T, Tuple extends unknown[]> = [T, ...Tuple];
type Append<Tuple extends unknown[], T> = [...Tuple, T];

// Compose two function signatures into a pipeline tuple
type Concat<A extends unknown[], B extends unknown[]> = [...A, ...B];

// Practical: middleware chain where each layer prepends a context arg
type WithContext<F extends (...args: any[]) => any> =
  (ctx: RequestContext, ...args: Parameters<F>) => ReturnType<F>;

interface RequestContext { userId: string }

function withContext<F extends (...args: any[]) => any>(
  fn: F
): WithContext<F> {
  return (ctx, ...args) => fn(...args);
}

function getOrder(orderId: string): Order { return {} as Order; }
interface Order {}
const getOrderWithCtx = withContext(getOrder);
// type: (ctx: RequestContext, orderId: string) => Order
```
Tradeoff: Variadic tuple types (`[...A, ...B]`) allow precise type-level list operations that previously required large union-based overloads. The main limitation is that TypeScript cannot always distribute through variadic spreads in complex higher-kinded scenarios — inference can fall back to `unknown[]` when constraints are too loose; tighten with explicit `extends unknown[]` bounds on every tuple type parameter.

---

**Pattern 230** — `Extract<T, U>` for Discriminated-Union Branch Isolation
```typescript
type Shape =
  | { kind: "circle"; radius: number }
  | { kind: "rect"; width: number; height: number }
  | { kind: "triangle"; base: number; height: number };

// Extract exactly the branch you need without writing the full shape again
type CircleShape = Extract<Shape, { kind: "circle" }>;
// { kind: "circle"; radius: number }

type AreaFn<S extends Shape> = (shape: Extract<Shape, { kind: S["kind"] }>) => number;

function area(shape: Shape): number {
  switch (shape.kind) {
    case "circle":   return Math.PI * shape.radius ** 2;
    case "rect":     return shape.width * shape.height;
    case "triangle": return 0.5 * shape.base * shape.height;
  }
}

// Utility: build a typed handler map keyed by discriminant
type HandlerMap = { [K in Shape["kind"]]: (s: Extract<Shape, { kind: K }>) => number };
```
Tradeoff: `Extract<Shape, { kind: "circle" }>` is more resilient than importing the branch type directly — when the union evolves (new properties added to `CircleShape`), `Extract` stays in sync automatically. The trade-off is readability: deeply nested `Extract` calls can obscure intent; give the extracted type a named alias at the module boundary.

---

**Pattern 231** — `ThisType<T>` Marker for Strongly Typed Object-Literal Methods
```typescript
interface DataLayer { x: number; y: number }
interface Methods {
  moveBy(dx: number, dy: number): void;
  reset(): void;
}

type Descriptor<D, M> = {
  data?: D;
  methods?: M & ThisType<D & M>;
};

function makeObject<D, M>(desc: Descriptor<D, M>): D & M {
  return { ...desc.data, ...desc.methods } as D & M;
}

const point = makeObject({
  data: { x: 0, y: 0 },
  methods: {
    moveBy(dx: number, dy: number) {
      this.x += dx; // TS knows this.x: number
      this.y += dy;
    },
    reset() {
      this.x = 0;
      this.y = 0;
    },
  },
});
point.moveBy(3, 4);
```
Tradeoff: `ThisType<T>` lets factory functions type `this` inside plain object literals without requiring a class, making it ideal for mixin and composition patterns. The requirement is that `noImplicitThis` (or `strict`) must be enabled in `tsconfig.json`; in its absence TypeScript ignores the marker and `this` falls back to `any`, silently erasing the benefit.

---

**Pattern 232** — `OmitThisParameter<T>` to Expose Bound Methods as Plain Callbacks
```typescript
class Formatter {
  private prefix: string;
  constructor(prefix: string) { this.prefix = prefix; }

  format(this: Formatter, value: string): string {
    return `${this.prefix}: ${value}`;
  }
}

// OmitThisParameter strips the explicit `this` constraint
type BoundFormat = OmitThisParameter<Formatter["format"]>;
// (value: string) => string   — safe to pass as a callback

function applyToList(list: string[], fn: BoundFormat): string[] {
  return list.map(fn);
}

const fmt = new Formatter("INFO");
const bound: BoundFormat = fmt.format.bind(fmt);
applyToList(["a", "b", "c"], bound);
// ["INFO: a", "INFO: b", "INFO: c"]
```
Tradeoff: `OmitThisParameter<T>` makes the relationship between a bound method and its callback signature explicit in the type system, preventing callers from accidentally passing an unbound method that crashes at runtime. The limitation is that the utility only removes one level of `this` typing — if you chain `.bind()` calls or reassign the bound function, TypeScript may re-infer a new `this` context and the type diverges from reality.

---

**Pattern 233** — `Lowercase` / `Uppercase` / `Uncapitalize` String Intrinsics for Typed Event Maps
```typescript
type EventNames = "Click" | "Focus" | "Blur" | "KeyDown";

// Build a fully typed DOM-style addEventListener signature
type EventHandlerMap = {
  [E in EventNames as `on${E}`]: (event: Event) => void;
};
// { onClick: ...; onFocus: ...; onBlur: ...; onKeyDown: ... }

// Reverse: derive the base name from a prefixed key using Uncapitalize
type StripOn<K extends string> =
  K extends `on${infer Rest}` ? Uncapitalize<Rest> : never;

type BaseEvents = StripOn<keyof EventHandlerMap>;
// "click" | "focus" | "blur" | "keyDown"

// Build a typed event-bus subscribe signature
type Subscribe<K extends string> = (
  event: Lowercase<K>,
  handler: () => void
) => () => void;
```
Tradeoff: Intrinsic string types (`Uppercase`, `Lowercase`, `Capitalize`, `Uncapitalize`) operate at the type level only and are applied at compile time, producing zero runtime overhead. They shine in code-generation scenarios (event maps, CSS class helpers, gRPC stub typing) but become confusing when the casing convention is mixed-case (camelCase, PascalCase) because `Lowercase` flattens all casing — combine with template literal reconstruction to preserve inner-word casing.

---

**Pattern 234** — Indexed Access on `typeof` Enumerations for Self-Describing Config Types
```typescript
const LOG_LEVELS = {
  debug: 0,
  info:  1,
  warn:  2,
  error: 3,
} as const;

type LogLevelName  = keyof typeof LOG_LEVELS;          // "debug" | "info" | "warn" | "error"
type LogLevelValue = (typeof LOG_LEVELS)[LogLevelName]; // 0 | 1 | 2 | 3

interface AppConfig {
  logLevel: LogLevelName;
  minLogValue: LogLevelValue;
}

function configure(cfg: AppConfig) {
  const numericLevel = LOG_LEVELS[cfg.logLevel];
  if (numericLevel < cfg.minLogValue) {
    console.warn("Effective log level is below minimum");
  }
}

configure({ logLevel: "warn", minLogValue: 1 }); // ok
// configure({ logLevel: "verbose", minLogValue: 1 }); // TS error
```
Tradeoff: Deriving `LogLevelName` and `LogLevelValue` from `typeof LOG_LEVELS` via indexed access keeps the type and the runtime constant in perfect sync — adding a new level to the object automatically expands the union types. The trade-off versus a TypeScript `enum` is that `keyof typeof` constructs lack reverse-mapping; if you need `LOG_LEVELS[0] === "debug"` you must build the reverse map manually with `{[V in LogLevelValue]: ...}`.

---

**Pattern 235** — `NonNullable<T>` as a Narrowing Constraint in Generic Utility Types
```typescript
// Ensure a generic does not silently accept null/undefined
type StrictRecord<K extends keyof any, V> = Record<K, NonNullable<V>>;

// Force unwrapping: build a mapped type that removes null/undefined from all values
type DeepNonNullable<T> = T extends object
  ? { [K in keyof T]: DeepNonNullable<NonNullable<T[K]>> }
  : NonNullable<T>;

interface ApiResponse {
  user: { name: string | null; age: number | undefined } | null;
}

type CleanResponse = DeepNonNullable<ApiResponse>;
// { user: { name: string; age: number } }

// Assertion utility leveraging NonNullable
function assertDefined<T>(val: T, label: string): NonNullable<T> {
  if (val == null) throw new Error(`${label} is null/undefined`);
  return val as NonNullable<T>;
}
```
Tradeoff: `NonNullable<T>` composed into recursive mapped types creates a `DeepNonNullable` utility that cleanly models validated/sanitised API shapes. The trade-off is that applying it too early — before the data has actually been validated — papers over nullability rather than handling it; always pair with a runtime assertion (like `assertDefined`) so the compile-time promise matches the runtime guarantee.

---

**Pattern 236** — Assertion Functions as Type-Narrowing Guards (`asserts x is T`)
```typescript
function assertIsString(val: unknown, label: string): asserts val is string {
  if (typeof val !== "string") {
    throw new TypeError(`Expected string for ${label}, got ${typeof val}`);
  }
}

function assertIsRecord(val: unknown): asserts val is Record<string, unknown> {
  if (typeof val !== "object" || val === null || Array.isArray(val)) {
    throw new TypeError("Expected a plain object");
  }
}

// After the assertion call, TS narrows the type in the current scope
function parseConfig(raw: unknown): { host: string; port: number } {
  assertIsRecord(raw);
  assertIsString(raw.host, "host");
  if (typeof raw.port !== "number") throw new TypeError("port must be number");
  return { host: raw.host, port: raw.port };
}
```
Tradeoff: Assertion functions (`asserts x is T`) narrow types imperatively — after the call, the compiler treats the value as the narrowed type for the remainder of the scope, making them ideal for validation-at-boundary patterns in parsers and deserialisers. The limitation is that the narrowing only applies within the same function scope; if the asserted value escapes (is stored in a mutable closure variable), TypeScript may widen it back to the original type at a later control-flow point.

---

**Pattern 237** — `infer R extends ConstraintType` (TypeScript 4.8) for Narrowed Inference
```typescript
// Before 4.8: required a second conditional to constrain the inferred type
type StringKeys<T> = T extends Record<infer K, unknown>
  ? K extends string ? K : never
  : never;

// TS 4.8+: constrain directly inside the infer clause
type StringKeysV2<T> = T extends Record<infer K extends string, unknown>
  ? K
  : never;

type ApiKeys = StringKeysV2<{ name: string; 42: number; sym: symbol }>;
// "name"

// Extract URL path segments constrained to non-empty strings
type PathSegments<T extends string> =
  T extends `/${infer Head extends string}/${infer Tail extends string}`
    ? Head | PathSegments<`/${Tail}`>
    : T extends `/${infer Last extends string}`
      ? Last
      : never;

type Segments = PathSegments<"/api/users/profile">; // "api" | "users" | "profile"
```
Tradeoff: `infer K extends SomeType` merges type extraction and constraint in a single step, eliminating the secondary conditional that was previously required. This dramatically improves readability of complex template-literal parsing utilities. The caveat is that the constraint narrows inference eagerly — if the inferred type has members both inside and outside the constraint, the entire inference branch evaluates to `never` rather than narrowing partially; model the constraint carefully to avoid silent `never` results.

---

**Pattern 238** — `using` Declarations (TypeScript 5.2) for Deterministic Resource Disposal
```typescript
// Implement the Disposable interface
class DbConnection implements Disposable {
  private conn: { query: (sql: string) => unknown; close: () => void };

  constructor(url: string) {
    this.conn = { query: (sql) => sql, close: () => console.log("closed") };
  }

  query(sql: string) { return this.conn.query(sql); }

  [Symbol.dispose]() {
    this.conn.close();
    console.log("DbConnection disposed");
  }
}

// `using` automatically calls [Symbol.dispose] at block exit (including on throw)
function runQuery(url: string, sql: string) {
  using db = new DbConnection(url);
  return db.query(sql);
  // db[Symbol.dispose]() called here even if query throws
}

// AsyncDisposable for async teardown
class FileHandle implements AsyncDisposable {
  async [Symbol.asyncDispose]() { await Promise.resolve(); /* flush & close */ }
}
```
Tradeoff: `using` declarations integrate TypeScript's type system with the ECMAScript Explicit Resource Management proposal, making resource lifecycle deterministic and exception-safe without try/finally boilerplate. The trade-off is adoption friction: target runtimes must support `Symbol.dispose` (Node 18.20+ or a polyfill), and `tsconfig.json` must include `"lib": ["ES2022", "ESNext.Disposable"]`; omitting this causes cryptic "Symbol.dispose not found" errors at runtime despite clean compilation.

---

**Pattern 239** — Template Literal `Split<S, Sep>` for Type-Level String Parsing
```typescript
type Split<S extends string, Sep extends string> =
  string extends S ? string[] :
  S extends "" ? [] :
  S extends `${infer Head}${Sep}${infer Tail}`
    ? [Head, ...Split<Tail, Sep>]
    : [S];

type Parts = Split<"a,b,c,d", ",">; // ["a", "b", "c", "d"]
type UrlParts = Split<"api/users/profile", "/">; // ["api", "users", "profile"]

// Build a typed deep-getter using Split and indexed access
type DeepGet<T, Path extends string> =
  Split<Path, "."> extends [infer Head extends keyof T & string, ...infer Tail extends string[]]
    ? Tail extends []
      ? T[Head]
      : DeepGet<T[Head], Join<Tail, ".">>
    : never;

type Join<T extends string[], Sep extends string> =
  T extends [infer F extends string, ...infer R extends string[]]
    ? R extends [] ? F : `${F}${Sep}${Join<R, Sep>}`
    : never;
```
Tradeoff: `Split` and `Join` at the type level unlock fully type-safe dot-path accessors (`get(obj, "user.address.city")`) with no runtime overhead. The cost is that TypeScript's recursive type depth limit applies — paths deeper than ~20 segments cause "Type instantiation is excessively deep" errors. For application-level code this is rarely a problem, but for deeply nested JSON schema paths, cap recursion with a depth counter parameter.

---

**Pattern 240** — `Record<K, V>` + `Partial` + `Required` Composition for Staged Builder Patterns
```typescript
type StepKeys = "database" | "cache" | "auth" | "logging";

// Phase 1: all steps are optional (config accumulation)
type BuilderState = Partial<Record<StepKeys, true>>;

// Phase 2: when all steps are provided, the builder is "sealed"
type SealedState = Required<Record<StepKeys, true>>;

class AppBuilder<S extends BuilderState = {}> {
  private state: S;
  constructor(state: S = {} as S) { this.state = state; }

  withDatabase(): AppBuilder<S & { database: true }> {
    return new AppBuilder({ ...this.state, database: true as const });
  }
  withCache(): AppBuilder<S & { cache: true }> {
    return new AppBuilder({ ...this.state, cache: true as const });
  }
  withAuth(): AppBuilder<S & { auth: true }> {
    return new AppBuilder({ ...this.state, auth: true as const });
  }
  withLogging(): AppBuilder<S & { logging: true }> {
    return new AppBuilder({ ...this.state, logging: true as const });
  }

  // Only callable when S satisfies SealedState
  build(this: AppBuilder<SealedState>): void {
    console.log("App configured", this.state);
  }
}

new AppBuilder().withDatabase().withCache().withAuth().withLogging().build(); // ok
// new AppBuilder().withDatabase().build(); // TS error: missing cache/auth/logging
```
Tradeoff: The staged builder pattern uses intersection accumulation on the generic parameter to track which configuration steps have been completed, making `.build()` unavailable until all mandatory steps are present. The downside is that each `.withX()` call allocates a new wrapper object — this is negligible for builders (called once at startup) but would be wasteful in hot paths. The approach also requires careful generic bookkeeping; each new step must extend the type parameter correctly or inference silently widens to `{}`.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G158** — `typeof` narrowing does not refine `object` subtypes — use discriminants or `instanceof`
Why this matters: `typeof value === "object"` narrows to `object | null` (because `typeof null === "object"`), but does not distinguish between plain objects, arrays, class instances, or Maps. Developers write a `typeof` guard expecting to handle "an object with a `.data` property" and are surprised when TS still reports `object` with no accessible members and `null` is not excluded.
Fix: Use `instanceof` for class types (`value instanceof MyClass`), a discriminant property check (`"data" in value && value !== null`) for plain objects, or `Array.isArray(value)` for arrays. For complete null exclusion pair with an explicit null check: `value !== null && typeof value === "object"`.

---

**G159** — Intersection types do not merge method overloads — they produce a single over-constrained signature
Why this matters: When intersecting two object types that both declare a method with the same name but different signatures (e.g., `{ log(msg: string): void } & { log(msg: Error): void }`), TypeScript does not create an overloaded function. Instead it produces a single function type requiring both signatures simultaneously — which is practically impossible to satisfy and causes confusing "no overload matches this call" errors at usage sites.
Fix: Instead of intersecting method types, declare explicit overloads on a single interface or use a union of parameter types: `{ log(msg: string | Error): void }`. When composing library types that share method names with different signatures, create a wrapper type that re-declares the method with a union signature rather than relying on intersection to merge them.

---

**G160** — `keyof` on an interface with optional properties includes `undefined` in the value union
Why this matters: `keyof` on an interface yields the union of all keys, and indexed access on optional properties includes `undefined` in the value type: `type V = MyInterface[keyof MyInterface]` where some properties are optional produces `string | number | undefined` even if you only intended to work with defined values. This propagates `undefined` silently through utility types like `Record<K, V>` and surprises developers who expect `V` to be the set of value types alone.
Fix: Filter out undefined from indexed-access results using `NonNullable`: `type DefinedValues = NonNullable<MyInterface[keyof MyInterface]>`. When building `Record` types from interface values, always intersect the value type with `NonNullable<...>` to preserve the intended constraint.

---

**G161** — Re-exported `const enum` causes runtime errors when consumed across module boundaries in isolatedModules mode
Why this matters: `const enum` values are inlined by the TypeScript compiler at each use site, which makes them zero-cost at runtime. However, under `isolatedModules: true` (required by esbuild, Vite, Babel, and SWC), each file is transpiled independently without cross-file type information. A `const enum` declared in one file and re-exported from an index barrel cannot be inlined in consuming files — the transpiler emits an object access that does not exist at runtime, producing `undefined` or a crash.
Fix: Replace `const enum` with a plain `enum` (which emits a runtime object) or with an `as const` object (`const Direction = { Up: 0, Down: 1 } as const`). The `as const` alternative is tree-shakeable, works in all transpiler modes, and produces the same literal union types as `const enum`. Enable the `@typescript-eslint/prefer-enum-initializers` and `no-const-enum` ESLint rules to catch new `const enum` introductions automatically.

---

**G162** — Excess property checking is skipped for `Pick<T, K>` and `Omit<T, K>` return types
Why this matters: `Pick<T, K>` and `Omit<T, K>` return structural types, not branded ones. When a function's return type is declared as `Pick<Config, "host">`, TypeScript accepts an object literal `{ host: "localhost", port: 3000 }` returned from the function body without flagging the extraneous `port` property. Developers assume `Pick` acts as a strict filter but the extra properties silently pass through to callers who spread the result into other objects.
Fix: Use `satisfies` on the return expression to trigger excess property checking: `return { host: "localhost", port: 3000 } satisfies Pick<Config, "host">` raises a compile error. Alternatively, explicitly pick properties in the return: `const { host } = fullConfig; return { host }` — destructuring ensures only the declared properties are included in the returned object.

---

## Cycle 61 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 241** — Key Remapping with `as` Clause to Build Getter Interfaces
```typescript
type Getters<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K];
};

interface Config {
  host: string;
  port: number;
  debug: boolean;
}

type ConfigGetters = Getters<Config>;
// { getHost: () => string; getPort: () => number; getDebug: () => boolean }

declare function attachGetters<T>(obj: T): T & Getters<T>;
const cfg = attachGetters({ host: "localhost", port: 8080, debug: false });
cfg.getHost();  // string
cfg.getPort();  // number
```
Tradeoff: The `as` clause with template literals elegantly derives accessor names without runtime codegen, but `Capitalize<string & K>` requires the explicit `string &` intersection because `keyof T` includes `number | symbol`; omitting that intersection produces a type error that is easy to misread as a mapped-type bug rather than a key-type constraint issue.

---

**Pattern 242** — Removing Mapped-Type Modifiers with `-readonly` and `-?`
```typescript
// Strip both readonly and optional in one pass
type Mutable<T> = {
  -readonly [K in keyof T]-?: T[K];
};

type FrozenConfig = {
  readonly host?: string;
  readonly port?: number;
  readonly debug?: boolean;
};

type EditableConfig = Mutable<FrozenConfig>;
// { host: string; port: number; debug: boolean }

// Inverse: add both modifiers
type Frozen<T> = {
  +readonly [K in keyof T]+?: T[K];
};

type ImmutableDraft = Frozen<EditableConfig>;
// { readonly host?: string; readonly port?: number; readonly debug?: boolean }
```
Tradeoff: The `-readonly` / `-?` modifier syntax is the only way to strip inherited modifiers in a mapped type — reassigning `readonly` or `?` without the minus prefix adds rather than removes — but the `+` prefix is optional (implicit), meaning `+?` and `?` are identical, which causes confusion when reading code where a developer used `+?` intending to "explicitly add" and another uses `?` assuming no change.

---

**Pattern 243** — Filtering Keys with `as never` Inside Mapped Types
```typescript
type PickByValue<T, V> = {
  [K in keyof T as T[K] extends V ? K : never]: T[K];
};

interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
  age: number;
  active: boolean;
}

type StringFields = PickByValue<User, string>;
// { name: string; email: string }

type NumericFields = PickByValue<User, number>;
// { id: number; age: number }

// Compose with Omit for inverse
type OmitByValue<T, V> = {
  [K in keyof T as T[K] extends V ? never : K]: T[K];
};
type NonStringFields = OmitByValue<User, string>;
// { id: number; age: number; active: boolean }
```
Tradeoff: Producing `never` in the `as` position completely removes a key from the resulting type — which is cleaner than wrapping the whole value in a conditional — but the pattern is non-homomorphic when applied to union inputs because the outer iteration distributes before the inner conditional fires, leading to unexpected key merging when `T` itself is a union type.

---

**Pattern 244** — `EventConfig` — Mapping a Discriminated-Union to a Handler Map
```typescript
type EventConfig<E extends { kind: string }> = {
  [Ev in E as Ev["kind"]]: (event: Ev) => void;
};

type ClickEvent  = { kind: "click";  x: number; y: number };
type KeyEvent    = { kind: "key";    key: string; ctrlKey: boolean };
type ResizeEvent = { kind: "resize"; width: number; height: number };

type AppEventConfig = EventConfig<ClickEvent | KeyEvent | ResizeEvent>;
// {
//   click:  (event: ClickEvent)  => void;
//   key:    (event: KeyEvent)    => void;
//   resize: (event: ResizeEvent) => void;
// }

function registerHandlers(config: AppEventConfig): void { /* ... */ }
registerHandlers({
  click:  e => console.log(e.x, e.y),
  key:    e => console.log(e.key),
  resize: e => console.log(e.width, e.height),
});
```
Tradeoff: Mapping a discriminated union through the `kind` discriminant directly to handler keys produces an exhaustive handler map that the compiler enforces, making it impossible to register an unrecognized event type; the downside is that adding a new event variant to the union immediately breaks all existing `registerHandlers` call sites — intentional for exhaustiveness, but painful when variants are added frequently in a large codebase.

---

**Pattern 245** — `NoInfer<T>` to Pin Default Values Against an Already-Inferred Parameter
```typescript
function createStateMachine<S extends string>(
  states: S[],
  initial: NoInfer<S>,
  transitions: Partial<Record<NoInfer<S>, NoInfer<S>>>
): { current: S; go(to: S): void } {
  let current = initial;
  return {
    get current() { return current; },
    go(to) {
      if (transitions[current]?.includes?.(to as never)) current = to;
    }
  };
}

// "idle" | "running" | "done" inferred from first arg only
const machine = createStateMachine(
  ["idle", "running", "done"],
  "idle",                          // must be one of the above
  { idle: "running", running: "done" }
);
// createStateMachine(["idle"], "paused", {}); // TS error: "paused" not in states
```
Tradeoff: `NoInfer<T>` (TypeScript 5.4) prevents the `initial` and `transitions` arguments from widening the inferred `S` union — without it TypeScript would add `"paused"` to `S` silently — but `NoInfer` is currently limited to preventing inference at specific call sites and cannot block widening caused by explicit type annotations on the call-site variable itself.

---

**Pattern 246** — Preserved Narrowing in Closures After Last Assignment (TypeScript 5.4)
```typescript
function buildQuery(input: string | URL, filters: string[]): string[] {
  if (typeof input === "string") {
    input = new URL(input);   // last assignment — TypeScript tracks this
  }
  // input is narrowed to URL here and stays URL inside the closure below
  return filters.map(f => {
    const u = new URL(input.toString());  // ok in TS 5.4+
    u.searchParams.set("filter", f);
    return u.toString();
  });
}

// Gotcha: any re-assignment inside the closure invalidates the narrowing
function badVersion(input: string | URL): void {
  if (typeof input === "string") input = new URL(input);
  setTimeout(() => {
    input = new URL("https://reset.example");  // invalidates narrowing
  }, 0);
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log(input.hostname);  // TS error: input possibly string
  }, 100);
}
```
Tradeoff: TypeScript 5.4's closure narrowing preservation eliminates spurious "possibly undefined/string" errors in common `if (typeof x === "string") { x = new URL(x); }` patterns, but the narrowing is invalidated by any assignment to the variable inside *any* closure in scope — not just the one performing the read — which means splitting logic across multiple `setTimeout` or `Promise` callbacks can still lose the narrowing even when the re-assignment logically cannot race with the read.

---

**Pattern 247** — Distributive vs. Non-Distributive Conditional Types with Tuple Wrapping
```typescript
// Distributive: applies to each union member separately
type IsString<T> = T extends string ? "yes" : "no";
type R1 = IsString<string | number>;   // "yes" | "no"

// Non-distributive: treats the union as a single type
type IsStringExact<T> = [T] extends [string] ? "yes" : "no";
type R2 = IsStringExact<string | number>;  // "no"

// Practical use: IsUnion check
type IsUnion<T> = [T] extends [T]
  ? Exclude<T, T> extends never
    ? [T] extends [Exclude<T, T>]
      ? false
      : true
    : false
  : false;

// Safer Equal check using non-distribution on both sides
type Equal<A, B> =
  (<T>() => T extends A ? 1 : 2) extends
  (<T>() => T extends B ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type E1 = Equal<string, string>;          // true
type E2 = Equal<string | number, string>; // false
```
Tradeoff: Wrapping in `[T]` to disable distribution is essential for type-equality checks and `IsUnion` helpers, but the tuple-wrapper pattern is a non-obvious hack: it works because `[string | number] extends [string]` evaluates the union as-is rather than distributing, relying on TypeScript internals that could theoretically change; the `Equal` implementation using higher-kinded inference is more robust but harder to explain during code review.

---

**Pattern 248** — Inferring Return Types from Function Overloads and the Last-Signature Rule
```typescript
// TypeScript infers the return type from the *last* overload signature
function parse(input: string): number;
function parse(input: number): string;
function parse(input: string | number): string | number {
  return typeof input === "string" ? parseInt(input) : String(input);
}

type ParseReturn = ReturnType<typeof parse>;  // string | number (last overload)

// Better approach: use a discriminated union + single generic instead of overloads
type ParseInput = string | number;
type ParseOutput<T extends ParseInput> = T extends string ? number : string;
function parseSafe<T extends ParseInput>(input: T): ParseOutput<T> {
  return (typeof input === "string" ? parseInt(input) : String(input)) as ParseOutput<T>;
}
type Safe1 = ReturnType<typeof parseSafe<string>>;  // number
type Safe2 = ReturnType<typeof parseSafe<number>>;  // string
```
Tradeoff: TypeScript's overload resolution picks the last overload signature for `ReturnType<>`, which silently loses precision for earlier overloads; replacing overloads with a single generic conditional-type signature preserves per-call-site return type accuracy at the cost of requiring an `as` cast in the implementation body because TypeScript cannot verify that the conditional type is satisfied in the implementation's broader union logic.

---

**Pattern 249** — `infer R extends Constraint` (TypeScript 4.8) for Narrowed Extraction
```typescript
// Without constraint: inferred type is widened
type GetLength<T extends readonly unknown[]> =
  T extends { length: infer L } ? L : never;
type L1 = GetLength<[1, 2, 3]>;  // number (widened)

// With constraint: narrows inferred type immediately
type GetLengthNarrow<T extends readonly unknown[]> =
  T extends { length: infer L extends number } ? L : never;
type L2 = GetLengthNarrow<[1, 2, 3]>;  // 3 (literal)

// Practical: extract discriminant value as literal
type Discriminant<T, K extends keyof T> =
  T extends Record<K, infer V extends string> ? V : never;

type Shape = { kind: "circle"; r: number } | { kind: "rect"; w: number; h: number };
type ShapeKind = Discriminant<Shape, "kind">;  // "circle" | "rect"
```
Tradeoff: `infer R extends Constraint` collapses the two-step pattern of inferring broadly then filtering with `& Constraint` into a single clause, but the constraint only narrows the inferred variable — it does not validate that the source type actually satisfies the constraint, meaning if the inferred value does not extend the constraint, the whole conditional branch returns `never` rather than raising a useful error.

---

**Pattern 250** — `PropEventSource<T>` — Template Literal Typed Event Subscriptions
```typescript
type PropEventSource<T> = {
  on<K extends string & keyof T>(
    event: `${K}Changed`,
    callback: (newValue: T[K]) => void
  ): void;
  off<K extends string & keyof T>(
    event: `${K}Changed`,
    callback: (newValue: T[K]) => void
  ): void;
};

function makeReactive<T extends object>(obj: T): T & PropEventSource<T> {
  const listeners = new Map<string, Set<(v: unknown) => void>>();
  return new Proxy(obj, {
    set(target, prop, value) {
      (target as Record<PropertyKey, unknown>)[prop] = value;
      listeners.get(String(prop))?.forEach(cb => cb(value));
      return true;
    }
  }) as T & PropEventSource<T>;
}

const user = makeReactive({ name: "Alice", age: 30 });
user.on("nameChanged", newName => newName.toUpperCase()); // string inferred
user.on("ageChanged",  newAge  => newAge.toFixed(2));    // number inferred
// user.on("emailChanged", ...);  // TS error: "email" not in keyof T
```
Tradeoff: The `K extends string & keyof T` constraint combined with template literal `${K}Changed` gives precise per-property callback typing without any runtime overhead, but the pattern creates a new generic instantiation per event name — in an object with dozens of properties, IDE completion can stall as TypeScript enumerates all `*Changed` combinations; for large models, splitting into domain-specific sub-objects keeps completion snappy.

---

**Pattern 251** — `Extract<T, U>` Applied to Discriminated Unions for Safe Sub-Dispatch
```typescript
type Action =
  | { type: "FETCH_USER";  userId: number }
  | { type: "SAVE_USER";   user: { id: number; name: string } }
  | { type: "DELETE_USER"; userId: number }
  | { type: "FETCH_POST";  postId: number }
  | { type: "SAVE_POST";   post: { id: number; title: string } };

type UserAction = Extract<Action, { type: `${"FETCH" | "SAVE" | "DELETE"}_USER` }>;
// { type: "FETCH_USER"; userId: number }
// | { type: "SAVE_USER"; user: {...} }
// | { type: "DELETE_USER"; userId: number }

function userReducer(action: UserAction): void {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "FETCH_USER":  console.log(action.userId); break;
    case "SAVE_USER":   console.log(action.user.name); break;
    case "DELETE_USER": console.log(action.userId); break;
  }
}

// Ensure userReducer only receives user actions at the call site
function dispatch(action: Action): void {
  if (action.type.endsWith("_USER")) userReducer(action as UserAction);
}
```
Tradeoff: Combining `Extract` with a template-literal pattern union narrows a broad action union to a meaningful sub-domain without manually listing every member, but the template pattern must exactly match discriminant string structure — changing `"FETCH_USER"` to `"user/FETCH"` in a refactor silently makes the `Extract` return `never` rather than raising an error, because `Extract` produces `never` for non-matching unions with no compiler diagnostic at the definition site.

---

**Pattern 252** — Aggressive Intersection Reduction with Primitive Constraints (TypeScript 5.4)
```typescript
declare function merge<T extends string, U>(value: T, extra: U): T & U;

// TS 5.4+: T constrained to string sub-literal; intersecting with number reduces to never
function process<T extends "a" | "b" | "c">(x: T) {
  const withStr = merge(x, "hello"); // T & string → T (string already satisfied)
  const withNum = merge(x, 42);      // T & number → never (literals can't be numbers)

  // Use this for type-level impossible-state elimination
  type MustBeString<V> = V extends string ? V : never;
  type MustBeNumber<V> = V extends number ? V : never;
}

// Practical: strip numeric excess from generic string params
type StringOnly<T> = T extends string ? T : never;
type Result = StringOnly<"hello" | 42 | "world">;  // "hello" | "world"

// Combining with branded types
type Brand<T, B extends string> = T & { __brand: B };
type UserId = Brand<string, "UserId">;
declare const id: UserId;
const s: string = id;    // ok — covariant direction
const u: UserId = "raw"; // error — "raw" & { __brand: "UserId" } → never
```
Tradeoff: TypeScript 5.4's more aggressive reduction of `T & primitive` intersections eliminates phantom `never` values that previously required explicit `Extract<T, string>` cleanup, but it introduces a subtle breaking change: code that previously relied on `T & string` remaining unevaluated (e.g., for branded-type building where `T extends "a"` and `T & string` was used as a loose `string` annotation) now collapses to `T`, which can cause type errors in downstream assignments expecting a plain `string`.

---

**Pattern 253** — `satisfies` Operator for Strict Object Shape Validation Without Type Widening
```typescript
type ColorMap = Record<string, [number, number, number] | string>;

// Without satisfies: type is widened to ColorMap, losing tuple/string specificity
const colors1: ColorMap = {
  red:   [255, 0, 0],
  green: "#00ff00",
};
colors1.red;   // [number, number, number] | string  (widened)

// With satisfies: validates against ColorMap but preserves inferred literal types
const colors2 = {
  red:   [255, 0, 0],
  green: "#00ff00",
} satisfies ColorMap;
colors2.red;    // [number, number, number]  (preserved)
colors2.green;  // string                   (preserved)
colors2.red[0]; // number                   (array access is safe)

// Also useful for config objects: validate shape, keep literal keys
const routes = {
  home:  "/",
  about: "/about",
  login: "/login",
} satisfies Record<string, `/${string}`>;
type RouteKeys = keyof typeof routes;  // "home" | "about" | "login" (not string)
```
Tradeoff: `satisfies` combines the structural validation of a type annotation with the inference preservation of no annotation, which is strictly more useful than `as const` + annotation in most cases, but it cannot be used on the left side of a destructuring assignment and does not flow into `typeof` when the `satisfies` expression is passed inline as a function argument — the widened inferred type is used at the call site, not the `satisfies`-narrowed one.

---

**Pattern 254** — Type-Safe Path Parameter Extraction via Recursive Template Literal Types
```typescript
type ExtractParams<Path extends string> =
  Path extends `${infer _Before}:${infer Param}/${infer Rest}`
    ? { [K in Param | keyof ExtractParams<Rest>]: string }
    : Path extends `${infer _Before}:${infer Param}`
      ? { [K in Param]: string }
      : Record<never, never>;

type UserParams    = ExtractParams<"/users/:userId/posts/:postId">;
// { userId: string; postId: string }

type ProductParams = ExtractParams<"/shop/:category/:productId">;
// { category: string; productId: string }

function route<P extends string>(
  path: P,
  handler: (params: ExtractParams<P>) => void
): void { /* router registration */ }

route("/users/:userId/posts/:postId", ({ userId, postId }) => {
  console.log(userId, postId);  // both string, typo-safe
});
// route("/users/:userId", ({ userId, typo }) => {}); // TS error: typo not in params
```
Tradeoff: Recursive template-literal parameter extraction gives zero-runtime-cost type-safe routing but TypeScript's recursion depth limit (approximately 100 levels for distributive recursion) means paths with many segments can hit the limit and produce `never`; keeping path segment count under 8–10 is safe in practice, and pre-splitting at the type level with a `Split<S, "/">` helper can reduce recursion depth.

---

**Pattern 255** — Variance Annotations (`in`/`out`) for Explicit Covariance and Contravariance
```typescript
// TypeScript 4.7+ variance annotations: `in` = contravariant, `out` = covariant
interface Consumer<in T> {
  consume(value: T): void;
}
interface Producer<out T> {
  produce(): T;
}
interface Transformer<in TIn, out TOut> {
  transform(value: TIn): TOut;
}

// Covariant Producer: Producer<Dog> assignable to Producer<Animal>
declare const dogProducer: Producer<{ breed: string; name: string }>;
const animalProducer: Producer<{ name: string }> = dogProducer;  // ok

// Contravariant Consumer: Consumer<Animal> assignable to Consumer<Dog>
declare const animalConsumer: Consumer<{ name: string }>;
const dogConsumer: Consumer<{ breed: string; name: string }> = animalConsumer; // ok

// Invariant (both in+out): no assignability in either direction
interface ReadWrite<in out T> {
  get(): T;
  set(value: T): void;
}
```
Tradeoff: Explicit variance annotations (`in`, `out`, `in out`) make covariance and contravariance relationships self-documenting and allow TypeScript to skip expensive structural variance checks for large generic hierarchies, improving compiler performance on deep type graphs; however, if the annotation is wrong (e.g., marking a type `out T` when it also consumes `T`), TypeScript raises an error at the annotation site rather than at the incorrect use site, which can be confusing when retrofitting annotations onto existing generic interfaces.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G163** — `NoInfer<T>` does not prevent widening caused by explicit type annotations at the call site
Why this matters: `NoInfer<T>` tells the compiler "do not use this position when inferring `T`", which prevents a default-value argument from widening the inferred union. However, if the caller writes `const x: string[] = createFn(["a", "b"], "c")` where `T` is declared as `string`, `NoInfer` has no effect — the explicit annotation overrides inference entirely and the constraint is still lost. Developers mistake `NoInfer` for a runtime or declaration-level constraint and are surprised when a caller with an explicit wider annotation bypasses the restriction.
Fix: Pair `NoInfer<T>` with a stricter generic constraint on the primary parameter (`T extends string` rather than `T extends string[]`) and add a runtime assertion if the invariant is safety-critical. Document that `NoInfer` only guards inference, not explicit annotations, in the function's JSDoc.

---

**G164** — `Extract<T, U>` silently returns `never` when a template-literal pattern no longer matches after a rename
Why this matters: `Extract<Action, { type: \`${"FETCH" | "SAVE"}_USER\` }>` returns `never` without any compiler warning if the discriminant strings in the `Action` union are later renamed (e.g., to `"user/FETCH"`). Because `Extract` returning `never` is not itself an error, downstream code that accepts the extracted type will silently accept `never` arguments — a variable typed as `never` can never be assigned a value, but function parameters typed as `never` accept any argument in practice because nothing is assignable to `never`.
Fix: Add a compile-time assertion after critical `Extract` usages: `type _AssertNonNever = [UserAction] extends [never] ? "ERROR: Extract returned never — check discriminant strings" : true`. A conditional type assertion that expands to a string literal error is caught at definition time and fails the build, making renames safe.

---

**G165** — `satisfies` does not narrow the type at inline call sites — the widened inferred type flows to the callee
Why this matters: `fn({ host: "localhost" } satisfies PickedConfig)` does not pass the `satisfies`-narrowed type to `fn`; TypeScript evaluates the expression's type as the inferred type of the object literal (widened), then `satisfies` validates it but does not change what type is passed. Developers use `satisfies` expecting `fn` to receive the constrained shape and are surprised when the callee's overload resolution uses the wider object type.
Fix: Assign the `satisfies` expression to a named `const` first: `const cfg = { host: "localhost" } satisfies PickedConfig; fn(cfg);`. The named constant's inferred type is the `satisfies`-preserved type and flows correctly into the function call. For inline usage, use an explicit type annotation on the parameter instead.

---

**G166** — Variance annotation errors appear at the annotation site, not at the incorrect usage
Why this matters: When retrofitting `out T` (covariant) onto an existing interface that also writes to `T` (e.g., a cache that both `get(): T` and `set(value: T): void`), TypeScript reports an error at the `interface Cache<out T>` line rather than at the `set` method. Developers unfamiliar with variance expect the error at the problematic method and waste time looking at usage sites rather than the interface declaration itself.
Fix: Read variance errors at the declaration level as "this annotation contradicts what the interface's members require." Use `in out T` for invariant types (mutable containers, read-write APIs), `out T` for covariant types (producers, read-only containers), and `in T` for contravariant types (consumers, write-only callbacks). When unsure, omit the annotation — TypeScript infers variance automatically and only annotations that conflict with structural inference are rejected.

---

**G167** — `Object.groupBy` returns `Partial<Record<K, T[]>>` — accessing the result without a null check is a type error under `strictNullChecks`
Why this matters: TypeScript 5.4 types `Object.groupBy(arr, fn)` as `Partial<Record<K, T[]>>` because not every possible key is guaranteed to appear in the output. Developers accustomed to `_.groupBy` (which returns `Record<K, T[]>`) write `Object.groupBy(items, f).myKey.map(...)` and encounter a compile error under `strictNullChecks` because `myKey` is `T[] | undefined`. Runtime behavior is the same — undefined is returned for missing keys — but TypeScript now enforces the null check that was previously ignored.
Fix: Use optional chaining and nullish coalescing: `Object.groupBy(items, f).myKey?.map(...) ?? []`. Alternatively, wrap in a helper that provides a default: `function groupByRequired<T, K extends PropertyKey>(items: T[], fn: (i: T) => K): Record<K, T[]> { return Object.groupBy(items, fn) as Record<K, T[]>; }` — acceptable when the calling code guarantees all keys will be present (e.g., grouping by a discriminant that covers all values).
