## Cycle 62 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**P256** — `Awaited<T>` for Recursive Promise Unwrapping

```typescript
// Awaited<T> recursively unwraps nested Promises to their resolved value type.
// This is essential when composing async utilities that return
// Promise<Promise<T>> (e.g., from dynamic imports or wrapped fetch helpers).

type NestedPromise = Promise<Promise<Promise<string>>>;
type Resolved = Awaited<NestedPromise>; // string

async function unwrapAll<T>(fn: () => T): Promise<Awaited<T>> {
  return fn() as Awaited<T>;
}

// Compose with ReturnType to extract what an async function ultimately resolves to
async function fetchUser(id: number): Promise<{ name: string; age: number }> {
  return { name: "Alice", age: 30 };
}
type UserShape = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof fetchUser>>;
// { name: string; age: number }
```
Tradeoff: `Awaited<T>` eliminates guessing games when deeply nested async chains produce opaque `Promise<Promise<…>>` types, making function return types self-documenting; however, it only operates at the type level and does not enforce that the runtime actually awaits all layers, so an incorrectly typed non-async wrapper that skips an await will silently produce a `Promise` at runtime while appearing resolved in the type system.

---

**P257** — `Parameters<T>` and `ReturnType<T>` for Adapter Wrappers

```typescript
// Use Parameters<T> and ReturnType<T> to write fully type-safe decorator or
// adapter wrappers without repeating the original function's signature.

function withLogging<F extends (...args: unknown[]) => unknown>(
  fn: F,
  label: string
): (...args: Parameters<F>) => ReturnType<F> {
  return (...args: Parameters<F>): ReturnType<F> => {
    console.log(`[${label}] called with`, args);
    const result = fn(...args) as ReturnType<F>;
    console.log(`[${label}] returned`, result);
    return result;
  };
}

function add(a: number, b: number): number {
  return a + b;
}

const loggedAdd = withLogging(add, "add");
loggedAdd(2, 3); // fully typed: (a: number, b: number) => number
```
Tradeoff: Using `Parameters<F>` and `ReturnType<F>` in a wrapper means the wrapper's type is always derived from the wrapped function, so renaming or retyping the original automatically propagates without touching the wrapper; the cost is that overloaded functions expose only the last overload signature to `Parameters` and `ReturnType`, which may cause the wrapper to silently lose overload resolution for callers expecting multiple call forms.

---

**P258** — `ConstructorParameters<T>` for Factory Helpers

```typescript
// ConstructorParameters<T> extracts the constructor's parameter tuple,
// enabling factory functions and dependency-injection containers that remain
// in sync with the class constructor without manual duplication.

class DatabaseConnection {
  constructor(
    private host: string,
    private port: number,
    private database: string
  ) {}
  query(sql: string): Promise<unknown[]> {
    return Promise.resolve([]);
  }
}

function createInstance<T extends new (...args: unknown[]) => unknown>(
  Ctor: T,
  ...args: ConstructorParameters<T>
): InstanceType<T> {
  return new Ctor(...args) as InstanceType<T>;
}

const db = createInstance(DatabaseConnection, "localhost", 5432, "mydb");
// db is typed as DatabaseConnection — host/port/db args are enforced
```
Tradeoff: `ConstructorParameters<T>` keeps factory functions structurally aligned with their target classes so constructor signature changes are caught at all factory call sites; however, when a class has multiple overloaded constructors TypeScript exposes only the last constructor in the overload list, which can cause the factory to accept argument shapes that the class never actually handles at runtime.

---

**P259** — `ThisParameterType<T>` and `OmitThisParameter<T>` for `this`-Bound Methods

```typescript
// ThisParameterType<T> extracts the explicit `this` parameter so callers can
// verify the required receiver type. OmitThisParameter<T> produces a clean
// function type after bind() or apply() has fixed the receiver.

interface Counter {
  value: number;
  increment(by: number): void;
}

function increment(this: Counter, by: number): void {
  this.value += by;
}

// Extract the required receiver type
type Receiver = ThisParameterType<typeof increment>; // Counter

// After .bind() the `this` parameter disappears from the callable type
const boundIncrement: OmitThisParameter<typeof increment> = increment.bind({
  value: 0,
  increment,
});
boundIncrement(5); // (by: number) => void — no `this` required
```
Tradeoff: Explicitly typing `this` parameters and using `OmitThisParameter` after `bind` makes receiver contracts visible in the type system and eliminates "lost context" bugs at the type level; the downside is that `this` parameters are a TypeScript-only concept erased at compile time, so JavaScript consumers of the same module cannot see the receiver constraint and can still call the function with an incorrect `this` at runtime.

---

**P260** — `Record<K, V>` as an Exhaustive Enum-Keyed Map

```typescript
// When K is a finite string union or enum, Record<K, V> guarantees that
// every member of K is present in the object literal — missing keys are a
// compile error. This is the idiomatic way to build look-up tables that
// stay exhaustive as the union grows.

type HttpMethod = "GET" | "POST" | "PUT" | "DELETE" | "PATCH";

const methodLabels: Record<HttpMethod, string> = {
  GET: "Fetch resource",
  POST: "Create resource",
  PUT: "Replace resource",
  DELETE: "Remove resource",
  PATCH: "Update resource",
  // Omitting any key is a compile-time error
};

// Adding "HEAD" to HttpMethod immediately flags every Record<HttpMethod, …>
// that doesn't include a "HEAD" entry.
type MethodHandler = Record<HttpMethod, (url: string) => Promise<Response>>;
```
Tradeoff: `Record<K, V>` turns union exhaustiveness into a structural property enforced at declaration time, so every addition to the key union immediately surfaces all gaps in existing tables; however, `Record` does not prevent extra keys — an object with keys beyond those in `K` still satisfies the type because TypeScript uses structural subtyping, so at a call site accepting `Record<HttpMethod, string>` a superset object with extra keys is silently accepted.

---

**P261** — `NonNullable<T>` as a Guard in Generic Constraints

```typescript
// Using NonNullable<T> in a constraint forces callers to supply values that
// are neither null nor undefined, centralising the nullability contract at the
// generic boundary rather than scattering null checks throughout the body.

function processAll<T>(
  items: Array<NonNullable<T>>,
  transform: (item: NonNullable<T>) => string
): string[] {
  return items.map(transform);
}

// The array element type itself must exclude null/undefined
processAll([1, 2, 3], (n) => n.toFixed(2));         // ok
// processAll([1, null, 3], (n) => n.toFixed(2));   // error: null not assignable

// Combine with a mapped type to strip nullability from all object fields
type StrictUser<T extends object> = {
  [K in keyof T]: NonNullable<T[K]>;
};

interface ApiUser {
  id: number;
  name: string | null;
  email: string | undefined;
}
type CleanUser = StrictUser<ApiUser>;
// { id: number; name: string; email: string }
```
Tradeoff: Embedding `NonNullable` in a generic constraint shifts the responsibility for null-safety to the caller, making function bodies cleaner and removing repetitive null-guard boilerplate; but it makes the function unusable in contexts where nullable inputs are legitimately expected, so callers sometimes resort to a pre-filter step (`.filter((x): x is T => x != null)`) that silently drops data rather than surfacing the null as an error.

---

**P262** — `Exclude<T, U>` for Subtract-Union Utility Types

```typescript
// Exclude<T, U> removes union members assignable to U from T.
// This is the building block for "subtract" utilities — types that strip
// specific capabilities from a larger union, keeping the remainder type-safe.

type AllEvents =
  | { kind: "click"; x: number; y: number }
  | { kind: "keydown"; key: string }
  | { kind: "resize"; width: number; height: number }
  | { kind: "scroll"; deltaY: number };

// Remove pointer events to get non-pointer events
type NonPointerEvents = Exclude<AllEvents, { kind: "click" | "scroll" }>;
// { kind: "keydown"; key: string } | { kind: "resize"; width: number; height: number }

// Build a generic "without" helper
type Without<T, K extends T> = Exclude<T, K>;
type NonScrollEvent = Without<AllEvents, { kind: "scroll"; deltaY: number }>;

function handleNonPointer(event: NonPointerEvents) {
  switch (event.kind) {
    case "keydown": console.log("Key:", event.key); break;
    case "resize": console.log("New size:", event.width, event.height); break;
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: `Exclude<T, U>` allows narrowing a union at definition time so that functions accepting a subset never need explicit member guards, keeping handlers lean; the subtle risk is that `Exclude` matches by assignability rather than identity — `Exclude<string | "literal", string>` returns `never` because `"literal"` is assignable to `string`, which surprises developers who expect only exact `string` to be removed while `"literal"` is preserved.

---

**P263** — Narrowing with Custom Type Predicates (`pet is Fish`)

```typescript
// A user-defined type guard narrows the type of its argument in the
// positive branch and the complementary type in the negative branch,
// enabling reusable narrowing logic that control-flow analysis can follow.

interface Fish { swim(): void; name: string; }
interface Bird { fly(): void; name: string; }
interface Reptile { crawl(): void; name: string; }

type Animal = Fish | Bird | Reptile;

function isFish(animal: Animal): animal is Fish {
  return "swim" in animal;
}

function isBird(animal: Animal): animal is Bird {
  return "fly" in animal;
}

const zoo: Animal[] = [
  { swim() {}, name: "Nemo" },
  { fly() {}, name: "Tweety" },
  { crawl() {}, name: "Rex" },
];

const fishOnly: Fish[] = zoo.filter(isFish);
const birdOnly: Bird[] = zoo.filter(isBird);
// Type-safe partition — no `as` casts needed
```
Tradeoff: Type predicates let narrowing logic live in a single, tested function and compose with `.filter`, `Array.find`, and conditional chains without `as` casts; the critical risk is that the predicate body is not structurally verified by the compiler — if `isFish` returns `true` for an object that is not a `Fish`, TypeScript trusts the annotation and the caller receives a badly typed value, so incorrect predicates introduce silent type-system lies that only surface at runtime.

---

**P264** — Exhaustiveness Checking with `never` in `switch` Default Branches

```typescript
// Assigning the discriminant to a `never`-typed variable in the default
// branch turns "unhandled union member" into a compile error, making
// discriminated unions safe to extend without silent omissions.

type Shape =
  | { kind: "circle"; radius: number }
  | { kind: "square"; side: number }
  | { kind: "triangle"; base: number; height: number };

function area(shape: Shape): number {
  switch (shape.kind) {
    case "circle":
      return Math.PI * shape.radius ** 2;
    case "square":
      return shape.side ** 2;
    case "triangle":
      return 0.5 * shape.base * shape.height;
    default: {
      // If a new variant is added to Shape without updating this function,
      // TypeScript emits: "Type 'NewVariant' is not assignable to type 'never'"
      const _exhaustive: never = shape;
      throw new Error(`Unhandled shape: ${JSON.stringify(_exhaustive)}`);
    }
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: The `never` sentinel in the default branch converts runtime omissions into compile-time errors, making discriminated union exhaustiveness automatic and continuous; the tradeoff is that this pattern requires the `switch` to handle every union member inline — if variants are handled in separate helper functions called from `default`, the exhaustiveness check is bypassed, and teams sometimes resist adding new variants to shared unions because they know it will break every existing switch across the codebase.

---

**P265** — `ThisType<T>` for Mixin Method Binding

```typescript
// ThisType<T> does not emit a type itself — it marks the `this` context for
// methods defined in an object literal, enabling fluent API builders and
// mixin factories where method bodies refer to sibling properties without
// explicit `this: T` annotations on every method.

type Point = { x: number; y: number };
type PointMethods = {
  translate(dx: number, dy: number): void;
  scale(factor: number): void;
  toString(): string;
};

function makePoint(
  x: number,
  y: number
): Point & PointMethods {
  const methods: PointMethods & ThisType<Point & PointMethods> = {
    translate(dx, dy) { this.x += dx; this.y += dy; },
    scale(factor) { this.x *= factor; this.y *= factor; },
    toString() { return `(${this.x}, ${this.y})`; },
  };
  return Object.assign({ x, y }, methods);
}

const p = makePoint(3, 4);
p.translate(1, 2);  // this.x and this.y are fully typed
console.log(p.toString()); // "(4, 6)"
```
Tradeoff: `ThisType<T>` keeps mixin object literals free of per-method `this:` annotations, resulting in cleaner, more readable factory code; it requires `noImplicitThis` to be enabled in `tsconfig.json` and only works when the object is typed through an intermediary type annotation — assigning the mixin to a plain untyped variable loses the `ThisType` context and silently falls back to an implicit `any` for `this`.

---

**P266** — Distributive `Exclude` vs. Non-Distributive `[T] extends [U]` for Union-Safe Filtering

```typescript
// Conditional types applied to bare type parameters distribute over unions.
// Wrapping in a tuple `[T] extends [U]` suppresses distribution and tests
// the whole union against U as a single type. Choose deliberately.

type IsNever<T> = [T] extends [never] ? true : false;

// Distributive — applies per member, returns union of results
type DistributedCheck<T> = T extends never ? "yes" : "no";
type D1 = DistributedCheck<never>;  // never  (distributes over empty union)
type D2 = DistributedCheck<string>; // "no"

// Non-distributive — tests the whole T
type NonDistCheck<T> = [T] extends [never] ? "yes" : "no";
type N1 = NonDistCheck<never>;  // "yes" (whole union IS never)
type N2 = NonDistCheck<string>; // "no"

// Practical: SafeUnion that checks if a computed type collapsed to never
type SafeUnion<T> = IsNever<T> extends true
  ? { error: "Computed type is never — check source union" }
  : T;

type GoodResult = SafeUnion<string | number>; // string | number
type BadResult  = SafeUnion<never>;           // { error: "..." }
```
Tradeoff: Deliberately choosing between distributive and non-distributive conditional types prevents hard-to-debug cases where `never extends never` resolves to `never` (not `true`) because the empty union distributes to nothing; the downside is that tuple-wrapping is a non-obvious convention that reads poorly to developers unfamiliar with the pattern, requiring a comment explaining why `[T] extends [U]` is used instead of `T extends U`.

---

**P267** — Branded / Opaque Types via Intersection with a Unique Symbol

```typescript
// Branded types use an intersection with a phantom marker to prevent
// structurally identical primitives from being used interchangeably,
// adding nominal typing on top of TypeScript's structural system.

declare const __brand: unique symbol;
type Brand<T, B extends string> = T & { readonly [__brand]: B };

type UserId  = Brand<string, "UserId">;
type OrderId = Brand<string, "OrderId">;

function createUserId(raw: string): UserId {
  return raw as UserId;
}
function createOrderId(raw: string): OrderId {
  return raw as OrderId;
}

function fetchUser(id: UserId): Promise<{ name: string }> {
  return Promise.resolve({ name: "Alice" });
}

const uid  = createUserId("u-123");
const oid  = createOrderId("o-456");

fetchUser(uid); // ok
// fetchUser(oid);  // Error: OrderId not assignable to UserId
// fetchUser("u-123"); // Error: plain string not assignable to UserId
```
Tradeoff: Branded types are zero-runtime-cost nominal guards that prevent domain-level confusion (passing an `OrderId` where a `UserId` is expected) without any runtime overhead; the price is that every branded value must be explicitly created through a constructor or cast, which adds boilerplate and can tempt developers into using `as UserId` at the construction site carelessly, undermining the safety guarantee at its origin.

---

**P268** — `infer` in Conditional Types for Generic Slot Extraction

```typescript
// The `infer` keyword inside a conditional type introduces a type variable
// that TypeScript fills in when the conditional matches, enabling extraction
// of nested generic slots without intermediate type aliases.

// Extract the element type from any array type
type ElementOf<T> = T extends (infer E)[] ? E : never;
type Str = ElementOf<string[]>;    // string
type Num = ElementOf<number[]>;    // number
type Mix = ElementOf<(string | number)[]>; // string | number

// Extract the value type from a Promise
type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? V : T;
type ResolvedStr = Unwrap<Promise<string>>;  // string
type Plain       = Unwrap<number>;           // number (no Promise)

// Extract both key and value from a Map
type MapKV<T> = T extends Map<infer K, infer V>
  ? { key: K; value: V }
  : never;
type KV = MapKV<Map<string, number>>; // { key: string; value: number }
```
Tradeoff: `infer` enables surgical slot extraction from arbitrarily nested generic types without requiring the original type definition to expose its inner parameters, making it the essential tool for writing library-level utility types; the limitation is that `infer` only captures one "matching" shape per position — when the same slot appears in multiple positions (e.g., `infer R` in both the key and value of a tuple), TypeScript intersects the inferences, which can produce unexpectedly wide or `never` results if the positions carry incompatible constraints.

---

**P269** — Recursive Conditional Types for Deep `Readonly<T>`

```typescript
// The built-in Readonly<T> only makes top-level properties read-only.
// A recursive conditional type descends into nested objects and arrays
// to make every property at every depth immutable.

type DeepReadonly<T> =
  T extends (infer E)[]
    ? ReadonlyArray<DeepReadonly<E>>
    : T extends object
      ? { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }
      : T;

interface Config {
  database: {
    host: string;
    port: number;
    credentials: { user: string; password: string };
  };
  features: string[];
}

type FrozenConfig = DeepReadonly<Config>;

declare const cfg: FrozenConfig;
// cfg.database.host = "x";                  // Error: read-only
// cfg.database.credentials.password = "y";  // Error: read-only
// cfg.features.push("z");                   // Error: ReadonlyArray
```
Tradeoff: `DeepReadonly<T>` enforces true immutability across nested structures so that a frozen configuration or state object cannot be mutated anywhere in the codebase without a compile error; the cost is that recursive conditional types can be slow on very deeply nested or wide types, and converting a `DeepReadonly` value back to a mutable type requires explicit `as` casts or a `DeepMutable` companion, making update patterns (e.g., immer-style mutations) awkward to type correctly.

---

**P270** — `satisfies` Operator to Preserve Literal Types While Validating Shape

```typescript
// The `satisfies` operator validates that a value matches a type without
// widening the inferred type to that type. The narrower inferred type is
// preserved, giving both safety and precision simultaneously.

type RouteConfig = Record<string, { method: "GET" | "POST" | "PUT" | "DELETE"; handler: string }>;

// Without `satisfies`: type is widened to RouteConfig — keys become `string`
const routesA: RouteConfig = {
  "/users": { method: "GET", handler: "getUsers" },
  "/users/create": { method: "POST", handler: "createUser" },
};
// routesA["/users"].method is "GET" | "POST" | "PUT" | "DELETE" (widened)

// With `satisfies`: shape is validated AND literal types are preserved
const routesB = {
  "/users": { method: "GET", handler: "getUsers" },
  "/users/create": { method: "POST", handler: "createUser" },
} satisfies RouteConfig;

// routesB["/users"].method is "GET" (preserved literal)
// Accessing a key that doesn't exist is still a compile error
const method = routesB["/users"].method; // type: "GET"
```
Tradeoff: `satisfies` is the preferred replacement for `as const` combined with a type annotation when you need both shape validation and literal-type preservation, eliminating the awkward two-step `as const satisfies T` pattern needed in earlier versions; the caveat is that `satisfies` does not change the variable's declared type — the inferred type remains the specific object literal shape, so it cannot be used directly where the broader type (e.g., `RouteConfig`) is required without an explicit upcast.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G168** — `typeof null === "object"` causes `typeof` guards to pass `null` as an object
Why this matters: TypeScript's control-flow analysis trusts `typeof strs === "object"` as a guard for object types, but JavaScript's infamous `typeof null === "object"` means `null` passes the guard. In TypeScript the narrowed type after `typeof x === "object"` is `T & object` which excludes `null` — however, if the variable's type is `string | string[] | null` and you check only `typeof x === "object"`, the compiler does narrow `null` out, but developers who combine `typeof` with truthiness (e.g., `if (strs && typeof strs === "object")`) are silently discarding the empty string `""` because falsy-check also excludes `""`. The cognitive overhead of mentally tracking which falsy value each check eliminates leads to bugs.
Fix: Always use explicit `!== null` checks instead of truthiness for nullability: `if (strs !== null && typeof strs === "object")`. For `strictNullChecks` projects, prefer discriminated unions or optional chaining over null-guard pyramids. Use a utility `isObject(x): x is Record<string, unknown>` that checks `typeof x === "object" && x !== null` to encapsulate the pattern once.

---

**G169** — `in` operator narrows both branches — types with optional matching properties appear in both the positive and negative branch
Why this matters: When `"swim" in animal` is used to distinguish `Fish` from `Bird | Human` where `Human` has an optional `swim?: () => void`, TypeScript narrows the positive branch to `Fish | Human` (both have `swim`, even optionally) and the negative branch to `Bird | Human` (neither is excluded). Developers assume `"swim" in animal` fully isolates `Fish` into the positive branch and are surprised to find that `Human` appears in both, requiring additional narrowing or a type predicate.
Fix: Replace `in`-based narrowing for optional properties with an explicit user-defined type predicate that checks for the property's presence AND its type: `function isFish(a: Fish | Bird | Human): a is Fish { return typeof (a as Fish).swim === "function"; }`. Alternatively, use a discriminant literal property (`kind: "fish"`) to ensure each branch is uniquely identified, which is the idiomatic TypeScript approach for multi-variant unions.

---

**G170** — `Partial<T>` does not make nested objects partial — only the top-level properties become optional
Why this matters: `Partial<Config>` makes `config.database` optional, but if `database` is present it is still typed as the full `{ host: string; port: number; credentials: { user: string; password: string } }` — `config.database.port` is still required. Developers building update-patch helpers expect `Partial<Config>` to allow `{ database: { host: "x" } }` (omitting `port` and `credentials`) and are surprised by compile errors.
Fix: Use a recursive `DeepPartial<T>` type: `type DeepPartial<T> = T extends object ? { [K in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[K]> } : T`. For simple two-level nesting, `Partial<T> & { [K in keyof T]?: Partial<T[K]> }` covers most practical cases. Libraries like `ts-essentials` export a battle-tested `DeepPartial` that handles arrays and edge cases, which is preferable to rolling a custom recursive type in production code.

---

**G171** — Exhaustiveness checks break silently when the `never` assignment is wrapped in a function call
Why this matters: The canonical exhaustiveness pattern `const _: never = shape` works because TypeScript verifies the assignment at the `default` branch. However, `assertNever(shape)` where `assertNever` is `function assertNever(x: never): never { throw new Error(…) }` only works if TypeScript can infer that `shape` has type `never` at the call site. If the `switch` statement is missing a case, TypeScript emits the error on the `assertNever(shape)` call. But if `shape` is re-assigned or passed through a generic intermediary before reaching `assertNever`, the `never` widening is lost and the error disappears — the union member silently falls through to `assertNever` without a compile error.
Fix: Prefer the inline assignment `const _: never = shape` over a helper function for exhaustiveness at switch sites, as it directly constrains the type at the point of assignment. When using `assertNever`, ensure the value passed is typed exactly as the switch discriminant — avoid intermediate variables or generic wrappers that might broaden the type before the call.

---

**G172** — Non-null assertions (`!`) on discriminated-union optional fields hide structural design problems
Why this matters: When a union uses a shared interface with optional properties instead of true discriminated union members (e.g., `interface Shape { kind: "circle" | "square"; radius?: number; side?: number }`), accessing `shape.radius` after checking `shape.kind === "circle"` still produces `number | undefined` because the type does not structurally link `kind: "circle"` to `radius: number`. Developers apply `shape.radius!` to silence the error, but this masks the fact that the type design allows a `{ kind: "circle" }` value with no `radius` to flow through the same code path, causing a runtime `NaN` or crash.
Fix: Replace shared-optional-property unions with proper discriminated union members where each variant carries only its own required fields: `type Shape = { kind: "circle"; radius: number } | { kind: "square"; side: number }`. This restructuring eliminates all `!` assertions by making the structural link between the discriminant and its payload explicit, and TypeScript narrows `radius` to `number` (not `number | undefined`) after the `kind === "circle"` check.

---

## Cycle 63 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 271** — Mapped Type Modifier Removal with `-readonly` and `-?`
```typescript
// Concrete<T> removes all optional and readonly modifiers simultaneously,
// converting a partially-specified config shape into a fully-required one
// that can be safely destructured without undefined guards.

type Concrete<T> = {
  -readonly [K in keyof T]-?: T[K];
};

interface PartialConfig {
  readonly host?: string;
  readonly port?: number;
  readonly timeout?: number;
  readonly retries?: number;
}

// All fields are now required and mutable
type ResolvedConfig = Concrete<PartialConfig>;
// { host: string; port: number; timeout: number; retries: number; }

function applyDefaults(overrides: PartialConfig): ResolvedConfig {
  return {
    host: overrides.host ?? "localhost",
    port: overrides.port ?? 3000,
    timeout: overrides.timeout ?? 5000,
    retries: overrides.retries ?? 3,
  };
}

const cfg = applyDefaults({ port: 8080 });
cfg.host = "example.com"; // ✅ mutable — not readonly any more
```
Tradeoff: Stripping `readonly` at the type level does not prevent accidental mutation in callers that received the value through a broader type annotation — if `ResolvedConfig` is stored in a variable typed as `PartialConfig`, TypeScript re-applies `readonly`; the safety benefit is therefore scoped to the function's internal logic, and using `Concrete<T>` in a public API can mislead callers into assuming the returned object is always safe to mutate.

---

**Pattern 272** — Key Remapping via `as` Clause in Mapped Types
```typescript
// Remap keys to getter/setter method names using template literals
// inside the `as` clause, building a full accessor interface from a
// plain data shape without any manual repetition.

type Getters<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K];
};

type Setters<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as `set${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: (value: T[K]) => void;
};

type Accessors<T> = Getters<T> & Setters<T>;

interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
}

// Accessors<User> expands to:
// { getId: () => number; getName: () => string; getEmail: () => string;
//   setId: (value: number) => void; setName: (value: string) => void;
//   setEmail: (value: string) => void; }

function makeAccessors<T extends object>(obj: T): Accessors<T> {
  const result = {} as Accessors<T>;
  for (const key of Object.keys(obj) as Array<keyof T & string>) {
    const capKey = (key[0].toUpperCase() + key.slice(1)) as Capitalize<typeof key>;
    (result as any)[`get${capKey}`] = () => obj[key];
    (result as any)[`set${capKey}`] = (v: T[typeof key]) => { obj[key] = v; };
  }
  return result;
}
```
Tradeoff: Key remapping with `Capitalize` only operates on `string & K` because symbol keys cannot be capitalized at the type level; if the source type contains symbol-keyed properties they are silently dropped from the remapped type, so this pattern is unsuitable for types that mix string and symbol keys (e.g., types using `Symbol.iterator`).

---

**Pattern 273** — Filtering Mapped Type Keys to `never` for Selective Inclusion
```typescript
// Produce a filtered view of a type that retains only properties whose
// value types extend a given target — for example, extract only the
// string fields from a mixed record.

type PickByValue<T, V> = {
  [K in keyof T as T[K] extends V ? K : never]: T[K];
};

interface FormData {
  userId: number;
  username: string;
  email: string;
  age: number;
  bio: string;
  verified: boolean;
}

// Picks only string fields
type StringFields = PickByValue<FormData, string>;
// { username: string; email: string; bio: string; }

// Picks only numeric fields
type NumericFields = PickByValue<FormData, number>;
// { userId: number; age: number; }

// Combine with template literals for typed form validation
type StringFieldKeys = keyof PickByValue<FormData, string>;
// "username" | "email" | "bio"

function validateStringField(key: StringFieldKeys, value: string): boolean {
  return value.trim().length > 0;
}
```
Tradeoff: Because `T[K] extends V` uses structural compatibility rather than exact type equality, a field typed as `string | null` does NOT extend `string` and is excluded, while a field typed as a string literal `"admin"` IS included because string literals extend `string`; this asymmetry is surprising when filtering nullable fields, requiring the caller to use `PickByValue<T, string | null>` explicitly when nullables should be retained.

---

**Pattern 274** — Template Literal Types for Type-Safe Event Emitter
```typescript
// Encode event names as template literal types so that registering a
// listener for "firstNameChanged" automatically infers the callback
// argument as `string` (the type of `firstName` on the source object),
// closing the gap between event name strings and their payload types.

type PropEventSource<T> = {
  on<K extends string & keyof T>(
    event: `${K}Changed`,
    cb: (newValue: T[K]) => void
  ): void;
  off<K extends string & keyof T>(
    event: `${K}Changed`,
    cb: (newValue: T[K]) => void
  ): void;
};

function makeObservable<T extends object>(target: T): T & PropEventSource<T> {
  const listeners = new Map<string, Set<Function>>();
  const proxy = new Proxy(target, {
    set(obj, prop: string, value) {
      obj[prop as keyof T] = value;
      listeners.get(`${prop}Changed`)?.forEach(fn => fn(value));
      return true;
    },
  });
  (proxy as any).on = (event: string, cb: Function) => {
    if (!listeners.has(event)) listeners.set(event, new Set());
    listeners.get(event)!.add(cb);
  };
  (proxy as any).off = (event: string, cb: Function) => {
    listeners.get(event)?.delete(cb);
  };
  return proxy as T & PropEventSource<T>;
}

const user = makeObservable({ firstName: "Alice", age: 30 });
user.on("firstNameChanged", name => name.toUpperCase()); // name: string ✅
user.on("ageChanged", age => age + 1);                   // age: number ✅
// user.on("firstName", () => {}); // ❌ compile error — must end in "Changed"
```
Tradeoff: Template literal inference requires that the generic `K` be resolved at the call site from the literal event name string; if the event name is stored in a `const` variable with a widened `string` type rather than a string literal type, TypeScript cannot narrow `K` and the callback argument degrades to `T[string & keyof T]` (the union of all property types), losing the per-property type safety that makes this pattern valuable.

---

**Pattern 275** — `infer` with Multiple Positions for Tuple Decomposition
```typescript
// Use `infer` in multiple positions within a single conditional type to
// decompose tuple types into their head and tail, enabling purely
// type-level list processing such as reversing, zipping, or flattening.

type Head<T extends readonly unknown[]> =
  T extends readonly [infer H, ...infer _] ? H : never;

type Tail<T extends readonly unknown[]> =
  T extends readonly [infer _, ...infer T] ? T : [];

type Last<T extends readonly unknown[]> =
  T extends readonly [...infer _, infer L] ? L : never;

type Reverse<T extends readonly unknown[]> =
  T extends readonly [infer H, ...infer Rest]
    ? [...Reverse<Rest>, H]
    : [];

// Usage examples
type H = Head<[string, number, boolean]>;   // string
type Ta = Tail<[string, number, boolean]>;  // [number, boolean]
type L = Last<[string, number, boolean]>;   // boolean
type R = Reverse<[1, 2, 3]>;               // [3, 2, 1]

// Practical: strongly typed pipe of two function steps
type PipeReturn<A extends (...args: any[]) => any, B extends (arg: ReturnType<A>) => any> =
  ReturnType<B>;

declare function pipe<A extends (...args: any[]) => any, B extends (arg: ReturnType<A>) => any>(
  a: A, b: B
): (...args: Parameters<A>) => PipeReturn<A, B>;
```
Tradeoff: TypeScript enforces a default recursion depth cap (roughly 100 levels) for recursive conditional types; `Reverse<T>` on a tuple with more than ~50 elements hits the instantiation depth limit and produces `Type instantiation is excessively deep` errors, making this approach unsuitable for variadic tuples of unbounded length — at which point a runtime approach with `as const` satisfies is more practical.

---

**Pattern 276** — Distributive vs. Non-Distributive Conditional Types via Bracket Wrapping
```typescript
// By default, a conditional type distributes over unions when the checked
// type is a bare type parameter. Wrapping both sides in brackets disables
// distribution, treating the union as a single atomic type — a subtle but
// critical distinction when building set-operation utilities.

// Distributive — checks each union member independently
type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;
type D = IsString<string | number>; // true | false (distributed)

// Non-distributive — checks the union as a whole unit
type IsStringND<T> = [T] extends [string] ? true : false;
type ND = IsStringND<string | number>; // false (union is not a subtype of string)

// Practical: build a non-distributive Equals check
type Equals<A, B> = [A] extends [B] ? ([B] extends [A] ? true : false) : false;

type E1 = Equals<string, string>;          // true
type E2 = Equals<string, string | number>; // false
type E3 = Equals<string | number, string>; // false
type E4 = Equals<never, never>;            // true

// Filter out union members that are exactly `never`
type NonNeverMembers<T> = T extends never ? never : T;
type NN = NonNeverMembers<string | never | number>; // string | number
```
Tradeoff: The `Equals<A, B>` double-bracket trick is reliable for most structural type comparisons but produces false positives for types involving `any`, because `[any] extends [string]` evaluates to `true` (`any` is simultaneously assignable to and from every type); code using `Equals` as a type guard in assertion helpers must document this limitation and add an explicit `Equals<A, any> extends true` early-exit guard if `any` values may appear.

---

**Pattern 277** — Recursive Mapped Types for Deep `Readonly<T>`
```typescript
// TypeScript's built-in `Readonly<T>` only freezes the top level of an
// object. A recursive variant uses a conditional type to descend into
// nested objects and arrays, giving a truly immutable type for use in
// state management or configuration modules.

type DeepReadonly<T> =
  T extends (infer U)[]
    ? ReadonlyArray<DeepReadonly<U>>
    : T extends object
      ? { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }
      : T;

interface AppState {
  user: { name: string; roles: string[] };
  settings: { theme: "light" | "dark"; features: { beta: boolean } };
}

type ImmutableState = DeepReadonly<AppState>;
// {
//   readonly user: { readonly name: string; readonly roles: ReadonlyArray<string> };
//   readonly settings: { readonly theme: "light"|"dark";
//                        readonly features: { readonly beta: boolean } };
// }

function reducer(state: ImmutableState): ImmutableState {
  // state.user.name = "Bob"; // ❌ compile error
  return { ...state, user: { ...state.user, name: "Bob" } };
}
```
Tradeoff: `DeepReadonly<T>` loses its protection when a property's type is a generic class instance (e.g., `Map<K, V>` or `Set<T>`), because those extend `object` and get their properties recursively frozen — but `Map.prototype.set` is still callable at runtime since the prototype chain methods are not included in the mapped type; for collections, wrap with `ReadonlyMap<K, V>` / `ReadonlySet<T>` explicitly.

---

**Pattern 278** — `NoInfer<T>` Utility Type to Suppress Contextual Inference
```typescript
// TypeScript 5.4 introduced `NoInfer<T>` to prevent a specific call-site
// argument from contributing to generic type inference, forcing the
// inferred type to be determined by other arguments alone. This eliminates
// a class of bugs where a default value silently widens an inferred union.

// Without NoInfer: `default` widens the inferred T to `string | number`
function createSlotBad<T>(initial: T, fallback: T): T {
  return initial ?? fallback;
}
const badResult = createSlotBad("active", 0);
// T inferred as string | number — not what the caller intended

// With NoInfer: `fallback` cannot influence T; T is inferred only from `initial`
function createSlot<T>(initial: T, fallback: NoInfer<T>): T {
  return initial ?? fallback;
}

const goodResult = createSlot("active", "inactive"); // T = string ✅
// createSlot("active", 0); // ❌ Argument of type 'number' is not assignable to NoInfer<string>

// Practical: typed config factory where defaults cannot change the key set
function defineConfig<const T extends Record<string, unknown>>(
  schema: T,
  defaults: Partial<NoInfer<T>>
): T & typeof defaults {
  return { ...defaults, ...schema } as T & typeof defaults;
}
```
Tradeoff: `NoInfer<T>` is only available from TypeScript 5.4 onwards; projects locked to earlier versions must replicate the behaviour by splitting the generic into two type parameters with a constraint (`function f<T, U extends T>(a: T, b: U): T`) which achieves the same "don't infer from this argument" semantics but is more verbose and does not integrate as cleanly with utility-type chains.

---

**Pattern 279** — `infer` with `extends` Constraints in the `infer` Clause
```typescript
// TypeScript 4.7+ allows placing an `extends` constraint directly on an
// `infer` variable, making the conditional type evaluate to `never` if
// the inferred type does not satisfy the constraint — enabling precise
// extraction without a secondary conditional layer.

// Old approach: two nested conditionals
type StringReturnOld<T> =
  T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R
    ? R extends string ? R : never
    : never;

// New approach (TS 4.7+): constraint directly on infer
type StringReturn<T> =
  T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R extends string ? R : never;

declare function getLabel(): "error" | "warning" | "info";
declare function getCount(): number;

type LabelType = StringReturn<typeof getLabel>; // "error" | "warning" | "info"
type CountType = StringReturn<typeof getCount>; // never

// Extract the resolved value from a Promise only if it is an array
type ArrayAwaited<T> =
  T extends Promise<infer V extends unknown[]> ? V : never;

type UnwrappedArray = ArrayAwaited<Promise<string[]>>;  // string[]
type UnwrappedScalar = ArrayAwaited<Promise<string>>;   // never
```
Tradeoff: Constrained `infer` only evaluates the constraint against the structurally inferred type, not against the full union after distribution; for a generic `T = Promise<string> | Promise<number[]>`, the distributive evaluation infers `string` (does not extend `unknown[]` → `never`) and `number[]` (extends `unknown[]` → `number[]`), giving `never | number[]` = `number[]`, which is correct — but developers not familiar with distribution may expect `never` when `T` is a union that mixes matching and non-matching members.

---

**Pattern 280** — Variance Annotation (`in`, `out`, `in out`) on Generic Type Parameters
```typescript
// TypeScript 4.7 introduced explicit variance annotations on type parameters
// to let the compiler skip expensive structural compatibility checks and to
// document the intended subtyping relationship directly in the type definition.

// `out T` = covariant (producer): a Container<Dog> is assignable to Container<Animal>
type Producer<out T> = { produce: () => T };

// `in T`  = contravariant (consumer): a Consumer<Animal> is assignable to Consumer<Dog>
type Consumer<in T> = { consume: (val: T) => void };

// `in out T` = invariant: no subtyping between different T
type ReadWrite<in out T> = { get: () => T; set: (val: T) => void };

interface Animal { breathe(): void; }
interface Dog extends Animal { bark(): void; }

declare const dogProducer: Producer<Dog>;
const animalProducer: Producer<Animal> = dogProducer; // ✅ covariance

declare const animalConsumer: Consumer<Animal>;
const dogConsumer: Consumer<Dog> = animalConsumer;    // ✅ contravariance

declare const dogStore: ReadWrite<Dog>;
// const animalStore: ReadWrite<Animal> = dogStore;   // ❌ invariant — blocked
```
Tradeoff: Variance annotations are enforced by the compiler — if you annotate `out T` but the type actually uses `T` in a consumer position (e.g., as a function parameter), TypeScript raises a `Type parameter 'T' is declared as 'out' but is used as 'in'` error, which acts as a useful correctness check; however, in complex types that are both produced and consumed (e.g., `Array<T>`), the annotation must be `in out T` (invariant), which means the annotation provides no inference speedup and simply documents intent without changing behavior.

**Pattern 281** — Template Literal Types for Route Parameter Extraction
```typescript
// Parse URL path parameters from a route pattern string at the type level,
// building a typed params object without any code generation step.

type ExtractRouteParams<T extends string> =
  T extends `${infer _Start}:${infer Param}/${infer Rest}`
    ? { [K in Param | keyof ExtractRouteParams<`/${Rest}`>]: string }
    : T extends `${infer _Start}:${infer Param}`
      ? { [K in Param]: string }
      : {};

type UserRoute = ExtractRouteParams<"/users/:userId/posts/:postId">;
// { userId: string; postId: string; }

type ShallowRoute = ExtractRouteParams<"/items/:id">;
// { id: string; }

type StaticRoute = ExtractRouteParams<"/health">;
// {}

declare function route<P extends string>(
  pattern: P,
  handler: (params: ExtractRouteParams<P>) => Response
): void;

route("/users/:userId/posts/:postId", ({ userId, postId }) => {
  // userId: string, postId: string — fully typed ✅
  return new Response(`User ${userId}, Post ${postId}`);
});
```
Tradeoff: This pattern works for simple `:param` style routes but breaks down for optional parameters (`:param?`), wildcard segments (`*`), or regex-constrained parameters (`/:id(\\d+)`), because template literal matching is purely structural string pattern matching with no notion of optionality; extending the extractor to handle these cases requires adding separate conditional branches for each syntax variant, quickly making the type definition unmaintainable — at which point a code-generation approach producing explicit param types per route is more robust.

---

**Pattern 282** — `const` Type Parameters for Literal Inference Without `as const`
```typescript
// TypeScript 5.0 introduced `const` on a type parameter, instructing
// the compiler to infer the argument as if `as const` were applied,
// preserving tuple structure, readonly arrays, and literal types without
// requiring the call site to annotate every argument.

// Without const: T is inferred as string[] (widened)
function tagsBad<T extends string[]>(tags: T): T { return tags; }
const t1 = tagsBad(["a", "b"]); // string[]

// With const: T is inferred as readonly ["a", "b"] (preserved literals)
function tags<const T extends readonly string[]>(values: T): T { return values; }
const t2 = tags(["a", "b"]); // readonly ["a", "b"]

// Practical: type-safe pick that returns a tuple of the picked keys
function pick<const K extends readonly (keyof any)[], T extends Record<K[number], unknown>>(
  obj: T,
  keys: K
): Pick<T, K[number]> {
  return Object.fromEntries(keys.map(k => [k, obj[k]])) as Pick<T, K[number]>;
}

const user = { id: 1, name: "Alice", role: "admin", password: "s3cr3t" };
const safe = pick(user, ["id", "name"] as const);
// Type: { id: number; name: string; } — password excluded ✅
```
Tradeoff: `const` type parameters work only when the argument is an inline array or object literal; if the value is stored in a variable before the function call, the variable's type has already been widened and the `const` modifier has no effect — the call site must still use `as const` on the variable declaration, which means `const` type parameters solve the ergonomics problem only for inline call patterns.

---

**Pattern 283** — Branded / Nominal Types Using `unique symbol` Intersection
```typescript
// TypeScript's structural type system treats `type UserId = string` and
// `type OrderId = string` as identical. Branding with a unique symbol
// creates a nominally distinct type that cannot be accidentally interchanged.

declare const _brand: unique symbol;
type Brand<T, B extends string> = T & { readonly [_brand]: B };

type UserId  = Brand<string, "UserId">;
type OrderId = Brand<string, "OrderId">;
type Dollars = Brand<number, "Dollars">;

// Constructor functions act as trusted entry points
const UserId  = (id: string): UserId   => id as UserId;
const OrderId = (id: string): OrderId  => id as OrderId;
const Dollars = (n: number): Dollars   => n as Dollars;

function fetchOrder(userId: UserId, orderId: OrderId): void { /* ... */ }

const uid = UserId("user-123");
const oid = OrderId("order-456");

fetchOrder(uid, oid);  // ✅
// fetchOrder(oid, uid); // ❌ Argument of type 'OrderId' not assignable to 'UserId'
// fetchOrder("user-123", "order-456"); // ❌ string is not Brand<string, "UserId">
```
Tradeoff: Branded types require every value to pass through a constructor function that casts with `as Brand<T, B>`, meaning the safety guarantee is only as strong as the discipline around those cast functions — a developer who writes `"raw-string" as UserId` bypasses the brand entirely; consider pairing with a linting rule or a runtime validator that returns the branded type only after validating format constraints (e.g., UUID format check) to prevent brand abuse.

---

**Pattern 284** — `satisfies` Combined with `as const` for Typed Constant Tables
```typescript
// Using `satisfies` with `as const` validates the shape of a constant
// table at definition time while preserving the most-specific literal
// types for all entries, enabling safe exhaustive lookups without widening.

type StatusConfig = {
  label: string;
  color: "green" | "yellow" | "red" | "gray";
  retryable: boolean;
};

const STATUS_MAP = {
  success:  { label: "Success",  color: "green",  retryable: false },
  pending:  { label: "Pending",  color: "yellow", retryable: true  },
  failed:   { label: "Failed",   color: "red",    retryable: true  },
  canceled: { label: "Canceled", color: "gray",   retryable: false },
} as const satisfies Record<string, StatusConfig>;

type Status = keyof typeof STATUS_MAP; // "success" | "pending" | "failed" | "canceled"

function getStatusColor(s: Status): typeof STATUS_MAP[Status]["color"] {
  return STATUS_MAP[s].color;
}

// Literal type preserved: STATUS_MAP.success.color is "green", not "green"|"yellow"|"red"|"gray"
const c = STATUS_MAP.success.color; // type: "green"
```
Tradeoff: The `as const satisfies T` idiom (TypeScript 4.9+) only validates that the object conforms to `T` at the point of declaration — it does not prevent runtime mutation if the object is passed to a function accepting `Record<string, StatusConfig>`, which does not carry the `as const` constraint; for tables that must never be modified at runtime, combine this pattern with `Object.freeze()` and ensure the exported symbol is typed as `typeof STATUS_MAP` rather than the broader `Record<string, StatusConfig>` to preserve narrowed types in consumers.

**Pattern 285** — Recursive Conditional Type for `Awaited<T>` Deep Promise Unwrapping
```typescript
// The built-in `Awaited<T>` utility type recursively unwraps nested
// Promises, but implementing a custom variant illustrates how to write
// a recursive conditional type that terminates safely and handles
// thenable objects (objects with a `.then` method) in addition to
// native Promises.

type DeepAwaited<T> =
  T extends null | undefined
    ? T
    : T extends object & { then(onfulfilled: infer F, ...args: infer _): any }
      ? F extends (value: infer V, ...args: infer _) => any
        ? DeepAwaited<V>
        : never
      : T;

// Scalar — no unwrapping needed
type A = DeepAwaited<string>;                         // string
// Single Promise
type B = DeepAwaited<Promise<number>>;                // number
// Nested Promises
type C = DeepAwaited<Promise<Promise<boolean>>>;      // boolean
// Custom thenable
type MyThenable = { then(cb: (v: Date) => void): void };
type D = DeepAwaited<MyThenable>;                     // Date
// null / undefined pass through unchanged
type E = DeepAwaited<null>;                           // null

// Practical: unwrap the resolved value of an async factory
async function fetchUser(): Promise<{ id: string; name: string }> {
  return { id: "1", name: "Alice" };
}
type UserPayload = DeepAwaited<ReturnType<typeof fetchUser>>;
// { id: string; name: string; }
```
Tradeoff: The recursive thenable-based `DeepAwaited<T>` matches any object with a `.then` method, including non-Promise classes that use `.then` for chaining (e.g., some query builder fluent APIs), inadvertently unwrapping their resolved value types; in codebases mixing Promises with fluent `.then` builders, prefer a more restrictive variant that checks for `Promise<infer V>` directly rather than the thenable protocol to avoid false unwrapping.

### Community Gotchas

**G173** — Template literal union cross-multiplication creates exponential type complexity
Why this matters: When multiple union types appear inside a template literal type (e.g., `` `${A | B}_${C | D}_${E | F}` ``), TypeScript eagerly computes the full Cartesian product at compile time. Three unions of four members each produce 64 string literal members; four unions of five members each produce 625 members. Beyond a few hundred members, the compiler emits `Expression produces a union type that is too complex to represent` and the type collapses to `string`, silently losing all type safety. This typically surfaces when combining HTTP methods, resource names, and lifecycle hooks into a single event-string type.
Fix: Decompose the event type into structured tagged objects (`{ resource: "user" | "order"; action: "created" | "updated"; lifecycle: "before" | "after" }`) and derive event names only when displaying them, rather than encoding all dimensions into a single string literal union. Alternatively, compute sub-unions per dimension and intersect them using a helper type, so the full cross-product is never materialized as a flat string union.

---

**G174** — `keyof` on an intersection type yields a union, not an intersection of keys
Why this matters: Developers expect `keyof (A & B)` to return only the keys present in both `A` and `B` (i.e., an intersection of key sets), but TypeScript returns `keyof A | keyof B` — every key from either type. This means a mapped type iterating `keyof (A & B)` will attempt to access properties that may not exist on one of the constituent types, and `(A & B)[K]` resolves to `never` for keys not shared, silently producing `never`-typed fields in the mapped result. The symmetric inverse also surprises: `keyof (A | B)` returns `keyof A & keyof B` (intersection of key sets), which is the behavior developers incorrectly expect from `&`.
Fix: When you need keys common to both `A` and `B`, use `keyof A & keyof B` explicitly rather than `keyof (A & B)`. When building a `Merge<A, B>` type that overlays B's properties on A, use `Omit<A, keyof B> & B` to ensure the mapped iteration produces correctly typed fields without `never` entries.

---

**G175** — Excess property checking only applies to fresh object literals, not to variables
Why this matters: TypeScript enforces excess property checking when an object literal is passed directly to a function or assigned to a typed variable, flagging `{ name: "x", unknownProp: true }` as an error if `unknownProp` is not in the target type. However, when the same object is first stored in a variable typed as `Record<string, unknown>` or inferred as a wider type and then passed, the excess property check is bypassed entirely — TypeScript only checks structural compatibility, which is satisfied. Developers relying on TypeScript to catch misspelled config keys (e.g., `retries` vs `retry`) are surprised when the misspelled key appears in a variable first.
Fix: Pass config object literals inline at the call site rather than through intermediate variables when the target type's excess property checking is the intended safety net. For runtime validation of external config objects (loaded from JSON or environment variables), use a schema validation library (zod, valibot) that checks properties at runtime independently of how the object reached the validator.

---

**G176** — `ReturnType<T>` resolves to the last overload signature, not the most specific
Why this matters: When `T` is an overloaded function, `ReturnType<typeof fn>` does not produce a union of all return types — it resolves to the return type of the last (most general) call signature in the overload list. For a function overloaded as `(x: string) => number` and `(x: number) => string`, the implementation signature `(x: string | number) => string | number` is what `ReturnType` sees if it is listed last, returning `string | number` instead of the per-call-type-dependent return. This causes type-narrowed callers to receive a broader type than expected.
Fix: Avoid `ReturnType` on overloaded functions; instead, define the per-input return types using conditional types: `type R<T extends string | number> = T extends string ? number : string`. For library functions whose overloads you do not control, extract the specific overload's type by casting: `type Specific = typeof fn extends (x: string) => infer R ? R : never`.

---

**G177** — Mapped types over `any` produce `any`, silently bypassing key constraints
Why this matters: When a mapped type iterates `keyof T` and `T` is `any`, `keyof any` evaluates to `string | number | symbol`, and the mapped result type is `any`. This means `Partial<any>`, `Required<any>`, and custom mapped types all return `any` rather than raising an error or returning the expected constrained shape. In generic utility code that accepts a type parameter without an explicit non-`any` constraint, passing `any` propagates `any` through the entire mapped type chain, erasing all type safety silently.
Fix: Add an explicit `extends object` (or a stricter non-`any` constraint) to the type parameter of mapped type utilities: `type MyPartial<T extends object> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }`. This causes `MyPartial<any>` to still satisfy the constraint (because `any` extends everything), but signals intent and prevents accidental `any` usage from collapsing complex mapped type chains in libraries that rely on those utilities for type inference.

### Patterns

**Pattern 286** — Mapped Type with `as` Clause for Getter Method Generation
```typescript
// Transform an interface into a companion object with strongly-typed getters
// using key remapping via the `as` clause (TypeScript 4.1+).
type Getters<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K];
};

interface Config {
  host: string;
  port: number;
  secure: boolean;
}

type ConfigGetters = Getters<Config>;
// { getHost: () => string; getPort: () => number; getSecure: () => boolean; }

// Compose with a concrete object that provides the getter implementations:
function makeGetters<T extends object>(obj: T): T & Getters<T> {
  const result = { ...obj } as T & Getters<T>;
  for (const key of Object.keys(obj) as (keyof T)[]) {
    const getter = `get${String(key).charAt(0).toUpperCase() + String(key).slice(1)}`;
    (result as Record<string, unknown>)[getter] = () => obj[key];
  }
  return result;
}

const cfg = makeGetters({ host: "localhost", port: 3000, secure: false });
cfg.getHost();   // string
cfg.getPort();   // number
```
Tradeoff: The `Capitalize<string & K>` intersection is required because `K` is `keyof T` (i.e., `string | number | symbol`), and `Capitalize` only accepts `string`; however, numeric keys (e.g., `0`, `1`) are silently dropped from the mapped output because `string & 0` evaluates to `never`, meaning tuple types or objects with numeric index keys produce an incomplete getter map without a compile-time warning.

**Pattern 287** — Conditional Type with `infer` for Flattening Nested Arrays
```typescript
// Recursively unwrap nested array types to their element type
// using a self-referential conditional type.
type DeepFlatten<T> = T extends ReadonlyArray<infer Item>
  ? DeepFlatten<Item>
  : T;

// Scalar — no unwrapping
type A = DeepFlatten<string>;                   // string
// Single nesting
type B = DeepFlatten<number[]>;                 // number
// Double nesting
type C = DeepFlatten<boolean[][]>;              // boolean
// Triple nesting with readonly
type D = DeepFlatten<readonly (readonly Date[])[]>;  // Date

// Practical: derive the leaf element type of any collection pipeline
declare function flattenDeep<T>(arr: T): DeepFlatten<T>[];
const result = flattenDeep([[[1, 2], [3]], [[4]]]);
// result: number[]

// Works with heterogeneous unions
type E = DeepFlatten<string[] | number[][]>;    // string | number
```
Tradeoff: Because TypeScript's recursion depth for conditional types is capped (approximately 100 levels), `DeepFlatten` will produce a `Type instantiation is excessively deep` error on arrays nested beyond ~20 levels deep at compile time; in practice this is rarely a problem, but when consuming deeply nested JSON schemas programmatically generated at compile time, prefer explicit depth-bounded variants (`Flatten1`, `Flatten2`, etc.) composed via union.
