**Pattern 288** — Template Literal Type for Type-Safe CSS Custom Properties
```typescript
// Build a typed interface for CSS custom properties (CSS variables)
// ensuring all keys begin with `--` and values are valid CSS value strings.
type CSSCustomProperty = `--${string}`;

type CSSVariableMap = Record<CSSCustomProperty, string>;

// Narrow to a specific design token vocabulary:
type ColorToken = "primary" | "secondary" | "accent" | "muted";
type SpacingToken = "xs" | "sm" | "md" | "lg" | "xl";

type DesignTokenVar =
  | `--color-${ColorToken}`
  | `--spacing-${SpacingToken}`;

type DesignTokens = Record<DesignTokenVar, string>;

const tokens: DesignTokens = {
  "--color-primary": "#3b82f6",
  "--color-secondary": "#64748b",
  "--color-accent": "#f59e0b",
  "--color-muted": "#94a3b8",
  "--spacing-xs": "4px",
  "--spacing-sm": "8px",
  "--spacing-md": "16px",
  "--spacing-lg": "24px",
  "--spacing-xl": "32px",
};

// Type error: "--color-danger" is not assignable to DesignTokenVar
// tokens["--color-danger"] = "red";

function applyTokens(el: HTMLElement, map: DesignTokens): void {
  for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(map)) {
    el.style.setProperty(key, value);
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: Using `Record<DesignTokenVar, string>` requires all 9 token keys to be present (it is not `Partial`), so adding a new token category demands updating every call site that constructs a full `DesignTokens` object; in large teams with many token consumers, prefer `Partial<Record<DesignTokenVar, string>>` or a builder pattern to allow incremental population.

---

**Pattern 289** — `satisfies` Operator for Validated Config Without Widening
```typescript
// `satisfies` (TypeScript 4.9) validates an expression against a type
// while preserving the narrowest inferred literal type for the variable.
type LogLevel = "debug" | "info" | "warn" | "error";

type AppConfig = {
  logLevel: LogLevel;
  port: number;
  origins: string[];
  features: Record<string, boolean>;
};

// With `as AppConfig`, logLevel would widen to LogLevel (string union).
// With `satisfies`, the literal type "info" is preserved.
const config = {
  logLevel: "info",
  port: 3000,
  origins: ["https://example.com"],
  features: { darkMode: true, betaApi: false },
} satisfies AppConfig;

// Narrow literal type is preserved:
type LogLevelType = typeof config.logLevel;  // "info" (not LogLevel)
type PortType = typeof config.port;           // 3000 (not number)

// Type safety is still enforced — this would error:
// const bad = { logLevel: "verbose", port: "not-a-number" } satisfies AppConfig;

// Also useful for validating exhaustive lookup tables:
const httpStatus = {
  ok: 200,
  notFound: 404,
  serverError: 500,
} satisfies Record<string, number>;

// Autocomplete on the exact keys works (not widened to Record<string, number>):
httpStatus.ok;        // 200 (literal, not number)
httpStatus.notFound;  // 404 (literal, not number)
```
Tradeoff: `satisfies` performs structural validation at the expression site only — it does not propagate the type constraint to downstream reassignment, so a variable declared with `let config = { ... } satisfies AppConfig` can still be reassigned to a structurally incompatible object without error if `config`'s inferred type (widened from the literal) happens to match; pair `satisfies` with `const` declarations or `as const satisfies` for full immutability and literal preservation.

---

**Pattern 290** — Distributive Conditional Type Suppression via Tuple Wrapping
```typescript
// By default, conditional types distribute over union members when the
// checked type is a bare type parameter. Wrapping in a tuple prevents this.
type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;

// Distributive (default): distributes over each union member
type D1 = IsString<string | number>;  // boolean  (true | false)
type D2 = IsString<string>;           // true
type D3 = IsString<number>;           // false

// Non-distributive: wrapping prevents distribution — treats union as a whole
type IsStringNonDist<T> = [T] extends [string] ? true : false;

type ND1 = IsStringNonDist<string | number>;  // false (string|number is not string)
type ND2 = IsStringNonDist<string>;           // true
type ND3 = IsStringNonDist<never>;            // false (not true like distributive)

// Practical use: exact union equality check
type Equals<A, B> = [A] extends [B] ? ([B] extends [A] ? true : false) : false;
type E1 = Equals<string | number, number | string>;  // true
type E2 = Equals<string, string | number>;           // false
type E3 = Equals<never, never>;                      // true

// Practical use: IsNever — distributive version gives wrong answer
type IsNeverDist<T> = T extends never ? true : false;
type Bad = IsNeverDist<never>;       // never (not true!)
type IsNever<T> = [T] extends [never] ? true : false;
type Good = IsNever<never>;          // true
```
Tradeoff: Non-distributive conditionals are necessary for `IsNever<T>` and union equality checks, but they make the mental model harder to follow because `[T] extends [string]` reads as "a 1-tuple is assignable to a 1-tuple" — reviewers unfamiliar with the pattern will question why a tuple is used instead of the direct form; always add a comment explaining the suppression intent to prevent well-meaning refactors from removing the brackets.

---

**Pattern 291** — `infer` with Constraints in the `infer` Clause for Narrowed Extraction
```typescript
// TypeScript 4.7+ allows `infer R extends SomeType` to constrain
// the inferred variable within a conditional type.
type FirstElement<T> = T extends [infer Head extends string, ...unknown[]]
  ? Head
  : never;

type A = FirstElement<["hello", number, boolean]>;   // "hello" (literal string)
type B = FirstElement<[string, number]>;             // string
type C = FirstElement<[42, string]>;                 // never (42 is not a string)

// Extract numeric values only from object types
type NumericValues<T> = {
  [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends infer V extends number ? V : never;
}[keyof T];

interface Metrics {
  responseTime: 250;
  errorRate: 0.01;
  name: string;
  version: "1.0";
}

type MetricNumbers = NumericValues<Metrics>;  // 250 | 0.01

// Extract the constructor parameter types constrained to object shapes
type ConstructorFirstArg<T> = T extends new (
  first: infer P extends object,
  ...rest: unknown[]
) => unknown
  ? P
  : never;

class EventEmitter {
  constructor(opts: { maxListeners: number; captureRejections?: boolean }) {}
}

type EmitterOpts = ConstructorFirstArg<typeof EventEmitter>;
// { maxListeners: number; captureRejections?: boolean }
```
Tradeoff: The `infer R extends Constraint` syntax requires TypeScript 4.7+; in codebases that target earlier versions (common in monorepos with legacy packages), this pattern must be replaced with a two-step approach (`infer R` followed by a nested `R extends Constraint ?`), which is verbose and can produce slightly different behavior around `never` distribution depending on where the constraint is placed.

---

**Pattern 292** — Recursive Mapped Type for `DeepPartial<T>`
```typescript
// Make every property optional at every nesting level,
// including arrays and tuple members.
type DeepPartial<T> = T extends (infer Item)[]
  ? DeepPartial<Item>[]
  : T extends readonly (infer Item)[]
  ? readonly DeepPartial<Item>[]
  : T extends object
  ? { [K in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[K]> }
  : T;

interface User {
  id: string;
  profile: {
    name: string;
    address: {
      city: string;
      zip: string;
    };
  };
  roles: string[];
  tags: readonly string[];
}

type PartialUser = DeepPartial<User>;
// {
//   id?: string;
//   profile?: { name?: string; address?: { city?: string; zip?: string } };
//   roles?: string[];
//   tags?: readonly string[];
// }

// Use as a patch/merge input type in REST APIs:
function patchUser(id: string, patch: DeepPartial<User>): Promise<User> {
  return fetch(`/api/users/${id}`, {
    method: "PATCH",
    body: JSON.stringify(patch),
  }).then(r => r.json());
}

patchUser("1", { profile: { address: { city: "Berlin" } } });
```
Tradeoff: Because `DeepPartial` recurses into every `object`-extending type, it also descends into class instances such as `Date`, `Map`, and `RegExp`, making `DeepPartial<Date>` resolve to `{ getTime?: () => number; ... }` (an object with optional method stubs) rather than the expected `Date | undefined`; exclude built-in class types explicitly by prefixing the conditionals with `T extends Date | RegExp | Map<any, any> | Set<any> ? T :` to short-circuit recursion for non-plain objects.

---

**Pattern 293** — Template Literal Type for Parsing Route Parameters
```typescript
// Extract named route parameters from a URL path template string type.
type ExtractParams<Path extends string> =
  Path extends `${infer _Prefix}:${infer Param}/${infer Rest}`
    ? Param | ExtractParams<`/${Rest}`>
    : Path extends `${infer _Prefix}:${infer Param}`
    ? Param
    : never;

type P1 = ExtractParams<"/users/:userId/posts/:postId">;
// "userId" | "postId"

type P2 = ExtractParams<"/orgs/:orgId/repos/:repoId/issues/:issueId">;
// "orgId" | "repoId" | "issueId"

type P3 = ExtractParams<"/health">;
// never

// Build a typed params record from the extracted names:
type RouteParams<Path extends string> = {
  [K in ExtractParams<Path>]: string;
};

function navigate<Path extends string>(
  path: Path,
  params: RouteParams<Path>
): string {
  return path.replace(/:(\w+)/g, (_, key) => params[key as keyof typeof params]);
}

const url = navigate("/users/:userId/posts/:postId", {
  userId: "42",
  postId: "99",
});
// "/users/42/posts/99"
// Type error if a param is missing or extra keys are provided
```
Tradeoff: The recursive template literal inference uses the pattern `` ${infer _}:${infer Param}/${infer Rest} `` which consumes segments greedily left-to-right; optional route segments (e.g., `/users/:id?`) are not handled by this pattern because `?` is not a path separator TypeScript can split on, so routes with optional params require a pre-processing step that normalizes `/:param?` to `/:param` before passing to `ExtractParams`.

---

**Pattern 294** — `NoInfer<T>` to Prevent Unwanted Contextual Inference Widening
```typescript
// `NoInfer<T>` (TypeScript 5.4+) blocks a type parameter from being
// inferred at that argument position, forcing inference from other sites.
declare function createReducer<State>(
  initial: State,
  // Without NoInfer, `action` would widen `State` if its payload type
  // includes extra properties not present in `initial`.
  handlers: {
    [K: string]: (state: State, payload: NoInfer<State>) => State;
  }
): (state: State | undefined, action: { type: string; payload: unknown }) => State;

// Practical: default parameter that must match, not influence, inferred type
function fillDefaults<T>(values: Partial<T>, defaults: NoInfer<T>): T {
  return { ...defaults, ...values } as T;
}

interface Options {
  timeout: number;
  retries: number;
  verbose: boolean;
}

// T is inferred from `values` as Options; `defaults` is checked against it,
// not used to widen T to `Options & { extraProp: string }`.
const opts = fillDefaults<Options>(
  { timeout: 5000 },
  { timeout: 1000, retries: 3, verbose: false }
);

// Older TypeScript (<5.4): achieve the same with an explicit generic:
function fillDefaultsCompat<T>(values: Partial<T>, defaults: T & {}): T {
  return { ...defaults, ...values } as T;
}
```
Tradeoff: `NoInfer<T>` was introduced in TypeScript 5.4 and is not available in earlier versions, requiring the `T & {}` workaround (which forces inference from other argument sites) for teams on TypeScript 4.x or early 5.x; additionally, `NoInfer<T>` only suppresses inference at that specific position — if there are multiple uninhibited inference sites that produce conflicting candidates, TypeScript still widens or errors as it would without `NoInfer`.

---

**Pattern 295** — Variance Annotation (`in`, `out`) for Explicit Covariance and Contravariance
```typescript
// TypeScript 4.7+ allows explicit variance annotations on generic parameters.
// `out T` = covariant (producer / read-only position)
// `in T`  = contravariant (consumer / write-only position)
// `in out T` = invariant (both read and write)

interface Producer<out T> {
  get(): T;
}

interface Consumer<in T> {
  accept(value: T): void;
}

interface Transformer<in Input, out Output> {
  transform(input: Input): Output;
}

// Covariant: Producer<Dog> assignable to Producer<Animal>
declare const dogProducer: Producer<{ breed: string }>;
const animalProducer: Producer<object> = dogProducer;  // OK

// Contravariant: Consumer<Animal> assignable to Consumer<Dog>
declare const objectConsumer: Consumer<object>;
const dogConsumer: Consumer<{ breed: string }> = objectConsumer;  // OK

// Invariant container (read + write):
interface Box<in out T> {
  value: T;
  set(v: T): void;
}

// Box<Dog> NOT assignable to Box<Animal> (invariant):
declare const dogBox: Box<{ breed: string }>;
// const animalBox: Box<object> = dogBox;  // Error: invariant

// Variance annotations make structural subtyping checks faster for
// deeply nested recursive types because the compiler skips full structural walks.
type Tree<out T> = {
  value: T;
  children: Tree<T>[];
};
```
Tradeoff: Variance annotations are advisory declarations — TypeScript still verifies structural variance and will emit an error if an annotation contradicts the actual structural variance of the type (e.g., annotating a mutable property type parameter as `out`); this means they are primarily a documentation and performance aid for deeply recursive types, not a tool for overriding the structural type system, and misapplied annotations produce confusing errors rather than silently bypassing checks.

---

**Pattern 296** — Intrinsic String Manipulation Types for Auto-Casing API Keys
```typescript
// TypeScript ships Uppercase<S>, Lowercase<S>, Capitalize<S>, Uncapitalize<S>
// as compiler-intrinsic types for string literal manipulation.

// Build a fully type-safe snake_case to camelCase transformer type:
type CamelCase<S extends string> =
  S extends `${infer Head}_${infer Tail}`
    ? `${Head}${CamelCase<Capitalize<Tail>>}`
    : S;

type C1 = CamelCase<"first_name">;           // "firstName"
type C2 = CamelCase<"created_at_timestamp">; // "createdAtTimestamp"
type C3 = CamelCase<"id">;                   // "id"

// Apply to an entire object type:
type CamelCaseKeys<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as CamelCase<string & K>]: T[K];
};

interface ApiResponse {
  user_id: string;
  created_at: string;
  is_active: boolean;
}

type FrontendModel = CamelCaseKeys<ApiResponse>;
// { userId: string; createdAt: string; isActive: boolean; }

// Combine with `satisfies` to validate the transform at compile time:
const response: ApiResponse = {
  user_id: "1",
  created_at: "2024-01-01",
  is_active: true,
};

function toCamel<T extends object>(obj: T): CamelCaseKeys<T> {
  const result: Record<string, unknown> = {};
  for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(obj)) {
    const camel = k.replace(/_([a-z])/g, (_, c) => c.toUpperCase());
    result[camel] = v;
  }
  return result as CamelCaseKeys<T>;
}
```
Tradeoff: The recursive `CamelCase<S>` type processes one underscore segment per recursion step and is subject to TypeScript's recursion depth cap (~100 levels), so strings with more than ~50 underscore-separated segments will hit the limit; more critically, `Capitalize<Tail>` only capitalizes the first character of the remainder, not each word's first character independently, so `CamelCase<"a_b_c">` requires the recursion to nest correctly — any deviation from the exact `${Head}_${Tail}` split pattern (e.g., double underscores) will leave underscores in the output without a compile-time error.

---

**Pattern 297** — Recursive Mapped Type for `DeepReadonly<T>` with Function Pass-Through
```typescript
// Make all nested properties readonly while leaving functions untouched,
// so methods remain callable and not accidentally wrapped in readonly records.
type DeepReadonly<T> = T extends (...args: infer A) => infer R
  ? (...args: A) => R  // functions pass through as-is
  : T extends (infer Item)[]
  ? ReadonlyArray<DeepReadonly<Item>>
  : T extends readonly (infer Item)[]
  ? ReadonlyArray<DeepReadonly<Item>>
  : T extends object
  ? { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }
  : T;

interface AppState {
  user: {
    id: string;
    preferences: {
      theme: string;
      notifications: boolean[];
    };
  };
  actions: {
    logout(): void;
    updateTheme(theme: string): void;
  };
}

type ReadonlyAppState = DeepReadonly<AppState>;
// user.id, user.preferences.theme — all readonly
// actions.logout() — still callable, not readonly-wrapped
// user.preferences.notifications — ReadonlyArray<boolean>

declare const state: ReadonlyAppState;
// state.user.id = "2";  // Error: readonly
state.actions.logout();   // OK: function passes through
state.actions.updateTheme("dark");  // OK
// state.user.preferences.notifications.push(true);  // Error: ReadonlyArray
```
Tradeoff: The function pass-through guard (`T extends (...args) => R`) must be the first branch; if it appears after the `object` check, all function types are captured by `{ readonly [K in keyof T] }` and transformed into objects with readonly `length`, `call`, `apply`, `bind` properties, producing a type that no longer behaves as a callable function and causes `This expression is not callable` errors throughout the codebase.

---

**Pattern 298** — `Extract` and `Exclude` Utility Types for Discriminated Union Routing
```typescript
// Use Extract and Exclude to split a discriminated union into subsets
// and dispatch to specialized handlers without losing type narrowing.
type AppEvent =
  | { type: "USER_CREATED"; userId: string; email: string }
  | { type: "USER_DELETED"; userId: string; reason: string }
  | { type: "ORDER_PLACED"; orderId: string; total: number }
  | { type: "ORDER_CANCELLED"; orderId: string; refund: boolean }
  | { type: "PAYMENT_SUCCEEDED"; paymentId: string; amount: number }
  | { type: "PAYMENT_FAILED"; paymentId: string; error: string };

// Extract only user-domain events:
type UserEvent = Extract<AppEvent, { type: `USER_${string}` }>;
// { type: "USER_CREATED"; ... } | { type: "USER_DELETED"; ... }

// Exclude payment events from processing pipeline:
type NonPaymentEvent = Exclude<AppEvent, { type: `PAYMENT_${string}` }>;

// Build typed handler maps per domain:
type HandlerMap<Events extends { type: string }> = {
  [E in Events as E["type"]]: (event: E) => void;
};

type UserHandlers = HandlerMap<UserEvent>;
// {
//   USER_CREATED: (event: { type: "USER_CREATED"; userId: string; email: string }) => void;
//   USER_DELETED: (event: { type: "USER_DELETED"; userId: string; reason: string }) => void;
// }

const userHandlers: UserHandlers = {
  USER_CREATED: (e) => console.log(`Creating user ${e.email}`),
  USER_DELETED: (e) => console.log(`Deleting ${e.userId}: ${e.reason}`),
};
```
Tradeoff: `Extract<AppEvent, { type: \`USER_${string}\` }>` uses a structural subtype check, not a string-pattern match on the discriminant value — TypeScript checks if the union member extends the constraint object `{ type: \`USER_${string}\` }`, so any union member with additional required properties that happen to include a `type` field matching the template will also be extracted; this is usually correct but can over-extract in unions where events share a `type` prefix for unrelated domain reasons.

---

**Pattern 299** — `ConstructorParameters<T>` and `InstanceType<T>` for Factory Abstraction
```typescript
// Use ConstructorParameters and InstanceType to build generic factory
// functions that preserve full constructor and instance types.
class Repository<T> {
  constructor(
    private readonly tableName: string,
    private readonly validator: (row: unknown) => T,
    private readonly ttl: number = 300
  ) {}

  async findById(id: string): Promise<T | null> {
    return null; // implementation omitted
  }
}

class CachedRepository<T> extends Repository<T> {
  constructor(
    tableName: string,
    validator: (row: unknown) => T,
    ttl: number,
    private readonly cacheKey: string
  ) {
    super(tableName, validator, ttl);
  }
}

// Generic factory that mirrors a class constructor signature:
function createInstance<C extends new (...args: unknown[]) => unknown>(
  Ctor: C,
  ...args: ConstructorParameters<C>
): InstanceType<C> {
  return new Ctor(...args) as InstanceType<C>;
}

// Full type safety: args must match CachedRepository constructor exactly
const repo = createInstance(
  CachedRepository<{ id: string; name: string }>,
  "users",
  (r) => r as { id: string; name: string },
  600,
  "user-cache"
);

// `repo` is correctly typed as CachedRepository<{ id: string; name: string }>
type RepoType = typeof repo;  // CachedRepository<{ id: string; name: string }>
```
Tradeoff: `ConstructorParameters<C>` captures the constructor signature as declared, not as overloaded — if the class has overloaded constructors, only the last (implementation) signature's parameters are returned, meaning the factory enforces the implementation signature rather than the public-facing overloads; for classes with meaningful overloads (e.g., accepting `string | Options` as the first argument with different semantics), callers must cast or use explicit overloads on the factory itself.

---

**Pattern 300** — `Parameters<T>` and `ReturnType<T>` for Middleware / Interceptor Typing
```typescript
// Build a generic middleware wrapper that preserves the wrapped function's
// full signature, using Parameters<T> and ReturnType<T>.
function withLogging<F extends (...args: unknown[]) => unknown>(fn: F): F {
  return function (...args: Parameters<F>): ReturnType<F> {
    console.log(`Calling ${fn.name} with`, args);
    const result = fn(...args) as ReturnType<F>;
    console.log(`${fn.name} returned`, result);
    return result;
  } as F;
}

function withRetry<F extends (...args: unknown[]) => Promise<unknown>>(
  fn: F,
  maxAttempts = 3
): F {
  return async function (...args: Parameters<F>): Promise<Awaited<ReturnType<F>>> {
    for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
      try {
        return await fn(...args) as Awaited<ReturnType<F>>;
      } catch (err) {
        if (attempt === maxAttempts) throw err;
      }
    }
    throw new Error("unreachable");
  } as F;
}

async function fetchUser(id: string): Promise<{ id: string; name: string }> {
  const r = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
  return r.json();
}

const loggedFetchUser = withLogging(fetchUser);
const resilientFetchUser = withRetry(withLogging(fetchUser), 3);

// Both preserve the original signature: (id: string) => Promise<{ id: string; name: string }>
const user = await resilientFetchUser("42");
```
Tradeoff: Casting the wrapper function `as F` bypasses TypeScript's check that the wrapper implementation fully satisfies `F`'s type — if the wrapper accidentally changes the return type (e.g., forgetting `await` causes a `Promise<Promise<T>>` instead of `Promise<T>`), the cast hides the mismatch and the error surfaces only at the call site where the incorrect return type is consumed, making the root cause difficult to trace; prefer returning an explicitly typed wrapper object instead of casting to `F` when the correctness of the wrapping logic is non-trivial.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G178** — `Uppercase<T>` and `Lowercase<T>` are not locale-aware and diverge from runtime behavior
Why this matters: The TypeScript intrinsic string manipulation types (`Uppercase`, `Lowercase`, `Capitalize`, `Uncapitalize`) are implemented in the compiler using JavaScript's `.toUpperCase()`, `.toLowerCase()`, `.charAt(0)`, and `.slice(1)` on the string literal at compile time. These methods are not locale-aware, so `Uppercase<"straße">` produces `"STRAßE"` rather than `"STRASSE"` (the correct German uppercase), and `Lowercase<"İSTANBUL">` (Turkish dotted I) does not match what `"İSTANBUL".toLowerCase()` produces in a Turkish locale at runtime. In i18n-heavy codebases that build locale-sensitive display strings from type-level computations, the compile-time types and runtime values can silently diverge.
Fix: Do not use `Uppercase`/`Lowercase` intrinsic types for user-facing string keys that depend on locale-sensitive casing. Reserve them for internal identifiers (enum-like string constants, CSS custom property names, HTTP header keys) where ASCII semantics are guaranteed. For locale-sensitive keys, represent them as opaque `string` at the type level and validate their shape with runtime schemas (zod, valibot) rather than compile-time type predicates.

---

**G179** — `infer` in multiple positions within the same clause infers the intersection, not a union
Why this matters: When the same type variable is inferred in multiple covariant positions within a single `extends` clause (e.g., `(...args: infer A) => infer A`), TypeScript infers the intersection of all candidate types for `A`, not their union. For a function `(x: string) => number`, inferring `A` from both `args[0]` (a `string`) and the return type (a `number`) yields `A = string & number` which is `never`. This silently produces `never`-typed inference results rather than an error, causing downstream utility types to return `never` for perfectly valid inputs and masking bugs in complex type utilities.
Fix: Always use distinct `infer` variable names for each position you want to capture independently: `(...args: infer Args) => infer Return`. Only reuse an `infer` variable across positions when you intentionally want the intersection (e.g., inferring a common base type). When debugging a utility type that returns `never` unexpectedly, inspect whether multiple `infer` clauses share a variable name.

---

**G180** — Mapped types over optional properties produce `T[K] | undefined`, not just `T[K]`
Why this matters: When iterating `[K in keyof T]` over a type with optional properties (e.g., `{ name?: string }`), `T[K]` evaluates to `string | undefined` because TypeScript includes `undefined` in the value type of optional properties. If you then apply a conditional type like `T[K] extends string ? "text" : "other"`, the `undefined` branch distributes and produces `"text" | "other"` instead of the expected `"text"` for a `string?` field. This causes utility types that categorize fields by their value type to miscategorize optional fields as ambiguous rather than as their base type.
Fix: Strip `undefined` from the value type before applying conditional logic: `Exclude<T[K], undefined> extends string ? "text" : "other"`. Alternatively, use the `-?` modifier on the iteration to make all properties required before inspecting their types: `{ [K in keyof T]-?: NonNullable<T[K]> extends string ? "text" : "other" }`. Choose the approach that best matches whether you want to treat optional-ness as part of the category.

---

**G181** — `as const` on an object does not prevent structural widening when passed to a generic
Why this matters: `as const` narrows an object literal to its deepest literal types and marks all properties `readonly`, but when the object is passed to a generic function whose type parameter is inferred from the argument, TypeScript widens the inferred type `T` to a mutable, non-literal version unless the generic is explicitly constrained. For example, `function id<T>(x: T): T` passed `{ color: "red" } as const` infers `T = { readonly color: "red" }` correctly, but `function wrap<T extends object>(x: T)` may infer `T = { color: string }` depending on the constraint, losing the literal. Developers add `as const` expecting the literal type to propagate and are surprised when the inferred generic type is widened.
Fix: Use `const` type parameters (TypeScript 5.0+): `function wrap<const T extends object>(x: T): T` preserves literal types without requiring callers to write `as const`. For older TypeScript, combine `as const` at the call site with a `satisfies` annotation to verify the shape while preserving literals: `wrap({ color: "red" } as const satisfies { color: string })`.

---

**G182** — `Partial<T>` combined with `Object.assign` merge loses non-optional field guarantees
Why this matters: A common pattern for merging a required config base with an optional override is `const merged = Object.assign({}, base, override)` where `override: Partial<T>`. TypeScript infers the return type of `Object.assign` as the intersection of its argument types, so the merged result is typed as `T & Partial<T>` which simplifies to `T` — all fields appear required. However, `Object.assign` performs a shallow copy, so nested required objects on the base are not deep-merged; they are replaced wholesale by the override's partial nested object, potentially omitting required nested fields at runtime while the type system falsely reports them as present. A service config with a required `database.host` field can be silently nulled out.
Fix: Replace `Object.assign` merging of nested config objects with a deep-merge utility that recurses into nested objects (`lodash.merge`, or a typed recursive merge function). Alternatively, flatten configuration so all required fields are at the top level and `Partial<T>` only applies to a single-depth override type, eliminating the deep-merge ambiguity entirely. For validation, run a schema check on the merged result using zod's `.parse()` to catch missing required fields at the boundary rather than trusting the type.

## Cycle 65 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 301** — Conditional Type with `infer` and Constraints for Narrowed Extraction
```typescript
// Extract the resolved value type of a Promise, constrained to objects only
type PromiseObjectValue<T> =
  T extends Promise<infer V extends object> ? V : never;

type A = PromiseObjectValue<Promise<{ id: number }>>;  // { id: number }
type B = PromiseObjectValue<Promise<string>>;           // never — string not an object
type C = PromiseObjectValue<string>;                   // never — not a Promise

// Constrained infer prevents matching primitive-resolving Promises
async function loadConfig(): Promise<{ debug: boolean; endpoint: string }> {
  return { debug: false, endpoint: "https://api.example.com" };
}

type ConfigShape = PromiseObjectValue<ReturnType<typeof loadConfig>>;
// ConfigShape = { debug: boolean; endpoint: string }
```
Tradeoff: The `infer V extends Constraint` syntax (TypeScript 4.8+) eliminates a downstream `Extract<V, Constraint>` call but changes semantics — the constraint is evaluated at inference time, so a type that is assignable only after narrowing (e.g., `unknown`) returns `never` rather than the narrowed form, surprising callers who expected the constraint to act as a filter rather than a guard.

**Pattern 302** — Mapped Type with `-readonly` and `-?` Modifiers for Full Mutability
```typescript
// Strips both readonly and optional from every property recursively
type DeepMutable<T> = T extends object
  ? { -readonly [K in keyof T]-?: DeepMutable<T[K]> }
  : T;

type FrozenConfig = {
  readonly host: string;
  readonly port?: number;
  readonly db: {
    readonly name: string;
    readonly poolSize?: number;
  };
};

type EditableConfig = DeepMutable<FrozenConfig>;
// { host: string; port: number; db: { name: string; poolSize: number } }

function patchConfig(base: FrozenConfig, patch: Partial<EditableConfig>): EditableConfig {
  return { ...base, db: { ...base.db }, ...patch } as EditableConfig;
}
```
Tradeoff: Applying `-?` recursively turns optional nested fields into required ones, which can over-specify the return type — callers who receive an `EditableConfig` must now supply every nested field even if their use case only needed mutability without requiredness; split into separate `DeepWritable<T>` (removes `readonly` only) and `DeepRequired<T>` types when those concerns differ.

**Pattern 303** — Template Literal Type for Type-Safe Event Emitter Payload Mapping
```typescript
type EventMap = {
  userCreated: { userId: string; email: string };
  orderPlaced: { orderId: string; total: number };
  paymentFailed: { orderId: string; reason: string };
};

type EventName = keyof EventMap;
type EventHandler<K extends EventName> = (payload: EventMap[K]) => void;

type HandlerMap = {
  [K in EventName as `on${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: EventHandler<K>;
};
// { onUserCreated: (p: {userId:string;email:string}) => void;
//   onOrderPlaced: (p: {orderId:string;total:number}) => void;
//   onPaymentFailed: (p: {orderId:string;reason:string}) => void; }

function createEmitterProxy(handlers: Partial<HandlerMap>) {
  return new Proxy({} as HandlerMap, {
    get: (_, prop: string) => (handlers as Record<string, unknown>)[prop],
  });
}
```
Tradeoff: Using `Capitalize<string & K>` in the `as` clause to remap keys to `onX` form ties the handler map's key shape to TypeScript's locale-insensitive `Capitalize` intrinsic — key names with non-ASCII initial characters (e.g., `çeşit`) produce compile-time keys that diverge from any sensible runtime camel-case implementation, so restrict event names to ASCII-initial identifiers and enforce this with an eslint rule or runtime schema rather than the type system alone.

**Pattern 304** — `satisfies` Operator to Validate Shape Without Widening Literal Types
```typescript
type PaletteColor = "red" | "green" | "blue";
type RGBTriple = [number, number, number];

// Without satisfies, TypeScript widens values to string[] or number[]
// With satisfies, literal/tuple types are preserved while shape is validated
const palette = {
  red:   [255, 0,   0  ],
  green: [0,   255, 0  ],
  blue:  [0,   0,   255],
} satisfies Record<PaletteColor, RGBTriple>;

// palette.red is [number, number, number], not number[] — tuples preserved
const [r, g, b] = palette.red;  // r: number, g: number, b: number (positional)

// Contrast: a full annotation loses literal tuple fidelity
const palette2: Record<PaletteColor, RGBTriple> = { red:[255,0,0], green:[0,255,0], blue:[0,0,255] };
const [r2] = palette2.red;  // r2: number — same, but palette2.red allows push/pop mutation
```
Tradeoff: `satisfies` validates the expression against the type at the declaration site but does not annotate the variable — the inferred type is the narrower literal/tuple form, which means downstream assignment of a conforming-but-different value (e.g., `palette.red = [0,0,0]`) is only blocked if the variable is also `const`; developers who want both shape validation and the wider annotated type must write `const x: T = expr satisfies T`, paying for a redundant check but gaining a clear contract for reassignment.

**Pattern 305** — Distributive Conditional Type Suppression via Tuple Wrapping for Exact Matching
```typescript
// Naked conditional type distributes over unions: IsNever<never> risks always being `never`
type IsNeverDistributive<T> = T extends never ? true : false;
type Broken = IsNeverDistributive<never>;  // never (distributes over empty union — no branches execute)

// Wrapped: prevents distribution, works correctly
type IsNever<T> = [T] extends [never] ? true : false;
type Fixed = IsNever<never>;  // true

type UnionToIntersection<U> =
  (U extends unknown ? (x: U) => void : never) extends (x: infer I) => void ? I : never;

type IsUnion<T> = [T] extends [UnionToIntersection<T>] ? false : true;

type CheckUnion = IsUnion<string | number>;  // true
type CheckSingle = IsUnion<string>;           // false
```
Tradeoff: Tuple-wrapping universally suppresses distributivity, which is correct for exact type identity checks like `IsNever` but wrong when you actually need per-member distribution — applying `[T] extends [U]` to a utility type that should distribute (e.g., a per-member transform) silently processes the full union as a single unit, producing an intersection result instead of a mapped-union; audit every `[T] extends [U]` usage to confirm non-distribution is the intended semantic.

**Pattern 306** — Recursive Conditional Type for Deep `Awaited<T>` Without Built-in Utility
```typescript
// Manual deep-await before TypeScript's built-in Awaited<T> (4.5+),
// still useful for understanding recursive conditional type mechanics
type DeepAwaited<T> =
  T extends null | undefined ? T :
  T extends object & { then(onfulfilled: infer F, ...args: infer _): unknown }
    ? F extends (value: infer V, ...args: infer _) => unknown
      ? DeepAwaited<V>
      : never
    : T;

async function nested(): Promise<Promise<Promise<{ id: number }>>> {
  return Promise.resolve(Promise.resolve({ id: 42 }));
}

type Resolved = DeepAwaited<ReturnType<typeof nested>>;
// { id: number }

// Modern equivalent (TypeScript 4.5+):
type ModernResolved = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof nested>>;
// { id: number } — same result, compiler-intrinsic performance
```
Tradeoff: Hand-rolled recursive conditional types for promise unwrapping are instructive but have worse performance than the compiler-intrinsic `Awaited<T>` (TS 4.5+) because intrinsics short-circuit at the compiler level instead of recursing through the type-checker; always prefer `Awaited<T>` in production code and reserve the hand-rolled form for TypeScript versions below 4.5 or for educational purposes.

**Pattern 307** — Mapped Type with `as never` to Filter Keys Conditionally
```typescript
// Remove all function-valued properties from a type, keeping only data fields
type DataOnly<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as T[K] extends (...args: unknown[]) => unknown ? never : K]: T[K];
};

class UserService {
  id: number = 0;
  name: string = "";
  createdAt: Date = new Date();
  save(): Promise<void> { return Promise.resolve(); }
  delete(): Promise<void> { return Promise.resolve(); }
}

type UserData = DataOnly<UserService>;
// { id: number; name: string; createdAt: Date }

function serializeUser(u: UserService): UserData {
  const { save: _s, delete: _d, ...data } = u;
  return data;
}
```
Tradeoff: Filtering with `as never` in a mapped type is evaluated at compile time using the structural type of each value — a property typed as `unknown` or `any` is not assignable to a function type and is therefore retained in the output, but if a field later receives a function-typed value at runtime (e.g., via `Object.assign`), the type system cannot see the divergence; use this pattern for strongly-typed class shapes and avoid it for dynamically-composed objects where `any` fields are present.

**Pattern 308** — Template Literal Type Parsing for Route Parameter Extraction
```typescript
// Extract named parameters from an Express-style route string at the type level
type ExtractParams<Route extends string> =
  Route extends `${infer _Before}:${infer Param}/${infer Rest}`
    ? Param | ExtractParams<`/${Rest}`>
    : Route extends `${infer _Before}:${infer Param}`
      ? Param
      : never;

type Params = ExtractParams<"/users/:userId/posts/:postId">;
// "userId" | "postId"

type RouteHandler<Route extends string> = (
  req: { params: Record<ExtractParams<Route>, string> }
) => Response;

const handler: RouteHandler<"/users/:userId/posts/:postId"> = ({ params }) => {
  const { userId, postId } = params;  // both typed as string, typo is a compile error
  return new Response(`User ${userId}, Post ${postId}`);
};
```
Tradeoff: Template literal type parsing via recursive `infer` splits produces correct results for static route strings known at compile time but fails silently for dynamically constructed route strings — the inferred `ExtractParams` collapses to `never` for plain `string` inputs rather than raising an error, so add a generic constraint `<Route extends string>` combined with a runtime assert that the route matches a known literal to expose the problem at the call site rather than silently at runtime.

**Pattern 309** — `infer` in Function Overloads to Extract the Last Overload's Return Type
```typescript
// TypeScript's built-in ReturnType<T> infers from the last overload only.
// This helper makes the behavior explicit and handles up to four overload signatures.
type LastOverloadReturn<T> =
  T extends {
    (...args: infer _A1): infer _R1;
    (...args: infer _A2): infer _R2;
    (...args: infer _A3): infer _R3;
    (...args: infer _A4): infer R4;
  } ? R4 :
  T extends {
    (...args: infer _A1): infer _R1;
    (...args: infer _A2): infer _R2;
    (...args: infer _A3): infer R3;
  } ? R3 :
  T extends { (...args: infer _A1): infer _R1; (...args: infer _A2): infer R2 } ? R2 :
  T extends (...args: infer _A) => infer R ? R : never;

function parse(input: string): string;
function parse(input: number): number;
function parse(input: string | number): string | number {
  return typeof input === "string" ? input.trim() : input * 2;
}

type ParseReturn = LastOverloadReturn<typeof parse>;  // string | number
```
Tradeoff: The ladder of conditional overload matches must be extended manually as the number of overloads grows (up to TypeScript's internal limit of ~23 overload resolution slots), and it only works on function types defined with overload syntax — a union of function types `((x: string) => string) | ((x: number) => number)` is not matched by this pattern because union types and overload types are structurally different in the type system.

**Pattern 310** — `Record<K, V>` with Discriminated Union Keys for Exhaustive Handler Tables
```typescript
type Shape =
  | { kind: "circle";    radius: number }
  | { kind: "rectangle"; width: number; height: number }
  | { kind: "triangle";  base: number;  height: number };

type ShapeKind = Shape["kind"];  // "circle" | "rectangle" | "triangle"

type AreaHandler = (shape: Shape) => number;

// Record forces you to handle every variant — missing a key is a compile error
const areaHandlers: Record<ShapeKind, AreaHandler> = {
  circle:    (s) => Math.PI * (s as Extract<Shape, { kind: "circle" }>).radius ** 2,
  rectangle: (s) => {
    const r = s as Extract<Shape, { kind: "rectangle" }>;
    return r.width * r.height;
  },
  triangle:  (s) => {
    const t = s as Extract<Shape, { kind: "triangle" }>;
    return 0.5 * t.base * t.height;
  },
};

function computeArea(shape: Shape): number {
  return areaHandlers[shape.kind](shape);
}
```
Tradeoff: Using `Record<ShapeKind, Handler>` guarantees exhaustiveness at declaration time (adding a new `Shape` variant forces a new key to be added to the table) but the handler function receives the full union type, requiring internal casts to the specific variant; a switch-statement or discriminated union `match` pattern provides exhaustiveness with narrower per-branch types and no casts — prefer the `Record` table pattern when handlers are registered dynamically or composed from separate modules.

**Pattern 311** — `NoInfer<T>` to Prevent Contextual Inference Widening in Generic Utilities
```typescript
// TypeScript 5.4+ built-in NoInfer<T>
// Forces a type parameter to be inferred from other sites, not this position
function createStore<T>(
  initialState: T,
  // Without NoInfer: reducer's `state` param could widen T to include action payload types
  reducer: (state: NoInfer<T>, action: unknown) => NoInfer<T>
): { getState(): T; dispatch(action: unknown): void } {
  let state = initialState;
  return {
    getState: () => state,
    dispatch: (action) => { state = reducer(state, action); },
  };
}

// T is inferred from initialState as { count: number }, not widened by reducer param
const store = createStore({ count: 0 }, (state, _action) => ({
  count: state.count + 1,  // state is { count: number }, not widened to a broader type
}));

const current = store.getState();  // { count: number }
```
Tradeoff: `NoInfer<T>` is a TypeScript 5.4+ compiler intrinsic that has no polyfill with identical semantics — the common pre-5.4 workaround `[T] extends [T] ? T : never` suppresses inference by making the position non-inferential but also disables distributivity in ways that `NoInfer` does not, so migrating from the workaround to the intrinsic can subtly change behavior for union-typed `T`; test edge cases with union inputs when upgrading from the workaround.

**Pattern 312** — Variance Annotations (`in`/`out`) for Explicit Covariance and Contravariance
```typescript
// TypeScript 4.7+ variance annotations communicate intent and improve checker performance
interface Animal { name: string }
interface Dog extends Animal { breed: string }

interface Producer<out T> {   // covariant: T only appears in output positions
  produce(): T;
}

interface Consumer<in T> {    // contravariant: T only appears in input positions
  consume(value: T): void;
}

interface Transformer<in TIn, out TOut> {
  transform(value: TIn): TOut;
}

// Valid: Producer<Dog> is assignable to Producer<Animal> (covariant — narrower to wider)
declare const dogProducer: Producer<Dog>;
const animalProducer: Producer<Animal> = dogProducer;  // OK

// Valid: Consumer<Animal> is assignable to Consumer<Dog> (contravariant — wider to narrower)
declare const animalConsumer: Consumer<Animal>;
const dogConsumer: Consumer<Dog> = animalConsumer;  // OK
```
Tradeoff: Variance annotations are checked by the compiler against actual usage — annotating `out T` on an interface that uses `T` in an input position (e.g., a method parameter) is a compile error, which surfaces incorrect variance assumptions early; however, the annotations only affect the declared interface, not all structurally compatible types, so an unannotated object literal that matches the interface shape is still subject to the usual bivariant method checks in non-strict mode.

---

**Pattern 313** — Template Literal Type for Type-Safe CSS Custom Property Names
```typescript
type CSSCustomProperty = `--${string}`;

function setCSSVar<K extends CSSCustomProperty>(
  element: HTMLElement,
  property: K,
  value: string
): void {
  element.style.setProperty(property, value);
}

// Only accepts strings starting with "--"
setCSSVar(document.body, "--primary-color", "#3b82f6");   // OK
// setCSSVar(document.body, "color", "#3b82f6");          // Error: "color" not assignable to `--${string}`

type ThemeVarMap = {
  "--color-bg":       string;
  "--color-fg":       string;
  "--spacing-base":   string;
  "--font-size-base": string;
};

function applyTheme(el: HTMLElement, vars: ThemeVarMap): void {
  for (const [key, val] of Object.entries(vars) as [CSSCustomProperty, string][]) {
    el.style.setProperty(key, val);
  }
}

// Composing with a record of known token names
type ThemeToken = "primary" | "secondary" | "accent";
type ThemeVars = Record<`--color-${ThemeToken}`, string>;
```
Tradeoff: `` `--${string}` `` as a type constraint validates the prefix at compile time but does not prevent invalid CSS custom property names that are syntactically valid at the type level yet semantically invalid in a browser (e.g., names with whitespace `"-- foo"`) — combine the type constraint with a runtime regex validation function at API boundaries to catch malformed names that slip past the prefix check.

**Pattern 314** — Utility Type Composition: `Required<Pick<T, K>>` for Partial-with-Mandatory-Fields
```typescript
// Pattern: a type where most fields are optional but specific ones are always required
type WithRequired<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K> & Required<Pick<T, K>>;

interface CreateUserInput {
  email?: string;
  name?: string;
  role?: "admin" | "user" | "guest";
  avatarUrl?: string;
  bio?: string;
}

// Email and role are always required; rest remain optional
type CreateUserRequest = WithRequired<CreateUserInput, "email" | "role">;
// { email: string; role: "admin"|"user"|"guest"; name?: string; avatarUrl?: string; bio?: string }

function createUser(input: CreateUserRequest): Promise<{ id: string }> {
  const { email, role, ...rest } = input;
  return fetch("/api/users", {
    method: "POST",
    body: JSON.stringify({ email, role, ...rest }),
  }).then((r) => r.json());
}

// Error: missing required email
// createUser({ role: "user" });  // TS error: Property 'email' is missing
```
Tradeoff: `Omit<T, K> & Required<Pick<T, K>>` produces an intersection type, and while required fields display correctly in IDE hover popups, some deep generic utilities that use `keyof` on the intersection see a flattened key set that may not preserve JSDoc comments or `@deprecated` markers from the original `T`; if documentation fidelity matters, prefer defining the required-fields variant as a standalone interface that extends `Partial<T>` to avoid losing metadata through intersection flattening.

**Pattern 315** — `ConstructorParameters<T>` and `InstanceType<T>` for Typed Factory Functions
```typescript
// Generic factory that accepts any class constructor and returns a typed instance
function createInstance<C extends new (...args: never[]) => unknown>(
  Ctor: C,
  ...args: ConstructorParameters<C>
): InstanceType<C> {
  return new (Ctor as new (...args: unknown[]) => InstanceType<C>)(...args);
}

class DatabaseConnection {
  constructor(
    public readonly host: string,
    public readonly port: number,
    public readonly database: string
  ) {}
  query(sql: string): Promise<unknown[]> { return Promise.resolve([]); }
}

class CacheClient {
  constructor(public readonly url: string, public readonly ttl: number) {}
  get(key: string): Promise<unknown> { return Promise.resolve(null); }
}

const db = createInstance(DatabaseConnection, "localhost", 5432, "mydb");
// db: DatabaseConnection — db.query() is available, positional args are type-checked

const cache = createInstance(CacheClient, "redis://localhost:6379", 300);
// cache: CacheClient — wrong arg count or wrong arg types are compile errors
```
Tradeoff: `ConstructorParameters<C>` requires the constructor type to be resolved to a concrete non-abstract class — using `abstract new (...args: never[]) => unknown` as the constraint permits abstract classes but loses positional arg types in the spread, forcing a cast in the implementation body; use `new (...args: never[]) => unknown` (non-abstract) when all instantiated classes are concrete, which removes the cast and keeps the implementation simpler at the cost of excluding abstract base classes.

### Community Gotchas

**G183** — `keyof` on an intersection type returns the union of both types' keys, not the intersection
Why this matters: For `type AB = A & B`, `keyof AB` evaluates to `keyof A | keyof B`, not `keyof A & keyof B`. This surprises developers who expect intersecting types to yield a narrower set of keys — in fact, intersecting two object types widens the key set because an `A & B` value has all properties of both `A` and `B`. Code that constructs `Record<keyof (A & B), V>` ends up with a record containing keys from both types, and a value typed as `A & B` that is missing `B`'s keys (structurally invalid at the intersection) is still accepted by the record type because the intersection constraint is checked at assignment, not at key enumeration.
Fix: When you want only shared keys, use `keyof A & keyof B` explicitly rather than `keyof (A & B)`. When you want all keys from both types (which is what `keyof (A & B)` gives you), name it clearly in a comment. Use `Extract<keyof A, keyof B>` to obtain the common keys in a way that is self-documenting and refactoring-safe.

---

**G184** — `as const` on a tuple does not prevent out-of-bounds access typed as a union member at compile time
Why this matters: `const arr = ["a", "b", "c"] as const` produces the type `readonly ["a", "b", "c"]`, and `arr[0]` correctly types as `"a"`. However, indexing with a variable typed as `number` (e.g., `arr[i]` where `i: number`) yields `"a" | "b" | "c"` rather than triggering an error — TypeScript does not track numeric range constraints, so `arr[99]` is `"a" | "b" | "c"` at the type level but `undefined` at runtime, causing unexpected `undefined` values to flow into code expecting a non-undefined union member.
Fix: Enable `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` in `tsconfig.json` — with that flag, tuple indexed access via a variable of type `number` returns `T | undefined`, forcing you to handle the undefined case. For statically-known indices, use the literal number type directly: `arr[2 as 0 | 1 | 2]`, or restructure to use destructuring to access specific positions by name rather than by index.

---

**G185** — Mapped types silently drop symbol-keyed properties
Why this matters: `[K in keyof T]` iterates over string, number, and symbol keys in theory, but in practice most built-in and custom mapped types (including TypeScript's own `Partial<T>`, `Required<T>`, and `Readonly<T>`) preserve symbol keys through the iteration. However, when a mapped type uses the `as` clause for key remapping (e.g., `` [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`] ``), the `string & K` intersection filters out symbol keys entirely, silently dropping `[Symbol.iterator]`, `[Symbol.toPrimitive]`, and other symbol-keyed properties from the output type. Code that passes the mapped result to a function expecting the original interface fails to compile with a confusing "missing property" error pointing at the symbol key.
Fix: After applying a key-remapping mapped type, verify with `keyof typeof result` that expected symbol properties are present. To preserve symbol keys through a remapping mapped type, combine the mapped type with an intersection: `RemappedVersion<T> & Pick<T, symbol & keyof T>` to re-attach symbol-keyed properties that the `as` clause dropped. Test custom utility types against interfaces that include `[Symbol.iterator]` or `[Symbol.toPrimitive]` to catch silent key omissions early.

---

**G186** — Template literal union explosion causes `Type instantiation is excessively deep` errors
Why this matters: Template literal types that cross-multiply multiple unions grow exponentially: a type with four union components of 10 members each produces 10,000 string literal members. TypeScript imposes a member limit on instantiated types, and complex downstream operations (`Extract`, conditional matching, indexed access) on large template literal unions cause the type checker to hit its recursion or memory budget, emitting `Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite` rather than a useful domain error. This manifests suddenly when adding the fifth or sixth union dimension to a locale/event/status key type that previously appeared fine.
Fix: Reduce union dimensions by representing high-cardinality components as `string` rather than a literal union (e.g., keep `Lang = "en" | "fr"` but replace dynamic `Region` with `string`). Split large combined key types into separate typed domains (`LocaleKey`, `EventKey`) rather than a single combined type. For validation at runtime, use a `Set<string>` lookup or zod `.enum()` instead of type-level exhaustive enumeration. Profile type-check time with `tsc --extendedDiagnostics` to identify which type alias is responsible for the instantiation budget breach.

---

**G187** — The `satisfies` operator validates at declaration but does not constrain future mutations
Why this matters: `const config = { ... } satisfies Config` checks that the object literal matches `Config` at the point of declaration, but the variable `config` is inferred as the narrower literal type, not as `Config`. Subsequent property assignments (`config.level = "verbose"`) are checked against the inferred literal type (e.g., `"debug"`) rather than the full `Config` union, so TypeScript may reject valid assignments that are allowed by `Config`'s declared type. Conversely, if the variable is `let`, later reassignment of the whole variable is not constrained to `Config` at all — `config = { level: 99 }` may be accepted if `99` satisfies the inferred type.
Fix: When you need both shape validation at initialization and a stable annotated type for later mutation, write the redundant form `const config: Config = { ... } satisfies Config` — the annotation governs future assignments while `satisfies` provides more-detailed error messages at the declaration site. Use `satisfies` alone (without annotation) only for `const` values that are never reassigned and where preserving the narrower inferred type (tuples, literal strings) is the explicit goal.

## Cycle 68 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 316** — `const` Type Parameter for Literal Tuple Inference Without `as const`
```typescript
// Without const modifier: argument is widened to string[]
function buildRoute<T extends readonly string[]>(segments: T): T {
  return segments;
}
const r1 = buildRoute(["users", "profile", "edit"]);
// r1: string[]  — literal tuple information is lost

// With const modifier: argument is inferred as a readonly literal tuple
function buildRouteConst<const T extends readonly string[]>(segments: T): T {
  return segments;
}
const r2 = buildRouteConst(["users", "profile", "edit"]);
// r2: readonly ["users", "profile", "edit"]  — exact literal tuple preserved

// Practical use: type-safe route registry
type RoutePath<T extends readonly string[]> = `/${T[number]}`;
function registerRoute<const T extends readonly string[]>(
  segments: T,
  handler: (path: RoutePath<T>) => void
): void {
  const path = `/${segments.join("/")}` as RoutePath<T>;
  handler(path);
}
registerRoute(["api", "users"], (path) => {
  // path: "/api" | "/users"  — union of literal segments, not just string
  console.log(path);
});
```
Tradeoff: The `const` modifier on a type parameter only applies to **inline literal arguments** — a pre-assigned variable `const arr = ["a", "b"]` passed to a `<const T>` function still infers `string[]` because const-ness was already resolved at the variable declaration; callers who store segments in a variable must still use `as const` at that declaration site, making the ergonomic gain partial when segments are assembled dynamically.

**Pattern 317** — Inferred Type Predicates for `Array.filter` Narrowing (TypeScript 5.5)
```typescript
interface User { id: number; name: string; }
interface AdminUser extends User { role: "admin"; permissions: string[]; }

const records: (User | AdminUser | undefined | null)[] = [
  { id: 1, name: "Alice", role: "admin", permissions: ["read", "write"] },
  { id: 2, name: "Bob" },
  undefined,
  null,
];

// Before TS 5.5: filter returned (User | AdminUser | undefined | null)[]
// requiring an explicit type predicate annotation
function isAdminUser(u: User | AdminUser | undefined | null): u is AdminUser {
  return u != null && "role" in u && u.role === "admin";
}

// TS 5.5+: predicate is inferred automatically when the function
// has a single return expression that refines the parameter
function isDefined<T>(value: T | undefined | null): value is T {
  return value != null;
}

const definedRecords = records.filter(isDefined);
// definedRecords: (User | AdminUser)[]  — undefined/null eliminated by inferred predicate

// Multi-step pipeline: all inference is preserved
const adminUsers = records
  .filter(isDefined)
  .filter((u): u is AdminUser => "role" in u && u.role === "admin");
// adminUsers: AdminUser[]

// Inline arrow predicate is also inferred in 5.5
const nonNullNames = ["Alice", null, "Bob", undefined].filter(x => x !== null && x !== undefined);
// nonNullNames: string[]  — no explicit predicate needed
```
Tradeoff: Inferred type predicates require that the filter function has **no explicit return type annotation, no parameter mutations, and exactly one return expression** — adding a multi-branch fallback (`if (debug) return true`) or an explicit annotation overrides inference and reverts the return type to `boolean`, silently losing the narrowing; teams must audit their filter callbacks for these conditions when upgrading to 5.5 to avoid unexpected regression from `T[]` back to `(T | null)[]`.

**Pattern 318** — `--isolatedDeclarations` Compatible Explicit Return Types on Exported Functions
```typescript
// tsconfig.json excerpt:
// { "compilerOptions": { "isolatedDeclarations": true } }

// ❌ Rejected under --isolatedDeclarations: return type must be inferable
//    without processing the function body
export function getUserCount() {
  return db.users.count(); // error TS9007: Function must have an explicit return type
}

// ✅ Correct: explicit return type allows parallel declaration emit
export function getUserCountOk(): Promise<number> {
  return db.users.count();
}

// ✅ Utility type compositions are fine as long as they don't require body inference
export function parseConfig<T extends Record<string, unknown>>(
  raw: unknown
): T {
  return raw as T;
}

// ✅ Re-exported constants also need explicit annotations
export const DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE: number = 25;
// Without `: number`, isolatedDeclarations cannot emit the .d.ts in parallel

// Example build pipeline benefit: transpile each file to .d.ts independently
// without type-checking the whole program, enabling 3-4x faster monorepo builds
// when combined with tsc --noCheck and a separate tsc --emitDeclarationOnly pass
export function formatDate(date: Date): string {
  return date.toISOString().split("T")[0];
}
```
Tradeoff: `--isolatedDeclarations` dramatically accelerates `.d.ts` generation in large monorepos by allowing each file to be processed independently, but it imposes explicit return type annotations on every exported function — this increases annotation boilerplate by roughly one line per exported function and creates a maintenance burden when return types change, since both the implementation and annotation must be updated; the tradeoff is worthwhile for projects with 50+ packages but adds friction in single-package repositories that do not benefit from parallel declaration emit.

**Pattern 319** — `using` Declarations with `Symbol.dispose` for Deterministic Resource Cleanup
```typescript
// TypeScript 5.2+: Explicit Resource Management via ECMAScript proposal
class DatabaseTransaction {
  private committed = false;

  constructor(private readonly conn: DatabaseConnection) {
    this.conn.beginTransaction();
  }

  commit(): void {
    this.conn.commit();
    this.committed = true;
  }

  // Symbol.dispose is called automatically at the end of the `using` scope
  [Symbol.dispose](): void {
    if (!this.committed) {
      this.conn.rollback();
    }
    this.conn.release();
  }
}

// Consumer: no try/finally required — disposal is guaranteed by the runtime
async function transferFunds(from: string, to: string, amount: number): Promise<void> {
  using tx = new DatabaseTransaction(getConnection());
  // If this throws, tx[Symbol.dispose]() is called before the error propagates
  await debit(from, amount);
  await credit(to, amount);
  tx.commit();
} // tx[Symbol.dispose]() runs here on normal exit

// Async disposal with Symbol.asyncDispose
class FileHandle {
  [Symbol.asyncDispose](): Promise<void> {
    return this.close();
  }
  async close(): Promise<void> { /* flush + close */ }
}

async function processFile(path: string): Promise<void> {
  await using handle = await FileHandle.open(path);
  await handle.read();
} // await handle[Symbol.asyncDispose]() runs here
```
Tradeoff: `using` declarations rely on the `Symbol.dispose` protocol introduced in TypeScript 5.2 and Node.js 18.20+ — in older runtimes or transpiled environments (e.g., Babel without the `@babel/plugin-proposal-explicit-resource-management` plugin), the `using` keyword is not recognized or the disposal is silently skipped, making resource leaks silent rather than compile errors; teams must verify their minimum runtime version and transpiler configuration before adopting `using` in production, and must add a `Symbol.dispose` polyfill for environments that lack it.

**Pattern 320** — `--erasableSyntaxOnly` Compatible Code: Replacing `enum` and Parameter Properties
```typescript
// tsconfig.json for Node.js 23.6+ type-stripping compatibility:
// { "compilerOptions": { "erasableSyntaxOnly": true } }

// ❌ Rejected: const enum cannot be erased safely — the erasure changes semantics
// const enum Direction { Up, Down, Left, Right }

// ✅ Correct: use a const assertion object map — erasing the type annotation
//    leaves a valid ES module with no semantic change
const Direction = { Up: 0, Down: 1, Left: 2, Right: 3 } as const;
type Direction = (typeof Direction)[keyof typeof Direction];

// ❌ Rejected: parameter properties require constructor body rewriting during erasure
// class ServiceA {
//   constructor(private readonly name: string, private count: number) {}
// }

// ✅ Correct: explicit property declarations are erasable
class ServiceB {
  private readonly name: string;
  private count: number;
  constructor(name: string, count: number) {
    this.name = name;
    this.count = count;
  }
}

// ❌ Rejected: namespace with runtime value (use plain module-level export instead)
// namespace MathUtils { export function clamp(...) {} }

// ✅ Correct: plain module-level export
export function clamp(n: number, min: number, max: number): number {
  return Math.max(min, Math.min(max, n));
}
```
Tradeoff: Migrating to `--erasableSyntaxOnly` eliminates all TypeScript-specific runtime constructs, enabling native type-stripping in Node.js 23.6+ without any compilation step — but it requires rewriting `enum` (which loses inlined constant values that bundlers optimize), parameter properties (which adds ~2 lines per field), and `namespace` merging (which loses the merging semantics that some library patterns depend on); the ergonomic cost is highest for codebases that rely on `const enum` for performance-sensitive code paths where the compiler inlines literal values at call sites.

**Pattern 321** — TypeScript 5.8 Granular Branch Return Type Checking in Conditional Expressions
```typescript
// TypeScript 5.8 checks each branch of a conditional expression in a return
// against the declared return type, rather than simplifying the union first.

declare const cache: Map<string, any>;

// Before TS 5.8: `any | string` simplified to `any`, masking the type error
// TS 5.8: the false branch `urlString` is checked as `string`, which fails `URL`
function resolveUrl(urlString: string): URL {
  return cache.has(urlString)
    ? cache.get(urlString)   // ok: any is assignable to URL
    : urlString;             // error TS2322: string is not assignable to URL
}

// Fix: add explicit cast or URL construction in the false branch
function resolveUrlFixed(urlString: string): URL {
  return cache.has(urlString)
    ? (cache.get(urlString) as URL)
    : new URL(urlString);  // correct: constructs URL from string
}

// Nested conditional expressions are each checked independently
function pickValue(flag: boolean, a: string, b: number): string {
  return flag
    ? a                     // ok: string → string
    : String(b);            // ok: number → string via String()
}

// The check applies to ternary inside arrow function bodies too
const formatId = (id: number | string): string =>
  typeof id === "number" ? id.toFixed(0) : id;
//                                          ^^ ok: string → string
```
Tradeoff: Granular branch checking catches real bugs (a string returned where URL was expected) that `any` previously swallowed, but it also surfaces pre-existing latent errors in codebases that relied on `any`-propagation through `Map.get()`, `JSON.parse()`, or untyped cache lookups — upgrading to TypeScript 5.8 may produce dozens of new errors in map-heavy code that was previously clean, and the fix (adding explicit casts or typed wrapper functions) requires a targeted audit rather than a bulk `@ts-ignore` suppression.

**Pattern 322** — `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` for `.ts`-Extension Imports in Direct Execution
```typescript
// tsconfig.json:
// { "compilerOptions": { "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true } }

// Source file: src/server.ts
// In-place execution with tsx/ts-node uses the .ts extension directly:
import { createRouter } from "./router.ts";       // works with tsx / Deno
import { applyMiddleware } from "./middleware.ts";

// After tsc compilation, rewrite turns them into .js extensions automatically:
// import { createRouter } from "./router.js";
// import { applyMiddleware } from "./middleware.js";

// Practical workflow: single source tree, two execution modes
// 1. Development: `tsx src/server.ts` — no compilation, .ts imports resolve directly
// 2. Production:  `tsc && node dist/server.js` — .ts → .js rewrite applied

// Explicit extension imports are required for ESM compatibility:
// (Node.js ESM resolution does not use extension elision)
export async function startServer(port: number): Promise<void> {
  const router = await import("./router.ts");   // tsx: works; tsc: rewrites to .js
  router.default.listen(port);
}

// Type-only imports are also rewritten (they erase entirely after compilation):
import type { RouterConfig } from "./router.ts"; // ok
```
Tradeoff: `--rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` only rewrites **relative path imports** — imports resolved through `baseUrl`, `paths` aliases, or bare package specifiers are untouched, so a mixed codebase using both path aliases (`@/utils`) and relative imports (`./utils.ts`) must ensure that path-aliased imports already use the `.js` extension or are transformed by a bundler; the flag is most useful in Deno or Node.js native ESM projects where the entire import graph uses explicit relative paths with `.ts` extensions and no path alias resolution.

**Pattern 323** — `Object.groupBy` and `Map.groupBy` Typed with `--target es2024`
```typescript
// tsconfig.json: { "compilerOptions": { "target": "es2024", "lib": ["es2024"] } }

interface Transaction {
  id: string;
  category: "food" | "transport" | "utilities";
  amount: number;
  date: string;
}

const transactions: Transaction[] = [
  { id: "t1", category: "food",       amount: 45.00,  date: "2026-05-01" },
  { id: "t2", category: "transport",  amount: 12.50,  date: "2026-05-01" },
  { id: "t3", category: "food",       amount: 30.00,  date: "2026-05-02" },
  { id: "t4", category: "utilities",  amount: 120.00, date: "2026-05-03" },
];

// Object.groupBy returns Partial<Record<K, T[]>>
// The return type is Partial because not every key is guaranteed to be present
const byCategory: Partial<Record<Transaction["category"], Transaction[]>> =
  Object.groupBy(transactions, (t) => t.category);

// Access requires undefined check — Partial<Record<K, V>>[K] is V | undefined
const foodTransactions = byCategory["food"] ?? [];
const totalFood = foodTransactions.reduce((sum, t) => sum + t.amount, 0);

// Map.groupBy returns Map<K, T[]> with the same key type
const groupedMap: Map<Transaction["category"], Transaction[]> =
  Map.groupBy(transactions, (t) => t.category);

// Map.get() returns T[] | undefined, so undefined check is still required
const utilitySpend = (groupedMap.get("utilities") ?? [])
  .reduce((sum, t) => sum + t.amount, 0);
```
Tradeoff: `Object.groupBy` returns `Partial<Record<K, T[]>>` rather than `Record<K, T[]>` because TypeScript cannot statically prove that every possible key is represented in the input array — this forces `?? []` fallbacks on every access and makes the type less ergonomic than a `Map`-based approach for code that needs to iterate over all present groups; `Map.groupBy` avoids the partiality footgun but requires `Map` iteration (`for...of`) instead of `Object.entries`, which is less familiar to code that handles plain objects.

**Pattern 324** — `infer extends` Constraint for Narrowing Inferred Types in Conditional Types
```typescript
// TypeScript 4.7+: infer with an extends constraint
// Extracts the resolved value type of a Promise but only when it is a string
type StringResolved<T> =
  T extends Promise<infer R extends string> ? R : never;

type A = StringResolved<Promise<"hello">>; // "hello"
type B = StringResolved<Promise<number>>;  // never
type C = StringResolved<string>;           // never

// More practical: extract function parameters that are all strings
type AllStringParams<T> =
  T extends (...args: infer P extends string[]) => unknown ? P : never;

function greet(firstName: string, lastName: string): void {}
type GreetParams = AllStringParams<typeof greet>; // [string, string]

// Extract the first element only when it is a literal string
type FirstStringArg<T> =
  T extends (first: infer F extends string, ...rest: unknown[]) => unknown
    ? F
    : never;

// Combining with template literal types for version string parsing
type ExtractVersion<T extends string> =
  T extends `${string}/v${infer V extends `${number}`}/${string}` ? V : never;

type V1 = ExtractVersion<"/api/v2/users">;     // "2"
type V2 = ExtractVersion<"/api/v12/products">; // "12"
type V3 = ExtractVersion<"/api/users">;        // never
```
Tradeoff: `infer X extends Constraint` narrows the inferred type to only match when the resolved type satisfies the constraint, but this **changes the semantics from extraction to filtering** — without the extends constraint, `T extends Promise<infer R>` would match `Promise<number>` and give `R = number`; adding `infer R extends string` causes the whole conditional to evaluate to `never` instead of `number`, which is surprising when used in utility types that are expected to be total rather than partial; document this filtering behavior explicitly in type aliases and prefer separate utility types for the "narrow" and "total" extraction variants.

**Pattern 325** — Validated JSON Import with `with { type: "json" }` Import Attribute Assertion
```typescript
// tsconfig.json: { "compilerOptions": { "module": "nodenext", "resolveJsonModule": true } }

// ✅ TypeScript 5.7+ with --module nodenext requires the import attribute
import packageJson from "./package.json" with { type: "json" };
// packageJson is typed as the literal structure of the JSON file
console.log(packageJson.version); // string — typed from actual JSON content

// Named exports are not allowed from JSON imports — only default import
// ❌ Error: JSON modules only support default imports
// import { version } from "./package.json" with { type: "json" };

// Dynamic import also requires the assertion
async function loadConfig(path: string): Promise<unknown> {
  const mod = await import(path, { with: { type: "json" } });
  return mod.default;
}

// Practical pattern: typed config loading with Zod validation
import rawConfig from "./app.config.json" with { type: "json" };
import { z } from "zod";

const ConfigSchema = z.object({
  port:    z.number().int().positive(),
  host:    z.string(),
  debug:   z.boolean().optional().default(false),
});

// TypeScript knows rawConfig shape at compile time; Zod validates at runtime
export const config = ConfigSchema.parse(rawConfig);
```
Tradeoff: Requiring `with { type: "json" }` on every JSON import adds four tokens per import and breaks existing codebases that import JSON without an attribute under `--module nodenext` — migrating requires a codemod pass, and the import attribute syntax is not supported in CommonJS (`require()`) contexts, so teams mixing CJS and ESM within the same project must use `fs.readFileSync` + `JSON.parse` in CJS files and the import attribute in ESM files, doubling the patterns for what was previously a uniform `require("./config.json")` call.

**Pattern 326** — Replacing `const enum` with `as const` Object Maps for `--erasableSyntaxOnly` Compatibility
```typescript
// const enum inlines values at call sites — useful but incompatible with type-stripping
// ✅ Equivalent as const map: values are preserved at runtime, fully erasable
const HttpStatus = {
  Ok:            200,
  Created:       201,
  BadRequest:    400,
  Unauthorized:  401,
  NotFound:      404,
  InternalError: 500,
} as const;

// Derive the union type of all status code values
type HttpStatus = (typeof HttpStatus)[keyof typeof HttpStatus];
// HttpStatus = 200 | 201 | 400 | 401 | 404 | 500

// Derive the union type of all status name keys
type HttpStatusName = keyof typeof HttpStatus;
// HttpStatusName = "Ok" | "Created" | "BadRequest" | ...

// Reverse mapping (code → name) using the derived types
const HttpStatusLabel: Record<HttpStatus, HttpStatusName> = {
  [HttpStatus.Ok]:            "Ok",
  [HttpStatus.Created]:       "Created",
  [HttpStatus.BadRequest]:    "BadRequest",
  [HttpStatus.Unauthorized]:  "Unauthorized",
  [HttpStatus.NotFound]:      "NotFound",
  [HttpStatus.InternalError]: "InternalError",
};

function describeStatus(code: HttpStatus): HttpStatusName {
  return HttpStatusLabel[code];
}

// Exhaustive check: adding a new key to HttpStatus without updating
// HttpStatusLabel triggers a compile error — same exhaustiveness as const enum
const _exhaustive: HttpStatus = 0 as never; // never compiles unless all cases listed
```
Tradeoff: `const enum` inlines literal values at every call site (e.g., `HttpStatus.Ok` becomes `200` in the emitted JS, reducing bundle size and eliminating the object lookup), whereas the `as const` map preserves the object at runtime — for hot paths where the enum is accessed millions of times per second (e.g., in a parser's inner loop), the loss of inlining can measurably increase memory pressure and indirection cost; in most application code the difference is negligible, but library authors targeting maximum tree-shakeability may prefer `const enum` in ambient `.d.ts` declaration files where type-stripping is not a concern.

**Pattern 327** — ECMAScript Set Methods (`union`, `intersection`, `difference`) with TypeScript `lib` es2024
```typescript
// tsconfig.json: { "compilerOptions": { "lib": ["es2024", "dom"] } }
// Requires: Node.js 22+, Chrome 122+, Firefox 127+, or a polyfill

// Feature flag management example
type FeatureFlag = "darkMode" | "betaSearch" | "aiSuggestions" | "newDashboard";

const enabledFlags    = new Set<FeatureFlag>(["darkMode", "betaSearch"]);
const premiumFlags    = new Set<FeatureFlag>(["aiSuggestions", "newDashboard", "darkMode"]);
const deprecatedFlags = new Set<FeatureFlag>(["betaSearch"]);

// union(): all flags that are enabled OR premium
const allRelevantFlags: Set<FeatureFlag> = enabledFlags.union(premiumFlags);
// Set { "darkMode", "betaSearch", "aiSuggestions", "newDashboard" }

// intersection(): flags that are both enabled AND premium
const premiumEnabled: Set<FeatureFlag> = enabledFlags.intersection(premiumFlags);
// Set { "darkMode" }

// difference(): flags that are enabled but NOT deprecated
const activeFlags: Set<FeatureFlag> = enabledFlags.difference(deprecatedFlags);
// Set { "darkMode" }

// symmetricDifference(): flags in either set but not both
const exclusiveFlags: Set<FeatureFlag> = enabledFlags.symmetricDifference(premiumFlags);
// Set { "betaSearch", "aiSuggestions", "newDashboard" }

// isSubsetOf / isSupersetOf for access-control checks
const userFlags = new Set<FeatureFlag>(["darkMode"]);
const hasAccess: boolean = userFlags.isSubsetOf(enabledFlags); // true
```
Tradeoff: The native `Set` methods introduced in ES2024 are significantly more readable than the previous `new Set([...a].filter(x => b.has(x)))` idioms, but they require Node.js 22+ or a polyfill — Node.js 18 LTS (end-of-life April 2025) lacks `Set.prototype.union`, so projects that still target Node.js 18 must either ship a polyfill (adding ~3 KB gzipped) or continue using spread-based idioms, making the adoption decision dependent on the project's minimum Node.js version policy.
