## Cycle 70 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 346** — `readonly T[]` Parameters in Public APIs for Mutable/Immutable Acceptance [official]
```typescript
// ❌ Accepts only mutable arrays — callers must spread `as const` arrays
function processTags(tags: string[]): string {
  return tags.join(", ");
}
const FIXED: readonly string[] = ["alpha", "beta"] as const;
// processTags(FIXED); // Error: Argument of type 'readonly string[]' not assignable to 'string[]'

// ✅ Accepts both mutable and readonly arrays — correct for read-only operations
function processTagsReadonly(tags: readonly string[]): string {
  return tags.join(", ");
}
processTagsReadonly(["dynamic", "tags"]);  // mutable array ✓
processTagsReadonly(FIXED);               // readonly array ✓

// ✅ Same applies to generic utilities
function first<T>(arr: readonly T[]): T | undefined {
  return arr[0];
}

// ✅ For object parameters, use Readonly<T> or ReadonlyArray<T>
interface Config { host: string; port: number; }
function printConfig(cfg: Readonly<Config>): void {
  console.log(`${cfg.host}:${cfg.port}`);
}
```
Tradeoff: Changing a parameter from `T[]` to `readonly T[]` is a non-breaking API change — every existing call site that was passing a mutable array continues to compile because mutable arrays are assignable to readonly arrays; the reverse migration (from `readonly T[]` back to `T[]`) IS breaking because readonly arrays cannot be assigned to mutable array parameters. Always prefer `readonly T[]` on public API boundaries where the function only reads the array, and reserve mutable `T[]` for parameters the function explicitly sorts, reverses, or splices in place — sourced from the Google TypeScript Style Guide.

---

**Pattern 347** — Interface Naming Without the `I` Prefix (Google Style Guide) [official]
```typescript
// ❌ Hungarian notation — common in C# / old Java, discouraged in TypeScript
interface IUserService {
  getUser(id: string): Promise<IUser>;
  updateUser(id: string, patch: Partial<IUser>): Promise<void>;
}
interface IUser { id: string; name: string; email: string; }

// ✅ Plain descriptive names — TypeScript convention
interface UserService {
  getUser(id: string): Promise<User>;
  updateUser(id: string, patch: Partial<User>): Promise<void>;
}
interface User { id: string; name: string; email: string; }

// ✅ Disambiguate by context, not prefix — add suffix when needed
// For class + interface pair, use the class name on the class, interface name on the interface:
interface Repository<T> { findById(id: string): Promise<T | null>; }
class UserRepository implements Repository<User> {
  async findById(id: string): Promise<User | null> {
    return null; // real impl would query DB
  }
}

// ✅ Type aliases follow the same rule — no T prefix
type UserId = string;           // not TUserId
type EventHandler<T> = (event: T) => void;  // not TEventHandler
```
Tradeoff: Dropping the `I` prefix for interfaces makes TypeScript code look more like idiomatic JavaScript (which has no interface construct at all) and avoids leaking implementation-language conventions into TypeScript's structurally-typed world; the downside is that in large codebases where both a class `UserService` and an interface `UserService` coexist (implementation class plus contract interface), naming collisions require one of them to be renamed — the convention is to keep the descriptive name on the interface and suffix the class with `Impl` (`UserServiceImpl`) or move the class to a separate file — sourced from the Google TypeScript Style Guide and the TypeScript Handbook declaration merging section.

---

**Pattern 348** — `--generateTrace` Performance Trace Privacy Awareness [community]
```typescript
// Running tsc --generateTrace emits a types.json and trace.json.
// These files are invaluable for diagnosing slow builds, BUT they contain
// sensitive information from your workspace.

// Example trace output (types.json excerpt):
// {
//   "id": 1,
//   "symbolName": "SECRET_API_KEY",
//   "recursionId": 0,
//   "flags": "512",
//   "display": "\"sk-prod-abc123...\"",    ← literal value in the trace
//   "filename": "/home/user/project/src/config.ts"  ← absolute path
// }

// Safe usage:
// 1. Generate locally only — never commit trace output to git
// 2. Redact before sharing with the TypeScript team or in issue reports
// 3. Add trace-output dirs to .gitignore:

// .gitignore
// trace-output/
// *.trace.json
// types.json

// 4. Scope the trace to the slow file/package:
// tsc --generateTrace ./trace-output --noEmit --project packages/api/tsconfig.json

// Reviewing the trace: open in Chrome Devtools (chrome://tracing) or
// https://www.speedscope.app — look for long "checkSourceFile" spans
// or "instantiateType" spans with large self-time.

// Community-discovered: the trace also captures full resolved module paths
// including any credential-adjacent filenames (api-keys.ts, secrets.ts),
// making unredacted sharing in public GitHub issues a security exposure.
const _traceWarning = "Always audit types.json before sharing in public issue trackers";
```
Tradeoff: `--generateTrace` is the definitive tool for understanding TypeScript build-time performance bottlenecks — it captures every type instantiation, every source file checked, and every module resolution decision — but the richness of the trace is exactly what makes it sensitive: literal type values derived from string constants in your code appear verbatim in `types.json`, absolute file paths expose your directory structure, and any `.env`-adjacent type definitions (e.g., `type ApiKey = "sk-prod-..."`) have their values visible in plaintext; the safe practice is to use `--generateTrace` only locally, never commit trace output, and always run `grep -r "secret\|key\|token\|password" trace-output/` before sharing — sourced from the TypeScript Performance wiki, which now explicitly warns that traces "may include information from your workspace, including file paths and source code."

**Pattern 349** — Project References Sweet Spot: 5–20 Sub-Projects for Optimal Monorepo Performance [community]
```typescript
// tsconfig.json (workspace root)
{
  "references": [
    { "path": "./packages/core" },
    { "path": "./packages/api" },
    { "path": "./packages/web" },
    { "path": "./packages/cli" },
    { "path": "./packages/testing" }
  ]
}

// packages/api/tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "composite": true,          // required for project references
    "declaration": true,        // required: downstream projects consume .d.ts
    "declarationMap": true,     // enables "go to source" across package boundaries
    "outDir": "./dist"
  },
  "references": [
    { "path": "../core" }       // only declare direct deps, not transitive
  ]
}

// Build only changed packages:
// tsc --build                  ← incremental, checks .tsbuildinfo
// tsc --build --force          ← rebuild all unconditionally
// tsc --build --dry            ← preview what would be rebuilt

// Too few packages (< 3): project references add overhead with no gain
// — use a single tsconfig.json with path aliases instead.

// Too many packages (> 30): the graph serialisation and .tsbuildinfo
// file management creates its own overhead.  Consider merging leaf packages.
```
Tradeoff: Project references deliver the greatest value in the 5–20 package range: below that threshold the per-package composite overhead (declaration emit, `.tsbuildinfo` files, dependency graph evaluation) costs more than the incremental-rebuild savings, while above ~20–30 packages the reference graph traversal and cache invalidation logic begins to introduce its own latency — monorepos with 50+ packages often achieve faster CI times by splitting into separate composite roots (one per team) rather than a single root that references every package; the TypeScript Performance wiki explicitly notes that "excessive numbers of small projects in a `--build` mode" is a known performance anti-pattern with the recommendation to consolidate into "fewer, larger" composites — sourced from the TypeScript Performance wiki.

**Pattern 350** — `getOrInsert` / `getOrInsertComputed` Atomicity Pitfall in Async Contexts [community]
```typescript
// ✅ Correct: getOrInsert is synchronous and atomic — safe in sync contexts
const cache = new Map<string, string[]>();

function getTags(key: string): string[] {
  return cache.getOrInsert(key, []);  // atomic: no race possible in single-threaded JS
}

// ❌ Pitfall: getOrInsertComputed with an async factory is NOT atomic
const asyncCache = new Map<string, Promise<string[]>>();

async function getTagsAsync(key: string): Promise<string[]> {
  // ❌ This is WRONG: getOrInsertComputed runs the factory synchronously —
  //    if the factory itself returns a Promise, the Map stores the Promise,
  //    not the resolved value.  Two concurrent callers each get the SAME
  //    Promise reference (correct), but if the factory throws, the rejected
  //    Promise is stored in the Map and all future callers get a rejected Promise.
  const promise = asyncCache.getOrInsertComputed(key, (k) => fetchTags(k));
  return promise;
}

// ✅ Correct async memoisation pattern — manually guard the Map:
async function getTagsSafe(key: string): Promise<string[]> {
  let promise = asyncCache.get(key);
  if (!promise) {
    promise = fetchTags(key).catch((err) => {
      asyncCache.delete(key);  // evict on failure so next call retries
      return Promise.reject(err);
    });
    asyncCache.set(key, promise);
  }
  return promise;
}

declare function fetchTags(key: string): Promise<string[]>;
```
Tradeoff: `Map.getOrInsert` and `Map.getOrInsertComputed` (ES2025 / TypeScript 6.0) solve the synchronous lookup-or-create pattern cleanly and correctly — in single-threaded JavaScript all synchronous operations are atomic from the event-loop perspective — but they do not help with asynchronous memoisation patterns where the "value" is itself a `Promise`; callers who use `getOrInsertComputed(k, () => asyncFetch(k))` correctly get shared-promise deduplication (all concurrent calls share the inflight `Promise` object), but they do not get automatic retry on rejection because the rejected `Promise` is permanently stored in the Map; the correct async memoisation pattern requires a manual `.catch()` eviction guard, which `getOrInsert` does not provide — sourced from the MDN documentation for `Map.prototype.getOrInsert` and the TypeScript 6.0 release notes.

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 70

**G198** — `--generateTrace` Output Leaks Source Code Values and Absolute Paths
Why this matters: Developers running `tsc --generateTrace` to investigate slow builds routinely paste the output into public GitHub issues. The `types.json` file contains the *string representation* of every resolved literal type — meaning `const API_URL = "https://internal.corp.example.com/api"` appears as `"display": "\"https://internal.corp.example.com/api\""` in the trace. Absolute file paths expose the developer's home directory, project structure, and any credential-adjacent filenames. Teams that have CI pipelines auto-uploading trace artifacts as build artefacts have inadvertently published sensitive data.
Fix: Before sharing any `--generateTrace` output publicly, run `grep -r "secret\|key\|token\|pass\|internal\|corp" ./trace-output/` to audit for sensitive values. Add `trace-output/` and `*.trace.json` to `.gitignore`. When sharing with the TypeScript team, use a minimal reproduction that replaces real string literals with `"REDACTED"` before tracing.

---

**G199** — Project References With More Than ~25 Sub-Projects Create Their Own Build Overhead
Why this matters: Teams adopting monorepo setups often create one TypeScript project per package, reasoning that "more granularity = better caching". In practice, `tsc --build` must evaluate the entire reference graph on every invocation — reading `.tsbuildinfo` files, checking timestamps, and resolving transitive dependencies — even if only one package changed. With 30+ packages this graph-traversal overhead can exceed the compilation time saved by incremental builds, making cold CI builds slower than a single monolithic `tsconfig.json`. The TypeScript Performance wiki explicitly lists "too many project references" as a known anti-pattern.
Fix: Merge packages that are always built together (especially `utils` → `core` pairs) into a single composite project. Aim for 5–20 sub-projects in the reference graph. Use `--build --dry` to see how many projects are rebuilding on each change — if it's always more than 3 times the number of files actually changed, the graph is too fine-grained.

---

**G200** — `Map.getOrInsertComputed` Permanently Caches Rejected Promises
Why this matters: `asyncCache.getOrInsertComputed(key, () => fetchData(key))` stores the `Promise` returned by the factory in the Map. If `fetchData` rejects (network error, auth failure, validation error), the rejected `Promise` is now permanently in the Map — all subsequent callers for that key receive the same rejected `Promise` without re-triggering the fetch. This is different from the synchronous `getOrInsert` case where the inserted default value is always valid. The bug is subtle because the first call appears to work normally (the rejection is handled by the caller) but every subsequent call silently returns the cached rejection.
Fix: Do not use `getOrInsertComputed` with async factories. Instead, use the manual guard pattern: `let p = cache.get(k); if (!p) { p = fetch(k).catch(e => { cache.delete(k); throw e; }); cache.set(k, p); } return p;`. This ensures failed promises are evicted from the cache, allowing retries on the next invocation.

**Pattern 351** — `--listFilesOnly` for Auditing Included Files Without Compilation [official]
```typescript
// tsc --listFilesOnly shows every file TypeScript will include WITHOUT
// running the full compilation (no type-checking, no emit).
// This is faster than --listFiles (which runs the full program construction).

// Usage:
// npx tsc --listFilesOnly --project tsconfig.json

// Sample output (abbreviated):
// /home/user/project/node_modules/typescript/lib/lib.es2022.full.d.ts
// /home/user/project/src/index.ts
// /home/user/project/src/utils/logger.ts
// /home/user/project/src/utils/config.ts

// Diagnose over-inclusion — spot unintended files:
// npx tsc --listFilesOnly 2>&1 | grep -v node_modules | wc -l
// If the count is unexpectedly high, your include glob is too broad.

// Compare --listFilesOnly vs --listFiles:
// --listFilesOnly   = list files only, stop before type-checking (fast)
// --listFiles       = list files, then continue with full compilation
// --explainFiles    = list files WITH the reason each was included (slowest but most detailed)

// Workflow: audit before adding a new path alias
// 1. npx tsc --listFilesOnly | sort > before.txt
// 2. Edit tsconfig.json (add new path entry)
// 3. npx tsc --listFilesOnly | sort > after.txt
// 4. diff before.txt after.txt
//    → Confirm only the expected new files appear
```
Tradeoff: `--listFilesOnly` is the fastest diagnostic for understanding what TypeScript sees during a build — it resolves the include/exclude/references/paths configuration and emits the file list without paying the cost of parsing, binding, or checking any of the files; it is significantly faster than `--listFiles` (which continues to full compilation) and `--explainFiles` (which reasons through every include decision for every file); the only scenario where you need the slower alternatives is when you want to understand *why* a file was included (`--explainFiles`) rather than merely *which* files are included — sourced from the TypeScript Performance wiki.

**Pattern 352** — `dexnode` + `--generateCpuProfile` for Deep TypeScript Compiler Profiling [official]
```typescript
// When --extendedDiagnostics identifies a high "Check time" but --generateTrace
// doesn't pinpoint the cause, a CPU profile gives function-level attribution.

// Step 1: Install dexnode (V8 isolate helper for CPU profiling)
// npm install -g dexnode

// Step 2: Generate a CPU profile of the TypeScript compiler
// npx dexnode -- ./node_modules/typescript/lib/tsc.js \
//   --generateCpuProfile tsc-profile.cpuprofile \
//   -p tsconfig.json --noEmit

// Step 3: Open in Chrome DevTools
// 1. Open chrome://inspect
// 2. Click "Open dedicated DevTools for Node"
// 3. Go to Profiler tab → Load profile → select tsc-profile.cpuprofile
// 4. Switch to "Chart" view — look for wide blocks in the "Check" or
//    "instantiateType" frames

// Step 4: Alternatively, use VS Code's built-in CPU profiler:
// 1. Open VS Code → Command Palette → "Developer: Start CPU Profile"
// 2. Trigger the operation you want to profile (e.g., open a slow file)
// 3. Command Palette → "Developer: Stop CPU Profile"
// 4. The .cpuprofile is saved to your desktop

// Shortcut: if your entire build is slow, use --extendedDiagnostics first:
// npx tsc --extendedDiagnostics --noEmit 2>&1 | tail -20
// Look for: "Check time" > 60% of "Total time" → type-checking bottleneck
//           "Parse time" > 30% of "Total time" → too many included files
//           "I/O Read" > 1s → disk speed / skipLibCheck candidate

// Anti-pattern: profiling with ts-node instead of tsc gives different
// timings because ts-node compiles one file at a time (no program-level caching).
```
Tradeoff: `--generateCpuProfile` is the most precise tool for identifying which internal TypeScript functions consume the most wall-clock time, but it requires `dexnode` (or equivalent V8 CPU sampler) to collect isolate-level samples — `node --cpu-prof` works as an alternative but produces `.cpuprofile` files with less stable frame labeling; the CPU profile approach is most useful after `--extendedDiagnostics` has already narrowed the bottleneck to a specific phase (Check, Instantiate, Bind) and you need to see *which type* or *which file* is the hot path; for most teams `--generateTrace` is sufficient because it provides type-instantiation counts without requiring a profiling tool — sourced from the TypeScript Performance wiki (`dexnode` section) and the TypeScript contributor guide.

**Pattern 353** — Unused Generic Type Parameters Are a Declaration File Anti-Pattern [official]
```typescript
// ❌ Anti-pattern: type parameter T is declared but never used
// TypeScript does NOT error on unused type parameters by default,
// but they create phantom flexibility that confuses callers.
interface ResponseWrapper<T> {
  status: number;
  message: string;
  // T is never used — callers must supply it but it has no effect
}

// Result: consumers are forced into meaningless ceremony:
const r: ResponseWrapper<User> = { status: 200, message: "ok" };
// ...but T is structurally inert — ResponseWrapper<User> === ResponseWrapper<string>

// ❌ Anti-pattern in declaration files (from TS Do's and Don'ts):
declare function format<T>(value: string): string; // T never used

// ✅ Fix: remove unused type parameters entirely
interface ResponseWrapper {
  status: number;
  message: string;
}

// ✅ Fix: use the parameter or replace with a concrete constraint
declare function format(value: string): string;

// ✅ Correct: type parameter that IS used
interface ResponseWrapper<T> {
  status: number;
  message: string;
  data: T;         // ← T is meaningful — callers get precise data type
}

const r: ResponseWrapper<User> = { status: 200, message: "ok", data: { id: 1, name: "Alice" } };

// ✅ Correct when T constrains behavior but doesn't appear in fields:
// Use a phantom brand field EXPLICITLY, not an implicit unused parameter
interface TaggedWrapper<TTag extends string> {
  readonly _tag: TTag;   // ← TTag IS used — it powers nominal discrimination
  status: number;
}
```
Tradeoff: Unused type parameters in public APIs and declaration files are not flagged by the TypeScript compiler (there is no `noUnusedTypeParameters` option), so they accumulate silently in codebases that follow a "maybe we'll need this later" philosophy; they create structural equivalence between superficially different types (callers discover that `Cache<string>` and `Cache<number>` are mutually assignable and conclude the typing is broken), they appear in documentation and IDE hover as required parameters that serve no purpose, and they complicate future refactoring because removing them is technically a breaking change to the public API; the TypeScript Do's and Don'ts documentation specifically lists "don't have unused generic type parameters" as a declaration file rule — sourced from `typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/declaration-files/do-s-and-don-ts.html`.

**Pattern 354** — TSServer Verbose Logging for Editor Performance Diagnosis [official]
```typescript
// When your IDE is slow (completions take >500ms, type errors lag) but
// `tsc --build` is fast, the bottleneck is in tsserver (the language service),
// not the compiler.

// Step 1: Enable verbose TSServer logging in VS Code settings.json:
// {
//   "typescript.tsserver.log": "verbose"
// }

// Step 2: Restart VS Code to apply

// Step 3: Open the "TypeScript" output channel
// View → Output → select "TypeScript" from dropdown

// Step 4: Navigate to a slow file and trigger the operation
// (hover over a type, trigger completions, open a large file)

// Step 5: Click "Open TS Server log" in the status bar (bottom right)
// or run: TypeScript: Open TS Server Log (Command Palette)

// Step 6: Analyze the log — look for:
// getSemanticDiagnostics  > 500ms → type-checking that file is slow
// completions             > 200ms → completion computation bottleneck
// getQuickInfoAtPosition  > 100ms → hover type computation slow
// getDefinitionAtPosition > 300ms → go-to-definition slow

// Turn it OFF after collecting data:
// {
//   "typescript.tsserver.log": "off"
// }

// Why off when done: verbose logs grow to hundreds of MB quickly and
// slow down the TypeScript output channel rendering in VS Code.

// Additional flag: enable editor tracing for even more detail:
// {
//   "typescript.tsserver.enableTracing": true
// }
// (This is the editor equivalent of --generateTrace for tsc)
```
Tradeoff: TSServer verbose logging captures a fundamentally different profile than `tsc --extendedDiagnostics` — the latter covers `tsc` invocations (CI builds), while tsserver logging covers interactive editing (local development); a project can have fast CI builds and slow editor experience if the language service is performing extra work that `tsc` does not (e.g., computing semantic classifications for hover, deduplicating suggestion diagnostics, or computing inlay hints on every keystroke); the log is human-readable JSON lines that are easy to `grep` but become enormous on large projects, so always disable after collection; this diagnostic was added as a first-class VS Code feature in TypeScript 4.0 and is documented in the TypeScript Performance wiki under "Editor Performance" — sourced from the TypeScript Performance wiki and VS Code TypeScript documentation.

**Pattern 355** — Prefer Inheritance Hierarchies Over Large Union Types for Performance [official]
```typescript
// ❌ Anti-pattern: large union of unrelated types
// Each new member adds O(n) comparison work — union comparison is quadratic
type AstNode =
  | { kind: "StringLiteral"; value: string }
  | { kind: "NumericLiteral"; value: number }
  | { kind: "BooleanLiteral"; value: boolean }
  | { kind: "Identifier"; name: string }
  | { kind: "BinaryExpression"; left: AstNode; operator: string; right: AstNode }
  | { kind: "CallExpression"; callee: AstNode; args: AstNode[] }
  | { kind: "ArrowFunction"; params: string[]; body: AstNode }
  | { kind: "BlockStatement"; statements: AstNode[] }
  | { kind: "IfStatement"; test: AstNode; consequent: AstNode; alternate?: AstNode }
  // ... 50 more variants
  ;

// ✅ Better for performance: base interface + specific sub-interfaces
// TypeScript can cache the base relationship and evaluate subtypes incrementally
interface AstNodeBase {
  kind: string;
  loc?: { line: number; col: number };
}

interface StringLiteral extends AstNodeBase {
  kind: "StringLiteral";
  value: string;
}

interface BinaryExpression extends AstNodeBase {
  kind: "BinaryExpression";
  left: AstNode;
  operator: string;
  right: AstNode;
}

// The union at the top level can be smaller — just the discriminating root:
type AstNode = StringLiteral | NumericLiteral | BooleanLiteral | BinaryExpression
             | CallExpression | ArrowFunction | BlockStatement | IfStatement;

// TypeScript caches interface relationships between checks.
// A union is re-evaluated pairwise on each use.

// ✅ When you MUST keep a large union: name the union type and reuse it
// (never inline a large union in every function parameter)
type AllEventTypes =
  | ClickEvent | InputEvent | FocusEvent | KeyboardEvent | MouseMoveEvent;

// ✅ Use this named alias everywhere — not the expanded union:
function handleEvent(event: AllEventTypes): void { /* ... */ }
// NOT: function handleEvent(event: ClickEvent | InputEvent | FocusEvent | ...): void
```
Tradeoff: The TypeScript compiler compares union type members pairwise to eliminate redundant members when composing types — so a union of N members requires N² comparisons, and a union of 50 members requires 2,500 comparisons every time that union appears in a type expression; by contrast, interface inheritance is cached between checks — once `StringLiteral extends AstNodeBase` has been verified, subsequent assignability checks can reference the cached result; the TypeScript Performance wiki explicitly calls out "large union types" as a key performance anti-pattern and recommends replacing them with interface inheritance hierarchies when the union members share common fields; the tradeoff is that interface hierarchies require more upfront boilerplate and lose the ability to add members to the union without updating the base — sourced from the TypeScript Performance wiki.

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 71

**G201** — `--listFilesOnly` Is Distinct from `--listFiles` — Don't Confuse Them
Why this matters: Developers looking up how to audit TypeScript's included file set often find references to `--listFiles` in older documentation and blog posts (pre-TypeScript 5.5). TypeScript 5.5 added `--listFilesOnly`, which stops immediately after file resolution without performing any type-checking. Using `--listFiles` on a slow project means waiting through the full compilation before getting the file list — on a 60-second build, this is a 60-second wait for information that `--listFilesOnly` can return in under a second.
Fix: Replace `tsc --listFiles` with `tsc --listFilesOnly` for all file-audit workflows. Use `--listFiles` only when you specifically want to verify the compilation succeeds AND see the file list — which is rarely useful outside of CI validation scripts.

---

**G202** — CPU Profiling `tsc` with `node --cpu-prof` Gives Misleading Frame Names
Why this matters: The most discoverable way to CPU-profile a Node.js program is `node --cpu-prof ./script.js`. When applied to `tsc`, this produces a `.cpuprofile` with V8 bytecode frame names that do not match TypeScript's source — internal functions appear as `checkTypeRelatedTo`, `getTypeFromTypeNodeWorker`, etc. without the higher-level context (which type alias, which source file) that makes the profile actionable. The TypeScript team's recommended approach is `dexnode`, which uses isolate snapshots to produce more stable frame labels aligned with TypeScript source map positions.
Fix: Use `npx dexnode -- ./node_modules/typescript/lib/tsc.js --generateCpuProfile out.cpuprofile` rather than `node --cpu-prof tsc.js`. Open the `.cpuprofile` in Chrome DevTools → Profiler for flame-chart analysis. Pair the CPU profile with `--generateTrace` to correlate CPU hot paths with specific type instantiations.

---

**G203** — Unused Generic Type Parameters Cause Invisible Structural Equivalence
Why this matters: `Cache<string>` and `Cache<number>` are structurally identical if the generic parameter `T` never appears in `Cache`'s body. TypeScript assigns them the same type, making the following code compile without error even though it looks like a type mismatch: `const strCache: Cache<string> = new Cache<number>()`. Teams that discover this behaviour late in a project have sometimes shipped production bugs where the wrong generic specialization was used — the type system appeared to validate the code but provided no protection. This is a known footgun documented in the TypeScript Do's & Don'ts.
Fix: Audit all generic interfaces and type aliases in your public API. Remove type parameters that are not referenced in any member. If the phantom typing is intentional (e.g., for branded types), add an explicit `_brand: T` or `readonly _phantom: T` field to make the usage visible in IDE tooltips and prevent accidental cross-assignment.
